provisions.heading: Apply Only Coarse Policies at the Endpoint
provisions.evidence: Does any endpoint policy decide target authorization instead of coarse authentication, role, or scope? Look at the endpoint policies beside the application guard.
provisions.statement: A WebApi endpoint MUST enforce only coarse authenticated, role, or scope policies, leaving target decisions to the application guard.
provisions.rationale: Authentication establishes who is calling, not whether the caller may act on this specific resource. An endpoint that decided target authorization would duplicate the business data access the guard already owns. Coarse policies at the endpoint check the caller; the application guard decides the target from the `access` the use-case record declares. Target authorization lives in `litespec/backend/application#enforce-target-authorization-in-the-pipeline`. An operation applies a stable forbidden or not-found policy when revealing that a resource exists would leak information.

provisions.heading: Apply PATCH to a Partial Update
provisions.evidence: Does every partial update arrive as PATCH with the merge-patch media type? Look at the partial update requests.
provisions.statement: A WebApi operation MUST apply a partial update with PATCH and the `application/merge-patch+json` media type.
provisions.rationale: A partial update names only the fields it changes. Sending them with PATCH and the merge-patch media type gives those semantics a standard meaning. A PUT body for a partial change either repeats fields the caller does not change or invents merge semantics per field. [RFC 5789](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc5789) defines PATCH and [RFC 7386](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc7386) defines the merge-patch media type.
provisions.example: A partial update sends only the changed members with `Content-Type: application/merge-patch+json`, and the endpoint reads the body as a sparse patch. A PUT keeps replacing the whole resource ([RFC 9110 section 9.3.4](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc9110#section-9.3.4)), and DELETE stays a hard-state transition.

provisions.heading: Authorize Every File Download Through Its Owning Use Case
provisions.evidence: Is every stored file reachable only through a download use case with its declared access? Look at the download endpoints and the storage addresses beside each owning use case.
provisions.statement: A caller MUST reach a stored file only through a download use case authorized from the access that use case declares.
provisions.rationale: A stored file carries the data of the record it belongs to. A direct storage address would serve that data to anyone holding the address, skipping the owning use case's grant and tenant scope. Routing each download through its owning use case keeps one authorization decision for the file and for the record it belongs to.
provisions.example: A Claimwick receipt photo downloads through the use case that owns the expense, so only an actor its access allows reads the photo, and no storage address serves it on its own.

provisions.heading: Avoid Noise Words in Field Names
provisions.evidence: Does any field name in contract schemas carry a type prefix or noise word? Look at the field names.
provisions.statement: Field names carry no type prefix and no noise word.
provisions.rationale: A type prefix repeats what the schema already declares, and a noise word names nothing an integrator acts on: `customerInfo` carries no more meaning than `customer`. The noise words are `data`, `info`, `item`, `object`, `value`, and `thing`; the type prefixes are `str`, `int`, `bool`, `num`, `obj`, and `arr`.
provisions.example: `customerInfo` becomes `customer`.

provisions.heading: Bound Collection Queries
provisions.evidence: Does every collection response apply deterministic order with the declared default and maximum limits? Look at the collection responses beside their records.
provisions.statement: A collection endpoint MUST apply deterministic ordering, its record's declared default limit, and its record's declared maximum limit of 100 or lower.
provisions.rationale: An unbounded collection read turns one caller into a source of unbounded database and serialization work. Deterministic ordering keeps pages stable, the declared default limit bounds the common case, and the declared maximum of 100 or lower caps the worst case. The use-case record declares its paging with order, cursor or offset, default limit, and maximum limit, and the endpoint applies exactly that. Cursor mechanics live in `litespec/backend/api#use-opaque-cursors-for-collection-paging` and `litespec/backend/api#version-cursors-with-stable-sort-values`.

provisions.heading: Bound Every File Upload
provisions.evidence: Does every upload operation declare its size and media-type bounds, and refuse files outside them? Look at each upload endpoint beside its use-case record.
provisions.statement: A file upload operation MUST accept no file larger than the size its use-case record declares and no media type outside the media types its use-case record declares.
provisions.rationale: An upload without a declared size or media-type bound lets one caller send work the server never agreed to store or inspect. Declaring both bounds on the use-case record lets the server refuse an oversize file or an undeclared type before storage, and lets a reviewer see the limit beside the use case that owns the file.
provisions.example: The Claimwick submit-expense upload declares the size and the image media types a receipt photo may carry. The server refuses a larger file or another media type before it stores anything.

provisions.heading: Commit the Generated Contract Its Consumers Read
provisions.evidence: Does every frontend or external consumer read a committed, current OpenAPI artifact? Look at the committed artifact beside its consumers.
provisions.statement: An application MUST commit its generated OpenAPI artifact when a frontend or external consumer reads it.
provisions.rationale: Without a committed file, a breaking contract change hides inside a code change. A committed artifact makes every contract change visible in review and lets CI fail when the document was not regenerated. Consumers read the artifact through the generated client, model, schema, and query-option packages.

provisions.heading: Declare a Smaller Collection Maximum
provisions.evidence: Does every lowered collection maximum carry its value and reason on the use-case record? Look at each lowered maximum.
provisions.statement: A use case with stricter needs declares its smaller maximum in its record's `paging` and states the reason on its use-case record.
provisions.rationale: Some collections cost more per item than others. A use case with stricter needs declares its smaller maximum in its record's `paging` with the reason on its use-case record, and the endpoint enforces it under `litespec/backend/api#bound-collection-queries`.

provisions.heading: Declare Stable Operation Metadata in the Contract
provisions.evidence: Does every operation in the generated contract declare its operationId, authorization, request, success, failure, and summary entries? Look at the operations in the generated contract.
provisions.statement: An operation MUST declare a stable `operationId`, its authorization, request, success, and Problem Details metadata, and a summary.
provisions.rationale: Generated clients name their methods from `operationId`. An unstable name renames client code on every generation. Authorization metadata cites the enforced policies and Problem Details metadata covers every documented failure status, so the client models security and failure before its first call. Comments on handlers are not contract documentation, so operations carry explicit summaries.

provisions.heading: Defer Error Mapping to the Global Handler
provisions.evidence: Does any endpoint body catch a use-case, domain, or validation failure? Look at the endpoint bodies beside the global handler.
provisions.statement: An endpoint MUST NOT catch a use-case failure, a domain failure, or a validation failure.
provisions.rationale: One global handler produces every error response from every failure type. When an endpoint catches a failure, it creates a second mapping for that failure, and the two mappings diverge: the same refusal answers different statuses or codes depending on which endpoint raised it.

provisions.heading: Expose Development Tooling in Development Only
provisions.evidence: Does any hosted environment serve exploration tooling, and does every Development host map it? Look at the mapped endpoints in each environment.
provisions.statement: An application MUST map its API exploration and diagnostic endpoints only when the host runs in the Development environment.
provisions.rationale: Development tooling exposes the full API surface for exploration. That is what development needs and what a hosted environment leaves unoffered. Mapping it in Development only keeps exploration local while hosted environments serve only the API.

provisions.heading: Generate the Contract Without Hosted Dependencies
provisions.evidence: Does every generation run avoid hosted dependencies with a recorded answer? Look at the generation runs beside the project record.
provisions.statement: The generation run contacts no hosted dependency and runs no schema change, and the project records its chosen answer.
provisions.rationale: Build-time generation boots the host, and a boot that needs a secret, a certificate, or a reachable dependency fails on a clean checkout. The project records which answer it uses: a generation environment that wires no hosted dependency for the generation run, or a deferred guard that moves each startup refusal from composition to first use. The document reflects the generation environment's endpoint set, and with a deferred guard a misconfiguration surfaces on the first request instead of at boot.

provisions.heading: Keep Business Dependencies Out of Endpoints
provisions.evidence: Does any endpoint constructor take more than mediators and HTTP-boundary services? Look at the endpoint constructors in the use case folders.
provisions.statement: An endpoint MUST NOT take an aggregate repository, a persistence session or context, a provider client, or an application service.
provisions.rationale: An endpoint that takes a repository, session, provider, or application service can reach business state or providers without passing the pipeline. Endpoints hold no request-scoped dependency because the application registers them at startup; they take only mediators and HTTP-boundary services such as an actor accessor. Handlers take neither, since a handler sends no message.

provisions.heading: Keep Numeric Transport Types Precise
provisions.evidence: Does every numeric field publish a plain schema, with the int64 union reserved for values beyond the safe range? Look at the numeric fields in the contract.
provisions.statement: Emit a plain numeric schema for an `int32` or `double` field, and reserve a string-or-number union for `int64` values beyond the JSON safe integer range.
provisions.rationale: A plain numeric schema lets consumers read `int32` and `double` directly. A string-or-number union is reserved for `int64` values beyond the JSON safe integer range, because an over-broad union forces every consumer to coerce plain numbers.

provisions.heading: Keep One Name for a Use Case Across Layers
provisions.evidence: Does every message type, operation id, and audit action carry its use case name? Look at each use case's message type, operation id, and audit action.
provisions.statement: Each use case MUST carry its name unchanged in its message type, operation id, and audit action.
provisions.rationale: A use case that reads one way in its record, another in its message type, and a third in its audit action forces every trace across layers through a translation table only the author holds. The record id is the name; the message type, the endpoint operation id, and the audit action repeat it in their own casing, so a reader follows one name from the page to the wire to the audit log.
provisions.example: `use-case/spending.reimburse-expense` travels as `ReimburseExpenseCommand`, operation id `ReimburseExpense`, and audit action `reimburse-expense`; an operation id of `PayExpense` is reported.

provisions.heading: Keep Routes Resource-Oriented
provisions.evidence: Does every route use plural segments, kebab-case subresources, identity parameters, filter queries, and body command data? Look at the route table entries.
provisions.statement: A route MUST use lowercase plural resource segments, kebab-case subresources, route parameters for identity, query parameters for filtering, and the body for command data.
provisions.rationale: A predictable route shape lets a caller derive an unfamiliar operation from a familiar one: plural resource segments, kebab-case subresources, route parameters for identity, query parameters for filtering, and command data in the body. A route that encoded actions or identities anywhere else would force the caller to read each route's documentation. For a transition beyond the five verbs, [AIP-136](https://google.aip.dev/136) defines the custom-method form.
provisions.example: A route carries the authenticated actor identifier only when that actor is intentionally addressing another actor as a resource.

provisions.heading: Map One Operation per Endpoint
provisions.evidence: Does every mapped route resolve to one endpoint type with one mediator dispatch? Look at the route table beside the use case folders.
provisions.statement: An endpoint MUST map one route operation, convert input to an Application message, dispatch through its mediator, and map the result.
provisions.rationale: When one endpoint class serves several operations, their input mappings, dispatches, and result mappings mix in one place, and one class changes for unrelated routes. One endpoint class per route operation gives each route a single owner, so its input mapping, dispatch, and result mapping live in one place.
provisions.example: At startup, the application discovers endpoint implementations, registers each one once, and maps them in deterministic name order. Discovery uses the platform's own reflection and dependency injection. It needs no separate scanning package.

provisions.heading: Mark Polymorphic Models with Discriminators
provisions.evidence: Does every data-bearing set publish a oneOf model with a required string discriminator? Look at the data-bearing sets in the contract.
provisions.statement: A data-bearing set MUST map to a polymorphic model with one case per variant, published as `oneOf` with a string discriminator.
provisions.rationale: A polymorphic payload without a discriminator forces the reader to guess the case from its fields. A required string discriminator names the case on every payload, so no payload validates without one. The strings equal the Domain union's stable case codes and stay stable across identifier renames.
provisions.example:
- Declare one polymorphic base with one registered case per variant.
- Carry the metadata on the type, not only in host options.
- Name the discriminator property, using a name such as `type` or `outcome`.
- Opt cases in explicitly, so an unregistered subtype fails serialization.
- A document or schema transformer completes discriminator metadata that the generator omits.

provisions.heading: Mirror Each Closed Set on the Wire
provisions.evidence: Does every transport model preserve the cases and data of its Domain set? Look at each transport model beside its Domain set.
provisions.statement: A WebApi transport model for a Domain closed set MUST preserve the shape of that set.
provisions.rationale: Each case of a closed set carries different data. A transport shape that differs from its Domain set discards information the Domain carries. Preserving the shape keeps every case and its data on the wire. Label-only sets follow `litespec/backend/api#publish-label-only-sets-as-string-enums`, and data-bearing sets follow `litespec/backend/api#mark-polymorphic-models-with-discriminators`. Narrowing follows `litespec/backend/application#record-a-decision-for-closed-set-narrowing`.
provisions.example: A label-only set maps to a string `enum`. A data-bearing set maps to a polymorphic model with one case per variant, published as `oneOf` with a discriminator.

provisions.heading: Model a Monetary Value as One Object
provisions.evidence: Does every monetary value travel as one Money object, with currency only where the caller chooses it? Look at the monetary fields in the contract.
provisions.statement: Carry a monetary value as one `Money` object in a response model and in a request where the caller chooses the currency.
provisions.rationale: Split sibling fields pair only by a server invariant invisible to the schema, so a report reads the two independently and mismatches them. One `Money` object holding `amount` and an ISO 4217 `currency` mirrors the Domain shape on the wire under `litespec/backend/domain#model-money-with-exact-decimal-values`. A caller with no currency choice carries `amount` alone, because a fixed currency arrives from the account, not the caller.
provisions.example: `unitPrice` and `currencyCode` become `price` of type `Money`. A request that references an account with a fixed currency carries `amount` alone.

provisions.heading: Name Boolean Fields as Conditions
provisions.evidence: Does every boolean field use the camel-case condition name of its code name? Look at the boolean fields in the contract.
provisions.statement: Boolean fields use the same condition names as code, in camel case.
provisions.rationale: Condition names state what the boolean means, and the camel-case form matches wire conventions. Boolean names live in `litespec/workspace/naming#use-intent-revealing-boolean-names`, and transport carries the camel-case form.
provisions.example: `IsBuyable` in code becomes `isBuyable` on the wire.

provisions.heading: Name Failure Pairs Code and Reason
provisions.evidence: Does every request body name failures with code and reason? Look at the failure pairs in request bodies.
provisions.statement: A request body names a failure with `code` for the class and `reason` for the explanation.
provisions.rationale: A request body names failures the same way responses do: `code` for the class, `reason` for the explanation, mirroring the Problem Details code and detail under `litespec/backend/api#return-stable-problem-details`. One pair in both directions lets clients reuse their failure handling.

provisions.heading: Name Path Parameters per Resource
provisions.evidence: Does every path parameter name its own resource identity? Look at the path parameters.
provisions.statement: Each path parameter names its own resource identity, and a `details` segment takes the aggregate name.
provisions.rationale: Each path parameter names its own resource identity, so `/api/posts/{postId}` is mistaken for no other resource's key. A shared `id` hides which resource it identifies.
provisions.example: `/api/posts/{postId}` names the post; `/details` takes the aggregate name.

provisions.heading: Name Routes from Resources
provisions.evidence: Does every route derive from its resource and subresource, with an action segment only where neither fits? Look at the route table.
provisions.statement: Derive each route from its resource and subresource, and use an action segment only when the operation maps to neither.
provisions.rationale: A route derived from its resource reads the same for every operation: the caller knows the record before opening the handler. An action segment reserved for operations that map to neither resource nor subresource keeps the exception visible instead of spreading verb-led routes.
provisions.example:
```text
POST   /api/posts
GET    /api/posts/{postId}
GET    /api/posts/{postId}/publication
GET    /api/posts?after={cursor}&limit=20
```

provisions.heading: Name the Use Case on Every Published Operation
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `operation-use-case-drift` (level S) for an operation in the committed contract whose `x-litespec-use-case` is missing or differs from the use case its endpoint's mark names.
provisions.statement: Every operation in the generated contract MUST carry `x-litespec-use-case` naming the use case its endpoint implements.
provisions.rationale: The `operationId` names an operation for client code and keeps its casing for method names, so it is not the record identifier. Carrying the identifier itself in an extension, which the OpenAPI specification reserves for this kind of metadata, lets an integrator, a gateway log, or a support person go from an operation straight to its specification page. The value comes from the generated map of operation names to use cases, so it is written once, in the endpoint's mark.
provisions.example: The Claimwick operation `SubmitExpense` carries `"x-litespec-use-case": "use-case/spending.submit-expense"`.

provisions.heading: Name Time Fields with At
provisions.evidence: Does every time field in contract schemas end in At? Look at the time fields.
provisions.statement: Time fields end in `At`, following [AIP-142](https://google.aip.dev/142).
provisions.rationale: A mixed suffix set hides which shape each field carries. One `At` suffix tells the reader every time field carries a timestamp.
provisions.example: `createdAt` names the creation time.

provisions.heading: Name Transport Types by Their Boundary Role
provisions.evidence: Does every transport type name carry the suffix its boundary role assigns? Look at the transport type names.
provisions.statement: Transport types take the names the suffix table assigns their roles.
provisions.rationale: A name that ends in its boundary role keeps transport concerns visibly separate from Application messages and results. The suffix table that assigns each role its suffix lives in `litespec/workspace/naming#use-architectural-suffixes`.
provisions.example: A passive HTTP DTO names its boundary role and ends in `Model`.

provisions.heading: Prove Every Upload Type from Its Content
provisions.evidence: Does every upload operation read the file type from the bytes rather than the claimed media type or file name? Look at the type check of each upload endpoint beside the declared media types.
provisions.statement: A file upload operation MUST determine the file type from the file content rather than the media type or file name the client claims.
provisions.rationale: A claimed media type and a file name are caller input. Either one can name an image while the bytes carry anything else. Reading the type from the content itself keeps the declared media-type bound honest, because the check runs on what the server stores rather than on what the caller says it sent.
provisions.example: A Claimwick receipt photo named as an image is stored as an image only when its bytes read as one of the declared image types. Bytes of another type are refused even when the name and claimed type agree.

provisions.heading: Publish Label-Only Sets as String Enums
provisions.evidence: Does every label-only set publish its string enum in the contract? Look at the label-only sets in the contract.
provisions.statement: A transport model for a label-only set MUST publish its values as an OpenAPI string `enum`.
provisions.rationale: A label-only set carries no case data, so its labels are the complete contract, and a string enum carries them exactly. The permission to use a plain enum for this one situation lives in `litespec/backend/domain#model-every-closed-set-as-a-type-hierarchy`.

provisions.heading: Publish Precise, Complete Schemas
provisions.evidence: Does every contract schema declare the value sets, bounds, formats, and required control headers of its fields? Look at the schemas in the generated contract.
provisions.statement: A generated schema MUST declare the closed value set, bounds, format, and required control headers of each field and parameter it describes.
provisions.rationale: A caller that learns limits from the document validates before sending. A caller that learns them from runtime rejections discovers one limit per failed request. Declaring the closed value set, bounds, format, and required control headers of each field and parameter moves every checkable limit into the contract.
provisions.example:
A label-only set publishes its values as an OpenAPI `enum`. A data-bearing set publishes a polymorphic `oneOf` model with a discriminator per `litespec/backend/api#mirror-each-closed-set-on-the-wire`. A converter on the boundary type keeps every serializer on the contract, including a test client using default options. Host-only conversion breaks readers that do not share host configuration.

An operation requiring a control header declares it as a required parameter, for example `Idempotency-Key` or `If-Match`. The implementation prefers results, enums, and parameter metadata derived from code over handwritten schemas that drift from code.

provisions.heading: Reflect Enforced Authentication in the Contract
provisions.evidence: Does every authenticated operation declare its security schemes and requirements in the generated contract? Look at the operations in the generated contract.
provisions.statement: A generated OpenAPI document MUST declare the security scheme and per-operation security requirement for every endpoint that enforces authentication.
provisions.rationale: A consumer that learns an authentication requirement from a runtime 401 has already built the wrong client. Declared security schemes and per-operation requirements let it build the right one before its first call. Handwritten security metadata drifts from registered schemes, so the document derives them from the registered authentication schemes.
provisions.example: The implementation reads the registered authentication schemes and adds the matching `securitySchemes` and `security` entries. Handwritten security metadata drifts from registered schemes. An operation whose `access` grant is `anonymous` declares no security requirement.

provisions.heading: Reject a Collapsed or Borrowed Wire Contract
provisions.evidence: Does any wire contract collapse a data-bearing set into an enum or reuse a Domain or Application type? Look at each wire contract.
provisions.statement: A WebApi transport model MUST NOT collapse a data-bearing set into an `enum` or reuse a Domain or Application type as the wire contract.
provisions.rationale: Collapsing a data-bearing set into an enum discards the data that distinguishes its cases. Reusing a Domain or Application type as the wire contract couples the public contract to inner shapes. Each layer owns its own contract type per `litespec/backend/architecture#own-each-layers-contract-types`, so the wire contract is always a dedicated transport model. Narrowing follows `litespec/backend/application#record-a-decision-for-closed-set-narrowing`.

provisions.heading: Require the Marker Header on Cookie-Authenticated Writes
provisions.evidence: Does every cookie-authenticated write without the marker header answer 401? Look at the write requests with cookie authentication.
provisions.statement: The API MUST refuse a cookie-authenticated write without the project's marker header.
provisions.rationale: Cookies travel with every request, including ones a malicious page triggers, so a cookie-authenticated write needs proof the project's own page sent it. A page on another site adds no custom header, so the header's absence exposes a cross-site forgery. A write is any request other than GET, HEAD, or OPTIONS. The header takes the form `X-<Project>-Request: 1`, with the exact name set in project configuration. The refused request is unauthenticated, so it answers 401 under `litespec/backend/api#use-consistent-status-codes`. The frontend pages own sending the header. This rule owns the API refusal.

provisions.heading: Return Stable Problem Details
provisions.evidence: Does every error response carry the stable code, the traceId, and one errors entry per field failure? Look at the error responses at the API boundary.
provisions.statement: An error response MUST use [RFC 9457](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc9457) Problem Details carrying a stable application `code`, the current `traceId`, and an `errors` entry for each field failure.
provisions.rationale: A stable machine-readable code lets a client branch on the failure without parsing prose, and the trace identifier connects the response to its diagnostics. One entry per field failure tells the caller everything wrong with the request in one answer. RFC 9457 defines the Problem Details media type the contract uses.
provisions.example:
The serialized contract is:

```json
{
  "type": "https://example.test/problems/validation",
  "title": "Request validation failed",
  "status": 400,
  "detail": "One or more values are invalid.",
  "instance": "/api/posts",
  "code": "validation-failed",
  "traceId": "4bf92f3577b34da6a3ce929d0e0e4736",
  "errors": [
    {
      "field": "title",
      "code": "required",
      "message": "Title is required."
    }
  ]
}
```

`type` is a stable absolute URI owned by the consumer. `errors` appears only when validity findings exist, carrying their member, code, and message. `code` carries the refusal result's stable code, and `detail` carries the free-form prose explanation. A request body names the same pair `code` and `reason` under `litespec/backend/api#name-failure-pairs-code-and-reason`.

WebApi maps Application member names to their public JSON field names. `traceId` carries the trace identifier from the current [W3C Trace Context](https://www.w3.org/TR/trace-context/) `traceparent`, with the request identifier as fallback. The same shape applies to authentication and authorization failures.

The global handler maps validation failures to 400, missing targets through the operation's disclosure policy, and forbidden failures to 403 or the declared 404. The derived `invalid-input` refusal answers 400, and the derived `forbidden` refusal answers 403 or the declared 404. It maps conflicts and state rejections to 409, and unexpected failures to 500 with code `internal-error`. It maps each known domain failure individually. It does not report cancellation from a disconnected request as an application error.

In the Claimwick product, reimbursing an expense that is not approved ends with `result/reimburse-expense.not-approved`, which carries the code `spending.not-approved` and the status 409. For example, the global handler answers:

```json
{
  "type": "https://example.test/problems/conflict",
  "title": "Not approved",
  "status": 409,
  "detail": "The expense is not approved.",
  "instance": "/api/expenses",
  "code": "spending.not-approved",
  "traceId": "4bf92f3577b34da6a3ce929d0e0e4736"
}
```

The endpoint catches no failure. The diagram shows how a domain failure or a validation failure reaches the global handler and becomes a status with a Problem Details body.

![A domain failure or a validation failure reaches the global handler, which no endpoint preempts. The handler selects the HTTP status and returns a Problem Details body carrying the stable code, the trace identifier, and one entry per field failure.](../assets/diagrams/backend-error-flow.svg)

provisions.heading: Shape Command Routes from the Aggregate and the Verb
provisions.evidence: Does every command route carry the aggregate plural and end with its verb? Look at the command routes.
provisions.statement: A command route carries the aggregate plural, and a custom action ends with the use-case verb as its last segment; a POST to the collection, a PUT, PATCH or DELETE on one resource, and a verb the HTTP method already says (POST for create, add and register; PUT or PATCH for change; DELETE for remove) keep the plain resource route.
provisions.rationale: A route that names the aggregate plural, its identity, and the verb as the last segment reads the same for every command: the reader knows the record and the act before opening the handler. A route that repeats the noun or hides the verb makes each command route a fresh puzzle.
provisions.example:
```text
POST   /api/expenses/{id}/reimburse
POST   /api/holds/{holdId}/cancel
```

provisions.heading: Store Every Upload Through Infrastructure
provisions.evidence: Does any endpoint or handler write file bytes to a storage provider directly? Look at the upload endpoints and handlers beside the Infrastructure storage code.
provisions.statement: File storage for an upload MUST live in Infrastructure.
provisions.rationale: Storing a file is provider work, like storing an aggregate, so the endpoint stays a transport adapter and the handler stays on behavior. Infrastructure owns the storage provider, its configuration, and its errors, so a project can change where files live without touching an endpoint or a handler.
provisions.example: The Claimwick endpoint for a receipt photo converts the request to its command and dispatches it, the handler stages the expense, and Infrastructure writes the photo bytes to the configured store.

provisions.heading: Treat OpenAPI as a Generated Contract
provisions.evidence: Does every Release build regenerate the OpenAPI artifact, with no contract gate passing on a changed tree? Look at the Release build output and the contract gate.
provisions.statement: An application MUST generate its OpenAPI document during the Release build.
provisions.rationale: A handwritten contract drifts from the code it describes with the first unmirrored change. Generating the document during the Release build keeps the contract a function of the code, so the file the pinned generator reads stays current.
provisions.example:
The API source artifact is `apps/api/openapi/{ProjectName}.json`.

Build-time generation boots the host, and a boot reaches every startup guard. A project whose composition refuses to start without a secret, a certificate, or a reachable dependency generates no contract from a clean checkout. Two answers are valid, and the project records which one it uses under `litespec/backend/api#generate-the-contract-without-hosted-dependencies`.

| Answer | What the project does | What it costs |
|:---|:---|:---|
| Generation environment | Set an environment for the generation run whose composition wires no hosted dependency. | The generated document reflects that environment's endpoint set. |
| Deferred guard | Move each startup refusal from composition to first use. | A misconfiguration surfaces on the first request instead of at boot. |

Generation without hosted dependencies follows `litespec/backend/api#generate-the-contract-without-hosted-dependencies`.

When a typed consumer reads the API, the pinned generator reads the source artifact. The generated client, its model types, its request schemas, and its query options are one workspace package, because every frontend and every command reads them.

provisions.heading: Use Consistent Status Codes
provisions.evidence: Does every operation response return the status the outcome table assigns? Look at each response beside the outcome table.
provisions.statement: A WebApi operation MUST return the status the outcome table assigns to its result.
provisions.rationale: A client branches on status before it reads a body, so a status that disagrees with the outcome table hides the real outcome. The stack derives the status from the use-case result: each success and refusal kind maps to exactly one status, with no recorded status on the record. The outcome table assigns each result its status once, and the operation returns exactly that status.
provisions.example:
| Outcome | Status |
|:---|:---:|
| Successful read | 200 |
| Successful creation of a readable resource | 201 with the resource location |
| Successful creation without a read route | 201 |
| Successful command without a response body | 204 |
| Structural validation failure | 400 |
| Missing or invalid authentication | 401 |
| Authenticated but forbidden | 403 |
| Resource unavailable under the disclosure policy | 404 |
| State, version, or idempotency conflict | 409 |
| Abuse limit exceeded | 429 with a `Retry-After` header |
| Accepted background operation | 202 with status location |
| Unexpected failure | 500 |

provisions.heading: Use Offsets for Proven Bounded Datasets
provisions.evidence: Does every offset-paged collection state the bound making it safe on the use-case record? Look at each offset-paged collection.
provisions.statement: A collection over a proven bounded dataset declares offset paging in its record while the public contract stays cursor-shaped.
provisions.rationale: Offsets skip rows the database still scans, so they stay cheap only while the dataset stays small. A collection over a proven bounded dataset declares offset paging while the public contract stays cursor-shaped, and the use-case record states the bound that makes it safe.

provisions.heading: Use Opaque Cursors for Collection Paging
provisions.evidence: Does every malformed cursor answer 400 with code invalid-cursor? Look at the collection endpoints.
provisions.statement: A collection endpoint MUST page with an opaque cursor and refuse a malformed cursor with 400 and code `invalid-cursor`.
provisions.rationale: A cursor that exposed offsets or internals lets callers craft requests against storage details, and breaks every stored cursor when those details change. An opaque cursor keeps paging state server-defined. The endpoint treats it as untrusted input: a malformed cursor, or an unsupported cursor version, answers 400 with code `invalid-cursor`.

provisions.heading: Use Standard Field Vocabulary
provisions.evidence: Does any field use placed, locale, or keyName over the standard vocabulary? Look at the field names in the contract.
provisions.statement: Field names use `created` over `placed`, `languageTag` over `locale`, and `displayName` over `keyName`.
provisions.rationale: Shared vocabulary stops the same field from appearing under different names on different operations. `languageTag` follows [RFC 5646](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc5646).
provisions.example: `defaultLanguageTag` replaces `defaultLocaleTag`.

provisions.heading: Use This Endpoint Layout
provisions.evidence: Does every endpoint sit in the `WebApi/` folder of its use case or in the host? Look at the endpoints beside the use case folders.
provisions.statement: Place each endpoint with its request and response models in the `WebApi/` folder of its use case, and host-only endpoints in the host.
provisions.rationale: When each endpoint sits in the `WebApi/` folder of its use case, the folder path matches the specification path, and a reader locates an operation from its use-case identifier without searching. Each use case owns its transport models, so a shape two use cases need is declared in each under `litespec/backend/architecture#give-each-use-case-its-own-models`. The host keeps the endpoints that have no handler to sit beside: protocol endpoints, static assets, and development-only tooling.
provisions.example:
The endpoints sit in the `WebApi/` folder of their use case inside the `UseCases/` folder of their module and aggregate:

```text
{Product}/
  Posts/                            single aggregate whose name matches the module
    UseCases/
      CreateDraft/
        Application/                message, result, handler, validator
        WebApi/                     endpoint, request model, response model
      GetPost/
        Application/
        WebApi/
  Customers/                        two aggregates: operations nest under each aggregate UseCases folder
    CustomerAccounts/
      UseCases/
        RestrictAccount/
          Application/
          WebApi/
    Consents/
      UseCases/
        GrantConsent/
          Application/
          WebApi/
```

Module nesting, including the single-aggregate flat form, follows `litespec/backend/architecture#organize-code-by-module-aggregate-and-use-case`.

provisions.heading: Version Cursors with Stable Sort Values
provisions.evidence: Does every cursor payload carry a version, the last sort values, and a unique tie-breaker, with no readable secret? Look at the cursor payloads.
provisions.statement: A paging cursor MUST carry a version and the last stable sort values, including a unique tie-breaker, and no sensitive value in readable form.
provisions.rationale: Paging reads a sorted sequence in order, so the cursor names exactly where the last page stopped. The version lets the sort evolve without breaking stored cursors, and the last stable sort values with a unique tie-breaker keep the read exact when values repeat. The tie-breaker matches the query's stable order under `litespec/backend/api#bound-collection-queries`. No sensitive value travels in readable form, because callers store and replay cursors.

provisions.heading: Answer Each Reaction in One Marked Class
provisions.evidence: Does every event handler answer its trigger in one class with one mark, send at most one command, retry no final refusal, and sit in the folder of what it runs? Look at each event handler class and its mark.
provisions.statement: A reaction implementation MUST answer the trigger its reaction record names, in one class carrying one mark naming that record.
provisions.rationale: A reaction without an explicit implementation leaves its trigger, its target, and its failure handling to whoever reads the code. One event handler class per reaction record answers the trigger the record names in `triggeredBy`, whether a domain event or an integration event, and dispatches only through the record's `effects` entries, sending at most one command. The class never writes an aggregate directly: an event handler that needs a write runs a command. It honors the record's `reads`, its idempotency, and its `onFailure`, and the mark is the link the stack reader follows. A conflict refusal from the command it runs is transient, so the reaction retries it under its `onFailure`; a declared final refusal ends the reaction without a retry. The class lives in the `Application/` folder of the use case it runs, or with the notification it sends or the system it calls, under `litespec/workspace/naming#place-each-trigger-with-what-it-runs`. The [automation page](../core/automation.md) states the trigger fields. An entry with `after-commit` timing uses durable delivery through the outbox extension.
provisions.example: The class `SendDueNoticeOnLoanBorrowedHandler` in `Lending/Notifications/LoanDue/` carries one mark naming `reaction/lending.send-due-notice-on-loan-borrowed`, answers `domain-event/loan.loan-borrowed`, and sends `notification/lending.loan-due`.

provisions.heading: Ask Another Module One Question Through a Decision Port
provisions.evidence: Does every port in `Contracts/Ports/` hold one method, read only, serve a command, and sit beside a use case stating why a read model is not enough? Look at each decision port beside its callers.
provisions.statement: A command whose decision needs another module's current value MUST ask for it through a decision port with one read-only method and one answer type named for its question, with the use case record stating why a read model's freshness is not enough.
provisions.rationale: Some decisions cannot accept a copy that lags: money that may still move, or capacity that may still sell. A decision port answers that one question with the owner's current value and nothing else, so it cannot grow into a general reader, and its name says what it decides. It only reads: a change the caller needs in the owning module is a fact that module's reaction answers. A query never needs one, because a screen accepts the lag or calls the owner's own query.
provisions.example: A sale asks a capacity module `IRemainingCapacity.FindAsync(variantId)` and receives a `RemainingCapacity` with the units left and the time it was read, instead of loading a whole event profile through a general reader.

provisions.heading: Build Collaborators Through the Container
provisions.evidence: Does any handler, job, or step class create collaborators inside its body, or take more than ten constructor dependencies? Look at each constructor the change adds.
provisions.statement: Each handler needing a collaborator MUST take it through the constructor from the container, never create it inside its own body.
provisions.rationale: A step class created inside a handler hides its dependencies: a handler that looks small is really hundreds of lines behind its helpers. Injected collaborators keep their dependencies visible in the constructor.
provisions.example: The reimburse handler takes its expense repository through its constructor, while a step created inside the handler that takes a repository is reported.

provisions.heading: Call External Systems Through Their Ports
provisions.evidence: Does every `calls` effect run in an event handler or job through its port, after the commit? Look at each provider call beside its record's `calls` entry.
provisions.statement: Each `calls` effect MUST run in an event handler or job through the port operation its record names, after the commit of the command that raised its trigger.
provisions.rationale: A command handler changes only its aggregate under `litespec/backend/application#dispatch-only-declared-effect-edges`, so a provider call runs in an event handler or job after the commit. The `calls` effect names one operation on one external system, and the operations entry states its timeout, its timeout behavior, its retries, its response, and its cache. The port carries that operation with project-owned types and carries a mark naming its system on the port interface, and Infrastructure implements it, so a provider change stops at the adapter. The stack reader counts a call as a `calls` edge only through such a marked port; any other injected interface is internal work. A call on a marked port that no `calls` entry declares fails `effect-undeclared`. A provider call whose result the command needs before it can answer is a waiver: the use case records the intent first, for example a pending charge, and an event handler calls the provider. A project that keeps an inline call records a waiver naming the compensation that undoes it.
provisions.example: An event handler that calls an expense payout operation names it through the record's `calls` entry and the port method; a direct provider call fails the check. The reimburse-expense command records a pending payment and answers at once, an event handler calls the payout provider after the commit, and the expense screen shows the pending state first and the later posted fact through the query.

provisions.heading: Declare a Port Where Its Consumers Meet
provisions.evidence: Does every port sit at the lowest folder holding every consumer that names it? Look at each port beside its consumers.
provisions.statement: A port MUST be declared at the lowest folder holding every consumer that names it, following `litespec/backend/architecture#place-a-type-at-the-lowest-folder-that-holds-its-consumers`.
provisions.rationale: A port in a product-wide folder is reviewed by nobody. A port declared beside the aggregate it serves is reviewed with that aggregate's specification. A port whose consumers sit in one module is declared in that module's layer folder beside the aggregate it serves, and only a port another module calls belongs in the owning module's `Contracts/Ports/` folder. A port in `Contracts/Ports/` only reads: a write another module needs is a fact its reaction answers. Collecting every port in one folder because they share the word "port" is grouping by technical type, and `litespec/backend/application#organize-application-by-use-case` rejects that grouping one level down for the same reason. Where a port serves aggregates in one module but is called from another, the declaring module is the one that owns the aggregates: the module whose rules change when the port changes.

provisions.heading: Declare Every Pipeline Position Beside the Message
provisions.evidence: Does every message declare a value or an exemption for each required pipeline position? Look at each message beside the baseline and selected extensions.
provisions.statement: A message MUST declare a value or an exemption for every pipeline position the baseline and the selected extensions require.
provisions.rationale: A pipeline stage that guesses a message's position guesses differently per message. Declaring a value or an exemption beside the message makes each position explicit, and composition refuses to start when a message states neither. The baseline holds one position: authorization, declared from the record's `access` on the message itself. The audit extension adds the audit selection position under `litespec/ext/audit#declare-which-commands-are-audited`.

provisions.heading: Declare Exclusive Holds Beside the Message
provisions.evidence: Does every command needing exclusive access declare its hold key and patience beside the message? Look at each such command message.
provisions.statement: Each command needing exclusive access MUST declare its hold beside the message, with its key and its patience.
provisions.rationale: A lock copied into each handler carries its own key, patience, and refusal at every site, and each copy drifts. Declaring the hold beside the message takes it in a pipeline step after validation and releases it on completion, refusing with the conflict code when the wait runs out.
provisions.example: The refund command declares its per-order hold with fifteen seconds of patience.

provisions.heading: Declare the Audit Target and Reason Beside the Message
provisions.evidence: Does any command handler add an audit target or reason that the message already carries? Look at each audit call in the command handlers.
provisions.statement: Each audited command MUST declare beside the message the audit target and reason that the message carries, leaving the handler to add only the values it learns while running.
provisions.rationale: A value read from the message is known before the handler runs, so the pipeline records it on every outcome, including a denial. Declaring the target and the reason beside the message evaluates both before the handler runs. The handler adds only a generated identity or a reason composed from loaded state.
provisions.example: The approve-expense command declares its expense id as the audit target with the reason the message carries, and the handler adds only the approval reference it learns while running.

provisions.heading: Define Narrow External Ports
provisions.evidence: Does every external port have the public interface shape, the noun or verb name, the single method or purpose, and the project-owned types? Look at each port declaration.
provisions.statement: Application MUST declare each external port as a public interface with a noun or verb name, one method or one purpose, and project-owned types.
provisions.rationale: A port is the seam where a provider change stops. It has one method or one purpose, named as a noun for the capability (`PostArchive`) or a verb for the act (`ArchivePosts`), typed with project-owned types. If provider names or transport models entered the interface, replacing the provider would rewrite Application. Keeping them in Infrastructure confines the change to the adapter.

provisions.heading: Dispatch Commands and Queries Through Separate Entry Points
provisions.evidence: Does every dispatch site call the command or query entry point rather than a unified bus? Look at each dispatch site.
provisions.statement: An application MUST dispatch a command and a query through two separate Application-facing entry points rather than one message bus abstraction.
provisions.rationale: Two entry points keep the write path and the read path distinguishable at every call site, and let the pipeline compose different stages for each path. A unified bus hides that difference behind one method, so a reader cannot tell whether a dispatch changes state or only reads. The backend's whole command and query split depends on that difference. The rule states the property, not the package. Each stack binding pins one library that supplies it. A consumer replacing that library names its own dispatch entry points in its Application documentation instead of touching this rule.

provisions.heading: Dispatch Only Declared Effect Edges
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `effect-undeclared` (level S) for a dispatch a handler, event handler, or job takes that its record declares no edge for, and `dotnet build` reports `LS2021` for a mediator held outside an endpoint, event handler or job.
provisions.statement: A command handler MUST change only its aggregate, leaving every declared `runs`, `sends` and `calls` edge to an event handler or job after the commit.
provisions.rationale: An undeclared edge is the defect: an event handler or job reaches a use case, notification, integration event, or external system the records never named, so review sees behavior the specification hides. Each declared entry names exactly one verb, its timing, and its failure handling, and the stack reader fails `effect-undeclared` on any dispatch the record does not declare. An outbound integration event is no effect: the pipeline stages it from the domain event it translates under `litespec/backend/application#emit-declared-integration-events-after-commit`. `sends`, `calls`, and `runs` effects run in an event handler or job after the commit, and only an entry point sends a message: an endpoint, an event handler, or a job, each sending one. A `sends` or `calls` effect on a command is `after-commit` or `async`, never `inline`, and `consistency: atomic` never reaches past the use case's own writes. The effect graph holds no cycles except through domain events with a stated end condition.
provisions.example: The send-approver-reminders reaction sends the approval reminder through the messenger port after the submit commit. A send its record does not declare fails the check.

provisions.heading: Emit Declared Integration Events After Commit
provisions.evidence: `dotnet build` reports `LS2022` for an event published outside the shared kernel, and `litespec model check` reports `effect-undeclared` for an event a handler, event handler or job publishes itself.
provisions.statement: Each outbound integration event MUST leave the commit only through the one pipeline step that stages raised domain events, built from the domain event its record `translates`, so no user code publishes an event.
provisions.rationale: When user code publishes events, two handlers publish one fact with two payloads, and a publisher in a handler emits state the act never announced. One global step, running in the command pipeline before the commit, stages each raised domain event for the reactions of its own module, and each integration event whose record translates that domain event, built by the integration event's own mapping from the domain event alone. Both commit with the business work, and the outbox extension delivers them. A command handler changes only its aggregate under `litespec/backend/application#dispatch-only-declared-effect-edges`, so the aggregate raises its fact and the pipeline does the rest. The domain event therefore carries every field its integration events publish. Settled by [decision/0064-raise-facts-and-send-nothing-from-handlers](decision/0064-raise-facts-and-send-nothing-from-handlers).
provisions.example: The expense raises its reimbursed fact, and the staging step stages it and `integration-event/expense-reimbursed`, built from that fact, in the same commit. The reimburse handler publishes nothing.

provisions.heading: Enforce Target Authorization in the Pipeline
provisions.evidence: Does every message reach the guard with the `access` its record declares, with no handler throwing a forbidden refusal or taking the authorization guard? Look at each handler body and the `access` on each message.
provisions.statement: The authorization guard, not the handler, MUST authorize every message from the `access` its use-case record declares.
provisions.rationale: Authorization decided in each handler is decided differently in each handler. The guard decides once from what the record declares: the `auth` kinds the caller presents, the `grant` naming a permission, a `self` scope over one, `anonymous`, or `system`, and the `tenant` scope naming the tenants the call reaches. Ownership, tenant, role, state, or delegated access resolves against the target data through a scope owner lookup for the record the message names. A handler never compares the caller with a target, and never throws the forbidden refusal itself. Code names no permitted action outside that grant, so the record stays the one list of who may run a use case. Where the stack generates code, it generates one constant per `permission/` record from the records. Declaring `access` beside the message also lets composition refuse to start when a message states no position at all. The guard reports a refusal as a denial rather than raising it, so a refused attempt reaches the audit trail beside the ones that succeeded. The audit extension records the denial under `litespec/ext/audit#record-refused-authorization`. A collection query has no single target record, so a scope owner lookup has nothing to resolve. Its authorized scope is a database predicate under `litespec/quality/security#restrict-a-protected-collection-in-the-database`, applied before paging. Filtering a loaded collection in memory satisfies neither rule. It matches the shape [OWASP names as broken object level authorization](https://owasp.org/www-project-top-ten/2021/A01_2021-Broken_Access_Control/). WebApi enforces coarse authenticated, role, or scope policies first under `litespec/backend/api#apply-only-coarse-policies-at-the-endpoint`, which replaces no decision that depends on business data.

provisions.heading: Expose Store State Through Ports
provisions.evidence: Does every `store` aggregate reach code only through its owner-naming port, with no aggregate root? Look at each store aggregate's code path.
provisions.statement: A `store` aggregate MUST reach code only through a port naming its owner, with no aggregate root.
provisions.rationale: A `store` aggregate is state no invariant guards: a library-owned table, a suppression list, or a delivery log. With no invariant, there is no root, no state record, and no domain repository; the port names the owning system and Infrastructure implements it. Staff actions on that state stay ordinary use cases calling the port.
provisions.example: The suppression list reaches code through a suppression port owned by the communications module, with no aggregate root.

provisions.heading: Implement One Outcome Path per Command
provisions.evidence: Does any command handler look up a record and then create one in the same method? Look at each command handler body for a lookup followed by a create.
provisions.statement: Each command MUST implement one use case with one success path, so a flow that finds a record or else creates it is two use cases that the boundary owning the flow chooses between.
provisions.rationale: A get-or-create command hides two use cases with different access, audit, and refusals behind one name. The boundary that owns the flow, an endpoint, an event handler, or a job, runs a query and then sends the command that fits. When the create loses a race, it refuses with its conflict under `litespec/backend/application#refuse-a-lost-race-as-a-conflict`, and the owner sends the other command. Where the record is usually present, the owner may instead send the command first and, on the record's not-found refusal, send the create and then the command again. One shared helper holds that sequence, so no endpoint repeats it.
provisions.example: Signing in to the library with an unknown reader card runs as a query and then one of two commands: the endpoint queries `query/loans.find-reader-by-card`, then sends either `use-case/loans.register-reader` or `use-case/loans.record-reader-sign-in`.

provisions.heading: Issue Per-Record Work from a Job
provisions.evidence: Does any command handler change records inside a loop body? Look at each loop in the command handlers.
provisions.statement: Work over many records MUST run as a job that selects the records and sends one command per record, each in its own unit of work, never as a command handler that changes records or sends commands in a loop.
provisions.rationale: When one command loops over many records, one failing record rolls back the batch, and the batch holds locks for its whole length. The job runs each command within its declared selection under `litespec/backend/application#run-each-job-within-its-declared-selection`, and persistence commits each record alone under `litespec/backend/persistence#commit-each-command-pipeline-once`.
provisions.example: The erase-expired-data job selects the expired expenses and sends one erase command per expense, each in its own unit of work, instead of a batch command looping over expenses. A condition the batch checked, such as the expense being past retention, moves into the erase act, so an expense changed in the meantime refuses the erase itself.

provisions.heading: Keep Command Handlers to Load, Call and Stage
provisions.evidence: `dotnet build` reports `LS2021` for a mediator a handler, validator, step or domain type holds, and `LS2022` for an event published outside the shared kernel.
provisions.statement: A command handler MUST load or create the aggregate its use case changes, call one domain method on it, stage it through its repository, and return the result, and send no command, query or event.
provisions.rationale: Everything else has an owner. Validation, authorization, idempotency, audit, the timestamp, holds, and the commit are pipeline stages. Decisions and invariants are the aggregate's. Uniqueness is persistence's under `litespec/backend/persistence#enforce-uniqueness-in-the-store`. Messages, provider calls, and changes to other aggregates are consequences that event handlers run after the commit under `litespec/backend/application#dispatch-only-declared-effect-edges`. A handler that does more widens the unit of work, so one failing step rolls back work that had no reason to fail with it, and agents copy the widened shape. A handler that sends a command nests one use case inside another, and a handler that publishes an event publishes state its act never announced; neither has a record that can declare it. The commit post-handler owns the transaction under `litespec/backend/persistence#commit-each-command-pipeline-once`, WebApi owns error mapping, the audit completion handler owns the trail, and the guard owns authorization. A use case whose record declares `consistency: atomic` over several aggregates is the one exception: the handler loads, calls, and stages each aggregate its `writes` names, one method each, and the record states why the change cannot be eventual. The handler takes its repositories under `litespec/backend/application#write-only-aggregates-the-record-names`, and returns only the results and refusals the record declares under `litespec/backend/application#return-only-declared-results-and-refusals`.
provisions.example:
In the Claimwick product, `use-case/spending.approve-expense` runs through the command pipeline: the endpoint maps the request to the approve command, the command entry point dispatches it, validation and the authorization guard run, the handler loads the expense, calls Approve on it, stages the expense, and returns the result. The handler body reads as three steps: it loads the expense through its domain repository, calls one domain method on it, and stages the expense. The handler commits nothing, and exactly one post-handler commits after it. The diagram shows each stage from the HTTP request to that single commit.

![An HTTP request reaches the endpoint, which maps it to a command and dispatches it through the command mediator. Validation checks structural input, then the authorization guard checks the permission and the target. The handler loads or creates one aggregate through its repository, calls one domain method, and stages it. The repository stages the aggregate, and exactly one commit post-handler commits the session once.](../assets/diagrams/backend-command-pipeline.svg)

The handler loads or creates, calls once, stages, and returns. Validation, authorization, idempotency, audit, the timestamp, holds, commit, and fault classification belong to their owners, so none appears in the handler.

provisions.heading: Keep Mappings at the Owning Boundary
provisions.evidence: Does any conversion live outside the layer owning its output shape? Look at each conversion beside its output.
provisions.statement: Own domain-to-result projection in Application, transport mapping in WebApi, and view models in the frontend.
provisions.rationale: A mapping changes when its output shape changes, so it lives with the boundary that defines that shape: domain-to-result projection in Application, transport mapping in WebApi, view models in the frontend. A mapping kept elsewhere breaks when the owning boundary evolves.

provisions.heading: Keep Messages Immutable
provisions.evidence: Do any commands, queries, results, or validation errors mutate? Look at each message declaration.
provisions.statement: Declare commands, queries, results, and validation errors as immutable values.
provisions.rationale: Immutable values give commands, queries, results, and validation errors a shape no handler mutates mid-pipeline. Typed identifiers and shared-kernel value objects cross the boundary; an aggregate-owned value object does not, so the message carries a primitive and the handler reconstructs it.

provisions.heading: Keep Query Handlers Free of Writes
provisions.evidence: Does any query handler stage, store, delete, or dispatch? Look at each query handler body.
provisions.statement: A query handler MUST NOT stage, store, delete or dispatch anything.
provisions.rationale: A read that writes makes retries, caching, and authorization of reads unsafe. An audited read is the pipeline's, not the handler's, under `litespec/ext/audit#declare-which-commands-are-audited`.
provisions.example: The list-expenses query projects its rows and stages nothing.

provisions.heading: Keep Repository Reads Out of Loops
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `repository-read-invalid` (level A) for a repository read inside a loop body.
provisions.statement: Each handler and job MUST read no repository inside a loop body.
provisions.rationale: A read inside a loop turns one handling into as many round trips as there are items, and the slowdown hides behind small test data. A batch read or a scoped query loads every item at once, so the handling costs one trip whatever the data holds.
provisions.example: The reminder job loads due loans with one scoped query instead of reading each loan inside its loop.

provisions.heading: Load a Required Record or Refuse It
provisions.evidence: Does every required record load through the required load, and does no optional lookup throw? Look at each load call in the handlers.
provisions.statement: Each handler needing a record MUST load it through the required load that throws the aggregate not-found refusal, and use the optional lookup only for optional records.
provisions.rationale: A lookup followed by a thrown not-found repeats the aggregate decision in every handler, and each copy names its own failure. The required load throws the aggregate's own not-found refusal, so the handler states that the record is required by the call it makes.
provisions.example: The approve handler loads its expense as a required record, while the optional coupon lookup returns nothing when the coupon is absent.

provisions.heading: Mirror a Domain Closed Set in the Result
provisions.evidence: Does any result carrying a Domain closed set flatten its shape or drop a case? Look at each such result beside its Domain set.
provisions.statement: An Application result carrying a Domain closed set MUST model that set with the same shape as its own union or code value.
provisions.rationale: Each case of a closed set can carry different data, and a caller that receives a flattened shape cannot tell which fields belong to which case. Flattening case data into an enumeration with nullable fields loses that mapping. Mirroring the Domain shape in the result keeps the layers aligned, so the data of each case survives to the caller. Application exposes no Domain union type. Narrowing follows `litespec/backend/application#record-a-decision-for-closed-set-narrowing`, and the set itself follows `litespec/backend/domain#model-every-closed-set-as-a-type-hierarchy`. The wire carries the same shape under `litespec/backend/api#mirror-each-closed-set-on-the-wire`.
provisions.example: A refund outcome result carries one case per Domain case with its data: pending, succeeded, failed, and reversed.

provisions.heading: Model Expected Use-Case Refusals Explicitly
provisions.evidence: Does every expected refusal carry its result code with a caller-safe message, and no transport status? Look at each refusal.
provisions.statement: An expected use-case refusal MUST carry its result code and a caller-safe message, with no transport status.
provisions.rationale: An expected refusal is part of the use case's contract: a missing resource, a forbidden act, or a conflicting write, carrying the refusal result's stable code and a caller-safe message. The refusal carries no transport result, provider detail, or stack detail, so the same refusal maps correctly at any transport, and handlers do not catch it. The use case lists every result it returns, and each refusal result carries its code. Generic refusals are derived, never written: a use case whose grant is a permission derives its `forbidden` result, and a use case with rules on its input derives its `invalid-input` result. A conflict refuses the same input the same way until the caller rereads the resource and retries with current state. A refusal that a blind retry can pass is transient and belongs to the [integrations extension](../ext/integrations.md). A module publishes no refusal type, so every refusal a use case returns is one its own module declares.

provisions.heading: Organize Application by Use Case
provisions.evidence: Does every command and query own one use case folder inside the `UseCases/` folder of its module and aggregate, with its message, result, validator, handler, mapping, and pipeline-read values? Look at the folders under each module.
provisions.statement: Each command or query MUST own one use case folder inside the `UseCases/` folder of its module and aggregate holding its message, result, validator, handler, mapping, and definition of pipeline-read values.
provisions.rationale: When handlers live in one folder, validators in another, and endpoints in a third, a single behavior spreads across the module. A change then touches six folders, and review misses one. One folder per use case keeps the message, result, validator, handler, mapping, and pipeline-read values together, with the endpoint and transport models beside them, so a reviewer judges the whole behavior from one place. Type names share the use-case prefix and follow the suffix table under `litespec/workspace/naming#use-architectural-suffixes`, and pipeline-read values sit beside the message under `litespec/backend/application#declare-every-pipeline-position-beside-the-message`.

provisions.heading: Parse Input in the Validator
provisions.evidence: Does every validator parse each value object in the input, leaving none for the handler? Look at each validator beside its input.
provisions.statement: Each validator MUST parse every value object in the input, so the handler construction cannot fail on input.
provisions.rationale: A validator that checks presence only leaves parsing to the handler, so one input is judged in two layers and the handler throws on caller data. Parsing in the validator keeps business refusals in the domain and input failures in validation, where each belongs.
provisions.example: The invite validator parses the email address into its value object, and the handler takes that value without a second check.

provisions.heading: Project Queries Directly
provisions.evidence: Does any query handler take a domain repository, load an aggregate, or call another module's port? Look at each query handler's constructor and body.
provisions.statement: A query handler MUST project directly to its result from its own module's store and read models, without loading an aggregate.
provisions.rationale: A read path acts on no invariant, so loading an aggregate for presentation pays for enforcement no read needs and couples the read shape to the write model. Projecting directly to the result keeps reads on the read boundary the persistence standards state. A query handler takes no domain repository, and reads no other module's reader: a query that only shows another module's data belongs to that module, and the screen joins the two answers under `litespec/frontend/data#compose-a-screen-from-each-owners-query`. The result type carries the `include` groups the record's `output` declares under `litespec/backend/application#shape-query-results-from-declared-output`. The command and query split lives in `litespec/backend/architecture#separate-command-and-query-behavior`.

provisions.heading: Read Another Module's State Through a Read Model
provisions.evidence: Does any use case call another module's reader for state a read model could hold, and does every read model have a use case naming it in `reads`? Look at each cross-module port call beside the module's read models.
provisions.statement: A use case MUST read another module's state through a read model its own module keeps, named in its `reads`, unless its decision needs the owner's current value and asks for it through a decision port.
provisions.rationale: A general reader in the owner's `Contracts/Ports/` folder couples every reading module to the owner's storage, uptime, and release cadence. It grows a method per caller until one interface returns one profile shape to every module. A read model is the reading module's own copy: its record names each field and the published field it comes from, a personal field names the event that erases it, and its projections keep it current from the owner's integration events. The reader pays with a lag up to the read model's declared `freshness`, which most decisions accept. This is the practice known as event-carried state transfer, declared as a record so a check can prove every field has a source. Settled by [decision/0065-read-another-module-through-a-read-model](decision/0065-read-another-module-through-a-read-model).
provisions.example: The reporting module's list-reimbursed-expenses query reads `read-model/reporting.reimbursed-expense`, which its projections fill from the expense-reimbursed integration event. It calls no spending reader.

provisions.heading: Read Settings Through Typed Options
provisions.evidence: Does every handler read its settings through a typed options value or stored tenant data, with no raw lookup? Look at each setting read in the handlers.
provisions.statement: A handler MUST read a setting record through a typed options value, or through stored tenant data where the record's `setBy` is `tenant`.
provisions.rationale: A raw configuration lookup bypasses the type, the range, and the bound the setting record owns, so no handler uses one. Binding decider-set and operator-set values to typed options the host validates at startup fails a bad value before traffic arrives. A setting record owns its type, its default, its range, its unit, and what happens at the bound. Tenant-set values are data nobody reviews: they live in stored tenant state the handler reads per tenant.
provisions.example: The receipt threshold binds to a spending options value. The handler reads the bound and refuses past it with `atBound: refuse`.

provisions.heading: Read Time from the Scoped Clock
provisions.evidence: Which handlers read the system clock directly, or take more than one timestamp for one message? Look at the clock reads in each handler.
provisions.statement: Each handler MUST read the message timestamp from the scoped clock the pipeline stamps once per message.
provisions.rationale: A handler that reads the clock two or three times in one decision records different times for one act, sometimes with an outside call in between. One timestamp per message fixes the moment the message starts, and every decision in the handling answers to the same time. The shared clock stays for infrastructure only.
provisions.example: The approve handler stamps its approval with the handled clock, not with a fresh clock read.

provisions.heading: Record a Decision for Closed-Set Narrowing
provisions.evidence: Does every narrowed closed set have a recorded decision with an updated specification? Look at each narrowed set beside the decision records.
provisions.statement: A layer MUST NOT narrow a Domain closed set without a recorded decision and an updated specification.
provisions.rationale: Narrowing silently drops cases the Domain can produce, so a caller meeting a dropped case gets a shape the contract left undescribed. A recorded decision with an updated specification makes the dropped cases visible and owned. The decision follows `litespec/core/model#record-each-technical-choice-as-a-decision`.

provisions.heading: Refuse a Lost Race as a Conflict
provisions.evidence: Does every command that loses a race at commit end with its use case conflict refusal? Look at the race outcomes beside the use case refusals.
provisions.statement: Each command that loses a race at commit MUST end with its use case's conflict refusal.
provisions.rationale: A duplicate key or a stale version reaches the commit as a store fault, and the pipeline classifies it as the use case's named conflict refusal, so the caller learns what happened and may reread and retry. No reservation, re-read, or retry lives in the handler. The store enforces uniqueness under `litespec/backend/persistence#enforce-uniqueness-in-the-store` and versions every aggregate under `litespec/backend/persistence#version-every-aggregate`.
provisions.example: Two clerks register the same book barcode at once. The second commit violates the barcode unique index, and the command refuses with `book-barcode-taken`.

provisions.heading: Report Input Problems as Validity Findings
provisions.evidence: Does every validator report validity findings with a member, a code, and a message, and no transport status? Look at the findings each validator reports.
provisions.statement: A validator MUST report its findings as validity findings, with each finding carrying a member, a code, and a message, and no transport status.
provisions.rationale: When validation stops at the first problem, one form turns into repeated round trips. Running every validator and merging the findings tells the caller everything wrong with the form in one answer. Each finding carries a member naming the input member, a code naming the stable reason, and a message explaining the problem in caller-safe language. Findings carry no transport status, because Application answers no transport.
provisions.example:
