A submit request with an empty expense identifier and an empty employee identifier reports one finding per member, two in total, with no transport status:

```json
[
  { "member": "ExpenseId", "code": "required", "message": "An expense is required." },
  { "member": "EmployeeId", "code": "required", "message": "An employee is required." }
]
```

The caller sees both problems at once, and the pipeline refuses the request before Domain runs.

provisions.heading: Return Only Declared Results and Refusals
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `result-undeclared` (level S) for a code a handler produces that no declared result names; a handler returns only the results and codes its record lists.
provisions.statement: A handler MUST return only the results, refusals, and codes its use-case record declares.
provisions.rationale: An observable outcome no result declares is behavior the specification hides, so the stack reader fails `result-undeclared` on it. Refusals return in the precedence order the record lists, first match wins, and a success carrying `codes` returns only those codes. Generic refusals derive from `access` and `input` and need no declaration. A use case refuses only with refusals its own module declares: when another module's port answers nothing, the use case refuses with its own declared refusal, never with the other module's exception.
provisions.example: A handler that returns a code its record never lists fails the check, even when the code is spelled correctly.

provisions.heading: Return Only What the Caller Needs
provisions.evidence: Does any Application result return more than the caller needs? Look at each result beside its caller.
provisions.statement: Return only the values the caller needs from an Application result.
provisions.rationale: A result carries only what the caller needs. An aggregate, session, provider response, or transport result leaving Application makes an inner concern part of the outward contract, and every change to that concern breaks callers.

provisions.heading: Run Each Job Within Its Declared Selection
provisions.evidence: Does every scheduled or one-off job run within its selection, batch size, lease, and cursor? Look at each job run beside its record.
provisions.statement: A scheduled or one-off job MUST run its declared commands once per item in its record's `selection`, honoring its batch size, lease, and cursor.
provisions.rationale: The job record owns what each run selects, how many items each batch takes, the lease that keeps two runs apart, and the cursor where a run resumes. The job runs its `effects` entries once per item, records its evidence where the record states, and follows its `onFailure` when an item fails. One execution host runs the job under `litespec/backend/architecture#name-the-host-for-work-that-outlives-a-request`. The job class lives in the `Application/` folder of the use case it runs, so the use case folder shows every way it starts.
provisions.example: The erase-expired-data job selects decided expenses past retention in batches of 200 under its lease, runs one erase command per expense, and resumes from its cursor.

provisions.heading: Run Heavy Work as a Request Then a Build
provisions.evidence: Does any command assembling a large artifact skip the recorded request and building job? Look at each heavy command.
provisions.statement: Record the request behind a command that assembles a large artifact, and let a job build the artifact for the requester to read back.
provisions.rationale: A command that reads many repositories to assemble a large response holds the caller waiting and times out under load. Recording the request answers at once, the build runs in the background, and the requester reads the state of its own request. Which artifact counts as large depends on the data and the load of the project, so that bound sits in the shape the project names.
provisions.example: The export-expenses command records its request, and a job builds the file the requester then downloads.

provisions.heading: Send Messages After Commit
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `effect-timing-invalid` (level S) for a command use case declaring a `sends` or `calls` effect with `inline` timing.
provisions.statement: Each command MUST leave its messages to an event handler after the commit, never send them from the command handler.
provisions.rationale: A message that leaves before its transaction commits promises work even when the transaction then fails. The aggregate raises its fact, and an event handler for that fact sends, so no message leaves for a write that never landed. A `sends` effect is `after-commit` or `async`, never `inline`.
provisions.example: The submit-expense aggregate raises its submitted fact, and an event handler sends the approver notice after the commit.

provisions.heading: Send Notifications Through the Messenger Port
provisions.evidence: Does every `sends` effect run in an event handler through the messenger port, after the commit? Look at each send beside its record's `sends` entry.
provisions.statement: Each `sends` effect MUST run in an event handler or job through the messenger port, after the commit of the command that raised its trigger.
provisions.rationale: A command handler changes only its aggregate under `litespec/backend/application#dispatch-only-declared-effect-edges`, so a notification send runs in an event handler after the commit. The notification record owns the template, the audience, the channel, the consent rule, the frequency, the dedup key, and the claims each message keeps. The `sends` edge names the notification, and the notification record carries its suppression in `suppressedWhen`. The messenger port carries the send with project-owned types. A reaction or job that only sends lives in the module `Notifications/` folder named for its notification, beside the notification's message model and any type only that notification uses. A send no edge declares fails `effect-undeclared`, and a second send of a `once` notification with the same dedup key sends nothing.
provisions.example: The due-notice event handler sends the loan-due notification through the messenger port. The template and consent rule stay on the notification record, not in the handler.

provisions.heading: Separate Input Validation from Invariants
provisions.evidence: Does every validator check structural input only, leaving aggregate state to Domain? Look at each validator body.
provisions.statement: A validator MUST limit its checks to structural input, leaving aggregate state decisions to Domain.
provisions.rationale: Structural input and aggregate state fail for different reasons at different times. Malformed input is rejected before Domain runs, while a state refusal needs the loaded aggregate. A validator that checked state would need the aggregate, which pulls persistence into validation and judges one input in two layers. Keeping validators to structural input, an empty title, a malformed identifier, or an invalid page size, leaves state decisions, such as whether an expense above the threshold carries a receipt, to Domain. Every validator for a message reports validity findings under `litespec/backend/application#report-input-problems-as-validity-findings`, so the caller learns the whole form in one answer.
provisions.example: Take the Claimwick expense submission, `use-case/spending.submit-expense`. Its command carries an expense identifier and an employee identifier, plus the amount, currency, and receipt. The validator checks the shape of that input: it rejects an empty expense identifier or an empty employee identifier, and it accepts every well-formed pair. It does not ask whether an expense above the threshold carries a receipt, because that is an aggregate state decision. Domain makes that call and rejects a receipt-less expense above the threshold with `result/submit-expense.receipt-missing`, which carries the stable code `spending.receipt-missing`.

provisions.heading: Shape Query Results from Declared Output
provisions.evidence: Does every query result type carry its declared `include` groups with their fields, freshness, and visibility? Look at each result type beside its record's `output`.
provisions.statement: A query result type MUST carry the `include` groups its record's `output` declares, with their fields, freshness, and visibility.
provisions.rationale: The record's `output` names each group with its fields, their classification, the aggregates it reads, and the freshness the caller can rely on: `immediate`, `snapshot`, or `eventual` with its `within`. The result type carries one member per group, with its fields, freshness, and visibility, so the caller reads what the record promises and nothing more. A group with `visibleWhen` appears only when its condition holds, and a group wider than its `reads` names the approved requirement widening it in `widenedBy`. A group showing a figure a command re-decides names the deciding command use case or its aggregate in `decidedBy`, as `litespec/core/use-cases#name-the-use-case-that-decides-a-stale-figure` states. A query whose `timing` is asynchronous carries an `eventual` freshness with its `within` and a lag scenario.
provisions.example: The expense-list result carries its `rows` group with the declared fields, freshness, and visibility.

provisions.heading: Use This Use-Case Layout
provisions.evidence: Does every use-case path, layer folder, trigger folder, and result part name follow the layout? Look at each path under the modules.
provisions.statement: Place each use case in a folder named for it inside the `UseCases/` folder of its module and aggregate, holding an `Application/` folder with its message, result, handler, validator, pipeline definitions, own steps and triggers, and a `WebApi/` folder with its endpoint and transport models when it has an endpoint.
provisions.rationale: One folder per use case inside its `UseCases/` folder holds everything a reviewer needs to judge it in one place, and the module tree lets a reader move from a handler to its endpoint without a map. Two layer folders inside it state each file's layer in the path, keep a large use case's listing readable, and show by their presence whether the use case has an endpoint. The reactions and job that run the use case sit in its `Application/` folder, so the folder shows every way the use case starts. Settled by [decision/0063-place-each-trigger-with-what-it-runs](decision/0063-place-each-trigger-with-what-it-runs).
provisions.example:
The layout reads as follows:

```text
{Product}/
  Application/                            product layer folder: pipeline positions and pipeline stages, and nothing else
  Posts/                                  single aggregate whose name matches the module: use cases sit in the module UseCases folder
    Contracts/
      Identifiers/  IntegrationEvents/  Ports/
    Application/                          a port several Posts use cases name sits here
    UseCases/
      CreateDraft/
        Application/                      Command, Result, Handler, Validator, mapping
        WebApi/                           Endpoint, RequestModel, ResponseModel
      GetPost/
        Application/
        WebApi/
      ListPosts/
        Application/
          ListPostsQueryResultItem        a result part named after its result
        WebApi/
      ArchiveStalePost/
        Application/                      no WebApi folder: no endpoint reaches this use case
          ArchiveStalePostsJob            the job that runs this use case once per stale post
          ArchiveStalePostOnPostReportedHandler   a reaction that runs this use case
    Notifications/
      NewPost/
        NotifySubscribersOnPostPublishedHandler   a reaction that only sends the new-post notification
  Customers/                              two aggregates: use cases nest under each aggregate UseCases folder
    Contracts/
      Identifiers/  IntegrationEvents/  Ports/
    CustomerAccounts/
      Application/                        aggregate-owned behavior sits in the aggregate layer folder
      UseCases/
        RestrictAccount/
          Application/  WebApi/
    Consents/
      UseCases/
        GrantConsent/
          Application/  WebApi/
    UseCases/                             use cases no single aggregate owns
    ReadModels/
      OrderHistories/                     a read model of another module's published facts
```

Module, aggregate, and use case order, including the single-aggregate flat form, follow `litespec/backend/architecture#organize-code-by-module-aggregate-and-use-case`.

Only a use case gets a folder below its `UseCases/` folder, so every folder name there names one use case. A use case's own models stay in its folder under `litespec/backend/architecture#give-each-use-case-its-own-models`, and any other type sits in the node layer folder that owns it, chosen by `litespec/backend/architecture#place-a-type-at-the-lowest-folder-that-holds-its-consumers`. An event handler or job lives with what it runs, under `litespec/workspace/naming#place-each-trigger-with-what-it-runs`, with its mark under `litespec/backend/application#answer-each-reaction-in-one-marked-class`. A folder named for a fact, a service, a technical kind, or a caller breaks that reading; it is drift rather than a second convention.

provisions.heading: Validate Query Input
provisions.evidence: Does every query with paging, filters, or ranges declare a query validator? Look at each such query beside the pipeline validators.
provisions.statement: Each query carrying paging, filters, or ranges MUST declare a query validator run by the pipeline.
provisions.rationale: An unvalidated page size or range reaches the store unchecked, and each query handler clamps its own input or none does. A query validator runs in the same pipeline step as command validators, so reads and writes answer to the same input rule.
provisions.example: The list-expenses query validates its page size through its query validator.

provisions.heading: Write Only Aggregates the Record Names
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `write-undeclared` (level S) for a handler that takes a repository whose aggregate sits outside the aggregates its record names in `writes` and `reads`; one domain repository serves each named aggregate.
provisions.statement: A command handler MUST write only the aggregates its record's `writes` names, through one domain repository per aggregate.
provisions.rationale: A write outside `writes` is behavior the record hides, so the stack reader fails `write-undeclared` on it. Under `litespec/backend/application#keep-command-handlers-to-load-call-and-stage`, the handler normally takes one domain repository for the one aggregate it changes, and stages only that aggregate. A use case whose record declares `consistency: atomic` over several aggregates takes one repository per named aggregate and stages each one. A query handler likewise projects only over the aggregates its record's `reads` names, through the read session.
provisions.example: The `approve-expense` handler takes the expense repository and no other. Staging a second aggregate fails the check unless the record declares `consistency: atomic` over both.

provisions.heading: Compose Each Process Explicitly
provisions.evidence: Is any host composing its process without calling the Infrastructure entry point, or building a second provider mid-registration? Look at each host entry point.
provisions.statement: A host MUST register its own transport services and call the Infrastructure entry point without building a second provider.
provisions.rationale: Each host registers its own services and calls the shared Infrastructure entry point, so the full composition of a process is visible in one place. A second provider built mid-registration resolves a different object graph than the host runs. WebApi and Worker are the only composition roots. Domain contains no registration code, and Application exposes contracts without resolving services.

provisions.heading: Create a Worker Project When Background Work Needs Its Own Process
provisions.evidence: Is any background work that needs independent scaling, deployment, or isolation running outside a Worker project? Look at the execution-host decision beside the solution project list.
provisions.statement: An application MUST create a Worker project when background work needs independent scaling, independent deployment, or isolation from request-path resource limits.
provisions.rationale: A shared process couples scaling, deployment, and resource limits. A restart to deploy an endpoint change interrupts a dispatch loop, and request load and dispatch load compete for one thread pool, where neither scales alone. When background work needs independent scaling, deployment, or isolation, it gets its own process. A product with one deployable unit and modest background load accepts that coupling deliberately, which is why the choice is declared rather than assumed.
provisions.example: An application whose outbox dispatches a few messages each minute can run it in WebApi. An application that dispatches continuously, or whose dispatch needs to survive an endpoint deployment, creates the Worker project.

provisions.heading: Give Each Use Case Its Own Models
provisions.evidence: `dotnet build` reports `LS2019` for a use case folder naming a type in another use case folder, and `litespec model check` reports `code-placement-drift` for a message, result or transport-model file outside a use-case folder.
provisions.statement: A message, result, result part, transport model or mapping MUST belong to exactly one use case and sit in its folder, so two use cases that need the same shape each declare their own.
provisions.rationale: A shared shape couples two slices that change for different reasons: one use case adds a field, and the other starts returning it. Counting consumers for shapes moved messages and results out of their use cases into aggregate and module folders as soon as a second caller named them, until those folders held more models than behavior. A copy costs a few lines that never drift into a wrong answer, because a shape decides nothing. A rule is different: two copies of a rule disagree, so a rule keeps one home in Domain under `litespec/backend/architecture#repeat-coordination-never-a-rule`. Settled by [decision/0063-place-each-trigger-with-what-it-runs](decision/0063-place-each-trigger-with-what-it-runs).
provisions.example: The submit-expense and approve-expense use cases each return the expense they acted on. Each declares its own result with the fields its caller needs, and neither result lives in `Expenses/Application/`.

provisions.heading: Keep Business Invariants in Domain
provisions.evidence: Is any state transition or invariant enforced outside its aggregate or value object, or repeated in a handler? Look at the handlers beside the aggregates they call.
provisions.artifact: aggregate, command-handler, job, query-handler, reaction, value-object
provisions.statement: An aggregate or value object MUST be the only place that enforces a state transition or invariant.
provisions.rationale: The aggregate or value object that owns data is the only code that sees every change to it. A rule duplicated in a handler drifts from the aggregate that owns it: one path allows what the other refuses.

provisions.heading: Keep Implementations Hidden and Closed
provisions.evidence: Is any handler, validator, definition, persistence implementation, or endpoint implementation visible outside its own layer, or inheritable? Look at the implementations in each layer.
provisions.artifact: command-handler, endpoint, query-handler, reaction, repository, validator
provisions.statement: An application MUST keep each handler, validator, definition, persistence implementation, and endpoint implementation inside its own layer and closed to extension.
provisions.rationale: Hidden implementations keep each layer's surface to the contracts other layers actually use. A public handler invites direct construction that bypasses the pipeline, and an inheritable one invites overrides that split behavior across subclasses. Messages, results, and ports stay public only when another layer uses them, and automatic discovery is not a reason to widen visibility.

provisions.heading: Keep Service Registration in Hosts
provisions.evidence: Is any service registered outside host entry points and host registration modules? Look at the registration calls in each layer.
provisions.statement: Keep service registration in host entry points and host registration modules.
provisions.rationale: Registration lives where the process is composed, so hosts and their registration modules hold every registration call. A registration call inside Domain or Application inverts the dependency direction, because those layers declare abstractions.
provisions.example:
Each outer layer keeps one registration entry point, so the call order stays visible.

```text
infrastructure: register providers and options
webapi: register transport, authentication, and documentation
```

The Infrastructure entry point receives the configuration and host environment values needed to bind and validate provider options. The WebApi entry point owns error details, authentication, authorization, endpoint discovery, and API documentation.

provisions.heading: Name the Host for Work That Outlives a Request
provisions.evidence: Does any durable dispatch, queue consumption, or scheduled work run without a Decision naming its execution host? Look for the decision record under `.litespec/intent/decisions/`.
provisions.statement: An application MUST declare the execution host that runs its durable dispatch, queue consumption, and scheduled work.
provisions.rationale: The declared host is either the WebApi process or a Worker project. A rule that only constrains a Worker, when one exists, leaves unsaid where the work runs without one, so a project can host background services inside WebApi while breaking no named rule and recording no decision. Naming the host makes the choice visible whichever way it goes. The declaration lives in a Decision record, following `litespec/core/model#record-each-technical-choice-as-a-decision`. Durable dispatch and queue consumption follow the outbox extension, and scheduled work follows the jobs extension. The host is a composition decision, not a code-placement decision. A job class lives with the use case it runs. The outbox dispatcher and the scheduler that drive reactions and jobs live in Worker when the project exists, otherwise in Infrastructure, and the host registers them.
provisions.example: A Decision naming WebApi as the execution host states that durable dispatch shares the request process, and what an unavailable process costs.

provisions.heading: Organize Code by Module, Aggregate and Use Case
provisions.evidence: Is any module, aggregate, use case, notification, external-system, or read-model folder naming no declared record, using a forbidden folder name, or carrying a technical-grouping name? Look at the folder paths in each module.
provisions.statement: Every module MUST organize its code as the module tree with one folder per declared aggregate, one `UseCases/` folder per aggregate and module, and one folder per declared use case inside its `UseCases/` folder holding its layer folders, using only the folder names its level allows.
provisions.rationale: One folder per declared aggregate and one folder per declared use case inside its `UseCases/` folder fix every type's address: a reader moves from a Domain aggregate to its handler, its repository, and its endpoint without a map. The closed folder names at each level keep that reading exact, because a folder outside the allowed set is refused and no second organization grows beside the tree. A module publishes what other modules may name in its `Contracts/` folder sorted by kind, the use cases no single aggregate owns sit in the module `UseCases/` folder, and each reaction and job sits in the folder of the use case it runs. A folder named for a fact would name the commands of other use cases and pull them out of their folders, and a fact's reactions span modules, so no fact folder ever showed them all. An aggregate stays flat only when its plural name equals the single module name. Settled by [decision/0063-place-each-trigger-with-what-it-runs](decision/0063-place-each-trigger-with-what-it-runs). A folder named for a technical grouping rather than a module defeats the rule: the next unrelated type fits it too. `Shared`, `Common`, `Util`, `Helpers`, `Core`, and `Misc` inside a layer are the names that do this.
provisions.example:
```text
# single-aggregate module whose aggregate name matches the module: the aggregate stays flat
Organizations/
  Contracts/
    Identifiers/  IntegrationEvents/  Ports/
  Domain/  Application/  Infrastructure/
  UseCases/
    CreateOrganization/
      Application/           Command, Result, Handler, Validator
      WebApi/                Endpoint, RequestModel, ResponseModel

# multi-aggregate module: module, then aggregate folder, then UseCases, then use case
Spending/
  Contracts/
    Identifiers/  IntegrationEvents/  Ports/
  Expenses/
    Domain/  Application/  Infrastructure/
    UseCases/
      SubmitExpense/
        Application/  WebApi/
      ErasePersonalData/
        Application/          the erase command, its handler, and the job that runs it
  Policies/
    Domain/  Application/  Infrastructure/
    UseCases/
      DefinePolicy/
        Application/  WebApi/

# module-level work beside the aggregates
Spending/
  UseCases/
    ReadExpenseDirectory/     a use case no single aggregate owns
  Notifications/
    ApprovalReminder/         the reaction that only sends the approval reminder
```

The placement check asserts these folder names directly, because a rule that only a reviewer checks stops holding at the first missed file.

```text
fail when a type path contains Shared, Common, Util, Helpers, Core, or Misc
```

provisions.heading: Own Each Layer's Contract Types
provisions.evidence: Is any inner layer's type reused as an outward contract, or any other module's port answer returned as-is, outside shared-kernel values and aggregate typed identifiers? Look at the results and transport models in each layer's folders.
provisions.statement: A layer MUST define its own outward contracts rather than reuse an inner layer's type or another module's contract type, except for shared-kernel values and aggregate typed identifiers.
provisions.rationale: When each layer defines its own outward contracts, a change to an inner shape stops at the boundary instead of rippling through every outer layer. Shared-kernel values cross because the kernel is shared by definition, and aggregate typed identifiers cross because messages need to name their targets. The module boundary works the same way: a use case maps another module's port answer at its edge and returns it in no result or transport model of its own, so the owner can change its answer without changing the reader's contract.

provisions.heading: Place a Type at the Lowest Folder That Holds Its Consumers
provisions.evidence: Is any type sitting above the lowest folder holding every consumer that names it? Look at each type beside its consumers, watching for Shared, Common, Util, Helpers, Core, or Misc folders.
provisions.statement: A type that is not a use case's own model MUST live at the lowest folder containing every consumer that names it.
provisions.rationale: Counting consumers gives each type exactly one folder, so placement needs no judgment call. The lowest folder is the use case folder when one use case names the type, the aggregate layer folder when several use cases of one aggregate name it, the module layer folder when several aggregates of one module name it, and the product layer folder when several modules name it with no module between them. A type another module names is published by its owning module in `Contracts/`; across modules a type is never shared. A use case file's layer comes from its role suffix, and a type only Infrastructure names is an Infrastructure type. Two kinds of type travel with something else rather than by their own consumer count. A type that exists only to shape one contract's input or output stays with that contract, and a closed enumerated set stays whole. A use case's own models are never counted: a message, result, result part, transport model, or mapping belongs to one use case under `litespec/backend/architecture#give-each-use-case-its-own-models`, so the count places behavior such as ports, rule calculations, and adapters. The product layer folders hold what remains after the count rather than a destination anyone chooses. A folder named for the absence of a reason (`Shared`, `Common`, `Util`, `Helpers`, `Core`, `Misc`) refuses nothing: it accumulates until a tenth of the layer sits outside the module tree, unreviewed, and named for no aggregate. Domain's shared kernel is the one product `Domain/` folder a solution keeps. Its membership is closed by `litespec/backend/architecture#own-each-layers-contract-types` rather than open to whatever needs a home. A service that coordinates several aggregates lives in the module that owns the aggregates it reads and writes, not with whichever module calls it first.

provisions.heading: Point Dependencies Inward
provisions.evidence: Is any outer layer named from an inner one? Look at the reference graph in the code.
provisions.statement: A reference MUST point inward, so Domain references no outer layer and WebApi composes the process.
provisions.rationale: Inner code names no outer code, so business rules compile and test without adapters or hosting. An outward reference drags technical concerns into Domain or coordination into Infrastructure. Application coordinates Domain, Infrastructure implements the boundaries both declare, and the reference matrix in [Dependencies](../workspace/dependencies.md) applies exactly.
provisions.example:
Every reference points from an outer layer to an inner one: Application names Domain, Infrastructure names both, and Domain names neither.

![The four layers and their references: WebApi references Application and WebApi, and from Domain only typed identifiers and shared-kernel values; Infrastructure references Domain, Application, and Infrastructure; Application references Domain and Application; Domain references only Domain.](../assets/diagrams/backend-dependencies.svg)

provisions.heading: Read Another Module Only Through Its Contracts
provisions.evidence: Does any cross-module read load another module's aggregate or repository, or call a general reader instead of a read model, a decision port, or a screen joining owner queries? Look at the cross-module reads beside the `Contracts/Ports/` folders.
provisions.statement: A module needing another module's data MUST read it through its own read model built from the owner's integration events, through a decision port in the owner's `Contracts/Ports/` folder, or, on a screen, through the owner's own query.
provisions.rationale: A module that loaded another module's aggregate or repository would couple its reads to the owner's consistency boundary and storage. A general reader in the owner's `Contracts/` is the same coupling one step removed: it grows a method per caller, and no record says which fields cross. The three allowed paths each name what crosses. A read model names each field it copies from a published event, under `litespec/backend/application#read-another-modules-state-through-a-read-model`. A decision port answers one current-value question, under `litespec/backend/application#ask-another-module-one-question-through-a-decision-port`. A screen joins each owner's query, under `litespec/frontend/data#compose-a-screen-from-each-owners-query`.
provisions.example: In the Claimwick product, the reporting module reads reimbursed expenses through its own `read-model/reporting.reimbursed-expense`, filled from the spending module's expense-reimbursed integration event. It loads no spending aggregate, no spending repository, and no spending reader.

provisions.heading: Repeat Coordination, Never a Rule
provisions.evidence: Is any shared Application type only coordinating, or any use-case step repeating a decision made elsewhere? Look at the shared Application types beside the use cases that call them.
provisions.statement: A step two use cases share MUST live once in Domain, or behind the owning module's port, when it decides something, while each use case holds its own copy of a step that only coordinates.
provisions.rationale: A step that decides, such as whether an expense needs a receipt, is a rule: two copies drift until one path allows what the other refuses, so the rule lives once on its aggregate, in a domain service marked with its `rule/`, or in the owning module behind its port. A step that only coordinates, such as mapping a request or loading two records in order, decides nothing, and a shared coordinator couples the use cases that call it. Once each follow-on act runs from a reaction, most shared coordinators disappear: the act raises its fact, and the other use case answers it.
provisions.example: The receipt threshold check lives once on the expense aggregate, while submit-expense and attach-receipt each map their own request.

provisions.heading: Restrict Commands to Their Own Module Aggregates
provisions.evidence: Is any command writing an aggregate outside its own module, or sending another module's command, instead of raising a fact that module's reaction answers? Look at each command handler beside its module.
provisions.statement: A command MUST change only the aggregates of its own module, so an act on another module's aggregate runs as that module's use case, triggered by an integration event its reaction answers.
provisions.rationale: Each module guards its own consistency boundaries, so a command from another module that wrote its aggregates would bypass the owning module's rules. An act on another module's aggregate is that module's use case instead: the caller raises its own fact, the owning module's reaction answers the published integration event, and the owning module enforces its own invariants. A module publishes no command, so no caller can send one across the boundary.
provisions.example: In the Claimwick product, a command that needs a policy change raises its own fact, and the policy module's reaction to the published integration event runs the policy use case. The command writes no policy aggregate and sends no policy command.

provisions.heading: Separate Command and Query Behavior
provisions.evidence: Is any command changing outside one aggregate or skipping the domain repository, or any query loading an aggregate or writing? Look at the command and query handlers in Application.
provisions.statement: A command MUST mutate one aggregate through its domain repository while a query projects read results without loading an aggregate or writing.
provisions.rationale: Reads that load aggregates pay for invariant enforcement no read needs, and writes that read from projections enforce rules against stale shapes. Commands change one aggregate through its domain repository, following `litespec/backend/application#keep-command-handlers-to-load-call-and-stage`, with a use case declaring `consistency: atomic` over several aggregates as the declared exception. Queries project read results without loading an aggregate and write nothing, following `litespec/backend/application#keep-query-handlers-free-of-writes`. An enabled persistence extension may replace the read boundary for named aggregate paths, but a command still enforces no invariant from a read projection.

provisions.heading: Subscribe Across Modules Only to Integration Events
provisions.evidence: Is any reaction triggered by another module's domain event instead of its published integration event? Look at each reaction trigger beside the integration events.
provisions.statement: A reaction to another module's fact MUST subscribe only to the published integration event.
provisions.rationale: A domain event stays inside the module that raised it, while the published integration event carries the fact outside. A reaction that subscribed to another module's domain event would couple to the owner's internals and break when they change. The integration event is the stable cross-module fact, so cross-module reactions answer it.
provisions.example: In the Claimwick product, a reaction in the reporting module answers the published expense reimbursed integration event, not the spending domain event behind it.

provisions.heading: Test Structural Boundaries
provisions.evidence: Does any structural boundary lack both an analyzer or `model check` finding and an architecture test, or does any architecture test repeat a boundary a check covers? Look at the architecture tests beside the analyzer and `model check` runs.
provisions.statement: A structural boundary that no LiteSpec analyzer or `model check` finding covers MUST have an architecture test.
provisions.rationale: Layer references, package boundaries, visibility, module folders, and aggregate inheritance are invisible at runtime: the application runs the same with or without them. Without mechanical proof on every run, each one erodes unnoticed. The analyzers and `model check` already prove the boundaries a stack page names as checked, and the rows in the table below: a check over method bodies, for one, reports an outer-layer call inside a method, which a test over compiled signatures misses. An architecture test that repeats a covered boundary holds a second copy of a rule the build or the check already enforces, and the copy drifts while the analyzer or the check keeps reporting the breach. Architecture tests hold the rest: a boundary the checks cover only in part, and a structural decision the project itself made that no LiteSpec tool names. | Structural boundary | Covered by | |:---|:---| | A folder sits outside the closed set its level allows, or a module folder names no declared module | `folder-invalid` and `module-undeclared` from `litespec model check` | | A marked code element, test, or folder sits outside the folder its record names, or a folder names no declared record | `mark-folder-drift` and `code-placement-drift` from `litespec model check` | | A folder or type carries a technical grouping name such as `Shared`, `Common`, or `Helpers` outside the declared shared kernel | `name-reason-missing` from `litespec model check` |
provisions.example: In the Claimwick product, no architecture test repeats the checks that report an outer-layer type in Domain, an enum in Domain, a command handler that holds a write session, or a handler that authorizes itself, because the stack's checks report each one. The architecture suite keeps a test that no module reaches another module outside its `dependsOn`, with a type in the other module's `Contracts/` folder staying allowed.

provisions.heading: Align ID Representations at Every Boundary
provisions.evidence: Is any identifier unreadable as the same value across Domain, persistence, transport, or generated clients? Look at one identifier in each boundary form.
provisions.statement: Represent an identifier the same way in Domain, persistence, transport, and generated clients.
provisions.rationale: One identifier takes a different form at each boundary, and each form is correct in its own place. Alignment means every form still reads as the same value, so a reader tracing one identifier follows it across boundaries without translation.
provisions.example: Domain and Application hold the typed identifier; the [HTTP API](api.md) states the route, query, JSON, and contract forms, and [Persistence](persistence.md) states the stored form. Alignment means a reader recognizes one identifier in every form.

provisions.heading: Change Each Aggregate Through Its Marked Act
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `use-case-act-missing` (level S) for a command handler changing an entity aggregate that calls no root method marked with its use case. The check runs in the CLI only, with no analyzer rule: the handler and the root method sit in different projects, and one compilation sees one project.
provisions.statement: A command handler changing an entity aggregate MUST change it by calling a root method marked with the handler's use case.
provisions.rationale: The use case names an act, and the aggregate performs it. The mark on the root method says which act the method is. A handler that changes its aggregate only through methods marked for other use cases performs an act its record never named, and a reader has no way to tell from the use case which method to open. The use-case verb, the method name, and the raised event's tense agree under `litespec/backend/domain#raise-the-past-tense-of-a-methods-own-verb`. This provision states the marked form of `litespec/backend/application#keep-command-handlers-to-load-call-and-stage`. A command that changes only stores, or that only runs other commands and lists nothing in `writes`, performs no act on a root, so it needs no marked call.
provisions.example: The handler for `use-case/spending.reimburse-expense` calls `Reimburse` on the expense root, and `Reimburse` carries the mark `use-case/spending.reimburse-expense`.

provisions.heading: Compare Collection Values by Their Content
provisions.evidence: Is any collection value compared by reference instead of content, or missing a matching hash for its declared ordering rule? Look at each collection value beside the module terms.
provisions.statement: A value object containing a collection MUST implement content equality and a matching hash for its declared ordering rule.
provisions.rationale: Default structural equality compares collection references rather than contents, so two value objects holding equal lists compare as different. Content equality with a matching hash compares what the value means. Creation copies incoming mutable collections, and members return read-only views, so later changes by the caller leave the value unchanged. The module terms state whether order is part of the value.
provisions.example: A post-tags value holding an ordered list compares element by element with a matching hash. Where order is not part of the value, creation normalizes to the documented comparison order before storing values.

provisions.heading: Create Valid Aggregates Through Named Factories
provisions.evidence: Can any aggregate root be created through a constructor or a factory that is not named for its business action? Look at the creation paths of each root.
provisions.statement: An aggregate root MUST create instances only through a factory named for its business action.
provisions.rationale: A constructor carries no business name, so creation through constructors spreads creation rules across call sites. A factory named for its business action accepts typed identifiers, rejects empty identity and violated creation rules, selects the initial state, records the required events, and returns a complete aggregate. A root created with its children composes them inside the same factory call. The factory builds the children itself from typed values the caller supplies, because a caller holding an already built child could change it after the invariant was checked.
provisions.example: In the Claimwick product, `use-case/spending.submit-expense` creates its expense through a factory named for submitting. The factory takes the expense and employee identifiers, rejects an empty identity, selects the submitted state, and records the submitted event.

provisions.heading: Declare Cross-Record Keys on the Aggregate
provisions.evidence: Is any cross-record uniqueness rule missing its `UniquenessKeys` declaration, or enforced by other code in Domain? Look at each aggregate with such a rule.
provisions.statement: An aggregate needing a cross-record uniqueness key MUST expose its current keys through `UniquenessKeys`.
provisions.rationale: `UniquenessKeys` is the only uniqueness code in Domain. The aggregate declares its current keys through it, and persistence claims and releases them in the commit that changes the aggregate, following `litespec/backend/persistence#claim-a-cross-record-key-at-commit`. The aggregate computes keys from its own state and validates nothing about other records, because only the store sees every concurrent write and arbitrates the race.
provisions.example: In the library product, a book holding a list of copy barcodes returns each barcode from `UniquenessKeys`, so adding a copy claims the new barcode at commit. In the Claimwick product, a payout carrying a reference that is unique across payouts and adjustments returns that reference, so a duplicate reference fails the commit on either record.

provisions.heading: Document Every Public Domain Contract
provisions.evidence: Is any public Domain type or member missing documentation of its business constraint, result, or refusal, or documented with a restated name? Look at the documentation on each public member.
provisions.statement: Every public Domain type and member MUST carry documentation stating the business constraint, result, or refusal it represents.
provisions.rationale: A reader meeting a public Domain member needs the business rule behind it, not just its signature. Documentation states the business constraint, result, or refusal the member represents. A mutation method names its source states, resulting state, protected invariant, and recorded event. A summary that restates the member name adds nothing.

provisions.heading: Express Transitions Through Business Methods
provisions.evidence: Does any public mutation skip its state check or invariant, or any lifecycle move skip replacement or its transition event? Look at the public mutation methods of each aggregate.
provisions.statement: A public aggregate mutation method MUST check current state and protect its invariants, replacing state and recording its transition event when it moves the lifecycle.
provisions.rationale: A business-named method lets the handler call the publish behavior without testing the state first: the method checks the current state and protects its invariants, then replaces state and records the transition event when it moves the lifecycle. A generic `Set`, `Update`, `Process`, or `Handle` name hides which business action ran. A mutation that changes no lifecycle state, such as `ChangeTitle` on a draft, checks state and assigns without recording a transition. Checks run before replacement, and replacement runs before recording: a method that replaces state before checking an invariant leaves a rejected aggregate holding the new state.
provisions.example:
In the Claimwick product, `use-case/spending.reimburse-expense` ends with `result/reimburse-expense.reimbursed` when the expense is approved, and with `result/reimburse-expense.not-approved` when it is not. The handler calls one business method, and the method checks the state, replaces it, and records `domain-event/expense.reimbursed`.

An unapproved expense keeps its state, and the refusal carries the stable code `spending.not-approved`.

provisions.heading: Give Each Use Case Its Own Act
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `mark-count-invalid` (level S) for a root method carrying more than one use-case mark, and `mark-unknown` (level S) for a mark on a method that changes no state.
provisions.statement: Each aggregate root method that changes state MUST perform the act of exactly one use case.
provisions.rationale: Each use case is its own path, with its own caller, setup, refusals, events, and scenarios. A method two use cases share couples them: a change made for one silently changes the other, and neither scenario set describes the method. One method per act keeps each path readable on its own; logic the acts share moves into a private method of the root that each act calls. A method that only reads or computes performs no act and carries no mark.
provisions.example: In the Claimwick product, a manager approving an expense and a delegate approving it for an absent manager both record an approval. The expense root offers `Approve` marked `use-case/spending.approve-expense` and `ApproveOnBehalf` marked `use-case/spending.approve-expense-on-behalf`: each raises its own event, and both call a private `RecordApproval`.

provisions.heading: Identify Each Aggregate with a Typed Version 7 Identifier
provisions.evidence: Does any aggregate identity escape the dedicated version 7 type, or does any conversion, alias, or creation path bypass its validation? Look at each identity type and its creation paths.
provisions.statement: An aggregate identity MUST be a dedicated type wrapping one version 7 UUID, with no conversion, alias, or creation path that bypasses its validation.
provisions.rationale: A bare identifier type lets one aggregate's identifier pass where another's is expected: an expense id lands in a parameter typed for an employee id, and the compiler stays silent. A dedicated identity type wrapping one version 7 UUID makes that a compile error. With no conversion, alias, or creation path around its validation, there is no quiet route back to a bare value. The type rejects the empty value, and each factory also rejects its default. New values arrive from the caller: a factory takes its identifier as an argument, and a method that needs several identifiers takes a generator. Domain reads no clock and calls no static source of time or randomness, so every Domain call stays a pure function of its inputs. Version 7 values come from the caller-supplied generator, so Domain observes no business time and decides nothing about clocks. Persistence rejects a duplicate key and the write fails, which follows the same path as any other write conflict, with the violation mapped to the use case conflict refusal under `litespec/backend/persistence#map-a-constraint-violation-to-its-refusal`.
provisions.example: A post identifier wraps one version 7 UUID, rejects the empty value, and parses from text through a named method.

provisions.heading: Keep Binary Floating Point Out of Exact Quantities
provisions.evidence: Is any monetary amount, rate applied to one, or exactly-compared quantity held in a binary floating-point type? Look at the field, parameter, and return types in Domain.
provisions.statement: A Domain value MUST NOT use binary floating point for a monetary amount, a rate applied to one, or a quantity compared for exact equality.
provisions.rationale: Binary floating point represents most decimal fractions only approximately, so two amounts a person reads as equal compare as different, and totals drift by fractions of a cent. Exact decimal types keep equality and arithmetic exact.
provisions.example: A tax rate multiplied into a `Money` amount uses an exact decimal type. A measured latency in a diagnostic log is not a Domain quantity and sits outside this rule.

provisions.heading: Keep Child Entities Inside the Aggregate Boundary
provisions.evidence: Does any child entity expose mutable state outside its root, including through a writable collection? Look at the child entities beside their root, including their collections.
provisions.statement: A child entity MUST expose no mutable state outside its aggregate root, surfacing its collection as a read-only collection.
provisions.rationale: A child that exposed mutable state would let outside code change aggregate data without passing the root's checks. The root creates, finds, and changes children through business methods, and collections surface as read-only collections. A child entity and the values only it holds sit in the part folder its data group names, under `litespec/backend/domain#organize-a-module-by-aggregate-and-concept`. A child with lifecycle states uses the same state types and no enumeration.

provisions.heading: Keep Domain Independent of Outer Layers
provisions.evidence: Does any Domain type reference code outside the language standard library and project-owned Domain types? Look at the references in the Domain code.
provisions.statement: The Domain code MUST reference only the language standard library and project-owned Domain types.
provisions.rationale: Domain that references only the language standard library and its own types compiles and tests with no infrastructure at all. Each banned reference would drag one outer concern into the business model: persistence metadata couples a rule to a store format, and dispatch plumbing couples it to delivery. Infrastructure registers a persisted discriminator instead, so Domain carries no serialization metadata.

provisions.heading: Limit Each Repository to One Aggregate
provisions.evidence: Is any domain repository serving more than one aggregate, exposing non-Domain types, or offering a composable query, session, or generic CRUD surface? Look at each repository interface.
provisions.statement: A domain repository MUST serve exactly one aggregate root, exposing only aggregate and Domain types, with no composable query, session, or generic CRUD surface.
provisions.rationale: One domain repository per aggregate keeps the write side shaped by the aggregates it loads. A required load looks the aggregate up by identity and reports a missing aggregate through the missing-resource refusal, so a handler repeats no absence check. An optional lookup stays reserved for cases where absence is normal. A composable query, session, or generic CRUD surface would expose store mechanics to every handler. This boundary is the write side only: a query uses a read model owned by Application and shaped by Infrastructure, with no Domain contract on that path. A repository that gained a projection method would put query shapes in Domain, which is the coupling this layer exists to prevent. A flow that finds a record or creates it is two use cases that the boundary owning the flow chooses between, following `litespec/backend/application#implement-one-outcome-path-per-command`.
provisions.example: A post repository loads a post by identity, reports a missing post through the missing-resource refusal, and stages the loaded aggregate through a staging call. The Infrastructure implementation owns the refusal, the command pipeline owns the commit, and the staging call stages the aggregate through the selected provider.

provisions.heading: Model Every Aggregate Lifecycle with State Types
provisions.evidence: Is any lifecycle exposed outside one state property and one closed hierarchy of per-state types? Look at the lifecycle declarations in each aggregate.
provisions.statement: An aggregate MUST expose its lifecycle only through one state property backed by one closed hierarchy of per-state types.
provisions.rationale: Each lifecycle state can carry different facts: a published post carries its publication time, and a draft has none. An enumeration, a string discriminator, a boolean flag, a parallel nullable field, or a computed state carries no state-specific data. State types hold each state's data on the state itself, and aggregate methods own the transitions between them. A switch over the state types names each case in its own arm where the language requires a fallback, and a case with no arm reaches that fallback at run time.
provisions.example:
A post defines one abstract post state with draft and published cases, and the published case carries its publication time. An aggregate with one current state still defines the hierarchy, so the second state has a home.

In the Claimwick product, `aggregate/spending.expense` records the `Submitted`, `Approved`, `Refused`, and `Reimbursed` states with their transitions: Submit from `use-case/spending.submit-expense` creates Submitted, Approve from `use-case/spending.approve-expense` moves Submitted to Approved, Refuse from `use-case/spending.refuse-expense` moves Submitted to Refused, and Reimburse from `use-case/spending.reimburse-expense` moves Approved to Reimbursed. The approved case carries the approver and the decided time, and the reimbursed case carries the reimbursed time.

![Submit from submit-expense creates a Submitted expense, Approve from approve-expense moves it to Approved carrying the approver and the decided time, Refuse from refuse-expense moves it to Refused carrying the reason, and Reimburse from reimburse-expense moves an Approved expense to Reimbursed carrying the reimbursed time.](../assets/diagrams/backend-aggregate-lifecycle.svg)

provisions.heading: Model Every Closed Set as a Type Hierarchy
provisions.evidence: Is any closed set escaping one type hierarchy with named label lookups? Look at each closed set and its boundary lookups.
provisions.statement: Domain code MUST model a closed set as one type hierarchy whose cases the type system can enumerate.
provisions.rationale: A closed set with case data needs a type per case. An enumeration carries no case data, admits undefined values, and forces parallel nullable fields the moment one case gains data. A closed hierarchy gives each case a named type that a switch can name in its own arm, and a case with no arm reaches the switch fallback at run time. A label arriving from outside converts to its case through a named lookup rather than through a string conversion, and an unrecognized label fails validation rather than landing on a default case.
provisions.example:
A refund outcome defines pending, succeeded, failed, and reversed cases, and each case carries its own data.

This provision owns the Domain form. Application mirrors the set in its result under `litespec/backend/application#mirror-a-domain-closed-set-in-the-result`, the wire mirrors it as a transport model of the same shape under `litespec/backend/api#mirror-each-closed-set-on-the-wire`, and storage mirrors it as a stable string discriminator under `litespec/backend/persistence#keep-serialization-behavior-out-of-domain`. Label-only sets cross the boundary as plain enumerations under `litespec/backend/api#publish-label-only-sets-as-string-enums`. A transport label converts to its type case before it reaches a Domain method.

provisions.heading: Model Money with Exact Decimal Values
provisions.evidence: Is any monetary amount held outside the shared `Money` value, missing its currency, or serialized in another shape? Look at each monetary amount in Domain.
provisions.statement: A monetary amount MUST use an exact decimal type inside one shared `Money` value object carrying an ISO 4217 currency code and serializing as `{ "amount": "12.50", "currency": "EUR" }`.
provisions.rationale: Money needs exact arithmetic and an explicit currency on every value, and one shared `Money` object gives both. The owning module record defines supported currencies, scale, rounding, sign rules, and cross-currency arithmetic, and Infrastructure maps that precision explicitly. A use case fixed to one currency accepts an amount alone and states that currency in its record.
provisions.example:
```json
{ "amount": "12.50", "currency": "EUR" }
```

The amount serializes as a string, so no reader parses it as binary floating point.

provisions.heading: Name Domain Types from Their Aggregate Root
provisions.evidence: Is any Domain name breaking the cited workspace naming provisions, or any state case breaking the one kept form? Look at each Domain name.
provisions.statement: Derive each Domain type name from the aggregate root it belongs to, following the workspace naming provisions cited below.
provisions.rationale: Aggregate-prefixed names keep each type readable at its call site without its namespace. Aggregate-owned names follow `litespec/workspace/naming#anchor-aggregate-owned-types-on-the-aggregate-root`, architectural suffixes follow `litespec/workspace/naming#use-architectural-suffixes`, and refusal names follow `litespec/workspace/naming#name-exceptions-by-failed-rule`. A project names every state case in one form and keeps it.
provisions.example: A post title reads as `PostTitle` at its call site, and a published post state as `PostPublishedState`. The stack page states the declaration form each name takes.

provisions.heading: Organize a Module by Aggregate and Concept
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `code-placement-drift` (level S) for a domain event outside its aggregate's `Events` folder.
provisions.statement: Give each aggregate a `Domain/` folder named with its plural root name, holding its own states, events, refusals, concepts, and one folder per part its record declares.
provisions.rationale: Each aggregate `Domain/` folder holds everything one aggregate owns: its states, events, refusals, and concepts. A reader finds the full aggregate in one place instead of hunting shared folders. A single aggregate stays flat only when its plural root name equals the module name; separate aggregates keep separate lifecycle, event, and refusal folders. A part is a data group the aggregate record declares with dotted field names, such as `parcel.*`. The part's child entity and the values only that child holds sit in a folder named for the part, such as `Parcels/`, while the part's events and refusals stay in the aggregate's `Events/` and `Refusals/` folders. A type that belongs to no part stays at the root.
provisions.example:
