Each aggregate's domain repository stays with the aggregate it loads. The module, aggregate, and use case order follows `litespec/backend/architecture#organize-code-by-module-aggregate-and-use-case`. Each stack page states the file names and extensions that carry this layout.

provisions.heading: Pass Nondeterministic Values into Domain
provisions.evidence: Is any clock read, random source, or new identifier reached from inside Domain instead of passed in as an argument? Look at the calls Domain code makes.
provisions.statement: Domain behavior MUST receive time, randomness, and new identifiers as arguments rather than read them, and read no clock.
provisions.rationale: Domain behavior that reads a clock or generates identifiers returns different results for the same call, which makes tests nondeterministic: the same test passes and fails with no code change. Receiving time, randomness, and new identifiers as arguments keeps every Domain call a pure function of its inputs: a test supplies explicit values and stays deterministic. Application obtains each value through an owned port and passes it in. A method that needs more than one value receives a clock or a generator through its arguments, and version 7 identifiers come from the caller-supplied generator.

provisions.heading: Place Every Part Type in Its Aggregate's Folder
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `part-parent-missing` (level S) for an unmarked Domain type whose folder holds no aggregate root and is not the product `Domain/` folder, and the model output lists each part under its aggregate.
provisions.statement: A Domain part type, meaning an identifier, a state type, a closed set, a child entity, a value object, or a repository interface, MUST sit in the `Domain/` folder of the aggregate it belongs to, or in the product `Domain/` folder, and a row or projection a port returns is no part.
provisions.rationale: A part serves no record of its own: it belongs to its aggregate, whose record already states the states, transitions, and data the part holds. A mark on each part would write that fact a second time, and the two copies would drift. The folder already says which aggregate a part belongs to, so the builder derives the link from it. A type in a folder that holds no aggregate root, and that is not the product `Domain/` folder, is the one place the derivation fails. A domain service that holds one rule calculation is not a part: it carries its `rule/` mark. A row or projection a read port returns is not a part either: it is the port's answer, shaped for a reader, and it sits with its port in Application.
provisions.example: In the Claimwick product, `ExpenseState` and `IExpenseRepository` sit beside the `Expense` root in `Spending/Expenses/Domain/` and carry no mark; the builder lists them as parts of `aggregate/spending.expense`. `Money` sits in the product `Domain/` folder and belongs to no aggregate.

provisions.heading: Raise Immutable Facts as Domain Events
provisions.evidence: Is any domain event mutable, named for the wrong aggregate or fact, or carrying more than business data? Look at each domain event.
provisions.statement: A domain event MUST be immutable and carry business data only.
provisions.rationale: A domain event records a completed fact for reactions to consume. The event carries business data only: typed identifiers and the values its reactions need, with no aggregate, session, service, mutable collection, or thrown error, because any of those would couple reactions to the raising aggregate. Envelope identity, such as message identity and causation identity, lives on the published integration event that carries the fact outside the process. That integration event names the domain event in `translates`. The event name states the aggregate and the completed fact, following `litespec/workspace/naming#anchor-aggregate-owned-types-on-the-aggregate-root` and `litespec/workspace/naming#use-architectural-suffixes`, so a reader knows which aggregate raised the fact without opening the file.

provisions.heading: Raise the Declared Events from the Marked Act
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `act-event-undeclared` (level S) for a marked method raising an event its use case does not list, and `act-event-unimplemented` (level S) for a listed event no marked method raises.
provisions.statement: The root methods marked with a use case MUST together raise exactly the events that use case lists in `raises`.
provisions.rationale: The use case record states the facts its act leaves behind, and reactions subscribe to those facts. A marked method that raises an event the record does not list starts a consequence nobody reviewed, and a listed event that no marked method raises is a promise the code does not keep. Each raised event carries every field its integration events publish, because each integration event is built from its domain event alone under `litespec/backend/application#emit-declared-integration-events-after-commit`.
provisions.example: `use-case/spending.submit-expense` lists `domain-event/expense.submitted` in `raises`, and the `Submit` method marked with it raises `ExpenseSubmittedEvent` and nothing else.

provisions.heading: Raise the Past Tense of a Method's Own Verb
provisions.evidence: Does any state-changing aggregate method raise an event named for a different verb than its own? Look at the events each changed aggregate method raises.
provisions.statement: Each aggregate method that changes state MUST raise a domain event named for the past tense of its verb.
provisions.rationale: The command raises nothing; the aggregate root raises its domain event inside its own method. An event named for another verb tells the reader the act finished under a name the code never spoke, and reactions subscribe to a vocabulary the aggregate does not own. The event name takes the past tense of the act's verb, as `litespec/core/domain-model#name-every-event-in-the-past-tense` requires for every event. The name may place the past tense as a whole word followed by a complement that opens with a preposition or particle. A method that sets a state names that state in its event, and a method may raise further events for the consequences of its act, as long as one of its events names the act itself.
provisions.example: In the Claimwick product, `Approve` on an expense raises `domain-event/expense.approved` and passes. `Approve` raising `domain-event/expense.signed-off` fails review, because that name belongs to another act.

provisions.heading: Reference Other Aggregates by ID
provisions.evidence: Does any aggregate field hold another aggregate as an object reference instead of a typed identifier? Look at the fields of each aggregate.
provisions.statement: An aggregate MUST store another aggregate's typed identifier rather than an object reference.
provisions.rationale: An object reference between aggregates loads one aggregate's data through another, which couples their consistency boundaries and their storage. A typed identifier keeps each aggregate loadable on its own, and Application loads each side through its own domain repository when a command coordinates several aggregates, with `consistency: atomic` citing the rule in `boundBy`.

provisions.heading: Reject Business Violations with Dedicated Refusals
provisions.evidence: Is any rejected business rule ending outside a dedicated refusal with its stable code, or carrying transport status? Look at each rejection beside its refusal.
provisions.statement: A rejected business rule MUST end its use case in a dedicated refusal carrying its stable code.
provisions.rationale: One refusal per rejected rule lets each boundary map outcomes without parsing messages: the refusal names the failed rule, and the stable code travels to the caller. The name leads with the aggregate root. Domain raises no standard library, validation, transport, or provider failure for a business rejection, and carries no transport status: the host maps refusals to transport errors through the mapping the API page documents under `litespec/backend/api#defer-error-mapping-to-the-global-handler`. Refusal names follow `litespec/workspace/naming#name-exceptions-by-failed-rule`; this provision owns the one-refusal-per-rule shape and the code each refusal carries.
provisions.example:
A refund allocation rule ends its use case in its own refusal, rather than sharing one refusal with a code passed at the call site.

Two rules that share a caller-visible refusal code because a boundary maps them to one response still get two refusals. The shared code lives in the two refusals, not in a value passed by the aggregate. One refusal serves more than one input only when one rule fails from more than one input and the differing values travel as creation parameters.

Application validators handle malformed caller input through validity findings. Aggregate and value-object refusals stay the last defense when direct Domain use violates a rule. Command handlers do not catch expected Domain refusals.

provisions.heading: Reuse the Shared Domain Contracts Across Modules
provisions.evidence: Is the root, event, identity, or refusal contract declared more than once across modules? Look at those contracts in each module.
provisions.statement: Declare the shared Domain contracts once in the product `Domain/` folder and reuse them across every module.
provisions.rationale: One declaration keeps the root, event, identity, and refusal mechanics identical in every module. A second declaration drifts from the first with the next fix.
provisions.example:
The shared contracts are the aggregate root, the domain event, the typed identity, and the refusal.

Event clearing is delivery mechanics, not a business mutation. Infrastructure calls it only after delivery accepts the pending events.

provisions.heading: Take Identity and Events from the Shared Root Contract
provisions.evidence: Does any aggregate root take identity or event mechanics from outside the project-owned root contract? Look at each aggregate root declaration.
provisions.statement: An aggregate root MUST take its identity and event mechanics from the project-owned root contract.
provisions.rationale: One shared root contract gives every aggregate the same identity and event mechanics, so Infrastructure collects pending events from any aggregate the same way. The contract stays small on purpose: it owns typed identity, pending events, recording, and clearing, plus the aggregate version as persistence metadata that Domain never reads or sets. A timestamp, audit, tenant, lifecycle, or other persistence behavior would couple every aggregate to a concern only some need.

provisions.heading: Treat Aggregates as Consistency Boundaries
provisions.evidence: Can any invariant be changed through a public mutation outside its aggregate root? Look at the public mutation entry points of each aggregate.
provisions.statement: An aggregate root MUST be the only public mutation entry point for every invariant its transaction protects.
provisions.rationale: If outside code could set properties or call child mutations directly, it would change data around the root's checks. With the root as the only public mutation entry point, every change passes the invariant its transaction protects. A command with `consistency: atomic` changes every aggregate its `writes` names in one transaction, citing the rule in `boundBy` when it changes more than one.

provisions.heading: Use Immutable Value Objects for Domain Concepts
provisions.evidence: Is any value object mutable, comparing by less than its complete value, or creatable without validation? Look at each value object and its creation paths.
provisions.statement: A value object MUST be immutable, compare by its complete value, and validate every value at creation.
provisions.rationale: Immutability with comparison by complete value lets two instances with the same data stand in for each other. The value exposes no mutation and no implicit conversion, because a primitive conversion hides validation and a value conversion erases the domain type. Reading uses the wrapped value or its text form, and creation through a named creation path keeps every value under the validation the type declares.
provisions.example: A post title accepts only non-blank text up to 200 characters: blank or longer input fails creation, and two titles with the same text compare as equal.

provisions.heading: Use One Ubiquitous Language
provisions.evidence: Does every Domain name match a term in the project glossary? Compare the Domain names with `glossary.yaml`.
provisions.statement: A Domain name MUST match a term in the project glossary.
provisions.rationale: When code and records use different names for one action, every reader translates between them. `SetStatus` in code hides which business action ran. With one shared name from the project glossary on both sides, the record and the code describe the same action in the same words.
provisions.example: The glossary names the business action `Publish`, so the root method is `Publish`, not `SetStatus`.

provisions.heading: Use Stateless Domain Services for Ownerless Rules
provisions.evidence: Is any domain service stateful, taking or returning non-Domain values, or calling persistence, messaging, logging, clock, authorization, or a provider? Look at each domain service and its calls.
provisions.statement: A domain service MUST be stateless, accept and return Domain values, and perform no persistence, messaging, logging, clock, authorization, or provider call.
provisions.rationale: Some calculations span concepts with no natural aggregate owner. Forcing one into an aggregate couples that aggregate to another's data. A stateless service holds the calculation instead, accepting and returning Domain values with no persistence, messaging, logging, clock, authorization, or provider call. Application loads the aggregates, calls the service, and passes its result into aggregate behavior. A domain service takes no port and holds no state, so its tests are Domain tests: they sit beside the aggregate tests in the unit tests mirroring the module tree, with no harness, no substitute, and no fixture.
provisions.example: An order-pricing service takes order lines and a currency and returns their total as `Money`, with no domain repository, clock, logger, or provider client. Application supplies the lines and passes the returned total into aggregate behavior.

provisions.heading: Compose the Host in Program.cs
provisions.evidence: Does `Program.cs` hold the recorded composition order with every step present? Look at `Program.cs`.
provisions.statement: `Program.cs` holds module registration, middleware order, endpoint discovery, health endpoints, OpenAPI, and host startup, ending with an empty partial `Program` class.
provisions.rationale: Middleware runs in registration order, so authentication registered after endpoints never runs. When one file shows the whole sequence, a reviewer sees the order at a glance; when registration scatters across files, a misplaced call hides. This file binds `litespec/backend/architecture#compose-each-process-explicitly` for WebApi.
provisions.example: The visible order is trusted forwarded headers, exception handling, transport security, authentication, authorization, endpoints, and then health. Forwarded headers appear only when the deployment boundary requires trusted proxies. OpenAPI and Scalar map only in Development.

provisions.heading: Declare Operation Metadata in the Contract
provisions.evidence: Does every operation declare a stable `operationId`, a summary, authorization, request, success, and Problem Details metadata, and typed results or `Produces` entries? Look at each operation.
provisions.statement: An operation MUST declare a stable `operationId`, a summary, its authorization, request, success, and Problem Details metadata, and typed results or `Produces` metadata.
provisions.rationale: Generated clients name their calls from `operationId`, so an unnamed or unstable operation breaks every client regeneration. Authorization and Problem Details metadata tell a client which policies apply and which failures to handle; without them the client guesses. Route-lambda comments never reach the contract, so the summary is declared explicitly. This provision binds `litespec/backend/api#declare-stable-operation-metadata-in-the-contract` for .NET.

provisions.heading: Derive HTTP Statuses from Refusal Codes
provisions.evidence: Does every refusal code map to its outcome-table status in the one `IExceptionHandler`? Look at the WebApi global handler.
provisions.statement: WebApi MUST map each refusal code to its HTTP status in one global handler.
provisions.rationale: The specification records each refusal with its stable `code` and no transport status, so the stack derives the status its transport needs. The outcome-to-status assignment lives in `litespec/backend/api#use-consistent-status-codes`; this provision binds it for .NET. The handler uses ASP.NET Core `AddProblemDetails` with one `IExceptionHandler`: - Validation failures answer 400. - Missing targets answer through the operation's 404 policy. - Forbidden failures answer 403 or the declared 404 disclosure policy. - Conflicts and state rejections answer 409. - Unexpected failures answer 500 with code `internal_error`. The derived `invalid-input` refusal answers 400 under the project's `refusals.invalidInput` code, and the derived `forbidden` refusal answers 403 or the declared 404 under the project's `refusals.forbidden` code. Known Domain exception types map individually, and a cancellation from a disconnected request is not reported as an application error.

provisions.heading: Exclude MVC Controllers from the Stack
provisions.evidence: `dotnet build` reports `LS2003` for a WebApi class deriving from `ControllerBase` or carrying `ApiController`.
provisions.statement: WebApi code MUST NOT route requests through MVC controllers or `ControllerBase`.
provisions.rationale: Controllers and endpoint classes route, filter, and map errors through different models. When both exist, a reviewer checks two mappings for every behavior, and error responses drift apart. One model means one place defines how requests reach handlers and how failures reach clients.

provisions.heading: Mark Polymorphic Transport Models with Discriminators
provisions.evidence: Does every data-bearing set map to an abstract base record with one sealed record per case and the discriminator the generic provision requires? Look at each data-bearing set.
provisions.statement: A data-bearing set MUST map to an abstract base record with one sealed record per case, carrying the discriminator that `litespec/backend/api#mark-polymorphic-models-with-discriminators` requires.
provisions.rationale: A concrete base record cannot mark the discriminator as required, so a client could send a payload that names no case. This provision binds `litespec/backend/api#mark-polymorphic-models-with-discriminators` for .NET and adds no discriminator rule of its own.
provisions.example:
- Declare an abstract base record carrying `JsonPolymorphic` and one `JsonDerivedType` per case, on the type itself rather than in host options.
- Name the discriminator through `TypeDiscriminatorPropertyName`, using a name such as `type` or `outcome`.
- Complete discriminator metadata that the generator omits with a document or schema transformer.

provisions.heading: Place Endpoints in Their Use Case Folders
provisions.evidence: Does every use case `WebApi/` folder hold the endpoint, request and response models, and mappings named for the use case? Look at each use case folder.
provisions.statement: Place each endpoint with its request and response models and mappings in the `WebApi/` folder of its use case inside the `UseCases/` folder of its module and aggregate.
provisions.rationale: The folder path matches the specification path, so a reader locates an operation from its use-case identifier without searching. Transport types take the names their boundary roles assign under `litespec/backend/api#name-transport-types-by-their-boundary-role`, and transport mapping lives in WebApi under `litespec/backend/application#keep-mappings-at-the-owning-boundary`. Response models carry the query's declared `include` groups. Each use case owns its transport models, so a shape two use cases need is declared in each under `litespec/backend/architecture#give-each-use-case-its-own-models`. Module nesting, including the single-aggregate flat form, follows `litespec/backend/architecture#organize-code-by-module-aggregate-and-use-case`.
provisions.example:
The endpoint layout is:

```text
{Product}.Modules/
  Posts/                            single aggregate whose name matches the module
    UseCases/
      CreateDraft/
        Application/                message, result, handler, validator
          CreateDraftCommand.cs
          CreateDraftCommandResult.cs
          CreateDraftCommandValidator.cs
          CreateDraftCommandHandler.cs
        WebApi/
          CreateDraftEndpoint.cs
          CreateDraftRequestModel.cs
          CreateDraftResponseModel.cs
          CreateDraftApiMappings.cs
      GetPost/
        Application/
          GetPostQuery.cs
          GetPostQueryResult.cs
          GetPostQueryValidator.cs
          GetPostQueryHandler.cs
        WebApi/
          GetPostEndpoint.cs
          GetPostResponseModel.cs
          GetPostApiMappings.cs
  Customers/                        two aggregates: use cases nest under each aggregate UseCases folder
    CustomerAccounts/
      UseCases/
        RestrictAccount/
          Application/
            RestrictAccountCommand.cs
            RestrictAccountCommandHandler.cs
          WebApi/
            RestrictAccountEndpoint.cs
            RestrictAccountRequestModel.cs
            RestrictAccountApiMappings.cs
    Consents/
      UseCases/
        GrantConsent/
          Application/
            GrantConsentCommand.cs
            GrantConsentCommandHandler.cs
          WebApi/
            GrantConsentEndpoint.cs
            GrantConsentRequestModel.cs
            GrantConsentApiMappings.cs
{Product}.WebApi/
  Errors/
    GlobalExceptionHandler.cs
    ProblemDetailsApiMappings.cs
  Security/
    CurrentActor.cs
  OpenApi/
  Program.cs
```

provisions.heading: Use One Endpoint per Operation
provisions.evidence: Does every mapped route run through one `IEndpoint` type that converts input, dispatches, and maps the result? Look at the endpoints in the use case folders.
provisions.statement: A WebApi endpoint MUST implement `IEndpoint`, map one route operation, convert input to an Application message, dispatch through its mediator, and map the result.
provisions.rationale: When one class owns one route, a reviewer finds the input mapping, the dispatch, and the result mapping for that route in one place. Without that rule, operations share classes or helpers, and a change to one route silently affects another, while a second routing pattern grows beside the first unnoticed. This provision binds `litespec/backend/api#map-one-operation-per-endpoint` for .NET.

provisions.heading: Bind Command Handlers to Load, Call, and Stage
provisions.evidence: `dotnet build` reports `LS2012` for a handler that throws a forbidden refusal or takes the authorization guard, `LS2013` for an audit call that reads the message, `LS2014` for a find followed by a create, `LS2015` for a store inside a loop, and `LS2021` for a handler holding a mediator.
provisions.statement: A command handler MUST load or create one aggregate through its repository, call one domain method on it, stage it, and return the result.
provisions.rationale: The handler body has three steps, the load or creation, the one domain call, and the stage. A required load uses the throwing `GetByIdAsync`, and an optional lookup uses the nullable `FindBy...Async`, under `litespec/backend/dotnet/domain#keep-repository-interfaces-in-domain`. The message carries the pipeline-stamped timestamp as `HandledAt` under `litespec/backend/application#read-time-from-the-scoped-clock` (see `litespec/backend/dotnet/application#bind-the-pipeline-to-the-pinned-litebus-apis`), so the handler stamps decisions without reading a clock. Validation, authorization, idempotency, audit, holds, and the commit are pipeline stages, not handler code. Messages, provider calls, and writes to other aggregates run in event handlers after the commit, under `litespec/backend/dotnet/application#dispatch-declared-effects-through-their-entry-points`. The handler takes no `ICommandMediator`, `IQueryMediator`, or `IEventMediator`. A use case whose record declares `consistency: atomic` over several aggregates is the one exception: the handler loads, calls, and stages each aggregate its `writes` names, one method each. This provision binds `litespec/backend/application#keep-command-handlers-to-load-call-and-stage` and `litespec/backend/application#load-a-required-record-or-refuse-it` for .NET, where `GetByIdAsync` and `FindBy...Async` are the forms.

provisions.heading: Bind the Pipeline to the Pinned LiteBus APIs
provisions.evidence: Does every pipeline position use its pinned LiteBus API? Check the command pipeline composition.
provisions.statement: An Application MUST compose its command pipeline through the LiteBus APIs this provision names for commit, authorization, audit, fault classification, delivery, event staging, and the timestamp.
provisions.rationale: One pinned binding per position keeps every project's pipeline identical. The commit runs through `commands.UseMartenUnitOfWork()`, which registers the LiteBus `IUnitOfWork` at `HandlerPriorities.UnitOfWork`, so the pipeline commits once under `litespec/backend/dotnet/persistence#commit-once-in-the-command-pipeline`. Authorization runs through a guard derived from `LiteBus.Messaging.Abstractions.DeclarationGuard<TMessage, TValue>`, reading the declaration from the message definition under `litespec/backend/application#enforce-target-authorization-in-the-pipeline`. Audit runs through `AuditDeclaration.Audited(...).WithTargetFrom<TCommand>(...).WithReasonFrom<TCommand>(...)` in an `IAuditDefinition<TCommand>`, declaring the target and reason beside the message under `litespec/backend/application#declare-the-audit-target-and-reason-beside-the-message`. Fault classification runs through `UseFaultRefusalClassifierInstance(new PostgreSqlConstraintRefusalClassifier(map))`, mapping each store fault to its refusal under `litespec/backend/persistence#map-a-constraint-violation-to-its-refusal`. Delivery runs through `outbox.EnablePerHandlerDelivery()`, reaching each handler separately under `litespec/ext/outbox#give-each-handler-its-own-delivery`. Event staging runs through `outbox.StageCollectedEvents()`, staging the facts `IDomainEventCollector` collected in the same commit as the aggregate change. The timestamp runs through `IExecutionContext.HandledAt`, stamping each message once for the handler to read as `HandledAt` under `litespec/backend/application#read-time-from-the-scoped-clock`.

provisions.heading: Dispatch Declared Effects Through Their Entry Points
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `effect-undeclared` for a dispatch no record declares, and `dotnet build` reports `LS2021` for a mediator held outside an endpoint, event handler or job and `LS2022` for an event published outside the shared kernel.
provisions.statement: An event handler or job MUST dispatch each declared `sends` effect through the messenger port, each declared `calls` effect through its external-system port, and its one declared `runs` effect through `ICommandMediator`, after the commit that stored the fact it answers, while the pipeline stages each raised domain event and each integration event translating it in the same commit.
provisions.rationale: A command handler changes its aggregate and returns; it dispatches nothing. The aggregate raises its facts, and the outbox stages them in the same commit through `outbox.StageCollectedEvents()` (see `litespec/backend/dotnet/application#bind-the-pipeline-to-the-pinned-litebus-apis`). The same commit stages each integration event whose record translates a raised domain event. The shared kernel collects it beside its domain event, built by the integration event's static `From` method from that domain event alone, so no module code publishes. After that commit, an event handler answers each fact through its entry point: the messenger port for `sends`, its external-system port for `calls`, and `ICommandMediator` for `runs`, sending one command in its own pipeline and commit. A scheduled or one-off job dispatches through the same entry points. Each handler gets its own delivery under `litespec/ext/outbox#give-each-handler-its-own-delivery`, so one failing handler retries alone. An undeclared dispatch fails `effect-undeclared`, whatever its entry point. This provision binds `litespec/backend/application#dispatch-only-declared-effect-edges` for .NET.

provisions.heading: Keep Query Handlers Free of Repositories and Writes
provisions.evidence: Does every query handler project through `IQuerySession`, with no repository and no stage, store, delete, or dispatch? Check each query handler; `dotnet build` reports LS2011 for a repository in a query handler and LS2012 for a forbidden refusal or the authorization guard.
provisions.statement: A query handler MUST take no repository and stage, store, delete, or dispatch nothing.
provisions.rationale: A read path acts on no invariant, so a repository in a query handler loads an aggregate the query has no write to justify. The handler projects through the read session under `litespec/backend/dotnet/persistence#query-through-iquerysession`. A read that writes makes retries and caching unsafe: repeating the query would repeat the write. An audited read is the pipeline's work, not the handler's. `dotnet build` reports a repository in a query handler as `LS2011`. This provision binds `litespec/backend/application#project-queries-directly` and `litespec/backend/application#keep-query-handlers-free-of-writes` for .NET.
provisions.example: The list-expenses query projects its rows through `IQuerySession`, taking no repository and staging nothing.

provisions.heading: Report Input Problems as Validity
provisions.evidence: Does every validator report through `Validity`, with member, code, and message on each finding and no HTTP status? Check each validator.
provisions.statement: A validator MUST report its findings as Validity, with each ValidationFailure carrying a member, a code, and a message, and no HTTP status.
provisions.rationale: Every validator for the message runs, and the pipeline merges the findings before it refuses the request, so the caller fixes the whole form at once. The member tells the caller which input failed, the stable code lets a client branch on the reason, and the message explains the problem in words safe to show. Validity values come from the pinned mediator's abstractions, named in `litespec/backend/dotnet/application#use-the-pinned-mediator-entry-points`, so every project reports the same shape. This provision binds `litespec/backend/application#report-input-problems-as-validity-findings` for .NET.

provisions.heading: Run Reactions in Dedicated Handlers
provisions.evidence: Does every reaction run in one handler class with its record's mark, sending at most one command from the folder of what it runs? Check each event handler beside its reaction record.
provisions.statement: A reaction MUST run in one class carrying one mark naming its reaction record.
provisions.rationale: One class per reaction answers the trigger the record names in `triggeredBy`, and dispatches only through its `effects` entries. The class carries the mark `reaction/<module>.<name>` in the declared style, so the stack reader links it without guessing. It lives in the `Application/` folder of the use case it runs, or in the module `Notifications/` or `ExternalSystems/` folder of what it only sends or calls, under `litespec/workspace/naming#place-each-trigger-with-what-it-runs`. It never writes an aggregate directly: a reaction that needs a write sends one command. It honors the record's `reads`, its idempotency, and its `onFailure`. This provision binds `litespec/backend/application#answer-each-reaction-in-one-marked-class` for .NET.

provisions.heading: Run Scheduled Jobs as Hosted Operations
provisions.evidence: Does every scheduled or one-off job run as one marked hosted operation honoring selection, batch size, lease, and cursor? Check each such job.
provisions.statement: A scheduled or one-off job MUST run as one hosted operation carrying one mark naming its job record.
provisions.rationale: The hosted operation lives in the `Application/` folder of the use case it runs, or in the module `Notifications/` or `ExternalSystems/` folder of what it only sends or calls, and registers on the declared execution host. It honors its record's selection, batch size, lease, and cursor, so a restart resumes where the last run stopped instead of reprocessing or skipping items. It sends its one command once per selected item, and records its evidence where the record states. This provision binds `litespec/backend/application#run-each-job-within-its-declared-selection` for .NET.

provisions.heading: Subscribe Each Reaction Handler to Its Declared Triggers
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `reaction-subscription-drift` (level S) for a marked handler subscribed to an event outside its reaction's `triggeredBy`, and `reaction-trigger-unhandled` (level S) for a declared trigger with no marked handler subscribed to it.
provisions.statement: The event handlers marked with a reaction MUST together subscribe to exactly the events the reaction names in `triggeredBy`.
provisions.rationale: The reaction record states the facts its handlers answer, and each handler subscribes by implementing its event-handler interface for one event type. A handler subscribed to an event the record does not name answers a fact nobody reviewed, while a named trigger with no subscribed handler is a promise the code does not keep. The check resolves each subscribed type through the event's own mark, so the mark on the event class is the link the reader follows. This provision binds `litespec/backend/application#answer-each-reaction-in-one-marked-class` for .NET, where the subscription is the event type of the handler's event-handler interface.
provisions.example: Claimwick's reaction `reaction/spending.send-approver-reminders-on-expense-submitted` names `domain-event/expense.submitted` in `triggeredBy`: `SendApproverRemindersOnExpenseSubmittedHandler` implements `IEventHandler<ExpenseSubmittedEvent>`, and `ExpenseSubmittedEvent` carries the mark `domain-event/expense.submitted`.

provisions.heading: Use the Pinned Mediator Entry Points
provisions.evidence: Does every dispatch site use `ICommandMediator.SendAsync` or `IQueryMediator.QueryAsync` from the pinned LiteBus version? Check each dispatch site.
provisions.statement: Dispatch a command through `ICommandMediator.SendAsync` and a query through `IQueryMediator.QueryAsync`, from the LiteBus version the manifest pins, only from an endpoint, an event handler, or a job.
provisions.rationale: With one pinned library, every dispatch site in every project reads the same way, and an agent finds all callers of a message with one search. A project that replaces the default still keeps commands and queries on separate entry points: that separation is required by `litespec/backend/application#dispatch-commands-and-queries-through-separate-entry-points`, and no replacement removes it.

provisions.heading: Use the Use Case Folder Layout
provisions.evidence: Does every use case folder hold its message, result, validator, and handler files in the right layer folders, with each event handler and job in the folder of what it runs? Check each use case folder.
provisions.statement: Place each use case in a folder named for it inside the `UseCases/` folder of its module and aggregate, with the files this provision names in its `Application/` and `WebApi/` folders.
provisions.rationale: The folder path matches the specification path, so a reader locates a use case from its use-case identifier without searching. Type names derive from the use-case identifier with the architectural suffix, so `use-case/spending.submit-expense` owns `SubmitExpenseCommand` under `litespec/workspace/naming#use-architectural-suffixes`. Only a use case gets a folder below its `UseCases/` folder: its own models stay in it under `litespec/backend/architecture#give-each-use-case-its-own-models`, any other type sits flat in the layer folder that owns it under `litespec/backend/architecture#place-a-type-at-the-lowest-folder-that-holds-its-consumers`, and the event handlers and job that run it sit in its `Application/` folder under `litespec/workspace/naming#place-each-trigger-with-what-it-runs`. Each result type carries one case per result, and each refusal carries the refusal `code` from its result record. A query result type carries one member per declared `include` group, and each result part is named after its result under `litespec/workspace/naming#name-result-parts-after-their-result`.
provisions.example:
The layout below shows a flat module, a two-aggregate module, and a reaction that only sends a notification:

```text
    Failures/

      UseCaseForbiddenException.cs
      UseCaseConflictException.cs
    Validation/
      ValidationErrors.cs
{Product}.Modules/
  Posts/                            single aggregate whose name matches the module: use cases sit in the module UseCases folder
    Application/
      IPostArchive.cs               a port several Posts use cases name
    UseCases/
      CreateDraft/
        Application/
          CreateDraftCommand.cs
          CreateDraftCommandResult.cs
          CreateDraftCommandValidator.cs
          CreateDraftCommandHandler.cs
        WebApi/
          CreateDraftEndpoint.cs
          CreateDraftRequestModel.cs
          CreateDraftResponseModel.cs
      GetPost/
        Application/
          GetPostQuery.cs
          GetPostQueryResult.cs
          GetPostQueryValidator.cs
          GetPostQueryHandler.cs
        WebApi/
          GetPostEndpoint.cs
      ListPosts/
        Application/
          ListPostsQuery.cs
          ListPostsQueryResult.cs
          ListPostsQueryResultItem.cs
          ListPostsQueryValidator.cs
          ListPostsQueryHandler.cs
        WebApi/
          ListPostsEndpoint.cs
      ArchivePost/
        Application/                no WebApi folder: only its reaction runs it
          ArchivePostCommand.cs

    Notifications/

        IPostPublicationNotifier.cs a port only this notification names
  Customers/                        two aggregates: use cases nest under each aggregate UseCases folder
```

Module and aggregate order, including the single-aggregate flat form, follow `litespec/backend/architecture#organize-code-by-module-aggregate-and-use-case`, and each use case file sits in the layer folder its role suffix names under `litespec/backend/dotnet/architecture#keep-closed-folder-sets-at-every-level`.

provisions.heading: Follow Declared Module Dependencies
provisions.evidence: Does every cross-module reference name a module its owner declares in `dependsOn`, with no dependency cycle? Check the cross-module references beside the module records.
provisions.statement: A module MUST reference only modules its record names in dependsOn.
provisions.rationale: The `dependsOn` list states which modules a module may know. An undeclared edge is a boundary the design never allowed. The rule covers code references and record links alike, and the graph stays acyclic.

provisions.heading: Follow Layer Direction in Every File
provisions.evidence: `dotnet build` reports `LS1001` for a Domain type naming an outer-layer type and `LS2018` for an Application or WebApi type naming a type outside its layer.
provisions.statement: A type MUST reference only the layers its own layer allows under the layer table of [Backend Architecture](../architecture.md#the-four-layers).
provisions.rationale: Layers are roles played by folders and use case files, whatever project holds them: a file takes its layer from its folder and, inside a use case folder, from its role suffix. Global usings import namespaces for every file, so the rule reads them too: they hide coupling from nothing. This provision binds `litespec/backend/architecture#point-dependencies-inward` for .NET.
provisions.example: Domain touches no Application, Infrastructure, or WebApi type, and none of the persistence, web, mediator, logging, and injection namespaces. Application touches no Infrastructure or WebApi type, and no ASP.NET Core type. WebApi touches no Domain type outside typed identifiers and shared-kernel values, and no repository.

provisions.heading: Keep Application Types in Their Layer Folders
provisions.evidence: Does every message, result, handler, validator, trigger, and port sit in its own use case `Application/` folder or its Contracts kind folder? Check the Application and Contracts folders beside the use case folders.
provisions.statement: An application MUST place each use case's messages, results, handlers, validators, and triggers in the use case's `Application/` folder, module ports in Application folders, and cross-module contracts in the sorted kind folders of its Contracts folder.
provisions.rationale: One use case keeps its command, query, result, handler, validator, and triggers in its `Application/` folder, and its endpoint and transport models in its `WebApi/` folder. A use case's own models never move up: two use cases with one shape each declare it, under `litespec/backend/architecture#give-each-use-case-its-own-models`. Ports and rules used by two or more use cases of one aggregate live in the aggregate Application folder, those used by two or more aggregates live in the module Application folder, and product-wide plumbing lives in the shared kernel Application folder. A module publishes its typed identifiers in `Contracts/Identifiers/`, its integration events in `Contracts/IntegrationEvents/`, and its read-only cross-module ports in `Contracts/Ports/`, so the public surface of a module stays visible at the module. It publishes no command and no refusal.

provisions.heading: Keep Closed Folder Sets at Every Level
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `code-placement-drift` for a folder outside its closed set or naming no declared record, for a file in the wrong layer folder of its use case, and for a reaction or job outside the folder of what it runs, and `mark-folder-drift` for a marked element outside the folder its mark names.
provisions.statement: Each level of the shared kernel and modules projects MUST hold only the folders the closed set table in this section allows.
provisions.rationale: A closed set refuses the catch-all folder by construction: anything outside the table has no home, so review refuses it. Product-wide plumbing lives in the product layer folders, and cross-module contracts live in each module Contracts folder. `litespec/backend/architecture#place-a-type-at-the-lowest-folder-that-holds-its-consumers` decides between a use case folder and the aggregate, module, and product layer folders. Module folders mirror record homes: use cases sit in `UseCases/` folders with their layer folders, each reaction and job sits with the use case, notification, or external system it runs, sends, or calls, and each read model sits in the module `ReadModels/` folder. Settled by [decision/0063-place-each-trigger-with-what-it-runs](decision/0063-place-each-trigger-with-what-it-runs).
provisions.example:
| Level | Allowed folders |
|:---|:---|
| Shared kernel project root | `Domain/`, `Application/`, `Infrastructure/`, `WebApi/` |
| Modules project root | `Composition/`, one per declared module |
| Module | `Contracts/`, `Domain/`, `Application/`, `Infrastructure/`, `UseCases/`, `Notifications/`, `ExternalSystems/`, `ReadModels/`, one per declared aggregate |
| Module `Contracts/` | `Identifiers/`, `IntegrationEvents/`, `Ports/` |
| Module `UseCases/` | one per declared module use case |
| Module `Notifications/` | one per notification a reaction or job of the module only sends |
| Module `ExternalSystems/` | one per external system a reaction or job of the module only calls |
| Module `ReadModels/` | one per declared read model of the module, in the plural |
| Aggregate | `Domain/`, `Application/`, `Infrastructure/`, `UseCases/` |
| Aggregate `UseCases/` | one per declared use case |
| Use case | `Application/`, and `WebApi/` when the use case has an endpoint |
| Use case `Application/` and `WebApi/`, and each folder under `Notifications/`, `ExternalSystems/` and `ReadModels/` | Files only |

```text
{Product}.SharedKernel/
  Domain/  Application/  Infrastructure/  WebApi/
{Product}.Modules/
  Composition/
  Organizations/
    Contracts/
      Identifiers/  IntegrationEvents/  Ports/
    Domain/  Application/  Infrastructure/
    Teams/
      Domain/          Team.cs  TeamState.cs  ITeamRepository.cs  Events/  Exceptions/
      Application/     ports and rules used by two or more Team use cases
      Infrastructure/  TeamRepository.cs
      UseCases/
        CreateTeam/
          Application/ CreateTeamCommand.cs  CreateTeamCommandResult.cs  CreateTeamCommandHandler.cs  CreateTeamCommandValidator.cs
          WebApi/      CreateTeamEndpoint.cs  CreateTeamRequestModel.cs  CreateTeamResponseModel.cs
        RemoveMember/
          Application/ RemoveMemberCommand.cs  RemoveMemberCommandHandler.cs  RemoveMemberOnAccountClosedHandler.cs
    UseCases/
      ReadTeamDirectory/        a use case no single aggregate owns
    Notifications/
      MemberRemoved/            a reaction that only sends this notification
    ReadModels/
      MemberAccounts/           a read model of another module's published facts
```

provisions.heading: Keep Composition in Hosts
provisions.evidence: Does every service registration call sit in `Program.cs` or a host registration module? Check the registration calls.
provisions.statement: Keep service registration in `Program.cs` and host registration modules.
provisions.rationale: Domain and Application declare abstractions for the hosts to implement. A registration call inside either layer makes the abstraction depend on the thing it abstracts, which inverts the dependency direction and drags Infrastructure into layers that must not name it. Each module registers its own Infrastructure types in its module Infrastructure folder, and `Program.cs` calls each module entry point in one visible order. This provision binds `litespec/backend/architecture#keep-service-registration-in-hosts` for .NET.
provisions.example:
One registration entry point per module, plus product plumbing:

```text
AddOrganizationsInfrastructure(...)
AddTeamsInfrastructure(...)
AddWebApi(...)
```

`Program.cs` keeps their call order visible, and the WebApi entry point owns Problem Details, authentication, authorization, endpoint discovery, and OpenAPI.

provisions.heading: Keep Host Endpoints in Hosts
provisions.evidence: Does every host endpoint without a handler live in its host project and carry its mark? Check the host endpoints beside the use case folders.
provisions.statement: Each host endpoint without a handler MUST live in its host project.
provisions.rationale: Protocol endpoints, static assets, and development-only tooling have no use case folder to sit beside, so the host keeps them. Each still carries its mark, and the placement check accepts a host endpoint in the host.

provisions.heading: Keep Implementation Types Internal
provisions.evidence: `dotnet build` reports `LS2001` for an implementation type that is not `internal sealed`.
provisions.artifact: command-handler, query-handler, validator, reaction, repository, endpoint
provisions.statement: A handler, validator, definition, persistence implementation, or endpoint implementation MUST be declared `internal sealed`.
provisions.rationale: A public type is an offer to every assembly, so an implementation left public invites callers it was never written for. Messages, results, markers, and ports turn public only when another assembly uses them, while handlers, validators, and implementations stay `internal sealed`. Assembly scanning reads internal types through the one public marker, so it never justifies widening visibility. This provision binds `litespec/backend/architecture#keep-implementations-hidden-and-closed` for .NET.

provisions.heading: Keep Use Case Folders Isolated
provisions.evidence: `dotnet build` reports `LS2019` for a use case folder naming a type in another use case folder.
provisions.artifact: use-case, command-handler, query-handler, validator, endpoint, reaction
provisions.statement: A use case folder MUST reference no type in another use case folder.
provisions.rationale: A use case folder holds one use case, so a reference between two such folders couples two slices that change for different reasons. A reaction or job that runs a use case lives in that use case's own `Application/` folder, so it names the message from inside, and no handler sends another use case's message. A shape two use cases need is declared in each, under `litespec/backend/architecture#give-each-use-case-its-own-models`. Behavior they share belongs in the aggregate, module, or shared kernel layer folder that holds every consumer, under `litespec/backend/architecture#place-a-type-at-the-lowest-folder-that-holds-its-consumers`. The rule applies to files and to global usings alike.

provisions.heading: Mirror Modules, Aggregates, and Use Cases in One Namespace Tree
provisions.evidence: Does every type in the shared kernel and modules projects carry the namespace its folder path implies? Compare the namespaces with the folders.
provisions.statement: Every type in the shared kernel and modules projects MUST live in the namespace tree that starts with the product name and follows the folders below the project root.
provisions.rationale: When the namespace reads like the folder path, `Claimwick.Spending.Expenses.UseCases.SubmitExpense.Application` names the product, module, aggregate, use case, and layer without a map. A reader moves from a Domain aggregate to its handler, its repository, and its endpoint by name alone, following folders under `litespec/workspace/naming#keep-namespaces-aligned-with-folders`. This provision binds `litespec/backend/architecture#organize-code-by-module-aggregate-and-use-case` for .NET.
provisions.example:
The Expenses aggregate of Claimwick's Spending module fills one branch:

```text
Claimwick.Modules/Spending/Expenses/Domain/Expense.cs
Claimwick.Modules/Spending/Expenses/UseCases/SubmitExpense/Application/SubmitExpenseCommandHandler.cs
```

The handler in the tree above lives in namespace `Claimwick.Spending.Expenses.UseCases.SubmitExpense.Application`.

provisions.heading: Place Each Read Model in Its Module Read Models Folder
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `code-placement-drift` for a class carrying a read-model mark outside its read-model folder, and for a folder under `ReadModels/` that names no declared read model.
provisions.statement: Each read model MUST live in a folder named for the read model in the plural inside its module `ReadModels/` folder, holding the read-model document, one projection per source integration event named `{ReadModel}On{Fact}Projection`, the reader interface `I{ReadModel}ReadModel` and its implementation, each carrying the read model's mark.
provisions.rationale: A read model's projections answer integration events like reactions, but they write only their read model and run no use case. Kept with a use case, they would read as reactions; kept with the read model, one folder shows every event that fills it and the one reader its module's use cases call. The mark links each class to the record that names its sources. A projection that wrote anything but its read model would be an unrecorded reaction. This provision binds `litespec/backend/application#read-another-modules-state-through-a-read-model` for .NET.
provisions.example:
```text
Claimwick.Modules/Reporting/ReadModels/ReimbursedExpenses/
  ReimbursedExpense.cs                                        the read-model document, keyed by ExpenseId
  ReimbursedExpenseOnExpenseReimbursedProjection.cs           one projection per source event
  ReimbursedExpenseOnExpensePersonalDataErasedProjection.cs
  IReimbursedExpenseReadModel.cs                              what Reporting use cases read
  ReimbursedExpenseReadModel.cs                               its store implementation
```

provisions.heading: Reach Another Module Only Through Contracts
provisions.evidence: `dotnet build` reports `LS2020` for a module reference naming another module type outside its Contracts folder.
provisions.statement: A module MUST reach another module only through types its Contracts folder publishes.
provisions.rationale: The Contracts folder is the public surface of a module, sorted by kind: typed identifiers in `Identifiers/`, integration events in `IntegrationEvents/`, and read-only ports other modules call in `Ports/`. Domain may name the typed identifiers; ports and integration events stay outside Domain. A module publishes no command and no refusal: another module triggers its acts through an integration event its reaction answers, and each module refuses with its own refusals. A module that needs another module's state keeps its own read model built from the owner's integration events, or asks one question through a decision port in the owner's `Contracts/Ports/` folder. It loads no foreign aggregate or repository. A reaction to another module's fact subscribes to the published integration event, never to the domain event.

provisions.heading: Separate the Shared Kernel from the Modules
provisions.evidence: Does the solution hold only the shared kernel, the modules project, and their hosts, with no reference from the shared kernel to the modules project? Check the solution file and the project references.
provisions.statement: Use a `{Product}.SharedKernel` project for what every module builds on and a `{Product}.Modules` project for the modules, with WebApi and optional Worker hosts, at every size.
provisions.rationale: The modules project then holds only business code and module slices: a reader opening it sees the modules of the product and nothing else, and one use case stays in one tree instead of spreading across layer projects. The shared kernel names no module, so a change to one module never touches it, and the build refuses a shared kernel type that reaches into a module, because the shared kernel project does not reference the modules project. Hosts stay separate projects, because two hosts can run the same modules.
provisions.example:
```text
apps/api/src/{Product}.SharedKernel/
apps/api/src/{Product}.Modules/
apps/api/src/{Product}.WebApi/
apps/api/src/{Product}.Worker/     only when background work needs its own process
```

provisions.heading: Use One Public Assembly Marker
provisions.evidence: Does the modules project expose exactly one public static assembly marker, with no unneeded marker in any other project? Check each project for its marker.
provisions.statement: Expose one public static assembly marker in the modules project for host endpoint discovery and scanning.
provisions.rationale: Scanners and the host need an assembly reference, and without a marker developers make handlers public to supply one, widening visibility for tooling convenience. One public static marker in the modules project gives the host and the scanners their reference while every handler stays internal.

provisions.heading: Centralize .NET Build Settings
provisions.evidence: Does `apps/api/Directory.Build.props` set the manifest target framework with nullable types, implicit usings, and warnings as errors? Look at that file.
provisions.statement: `apps/api/Directory.Build.props` MUST set the target framework of the manifest .NET stack release, and enable nullable types, implicit usings, and warnings as errors.
provisions.rationale: Build settings drift project by project when each project owns its own: one project targets an older framework, another drops nullable types, and warnings pile up where nobody reads them. One file owns the framework, nullability, usings, and warnings-as-errors, so a change applies to every project and review sees it in one diff.

provisions.heading: Centralize NuGet Versions
provisions.evidence: Does `apps/api/Directory.Packages.props` enable central management with the manifest pins, with versions in no project file? Look at the central file beside the project files.
provisions.statement: `apps/api/Directory.Packages.props` MUST enable central package management and carry an exact version within each manifest pin.
provisions.rationale: A version written in a project file is invisible to the manifest that owns it, and two projects drift to two versions of one package. Central management leaves project files naming packages only, while one file carries the exact version within each manifest pin, so an upgrade touches one place.

provisions.heading: Commit the Tool Manifest
provisions.evidence: Does the root `.config/dotnet-tools.json` pin every local tool a documented command invokes, including the Stryker.NET runner? Look at the tool manifest.
provisions.statement: The root `.config/dotnet-tools.json` MUST pin every local .NET tool that a documented command invokes.
provisions.rationale: A tool installed by version range resolves differently on two machines, and a build that passes locally fails in CI. Pinning every tool a documented command invokes keeps local and CI runs on one version; when a tool ships in the manifest's .NET release, its pin matches that release. The manifest pins the Stryker.NET runner that `litespec/quality/testing#refuse-surviving-mutants-on-changed-lines` names.

provisions.heading: Set the SDK Floor at the Workspace Root
provisions.evidence: Does the root `global.json` set the manifest major release's first feature band with `latestFeature` roll-forward? Look at the root `global.json`.
provisions.statement: The root `global.json` MUST set the first feature band of the manifest .NET major release as its SDK version and roll forward with `latestFeature`.
provisions.rationale: The first feature band of the manifest's major release is the lowest SDK that builds the workspace, and `latestFeature` roll-forward lets a later feature band of the same major release build it too. A newer major release needs a workspace change, so a local machine and CI stay on one major line. The compiler and its analyzers ship with the SDK, so a different SDK can still build different output within that line; the floor sets the minimum, not identical output. The manifest names the major release; `Directory.Build.props` sets its target framework.

provisions.heading: Define the Shared Domain Contracts Once
provisions.evidence: Is every shared Domain contract declared once, with `DomainException` and `AggregateRoot<TId>` in their declared shapes? Check the shared contracts.
provisions.statement: Declare the shared Domain contracts once in the shared kernel Domain folder and reuse them across every module.
provisions.rationale: Every module raises events, throws domain exceptions, and identifies aggregates. A shared contract declared twice becomes two contracts that drift. Declaring `IDomainEvent`, `DomainException`, `IStronglyTypedId`, `Entity<TId>`, `IAggregateRoot`, and `AggregateRoot<TId>` once in the shared kernel Domain folder gives every module the same mechanics. Generic handling constrains its parameters with `IAggregateRoot`, as in `IRepository<T> where T : IAggregateRoot`. This provision binds `litespec/backend/domain#reuse-the-shared-domain-contracts-across-modules` for .NET.

provisions.heading: Document Every Public Domain Contract
provisions.evidence: `dotnet build` reports `LS1011` for a public Domain type or member without XML documentation.
provisions.statement: Every public Domain type and member MUST carry XML documentation stating the business constraint, result, or failure it represents.
provisions.rationale: A public Domain member is a business promise, and without documentation stating the constraint, result, or failure it represents, callers infer the contract from the implementation and miss the rule. A summary that restates the member name adds nothing; a mutation method names its source states, resulting state, protected invariant, and recorded event. This provision binds `litespec/backend/domain#document-every-public-domain-contract` for .NET.

provisions.heading: Hold Every Monetary Amount in the Shared Money Object
provisions.evidence: Does every monetary amount live in the shared `Money` object as a `decimal` with amount and currency? Check each monetary amount.
provisions.statement: A monetary amount MUST use `decimal` inside one shared `Money` value object carrying an ISO 4217 currency code and serializing as `{ "amount": "12.50", "currency": "EUR" }`.
provisions.rationale: Binary floating point cannot represent most decimal amounts exactly, so money computed in `double` drifts by cents. The shared `Money` object keeps a `decimal` amount with an ISO 4217 currency code. The owning module record defines supported currencies, scale, rounding, sign rules, and cross-currency arithmetic, and Infrastructure maps that precision explicitly. A use case fixed to one currency accepts an amount alone while stating that currency in its record. This provision binds `litespec/backend/domain#model-money-with-exact-decimal-values` for .NET.

provisions.heading: Implement Domain Services as Stateless Classes
provisions.evidence: Does every domain service stay stateless, take only Domain values, and avoid provider calls? Check each domain service.
provisions.statement: A domain service MUST be a stateless sealed class accepting and returning Domain values.
provisions.rationale: Some calculations span concepts with no natural aggregate owner, such as pricing an order from its lines. A stateless service holds that calculation with no persistence, messaging, logging, clock, authorization, or provider call. Application loads the aggregates, calls the service, and passes its result into aggregate behavior. The service carries a mark naming its rule, and the builder links it to the rule it computes. This provision binds `litespec/backend/domain#use-stateless-domain-services-for-ownerless-rules` for .NET.

provisions.heading: Keep Clock Reads and Random Values Out of Domain
provisions.evidence: `dotnet build` reports `LS1009` for a clock, randomness, or identifier read in Domain.
provisions.statement: Domain code MUST NOT read a clock, a random source, or a new `Guid`, so every such value arrives as an argument.
provisions.rationale: Each of `DateTime`, `DateTimeOffset`, `TimeProvider`, `Random`, `RandomNumberGenerator`, `Guid.NewGuid`, and `Guid.CreateVersion7` returns a different value on every call, so a Domain method that reads one cannot run twice with the same result and cannot be tested with a fixed value. Receiving each value as an argument keeps every Domain call a pure function of its inputs. The Application layer obtains each value through the port it owns and passes it in. This provision binds `litespec/backend/domain#pass-nondeterministic-values-into-domain` for .NET.

provisions.heading: Keep Domain Free of Outer-Layer Concerns
provisions.evidence: `dotnet build` reports `LS1001` for Domain code naming an outer-layer type.
provisions.statement: Domain code MUST reference only the .NET base class library and product-owned Domain types.
provisions.rationale: A package reference points one way, and once Domain names a persistence or web type, business rules depend on the framework instead of the framework depending on them. Keeping Domain to the base class library and product-owned types means a provider change cannot reach business behavior. Infrastructure registers persisted discriminators and mappings, so Domain carries no serialization attribute. This provision binds `litespec/backend/domain#keep-domain-independent-of-outer-layers` for .NET.

provisions.heading: Keep Double and Float Out of Exact Quantities
provisions.evidence: `dotnet build` reports `LS1008` for a `double` or `float` type in Domain.
provisions.statement: Domain code MUST NOT declare a `double` or `float` for a monetary amount, a rate applied to one, or a quantity compared for exact equality.
provisions.rationale: `double` and `float` represent most decimal fractions only approximately, so two amounts that read as equal compare as different. The shared `Money` object holds a `decimal`, and a rate applied to a `Money` amount is a `decimal` too. The analyzer reports the Domain declaration that breaks this form. This provision binds `litespec/backend/domain#keep-binary-floating-point-out-of-exact-quantities` for .NET.

provisions.heading: Keep ID Representations Aligned at Every Boundary
provisions.evidence: Does every identifier keep the same UUID text form across Domain, persistence, transport, and client boundaries? Trace one identifier through each boundary form.
provisions.statement: Represent an identifier the same way in Domain, persistence, transport, and generated clients.
provisions.rationale: An identifier crosses every boundary in the table below, and each boundary that invents its own text form forces converters at both ends. One UUID text form everywhere means a value copied from a log, a route, or a JSON payload parses at the next boundary without translation. This provision binds `litespec/backend/domain#align-id-representations-at-every-boundary` for .NET.

provisions.heading: Keep Repository Interfaces in Domain
provisions.evidence: `dotnet build` reports `LS1010` for a repository interface exposing a query surface.
provisions.statement: A repository interface MUST expose only aggregate and Domain types for exactly one aggregate root, without `IQueryable`, a session, or a generic CRUD surface.
provisions.rationale: One repository per aggregate keeps the write boundary aligned with the consistency boundary: the interface loads and stages complete aggregates of its own type, and nothing else. `GetByIdAsync` throws `{Aggregate}NotFoundException` for a required load, which frees handlers from repeating null checks, while a nullable `FindBy...Async` stays reserved for lookups where absence is normal. A flow that finds a record or creates it is two use cases, and the boundary owning the flow chooses between them, following `litespec/backend/application#implement-one-outcome-path-per-command`. `IQueryable`, sessions, and generic CRUD surfaces would leak query shaping and provider behavior into Domain, so the interface exposes none of them. This provision binds `litespec/backend/domain#limit-each-repository-to-one-aggregate` for .NET. The repository is the write side only. A query reads through a read model owned by Application and shaped by Infrastructure, and that path declares no Domain interface. A repository that gained a projection method would put query shapes in Domain, which is the coupling this layer exists to prevent. A `store` aggregate owns no repository interface; its port carries the state its owner holds.

provisions.heading: Mark Each State-Changing Root Method with Its Use Case
provisions.evidence: `dotnet build` reports `LS5003` for a root method carrying other than one use-case mark, and `LS5002` for a mark on a reading or private method.
provisions.statement: A root method that changes state MUST carry exactly one `<implements>` mark naming its use case.
provisions.rationale: The `<implements>` mark is the XML documentation tag that ties a method to the use case whose act it performs, and the builder and the analyzer read the same link from it. A reading or private method performs no act and carries no use-case mark, and `LS5002` reports one that does. This provision binds `litespec/backend/domain#give-each-use-case-its-own-act` for .NET, and the model check for the same rule stays on that generic provision.

provisions.heading: Model Child Entities as Sealed Classes
provisions.evidence: Does every child entity stay a sealed class derived from `Entity<TId>`, created only through its root's methods? Check each child entity.
provisions.statement: A child entity MUST be a sealed class deriving from the project-owned `Entity<TId>`.
provisions.rationale: Deriving from the project-owned `Entity<TId>` gives the child typed identity and identity equality, so it declares only its own data and behavior. The root creates, finds, and changes its children through business methods, and a child exposes no mutable state outside the root. A child is a design choice inside its aggregate: it appears in code and the glossary, never as a record. This provision binds `litespec/backend/domain#keep-child-entities-inside-the-aggregate-boundary` for .NET.

provisions.heading: Model Every Aggregate Lifecycle with State Records
provisions.evidence: `dotnet build` reports `LS1003` for an aggregate with no `State` property, `LS1004` for a state case left unsealed, and `LS1013` for a switch that leaves a sealed state case to its discard arm.
provisions.statement: An aggregate MUST expose its lifecycle only through one `State` property backed by an abstract `{Aggregate}State` record with sealed per-state records.
provisions.rationale: An enum, a status string, a boolean flag, a parallel nullable field, or a computed state cannot carry state-specific data such as a publication time. State records hold each state's data where it belongs, and aggregate methods own the transitions between them. Even a one-state aggregate defines its hierarchy, so later states have a home. The C# compiler does not check that a switch over the hierarchy covers every sealed case: a switch expression needs a discard arm to compile without warning CS8509, and a sealed case with no arm of its own reaches that discard arm at run time. `LS1013` reports a switch that leaves a sealed case to its discard arm, and tests cover the discard path for a case added later. The sealed set matches the aggregate's declared `states`, which is the link the builder follows. This provision binds `litespec/backend/domain#model-every-aggregate-lifecycle-with-state-types` for .NET.

provisions.heading: Model Every Closed Set of Domain Values Without Enums
provisions.evidence: `dotnet build` reports `LS1002` for an enum declared in Domain and `LS1013` for a switch that leaves a sealed case to its discard arm.
provisions.statement: Domain code MUST model every closed set as an abstract record base with sealed cases exposing one stable `Code`, converting labels through `FromCode`.
provisions.rationale: An enum is a named integer, so it carries no case data and admits undefined values through a cast. When a case later gains data, the enum grows parallel fields. A record hierarchy carries each case's data in its own sealed record. A boundary converts a label through `FromCode` instead of `ToString`, which turns an unrecognized label into a validation failure rather than a silent default. The C# compiler does not check that a switch over the hierarchy covers every sealed case: a switch expression needs a discard arm to compile without warning CS8509, and a sealed case with no arm of its own reaches that discard arm at run time. `LS1013` reports a switch that leaves a sealed case to its discard arm, and tests cover the discard path for a case added later. A static class of string constants, such as a set of reason codes, is the same closed set without its cases: the compiler cannot tell a valid code from a typo, so it becomes a record hierarchy too. This provision binds `litespec/backend/domain#model-every-closed-set-as-a-type-hierarchy` for .NET.

provisions.heading: Model Value Objects as Records
provisions.evidence: Is every value object an immutable record with static creation and no base type? Check each value object.
provisions.statement: A value object MUST be an immutable C# record with no base type.
provisions.rationale: Comparison by complete value lets two instances with the same data stand in for each other. The type exposes no setter and no implicit conversion, and creation through a named static method keeps every construction path under the validation the type declares. A value object that holds a collection implements content equality and a matching hash for its declared ordering rule, copying incoming collections and returning read-only views. This provision binds `litespec/backend/domain#use-immutable-value-objects-for-domain-concepts` and `litespec/backend/domain#compare-collection-values-by-their-content` for .NET.

provisions.heading: Raise Immutable Domain Facts
provisions.evidence: `dotnet build` reports `LS1007` for a domain event that is not an immutable record.
provisions.statement: A domain event MUST be a public immutable record named `{Aggregate}{PastFact}Event` implementing `IDomainEvent`, carrying business data only and one mark naming its domain-event record.
provisions.rationale: The `{Aggregate}{PastFact}Event` name tells a reader which aggregate raised the fact without opening the file. The event carries business data only: the typed identifiers and the values its reactions need. It carries no aggregate, session, service, mutable collection, or exception, because a mutable payload lets a reaction observe state that changed after the fact. Envelope identity, such as message and causation identity, lives on the published integration event that carries the fact outside the process. Its `Classification` comes from the domain-event record its mark names, under `litespec/backend/dotnet/stack#generate-runtime-values-from-the-records`. Only the aggregate root raises events, through `RaiseDomainEvent` on the shared base. This provision binds `litespec/backend/domain#raise-immutable-facts-as-domain-events` for .NET.

provisions.heading: Reject Business Violations with Domain Exceptions
provisions.evidence: `dotnet build` reports `LS1005` for a throw outside a `DomainException` subclass and `LS1006` for a domain exception that is misnamed or open.
provisions.statement: A rejected business rule MUST throw a `DomainException` subclass named `{DomainType}{Reason}Exception`, carrying the refusal `code` and one mark naming its rule.
provisions.rationale: One exception type per rule puts the stable code and the message in the type, so the call site passes only domain values and two rules never share a type by accident. A shared rule exception with caller-supplied codes lets any caller invent a code and lets unrelated rules merge silently. Its `Code` comes from the refusal result its rule names, under `litespec/backend/dotnet/stack#generate-runtime-values-from-the-records`, and each exception's code equals the refusal `code` on the result record it answers. The root's factory and methods check an invariant rule, and the use-case validator or the root's method checks a precondition rule. Names lead with the aggregate root and follow `litespec/workspace/naming#name-exceptions-by-failed-rule`; this provision owns the one-type-per-rule shape and the code each type carries. Domain throws no `InvalidOperationException`, `ArgumentException`, validation, HTTP, or provider exception for a business rejection, and carries no transport status. This provision binds `litespec/backend/domain#reject-business-violations-with-dedicated-refusals` for .NET.

provisions.heading: Throw Only Refusal Codes the Module Owns
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `refusal-module-foreign` (level S) for a refusal code carried from another module's code, and `refusal-code-duplicate` (level S) for a refusal code two exception types carry.
provisions.statement: Each refusal code a module declares MUST be carried by at most one exception type, in the module that declares it.
provisions.rationale: A refusal code tells the caller which module refused and why. An exception in one module that carries another module's code blames the wrong owner, and two exception types carrying one code leave the caller unable to tell which rule failed, so the code stops meaning anything once it travels. Each module declares its codes once in its refusal set, under `litespec/core/use-cases#declare-each-modules-refusals-once`, and each exception type carries its rule's code from that set, under `litespec/backend/dotnet/domain#reject-business-violations-with-domain-exceptions`. One carrying type per code in the declaring module keeps the blame and the rule behind each code fixed. This provision binds `litespec/backend/domain#reject-business-violations-with-dedicated-refusals` for .NET.

provisions.heading: Use Strongly Typed Version 7 Identifiers
provisions.evidence: `dotnet build` reports `LS1012` for an `Id` struct outside the strongly typed form, or a raw `Guid` as an aggregate identity.
provisions.statement: An aggregate identity MUST be a `readonly record struct` wrapping one version 7 `Guid`, declaring no implicit conversion, primitive alias, or public parameterless creation path.
provisions.rationale: A bare `Guid` parameter accepts any identifier, including an empty one and one meant for another aggregate. The typed struct rejects `Guid.Empty` and the struct default in every factory, implements `IStronglyTypedId` and `IParsable<TId>`, and declares no implicit conversion or parameterless creation, so a wrong identifier fails at the boundary. New values arrive from the caller: a factory takes its identifier as an argument, and a method that needs several takes a generator. Domain reads no clock and calls no static source of time or randomness, which keeps business behavior deterministic and testable. This provision binds `litespec/backend/domain#identify-each-aggregate-with-a-typed-version-7-identifier` for .NET. When two callers generate the same value, persistence rejects the duplicate key, and the operation fails on the same path as any other write conflict, with the violation mapped to the use case conflict refusal under `litespec/backend/persistence#map-a-constraint-violation-to-its-refusal`.

provisions.heading: Use the Domain Layer Folder Layout
provisions.evidence: Does every aggregate Domain folder follow the states, events, exceptions, and concepts layout, with no named-by-another-module identifier inside? Check each Domain folder beside its Contracts folder.
provisions.statement: Give each aggregate Domain folder its states, events, exceptions, and concepts in the files this provision names.
provisions.rationale: Each aggregate Domain folder holds everything one aggregate owns in the files the layout names, so a reader finds the full aggregate in one place. Namespaces follow the folders under `litespec/workspace/naming#keep-namespaces-aligned-with-folders`, and each file sits at the lowest folder holding its consumers under `litespec/backend/architecture#place-a-type-at-the-lowest-folder-that-holds-its-consumers`. A typed identifier that another module names lives in its owner's `Contracts/Identifiers/` folder. Shared values live in the shared kernel `Domain/` folder with the exceptions of the rules they enforce, which take the product as their home, such as `rule/claimwick.amount-is-never-negative`. This provision binds `litespec/backend/domain#organize-a-module-by-aggregate-and-concept` for .NET.
provisions.example:
The layout below shows the Domain folders for a flat module, a module with a concept folder, and a module with two aggregates:

```text

{Product}.Modules/
```
