Each aggregate repository interface stays with the aggregate it loads, and module and aggregate folders keep the same names at every layer, per `litespec/backend/architecture#organize-code-by-module-aggregate-and-use-case`.

provisions.heading: Use the Project Aggregate Root Contract
provisions.evidence: Does every aggregate root stay a sealed class derived from the project-owned `AggregateRoot<TId>`? Check each root declaration.
provisions.statement: An aggregate root MUST be a sealed class deriving from the project-owned `AggregateRoot<TId>`, taking identity and event mechanics from that base.
provisions.rationale: One project-owned base gives every aggregate the same mechanics: typed identity, a pending event collection with protected recording, and clearing. The shared base supplies exactly those mechanics and nothing else: no timestamps, audit, tenancy, lifecycle, or persistence that would force every aggregate to carry behavior most never need. It carries the aggregate version only as persistence metadata, which Domain never reads or sets. The root stays a sealed class, so no behavior extends an aggregate by inheritance, and it carries a mark naming its aggregate record for the builder to link. This provision binds `litespec/backend/domain#take-identity-and-events-from-the-shared-root-contract` for .NET.

provisions.heading: Assert Observable Outcomes
provisions.evidence: Does every BDD scenario assert a response, read, event, record, or other observable outcome? Look at each BDD scenario in the acceptance suite.
provisions.statement: A BDD scenario MUST assert a response, later read, durable event, audit record, or other observable outcome.
provisions.rationale: A scenario that runs requests without asserting proves only that nothing threw. Asserting a response, a later read, a durable event, an audit record, or another observable outcome shows the public boundary achieved the expected behavior.

provisions.heading: Avoid Routine Scenario Duplication
provisions.evidence: Does any unit or validation test repeat as a duplicate BDD scenario? Look at the narrower suites beside the acceptance suite.
provisions.statement: A test author MUST NOT duplicate every unit or validation test as a BDD scenario.
provisions.rationale: A unit test fails at the exact rule and runs in milliseconds; the same test duplicated as a BDD scenario fails at a public boundary after a full setup. Duplication slows the suite and moves the failure away from its cause, so routine behavior stays in its narrower tests.

provisions.heading: Call Public Boundaries from BDD Steps
provisions.evidence: Does every step definition stay within the HTTP API and the declared public boundaries? Look at each step definition in the acceptance suite.
provisions.statement: A BDD step MUST call the HTTP API or another declared public system boundary.
provisions.rationale: A step that calls the HTTP API or another declared public boundary proves what a caller can observe. A step that reaches past the boundary depends on implementation details, so a refactoring breaks the scenario without breaking the behavior.

provisions.heading: Exclude Production Internals
provisions.evidence: Does any step definition resolve a repository, handler, session, or the production service provider? Look at each step definition in the acceptance suite.
provisions.statement: A BDD step definition MUST NOT resolve repositories, handlers, sessions, or the production service provider.
provisions.rationale: Resolving a repository, handler, session, or the production service provider runs the behavior without the boundary the scenario claims to verify. The scenario then passes while the public path stays untested, so step definitions resolve none of them.

provisions.heading: Group Feature Classes by Module
provisions.evidence: Does every feature class sit under its module folder, or under a documented grouping? Look at `Acceptance.Tests` beside the project documentation.
provisions.statement: Group feature classes under module folders in `Acceptance.Tests`.
provisions.rationale: A scenario filed by business module sits beside the vocabulary it exercises, so a reader finds every example of one module in one folder. A flat or technically grouped suite scatters them.

provisions.heading: Isolate Scenario Execution
provisions.evidence: Does every scenario pass alone and in any order, with state reset between runs? Look at the acceptance suite runs.
provisions.statement: The acceptance suite MUST reset database state between scenarios and avoid scenario-order dependencies.
provisions.rationale: State left by one scenario becomes a hidden precondition of the next, and the suite passes only in one order. Resetting database state between scenarios removes that coupling, so any scenario runs alone or in any order.

provisions.heading: Keep Steps Vocabulary-Scoped
provisions.evidence: Does every reusable step set serve one business vocabulary, or a documented scope? Look at each reusable step set beside the project documentation.
provisions.statement: Keep step definitions narrow and reusable only within one business vocabulary.
provisions.rationale: A step reused across vocabularies, such as a generic success step, means something subtly different in each place and couples unrelated modules to one definition. Steps narrow to one business vocabulary keep their meaning exact.

provisions.heading: Limit Database Assertions
provisions.evidence: Does every direct database assertion name a documented durable boundary? Look at each direct database assertion in the acceptance suite.
provisions.statement: A BDD scenario MUST use direct database assertions only for a documented durable boundary.
provisions.rationale: The database is an implementation detail, so asserting its rows couples the scenario to storage shapes. A direct assertion is allowed only for a documented durable boundary, such as an outbox record, where the stored row is itself the promised evidence.

provisions.heading: Limit Scenario Context
provisions.evidence: Does every scenario context object hold only scenario state, or a documented use? Look at the scenario context beside the project documentation.
provisions.statement: Store values for one scenario in a scenario context object.
provisions.rationale: One context object holding the scenario's own values keeps shared state visible and small. Resolving services from it turns it into a service locator that hides what the scenario depends on.

provisions.heading: Mark Pull-Request Scenarios
provisions.evidence: Does the marked pull-request subset stay within its stated bound with its owner named? Look at the marked subset beside the proves claims.
provisions.statement: Mark the small pull-request subset separately from the proves claim, with a critical test trait on the LightBDD scenario.
provisions.rationale: The critical trait selects the small subset whose failure stops a release, for fast pull-request feedback. The marking stays separate from the proves claim, which records scenario proof rather than release gating. A marking that every scenario carries selects nothing, so the subset keeps a stated size bound and an owner who keeps it there.

provisions.heading: Own Scenario Data
provisions.evidence: Does every BDD scenario own its identifiers, actor context, requests, responses, and expected state? Look at each BDD scenario in the acceptance suite.
provisions.statement: Each BDD scenario MUST own its identifiers, actor context, requests, responses, and expected state.
provisions.rationale: A scenario that borrows identifiers or state prepared elsewhere breaks when that other setup changes. Owning its identifiers, actor context, requests, responses, and expected state keeps each scenario self-contained and runnable alone.

provisions.heading: Preserve Scenario Failures
provisions.evidence: Does every hook await setup and cleanup without replacing the original scenario failure? Look at each hook in the acceptance suite.
provisions.statement: A BDD hook MUST await asynchronous setup and cleanup without replacing the original scenario failure.
provisions.rationale: Setup and cleanup are asynchronous, and an unawaited hook leaves the next scenario running against a half-reset database. A hook that throws during cleanup can also replace the scenario's own failure, hiding the real cause. Awaiting both without replacing the original failure keeps the evidence trustworthy.

provisions.heading: Select Shared Critical Examples
provisions.evidence: Does every BDD scenario trace to a cross-layer example the team discusses in business language? Look at each BDD scenario in the acceptance suite.
provisions.statement: A test author MUST create a BDD scenario only when business-language form improves shared understanding of cross-layer behavior.
provisions.rationale: A scenario costs maintenance on every behavior change, so the suite earns that cost only where business-language form improves shared understanding of cross-layer behavior. Each selected scenario gives product, domain, engineering, and testing discussions one executable example instead of four retellings.

provisions.heading: Trace Every BDD Scenario to Its Scenario
provisions.evidence: Does every BDD scenario carry one `proves` claim naming its scenario? Look at each BDD scenario in the acceptance suite.
provisions.statement: Every BDD scenario MUST carry one `proves` claim naming the scenario it proves.
provisions.rationale: A scenario pairs one `given` situation and `when` action with the `then` result they lead to, and the proves claim is what ties the BDD scenario to that record. The claim names it, the steps call the proved use case, and the assertion checks its result; without the claim, the model builder cannot tell which scenario the BDD scenario proves. A LightBDD scenario carries the claim as a proves mark on the scenario method, in the style the project declares. The model builder reads proves marks on C# methods, so a Gherkin feature file would not count as proof and would state each scenario twice beside its scenario record.
provisions.example: `/// <proves>scenario/cancel-order.canceling-twice-is-refused</proves>` traces a cancellation BDD scenario to its scenario record.

provisions.heading: Translate Business Phrases into Test-Driver Calls
provisions.evidence: Does every step definition translate its phrase through a typed test-driver call? Look at each step definition in the acceptance suite.
provisions.statement: A BDD step definition MUST translate a business phrase into a typed test-driver call.
provisions.rationale: HTTP calls, JSON shapes, and assertion mechanics in a step definition hide the business phrase the scenario promises. Translating each phrase into a typed test-driver call keeps the scenario readable while the driver owns the boundary mechanics.

provisions.heading: Assign Each Baseline Package to Its Owning Project
provisions.evidence: Does every baseline package reference sit in the project the ownership table assigns? Look at each package reference beside the ownership table.
provisions.statement: Assign each baseline package to the owning layer named in the table in this section.
provisions.rationale: Without an owner, a package lands in the project that first needs it and spreads from there. The table assigns each baseline package to its one owning project, so the narrowest project holds each package and review can refuse it anywhere else. This provision states the .NET form of `litespec/workspace/dependencies#assign-each-baseline-package-to-its-owning-layer`.
provisions.example:
| Project | Direct package groups |
|:---|:---|
| Domain | None |
| Application.Abstractions | Required LiteBus module abstractions only |
| Application | Required LiteBus module abstractions; `Marten` for the selected `IQuerySession` read boundary; Microsoft abstractions used by public ports |
| Infrastructure | `Marten`; LiteBus registration modules. Provider, resilience, service discovery, and configuration packages required by implemented adapters |
| WebApi | JWT Bearer [REDACTED], ASP.NET Core OpenAPI, build-time OpenAPI generation, Scalar, and required LiteBus mediator abstractions |
| Worker | LiteBus registration modules; the provider, resilience, and configuration packages its hosted operations need |
| ServiceDefaults | Health checks, service discovery, HTTP resilience, and OpenTelemetry registration and instrumentation |
| AppHost | Aspire AppHost and resource hosting packages |
| Domain.Tests | xUnit v3, assertions, and FsCheck |
| Application.Tests | xUnit v3, assertions, and NSubstitute for outside providers and the clock |
| Integration.Tests | xUnit v3, assertions, test host, Testcontainers PostgreSQL, and the Microsoft.Testing.Platform report and coverage extensions |
| Architecture.Tests | xUnit v3 and assertions |
| Acceptance.Tests | xUnit v3, assertions, the behavior runner its extension selects, test host, and the report and coverage extensions |

Application.Tests run each handler against the real repositories on the test database. A test substitutes only the outside providers and the clock, as `litespec/quality/testing#use-one-mock-rule-for-every-stack` requires.

Test projects reference xUnit v3 and run on Microsoft.Testing.Platform. The consumer `global.json` sets `"test": { "runner": "Microsoft.Testing.Platform" }`, because the .NET 10 `dotnet test` command refuses the VSTest mode for these projects. Domain.Tests carries FsCheck at the 3.6.0 pin `litespec.manifest.yaml` states for the property tests that `litespec/backend/testing#prove-every-calculation-with-property-tests` names and the model-based tests that `litespec/backend/testing#prove-every-aggregate-with-a-model-based-test` names.

The example adds a package to the narrowest owning project. A central version entry does not authorize every project to reference that package. Conditional packages such as LightBDD, SignalR, and WireMock are referenced only after their extension activates. The manifest pins no architecture-test library; a project that wants one adds it with owner approval.

provisions.heading: Keep Application Dependencies Narrow
provisions.evidence: Does the Application project file reference anything beyond the permitted abstractions and the one read boundary? Look at the Application project file.
provisions.statement: Application MUST reference only LiteBus command and query abstractions, required read abstractions, and needed Microsoft abstractions, plus the `IQuerySession` read boundary.
provisions.rationale: Application coordinates work; Infrastructure hides technology. A provider package in Application makes the coordination layer depend on the technology it was meant to stay free of. The Statement names the one permitted read boundary; everything else provider-shaped stays out. This provision states the .NET form of `litespec/workspace/dependencies#keep-application-free-of-provider-packages`.

provisions.heading: Keep Domain Package-Free
provisions.evidence: Does the Domain project file reference any package beyond the base class library? Look at the Domain project file.
provisions.statement: The Domain project MUST reference no package beyond the .NET base class library.
provisions.rationale: A package in Domain makes business rules depend on a framework, a provider, or a messenger. Marten, LiteBus, ASP.NET Core, injection, serialization, and logging packages all stay outside, so Domain builds on the base class library alone. This provision states the .NET form of `litespec/workspace/dependencies#keep-domain-dependency-free`.

provisions.heading: Keep .NET Production and Test Projects Separate
provisions.evidence: Does every production project, test project, and solution file sit at its fixed address? Look at `apps/api/`.
provisions.statement: Production projects MUST live under `apps/api/src/` and test projects under `apps/api/tests/`, with the solution directly under `apps/api/`.
provisions.rationale: Production under `apps/api/src/` and tests under `apps/api/tests/` make a test dependency reaching production visible in the path itself. The solution sits directly under `apps/api/`, beside both. A workspace AppHost is the one production project outside `src/`, placed by `litespec/backend/dotnet/workspace#place-a-workspace-apphost-beside-the-applications-it-runs`. This provision states the .NET form of `litespec/workspace/structure#keep-production-and-test-code-separate`.
provisions.example:
The baseline tree is:

```text
apps/api/
  {ProjectName}.slnx
  Directory.Build.props
  Directory.Packages.props
  src/
    {ProjectName}.Domain/
    {ProjectName}.Application.Abstractions/
    {ProjectName}.Application/
    {ProjectName}.Infrastructure/
    {ProjectName}.WebApi/
    {ProjectName}.Worker/             when background work needs a host
    {ProjectName}.AppHost/            when an orchestration host runs the API alone
    {ProjectName}.ServiceDefaults/    when a local orchestration host is used
  tests/
    {ProjectName}.Architecture.Tests/
    {ProjectName}.Integration.Tests/
    {ProjectName}.Acceptance.Tests/   when size is large
    {ProjectName}.Domain.Tests/       optional unit tests
    {ProjectName}.Application.Tests/  optional unit tests
```

Worker is conditional on the extension that runs background work. Acceptance.Tests is required when `size` is large and optional otherwise. Domain.Tests and Application.Tests are optional in both sizes. `AppHost` and `ServiceDefaults` are local hosting and diagnostics projects rather than application layers. An application that orchestrates its local dependencies another way ships neither and records no waiver for their absence.

provisions.heading: Keep One Application Assembly
provisions.evidence: Does every command, query, result, validator, handler, event handler, and job file sit in the Application project, with cross-module contracts in Application.Abstractions or the merged Application? Look at the Application project files beside the shared contracts.
provisions.statement: An application MUST place commands, queries, results, validators, handlers, event handler classes, job classes, and module-owned ports in one Application project, and cross-module contracts in Application.Abstractions, or in Application where the project merges them under `litespec/backend/dotnet/ext/layer-projects#package-each-layer-as-its-own-project`.
provisions.rationale: One assembly holds commands, queries, and their handlers because the stack never deploys them separately. Splitting Application into Write, Read, Contracts, and event-handler assemblies would buy a deployment boundary the stack never uses, and every use case would pay for it with a project reference to cross. The separation this stack keeps is the one [Fowler describes as CQRS](https://www.martinfowler.com/bliki/CQRS.html): the command and query models differ, while one assembly holds them. Event handlers and jobs live with the use case they run inside the Application project, in that use case's operation folder; one that runs none lives in the module `Notifications/` folder of the notification it sends or the `ExternalSystems/` folder of the system it calls. Job scheduling stays in Worker or Infrastructure with the scheduling concerns, under `litespec/backend/architecture#name-the-host-for-work-that-outlives-a-request`.

provisions.heading: Keep Persistence in One Infrastructure Folder
provisions.evidence: Does every Marten configuration, repository, commit, and serialization file sit in the one Infrastructure persistence folder? Look at the persistence files.
provisions.statement: Place Marten configuration, repositories, commit behavior, and serialization under one Infrastructure persistence folder.
provisions.rationale: One persistence folder holds Marten configuration, repositories, commit behavior, and serialization, so every persistence type has one discoverable home. Scattered configuration hides the provider setup across the project. This provision states the .NET form of `litespec/backend/persistence#use-one-persistence-folder`.
provisions.example:
```text
{ProjectName}.Infrastructure/
  Persistence/
    Marten/
      MartenServiceRegistration.cs
      MartenStoreConfiguration.cs
      Commit/
        SaveChangesCommandPostHandler.cs
      Events/
        DomainEventBuffer.cs
      Posts/                        single aggregate whose name matches the module: files directly under the module
        PostRepository.cs
        PostMartenConfiguration.cs
      Customers/                    two aggregates: one folder per aggregate
        CustomerAccounts/
          CustomerAccountRepository.cs
          CustomerAccountMartenConfiguration.cs
        Consents/
          ConsentRepository.cs
          ConsentMartenConfiguration.cs
```

The module folders follow `litespec/backend/architecture#organize-code-by-module-aggregate-and-use-case`. A single-aggregate module stays flat when its aggregate root's plural name equals the module name. For example, `Post` stays flat under `Posts`. Otherwise, each aggregate takes its own folder.

Aggregate-specific configuration stays beside its aggregate, while session and commit plumbing stay under the Marten root.

provisions.heading: Keep the Test Projects the Size Requires
provisions.evidence: Does the solution tree hold Architecture and Integration test projects, with Acceptance only where size large or the BDD extension requires it? Look at `apps/api/tests/` beside the declared size.
provisions.statement: A backend solution MUST hold exactly the test projects its size requires: Architecture and Integration for small, adding Acceptance for large.
provisions.rationale: The required suites match the size: Architecture and Integration for small, adding Acceptance for large. Unit test projects stay optional in both sizes, and Acceptance stays optional for small. An Acceptance project without the executable BDD extension is an unnamed baseline project: select the extension, or name the project for what it actually is. This provision states the .NET form of `litespec/backend/testing#keep-the-test-suites-the-size-requires`.
provisions.example:
A test suite can contain:

```text
{ProjectName}.Architecture.Tests/
{ProjectName}.Integration.Tests/
{ProjectName}.Acceptance.Tests/
```

A small solution holds the first two; Acceptance appears when the executable BDD extension activates.

provisions.heading: Mirror Modules in Folders and Namespaces
provisions.evidence: Does every project give each module one folder and namespace under its module name? Look at the module folders and namespaces in every project.
provisions.statement: Every project MUST give each module one folder and namespace.
provisions.rationale: The folder name derives from the module identifier, so `module/spending` owns the `Spending` folder in every project, and the namespace follows the folder under `litespec/workspace/naming#keep-namespaces-aligned-with-folders`. The same module names in every layer let a reader move from a Domain aggregate to its handler, its repository, and its endpoint without a map. This provision states the five-project form of the module organization that `litespec/backend/architecture#organize-code-by-module-aggregate-and-use-case` states for the module layout.
provisions.example:
The `Spending` module owns one folder in every project, and each namespace follows its folder:

```text
Claimwick.Domain/Spending/Expenses/Expense.cs
Claimwick.Application/Spending/Expenses/SubmitExpense/SubmitExpenseCommandHandler.cs
```

The handler above lives in namespace `Claimwick.Application.Spending.Expenses.SubmitExpense`.

provisions.heading: Package Each Layer as Its Own Project
provisions.evidence: Does every project fit the five baseline projects, the merged small layout, or the allowed hosts and Worker? Look at the solution file beside the declared project size.
provisions.statement: Use Domain, Application.Abstractions, Application, Infrastructure, and WebApi as the five baseline projects at every size, with a small project merging Application.Abstractions into Application and hosts and a Worker project as allowed extras.
provisions.rationale: `Application.Abstractions` holds the contracts that more than one module names: the pipeline's own positions, the cross-module ports, the transport-neutral failures, and the published integration events. It references Domain and the required LiteBus module abstractions, and nothing else, so no type in it can name a use case, a handler, or a module. That refusal is why shared contracts get a project rather than a folder. A folder inside Application cannot decline what a developer puts in it, so the folder meant for shared contracts becomes the drawer every unplaced type lands in. A small project with few cross-module contracts may merge them into Application, trading that compiler-held separation for one less project. The project name states the admission test: anything that is not a shared abstraction fails it. An implementation never belongs there, and a type that cannot pass the test belongs to a module under `litespec/backend/architecture#place-a-type-at-the-lowest-folder-that-holds-its-consumers`. Hosts support local hosting and diagnostics. They are hosts rather than layer projects, and a Worker project hosts background work under `litespec/backend/architecture#create-a-worker-project-when-background-work-needs-its-own-process`.
provisions.example:
```text
apps/api/src/{ProjectName}.Domain/
apps/api/src/{ProjectName}.Application.Abstractions/
apps/api/src/{ProjectName}.Application/
apps/api/src/{ProjectName}.Infrastructure/
apps/api/src/{ProjectName}.WebApi/
```

provisions.heading: Run the LiteSpec Analyzers in Every Layer Project
provisions.evidence: Does every layer project file reference `LiteSpec.Analyzers` at the manifest pin with `PrivateAssets="all"`? Look at each layer project file.
provisions.statement: Reference `LiteSpec.Analyzers` at the manifest pin, with `PrivateAssets="all"`, from every Domain, Application.Abstractions, Application, Infrastructure, and WebApi project.
provisions.rationale: The analyzers report a breach of a .NET provision in the editor and the build, at the line that breaks it, with a link to the provision. Without them, a breach surfaces only in review, if at all. The package is a development dependency: it adds nothing to the built assemblies, so Domain stays package-free at run time. `LS2016` reports a pipeline-owned collaborator in a handler constructor; its default list covers the LiteBus unit of work, idempotency store, and outbox, and a project adds its uniqueness claim service. [Check .NET code with the analyzers](../../../analyzers/check-dotnet-code-with-the-analyzers.md) sets it up, and [Analyzer rules](../../../analyzers/README.md) lists what each rule reports.
provisions.example:
```xml
<ItemGroup>
  <PackageReference Include="LiteSpec.Analyzers" PrivateAssets="all" />
</ItemGroup>
```

provisions.heading: Use the Domain Module Layout
provisions.evidence: Does every Domain module folder hold one plural folder per aggregate with states, events, exceptions, and concepts? Look at each module folder.
provisions.statement: Give each aggregate a folder named with its plural root name, holding its states, events, exceptions, and concepts in the files this provision names.
provisions.rationale: Each aggregate folder holds everything one aggregate owns in the files the layout names, so a reader finds the full aggregate in one place. Namespaces follow the folders under `litespec/workspace/naming#keep-namespaces-aligned-with-folders`, and each file sits at the lowest folder holding its consumers under `litespec/backend/architecture#place-a-type-at-the-lowest-folder-that-holds-its-consumers`. Each aggregate-specific repository interface stays with the aggregate it loads. Application, Infrastructure, and WebApi use the same module and per-aggregate folder names, per `litespec/backend/dotnet/ext/layer-projects#mirror-modules-in-folders-and-namespaces`.

provisions.heading: Use the Endpoint Folder Layout
provisions.evidence: Does every endpoint folder hold the endpoint, request and response models, and mappings named for the use case? Look at each endpoint folder.
provisions.statement: Place each endpoint in a folder named for its use case under its module and aggregate, with the files this provision names.
provisions.rationale: The folder path matches the specification path, so a reader locates an operation from its use-case identifier without searching. Transport types take the names their boundary roles assign under `litespec/backend/api#name-transport-types-by-their-boundary-role`, and transport mapping lives in WebApi under `litespec/backend/application#keep-mappings-at-the-owning-boundary`. Response models carry the query's declared `include` groups. Module nesting, including the single-aggregate flat form, follows `litespec/backend/architecture#organize-code-by-module-aggregate-and-use-case`.

provisions.heading: Use the Operation Folder Layout
provisions.evidence: Does every operation folder hold message, result, validator, and handler files named for the use case, with event handlers and jobs in the folder of what they run? Look at each operation folder.
provisions.statement: Place each operation in a folder named for its use case under its module and aggregate, with the files this provision names.
provisions.rationale: The folder path matches the specification path, so a reader locates an operation from its use-case identifier without searching. Type names derive from the use-case identifier with the architectural suffix, so `use-case/spending.submit-expense` owns `SubmitExpenseCommand` under `litespec/workspace/naming#use-architectural-suffixes`. Only a use case gets an operation folder: any other type sits flat in the folder that owns it under `litespec/backend/architecture#place-a-type-at-the-lowest-folder-that-holds-its-consumers`. An event handler or job that runs a use case sits in that use case's operation folder; one that runs none sits in the module `Notifications/` or `ExternalSystems/` folder named for what it sends or calls, under `litespec/workspace/naming#place-each-trigger-with-what-it-runs`. Each result type carries one case per result, and each refusal carries the refusal `code` from its result record. A query result type carries one member per declared `include` group, and each result part is named after its result under `litespec/workspace/naming#name-result-parts-after-their-result`.

Module and aggregate order, including the single-aggregate flat form, follow `litespec/backend/architecture#organize-code-by-module-aggregate-and-use-case`.

provisions.heading: Use the Project Reference Graph
provisions.evidence: Does every project file reference only the permitted edges of the graph table? Look at each project file beside the graph table.
provisions.statement: A project reference MUST follow the graph in the table in this section and add no other edge.
provisions.rationale: An undeclared reference lets a layer reach past its boundary. The table names every permitted edge, so composition stays in the hosts, each project names only the layers its job needs, and review has a written graph to hold new references against. A small project merged under `litespec/backend/dotnet/ext/layer-projects#package-each-layer-as-its-own-project` has no Application.Abstractions row; its remaining rows still bind. This provision states the project form of the layer graph that `litespec/workspace/dependencies#follow-the-declared-dependency-graph` declares.
provisions.example:
| Project | may reference |
|:---|:---|
| Domain | None |
| Application.Abstractions | Domain |
| Application | Domain, Application.Abstractions |
| Infrastructure | Domain, Application.Abstractions, Application |
| WebApi | Application.Abstractions, Application, Infrastructure |
| Worker | Application.Abstractions, Application, Infrastructure |
| AppHost | Deployable host projects through Aspire resource references |
| Test projects | Only production projects and test support needed by their test category |

`WebApi` references Infrastructure for composition in `Program.cs`. Endpoint implementations take their dependencies from Application abstractions, not from Infrastructure repositories, sessions, or provider clients.

provisions.heading: Apply Architectural Role Suffixes
provisions.evidence: `dotnet build` reports `LS2005` for a handler missing its command or query suffix, `LS2006` for an endpoint missing its suffix, and `LS2007` for a reaction or job whose name hides its kind.
provisions.statement: In the dotnet stack, a handler, endpoint, reaction, or job MUST carry the suffix its role assigns in the Role Suffixes table.
provisions.rationale: The suffix states the architectural role in the name, so a reader and a tool tell command coordination, projection, and boundaries apart without opening the file. This provision binds `litespec/workspace/naming#use-architectural-suffixes` for .NET.

provisions.heading: Keep Implementation Style Consistent
provisions.evidence: `dotnet build` reports `LS3004` for a concrete class with no derived type that is not sealed.
provisions.statement: Production C# MUST use file-scoped namespaces, braces on every body, explicit access modifiers, and sealed concrete classes.
provisions.rationale: File-scoped namespaces, braces on every body, explicit access modifiers, and sealed concrete classes change diff readability rather than behavior. One shared setting removes the debate from every review and keeps generated and hand-written code alike.

provisions.heading: Match C# Files and Primary Types
provisions.evidence: `dotnet build` reports `LS3003` for a C# file whose name differs from its primary type.
provisions.statement: A C# file MUST contain one primary top-level type and take that type's exact name.
provisions.rationale: A file named for its type lets a reader and a tool find the type by the path. Two top-level types in one file break that lookup and merge their histories in review. Only a small private or file-scoped nested type stays with its owner.

provisions.heading: Name Every Folder and Type for Its Reason
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `name-reason-missing` (level S) for a folder or type named for the absence of a reason outside the declared shared kernel.
provisions.statement: No folder is named `Shared`, `Common`, `Util`, `Utils`, `Helpers`, or `Misc`, and no type carries one of those names or ends in `Helper`, `Manager`, `Util`, or `Utils`, outside the declared shared kernel.
provisions.rationale: A folder named `Shared` or a type ending in `Manager` tells the reader the author found no reason to name, and each such name becomes the drawer where unrelated code gathers. The shared kernel project is the one declared exception, named in one place, so the exception stays visible instead of spreading.
provisions.example: The declared shared kernel project passes; `Billing/Helpers/` and `OrderManager` outside it are reported.

provisions.heading: Name Repository Variables After Their Interface
provisions.evidence: `dotnet build` reports `LS2010` for a repository parameter, field, or local whose name does not follow its interface.
provisions.statement: In the dotnet stack, a repository parameter, field, or local MUST be named after its interface without the `I` prefix.
provisions.rationale: Naming the variable after its interface keeps one name per repository at every use site. This provision binds `litespec/workspace/naming#name-repository-variables-after-their-interface` for .NET.

provisions.heading: Name Result Parts After Their Result
provisions.evidence: `dotnet build` reports `LS2009` for a type a use-case result reaches through its properties whose name does not start with the result name.
provisions.statement: In the dotnet stack, a type a use-case result reaches through its properties MUST be named after the result it belongs to.
provisions.rationale: A result part named for its result keeps each part beside the result it belongs to and avoids collisions between use cases shaping the same concept. This provision binds `litespec/workspace/naming#name-result-parts-after-their-result` for .NET.

provisions.heading: Put the Cancellation Token Last
provisions.evidence: `dotnet build` reports `LS3002` for a cancellation token that is misplaced or misnamed.
provisions.statement: In the dotnet stack, a method that takes a `CancellationToken` MUST place it last, or second to last before a `params` array, and name it `cancellationToken`.
provisions.rationale: A token in a fixed trailing position lets every caller pass cancellation without reading the signature, and one name lets every reader tell the token from the data beside it. A token buried mid-signature is passed in the wrong position, and a renamed token hides what it is where the method is called.
provisions.example: `SubmitExpenseCommandHandler.HandleAsync` takes `SubmitExpenseCommand command` and then `CancellationToken cancellationToken`, so a caller passes the data first and cancellation last.

provisions.heading: Raise the LiteBus Handler Analyzers to Errors
provisions.evidence: Does `.editorconfig` set `LB1023` and `LB1024` to error and list `litebus.LB1024.forbidden_types`? Look at `.editorconfig`.
provisions.statement: A project using LiteBus sets `LB1023` and `LB1024` to `error` in `.editorconfig` and lists its outside-world client types in `litebus.LB1024.forbidden_types`.
provisions.rationale: Both LiteBus rules are off by default, so a command handler can quietly send a second message or call an outside system with no report. `LB1023` reports nested mediation in a command handler and `LB1024` reports an outside-world client in a command handler, so consequences leave through event handlers after the commit under `litespec/backend/application#keep-command-handlers-to-load-call-and-stage`. The client list replaces the defaults, so it names every port that leaves the process. The same file lists the project pipeline-owned collaborators under the key the [Configuration section of the LS2016 rule page](../../analyzers/rules/ls2016.md#configuration) names, such as its uniqueness claim service.
provisions.example:
```text
dotnet_diagnostic.LB1023.severity = error
dotnet_diagnostic.LB1024.severity = error
litebus.LB1024.forbidden_types = Claimwick.Payouts.PayoutBankClient
litespec.LS2016.pipeline_owned_types = Claimwick.Spending.ExpenseKeyClaims
```

provisions.heading: Reference Only the LiteBus Module Required
provisions.evidence: Does every project file reference only the LiteBus modules its code dispatches? Look at each project file.
provisions.statement: Reference the LiteBus command, query, or event module that the code actually uses.
provisions.rationale: A unified bus package pulls contracts for commands, queries, and events into a layer that dispatches only some of them. Referencing only the module the code uses keeps each dispatch surface exact.

provisions.heading: Run LiteSpec Analyzers in the Business Projects and Hosts
provisions.evidence: Does every shared kernel, modules, and host project file reference `LiteSpec.Analyzers` at the manifest pin with `PrivateAssets="all"`? Look at each business and host project file.
provisions.statement: Reference `LiteSpec.Analyzers` at the manifest pin, with `PrivateAssets="all"`, from the shared kernel and modules projects and each host project.
provisions.rationale: The analyzers report a breach of a .NET provision in the editor and the build, at the line that breaks it, with a link to the provision. Without them, a breach surfaces only in review, if at all. The package is a development dependency: it adds nothing to the built assemblies, so Domain stays package-free at run time. `LS2016` reports a pipeline-owned collaborator in a handler constructor; its default list covers the LiteBus unit of work, idempotency store, and outbox, and a project adds its uniqueness claim service. [Check .NET code with the analyzers](../../analyzers/check-dotnet-code-with-the-analyzers.md) sets it up, and [Analyzer rules](../../analyzers/README.md) lists what each rule reports.
provisions.example:
```xml
<ItemGroup>
  <PackageReference Include="LiteSpec.Analyzers" PrivateAssets="all" />
</ItemGroup>
```

provisions.heading: Apply Optimistic Concurrency to Every Aggregate Document
provisions.evidence: Does every Marten aggregate document type enable optimistic concurrency? Look at each document type and the document policy.
provisions.statement: Each Marten aggregate document type MUST enable optimistic concurrency.
provisions.rationale: The store compares the version each command loaded with the version it commits against, so a stale write fails the commit instead of silently overwriting newer work. Each aggregate document type enables it with `UseOptimisticConcurrency(true)`, or one `Policies.ForAllDocuments` policy covers every aggregate document type at once; no aggregate document type is left without it. This provision binds `litespec/backend/persistence#version-every-aggregate` for .NET.
provisions.example:
The expense document enables the check on its own type:

```csharp
options.Schema.For<ExpenseDocument>().UseOptimisticConcurrency(true);
```

provisions.heading: Claim Cross-Record Keys with a Claims Document
provisions.evidence: Is every cross-record key claimed through a claims document written with `session.Insert`, never with `Store`? Look at each key claim.
provisions.statement: Each cross-record uniqueness key MUST be claimed through a claims document keyed by the key text and written with `session.Insert`, never with `Store`.
provisions.rationale: Some keys admit no index: Marten cannot index elements of a list inside a document, cannot enforce uniqueness across document types, and computed indexes do not work on `DateTime` or `DateTimeOffset` members. Those keys are claimed through a small document whose id is the key text, so the store still arbitrates the race. The write uses `Insert`, which fails when the key document already exists; `Store` upserts, so it would overwrite a competing claim instead of colliding with it. The repository compares the aggregate keys at load with the keys at commit, and inserts the added key documents and deletes the removed ones in the same transaction. This provision binds `litespec/backend/persistence#claim-a-cross-record-key-at-commit` for .NET.

provisions.heading: Commit Once in the Command Pipeline
provisions.evidence: Does exactly one post-handler file call `SaveChangesAsync` in each pipeline? Look at the `SaveChangesAsync` calls in each pipeline.
provisions.statement: Exactly one global command post-handler MUST call `SaveChangesAsync` for a command pipeline.
provisions.rationale: When exactly one post-handler commits, a failed command leaves the scoped session uncommitted and no partial work persists. A second committer, in a handler, repository, validator, reaction, job, or endpoint, would store work the pipeline later refuses. This provision binds `litespec/backend/persistence#commit-each-command-pipeline-once` for .NET. The obligation is one commit per pipeline, not one named method. Under the baseline provider that commit is `IDocumentSession.SaveChangesAsync`. Under `consistency: atomic` it covers everything the handler staged. Other modes split work across commands: each command still commits once, and the job resumes from its cursor or runs the declared compensation.

provisions.heading: Enforce Uniqueness with Marten Unique Indexes
provisions.evidence: Does every Marten aggregate document with a uniqueness rule carry a unique index or an owner-derived identity? Look at the store configuration.
provisions.statement: Each Marten aggregate document MUST enforce its uniqueness rules through a unique index over the stored value or an identity derived from its owner.
provisions.rationale: A unique index makes the store arbitrate the race at commit, where every concurrent write is visible. The index is declared with `options.Schema.For<T>().UniqueIndex`, or as a computed index carrying `IsUnique`, and the index name follows `litespec/backend/persistence#use-database-naming-conventions`. A record that exists at most once per owner takes a document id equal to the owner id instead, so a second record for the same owner collides on identity. This provision binds `litespec/backend/persistence#enforce-uniqueness-in-the-store` for .NET.
provisions.example:
The payout number is unique per spending owner:

```csharp
options.Schema.For<PayoutDocument>().UniqueIndex(
    UniqueIndexType.Computed,
    "uq_payout_owner_number",
    x => x.PayoutNumber);
```

A payout exists at most once per expense, so its document id is the expense id:

```csharp
// The payout document id equals the expense id: one payout per expense.
session.Store(new PayoutDocument(expense.Id, payoutNumber));
```

provisions.heading: Keep Pipeline-Owned Collaborators Out of Handlers
provisions.evidence: `dotnet build` reports `LS2016` for a command or query handler whose constructor takes a pipeline-owned type.
provisions.statement: A command or query handler MUST NOT take a pipeline-owned collaborator, such as `IUnitOfWork`, `IIdempotencyStore`, or `ITransactionalOutbox`, through its constructor.
provisions.rationale: The pipeline owns the unit of work, the idempotency store, the outbox, and the uniqueness claim service. A handler that takes one of them commits or reserves work outside the post-handler that owns the commit. The analyzer's default list names the LiteBus types, and a project adds its own claim service to the `litespec.LS2016.pipeline_owned_types` key. This provision binds `litespec/backend/persistence#keep-uniqueness-out-of-handlers` for .NET.
provisions.example: The submit-expense handler takes its Domain repository and no unit of work, so the commit stays in the one post-handler. A handler constructor that adds `IUnitOfWork` is reported at the parameter.

provisions.heading: Map Constraint Violations with the PostgreSQL Refusal Classifier
provisions.evidence: Does every unique index name map to its conflict refusal code in the PostgreSQL refusal classifier? Look at the service registration.
provisions.statement: Each Marten unique index MUST map by name to its conflict refusal code in `PostgreSqlConstraintRefusalClassifier`.
provisions.rationale: The `LiteBus.Storage.PostgreSql.PostgreSqlConstraintRefusalClassifier` carries the map from index name to refusal code and is registered through `UseFaultRefusalClassifierInstance`, so the pipeline fault classification turns a unique violation into the use case named conflict refusal under `litespec/backend/application#refuse-a-lost-race-as-a-conflict`. This provision binds `litespec/backend/persistence#map-a-constraint-violation-to-its-refusal` for .NET.

provisions.heading: Map Marten Concurrency Faults to Conflict Refusals
provisions.evidence: Does every `ConcurrencyException` path at commit reach the use case conflict refusal? Look at the registered classifier.
provisions.statement: A classifier MUST translate Marten's `ConcurrencyException` into the use case conflict refusal.
provisions.rationale: A `ConcurrencyException` names a provider type that Application does not expose. The registered classifier translates it into the use case named conflict refusal, following `litespec/backend/application#refuse-a-lost-race-as-a-conflict`, so a version race and a uniqueness race reach the caller through the same refusal path. This provision binds `litespec/backend/application#refuse-a-lost-race-as-a-conflict` for .NET.
provisions.example: Two approvers race on one submitted expense; the loser throws `ConcurrencyException` at commit, and the classifier returns the approve conflict refusal so the caller re-reads the expense before deciding again.

provisions.heading: Query Through IQuerySession
provisions.evidence: Does every query handler project through `IQuerySession`, with filter, scope, ordering, and limit applied before materialization? Look at each query handler file.
provisions.statement: A query handler MUST project through `IQuerySession`, applying filter, scope, ordering, and limit before materialization.
provisions.rationale: The read session already filters, orders, pages, and projects. A read-store interface per aggregate, a generic read repository, or a callback wrapper adds a layer that repeats it. Ordering and paging follow `litespec/backend/api#bound-collection-queries`. This provision binds `litespec/backend/persistence#query-through-the-read-session` for .NET. | Provider | Query surface | |:---|:---| | Marten baseline | `IQuerySession` | The table names the binding per provider. The obligation to project with filter, scope, ordering, and limit holds under each. A table the project keeps beside its documents, such as a counter or an append-only ledger written through plain SQL, is read through the same session. Under Marten, `AdvancedSql.QueryAsync<TRow>` returns any JSON-serializable type, so the SQL selects one JSON object per row, keyed in the casing the store's serializer uses, with the filter, ordering, and limit in its `WHERE`, `ORDER BY`, and `LIMIT`. The handler keeps no repository for such a table, and the project adds no read interface for it.
provisions.example:
In the Claimwick product, each spending owner's running totals live in a `spending_totals` table that a command updates in place. The read-spending-totals query reads it through the session:

```csharp
internal sealed record SpendingTotalRow(Guid OwnerId, string Currency, decimal Submitted, decimal Approved);

var rows = await session.AdvancedSql.QueryAsync<SpendingTotalRow>(
    """
    select jsonb_build_object(
        'ownerId', owner_id, 'currency', currency, 'submitted', submitted, 'approved', approved)
    from spending_totals
    where owner_id = ?
    order by currency
    limit 100
    """,
    cancellationToken,
    query.OwnerId.Value);
```

provisions.heading: Register One Scoped Session
provisions.evidence: Does the service registration wire `IDocumentSession` once per WebApi request or Worker operation scope? Look at the service registration.
provisions.statement: Register `IDocumentSession` with the WebApi request or Worker operation scope.
provisions.rationale: One session per WebApi request or Worker operation means the repositories and the commit handler in one command resolve the same instance. Two sessions would stage and commit separately, splitting one command across two units of work. This provision binds `litespec/backend/persistence#use-one-session-per-command` for .NET.

provisions.heading: Stage Aggregate Writes Through Repositories
provisions.evidence: `dotnet build` reports `LS2004` for a command handler writing through a document session or database context.
provisions.statement: A command handler MUST reach persistence only through a Domain repository, never through `IDocumentSession`.
provisions.rationale: Infrastructure implements each Domain repository with the scoped session, so the handler stages work without naming a provider type. A repository that exposed the session, a generic query, or a save operation would hand the handler the provider surface the layer exists to hide. This provision binds `litespec/backend/persistence#stage-aggregate-writes-through-domain-repositories` for .NET.

provisions.heading: Use the Persistence Layer Folder Layout
provisions.evidence: Does every Marten configuration, repository, commit, and serialization file sit in its shared kernel or module Infrastructure folder? Look at the persistence files.
provisions.statement: Place Marten configuration, repositories, commit behavior, and serialization in the shared kernel and module Infrastructure folders this provision names.
provisions.rationale: One store stays the default, configured in the shared kernel Infrastructure folder, while each module's mappings and repositories live in its own Infrastructure folders, so every persistence type has one discoverable home. Scattered configuration hides the provider setup across the product. This provision binds `litespec/backend/persistence#use-one-persistence-folder` for .NET.
provisions.example:
```text
{Product}.SharedKernel/
  Infrastructure/
    Marten/
      MartenServiceRegistration.cs
      MartenStoreConfiguration.cs
      Commit/
        SaveChangesCommandPostHandler.cs
      Events/
        DomainEventBuffer.cs
{Product}.Modules/
  Posts/                            single aggregate whose name matches the module: files directly under the module
    Infrastructure/
      PostRepository.cs
      PostMartenConfiguration.cs
  Customers/                        two aggregates: one folder per aggregate
    CustomerAccounts/
      Infrastructure/
        CustomerAccountRepository.cs
        CustomerAccountMartenConfiguration.cs
    Consents/
      Infrastructure/
        ConsentRepository.cs
        ConsentMartenConfiguration.cs
```

The module folders follow `litespec/backend/architecture#organize-code-by-module-aggregate-and-use-case`. A single-aggregate module stays flat when its aggregate root plural name equals the module name. For example, `Post` stays flat under `Posts`. Otherwise, each aggregate takes its own folder.

Aggregate-specific configuration stays beside its aggregate, while session and commit plumbing stay in the shared kernel Infrastructure folder.

provisions.heading: Declare `dotnet` as the Backend Stack
provisions.evidence: Does `.litespec/project.yaml` list `dotnet` in `stacks` when the backend runs on .NET? Check `.litespec/project.yaml`.
provisions.statement: A project whose backend runs on .NET MUST name `dotnet` in the `stacks` of `.litespec/project.yaml`.
provisions.rationale: The `stacks` entry applies every page in this folder with its checks and analyzers. An undeclared backend follows no .NET rule, and the model builder selects no readers for its C# handlers, events, refusal codes, and scenarios.

provisions.heading: Declare Marked Events and Exceptions as Partial Types
provisions.evidence: `dotnet build` reports `LS5006` for a marked domain event or rule exception that is not `partial`, in every project that references the analyzer package.
provisions.statement: A project that references the analyzer package MUST declare every marked domain event and rule exception as a `partial` type.
provisions.rationale: The source generator adds the runtime value as a second part of the type, and a type that is not `partial` cannot take one. The generator writes a value only where no member of that name is declared in source, so a hand-written value is compared with the record rather than duplicated. A code fix adds `partial` and deletes a hand-written value that equals the record.
provisions.example: The declaration `public sealed partial record ExpenseSubmittedEvent(...)` takes its generated `Classification`, while the same record without `partial` is reported.

provisions.heading: Generate Runtime Values from the Records
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `runtime-value-drift` (level S) for a hand-written value that differs from its record, and `dotnet build` reports `LS5005` for the same value.
provisions.statement: A domain event `Classification` and a domain exception `Code` MUST equal the values their records state.
provisions.rationale: The record states each identifier and refusal code once. A second hand-written copy in code is a second source that drifts. With the analyzer package installed, its source generator writes the value into the `partial` type from the mark and the record: the event `Classification` is the event identifier, and the exception `Code` is the `code` of the refusal result its rule names. Without the analyzer package, the value stays hand-written, and the check compares it with the record.

provisions.heading: Generate the Registry, Permissions, and Roles from the Records
provisions.evidence: `dotnet build` reports `LS5009` for two records generating one constant name, `LS5011` for a message two marked handlers serve with different use cases, and `LS5012` for a role allowing a permission no record declares.
provisions.statement: Code MUST read a use case's identity, its grant, a permission's facts, and a role's permission set from the classes the analyzer package generates from the marks and the records, never from a hand-written copy.
provisions.rationale: Each of these facts is written once, on a record or in a mark. A hand-written table of them is a second source that drifts the first time a record changes. The generator writes them per project: `LiteSpecRegistry` answers a message type's use case (`UseCaseOf`), a marked type's use case (`UseCaseOfType`), a message type's grant (`GrantOf`), and in an API project an operation name's use case (`UseCaseOfOperation`); `LiteSpecPermissions` holds one constant and one entry per `permission/` record; and `LiteSpecRoles` holds each role's scope and the permissions its record allows. In the module layout the modules project generates all three, and the host beside it reads them from there; the shared kernel project generates none, and the host generates only `LiteSpecHostOperations`, which answers `UseCaseOfOperation` for the endpoints the host itself holds. A role that names a permission no record declares, and two records that generate one name, stop at build time.
provisions.example: When Claimwick's `role/finance` record gains a permission, `LiteSpecRoles.Of("role/finance").Allows` carries it at the next build with no hand-written table to update, and `LiteSpecRegistry.GrantOf(typeof(ReimburseExpenseCommand))` answers the reimbursement grant.

provisions.heading: Identify an Aggregate Root by Its Mark and State Record
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `aggregate-unimplemented` (level S) for an aggregate record that no type with its mark and its state record, and no type deriving the aggregate root base, implements.
provisions.statement: The .NET stack reader MUST recognize a type that carries an `aggregate` mark and a `State` property backed by an abstract state record as an aggregate root.
provisions.rationale: A project that claims Implementation with `own` keeps its own code layout and its own aggregate base, so a root that follows the LiteSpec base type is not the only root the code holds. The aggregate mark names the record the type implements, and the state record states its lifecycle; together they identify the root without the base type. A type with only the mark, or only the state record, does not state both facts, so it stays unrecognized. This provision states the `trace: yes` reading of the aggregate root beside `litespec/backend/dotnet/domain#use-the-project-aggregate-root-contract`, which governs the full contract.
provisions.example: The library loan type carries `/// <implements>aggregate/lending.loan</implements>` with a `LoanState State` property backed by the abstract `LoanState` record, so the reader treats it as the loan aggregate root and reads its public methods as aggregate methods.

provisions.heading: Pin the Test Packages in the Manifest
provisions.evidence: Does every test project reference each test package at its manifest-pinned version? Check each test project file beside the package pins in `litespec.manifest.yaml`.
provisions.statement: A .NET test project MUST reference each test package at the version `litespec.manifest.yaml` pins.
provisions.rationale: A test package that moves to a newer version changes what the tests prove without any change to the code under test. The manifest is the one place the release names its pins, so the test SDK, the Microsoft.Testing.Platform extensions, the xUnit runner, the property-test and mock libraries, and the PostgreSQL container each resolve to the version the release reviewed.

provisions.heading: Read Every Declared Web and Worker Host
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `reader-missing` (level S) for a named host folder that does not exist, and reads the handlers, endpoints and jobs of each named host that does.
provisions.statement: The .NET stack reader MUST read every project that `stackConfig.dotnet.webapi` and `stackConfig.dotnet.worker` name, whether each field holds one glob string or a list of glob strings.
provisions.rationale: A backend can serve its use cases from more than one web host and run more than one worker host, and each host holds endpoints or jobs the others do not. Reading only the first host leaves the use cases that only the other hosts serve looking unimplemented. Each named host is therefore a source root of the read. A host that is not a WebApi or worker project, such as a command-line host, is not a stack root.
provisions.example: Claimwick serves member requests from one web host and partner requests from a second, so `webapi` lists both host projects and the reader reads the endpoints of each.

provisions.heading: Read .NET Code Through the Stack Reader
provisions.evidence: Does the .NET reader read every shape the statement names? Check the stack reader source for marks, injected repositories, returned codes, dispatch calls, aggregate method calls, raised events, and test results.
provisions.statement: The .NET stack reader MUST read marks in both styles, injected repositories, returned codes, dispatch calls, aggregate method calls, raised events, and test results.
provisions.rationale: Each level S check reads one of those shapes. The mark links a code element to its record: a handler, an event handler, an endpoint, an aggregate root and its methods, a domain event, a refusal type, and a test each name what they serve. The reader reads a mark in either style and reports the style the project did not declare. Injected repositories prove `writes`: a repository serves the aggregate its implementing class names in an `implements` mark, or, with no such mark, the aggregate its interface names. Returned codes prove declared results and refusals, and dispatch calls prove declared effects, so the reader reports `behavior-unrecorded`, `use-case-unimplemented`, `write-undeclared`, `result-undeclared`, `effect-undeclared`, and `refusal-unimplemented` from code. Test marks with the latest test run prove each scenario, so the reader reports `proves-unreached` and `use-case-scenario-missing` from tests. The reader also reads the options classes that bind keyed settings, through each class's `SectionName` constant and properties, and the template store `stackConfig.dotnet.templateStore` names: one C# file whose top-level dictionary initializer keys are the template keys and whose texts write each parameter as `{{PascalCaseName}}`. Level S checks block where this reader is qualified and report elsewhere.
provisions.example: Claimwick's reimburse-expense handler carries `/// <implements>use-case/spending.reimburse-expense</implements>`, and its approver-reminder event handler carries `/// <implements>reaction/spending.send-approver-reminder-on-expense-submitted</implements>`.

provisions.heading: Report a Stack Root That Matches No Folder
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `reader-missing` (level S) naming the field, the written pattern and the resolved folder that does not exist.
provisions.statement: The model builder MUST report `reader-missing` for a configured .NET stack root that matches no folder, and for the default modules root, and the default Domain and Infrastructure roots under the layer-projects layout, when that default matches no folder in a project that selects the .NET reader.
provisions.rationale: A root that matches no folder reads no source, so the records that source would implement are not gaps in the product: the tool read nothing where it expected code. Reporting the missing root beside the unimplemented findings lets a reader tell a reader gap from a product gap. The WebApi, worker, and shared kernel defaults name hosts and a kernel that a valid project may omit, so a missing default for those roots stays silent, and only a configured host or kernel path reports.
provisions.example: A library project that keeps its code under a product folder and names no stack root reports `reader-missing` for the default modules root instead of reporting every aggregate and use case as unimplemented.

provisions.heading: Run Mutation Testing with Stryker.NET
provisions.evidence: Does the mutation gate run Stryker.NET at the version the root tool manifest pins? Check `.config/dotnet-tools.json` and the mutation job's command.
provisions.statement: Run the mutation gate with the Stryker.NET runner that the root tool manifest pins.
provisions.rationale: Stryker.NET is the .NET runner for the mutation gate that `litespec/quality/testing#refuse-surviving-mutants-on-changed-lines` names, and the root tool manifest pins its version, so a developer and CI run the same mutants against the same tool.

provisions.heading: Start the Integration Database in a Container
provisions.evidence: Does the integration test project start the pinned PostgreSQL in a Testcontainers container for every run? Check the integration fixture and the Testcontainers package reference.
provisions.statement: The .NET integration test project MUST start the pinned PostgreSQL in a Testcontainers container.
provisions.rationale: A container from the pinned image gives every test run the database version the release runs. It starts and stops with the test run, so no shared server carries state from one run to the next. The fixture that owns the container is the one `litespec/backend/testing#share-one-production-faithful-integration-harness` names.

provisions.heading: Test with xUnit v3 on Microsoft.Testing.Platform
provisions.evidence: Does every test project reference xUnit v3 and run on Microsoft.Testing.Platform, with `global.json` naming that runner? Check each test project file and `global.json`.
provisions.statement: A .NET test project MUST reference xUnit v3 and run on Microsoft.Testing.Platform, with `global.json` naming that runner.
provisions.rationale: The .NET 10 `dotnet test` command refuses the VSTest mode for xUnit v3 projects. Each test project therefore runs on the platform runner, and the root `global.json` states that choice once for every project beneath it. A project that runs on another runner reports its results in a shape the model builder does not read, so its passing tests prove nothing.

provisions.heading: Write Each Mark in the Declared Style
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `mark-style-invalid` (level S), and `dotnet build` reports `LS5004`, for a mark written in the style the project did not declare.
provisions.statement: A .NET mark MUST be an `implements`, `proves`, or `follows` documentation tag when `marks` is `xml`, and an `Implements`, `Proves`, or `Follows` attribute when `marks` is `attribute`.
provisions.rationale: The `xml` style keeps business code free of attributes that are not of the business, with the mark as a documentation tag read by the stack reader and the analyzers, which need the documentation file every LiteSpec project already generates. The `attribute` style carries the mark into metadata, so it survives compilation and reflection can read it. Its attribute types are generated into each project as internal types by the analyzer package, so no runtime package is referenced, and Domain stays free of outer-layer dependencies. A code element takes one mark per record, and a code fix converts a mark between the styles. This provision states the .NET form of `litespec/core/model#declare-one-mark-style`.
provisions.example:
In the `xml` style, Claimwick's reimbursement handler carries its marks as documentation tags:

```csharp
/// <summary>Reimburses an approved expense.</summary>
/// <implements>use-case/spending.reimburse-expense</implements>
/// <follows>litespec/backend/application#keep-command-handlers-to-load-call-and-stage</follows>
internal sealed class ReimburseExpenseCommandHandler(IExpenseRepository expenseRepository)
```

In the `attribute` style, the same handler carries them as attributes:

```csharp
[Implements("use-case/spending.reimburse-expense")]
[Follows("litespec/backend/application#keep-command-handlers-to-load-call-and-stage")]
internal sealed class ReimburseExpenseCommandHandler(IExpenseRepository expenseRepository)
```

provisions.heading: Write Test Results the Model Builder Reads
provisions.evidence: Does every test run write TRX or JUnit XML under `paths.testResults`? Check the test run output beside `paths.testResults` in `.litespec/project.yaml`.
provisions.statement: A .NET test run MUST write its results as TRX or JUnit XML under `paths.testResults`.
provisions.rationale: The model builder computes verified status from TRX and JUnit XML only. A run written in another format, or outside `paths.testResults`, proves no scenario even when every test passes, so green tests would show as unproven. A JUnit `testcase` proves a Behavior scenario without a `proves` mark by carrying the scenario id in a `litespec.proves` property, one property per scenario or several ids separated by commas in one value; the case proves each id it names with the same rules as a `proves` mark on a test method.

provisions.heading: List Every Deployable Unit in the Root Solution
provisions.evidence: Does the root solution list more than one deployable unit, with builds, test runs, and configuration still naming the API solution? Look at the solution files beside the build configuration.
provisions.statement: A root solution MUST list the .NET projects of more than one deployable unit, with builds, test runs, and configuration still naming the API solution.
provisions.rationale: A workspace with a second .NET deployable, such as a command-line tool, otherwise has no single file an editor can open across both. The root solution gives editors that view, while the API solution stays at `apps/api/` and remains the one builds and test runs name. Two solution files listing overlapping projects are a supported MSBuild arrangement, and the projects stay where `litespec/workspace/structure#keep-production-and-test-code-separate` puts them.
provisions.example: A workspace with an API and a command-line tool carries `apps/api/{Product}.slnx`, `apps/cli/{Product}.Cli.slnx` where one exists, and a root `{Product}.slnx` listing both sets.

provisions.heading: Place a Workspace AppHost Beside the Applications It Runs
provisions.evidence: Does every AppHost sit in the placed home for what it runs? Look at each AppHost path beside the applications it runs.
provisions.statement: An AppHost that runs more than one application under `apps/` MUST live at `apps/apphost/{ProjectName}.AppHost/` rather than under `apps/api/src/`.
provisions.rationale: An AppHost that runs the API and its dependencies alone stays under `apps/api/src/` with the projects it hosts. An AppHost that also runs the frontends orchestrates the workspace rather than the API: under `apps/api/src/` it reads as one of the API's layers while reaching out of that tree for every frontend it starts. Beside the applications it runs, its path says what it serves. `ServiceDefaults` stays under `apps/api/src/`, because the API references it and the AppHost does not.
provisions.example:
A workspace with an API and three frontends carries:

```text
apps/
  api/
    src/
      {Product}.WebApi/
    tests/
      {Product}.Architecture.Tests/   references the AppHost for its model tests
  apphost/
    {Product}.AppHost/
      {Product}.AppHost.csproj
      Program.cs
  {frontend}/
```

The workspace solution of `litespec/backend/dotnet/workspace#list-every-deployable-unit-in-the-root-solution` lists the AppHost, and the API solution lists it too when a test project references it.

provisions.heading: Add Read Documents for Query-Shaped Data
provisions.evidence: Is any read document missing recorded consistency and rebuild behavior beside its owning use case? Look at each read document.
provisions.statement: Add a module-owned read document for repeated cross-aggregate composition, deep traversal, or a distorting index shape.
provisions.rationale: Aggregate documents serve simple reads. Repeated cross-aggregate composition or deep traversal through them loads whole aggregates to show a few fields. A module-owned read document carries that shape directly, and its owning use case defines its consistency and rebuild behavior.

provisions.heading: Assign Document Numbers from a Sequence
provisions.evidence: Is any legal document number allocated outside a per-owner sequence taken in the command transaction? Look at each number allocation.
provisions.statement: Each legal document number MUST allocate from a per-owner sequence taken in the command transaction.
provisions.rationale: A number computed from a count plus one hands two concurrent issues the same legal number. A per-owner counter row taken in the command transaction allocates each number once, no matter what races it.
provisions.example: The reimburse-expense command takes its number from the spending payout sequence, not from a list count.

provisions.heading: Claim a Cross-Record Key at Commit
provisions.evidence: Is any cross-record uniqueness rule missing declared keys, or claiming and releasing them outside the committing transaction? Look at each such rule beside its commit.
provisions.statement: A uniqueness rule that no single-record constraint can express MUST be declared by the aggregate as a key and claimed and released by persistence in the commit that changes the aggregate.
provisions.rationale: Some rules fit no single-record constraint: a value held in a list inside the aggregate, or a value that is unique across two record kinds. A check in code sees only its own transaction and passes two racing writers. For those rules, the aggregate declares its current keys through `UniquenessKeys` (see `litespec/backend/domain#declare-cross-record-keys-on-the-aggregate`). Persistence compares the keys at load with the keys at commit, inserting the added keys and deleting the removed ones in the same transaction, so the database still arbitrates the race.
provisions.example: In the library product, a book holds a list of copy barcodes and each barcode belongs to one book: the book declares each barcode as a key, and the commit that adds a copy claims the new barcode while releasing a removed one. In the Claimwick product, a payout reference that is unique across payouts and adjustments is declared by each aggregate that carries it, so a reference already used by either record blocks the other at commit.

provisions.heading: Collect Events Without a Public Unit of Work
provisions.evidence: Is any touched aggregate missing from the internal event buffer, or any event mechanics exposed through a public type? Look at the repository staging calls beside the post-handler.
provisions.statement: A repository MUST register each touched aggregate with the internal event buffer that the post-handler drains.
provisions.rationale: Pending events leave the process exactly when their write commits, so the post-handler drains the buffer and commits in one place. A public unit-of-work type would expose that mechanics to every handler. The internal buffer keeps it inside the pipeline. Async delivery leaves after the commit succeeds.

provisions.heading: Commit Each Command Pipeline Once
provisions.evidence: Does any pipeline commit outside one command post-handler, or do any handlers, repositories, validators, reactions, jobs, or endpoints commit? Look at the commit calls in each pipeline.
provisions.statement: Exactly one global command post-handler MUST commit the session for a command pipeline.
provisions.rationale: One commit point makes the transaction boundary visible: everything the handler staged succeeds or fails together, and a failed command leaves the session uncommitted. If handlers or repositories committed, a later failure in the same pipeline would leave a partial write behind. Handlers, repositories, validators, reactions, jobs, and endpoints commit nothing. Every command runs as a top-level pipeline with its own commit, because no handler sends a command, so a command rides on no caller's commit. A declared consistency mode other than `atomic` splits work across commands, and each command still commits once.
provisions.example:
In the Claimwick product, `use-case/spending.submit-expense` stages the expense through its Domain repository, and one post-handler commits once after the handler returns:

```text
handler stages the expense through its repository
post-handler collects the pending events
post-handler commits the session once
```

A failed submission leaves the session uncommitted, so no partial expense is stored.

provisions.heading: Control Production Schema Changes
provisions.evidence: Is any hosted schema change applied outside a reviewed step before traffic shifts, or from a starting replica? Look at the deployment steps beside the startup paths.
provisions.statement: A hosted environment MUST apply schema changes through a reviewed step before traffic shifts, not from a starting replica.
provisions.rationale: A schema change that runs from a starting replica races every other starting replica, and the winner is nondeterministic. A reviewed step produces the migration artifact instead, and a deployment step applies that artifact before traffic shifts. Development and disposable integration databases still apply schema automatically. A tool that alters the schema from application startup is no reviewed step, whichever provider runs it.

provisions.heading: Enforce Uniqueness in the Store
provisions.evidence: Is any uniqueness rule missing a store unique index or an owner-derived identity, or indexing a denormalized field? Look at the store configuration for each rule.
provisions.statement: Each uniqueness rule MUST be enforced by the store, through a unique index over the stored value or, for a record that exists at most once per owner, through an identity derived from its owner.
provisions.rationale: The store is the only place that sees every concurrent write. A check in code sees only its own transaction, so two commands that both check and then both write store the same value twice. A unique index or an owner-derived identity makes the second write fail in the store instead. When the rule ignores case or spacing, the stored value is normalized before writing and the index covers the normalized field, so differently cased writes still collide.
provisions.example: In the Claimwick product, each payout carries a legal document number that is unique per spending owner. The store holds a unique index over the owner and number pair, so two concurrent reimbursements collide on the index and the loser ends with the use case conflict refusal instead of sharing one number. In the library product, each book barcode is unique across books: two clerks registering the same barcode at once collide on the barcode unique index, and the second commit refuses with `book-barcode-taken`.

provisions.heading: Evolve Stored Document Contracts Explicitly
provisions.evidence: Is any rename, removal, type change, member move, or discriminator change shipping without a reviewed transformation or an expand-and-contract rollout? Look at each stored-contract change.
provisions.statement: A rename, removal, type change, member move, or discriminator change MUST have a reviewed data transformation or an expand-and-contract rollout.
provisions.rationale: Stored JSON member names, required values, and discriminator values are database schema: old documents stay on disk after the code changes. Without a reviewed transformation or an expand-and-contract rollout, a rename or type change makes old documents unreadable.
