An additive member still defines its behavior for documents written earlier. An additive change is the only kind that needs no transformation, and it counts as additive only when every earlier document stays valid. A new member with a defined absent-value behavior qualifies. A new required member, a narrowed type, or a new discriminator value that an earlier reader rejects does not.

provisions.heading: Honor the Declared Consistency Mode
provisions.evidence: Is any command committed in a shape its record's `consistency` mode does not declare? Look at each commit beside the record's mode.
provisions.statement: Persistence MUST commit a command exactly as its use-case record's `consistency` mode states.
provisions.rationale: Under `atomic`, everything the handler staged commits in one unit of work, citing the rule in `boundBy` when `writes` names more than one aggregate. Under `per-record`, each record's command commits alone, and the job resumes from its cursor after a failure. A second commit inside one command splits one unit of work across two transactions, and a failure between them leaves a partial write.
provisions.example: The erase-expired-data job commits each expense alone under `per-record`, while the submit-expense command commits its staged aggregates together under `atomic`.

provisions.heading: Keep Mappings and Aliases Explicit
provisions.evidence: Is any stored aggregate missing a stable document alias, a typed-identifier mapping, or the indexes its accepted queries need? Look at the store configuration for each aggregate.
provisions.statement: Each stored aggregate MUST declare a stable document alias, typed-identifier mapping, and the indexes its accepted queries need.
provisions.rationale: Document types and collection names are storage identity. If they followed code names, renaming a class would orphan every stored document. An explicit alias, identifier mapping, and index list keeps storage identity independent of code names. The store configuration owned in Infrastructure holds all three.

provisions.heading: Keep Serialization Behavior Out of Domain
provisions.evidence: Is any serialization metadata sitting on a Domain type, or any stored JSON contract owned outside Infrastructure? Look at the Domain types beside the Infrastructure JSON contract.
provisions.statement: Infrastructure MUST own the JSON contract for stored documents, including member names, constructors, converters, and polymorphic registration.
provisions.rationale: Serialization metadata on Domain types couples the business model to one store's format, so changing the format means editing the rules. Infrastructure owns member names, constructors, converters, and polymorphic registration, and Domain stays free of serialization metadata. Every concrete type behind a base or interface is registered, because an unregistered subtype fails at read time. Registration covers the types this store actually persists. The store that writes a union referenced from another aggregate registers it once, instead of every store that names the referencing type. A type reachable only through an identifier is persisted by no store here, so it needs no registration.

provisions.heading: Keep Unbounded Collections Out of Aggregate Documents
provisions.evidence: Is any collection with no accepted business bound embedded in an aggregate document? Look at the embedded collections in each document.
provisions.statement: An aggregate document MUST NOT embed a collection that has no accepted business bound.
provisions.rationale: A document grows with every write to its collection. An unbounded embedded collection eventually exceeds size limits and slows every load of its aggregate. Data with no accepted business bound belongs in another aggregate, an owned document record, or a separate query-shaped document, depending on the consistency boundary it needs.

provisions.heading: Keep Uniqueness Out of Handlers
provisions.evidence: Is any handler reserving, claiming, checking, or releasing a uniqueness key? Look at each handler body.
provisions.statement: A handler MUST NOT reserve, claim, check or release a uniqueness key.
provisions.rationale: A reservation made in a handler runs outside the commit that needs it. It can leak when the command fails later, and it teaches every later handler to coordinate with the store directly. The store enforces the rule at commit through `litespec/backend/persistence#enforce-uniqueness-in-the-store` and `litespec/backend/persistence#claim-a-cross-record-key-at-commit`, and the pipeline turns a lost race into the use case conflict refusal under `litespec/backend/application#refuse-a-lost-race-as-a-conflict`, so the handler carries no reservation, check, or cleanup.
provisions.example: The register-reader handler creates the reader aggregate and stages it through its Domain repository. It reserves no card number and checks no registry first. When two registrations race for one card number, the second commit violates the unique index and refuses with the use case conflict, with no reservation or cleanup code in the handler. The submit-expense handler likewise stages the expense and leaves the payout number to the store sequence.

provisions.heading: Map a Constraint Violation to Its Refusal
provisions.evidence: Is any unique constraint missing a conflict refusal mapping for the use cases that can violate it? Look at the fault classification map.
provisions.statement: Each unique constraint MUST map by name to the conflict refusal of the use cases that can violate it.
provisions.rationale: When the store refuses a commit, pipeline fault classification turns that fault into the use case named conflict refusal, following `litespec/backend/application#refuse-a-lost-race-as-a-conflict`. The map keys each unique constraint by name, so the classifier knows which refusal the violation answers. An unmapped violation still fails the commit, but it reaches the caller as a generic conflict that names no rule and suggests no next step. A classifier that builds the code from the lost key, one code per key scope, declares its template in the project file `refusals.composed`, so the model checks read each code as raised where its key scope is declared.
provisions.example: The barcode unique index is named `uq_book_barcode`, and the map pairs it with `book-barcode-taken`, so a registration that loses the barcode race refuses with that code. The payout number index is named `uq_payout_owner_number`, and the map pairs it with the reimburse conflict refusal, so each racing command names the number it lost.

provisions.heading: Model a Once-Only Rule as Aggregate State
provisions.evidence: Is any at-most-once rule held outside its aggregate's state, or any repeated action escaping the refusal? Look at each such rule beside its aggregate.
provisions.statement: Each rule that an action happens at most once for a record MUST be state on that record's aggregate.
provisions.rationale: A flag on the aggregate travels with the record it guards, so the rule is checked where the record is changed. The aggregate sees the earlier action in its own state and refuses the repeat, or leaves it without effect. A counter or marker kept anywhere else splits the rule from the record, and the two disagree under concurrent writes.
provisions.example: In the library product, a loan charges its overdue fee at most once. The loan records that it charged the fee, and a repeat command finds the flag and refuses with the loan conflict refusal. In the Claimwick product, an expense is reimbursed at most once: the reimbursed state carries the fact, so a second reimbursement finds an already reimbursed expense and ends with `spending.not-approved`.

provisions.heading: Page and Filter Collection Queries in the Store
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `query-filter-invalid` (level A) for a query handler filtering a repository list in memory.
provisions.statement: Each collection query MUST page and filter in the store, never load a whole list to shape it in memory.
provisions.rationale: A query that loads a whole list to filter, sort, or page it in memory pays the full read on every call, and breaks when the data grows. Repository list methods take the scope and the page and filter in the database instead, through the shared page request and page shapes.
provisions.example: The list-expenses query passes its employee scope and page to the repository. A handler that filters a full list in memory is reported.

provisions.heading: Persist One Explicit State Object
provisions.evidence: Is any aggregate document flattening its state object, or any state failing to round-trip through the serializer? Look at each stored state in the integration tests.
provisions.statement: Persist the aggregate state object itself rather than a flattened projection, round-tripping every state object through the configured serializer in integration tests.
provisions.rationale: The stored state object keeps the aggregate's lifecycle and its state-specific facts in one value. A read then materializes the same state the command stored. A flattened projection splits that value across members the store cannot version together, and a flag beside the object disagrees with it after the next transition.

provisions.heading: Query Through the Read Session
provisions.evidence: Is any query handler projecting outside the read session, or applying filter, scope, ordering, or limit after materialization? Look at each query handler body.
provisions.statement: A query handler MUST project through the read session, applying filter, scope, ordering, and limit before materialization.
provisions.rationale: The session already projects, filters, and pages, so a read-store interface per aggregate, a generic read repository, or a callback wrapper adds a layer that only repeats it. Applying filter, scope, ordering, and limit before materialization keeps that work in the database; materializing first loads rows the caller does not see. Ordering and paging follow `litespec/backend/api#bound-collection-queries`.

provisions.heading: Review Query Plans for New Indexes
provisions.evidence: Is any new index missing an accepted query or a justifying plan on representative data? Look at each new index beside its query.
provisions.statement: Add an index only from an accepted query or a measured operating need, and inspect its plan on representative data.
provisions.rationale: Every index costs write throughput on each change to its table. An index added without reading its plan on representative data pays that cost for a read with no measured need. So each index starts from an accepted query or a measured operating need.

provisions.heading: Stage Aggregate Writes Through Domain Repositories
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `repository-unimplemented` (level S) for an aggregate a use case changes that has no Infrastructure repository implementing its domain repository.
provisions.statement: A command handler MUST reach persistence only through a Domain repository, never through the session directly.
provisions.rationale: The repository is the one reviewable path from a handler to the store, shaped around one aggregate type. Without it, handlers reach the session directly, bypass aggregate loading, and scatter store calls through Application. Infrastructure implements each repository with the command session, and the repository exposes no session, generic query, or save operation.
provisions.example: The submit-expense handler stages the new expense through the expense repository; it names no session and issues no store call of its own.

provisions.heading: Test Persistence Against the Pinned Database
provisions.evidence: Is any repository behavior, projection, mapping, correctness index, commit behavior, or schema application tested outside the pinned database, or against an in-memory substitute? Look at the persistence test fixtures.
provisions.statement: Repository behavior, projections, mappings, correctness indexes, commit behavior, and schema application MUST run against the pinned database.
provisions.rationale: Only the pinned database runs the real query planner, constraints, and type behavior. An in-memory substitute proves the test's own model of the database, so a query that passes against it fails in production. HTTP integration through the real host is covered under `litespec/backend/testing#test-http-integration-through-the-real-application-host`.

provisions.heading: Use Database Naming Conventions
provisions.evidence: Is any schema, table, column, index, constraint, document alias, or SQL identifier breaking `snake_case`? Look at the schemas, tables, columns, and indexes.
provisions.statement: A database schema, table, column, index, constraint, document alias, or SQL identifier MUST use `snake_case`.
provisions.rationale: One casing rule lets anyone predict a table or column name from the code type without opening the mapping. Code types keep normal language naming while the mapping layer converts once. The store configuration sets the casing, so no configuration repeats the rule per entity.

provisions.heading: Use One Persistence Folder
provisions.evidence: Is any store setup, repository, or commit file sitting outside the product or module `Infrastructure/` folders? Look at the persistence files beside the module tree.
provisions.statement: Place store setup in the product `Infrastructure/` folder and each module's repositories, mappings, and serialization in its own `Infrastructure/` folders.
provisions.rationale: The product `Infrastructure/` folder holds store setup, session and commit plumbing, and serialization shared by every module, so every persistence type has one discoverable home. Each module keeps its repositories and mappings in its own `Infrastructure/` folders, beside the aggregates they store. Scattered configuration hides the provider setup across the product.
provisions.example:
```text
{Product}/
  Infrastructure/                   store setup: registration, configuration, commit handler, event buffer
    StoreServiceRegistration
    StoreConfiguration
    Commands/
      CommitCommandPostHandler
    Events/
      DomainEventBuffer
  Posts/                            single aggregate whose name matches the module: files directly under the module
    Infrastructure/
      PostRepository
      PostStoreConfiguration
  Customers/                        two aggregates: one folder per aggregate
    CustomerAccounts/
      Infrastructure/
        CustomerAccountRepository
        CustomerAccountStoreConfiguration
    Consents/
      Infrastructure/
        ConsentRepository
        ConsentStoreConfiguration
```

The module folders follow `litespec/backend/architecture#organize-code-by-module-aggregate-and-use-case`. A single-aggregate module stays flat when its aggregate root's plural name equals the module name: `Post` stays flat under `Posts`, and otherwise each aggregate takes its own folder.

Aggregate-specific configuration sits beside its aggregate, and session and commit plumbing sit under the product store root.

provisions.heading: Use One Session per Command
provisions.evidence: Is any command resolving more than one session across its repositories and commit handler? Look at the session wiring in each command.
provisions.statement: Resolve one session for the repositories and the commit handler in one command.
provisions.rationale: One session per command means the repositories and the commit handler stage and commit the same unit of work. Two sessions in one command commit separately, and a failure between them leaves a partial write behind.

provisions.heading: Version Every Aggregate
provisions.evidence: Is any stored aggregate committed without a compared version, or any stale write escaping the use case conflict refusal? Look at each stored aggregate beside its commit.
provisions.statement: Each stored aggregate MUST carry a version that the store compares at commit, so a lost update fails the commit.
provisions.rationale: Without a compared version, two commands can load the same aggregate and both commit, and the second silently overwrites the first. The store compares the version each command loaded with the version it commits against, so a stale write fails the commit instead of erasing newer work. A failed comparison ends with the use case conflict refusal, following `litespec/backend/application#refuse-a-lost-race-as-a-conflict`.
provisions.example: Two approvers open the same submitted expense. The first approval commits and moves the version forward, and the second approval fails its version comparison and refuses with the approve conflict instead of overwriting the first decision. In the library product, two clerks extending one loan race the same way, and the loser re-reads the loan before deciding again.

provisions.heading: Isolate Integration State
provisions.evidence: Is any mutable business state shared across tests, or any reset strategy missing from the testing documentation? Look at the tests beside the testing documentation.
provisions.statement: An integration test MUST reset database state between tests through one documented strategy and depend on no test order.
provisions.rationale: Two tests that share mutable business state pass or fail depending on which runs first, and the failure disappears when either test runs alone. One documented reset strategy removes that coupling, so order stops mattering. Container and host fixtures stay shared for cost, because only mutable business state leaks between tests. The default strategy is one database per test class, cloned from a migrated template. The harness applies the schema once per run to a template database. Each test class then receives its own database cloned from that template and drops it when the class finishes. A clone takes milliseconds, so every class starts from an empty migrated schema without a second container. A project that resets tables between tests instead records that strategy in its testing documentation.

provisions.heading: Keep Assertions Focused
provisions.evidence: Is any test body asserting outside its named outcome, or snapshotting whole objects? Look at each test body.
provisions.statement: Assert only the state, event, call, response, or error that the test covers.
provisions.rationale: A focused assertion fails only when the behavior it covers breaks. A broad object snapshot fails on an unrelated field addition, which trains readers to update it without reading it.

provisions.heading: Keep the Test Suites the Size Requires
provisions.evidence: Is any required suite missing a folder, or any extra folder holding an unnamed suite? Look at the test folders beside the declared project size.
provisions.statement: A backend codebase MUST hold exactly the test suites its size requires: architecture and integration for small, adding acceptance for large.
provisions.rationale: Each suite owns one boundary and one harness, so a project that keeps exactly its suites knows where each new test belongs. A missing suite pushes its tests into another suite's harness, where they run with the wrong fixtures: an integration test in a unit harness gets no database. An extra suite with no stated boundary collects the tests nobody placed, and nobody knows what those tests prove. Unit suites stay optional at both sizes, and acceptance stays optional at size small. An acceptance suite without the executable BDD extension is an unnamed baseline suite: the project either selects the extension or names the suite for what it actually is.
provisions.example:
These are the suite folders:

```text
architecture-tests/
integration-tests/
acceptance-tests/
```

A small codebase holds the first two. The acceptance folder appears when the executable BDD extension activates.

provisions.heading: Match Tests by Fully Qualified Name
provisions.evidence: Is any test result matched by a short name, or carrying data-row arguments? Look at the test result files.
provisions.statement: A test run MUST match results to tests by fully qualified name.
provisions.rationale: Result files name each test in full: its namespace, its containing types joined with dots, and its method, without data-row arguments. A renamed test then matches nothing instead of matching another test's same-named method, so the rename fails loudly instead of lingering as an awaited run. Matching by short name hides the rename behind a passing name the test no longer owns.
provisions.example: A renamed submit-expense test leaves its old qualified name with no matching result, so the use case stays coded until the new name runs and passes.

provisions.heading: Mirror Production Module Names
provisions.evidence: Is any test tree breaking the production module folders outside the exempt harness files and adapter tests? Look at each test tree beside production.
provisions.statement: Mirror the production module, aggregate, `UseCases/`, and use case folder names inside each test suite.
provisions.rationale: When test folders mirror production folders, a reader finds the tests for a module without searching. Harness and flat files stay exempt: a `Support` folder and flat Architecture test files need no production counterpart. Adapter tests sit under the adapter's `Infrastructure/` path and are exempt by kind, because they prove a scenario through an adapter that owns no use case folder.
provisions.example:
Each test tree mirrors the production module folders, including the `UseCases/` level:

```text
Unit tests/
  Posts/
    UseCases/
      CreateDraft/
      GetPost/
Integration tests/
  Posts/
    UseCases/
      CreateDraft/
  Support/
Architecture tests/
```

The same module names appear in every test tree, apart from the exempt harness files and adapter tests.

provisions.heading: Name Tests by Observable Behavior
provisions.evidence: Is any test name missing operation, condition, or expected result, or any test class missing its production type? Look at the test names.
provisions.statement: Name a test `{MethodOrOperation}_{Condition}_{ExpectedResult}` and its class after the production type it covers.
provisions.rationale: The failing test name is often the first thing anyone reads in a broken build. A name that states operation, condition, and expected result identifies the broken behavior without opening the file. A name such as `Test1` or `HappyPath` describes the author's intent instead of the behavior that failed, so the reader opens the file to learn what broke.

provisions.heading: Prove Every Aggregate with a Model-Based Test
provisions.evidence: Is any aggregate at size large missing a model-based test walking its declared transitions? Look at the aggregates beside their model-based test files and the declared project size.
provisions.statement: Prove every aggregate with a model-based test generated from its declared transitions at size large; model-based tests stay optional at size small.
provisions.rationale: The transitions table declares every allowed move between states. A model-based test walks generated sequences through that model, checking that allowed moves succeed and rejected moves refuse. Generating from the declared table keeps the model and the test in agreement by construction. The table lives on the aggregate page, as `litespec/core/domain-model#connect-every-state-through-transitions` requires.
provisions.example: An expense test generates walks across submitted, approved, refused, and reimbursed, checking each move against the declared transitions. A walk attempting reimbursement from submitted ends in the refusal the transitions table allows.

provisions.heading: Prove Every Calculation with Property Tests
provisions.evidence: Is any calculation rule at size large missing property tests seeded from its scenario examples? Look at the calculation rules beside their property test files and the declared project size.
provisions.statement: Prove every calculation rule with property tests seeded from its scenario examples at size large; property tests stay optional at size small.
provisions.rationale: An examples table holds the debated rows, and property tests range beyond them: each generated input checks the same stated property the rows illustrate. Seeding from the table ties the properties to reviewed values instead of invented ones. The table itself lives on a scenario proving the rule, as `litespec/core/domain-model#tabulate-every-calculation-with-examples` requires.
provisions.example: A rounding rule with three reviewed rows seeds a property test that asserts the rounded total against the stated bound for every generated input.

provisions.heading: Share One Production-Faithful Integration Harness
provisions.evidence: Is any integration suite missing its container fixture, host factory, or isolation helper, or holding a second of one? Look at the integration suite.
provisions.statement: The integration suite MUST own one database container fixture, one application host factory, and one database isolation helper.
provisions.rationale: One fixture, one host factory, and one reset helper give every integration test the same database and configuration. A container per test group multiplies run time by the group count and buys no isolation that a cloned database lacks. The fixture starts the pinned PostgreSQL once per test run and supplies each test group its connection string before the host builds. The integration suite still owns one harness. An activated BDD extension brings its own host for the acceptance suite, because the two suites run different lifetimes, and that host reuses this fixture's container and reset helper instead of starting another database.

provisions.heading: Test Domain in Isolation
provisions.evidence: Is any Domain test using a database, HTTP host, container, clock, or mock instead of explicit inputs alone? Look at the Domain test files.
provisions.statement: A Domain test MUST use explicit inputs with no database, HTTP host, container, clock, or mock.
provisions.rationale: Domain behavior is deterministic: the same explicit inputs produce the same new state or the same refusal. A database, host, container, clock, or mock in a Domain test hides nondeterminism behind the call, so the same test passes and fails without a code change. The suite covers factories, every lifecycle state, allowed and rejected transitions, invariants, value equality, collections, money rules, exceptions, and raised events.

provisions.heading: Test HTTP Integration Through the Real Application Host
provisions.evidence: Is any HTTP integration test bypassing the real host factory or production configuration, or skipping Problem Details, authentication, or resource authorization? Look at the HTTP integration tests.
provisions.statement: An HTTP integration test MUST run through the real application host with the real configuration, covering Problem Details, authentication, and resource authorization.
provisions.rationale: The real host is the only place where routing, serialization, authentication, and authorization are wired together. A test that bypasses the host proves the handler a second time and misses the boundary where status codes, Problem Details shapes, and policy denials actually come from. Persistence behavior runs against PostgreSQL under `litespec/backend/persistence#test-persistence-against-the-pinned-database`, and both run on the harness that `litespec/backend/testing#share-one-production-faithful-integration-harness` owns.

provisions.heading: Use Builders for Valid Defaults
provisions.evidence: Is any test data builder starting outside valid state, or customizing without business names? Look at each builder.
provisions.statement: Create a test data builder that produces valid state by default and exposes business-named customization.
provisions.rationale: A builder that starts from valid state keeps each test focused on the one value it changes. Building state by bypassing Domain methods is reserved for a persistence compatibility test, because only that test needs state the Domain would refuse.

provisions.heading: Authenticate Every Caller Through a Declared Auth Kind
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `field-invalid` for an `auth` kind outside session, token, device, link, app, and none.
provisions.statement: Each entry point MUST name its auth kinds from session, token, device, link, app, and none.
provisions.rationale: The auth kind says how the caller proves identity before the grant is checked: a session for a signed-in person, a device for a managed scanner, a link for a single-purpose link, an app for a calling application, a token for a bearer token, and none for open calls. Without a declared kind, open calls and authenticated calls look alike, and a reviewer cannot tell which identity the grant was checked against.
provisions.example: An expense submission names `session`, a library self-checkout kiosk names `device`, and a public catalog names `none`.

provisions.heading: Authorize Every Use Case Through a Declared Grant
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `field-invalid` for a grant outside permission, self, signed-in, anonymous, and system, and `reference-unknown` for a permission no record defines.
provisions.statement: Each access declaration MUST name its grant as a permission, a self grant, signed-in, anonymous, or system.
provisions.rationale: The grant is the check the call passes: a permission for role-held action, a self grant for action on records the caller owns, signed-in for an authenticated caller with no permission, anonymous for open calls, and system for work an internal trigger runs with no outside caller. A grant outside these five forms gives the checker no stated check to enforce, so each caller invents its own test. System never authorizes an outside request, and a call with no authentication where one is needed ends in the derived unauthenticated result. Settled by [decision/0079-cover-the-behavior-reviewers-found-missing](decision/0079-cover-the-behavior-reviewers-found-missing) and [decision/0083-evaluate-access-in-one-order](decision/0083-evaluate-access-in-one-order).
provisions.example: `permission/manage-copies` guards staff work, `self(permission/read-loans)` lets a reader read their own loans, `signed-in` opens a workspace to any signed-in person with no permission, `anonymous` opens a public catalog, and `system` covers an archive use case only its retention job runs.

provisions.heading: Cite the Setting or Plan Behind Every Entitlement
provisions.evidence: Does every entitlement grant cite its setting or plan? Check each grant beside the settings its use case cites.
provisions.statement: A grant that depends on a setting or a plan MUST cite that setting or plan.
provisions.rationale: An entitlement allows one tenant what another is refused, so the grant alone reads as unequal treatment. Citing the setting or plan shows the commercial or configured reason behind the difference, and gives the reviewer the range and setter to judge it against.
provisions.example: A submit command cites `setting/spending.receipt-threshold`, so an expense above the line with no receipt is refused by the policy setting rather than by role.

provisions.heading: Declare Access on Every Use Case
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `record-invalid` for a use case without `access`, `grant`, or `tenant`.
provisions.statement: Each use case MUST declare its grant and its tenant scope in `access`.
provisions.rationale: The grant and the tenant scope answer the two access questions together: what check the call passes, and which tenant data it may touch. A use case missing one part leaves that question to code, and two implementations of the same record enforce different boundaries. The entry point the call arrives through declares how the caller proved identity.

provisions.heading: Declare Erasure for Every External System
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `record-invalid` for an external system without `erasure` and `reference-unknown` for an unsupported, manual or not-applicable erasure without an Intent decision.
provisions.statement: An external system MUST declare how personal data it holds is erased in `erasure`.
provisions.rationale: Personal data sent outside stays outside unless some operation or event removes it. The erasure declaration states the call, the integration event, or why removal does not run. An unsupported, manual, or not-applicable erasure cites the Intent decision that accepts the limit, so the gap reads as an accepted decision rather than a missed edge.
provisions.example: A payout archive declares `{"mode": "unsupported", "reason": "settled payouts belong to the bank"}` with the decision that accepts the limit, plus the sentence employees see.

provisions.heading: Define Each Scope Level in the Glossary
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `scope-term-missing` for a role scope with no glossary term titled with the level and Scope.
provisions.statement: Each scope level a role names MUST have a glossary term titled with the level and Scope, stating what the level covers in this product.
provisions.rationale: A bare level such as `platform` or `tenant` reads the same in every product, and each product means a different reach by it. The glossary term states that reach once, so a reviewer reads what `platform` covers in this product rather than guessing it from the word. Proposed by [decision/0055-state-each-access-scope-once](decision/0055-state-each-access-scope-once).
provisions.example: Claimwick's `platform` scope has a glossary term, Platform Scope, that states it covers every expense in the Claimwick installation.

provisions.heading: Describe Every Served Content Entry Point with Its Serving Fields
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `record-invalid` for a served content entry point without path, contentType, cacheControl, versioning, or fulfills.
provisions.statement: A served content entry point MUST carry path, contentType, cacheControl, versioning, and fulfills.
provisions.rationale: Served content is a file the product hands out, not behavior it runs, so the serving fields are the whole contract: where it lives, what it is, how long it caches, how it versions, and which requirement it carries. Without them, a legal text or a static script ships as an unreviewed file with no stated requirement or freshness.
provisions.example: A terms text carries its path, `text/html`, its cache window, its version rule, and the requirement it fulfills.

provisions.heading: Evaluate Access in One Order
provisions.evidence: Does every call evaluate principal, assignments, permission, tenant scope, ownership, and delegation in that order? Walk one allowed and one refused call through the steps.
provisions.statement: Access MUST be evaluated in one order: the authenticated principal, then the role assignments whose bound scope instance matches the target, then the permission, then the use case tenant scope, then the self-ownership restriction, then delegation validity, with several assignments combining as a union.
provisions.rationale: Each step narrows what the next step checks: identity before assignments, assignments before the permission they carry, the permission before the reach it is used at, and ownership and delegation last as restrictions on an otherwise allowed call. One order means two implementations allow and refuse the same calls. A role assignment binds a scope instance as well as a level: the tenant the hold reaches, or the person for a self grant. Several assignments combine as a union: any assignment that allows the call allows it. Settled by [decision/0083-evaluate-access-in-one-order](decision/0083-evaluate-access-in-one-order).
provisions.example: A Claimwick approver holds the approver role for one cost center. A call to approve an expense evaluates as the session principal, then the approver assignment whose cost center matches the expense, then the approve-expense permission, then the own tenant scope, then ownership and delegation. An assignment for another cost center does not match, so the call ends in the derived forbidden result.

provisions.heading: Grant Across Tenants Only Through Declared Delegation
provisions.evidence: Does every cross-tenant delegation grant declare its grant on both sides? Check the delegation grants the tenancy extension declares.
provisions.statement: A grant that acts across tenants through delegation MUST declare its delegation grant on both sides.
provisions.rationale: Delegation lets one actor act for another, so a grant on one side alone leaves the other side unreviewed. Declaring the grant on both sides shows who may delegate and who may be acted for, and the tenancy extension states the fields each side carries.
provisions.example: An assistant acts for a manager only where the manager delegation grant and the assistant acting grant both name the pairing.

provisions.heading: Grant Permissions Through Roles
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `record-invalid` for a role with no `allows` entry, and `permission-unused` for a permission allowed by no role.
provisions.statement: A role MUST name the permissions it allows in `allows`.
provisions.rationale: The `allows` list is the middle of the chain: it joins the actors that hold the role to the use cases that cite its permissions in their grants. A role that names no permission grants nothing, so every use case its holders run breaks the chain at the middle link. The role lives in Intent and the permission lives in Behavior, so `allows` is a declared down-link from Intent to Behavior.
provisions.example: `role/employee` allows `permission/request-expense`, which the submit use case cites in its grant.

provisions.heading: Keep Access Records in Their Homes
provisions.evidence: Does every access record sit in the home its type names? Check the actor, role, permission, entry point, and external system homes.
provisions.statement: An access record MUST live in the home its type names.
provisions.rationale: A reader who wants an actor opens the actors home, and the book renders each record from its home too. A record kept anywhere else looks written while everyone opens the home and finds nothing there.

provisions.heading: Keep Permission Sets to Entries
provisions.evidence: Does the explanation beside each permissions file state only risks and boundaries, without restating a meaning, adding a grant, or naming a future role? Check the Risk and Boundaries sections beside each permissions file.
provisions.statement: A module permissions file MUST hold permission entries only, and its explanation states only the risks and boundaries of those entries, without restating a permission's meaning or adding a grant.
provisions.rationale: Each permission is defined once, in its entry: its `meaning` is the one statement of what it allows, and prose that repeats it drifts from the entry. A boundary is what a reader might assume a permission allows but it does not, which the meaning does not say, so the explanation holds what the entries cannot. A permission that guards a query or use case disclosing personal or financial data carries the `personal-data` or `access` risk, like a permission for a write. Proposed by [decision/0055-state-each-access-scope-once](decision/0055-state-each-access-scope-once). Settled by [decision/0079-cover-the-behavior-reviewers-found-missing](decision/0079-cover-the-behavior-reviewers-found-missing).

provisions.heading: Name Each Permission by a Use-Case Verb
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `permission-verb-unknown` as advisory for a permission name whose opening verb is neither in the table, nor a glossary verb of kind command or either, nor `manage`.
provisions.statement: Each permission name SHOULD open with a verb from the use-case verb table, a glossary verb of kind command or either, or with `manage`.
provisions.rationale: The first word of a permission name tells a reader whether the grant reads or changes, and which kind of use case it covers. A name such as `handle-documents` says nothing about what it includes, so a reader cannot tell whether it reads, writes, or removes. The verb table gives each opening word one meaning across the product, and a project verb carries its kind in its glossary verb term, so a permission opens with a command or either verb from either list. The opening verb is a naming convention only: no permission implies another by its name, and `manage-` grants nothing beyond the use cases that cite the permission. Proposed by [decision/0055-state-each-access-scope-once](decision/0055-state-each-access-scope-once), and glossary verbs by [decision/0062-declare-project-verbs-in-the-glossary](decision/0062-declare-project-verbs-in-the-glossary). Settled by [decision/0083-evaluate-access-in-one-order](decision/0083-evaluate-access-in-one-order) and [decision/0087-keep-prose-checks-advisory-and-names-per-type](decision/0087-keep-prose-checks-advisory-and-names-per-type).
provisions.example: `permission/approve-expense` opens with `approve` and `permission/manage-policy` opens with `manage`, so both pass. `permission/submit-expense` opens with the glossary verb `submit` and passes. `permission/handle-documents` opens with a word neither list states, so it is reported.

provisions.heading: Name Every Actor with Its Kind
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `record-invalid` for an actor without `kind` and `field-invalid` for a kind outside person and organization.
provisions.statement: An actor MUST name its kind in `kind`.
provisions.rationale: The kind says whether a human or an organization stands behind the actor, and that decides who answers for what the actor does. Without it, a reviewer assigns responsibility without knowing who stands behind the actor. Software stands behind no actor.
provisions.example: An employee actor carries `person`, and the library as a lending party carries `organization`.

provisions.heading: Prove Hierarchies Derived Trust and Delegation with Scenarios
provisions.evidence: Does every hierarchy, trust, or delegation pattern carry an allowed and a refused scenario? Check the scenarios on the use cases that carry the pattern.
provisions.statement: A hierarchy, derived trust, or delegation pattern MUST prove its allowed and refused calls with scenarios.
provisions.rationale: These patterns compose the same access parts into wider reach, so prose alone cannot show where the wider grant stops. Scenarios that walk an allowed call and a refused call pin the boundary as checked facts, and the checker confirms each one through the public boundary.
provisions.example: A delegation story shows an assistant acting for a manager succeeding, and the same assistant acting without delegation ending in the derived forbidden result.

provisions.heading: Record a Delegated Grant Inside One Tenant as a Role Assignment
provisions.evidence: Does every delegated or temporary grant inside one tenant sit on a role assignment with `validFrom`, `validUntil`, and the bound scope instance, with its own granting and revoking use cases? Check the assignments beside the actor holds and the use cases that act under them.
provisions.statement: A delegated or temporary grant inside one tenant MUST be recorded as a role assignment with a validity window in `validFrom` and `validUntil` and the bound scope instance, held on an aggregate the access model reads and granted and revoked by its own use cases.
provisions.rationale: Inside one tenant, delegation changes who holds a role for a time, not which grant forms exist. Recording the assignment with its window on an aggregate the access model reads gives the guard one stated source for the deputy, the role, and the dates, and the granting and revoking use cases make the start and the end reviewable acts. A use case acting under the assignment declares its permission as usual, so no new access form appears. The assignment binds the scope instance the deputy reaches, the tenant or team, beside the dates. The tenancy extension adds only the cross-tenant form of delegation; it adds no form inside one tenant. Settled by [decision/0083-evaluate-access-in-one-order](decision/0083-evaluate-access-in-one-order).
provisions.example: In Claimwick, a manager delegating team management to a deputy for 2026-12-20 to 2027-01-05 is recorded as an assignment of the manager role to the deputy, bound to the manager's team, with `validFrom` of 2026-12-20 and `validUntil` of 2027-01-05, granted by its own grant use case and ended by its own revoke use case. The manage use case acting under it still declares `permission/manage-team`.

provisions.heading: Record Every Role an Actor Holds
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `role-unused` for a role held by no actor, and `record-invalid` for a hold that is not a role identifier, such as a hold carrying a scope.
provisions.statement: An actor that acts through a role MUST list the role's identifier in `holds`.
provisions.rationale: The hold is what connects an actor to its grant. Without it, the actor and the role sit on separate pages with no stated connection, and no reviewer can tell what the actor may do. The hold names only the role, because the role holds the scope of its grant, and one actor's hold cannot widen or narrow the reach the role states. Proposed by [decision/0055-state-each-access-scope-once](decision/0055-state-each-access-scope-once).
provisions.example:
```json
"holds": ["role/employee"]
```

provisions.heading: Remove a Target That Must Be the Caller
provisions.evidence: Which use cases still read a target identifier from their input when the guard allows only the signed-in person? Check their inputs and handlers beside the self grants.
provisions.statement: A message whose target must be the caller MUST carry no target and act on the caller, or declare a self grant that the authorization guard enforces.
provisions.rationale: A target that must equal the caller is a value the caller could forge. Each handler would compare it with the verified identity, and each comparison is authorization logic sitting in a handler. Carrying no target leaves nothing to forge: the call acts on the caller from verified claims. Where the target must stay on the message, a self grant states the scope beside the use case, and the guard enforces it.
provisions.example: "My loans" lists the signed-in reader's loans and takes no reader id.

provisions.heading: Require a Recent Sign-In by Setting
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `record-invalid` for a `recentSignIn` that names no `setting/` identifier and `reference-unknown` for a setting no record defines.
provisions.statement: A use case that requires a recent sign-in MUST name the window in `recentSignIn` with a `setting/` identifier.
provisions.rationale: Some operations need a fresh sign-in: changing a sign-in method or approving a large payout on a week-old session is not the same as doing it just after signing in. The window is a product decision, so it lives in a setting that states its range and setter, and every use case that needs it names the same setting instead of typing its own duration. A call whose sign-in is older than the window ends in the derived sign-in-too-old result. Settled by [decision/0074-declare-access-settings-and-deadlines](decision/0074-declare-access-settings-and-deadlines).
provisions.example: Claimwick payout approval above the threshold names `setting/spending.sign-in-window` in `recentSignIn`; a session older than the window ends in the derived sign-in-too-old result.

provisions.heading: Scope Every Grant to Its Tenant Reach
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `field-invalid` for a tenant scope outside own, cross, public, and none.
provisions.statement: Each access declaration MUST name its tenant scope as own, cross, public, or none.
provisions.rationale: The tenant scope bounds which tenant data the call may touch: `own` stays inside the caller tenant, `cross` reaches across tenants, `public` works beyond tenant boundaries, and `none` touches no tenant data. Without the scope, a read inside one tenant and a read across all tenants look the same, and the widest reach hides inside the narrowest grant.
provisions.example: An expense report names `own`, a staff search across tenants names `cross`, a public catalog names `public`, and a health check names `none`.

provisions.heading: Scope Every Role to Its One Reach
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `record-invalid` for a role without `scope` and `field-invalid` for a scope outside kebab-case form. A `scope` on a permission entry or on a hold fails the schema as an unknown property.
provisions.statement: A role MUST name its one scope in `scope`.
provisions.rationale: The role is the only home of a grant's reach. The same permission allows platform-wide action in one grant and own-record action in another, so the scope decides what each grant actually reaches. Stating the reach on each hold or each permission as well would keep three copies of one value, and the copies would drift apart, so the role states it once and every permission reads its reach from the roles that allow it. Without a named scope, every grant reads as product-wide, and the narrowest grant gets the widest reach. Proposed by [decision/0055-state-each-access-scope-once](decision/0055-state-each-access-scope-once).
provisions.example: A scope of `team` bounds the role to one team, while `platform` bounds it to the whole product.

provisions.heading: State Every Permission with Its Meaning
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `record-invalid` for a permission without `meaning`.
provisions.statement: A permission MUST state what it allows in `meaning`.
provisions.rationale: The `meaning` is the one sentence a reviewer reads to decide whether the grant fits the role. A name alone carries no boundary: two permissions with the same name pattern and no meanings drift into overlapping grants that no audit can separate.
provisions.example: `permission/request-expense` carries "Submit an expense for reimbursement."

provisions.heading: Use Three Conventional Scope Levels
provisions.evidence: Does every role scope use `platform`, `tenant`, or `self`, or a recorded project convention? Check `scope` on each role page.
provisions.statement: Use `platform`, `tenant`, and `self` as role scopes.
provisions.rationale: Three levels cover the grants most products need: product-wide administration, tenant-wide operation, and action on one's own records. A project with different boundaries names its own levels, and every role still carries exactly one scope.

provisions.heading: Write a Summary on Every Actor and Role Page
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `prose-missing` as advisory for an actor or role page without `summary`.
provisions.statement: An actor or role page SHOULD carry a `summary` field.
provisions.rationale: The `summary` states in plain sentences who the party is and what the grant is for, which the fields alone do not say. A reviewer meets the story first and the fields after, so the grant reads as a decision rather than a row. Settled by [decision/0087-keep-prose-checks-advisory-and-names-per-type](decision/0087-keep-prose-checks-advisory-and-names-per-type).

provisions.heading: Write a Summary on Every External System Page
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `prose-missing` as advisory for an external system page without `summary`.
provisions.statement: An external system page SHOULD carry a `summary` field.
provisions.rationale: The `summary` states in plain sentences what the outside system does for the product, which the message lists alone do not say. A reviewer meets the relationship first and the messages after, so the dependency reads as a decision rather than a row. Settled by [decision/0087-keep-prose-checks-advisory-and-names-per-type](decision/0087-keep-prose-checks-advisory-and-names-per-type).

provisions.heading: Advise Without Gating
provisions.evidence: Does the agent output record findings as advice with evidence, with decisions left to the owner? Check the output beside the changed records.
provisions.statement: An agent MUST report its findings as advice with evidence, never as a decision.
provisions.rationale: Decisions belong to the owner: the pull request that changes a record is its review. An agent that records a decision spends authority it was never given. Advice with evidence lets the owner decide faster without moving the decision to the agent.

provisions.heading: Apply Guidance Precedence
provisions.evidence: Does the design apply the project waiver, the extension, the deeper page, and the shallower page in that order? Check the design beside the overlapping guidance.
provisions.statement: An agent MUST apply the project waiver, the extension, the deeper page, and the shallower page in that order.
provisions.rationale: Overlapping guidance is normal: a project waiver narrows a shared provision, an extension replaces a baseline default, and a stack page refines its area page. Without a fixed order, two agents resolve the same overlap differently and the workspace drifts. The order puts the most local decision first, so the broader baseline fills only the gaps it leaves.

provisions.heading: Escalate Decisions That Specify Forbids
provisions.evidence: Does each figure the owner sets that the change needs sit in an owner question or a backlog item, not in an agent-written decision? Check the owner questions and the backlog board beside the change.
provisions.statement: An agent MUST NOT decide a figure the owner sets.
provisions.rationale: The Specify rule reserves the figures the owner sets for Intent, because each one binds the product to buyers, markets, or law; the [Intent page](intent.md) states the Specify boundary. An agent that picks a figure silently takes a decision that belongs to the owner. Each undecided figure becomes a question to the owner with a recommendation, or a backlog item.
provisions.example: A setting needs a default queue cap; the agent raises a question to the owner with a recommendation instead of writing the default into the record.

provisions.heading: Inspect Existing Work Before Editing
provisions.evidence: Does `git status` output precede the edits, with user changes, untracked files, and unrelated generated output untouched? Check the session log beside the working tree.
provisions.statement: An agent MUST read `git status` before editing and preserve user changes, untracked files, and unrelated generated output.
provisions.rationale: A working tree can hold the user's own uncommitted edits, untracked files, and generated output from an unrelated task. An agent that edits without looking overwrites or deletes work outside its scope. Reading `git status` first marks that work as untouchable.

provisions.heading: Inspect Local Examples After Standards
provisions.evidence: Does the change name the neighboring files that shaped it after the standards? Check the change beside its neighbors.
provisions.statement: Inspect neighboring consumer files after loading applicable standards.
provisions.rationale: Standards state the required shape, while neighboring files show the names, folders, and idioms this project chose for it. An agent that skips them writes compliant but foreign-looking code that the next edit rewrites.

provisions.heading: Keep Agent Working Files Under Agents
provisions.evidence: Does every agent working file sit under `.agents/` or the path the working-files convention names? Check the working files beside the convention.
provisions.statement: Keep agent working files under `.agents/`, with tracked `skills/` and `records/` folders and ignored `scratch/` and `delegate/` folders.
provisions.rationale: Agent work with no agreed home lands beside authored records, where it pollutes review, or vanishes with the session, where nobody can audit it. The split keeps durable work in `skills/` and `records/` and machine-local work in the ignored `scratch/` and `delegate/` folders.
provisions.example:
```text
.agents/
  skills/
  records/
  delegate/
  scratch/
```

provisions.heading: Keep the Agent Protocol Current
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `agent-protocol-drift` (level S) when the region differs from what `render` would write, `agent-protocol-missing` (level S) when `AGENTS.md` holds no region, and `skill-drift` (level S) when a project-scope skill copy differs from what the carried release generates.
provisions.statement: A project MUST keep its agent protocol region and its project-scope skill copies equal to what its LiteSpec release generates.
provisions.rationale: The region carries the commands and rules every session loads first. A stale region points agents at an old release, an old selection, or commands that changed, while the tool output stays current. The project-scope skill copies carry the same procedure to tools that load skills on demand, and a stale copy points at the same old release. The release template plus the project file regenerate the region and the project-scope skill copies in one command, so drift is always fixable. Global copies live outside the project and stay outside the check. Settled by [decision/0037-generate-the-agent-protocol](decision/0037-generate-the-agent-protocol) and [decision/0039-ship-a-litespec-skill](decision/0039-ship-a-litespec-skill).
provisions.example: Claimwick upgrades its LiteSpec release and runs `litespec model render`; the region in its `AGENTS.md` and its project-scope skill copies match what the new release generates.

provisions.heading: Load Applicable Extensions
provisions.evidence: Does the change name each extension loaded before editing inside its boundary? Check the change record beside the extensions the project selects.
provisions.statement: An agent MUST load selected project extensions and selected applicable local extensions before editing code or prose inside the extension's boundary.
provisions.rationale: An extension replaces baseline guidance inside its boundary. An agent that edits there without loading the extension follows the baseline the extension replaced, and the change contradicts the project's own selection.
provisions.example: A change to the cached catalog reads the selected caching extension before touching the code its boundary covers.

provisions.heading: Load Applicable Provisions Before Editing
provisions.evidence: Does the completion report answer every judgment provision `litespec rules --since <base>` listed? Compare the rules output with the report.
provisions.statement: An agent MUST run `litespec rules <path>` before editing a file and answer each judgment provision `litespec rules --since <base>` lists before reporting done.
provisions.rationale: Provisions are only usable when retrieved by situation: the query returns what governs the change, grouped by strength, with project conventions and waivers merged in. `litespec rules <...> --full` adds rationale and example when a statement is not enough. Settled by [decision/0038-narrow-rules-output-per-file-and-change-set](decision/0038-narrow-rules-output-per-file-and-change-set).
provisions.example: `litespec rules use-case/spending.submit-expense` returns the provisions that govern the change, grouped by strength.

provisions.heading: Make Coherent Scoped Changes
provisions.evidence: Does every changed artifact trace to the authorized request? Check the changed files beside the task text.
provisions.statement: An agent MUST make the smallest coherent change that satisfies the authorized request.
provisions.rationale: A change that stops at code and skips its records, tests, or operating evidence leaves the workspace claiming behavior nothing proves. A change that sprawls past the request drags unrelated files into review. The smallest coherent change keeps the records, code, tests, and evidence that belong together in one reviewable unit.

provisions.heading: Name Judged Provisions in the Completion Report
provisions.evidence: Does the completion report name every judged provision with its judgment? Check the report beside the provisions the query returned.
provisions.statement: A completion report MUST name each provision the agent judged and how it judged it.
provisions.rationale: The report shows which required provisions, defaults, and advisory provisions the change met and the judgment for each, so the owner checks the reasoning without re-reading the change. A provision the query returned but the report skips is a judgment nobody can check.
provisions.example: The report names each returned provision with its judgment: followed, replaced by a named convention, or parked by a waiver.

provisions.heading: Protect Proofs from Implementation Edits
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check --since <ref>` reports `proof-hash-drift` as advisory for each scenario whose proving test method changed since the base while the scenario did not.
provisions.statement: An agent MUST NOT delete, skip, or weaken a test that proves a scenario, or change its expected values, unless the scenario changed in the same change; it reports a test it believes is wrong instead of editing it.
provisions.rationale: A proof that changes with the implementation stops proving the decided behavior and starts restating the code. The proof ledger records each scenario's hash and the hash of each test that proves it, so `model check --since` can report, as an advisory finding, each scenario whose proving test changed while the scenario did not. Hashing the proving test method rather than its file keeps an unrelated edit in the same file from reporting a change. Settled by [decision/0033-agents-never-weaken-proving-tests](decision/0033-agents-never-weaken-proving-tests).
provisions.example: A handler change makes a proving test fail; the agent reports the failing test and the mismatch instead of changing the expected value to fit the new result.

provisions.heading: Raise Open Figures to the Owner
provisions.evidence: Does every open figure have an owner question with a recommendation or a backlog item? Check the owner questions and the backlog board beside the change.
provisions.statement: An agent MUST raise each open figure to the owner with a recommendation, or place it on the backlog board.
provisions.rationale: A figure without a recommendation asks the owner to research from nothing, while a recommendation gives a default to accept or correct. Grouping figures by subject lets the owner answer one set at a time. A figure never becomes a silent agent decision or code written on a guess.
provisions.example: Two open figures land in one owner question set, each with a recommendation.

provisions.heading: Read the Full Record Before Changing a Boundary
provisions.evidence: Does each file generation or boundary change cite the full record it matched? Check the change beside the cited records.
provisions.statement: Read the full record, the record file with its explanation file, before generating a file, changing a public boundary, or choosing between patterns.
provisions.rationale: Generating a file or changing a public boundary from a summary risks baking a paraphrase into a contract. The full record carries the exact fields, links, and wording the new surface matches. A small edit that follows an existing local pattern can rely on neighboring code instead.

provisions.heading: Replace Only Declared Conventions
provisions.evidence: Does each convention replacement resolve to a recorded local convention? Check the replacements beside the project documentation.
provisions.statement: An agent MUST apply a replacement for a convention only when the project documentation records that replacement.
provisions.rationale: Conventions exist to be replaced, but only through a recorded decision. An undocumented local preference that silently replaces a baseline default looks identical to a mistake, so the next agent fixes it back. The recorded convention keeps the replacement visible and reviewable.

provisions.heading: Restrict Unapproved Side Effects
provisions.evidence: Does an explicit task instruction naming the action and its bounds cover each consequential action beyond the task, or does the project's `AGENTS.md` grant the wider authority? Check the task text beside the actions taken.
provisions.statement: An agent MUST stay inside its authorized task and take no consequential action beyond it without an explicit task instruction that names the action and its bounds.
provisions.rationale: Inside the task, the agent applies an approved standard or decision, drafts records and proposed decisions, implements the change, and reports findings, including a failed check or a conflict between provisions. It approves no product-policy proposal of its own, widens no scope, invents no business value, and takes no consequential outside action beyond the task. Packages, migrations, authentication, a public API, production data, releases, spending, and outside calls that change state each need an explicit task instruction that names the action and its bounds, because none of them can be judged from the task text alone. A project may grant wider authority in its `AGENTS.md`. Settled by [decision/0086-set-one-agent-authority-boundary](decision/0086-set-one-agent-authority-boundary).
provisions.example: A task that names the migration and its scope approves it; a task silent on releases leaves a release unmade.

provisions.heading: Scope Every Convention to Files It Governs
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `convention-unreached` (level G) for a project convention whose Applies to matches no file in the project tree and no record.
provisions.statement: A project convention MUST state an Applies to that matches at least one file in the project tree or one record the project writes.
provisions.rationale: `rules` returns a convention only when its Applies to meets the queried path or record. A convention that meets nothing reaches no agent, so its rule stays unread while the project believes it is stated. One match keeps every stated convention live.
provisions.example: Claimwick records that every command handler logs its outcome, with `stack: dotnet; artifact: command-handler`; the convention meets each handler file, so `rules` returns it before an agent edits one.

provisions.heading: Search the Provisions Before Recording a Decision
provisions.evidence: Does any technical decision restate a choice a provision already makes? Compare each decision with the `rules` output for its subject.
provisions.statement: Query `litespec rules` for the decision's subject, and where a provision makes the choice, follow that provision instead of recording a decision.
provisions.rationale: Many technical choices are already decided: a provision names the shape, the baseline, or the boundary the code follows. A decision that restates such a choice splits authority between the provision and the record, and the two drift. Searching first keeps one home for each decided choice.
provisions.example: An agent about to record how Claimwick declares integration edges queries `litespec rules` for the subject; the provision declares every edge in a record, so the code follows it and no decision is recorded.

provisions.heading: Select Task Context
provisions.evidence: Does the completion report name the model query that selected the cited records, or the prose-only correction and the record it read? Check the report beside the cited records.
provisions.statement: An agent MUST query the project model for the records that cover the request, and read the query output, before changing behavior, access, a contract, or a trace link; a prose-only correction of an existing record needs only the record and its explanation file.
provisions.rationale: Without the query, an agent reads either too little and invents the missing rules, or half the repository and buries the task in unrelated guidance. The query returns the smallest record set that covers the request, with the links the builder joined between records, so the agent starts from decided Intent. A change that touches behavior, access, a contract, or a trace link always needs that set. A prose-only correction of an existing record needs no joined links: the record and its explanation file show the decided shape, and a query would slow ordinary work without adding information.
provisions.example: `litespec model query use-case/spending.submit-expense` returns the use case with its rules, results, and scenarios. A spelling fix in a setting record reads the record and its explanation file, then edits without querying the model.

provisions.heading: Stop on Unresolved Conflict
provisions.evidence: Does the stopped work quote the conflict with both provision IDs and paths? Check the handoff beside the disagreeing provisions.
provisions.statement: An agent MUST stop when applicable provisions disagree without declared precedence and quote both provision IDs and paths.
provisions.rationale: When two provisions disagree and no precedence decides, any continuation invents a compromise neither provision states. Stopping with both provision identifiers and paths hands the decision to a person with exactly the evidence the decision needs.

provisions.heading: Take Expected Values from the Scenario
provisions.evidence: Do each test's expected values match the scenario's Then, with none taken from a code run? Check the assertions beside the scenario Thens.
provisions.statement: An agent MUST take a test's expected values only from the scenario's Then, never from running the code.
provisions.rationale: Expected values read from a passing run restate what the code already does, so the test stays green while behavior drifts. The scenario's Then states the decided intent, which makes the test check the behavior rather than copy it.
provisions.example: A scenario whose Then names a total of `42.50` keeps `42.50` as the asserted value even when the code returns `42.51`: the mismatch fails the test instead of updating the expectation.

provisions.heading: Verify Money Calculations and Refusals Against Held-Back Examples
provisions.evidence: Does the check log show money-risk refusal and calculation rows written by a different author, withheld during implementation, and run after? Check the log beside the withheld rows.
provisions.statement: An agent MUST verify a refusal or calculation implementation that carries the money risk against example rows held back from the agent that wrote it.
provisions.rationale: Money rules decide amounts a customer pays or receives, so fitting the code to the examples instead of the rule moves money. A different author than the implementing agent writes the held-back rows. They sit under `proof/withheld/`, which the implementing agent's instructions exclude. Their expected values cite the scenario's rule, and they run in CI. The money risk is the risk on the permission guarding the use case. Settled by [decision/0085-bind-proof-to-code-and-outcomes](decision/0085-bind-proof-to-code-and-outcomes).
provisions.example: The implementing agent writes a discount calculation from its rule and scenario; a CI check runs the withheld rows from `proof/withheld/` against the result.

provisions.heading: Verify Refusals and Calculations Against Held-Back Examples
provisions.evidence: Does the check log show refusal and calculation example rows withheld during implementation and run after? Check the log beside the implementing change.
provisions.statement: An agent SHOULD verify a refusal or calculation implementation against example rows held back from the agent that wrote it.
provisions.rationale: An agent that sees the examples while implementing fits the code to the rows instead of the rule. Held-back rows turn the examples into an independent check: the implementing agent works from the rule and the scenario, and a later check runs the withheld rows against the result. For a calculation or refusal rule that carries the money risk, held-back verification is required, as [Verify Money Calculations and Refusals Against Held-Back Examples](#verify-money-calculations-and-refusals-against-held-back-examples) states. Settled by [decision/0085-bind-proof-to-code-and-outcomes](decision/0085-bind-proof-to-code-and-outcomes).
provisions.example: The implementing agent writes a discount calculation from its rule and scenario; a later check runs the withheld example rows against the result.

provisions.heading: Write Pages Below Decided Intent
provisions.evidence: Does each written page trace to a decided Intent record, with no invented promise? Check the written pages beside the Intent records.
provisions.statement: An agent MUST write every page below decided Intent.
provisions.rationale: Intent holds the decided promises, and everything below those decisions is written by agents: Behavior records, code, and tests that carry the decisions down. An agent that invents promises writes commitments nobody decided, while an agent that waits for dictation wastes the reading the owner gives to finished work. Writing below decided Intent keeps authorship with the agent and decisions with the owner.
provisions.example: Given a requirement for expense reimbursement, an agent writes the use case, its scenarios, and the handler without asking what the promise means.

provisions.heading: Attach Examples to Their Provisions
provisions.evidence: `litespec-maintain validate` emits no `STANDARD_EXAMPLE_LABEL`, `PAGE_UNKNOWN_SECTION`, or `REFERENCE_EXAMPLE_DECLARATION` diagnostic.
provisions.statement: An informative example MUST belong to its provision or to a Reference Example that names every provision it demonstrates.
provisions.rationale: An example floating free of its provision reads as a second rule, and readers obey the illustration instead of the obligation. Sitting inside its provision, or inside a Reference Example that names every provision it demonstrates, marks it as illustration.

provisions.heading: Cite Owned Content Instead of Copying It
provisions.evidence: Does any passage restate content another page owns? Compare repeated passages with the owning page.
provisions.statement: A page MUST link to content another page owns instead of restating it.
provisions.rationale: The next unrelated edit updates the source and misses the copy, and readers follow the stale text. One home for each fact keeps every reader on the current text. A link to a record names its identifier, not its file.

provisions.heading: Copy Each Template from the Example
provisions.evidence: `litespec-maintain validate` (`TEMPLATE_SOURCE_DIFFERS`, `TEMPLATE_SOURCE_MISSING`) and `litespec model check` (`template-value-unchanged`).
provisions.statement: Each record template in `templates/consumer/` MUST equal the Claimwick example record its identifier names, and a scaffold that `litespec new` writes keeps no copied text or number.
provisions.rationale: A template doubles as a worked example, so it stays coherent only as one record of the reference product. `litespec-maintain validate` reports a template that differs from its example record, and `litespec model check` reports `template-value-unchanged` on a scaffold that keeps a copied value, so a copied period or a copied statement cannot pass as a decision. Proposed by [decision/0056-copy-each-template-from-claimwick](decision/0056-copy-each-template-from-claimwick).

provisions.heading: Define Each Glossary Term Under Its Heading
provisions.evidence: Does every glossary entry open with its definition and carry no Term line? Check `docs/reference/glossary.md`.
provisions.statement: A glossary entry MUST hold its definition in the paragraph under its term heading.
provisions.rationale: The heading anchor already carries the term identifier, so a `Term` line would repeat it. The paragraph under the heading holds the definition, and the lines after it name the record layer, established aliases, the source, and rejected synonyms where they exist.

provisions.heading: End Each Provision with One Verification Line
provisions.evidence: `litespec-maintain validate` emits no `VERIFY_MISSING_ID`, `VERIFY_DUPLICATE_ID`, `VERIFY_ORDER`, or `VERIFY_HEADER` diagnostic.
provisions.statement: Every provision MUST end its fields with exactly one verification line.
provisions.rationale: A provision with no verification line is a rule nobody checks. Each team assumes a tool covers it while no tool was told. One line per provision, beside the rule it checks, makes each rule reviewable by a person or a tool.

provisions.heading: Exclude a Sequence Number from the Identifier
provisions.evidence: Does any new identifier carry a sequence number? Check the provision IDs the change adds.
provisions.statement: A provision ID MUST NOT contain a sequence number.
provisions.rationale: A counter says where a provision sits among its siblings and nothing about what it requires. Words name the obligation. Numbers would renumber every sibling on each insertion and break citations for no gain.

provisions.heading: Exclude Cross-Release Compatibility Work
provisions.evidence: Does any page promise migration, mapping, or alias between releases? Check the release material the change adds.
provisions.statement: The LiteSpec repository MUST NOT publish a compatibility guarantee, migration path, deprecation period, or identifier alias between its own releases.
provisions.rationale: LiteSpec is a pinned contract, not a running service: consumers adopt a release whole, on their own schedule. Compatibility guarantees, migration paths, deprecation periods, and identifier aliases between LiteSpec releases would promise a continuity the model does not offer. A consumer product keeps its own API compatibility, migration, deprecation, and rollback provisions for its own users.

provisions.heading: Exclude Generated Regions from Prose Checks
provisions.evidence: Do any findings point inside generated-region fences? Check the findings the checks report.
provisions.statement: An authoring check MUST skip every generated region.
provisions.rationale: A generated region holds tool output: no author wrote it, and no author can fix it by editing the page. Checking it would fail pages for words outside author control, and writers would learn to ignore diagnostics.

provisions.heading: Exclude Historical Transition Material
provisions.evidence: Does any active file carry history-specific paths, aliases, or migration material? Check the files the change adds.
provisions.statement: Current standards material MUST NOT contain history-specific paths, IDs, terms, aliases, replacement maps, release migration material, compatibility rules, or transition checks other than the generated provision identifier list in the changelog.
provisions.rationale: A snapshot that carries aliases, maps, migration notes, or transition checks for other releases forces every reader to learn releases they did not pin. The published snapshot states its own contract and nothing else. An extension's `Baseline Relationship` section names a provision it replaces inside this release, which is a current replacement rather than history. The changelog's generated list of added, removed, and renamed provision identifiers states a fact about the release it ships in; it offers no alias, mapping, or migration path, so it stands as the one exception this provision allows.

provisions.heading: Generate the Provision Diff for Each Release
