provisions.rationale: A step written as a product sentence reads in flow detail with no Behavior knowledge: it states what a person experiences, not which handler runs. The sentence states one act of its performer and may end with the product's observable response after the act, as in "Finance reimburses the approved expense, and Claimwick pays the amount into the employee's account". How the product computes that response stays in the cited requirement, and a second act of a person is a second step. Numbers, limits, and conditions stay in the cited requirement; the step states the experience only. Proposed by [decision/0048-state-the-start-and-branches-of-each-flow](decision/0048-state-the-start-and-branches-of-each-flow). The `id` (`s1`, `s2`, and so on) gives Behavior a stable target: use cases, reactions, and jobs point up with `serves` to `flow/<name>#s1`. A step naming its use case drags Behavior into Intent and breaks the flow detail every time Behavior renames. The performer and the failure text are optional: a step names the actor taking the flow only at a handoff in `actor`, or the external system performing it in `system` when no person acts, and carries `failure` where the flow can fail. Reworded by [decision/0049-literal-flow-words-concrete-consequences](decision/0049-literal-flow-words-concrete-consequences). Settled by decision 0067.
provisions.example: Step `s4` states `Finance reimburses the approved expense.` in `statement` and names no use case; `use-case/spending.reimburse-expense` names `flow/submit-and-reimburse#s4` in `serves`.

provisions.heading: Cite Shared Provisions in Their Published Form
provisions.evidence: `litespec-maintain validate` emits no `ID_UNKNOWN_REFERENCE` diagnostic.
provisions.statement: A shared provision citation MUST use its published identifier.
provisions.rationale: A shared provision is cited across projects, so its identifier looks the same everywhere. The published `litespec/<page>#<slug>` form stays fixed, while project records use the type forms above.

provisions.heading: Exclude Declared Content Paths from the ASCII Check
provisions.evidence: Does any non-ASCII prose sit outside the paths the project record declares? Check the content files against the declaration.
provisions.statement: An ASCII check MUST exclude only the natural-language content paths that the project record declares.
provisions.rationale: A product whose subject is another language carries that language in its content files, where a diacritic is part of a word rather than a styling choice. Excluding only the declared content paths keeps the check strict everywhere else: documents about that content stay in scope, so styled prose filed beside content still meets the check.

provisions.heading: Follow the Identifier Form of Each Record Type
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `identifier-invalid` for an identifier outside the form its type uses.
provisions.statement: A record identifier MUST follow the form the model states for its record type.
provisions.rationale: A reader who meets `use-case/spending.submit-expense` knows it is a use case in the spending module without opening it. If two types shared one form, a citation needs its surrounding page to make sense, and search returns the wrong records.
provisions.example: `domain-event/expense.submitted` names a domain event of the expense aggregate.

provisions.heading: Keep Names an Outside Standard Fixes
provisions.evidence: Was any fixed name renamed to fit the grammar? Check the Gherkin fields and CloudEvents attributes the change touches.
provisions.statement: Every name an outside standard fixes MUST stay exactly as that standard spells it.
provisions.rationale: A name an outside standard fixes belongs to that standard: renaming `given` to fit the word classes breaks every Gherkin reader. The grammar stays complete by exempting exactly these names instead of growing an exceptions list. Gherkin and CloudEvents names are the only exemptions.
provisions.example: A Claimwick scenario keeps `given`, `when`, and `then`, which the word-class table gives no class.

provisions.heading: Keep Wire Codes Stable
provisions.evidence: Does any wire code in the contract break the values deployed clients branch on? Check the wire codes in the contract against the deployed clients.
provisions.statement: A wire code MUST stay unchanged once clients read it.
provisions.rationale: Wire codes travel to deployed clients, which branch on their exact values. Renaming a code that clients already read breaks every deployed reader that compares the old value, with no record the reader opens to learn the new one.

provisions.heading: List the Compounds a Rejection Does Not Cover
provisions.evidence: Does any compound use a rejected word for another concept without an `except` entry? Check the compounds against the rejection's `except` list.
provisions.statement: A glossary rejection MUST list, in `except`, every compound in which a rejected word names a concept other than the one the rejection is about.
provisions.rationale: A rejection matches a word, and a word can belong to more than one term: Claimwick rejects `docket` in favor of `receipt` for payment proof while a docket still names the shipping list. Without the `except` list, the check would force the project to rename an unrelated concept or drop a sound rejection.
provisions.example:
The exemption covers the compound only, so the bare word stays rejected.

```json
{ "word": "docket", "reason": "one word for a payment receipt and a shipping list",
  "scope": "^.litespec/domain/modules/spending/", "except": ["shipping docket"] }
```

provisions.heading: Name a Boolean as a Predicate
provisions.evidence: Does every boolean field read as a predicate with no `is` or `has` prefix? Check the boolean fields the change adds.
provisions.statement: Every boolean field MUST read as a present-tense predicate that is true about the record when the value is true.
provisions.rationale: A boolean without a prefix reads as a fact about the record: `applies` says the constraint applies, and `recorded` says the entry is recorded. An `is` or `has` prefix adds a word that says nothing the value does not already say. The predicate form keeps every boolean readable in a sentence about its record.
provisions.example: Claimwick marks an applying constraint with `applies: true` instead of `isApplicable: true`.

provisions.heading: Name Commands as Verbs and Flags by What They Set
provisions.evidence: Does every subcommand read as a verb and every flag as its mode or value? Check the commands and flags the change adds.
provisions.statement: Every subcommand MUST read as a verb and every flag as the mode or value it sets.
provisions.rationale: A verb names what the command does, so `check` reads as an action before its arguments are weighed. A flag that names its mode or value reads the same way at every call site, and kebab-case keeps multiword flags writable without quotes. Stable exit codes let scripts tell a clean run from a blocking finding from bad arguments.
provisions.example: The release check runs as `litespec model check --release` and exits 1 on a blocking finding.

provisions.heading: Name Each Date by What It Marks
provisions.evidence: `litespec-maintain validate` emits no `FIELD_NAME_SHAPE` diagnostic for a date field.
provisions.statement: Every date field MUST end in `On` for a recorded date or carry a name that states what the date does.
provisions.rationale: A recorded date says when something happened or until when it holds: `readOn` says when an outside source was read, and `expiresOn` says when a waiver ends. `effectiveFrom` opens a validity span. The shape tells a reader which dates record the world and which open a span.
provisions.example: A Claimwick constraint carries `readOn` on each source with the date the source was read, and a waiver carries `expiresOn` with the date it ends.

provisions.heading: Name Each Field by Its Word Class
provisions.evidence: Does every field use the name its word class gives it? Check the field names the change adds against the word-class table.
provisions.statement: Every record field MUST use the name its word class gives it in the word-class table.
provisions.rationale: One grammar with no exceptions list means a reader who learned `cites` on a flow reads `cites` on a requirement without a second look. Each class answers one question about the field: whether it identifies, links, classifies, narrates, conditions, or reasons. Only names an outside standard fixes stand outside this grammar. Settled by [decision/0006-one-field-naming-grammar](decision/0006-one-field-naming-grammar) on the evidence in [research/field-naming-evidence](research/field-naming-evidence) and [research/cross-layer-trace-evidence](research/cross-layer-trace-evidence).
provisions.example: The Claimwick flow `submit-an-expense` names its goal in `serves` and states each step in `statement`.

provisions.heading: Name Each Finding Code by Subject and Problem
provisions.evidence: Does every finding code read as subject-problem with a problem word from the table? Check the finding codes the change adds against the problem-word table.
provisions.statement: Every finding code MUST read as `<subject>-<problem>` with the problem drawn from the problem-word table.
provisions.rationale: A code in subject-problem form tells a reader what the finding is about and what is wrong with it before the message is opened. A closed set of problem words, each with one meaning, keeps codes comparable across tools: one word for absent, one for expired, and no synonyms. The problem-word table holds each word with its meaning and an example.
provisions.example: A use case with no scenario takes the code `use-case-scenario-missing`.

provisions.heading: Name Each Record by Its Type's Name Form
provisions.evidence: Does every record name use the name form of its type? Check the identifiers the change adds against the record-name table.
provisions.statement: Every record name MUST use the name form the record-name table gives its type.
provisions.rationale: A name in the word class of what the record is tells a reader the type before the identifier is opened: a verb opens a use case, a noun phrase opens a goal, and a past participle opens a domain event. One name form per type keeps listings scannable and citations writable by hand. The record-name table holds the Intent forms beside the Behavior and governance forms. Settled by [decision/0077-use-the-standard-term-for-each-concept](decision/0077-use-the-standard-term-for-each-concept).
provisions.example: Claimwick names the flow `submit-an-expense`, the use case `submit-expense`, and the setting `receipt-threshold`.

provisions.heading: Name Records with One to Six Words
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `identifier-invalid` for a name outside one to six lowercase hyphenated words.
provisions.statement: A name MUST carry one to six lowercase hyphenated words.
provisions.rationale: A short hyphenated name reads aloud in review and stays stable when the wording of the record changes. A long name gets shortened differently at each citation, and the shortcuts drift into competing names for one record.
provisions.example: `decision/0001-receipt-threshold` counts its number as one word.

provisions.heading: Record the Project Vocabulary as Data
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `glossary-invalid` for a glossary that fails the glossary schema.
provisions.statement: A consumer MUST record each term, its rejected synonyms, the scope of each rejection, and its mannered terms in the project glossary satisfying `schemas/glossary.schema.yaml`.
provisions.rationale: A glossary column headed "Avoid" speaks to a reader and to nothing else: no tool can check it. A rule held as data reaches the reader and the validator alike, so the same rejection appears in prose guidance and in diagnostics.
provisions.example:
A rejection carries the scope that binds it, because a word that is right in one module is wrong in another.

```json
{ "id": "term/customer", "term": "customer", "meaning": "A person or company that buys.",
  "rejected": [{ "word": "client", "scope": "^domain/modules/orders/",
    "reason": "client names the API consumer" }] }
```

provisions.heading: Reject a Recorded Synonym Inside Its Scope
provisions.evidence: Does any word on the page use a synonym the glossary rejects for this scope? Check the page against the project glossary.
provisions.statement: Authored prose MUST NOT use a synonym that the project glossary rejects for the scope the page sits in.
provisions.rationale: Term drift is invisible one page at a time and plain across a module: each page looks fine while the project slowly speaks two languages. The expensive case is a synonym that is a defined term elsewhere, because one word then names two things and every reader guesses which one.

provisions.heading: Resolve Every Identifier Citation
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `reference-unknown` for a citation naming no written record.
provisions.statement: Every identifier citation MUST resolve to a written record.
provisions.rationale: A citation is a promise that a record exists at the other end. A citation that names nothing sends the reader searching for a record nobody wrote, so the model check fails it.

provisions.heading: Review Each Term for Its Lookalikes
provisions.evidence: Does any term differ from another only in hyphenation, spelling, plurality, or a compound split? Check the terms the change adds against the glossary.
provisions.statement: A project MUST resolve each pair of terms that differ only in hyphenation, spelling variant, plurality, or a compound split.
provisions.rationale: Two spellings of one concept split every search and every listing, and a reader cannot tell whether they name one concept or two. One spelling per concept keeps each term defined once and checked once. A hyphenated pair whose first part is a function word is two words side by side, not one compound split in two, so the check skips it: `a`, `an`, `as`, `at`, `by`, `in`, `of`, `on`, `or`, `to`, and `with`.
provisions.example: The notification `send-receiptreminder-confirmation` and the reaction `send-receipt-reminder-on-expense-submitted` name one concept with two spellings; the project picks one and renames the other. `send-on-line-notice` beside `send-online-notice` is not reported, since `on` opens no compound.

provisions.heading: State Mannered Terms Literally
provisions.evidence: Does any mannered term stand where the glossary asks for the literal word? Check the page against the project glossary.
provisions.statement: Authored prose MUST NOT use a mannered term the project glossary lists.
provisions.rationale: A metaphor or stock phrase reads smoothly while hiding what the project means: each reader pictures a different act behind the same flourish. The glossary lists each mannered term with the literal phrase that carries its meaning, so the check points at the flourish and names the plain words to reach for.
provisions.example: The glossary lists `{ "term": "leverage", "instead": "use" }`, so prose reads "use the retry queue" rather than "leverage the retry queue".

provisions.heading: Use Every Identifier Once
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `identifier-duplicate` for an identifier used twice.
provisions.statement: A record identifier MUST name exactly one record.
provisions.rationale: An identifier used twice names two records at once, so every citation of it points both ways. One use per identifier keeps each citation single-valued.
provisions.example: Two records named `use-case/spending.submit-expense` leave the model check reporting the duplicate on the second record.

provisions.heading: Use the Declared Record Identifier Grammar
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `identifier-invalid` for a record identifier outside the declared grammar.
provisions.statement: A consumer record identifier MUST be `type/home.name` in kebab-case, using the form the Project Model states for its type.
provisions.rationale: The type names the record kind and `home.name` names the owning module or set, so an identifier resolves with no lookup table. One grammar for every record kind keeps identifiers writable by hand and checkable by tool. The [Project Model](model.md) states the form each type uses, and the Identifier Forms section above states the name rules and checks.
provisions.example: `reaction/spending.send-receipt-reminder-on-expense-submitted` is a reaction owned by the spending module, and `flow/submit-and-reimburse#s2` is the second step of a flow.

provisions.heading: Write Each Finding Message as a Fact
provisions.evidence: Does every finding message state one present-tense fact opening with the subject and identifier? Check the messages the change adds.
provisions.statement: Every finding message MUST state one present-tense fact that opens with the subject title and its quoted identifier.
provisions.rationale: A message that states a fact survives every reader: the terminal and the book both show what is true. Advice belongs in the finding table on the [model page](../tools/model.md), where it is written once beside the code instead of repeated in every occurrence. Analyzer diagnostics keep their `LS` numbers and follow the same message rule.
provisions.example: A flow step with no serving use case reports `Flow step 'book-a-room#s3' is served by no use case.`

provisions.heading: Write Each Text Kind in Its Own Form
provisions.evidence: Does every text use the form of its kind? Check the statements, steps, and meanings the change adds against the text-kind table.
provisions.statement: Every project text MUST use the form the text-kind table gives its kind.
provisions.rationale: Each kind of text has one reader and one job: a requirement promises, a domain event reports, and a runbook step instructs. One form per kind means the tense and voice tell the reader what the text does before a word is weighed. Record values stay in the third person, Intent chapter prose says `we` for the business, and nothing says `you`.
provisions.example: A Claimwick requirement states "An expense above the threshold waits for its approver."

provisions.heading: Write Each Value in the Value Style
provisions.evidence: Does every statement, meaning, rationale, condition, failure, and title value use its row's style? Check the values the change adds against the value-style table.
provisions.statement: Every `statement`, `meaning`, `rationale`, `*Because`, `*When`, `condition`, `failure`, and `title` value MUST use the value style the value-style table states.
provisions.rationale: Values are read far more than they are written, in records, in the book, and in tool output. One written form per value means a period or a capital letter is never a styling choice but part of the value. The value-style table ends each row with the mechanical test the value meets. Settled by [decision/0011-one-grammar-for-names-and-values](decision/0011-one-grammar-for-names-and-values) on the evidence in [research/naming-grammar-evidence](research/naming-grammar-evidence).
provisions.example: A Claimwick flow step states "The traveller pays for the booking."

provisions.heading: Write in American English
provisions.evidence: Does any word use British spelling? Check the field names, enum values, and prose the change adds.
provisions.statement: Every field name and enum value MUST use American spelling.
provisions.rationale: One spelling per word keeps each term defined once and checked once: `license` in one record and `licence` in another split every search and every listing. American spelling is the project spelling for field names and enum values; prose spelling follows the [Writing Standard](writing.md). Each British form reads as a rejected word beside its American spelling.
provisions.example: Claimwick writes `license` and `pseudonymize` in field names, values, and prose.

provisions.heading: Write Quantities in Standard Units
provisions.evidence: Does every quantity use a standard unit? Check the dates, durations, money values, and numbers the change adds.
provisions.statement: Every quantity in a record MUST use an ISO 8601 date, an ISO 8601 duration, an amount with an ISO 4217 currency, or a number with its unit.
provisions.rationale: Free-text quantities hide behind local habits: one record writes `7 years`, another writes `seven years`, and a check matches neither. ISO dates, ISO durations, and ISO currency codes give every quantity one written form across records and tools. Prose keeps numbers readable by writing each with its unit.
provisions.example: Claimwick holds a room for `PT10M` and writes "95 percent of checkouts complete" in prose.

provisions.heading: Add Behavior Detail When Specifying Intent
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` emits no `requirement-fulfillment-missing`, `record-link-missing`, `step-use-case-missing`, `erasure-undeclared`, or `setting-requirement-missing` finding across Behavior records.
provisions.statement: Behavior that fulfills an Intent record MUST add the states, invariants, refusals, consistency, data classes with erasure positions, freshness, and tenant-scoped access the Intent record leaves unstated.
provisions.rationale: An Intent promise says what the product owes in product words, without saying how the system keeps it. Behavior turns each promise into the states, invariants, refusals, consistency, data classes with erasure positions, freshness, and tenant-scoped access that keep it. Only Behavior records fulfill a requirement, as `litespec/core/intent#restrict-requirement-fulfillment-to-behavior` states. Without that detail, each implementer fills the gap with a guess, and two guesses about the same promise diverge.
provisions.example: Claimwick's reimbursement promise gains an entity with Approved and Reimbursed states, a refusal for an expense that is already reimbursed, and atomic consistency over one aggregate.

provisions.heading: Build Ahead of a Regulation Only Under Its Constraint
provisions.evidence: Does every anticipatory behavior cite its constraint without blocking a release before the statutory date? Check the regulation-driven Behavior records against the constraint and its date.
provisions.statement: Behavior that anticipates a regulation with a deadline MUST follow that regulation's constraint.
provisions.rationale: A regulation with a deadline needs working behavior before its requirement exists, so the constraint carries the rule in the meantime, with its statutory date in `effectiveFrom`. The release stays shippable until the statutory date, and only then does the missing behavior block it. Without this path, teams either ship late or build the rule where no record owns it.
provisions.example: A privacy regulation taking effect next year enters as a Claimwick constraint with its statutory date, and the anticipatory erasure behavior follows that constraint until the requirement exists.

provisions.heading: Enter World Facts as Cited Research or Constraints
provisions.evidence: Did every world fact enter as a cited and dated research or constraint record? Check the provider, regulation, and incident facts the change relies on.
provisions.statement: A fact learned from the world MUST enter Intent as research, or as a constraint whose `sources` cite its source with the date it was read.
provisions.rationale: Commitments flow down, and facts from the world flow up: a provider's behavior, a regulation, or an incident enters Intent where people can weigh it. The citation and the `readOn` date show where the fact came from and when someone read it, so a later change rechecks the source instead of trusting memory. A constraint names the research it rests on in `basedOn`, as the constraint fields state. Proposed by [decision/0047-cite-a-source-for-each-constraint-rule](decision/0047-cite-a-source-for-each-constraint-rule).
provisions.example: Claimwick's observed two-day payout settlement window enters as research, then as a constraint citing that research.

provisions.heading: Implement Only Declared Behavior
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` emits no `behavior-unrecorded`, `write-undeclared`, `result-undeclared`, `effect-undeclared`, or `refusal-unimplemented` finding across the implementation.
provisions.statement: Implementation MUST add only the code shapes its stack pages fix and no observable outcome, edge, write, or access grant its Behavior records leave undeclared.
provisions.rationale: Stack pages fix the code shapes: the handler, the repository call, and the published domain event each have one prescribed form. An extra outcome, edge, write, or access grant splits the project into a specification that says one thing and code that does another. A handler that authorizes itself is one such extra grant, which analyzer `LS2012` reports.
provisions.example: Claimwick's submit-expense handler returns a code no result declares. The run fails `result-undeclared`, and the fix declares the result or removes the code.

provisions.heading: Prove Each Scenario Through the Public Boundary
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` emits no `use-case-scenario-missing` or `proves-unreached` finding across scenarios and tests.
provisions.statement: At large size or with the `bdd` extension, each scenario MUST be proved by one test through the public boundary.
provisions.rationale: Small projects carry no scenarios unless the `bdd` extension switches them on, so the rule binds large projects and small projects with the extension. A scenario is the leaf of the record tree, so one test through the public boundary ties each leaf to running behavior.
provisions.example: Claimwick, a large project, carries a scenario for its missing-receipt refusal, and one test proves it by submitting an expense without a receipt through the endpoint.

provisions.heading: Raise Open Needs as Owner Questions or Backlog Items
provisions.evidence: Does every unstated need have a question to the owner or a backlog item? Check the added records from a lower record layer beside the owner questions and the backlog.
provisions.statement: A need a lower record layer meets that the upper record layer leaves unstated MUST travel up as a question to the owner or a backlog item, never as code.
provisions.rationale: The lower layer does not decide what the upper layer left unstated, so the need travels up with its context instead of turning into a guess. A question carries product choices to the person who answers for them. A backlog item holds the rest where it stays visible until it is specified. The specification is closed: an agent builds what it states and nothing more.
provisions.example: Claimwick's missing reimbursement policy becomes a question to the owner, not a rule the agent writes.

provisions.heading: Record Changed Provider Behavior as Observed Research
provisions.evidence: Does every provider change have observed research and a citing constraint? Check the provider facts the change relies on beside the research records.
provisions.statement: A changed provider behavior MUST enter as research recording the observed behavior, then as a constraint citing that research.
provisions.rationale: The provider's behavior is a fact from the world, and research is where such facts enter. The constraint that follows names the research in `basedOn`, so the constraint carries its evidence. Code is not the source: a failed reimbursement in production points at the world, and the world is cited.
provisions.example: Claimwick's payout provider starts settling every two days instead of daily: that enters as research with the observed dates, and a settlement-window constraint cites that research.

provisions.heading: Send Commercial and Observable Figures to the Owner
provisions.evidence: Did Behavior fix any figure the owner sets without asking? Check the settings and rules the change adds beside the list of owner-set figures on the model page.
provisions.statement: Behavior that meets a figure the owner sets MUST send it to the owner instead of fixing it.
provisions.rationale: The [model page](model.md) holds the one list of figures the owner sets: prices, fees, rates, terms, markets, payers, retention periods, freshness, and figures that differ by tenant, market, or date. Each figure is a business choice, and only an accountable person makes it. An agent that fixed one would bury a commitment in a Behavior record nobody chose. The figure becomes a question to the owner or a backlog item, never a silent default.
provisions.example: Claimwick's receipt threshold of EUR 25 waits for the owner instead of entering the setting silently.

provisions.heading: Write Each Layer from the Layer Above It
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` emits no `behavior-unrecorded` finding for a refusal literal or a screen call to no endpoint, and reports `mark-missing` for a code element that carries no mark.
provisions.statement: Each record below Intent MUST be written from a record in the record layer above it.
provisions.rationale: Without a parent above it, a lower record could be a carried promise or an invented one, and reviewers cannot tell which. Implementers then build from guesses, and two guesses about the same gap diverge. Writing each record from the layer above keeps one chain from promise to proof, so a gap shows as a missing parent instead of silent invention. Derivation between records follows the same direction: generic refusals derive from `access` and `input` without new records.
provisions.example: Claimwick's submit-expense handler holds a positivity guard with no rule above it. The agent writes the missing rule or reports the gap, and the guard stays until the record lands. Behavior with no parent is recorded or reported, never deleted for lacking one.

provisions.heading: Keep Provision Identifiers Stable Within a Major Version
provisions.evidence: Did a minor release remove or rename any provision identifier? Compare the provision index at the previous tag with the provision index of the release, beside the changelog entry that lists the generated diff.
provisions.statement: A minor LiteSpec release MUST keep every provision identifier of its major version, adding provisions and rewording provision text without removing or renaming an identifier.
provisions.rationale: Consumers cite provision identifiers in code marks, records, and waivers, each written against the major version the project pins. A minor release that removes or renames an identifier breaks those citations inside a version line the consumer took as stable, with no major release to signal the break. A major release may remove or rename identifiers, and the generated provision diff in its changelog lists every added, removed, and renamed identifier, so a consumer moving across a major version finds each change in one place.
provisions.example: A minor release adds `litespec/core/scope#claim-the-record-layers-the-project-uses` and rewords a neighboring provision; both keep their identifiers, so every mark and waiver written against the major version still resolves.

provisions.heading: List Every Stack, Shape, and Extension in the Manifest
provisions.evidence: `litespec-maintain validate` emits `EXTENSION_UNLISTED` for an extension page no manifest entry lists, `LAYER_UNREACHABLE` for a page no stack selection reaches, and `MANIFEST_ANALYZER_PIN` for an analyzer pin that differs from the analyzer project version.
provisions.statement: The LiteSpec manifest MUST list every stack, shape, extension, and version pin the release carries.
provisions.rationale: The manifest is the release record that tools read: stacks and shapes decide which pages apply, extensions decide which conditional bundles a project selects from, and pins decide which versions build. A stack, shape, extension, or pin the manifest omits is one no consumer selects and no tool resolves. Listing all of them in one file keeps the release reproducible from its tag.
provisions.example: The manifest lists the `cache` extension with its page path `docs/ext/cache.md` and its `local` activation scope.

provisions.heading: Mark the Tools with the Provisions They Follow
provisions.evidence: `litespec-maintain validate` emits `MARK_MISSING` for a class with a method and no `follows` mark in a source project under `apps/`, and `MARK_UNRESOLVED` for a `follows` or `proves` mark in a .NET project under `apps/`, outside its `Fixtures` folders, that names no provision in `docs/reference/provisions.md`.
provisions.statement: Every top-level class that declares a method in a .NET source project under `apps/`, and every test that verifies a provision, MUST name its provision in a mark: a `follows` mark on the class and a `proves` mark on the test.
provisions.rationale: LiteSpec's own tools are technical classes: they serve no product record, and each exists because a provision requires a check, a reader, or a generator of its shape. A `follows` mark is the reverse index from that code to the provision, so a retired or renamed provision finds every class still built for it. A `proves` mark finds the tests that keep its check honest. LiteSpec keeps the research and decisions behind its provisions as records under `docs/intent/`, in the shapes a consumer uses; its provisions remain its specification, and the marks point at them directly. The site under `apps/site` is TypeScript with no mark form in the maintainer tool, so it carries no marks.
provisions.example: The .NET scenario reader carries `/// <follows>litespec/core/model#name-the-lowest-record-each-test-proves</follows>`, and the test that confirms a scenario driven through a shared probe step carries `/// <proves>litespec/core/model#name-the-lowest-record-each-test-proves</proves>`.

provisions.heading: Publish a LiteSpec Release from a Tag
provisions.evidence: `dotnet test --solution LiteSpec.slnx` fails `ReleaseVersionTests` when the changelog, the template, or either package version differs from the manifest version, and `.github/workflows/release.yml` refuses a tag that does not name the manifest version, a release tag whose commit is not on `main`, and a candidate tag whose commit is not on `release/<version>`.
provisions.statement: A LiteSpec tag that publishes MUST be `v<version>` on `main`, or a release candidate `v<version>-rc.<n>` on `release/<version>`, and the changelog entry, the consumer template version, and the tool and analyzer package versions name the same manifest version.
provisions.rationale: A git tag is the only durable artifact that names a release: branches move and files change, but the tag stays. Reading the current release from the highest tag gives maintainers, consumers, and tools one shared answer. Writing that version into the manifest, the changelog, the template, and the tool package in the same release keeps the four from disagreeing. A candidate lets a consumer test the packages a release will publish before the release branch merges. Its suffix keeps its packages apart from the release's, and the committed files keep the plain version, so a candidate never changes what `main` names. Each release publishes the CLI as one native executable per platform, in the tool packages and in standalone archives, so the version reaches a consumer with or without .NET, settled by [decision/0021-native-command-line](decision/0021-native-command-line) on the evidence in [research/native-command-line-evidence](research/native-command-line-evidence).

provisions.heading: Publish Each Release Candidate from Its Release Branch
provisions.evidence: Does every release candidate tag name a commit on `release/<version>`, with no candidate packages published from `main`? Check the candidate tags and the release workflow runs that published them.
provisions.statement: Every release candidate MUST publish from its release branch, `release/<version>`, and no candidate publishes from `main`.
provisions.rationale: A consumer validates a candidate before the final release reaches `main`, so the candidate must hold the release branch's commit and nothing newer on `main`. Publishing from the branch keeps the tested packages the packages the release will publish, and the release's final tag still comes from `main`. Proposed by [decision/0059-publish-candidates-from-release-branches](decision/0059-publish-candidates-from-release-branches).

provisions.heading: Record the Reasoning Behind Each Release
provisions.evidence: `litespec-maintain validate` emits no `RECORD_SCHEMA`, `RECORD_ID_MISMATCH`, `RECORD_SOURCE`, `RECORD_UNKNOWN_REFERENCE`, or `RECORD_DECISION_UNCITED` diagnostic.
provisions.statement: A maintainer MUST keep the research and decisions behind each release as records under `docs/intent/`.
provisions.rationale: Provisions state obligations without the questions, sources, or conclusions behind them. Without that reasoning on record, a later change cannot tell why a rule reads as it does. Settled by [decision/0001-keep-release-reasoning-as-records](decision/0001-keep-release-reasoning-as-records) on the evidence in [research/comparable-rationale-practice](research/comparable-rationale-practice).
provisions.example: Claimwick states its five-day reimbursement target in a provision, with the benchmark behind the number in a research record beside it.

provisions.heading: Replace Every Citation on a Rename
provisions.evidence: `litespec-maintain validate` emits no `ID_UNKNOWN_REFERENCE` diagnostic.
provisions.statement: A provision rename MUST replace every citation of the old identifier in one change.
provisions.rationale: An identifier rename changes the ID line, and no alias catches stragglers. Every citation the rename misses names a provision that no longer exists, and readers follow it nowhere. Replacing all of them in one change keeps the repository resolvable at every commit. A heading reword leaves the identifier unchanged, so it needs no citation sweep.
provisions.example: A rename changes the ID line and every citation of it in the same change.

provisions.heading: State the Provision Lifecycle
provisions.evidence: Does every provision sit in exactly one lifecycle state, with no citations to retired identifiers? Check the provisions beside their citations.
provisions.statement: A maintainer MUST keep each provision in exactly one of three states: draft, active, or retired.
provisions.rationale: The three states tell a maintainer what an identifier promises. An active identifier names a rule that holds, with its verification line saying how to check it. A retired identifier names nothing, so a citation to it is a defect rather than a reference. Without the lifecycle, a half-written provision and a removed one look identical to a cited one.
provisions.example: A new provision starts in draft. When its verification line is written, it becomes active. When a richer provision folds its assertion in, it retires.

provisions.heading: Add a Missing Fact to LiteSpec Before the Book Shows It
provisions.evidence: Does every fact the book shows come from LiteSpec? Look at the book beside the model output and the finding codes: each fact is a record field, a computed status, or a check.
provisions.statement: A fact the book needs that LiteSpec does not define MUST become a record field, a computed status, or a check in LiteSpec before the book shows it.
provisions.rationale: Rendering the book is a probe: what it cannot show is a gap in the specification. Closing the gap in LiteSpec gives every project the fact, checked; closing it in the book gives one view an unchecked fact. Settled by [decision/0008-book-follows-record-layers](../intent/decisions/0008-book-follows-record-layers/0008-book-follows-record-layers.md) on the evidence in [research/book-outline-evidence](../intent/research/book-outline-evidence/book-outline-evidence.md), [research/behavior-containment-evidence](../intent/research/behavior-containment-evidence/behavior-containment-evidence.md), and [research/check-coverage-evidence](../intent/research/check-coverage-evidence/check-coverage-evidence.md).
provisions.example: The book needs to say that a refusal has no scenario, so LiteSpec gains a check for it, and the book shows that check's findings.

provisions.heading: Author One Slice at a Time
provisions.evidence: Does every Behavior record show the Intent above it? Follow its `fulfills` and `decides` links.
provisions.statement: Authoring MUST complete one feature from problem to scenario before starting the next.
provisions.rationale: A feature worked from problem to scenario stays complete at every level: each record lands with the Intent above it already written. Parallel slices leave Behavior records resting on Intent nobody wrote yet.

provisions.heading: Classify Every Specification File
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports no `explanation-orphaned` finding, and fails a `.yaml` file with no record type outside a declared unstructured path.
provisions.statement: Every file under the consumer documentation root MUST be a record file, an explanation file beside its record file, or a document, or sit under a declared unstructured path.
provisions.rationale: A file the validator leaves unclassified is skipped, and a skipped file looks sound: its errors stay hidden. Requiring every file to be a record file, an explanation, or a document, or to sit under a declared unstructured path, leaves no page unchecked. A directory index that owns no record uses the index style, and a `README.md` with no frontmatter is a document.

provisions.heading: Compute Completion in the Builder
provisions.evidence: Which features read below `verified`, and which children hold each one back? Look at `completion` on each feature in the model.
provisions.statement: The builder MUST compute one completion stage for every requirement, use case, flow, feature and goal, and write it as `completion` with `stage`, `proof`, `heldBy` and `counts`, with a parent only as far as its weakest in-scope child and `heldBy` naming at most ten children at that stage.
provisions.rationale: Completion is a fact the builder can count from fulfillment, code, and proof, so no record carries a shorthand saying how far it is. One ladder reads the same everywhere: `unfulfilled` when no Behavior record fulfills a record, `specified` when it is fulfilled and no code is found, `coded` when code is found for every in-scope child, and `verified` when every in-scope child is verified with fresh proof. When the model holds no test run, a coded record stays `coded` with proof `unknown`, so proof unknown never reads as a failure. A requirement a waiver parks stays out of the stage and the counts and names itself in `heldBy`, so deferred work stays visible. A goal's completion shows delivery only; its outcome reads `not measured` until the goal records `observations`.
provisions.example: In Claimwick, `feature/expense-submission` shows `coded` with proof `unknown` before any test run, held by the one requirement with no fulfiller; after a passing run proves every fulfiller, the same feature shows `verified` with no held-by entries.

provisions.heading: Compute Proof Statuses in the Builder
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `use-case-unimplemented`, `proves-unreached`, and `refusal-unimplemented` for a use case whose handler, proof, or refusal code is missing, and `proof-invalid` (level A) for a test that both passed and failed within the runs read.
provisions.statement: Coded, verified, tested, exercised, stale, flaky, and reachable MUST come from the builder, never from handwriting.
provisions.rationale: Handwritten state drifts: a record marked coded stays marked after its handler is deleted. Computed state cannot drift, because the builder re-derives it from handlers, routes, scenarios, and test runs on every run. A use case reads coded when a handler, reaction, job, or endpoint marked with it carries it out, verified when every scenario has a passing proof through the public boundary that is not stale, and stale when the scenario, the test body, or a file carrying the mark of the behavior it proves changed after the run, which records its commit. A requirement reads verified when everything fulfilling it is verified and its measure's check passes. A record reads tested when a passing test that asserts something links to it. A flow step reads exercised when a passing proof of a use case, reaction, or job serves it. A proof reads flaky when its test both passed and failed within the runs read. Nothing above Implementation is computed from code: derivation from code into any other record is forbidden, and code-computed facts live in the book and the model output. Settled by [decision/0017-proof-that-holds](decision/0017-proof-that-holds) on the evidence in [research/lower-layers-practice](research/lower-layers-practice).
provisions.example: A use case reads coded when its handler exists.

provisions.heading: Connect Across Modules Only Through Declared Dependencies
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `link-locality-invalid` for a record under a module that is linked from another module with no declared dependency or integration event.
provisions.statement: Within one layer, a record under a module MUST be linked from another module only along a declared module dependency or through an integration event.
provisions.rationale: A record linked from another module with no declared tie is not local: it belongs at product level. The declared dependency or the integration event names the tie, so the seam where a monolith would split stays visible. Links from one layer down to the next may cross modules, because that is how one capability spans modules. This provision is the one rule for links across modules.
provisions.example: A spending rule cited from the finance module with no `dependsOn` tie and no integration event between them is reported; the rule moves to product level or the modules declare the tie.

provisions.heading: Connect Every Behavior Record to Intent
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `record-link-missing` for a use case, reaction, job, notification, or setting with neither `serves` nor `fulfills`, and `use-case-flow-missing` (level G) at large size for a use case that no reaction, job or other use case runs and that serves no flow step.
provisions.statement: A use case, reaction, job, notification, or setting MUST carry `serves`, `fulfills`, or both.
provisions.rationale: A behavior record with no served flow step and no fulfilled requirement answers to nothing above it: no promise explains why it exists. Pointing up with `serves` or `fulfills` ties every behavior to the Intent that asks for it. A use case is background-only when a reaction or job runs it, so `use-case-flow-missing` skips it.

provisions.heading: Declare One Mark Style
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `mark-style-invalid` (level S) for a mark written in a form its language does not take.
provisions.statement: A project MUST write each C# mark in the one style that `marks` in `.litespec/project.yaml` declares, each TypeScript mark as a typed constant, and each operations mark as a comment.
provisions.rationale: Two styles in one language are two ways to do one job: a reader learns both, a check covers both, and a search for a record finds half its code. The C# style is a project choice made once, so every tool reads it from the project file and refuses the other style within C#. TypeScript and operations files have one form each, so a typed constant beside a C# documentation tag is two languages, not two styles. A code fix converts a mark to the form its language takes.
provisions.example: The Claimwick product declares `"marks": "xml"`, so its submit-expense handler carries a documentation tag naming `use-case/spending.submit-expense`, and an attribute naming the same use case is reported. Its use-case module carries the same identifier as a typed constant, and its deployment file carries its `follows` mark as a comment.

provisions.heading: Declare Size and Stacks
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `size-type-missing` and `record-invalid` for a project missing its declaration or a required type.
provisions.statement: A project MUST declare its size and stacks.
provisions.rationale: Size decides which record types and test projects the checks require, while stacks decide which technology pages and checks apply. Without the declaration, the builder cannot tell a missing record from one the project never needed.
provisions.example: The running Claimwick example declares large with a server shape and two stacks.

provisions.heading: Derive a Computed Fact Instead of Restating It
provisions.evidence: Does every count, census, and membership list name its source or command? Look at the numbers the change adds.
provisions.statement: A specification MUST name the source or the command that produces any count, census, or membership list derived between records.
provisions.rationale: A restated number is right until the next unrelated edit changes the records it counts, and nothing reports when it goes stale. Naming the source or the command gives every reader the current figure instead of the figure from commit day. Derivation between records is allowed: generic refusals derive from `access` and `input`, and computed completion appears in the book and the model output only.
provisions.example:
A chapter states where its numbers come from rather than copying them.

```markdown
The figures below render from the retention schedule at build time.
```

provisions.heading: Explain Each Record Beside Its Record File
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `explanation-orphaned` for a Markdown file under a record root with no frontmatter and no record file beside it.
provisions.statement: An explanation file MUST sit beside its record file in the record's own folder, with the same name, and hold plain Markdown with no frontmatter.
provisions.rationale: The shared file name is the link: no field joins the two files, so a rename moves both and nothing else. Plain Markdown with no frontmatter stays readable in any reader and tells every check to read fields from the record file only. The file opens with the record title and uses H2 sections, so each explanation has one shape.
provisions.example: `submit-expense.yaml` explains its Example and Notes in `submit-expense.md` beside it.

provisions.heading: Explain the Book from LiteSpec Definitions
provisions.evidence: Does every book explanation come from a LiteSpec definition? Look at the book's explanations beside the glossary and the record type table.
provisions.statement: Every explanation the book shows MUST come from the glossary definition of the term or from the question its record type answers on this page.
provisions.rationale: The book explains itself so nobody needs a learning curve, and the explanation stays true only when it has one source. An explanation written for the book drifts from the definition the records follow. Settled by [decision/0008-book-follows-record-layers](../intent/decisions/0008-book-follows-record-layers/0008-book-follows-record-layers.md) on the evidence in [research/book-outline-evidence](../intent/research/book-outline-evidence/book-outline-evidence.md), [research/behavior-containment-evidence](../intent/research/behavior-containment-evidence/behavior-containment-evidence.md), and [research/check-coverage-evidence](../intent/research/check-coverage-evidence/check-coverage-evidence.md). Settled by [decision/0090-make-the-book-an-explorer](decision/0090-make-the-book-an-explorer): the book states a definition on hover and in the lexicon, and shows no teaching text beside each use.
provisions.example: The book explains a waiver with the glossary definition of Waiver.

provisions.heading: Follow the Authority Order
provisions.evidence: When records conflict, does the decision name the higher record that won? Look at the conflict decisions under `.litespec/intent/decisions/`, in the order this page states.
provisions.statement: A conflict MUST resolve toward the higher authority.
provisions.rationale: Intent records outrank Behavior records: constraint over product, product over requirement, requirement over rule, rule over use case, use case over result, and result over scenario. A use case asking for behavior its rule forbids loses to the rule, and the contradiction is reported and resolved by updating the inconsistent records. Where Intent has spoken, the specification wins over code; where the specification is silent, an agent builds nothing, as the Authority section states. Goals, problems, features, flows, actors, research, and prose carry no authority, so none outranks the ladder. Only an explicit product `excludes` overrides a requirement.

provisions.heading: Give Every Record One Parent
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `record-parent-missing` (level G) for a record whose required parent is missing.
provisions.statement: Every record except the product MUST have exactly one parent from the Placement Table on this page.
provisions.rationale: A record with no parent has no place in the book, and a record with two parents appears twice. One parent per record places every record exactly once: the container is the parent, so an entry sits under the record file that holds it, a scenario sits under its use case, reaction, or job, and a record file sits under its scope node. A feature requirement sits under its feature in its own folder, and types at product level, including a product-level requirement, sit under the product with no field written. The product is the root of the tree and stands above every record layer, settled by [decision/0091-place-the-product-above-layers](decision/0091-place-the-product-above-layers). Settled by [decision/0002-parent-for-every-record](../intent/decisions/0002-parent-for-every-record/0002-parent-for-every-record.md) on the evidence in [research/behavior-containment-evidence](../intent/research/behavior-containment-evidence/behavior-containment-evidence.md), [research/intent-hierarchy-evidence](../intent/research/intent-hierarchy-evidence/intent-hierarchy-evidence.md), [research/book-outline-evidence](../intent/research/book-outline-evidence/book-outline-evidence.md), and [research/established-traceability-practice](../intent/research/established-traceability-practice/established-traceability-practice.md).
provisions.example: In the Claimwick product, `requirement/approval-reminders.receipt-over-threshold` sits under `feature/approval-reminders` in `intent/features/approval-reminders/requirements/receipt-over-threshold/`; `use-case/spending.submit-expense` sits beside its aggregate; and `scenario/submit-expense.submitting-with-a-receipt-succeeds` sits in the file of `use-case/spending.submit-expense`.

provisions.heading: Hold Every Record File and Frontmatter Block to the Schema
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `record-invalid` for each record file and document frontmatter block that fails the record schema.
provisions.statement: Every record file and every document frontmatter block MUST satisfy the record schema for its declared type.
provisions.rationale: The record schema owns the field list of every record type and page style. A record file is one YAML mapping with its entries in `records`, holding no Markdown and no frontmatter fences. A document frontmatter block is YAML between two lines that hold only `---`, holding only the page style and its common fields. This page states the record types and their homes.
provisions.example:
A use-case record file opens with its identity fields.

```yaml
type: use-case
id: use-case/spending.submit-expense
title: Submit Expense
```

provisions.heading: Hold Module Rules in Rule Sets
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `record-placement-invalid` for a rule in `module.yaml`.
provisions.statement: A module-level rule MUST live in a rule-set file under `behavior/modules/<m>/rules/`, never in `module.yaml`.
provisions.rationale: The module record declares the module; rules are behavior and live with Behavior. A rule written into `module.yaml` hides behavior in a declaration no rule check scans.
provisions.example: A spending rule lives in a rule-set file under `behavior/modules/spending/rules/`; the same rule written into `module.yaml` is reported.

provisions.heading: Implement Each Mapped Behavior Record Behind a Mark
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `aggregate-unimplemented`, `reaction-unimplemented`, `job-unimplemented`, `external-system-unimplemented`, and `use-case-endpoint-missing` (level S) for a record no mark names, where `aggregate-unimplemented` fires only for an entity aggregate, and `use-case-unreached` (level S) for a browser use case no screen calls.
provisions.statement: Every entity aggregate, every reaction, job, and external system, and every use case reached through a `browser` or `api` entry point, MUST be named by a mark on the code element the marks table gives it.
provisions.rationale: A mark points up, so a check reading marks alone finds code nobody recorded but misses a record nobody built. Checking each record that the marks table maps to code from the top closes the loop in the other direction: an entity aggregate with no root, a reaction with no event handler, a job with no host, an external system with no port, and a use case people reach with no endpoint. A store has no root, so it needs no mark. A use case with no screen calling it blocks at level S: the link between a use case and the screens that call it is never advisory.
provisions.example: `reaction/spending.send-approver-reminder-on-expense-submitted` has no event handler carrying its mark, so the check reports `reaction-unimplemented` and blocks.

provisions.heading: Keep Code Out of Intent and Behavior Fields
provisions.evidence: Does any Intent or Behavior field copy a value from code? Look at the fields the change fills, beside the implementation.
provisions.statement: A project MUST fill no field on an Intent or Behavior record from code.
provisions.rationale: Code implements Behavior, so a field filled from an implementation restates what already ships instead of stating the promise under review. A fact learned from the world enters Intent as research or a constraint, cited and dated, and a need the upper record layer does not state becomes a backlog item outside the repository. Derivation between records stays allowed.
provisions.example: A positivity guard found in a handler becomes a backlog item for a rule, while the code stays untouched until the rule lands.

provisions.heading: Keep Each Name Unique in Its Record Type
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `name-duplicate` for a name that occurs twice in one record type, and for a use case, reaction or job name that occurs in another of the three types.
provisions.statement: Each name MUST stay unique in its record type.
provisions.rationale: Short identifiers resolve with no lookup table only when each name means one record of its type. Two records of one type with one name collide everywhere the identifier is read, while two records of different types with one name coexist: `actor/owner` and `role/owner` are different records. Folders do not narrow uniqueness within a type. Use case, reaction, and job names share one namespace, so a scenario cites its parent without ambiguity.
provisions.example: Claimwick names one feature `approval-reminders`; a second feature with that name is reported even though the folders differ. An actor named `owner` and a role named `owner` coexist.

provisions.heading: Keep Every Field Value in the Record File
provisions.evidence: Does any page carry field values outside the record file? Look at the explanation files beside the changed record files.
provisions.statement: A consumer page MUST use its record file as its only metadata carrier.
provisions.rationale: Two metadata carriers on one page disagree sooner or later: source links, paths, and evidence drift between the record file and the explanation file. One record file keeps every field a check reads in one place, while the explanation file beside it explains without stating a field value. A generated region that `model render` writes from the record file is not a second carrier, because no person edits it and `model check` reports any drift from the record. The source-links region of a research or constraint explanation is one such region.

provisions.heading: Keep Module Dependencies Free of Cycles
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `module-dependency-invalid` for a module dependency cycle.
provisions.statement: Module `dependsOn` links MUST NOT form a cycle.
provisions.rationale: A dependency cycle says each module builds on the other, so neither has a seam to split along. The module order stays a directed graph with no cycle, like the effect edges.
provisions.example: Spending depends on finance and finance depends on spending, so the cycle is reported.

provisions.heading: Keep Rules and Targets Out of Technical Decisions
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `decision-basis-missing` (level G) for a technical decision whose `basedOn` names nothing, and counts a quality requirement as fulfilled when a technical decision names it in `basedOn`.
provisions.statement: A technical decision MUST leave each rule the product obeys whatever its design to a constraint and each measurable target to a quality requirement, and name the ones it serves in `basedOn`.
provisions.rationale: A technical decision chooses one way among alternatives, and a better alternative may replace it tomorrow. A rule such as keeping personal data in the European Union, or a target such as answering checkout within two seconds, does not change when the library does: overriding it needs a business, legal, or organizational change. Written inside a decision, the rule disappears the day the decision is replaced, and nobody holds it as the promise it is. Kept in Intent, the rule and the target stand as the promises they are, the decision points up to them, and the chain runs unbroken from code through the decision to the constraint or requirement and the goal above it. A decision with no basis blocks at level G, like a product decision that decides nothing: a technical choice among equal options may serve no rule or target yet and still govern the code that follows it, but a product decision that settles no record governs nothing.
provisions.example: Claimwick keeps each receipt for the tax file because `constraint/tax-receipt-retention` requires it, and answers submissions quickly because `requirement/approval-reminders.month-end-submission` sets the target. `decision/0005-render-receipts-as-pdf` names the constraint in `basedOn`, and `decision/0004-serve-receipts-behind-one-proxy` names the requirement in `basedOn`; neither the seven years nor the two seconds is written in a decision.

provisions.heading: Keep Shape Rules in the Schema
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `record-invalid` for a record that breaks a shape rule and `record-key-duplicate` for two entries of one record that share a key, and the parity test `RecordSchemaParityTests` fails when the schema and the model check disagree on a rule both carry.
provisions.statement: Each rule on the shape of one record MUST be written in the record schema, and each rule on the graph between records stays in the model check.
provisions.rationale: An editor validates a record against the schema alone, so a shape rule the schema lacks lets a record pass in the editor and fail in the check. Graph rules, such as reference resolution, ownership, and consistency across records, need every record at once, which a schema cannot read. The schema holds required properties, minimum counts, conditional requirements, and allowed values. A list of objects does not use `uniqueItems`, since that compares whole objects, so the model check reports each key that two entries of one record share. Proposed by [decision/0058-keep-shape-rules-in-the-schema](../intent/decisions/0058-keep-shape-rules-in-the-schema/0058-keep-shape-rules-in-the-schema.md) on the disagreements between the schema and the check.
provisions.example: A Claimwick research record with an empty `sources` list fails the schema in an editor and the model check alike, and a research record that names source key `benchmark-report` twice is reported as `record-key-duplicate`.

provisions.heading: Mark Every Check with Its Level
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `reader-missing` (level S) for a frontend whose reader is missing or failing, prints the level beside each finding, and `litespec model check --release` blocks on `reader-missing` for a claimed layer.
provisions.statement: Every check MUST carry the level its finding rests on, and block or report as the strength of its provision states.
provisions.rationale: The level tells a reader what a finding rests on: G rests on records only, S rests on code read through a stack reader, and A rests on prose, names, or proof state. Whether a finding blocks follows the strength of the provision it reports: a finding on a required provision blocks unless a waiver parks it, and a finding on an advisory provision never blocks. `litespec model check` prints the level beside each finding, so a reader tells what each finding rests on at a glance. A missing required link is level G.

provisions.heading: Match Each Backend Mark to Its Folder
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `mark-folder-drift` (level S) for a handler, endpoint, event handler, job host or aggregate root whose mark names a record outside its module and folder, and `code-placement-drift` (level S) for a code element, test, or folder outside the code folder its record's placement names.
provisions.artifact: command-handler, query-handler, endpoint, reaction, job, aggregate
provisions.statement: A backend handler, endpoint, event handler, job host or aggregate root MUST carry a mark naming a use case, reaction, job, or aggregate in the module and folder it sits in.
provisions.rationale: Copying a handler and forgetting its mark is the most common agent mistake, and the folder already says what the mark should be. A handler that sits in one use-case folder while naming another sends readers and checks to the wrong record. An aggregate method and a technical class carry the mark of the use case that calls them, which may sit in another module, so their folder says nothing about their mark. The frontend mirror already compares each mark with its module; the backend check applies the same comparison to handlers, endpoints, and aggregates.
provisions.example: A handler in `Booking/Holds/HoldRoom/` marked `use-case/booking.release-hold` is reported, because the folder holds `use-case/booking.hold-room`.

provisions.heading: Move Each Identifier with Its Module
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `identifier-folder-drift` for an identifier whose home segment disagrees with its folder.
provisions.statement: A record that moves to another module MUST change the module segment of its identifier and every citation in the same change.
provisions.rationale: The folder wins: an identifier whose home segment disagrees with its folder names a home the record left. Only identifiers whose first segment names a module change with a module move. A rule identifier keeps its home segment, because the segment names the aggregate or module the rule is about rather than the folder that holds it. A move between product and module level changes no identifier, so no citation changes.
provisions.example: Claimwick moves `use-case/spending.submit-expense` from the spending module to the finance module, so the use case becomes `use-case/finance.submit-expense` and every citation changes in the same change.

provisions.heading: Name Book Labels with LiteSpec Terms
provisions.evidence: Does every book label use a LiteSpec term? Look at the book beside the glossary and the Links table: each label is a record type, a field name, a computed state, a glossary term, or a reads-as phrase.
provisions.statement: Every label in the book MUST be a record type, a field name, a computed state, a glossary term, or the reads-as phrase the Links table states for a connection.
provisions.rationale: LiteSpec already names every concept once, for people and agents alike. A friendlier synonym in the book, such as promise for requirement, is a second word for one concept: the reader learns it, then meets the real word in the records and the checks, and has to translate. Settled by [decision/0008-book-follows-record-layers](../intent/decisions/0008-book-follows-record-layers/0008-book-follows-record-layers.md) on the evidence in [research/book-outline-evidence](../intent/research/book-outline-evidence/book-outline-evidence.md), [research/behavior-containment-evidence](../intent/research/behavior-containment-evidence/behavior-containment-evidence.md), and [research/check-coverage-evidence](../intent/research/check-coverage-evidence/check-coverage-evidence.md).
provisions.example: A use case page heads its results "Results" and its scenarios "Scenarios", never "Endings" and "Examples".

provisions.heading: Name Each Identifier from Its Title
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `identifier-title-invalid` for a page record whose identifier name is no word subsequence of its title, or whose record file is named for neither its identifier name nor the fixed file name of its type.
provisions.artifact: record:product, record:goal, record:vision, record:problem, record:feature, record:requirement, record:constraint, record:decision, record:research, record:flow, record:actor, record:role, record:module, record:aggregate, record:use-case, record:reaction, record:job, record:notification, record:integration-event, record:entry-point, record:screen, record:external-system, record:runbook, record:waiver
provisions.statement: Every page record MUST take its identifier name, and so its folder and file names, from the words of its title in title order.
provisions.rationale: Readers browse the folders before they open a record, so the folder name must say what the record says. A retitle that keeps the identifier leaves the folder and file saying the old name while the record says the new one, and no listing shows the gap. Taking the name from the title's words keeps the identifier, the file, and the folder on what the record says. Proposed by [decision/0061-name-each-identifier-from-its-title](../intent/decisions/0061-name-each-identifier-from-its-title/0061-name-each-identifier-from-its-title.md).
provisions.example: Claimwick titles a requirement "Nobody Approves Their Own Expense", so the requirement is `requirement/approval.nobody-approves-own-expense` in `nobody-approves-own-expense/nobody-approves-own-expense.yaml`. The name `no-self-approval` holds words the title does not hold, so it is reported.

provisions.heading: Name Records in Prose by Their Identifiers
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `prose-reference-unknown` for a backticked identifier that names no written record and for a backticked provision the carried release does not ship.
provisions.statement: Prose in a record field, an explanation file, a document, or the `AGENTS.md` file at the consumer root MUST name every record by its identifier in backticks and every provision by the published identifier the carried release ships.
provisions.rationale: A name in plain words, such as a decision number without its identifier, cannot be resolved: nothing tells whether the record still exists after a rename or a move. The identifier in backticks is the one form every check reads, so a stale name fails the check at the line that names it instead of sending the reader after a record nobody wrote.
provisions.example: A waiver exit reads "The gap closes when `decision/0005-render-receipts-as-pdf` lands." rather than "The gap closes when Decision 5 lands."

provisions.heading: Name the Lowest Record Each Test Proves
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `mark-missing` and `mark-unknown` (level S) for a test that names no record or a record of a kind a test does not take.
provisions.statement: Every test MUST name in a `proves` mark the lowest record it verifies, from the kinds the marks table on this page lists for a test.
provisions.rationale: A test outside the record tree is either proof of something the specification forgot to state or a test that verifies nothing anyone promised. Naming the lowest record it verifies places each test: a scenario or rule for behavior, a quality requirement for how well the product behaves, a technical decision for a technical choice, an external system or integration event for an agreement with the outside, a provision for a structural rule the code must keep, and a project convention for a standing rule the code must keep. A test that verifies a choice no record states shows a missing record, which is written at the level where the choice lives, as safety-critical standards resolve derived requirements; a test that verifies nothing a record should state is deleted. Proof stays layered: only scenario and rule proofs verify a use case, and a passing test that asserts something links to a quality requirement, a technical decision, an external system, an integration event, or a provision marks that record tested, so "the adapter is right" never reads as "the promise is kept". A background use case is verified through the passing proofs of the use cases it serves. A browser success proof asserts the result sentence or the scenario Then text.
provisions.example: In Claimwick, the submit-expense acceptance test proves `scenario/submit-expense.submitting-with-a-receipt-succeeds`; a load test of month-end submissions proves `requirement/approval-reminders.month-end-submission`; a receipt-rendering test proves `decision/0005-render-receipts-as-pdf`; and the layering test that Domain references no persistence package proves `litespec/backend/architecture#point-dependencies-inward`.

provisions.heading: Name What Every Decision Decides
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `decision-decides-missing` for a product decision with an empty `decides` field, and `decision-decides-duplicate` for two decisions deciding one record.
provisions.statement: Every product decision MUST name at least one record it settles in `decides`.
provisions.rationale: A decision that names nothing governs nothing. Naming at least one settled record gives the decision something to govern. A technical decision governs the code that follows it instead.

provisions.heading: Organize the Book by the Record Layers
provisions.evidence: Which book headings or groupings are not a record layer, a record type, or a record the identifier names? Look at the book's outline beside this page's record type table.
provisions.statement: The book MUST outline a project by the four record layers, with the governance records beside them, and place each record under the record its folder and links name, or at the top of its own layer when the product parents it.
provisions.rationale: The book is how people read the model, so it shows the model's own hierarchy. A reader who learns Intent, Behavior, Implementation, and Proof in the book reads the same structure in the docs folder, in the model output, and in every other LiteSpec project. An outline of the book's own invention is a second hierarchy to learn, and it drifts from the one the records keep. Settled by [decision/0002-parent-for-every-record](../intent/decisions/0002-parent-for-every-record/0002-parent-for-every-record.md) on the evidence in [research/behavior-containment-evidence](../intent/research/behavior-containment-evidence/behavior-containment-evidence.md), [research/intent-hierarchy-evidence](../intent/research/intent-hierarchy-evidence/intent-hierarchy-evidence.md), [research/book-outline-evidence](../intent/research/book-outline-evidence/book-outline-evidence.md), and [research/established-traceability-practice](../intent/research/established-traceability-practice/established-traceability-practice.md). Settled by [decision/0008-book-follows-record-layers](../intent/decisions/0008-book-follows-record-layers/0008-book-follows-record-layers.md) on the evidence in [research/book-outline-evidence](../intent/research/book-outline-evidence/book-outline-evidence.md), [research/behavior-containment-evidence](../intent/research/behavior-containment-evidence/behavior-containment-evidence.md), and [research/check-coverage-evidence](../intent/research/check-coverage-evidence/check-coverage-evidence.md). Settled by [decision/0088-serve-the-book-live-and-export-it](decision/0088-serve-the-book-live-and-export-it).
provisions.example: In the Claimwick product, `use-case/spending.submit-expense` sits under Behavior, its module and its aggregate; its results under it; each scenario under the result it shows; and the handler that carries its mark under Implementation.

provisions.heading: Place a Record by Its Content and Link It by Its Reason
provisions.evidence: Does any record sit under a record that holds only part of its content, and does any record type in the Placement Table take a parent whose scope is narrower than its content? Compare each record's folder with the records it cites and the records that serve it.
provisions.statement: A record MUST nest under another record only when its whole content lies within that record, and otherwise sit at the lowest scope node that holds all of its content and name the record it exists for in a link field.
provisions.rationale: A folder states that everything inside it belongs to the record above it. Content is what a record states and what it changes; its links are its reasons, not its content. A record filed under one of several records its content spans claims a scope it does not hold, and a reader looking for every record of its type must search the folder of every possible parent. The reason a record exists can change while its content stays the same, so a link field keeps that change to one line where a folder would move the record. Settled by [decision/0078-place-each-record-by-its-content](decision/0078-place-each-record-by-its-content).
provisions.example: In the Claimwick product, `flow/submit-and-reimburse` cites requirements of both `feature/approval` and `feature/approval-reminders`, so it sits in `intent/flows/` under the product and names its goal in `serves`. A reaction answering another module's integration event sits with the module whose records it changes, and names the event in `triggeredBy`.

provisions.heading: Place Child Records in Typed Folders
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `record-placement-invalid` for a child record outside its typed folder, and for a module subfolder that names no typed folder.
provisions.statement: A project MUST hold each child record stored as its own file in a folder named for its type in the plural, inside its parent's folder, and each child stored as an entry in its parent's file.
provisions.rationale: A reader who opens a parent folder sees its own files with each kind of child kept apart, without opening each file. One rule for every parent replaces a placement sentence per type and gives every module one layout. A child stored as an entry has no file of its own, so a folder for it would hold nothing.
