Proposed by [decision/0060-put-child-records-in-typed-folders](decision/0060-put-child-records-in-typed-folders).
provisions.example: A feature's requirements sit in `features/approval/requirements/`, and an aggregate's use cases sit in `aggregates/expenses/use-cases/`, while a result stays in its use case file.

provisions.heading: Point Every Book Entry to Its Source
provisions.evidence: Does every book entry link to its file and line? Look at the book's record, code, test, and finding entries.
provisions.statement: Every record, code element, test and finding the book shows MUST link to the file and line it comes from.
provisions.rationale: The book is where a reader notices what to change, and the source is where the change is made. A link to the file and line makes the next step one click, and it shows that every entry comes from a written record or from code, not from the book. Settled by [decision/0008-book-follows-record-layers](../intent/decisions/0008-book-follows-record-layers/0008-book-follows-record-layers.md) on the evidence in [research/book-outline-evidence](../intent/research/book-outline-evidence/book-outline-evidence.md), [research/behavior-containment-evidence](../intent/research/behavior-containment-evidence/behavior-containment-evidence.md), and [research/check-coverage-evidence](../intent/research/check-coverage-evidence/check-coverage-evidence.md).
provisions.example: The submit-expense use case page links to `.litespec/behavior/modules/spending/aggregates/expenses/use-cases/submit-expense/submit-expense.yaml` at its first line, and its handler to the handler file at the class.

provisions.heading: Publish Each Integration Event from One Module
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `event-publisher-invalid` for an integration event with a second publishing module.
provisions.statement: An integration event MUST have exactly one publishing module.
provisions.rationale: An event with two publishers has two writers of one fact: readers cannot tell which module states it. One publishing module gives the fact one home, and every other module reads it through the event. The publishers follow from the records: the use cases whose `raises` holds the domain event the integration event `translates`.
provisions.example: `integration-event/expense-submitted` translates `domain-event/expense.submitted`, which only spending use cases raise, so the spending module publishes it.

provisions.heading: Record Each Screen's Captures from the Gallery
provisions.evidence: Which screens with a route have no capture? Look at `captureState` `route-not-captured` on screen records in the model.
provisions.statement: The builder MUST record each screen's captures from the gallery folders and file-name pattern the project file names, as `captures` with `path`, `theme`, `width` and `capturedOn`, and its `captureState` as `captured`, `route-not-captured` or `no-route`.
provisions.rationale: A reader judging a screen needs to see it, and a capture named by its route, theme, and width is the copy the built screen makes. The route slug names the file the same way everywhere: the leading slash dropped, segments joined with a hyphen, a parameter reduced to its name, and the root route named `home`. A missing gallery folder captures nothing and fails nothing, so a project with no photography yet still builds its model.
provisions.example: The Claimwick web gallery holds `expenses--light--1440.png`, so `screen/expenses.list` at `/expenses` shows that capture at theme `light` and width 1440 with `captureState` `captured`; a screen with no address shows `no-route`.

provisions.heading: Record Each Technical Choice as a Decision
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `decision-unimplemented` (level S) for a technical decision that no code element follows. It reports `decision-kind-missing` (level A) for a technical decision with no `kind`, `decision-scope-invalid` (level A) for a technical decision whose followers all sit in one module and each already carry an `implements` mark, and `decision-home-drift` (level A) for a technical decision kept at a level its followers do not match. The check runs in the CLI only, with no analyzer rule: whether any code follows a decision is known only across every project, and one compilation sees one project.
provisions.statement: A technical choice of one of the six kinds that code follows and no LiteSpec provision makes MUST be a decision under `.litespec/implementation/decisions/` that at least one code element follows.
provisions.rationale: Why a pattern, a library, or a configuration value was chosen is the first thing a maintainer asks before changing it. Written in a comment, the answer drifts and no tool finds it. Written as a decision, it carries its options, what speaks for and against each, and what would reopen it, and every code element shaped by it names it in a `follows` mark. A choice a LiteSpec provision already makes needs no decision, because the provision is the record. The six kinds are provider, package, format, boundary, topology, and replacement, as the [decision records page](../reference/decision-records.md) states: a choice of no kind is not a decision. A choice of no kind states its reason in the class documentation, and the mark on the class names the record the class serves. Technical decisions sit under Implementation because they name technologies and code, which Intent never holds, and they share the numbered sequence of product decisions, so all decisions share one identifier space. Settled by [decision/0040-decisions-only-for-six-kinds-of-choice](decision/0040-decisions-only-for-six-kinds-of-choice).
provisions.example: Claimwick renders each receipt as a PDF file. `decision/0005-render-receipts-as-pdf` weighs a PDF library against an HTML-to-PDF browser, chooses the PDF library, and names what reopens the choice: receipts no longer needing a downloadable file. The decision carries `kind: package`. The receipt PDF renderer carries `/// <follows>decision/0005-render-receipts-as-pdf</follows>`.

provisions.heading: Render Generated Regions from the Model
provisions.evidence: Does any generated region outside an index region render code-computed facts? Look inside the generated fences beside the book and the model output.
provisions.statement: A generated region renders only facts derived from records, and a `decision-index` or `waiver-index` region also renders the computed follower facts its rows name.
provisions.rationale: A generated region sits inside a record page, so everything in it reads with record authority. Facts computed from code, such as coded and verified counts, describe the world rather than the promise, and rendering them beside records would lend them authority they do not hold. The book and the model output carry code-computed facts where readers meet them as computed. An index region is the exception: it lists the records beside it, so each row names the computed followers, concerns, and flags the reader needs to read the list. Settled by [decision/0072-generate-the-links-table-from-the-schema](decision/0072-generate-the-links-table-from-the-schema).

provisions.heading: Report Unverified Use Cases
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `use-case-unverified` (level A) for a use case whose scenarios are not all proved, and `litespec model check --release` blocks on it.
provisions.statement: A use case whose scenarios are not all proved MUST be reported as `use-case-unverified`.
provisions.rationale: Nothing blocks on an unverified scenario day to day, so the release gate would depend on someone reading the book. Reporting the use case keeps daily work loose, and `litespec model check --release` makes the finding block, so the release stays honest without slowing ordinary work.
provisions.example: Claimwick adds `use-case/spending.export-expenses` with two scenarios and one passing proof: `litespec model check` reports `use-case-unverified` for it and exits zero, and `litespec model check --release` blocks on it.

provisions.heading: Require an Explanation File for Article Types
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `explanation-missing` for an article type with no explanation file or with a required H2 section missing or its sections out of order.
provisions.statement: A research or decision page MUST carry its explanation file with the required H2 sections.
provisions.rationale: Research and decision records are read as prose: a research's Findings and a decision's Decision are what the reader comes for. The required sections keep each article complete: Findings for research, and Context, Options, Decision, Consequences, and Revisit Conditions for decision.
provisions.example: `research/approval-time-benchmarks` carries its Findings in `approval-time-benchmarks.md`.

provisions.heading: Require Explanation Files on the Layers a Project Names
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `explanation-missing` for a record page on a listed layer with no explanation file or with a required H2 section missing or its sections out of order.
provisions.statement: A record page on a layer the project lists in `explanations.layers` MUST carry its explanation file with the required H2 sections.
provisions.rationale: On a complex product, every record needs explaining for people who did not write it. Listing a layer in `explanations.layers` makes the explanation a gate instead of a habit.
provisions.example: Claimwick lists `intent` and `behavior` in `explanations.layers`, so its problem `problem/expenses-wait-weeks` carries `expenses-wait-weeks.md` with the sections Affected Users, Failure Cases, Current Workaround, Cost, Evidence and Resolution Criteria. A problem without that file, or without one of those sections, fails the check.

provisions.heading: Resolve Every Page Link
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `link-unknown` for a link that resolves to no file and no written record identifier.
provisions.statement: Every Markdown link outside code in a record field, an explanation file, or a document MUST resolve to an existing file or to a written record identifier.
provisions.rationale: A link that points at a moved file or an unknown identifier reads as navigation and leads nowhere. A link whose target is a record identifier, with an optional `#<step-id>`, cites that record: link checks resolve it against the model's identifiers, citation checks count it, and the book links it to the record. Prose cites a record by its identifier, never by its file path.
provisions.example: The Claimwick receipt rule is cited as `[the receipt rule](rule/expense.approver-is-not-submitter)`.

provisions.heading: Rewrite Every Link on a Rename
provisions.evidence: `litespec rename` leaves no citation of the old identifier, and `litespec-maintain validate` emits no `ID_UNKNOWN_REFERENCE` diagnostic.
provisions.statement: An author MUST rename a record identifier with `litespec rename <old> <new>`, which rewrites every link and keeps the record at its level and in its owner's folder unless `--move` names another owner.
provisions.rationale: An identifier rename touches the record file, its explanation file, and every record that points at it. Rewriting every link in the same command leaves no citation pointing at the old name, so the repository stays resolvable at every commit. When the file name follows the identifier, both files move together. A plain rename changes no owner, so a record never changes level by accident, and a move to another owner is an explicit choice. Proposed by [decision/0060-put-child-records-in-typed-folders](../intent/decisions/0060-put-child-records-in-typed-folders/0060-put-child-records-in-typed-folders.md).
provisions.example: `litespec rename use-case/spending.close-run use-case/spending.complete-run` updates the page and every citation together.

provisions.heading: Scaffold Pages and Reserve Identifiers
provisions.evidence: Does every new page carry a reserved identifier? Look for pages created without `litespec new`.
provisions.statement: An author MUST scaffold a new page with `litespec new <type> <id>`, which reserves its identifier.
provisions.rationale: Two agents working in parallel mint the same identifier when each writes a file by hand, and the collision surfaces only at merge time. Scaffolding reserves the identifier before any prose exists, so the second author learns the clash at creation and picks another name. For an article type the command also writes the explanation file, and for a document style it writes the document.
provisions.example: `litespec new reaction spending.send-receipt-reminder-on-expense-submitted` creates the reaction record file with its reserved identifier.

provisions.heading: Serve Every Flow Step
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `step-use-case-missing` for a flow step with no serving use case, reaction, or job, beside `step-screen-missing` for a step a browser or device use case serves that no screen serves.
provisions.statement: Every flow step MUST have a serving use case, reaction, or job.
provisions.rationale: A step no use case, reaction, or job serves promises a moment the product never builds. Use cases, reactions, and jobs point up with `serves`, so each step id collects the behaviors that carry the actor through it. The pair sits side by side: `step-use-case-missing` names a step no use case, reaction, or job serves, and `step-screen-missing` names a step a browser or device use case serves that no screen serves. Reworded by [decision/0049-literal-flow-words-concrete-consequences](decision/0049-literal-flow-words-concrete-consequences).

provisions.heading: Show Only Computed Judgments in the Book
provisions.evidence: Does every status, count, order, and finding in the book come from the builder or a check? Look at the book beside the model output.
provisions.statement: Every status, count, order and finding the book shows MUST be one the builder or a check computes.
provisions.rationale: The book is a view of the model, not a second authority. A judgment only the book makes, such as its own idea of what to do next, cannot be checked, cannot fail a build, and cannot be found by an agent reading the model output. Settled by [decision/0008-book-follows-record-layers](../intent/decisions/0008-book-follows-record-layers/0008-book-follows-record-layers.md) on the evidence in [research/book-outline-evidence](../intent/research/book-outline-evidence/book-outline-evidence.md), [research/behavior-containment-evidence](../intent/research/behavior-containment-evidence/behavior-containment-evidence.md), and [research/check-coverage-evidence](../intent/research/check-coverage-evidence/check-coverage-evidence.md).
provisions.example: The book orders features by the completion the builder computes.

provisions.heading: Split Record Fields from Explanation
provisions.evidence: Does any explanation file state a fact a check reads? Compare each explanation file with its record file.
provisions.statement: A fact a check reads MUST live as a field in the record file rather than in the explanation file.
provisions.rationale: Fields are checked and prose is not, so a check-read fact sitting in prose is invisible to its check. The page explanation cites entries by identifier, so entries need no file of their own.
provisions.example: The submit-expense summary lives in the `summary` field of `submit-expense.yaml`, while why the flow reads well lives under Notes in `submit-expense.md`.

provisions.heading: Start Each Explanation File with Its Title
provisions.evidence: Does every explanation file open with its H1 title and section content under H2? Look at the explanation files beside the changed record files.
provisions.statement: An explanation file MUST open with one H1 title and section its content with H2 sections.
provisions.rationale: One shape puts the title and each section in the same place on every explanation. The H1 carries the record title, and each H2 carries one section from the table on this page or a free section; Notes take free `###` headings under their H2.

provisions.heading: State the Common Fields on Every Record
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `record-invalid` for a record missing a common field.
provisions.statement: Every written record MUST carry its type, identifier, and title.
provisions.rationale: Type, identifier, and title are the fields every join needs. Without them on every record, the builder cannot connect decisions to requirements, scenarios to results, or records to terms, and the model falls apart into loose pages. A record adds `terms` when it uses glossary terms and `records` when it holds entries.

provisions.heading: State What a Reader Needs on the Record and Check Each Copy
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `rule-governs-drift`, `exposure-reference-drift`, `exposure-missing`, `classification-drift` and `data-class-fields-drift` for a stated copy that differs from its source.
provisions.statement: A record MUST state the links and facts a reader needs to read it alone, with every stated fact the model can also derive held by a check that reports a difference.
provisions.rationale: An isolated file reads whole by eye and by tool, without opening the files it links to. The copy stays honest because a check compares it with its source on every run: `governs` against the links naming the rule, `exposure` against the entry points and permissions the use case declares, a field `classification` against its data class, a data class `fields` list against the fields naming the class, and a screen `serves` against the steps its use cases serve. Judgments stay computed and are never typed: completion, coverage, proof status, counts, and censuses. Settled by [decision/0070-keep-one-source-for-each-fact](decision/0070-keep-one-source-for-each-fact).
provisions.example: The Claimwick submit-expense use case states its `exposure` in plain words, and `exposure-reference-drift` reports an entry point it names that `reachedThrough` lacks.

provisions.heading: State What Happens in Every Behavior Statement
provisions.evidence: Does any rule statement, scenario step, or result meaning hide its behavior behind a vague word? Look at the statements the change adds.
provisions.statement: A rule statement, scenario step, and result meaning SHOULD avoid words that hide behavior.
provisions.rationale: The vague words are handle, handles, handled, process, processes, manage, manages, various, etc., appropriate, appropriately, properly, as needed, and so on: each says that something happens without saying what. A reader cannot check a statement that hides its behavior, so each statement names the act in words a test could assert.
provisions.example: A scenario step reads "The member borrows the copy" rather than "The member handles the copy".

provisions.heading: Take Decision Numbers from One Sequence
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `decision-number-duplicate` for two decisions sharing one number.
provisions.statement: A decision number MUST come from one sequence across every home.
provisions.rationale: Product and technical decisions share one identifier space, so a number identifies one decision wherever it sits. `litespec new decision` takes the next free number, and no two decisions share it.
provisions.example: `decision/0005-render-receipts-as-pdf` is the fifth decision, whether it sits under Intent or under Implementation.

provisions.heading: Validate a Single Page Before Committing
provisions.evidence: Does the change report show each touched page passing single-page validation before commit?
provisions.statement: An author MUST validate a single page before committing it.
provisions.rationale: Full validation walks the whole repository, which grows slow exactly when many authors commit often. A single-page check reports shape and link errors for the page at hand in seconds, so each commit arrives already sound.
provisions.example: The author validates the touched page, fixes the reported diagnostics, and commits only when the page passes.

provisions.heading: Write Every Record File in Canonical Form
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `format-drift` for a record file whose text differs from its canonical form.
provisions.statement: Every record file MUST match the canonical text the record writer produces for it.
provisions.rationale: One layout for every record keeps diffs small and readers on content: a change shows the moved fact, never reflowed prose or reordered keys. The tool owns the layout, so `litespec model format` rewrites every record file into canonical form and the check reports any file that differs.
provisions.example: A use-case file opens with `type`, `id`, and `title`, holds its own fields in schema order, and closes with `records`.

provisions.heading: Write Every Record in Its Home
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `folder-invalid` for a folder outside the closed set of its layer and level, `module-undeclared` for a `modules` folder naming no declared module, and `record-placement-invalid` for a record outside its home.
provisions.statement: A project MUST keep every record in the home its type names.
provisions.rationale: A fixed home tells a reader where to open a record and tells the builder where to read it. A record kept anywhere else misses the checks that scan its home, so it looks sound while nothing validates it. Settled by [decision/0042-record-named-folders](../intent/decisions/0042-record-named-folders/0042-record-named-folders.md), which puts each named record in its own folder beside its explanation.
provisions.example: A decision lives at `.litespec/intent/decisions/0001-receipt-threshold/0001-receipt-threshold.yaml`.

provisions.heading: Write Every Record in Its Record File
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `record-invalid` for a record file that does not parse or whose top level names no record type or container page style.
provisions.statement: Every record page MUST live in one record file holding one YAML mapping with its entries in `records`.
provisions.rationale: One file per page tells a reader where to open a record and tells the builder where to read it. The mapping holds exactly the fields the schema defines for its type, with entries in `records`, so every record has one shape and the checks read every record the same way. A record kept anywhere else misses the checks that scan its home. Settled by [decision/0020-records-in-yaml](decision/0020-records-in-yaml) on the evidence in [research/record-format-evidence](research/record-format-evidence).
provisions.example: Claimwick keeps `use-case/spending.submit-expense` in `.litespec/behavior/modules/spending/aggregates/expenses/use-cases/submit-expense/submit-expense.yaml`, with its results and scenarios in `records`.

provisions.heading: Write Links on the Record That Points
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `reference-unknown` for a link whose target no record carries.
provisions.statement: A link MUST live as a field on the record it starts from, with an inverse stated only where a reader needs it and held by an agreement check.
provisions.rationale: One writing site keeps a link and its source in one edit: changing the source updates the link in the same change. Links written on the target instead would scatter each relationship across every page it touches. A record states the inverse only when a reader needs it there, and the agreement check holds the copy to its source, as `litespec/core/model#state-what-a-reader-needs-on-the-record-and-check-each-copy` states. The Links table states how each link reads in both directions. Settled by [decision/0002-parent-for-every-record](../intent/decisions/0002-parent-for-every-record/0002-parent-for-every-record.md) on the evidence in [research/behavior-containment-evidence](../intent/research/behavior-containment-evidence/behavior-containment-evidence.md), [research/intent-hierarchy-evidence](../intent/research/intent-hierarchy-evidence/intent-hierarchy-evidence.md), [research/book-outline-evidence](../intent/research/book-outline-evidence/book-outline-evidence.md), and [research/established-traceability-practice](../intent/research/established-traceability-practice/established-traceability-practice.md).

provisions.heading: Add New Machinery Only for a Current Requirement
provisions.evidence: Does each added package, project, wrapper, process, cache, queue, or pattern cite a current use case, decision, or requirement? Check the added machinery beside the use cases, decisions, and requirements it cites.
provisions.statement: A consumer MUST add packages, projects, wrappers, background processes, caches, queues, or distributed patterns only for a current documented requirement, and never for a vision alone.
provisions.rationale: Each package, project, wrapper, background process, cache, queue, or distributed pattern adds maintenance, failure modes, and concepts every later reader learns. A current use case, decision, or requirement justifies that cost by naming the activation criterion. Preference and possible future need justify nothing, so speculative machinery stays out. A vision may justify the shape of a record or a model, such as a field that keeps a later destination reachable, but it activates no machinery: that cost waits for the requirement that cites the vision.

provisions.heading: Avoid Generic Boundary Names
provisions.evidence: Does each changed boundary name carry the narrowest accurate business name, with no bare `bus`, `manager`, `helper`, `processor`, or `service`? Check the changed names for bare mechanism words.
provisions.statement: A consumer MUST NOT use generic `bus`, `manager`, `helper`, `processor`, or `service` names when a narrower name exists.
provisions.rationale: Names such as `bus`, `manager`, `helper`, `processor`, and `service` say nothing about the business action, so unrelated responsibility collects behind them with every change. The narrower name keeps each boundary to the action it names.
provisions.example: Claimwick's receipt-reminder notifier names its action, while one named only `service` does not.

provisions.heading: Complete Work Before Merging
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` blocks on unreached records, such as `intent-unreached` and `constraint-unreached`, in every run, locally and in the pull-request check alike.
provisions.statement: What merges MUST be complete.
provisions.rationale: A branch may be incomplete, but what merges is complete. A record that must stay unreached past a merge carries a gap waiver with `expiresOn` and `closedBy`, which parks reachability for that record until the waiver expires.
provisions.example: A Claimwick use case with no endpoint stays on its branch until the endpoint lands, or until a gap waiver with `expiresOn` and `closedBy` parks it.

provisions.heading: Compute Completion from Code and Tests
provisions.evidence: Does any record state its own completion? Compare the record fields with the completion the model computes.
provisions.statement: A consumer MUST NOT write completion by hand, because the model computes it from code, tests, and passing scenarios.
provisions.rationale: A reader's first question is how much of a thing is coded and verified. Completion typed by hand answers with a report the next commit falsifies. The [model page](model.md) defines what the model computes.
provisions.example: Claimwick's book marks a use case complete when its handler exists and its scenarios pass, with the model deriving that from the runs.

provisions.heading: Compute Nothing Above Implementation from Code
provisions.evidence: Does every record above Implementation state a decided promise rather than restating code? Compare each new record with the code beside it.
provisions.statement: A consumer MUST NOT compute a record above Implementation from code.
provisions.rationale: A record computed from code turns what exists into what is promised: drift becomes the plan, and the record restates what the code already does. Records above Implementation state decided promises instead, and code points up to the record it serves through a mark that names that record.

provisions.heading: Confine Atomic Consistency to One Use Case
provisions.evidence: Does every atomic use case rely only on its own writes, with every rule across use cases held by a state guard? Check the consistency field and the rules it cites beside the reactions that follow.
provisions.statement: Atomic consistency MUST cover only the writes of one use case, never an edge to another record.
provisions.rationale: Every edge crosses a commit boundary, so work past it can fail after the caller succeeded. Atomic consistency promises one shared outcome, and that promise holds only inside the one commit a use case owns. A rule that spans two use cases is held by a state guard instead: the later act refuses until the earlier fact arrived.
provisions.example: The library's hold request waits for its copy in an awaiting-copy state, and lending the copy refuses until the hold fact arrives.

provisions.heading: Cover Other Mechanisms with Extensions
provisions.evidence: Does every mechanism outside the favored set have an extension? Check the selected extensions beside the changed records.
provisions.statement: A mechanism outside modules, aggregates, domain events, use cases, reactions, and jobs MUST live in an extension.
provisions.rationale: LiteSpec favors one set of mechanisms and states that choice openly instead of claiming neutrality. An extension states how its mechanism composes with the core fields, so a project that needs it selects one place holding the whole contract.

provisions.heading: Derive Records Only from Records
provisions.evidence: Can every derived value be traced to the record that authors it? Trace each derived value to the record it cites.
provisions.statement: A record MUST take each derived value from another record.
provisions.rationale: Derivation between records keeps one authored source behind every value: the source changes once, and each derived read model follows. Generic refusals derive from access and input, and each read model derives from the records it lists, so readers trace every derived value to the record that states it.

provisions.heading: End Every Effect Cycle in a Domain Event
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports no `effect-loop-invalid` finding on the changed records.
provisions.statement: An effect graph MUST NOT hold a cycle except through a domain event with a stated end condition.
provisions.rationale: A cycle without an end condition runs until something outside the records stops it, so no reader can say when the work finishes. Routing each cycle through a domain event with a stated end condition names the loop and its exit in the records the graph checks.

provisions.heading: Follow Intent Where It States the Promise
provisions.evidence: Does the changed code agree with the Intent records it serves? Compare the changed code with the stated promises.
provisions.statement: Behavior and Implementation MUST follow Intent where Intent states the promise.
provisions.rationale: Intent holds the decided promises, and Behavior and code keep one chain from promise to product by following them. Where Intent states the promise, code that disagrees is the defect, and the fix changes the code.

provisions.heading: Keep Git as the Decision Record
provisions.evidence: Did every changed record go through its pull request? Check the pull request behind the change.
provisions.statement: A consumer MUST treat a record in the repository as decided, with the pull request that changes it as its review.
provisions.rationale: A record in git is the decision, and the pull request that changes it is its review. A record nobody wants is deleted, while git keeps who changed what and when, so records carry no history of their own.
provisions.example: A Claimwick feature nobody wants is deleted from the repository, and its history stays in git.

provisions.heading: Keep One Authored Source
provisions.evidence: Does every fact on the changed pages trace to one authored source, with every stated copy equal to its source under its check? Check the changed pages against their sources and checks.
provisions.statement: A consumer MUST author each fact once as its source and state it elsewhere only under a check that compares the copy with the source.
provisions.rationale: One source behind every fact lands each change in one place: the source changes once, and each stated copy follows under its check. A record repeats a fact from another record only when a reader needs it there, and the check reports a copy that drifts from its source. Judgments stay computed: completion derives from the model, and nobody types it by hand. Settled by [decision/0069-state-each-copy-under-a-check](decision/0069-state-each-copy-under-a-check).

provisions.heading: Keep Tools Small
provisions.evidence: Does every added command, check, generated file, or package have an owner approval and a user? Check the tooling the change adds beside its users.
provisions.statement: A command, check, generated file, or package MUST exist only while the owner approves it and something uses it.
provisions.rationale: Each command, check, generated file, or package adds maintenance, failure modes, and concepts every later reader learns. A tool nothing uses is removed instead of kept beside its replacement. Settled by [decision/0029-delete-the-unwired-language-checker](decision/0029-delete-the-unwired-language-checker), [decision/0031-remove-only-the-timing-variable](decision/0031-remove-only-the-timing-variable), and [decision/0034-measure-mutation-before-gating](decision/0034-measure-mutation-before-gating), and the same rule removes project fields in [decision/0025-remove-fields-nothing-reads](decision/0025-remove-fields-nothing-reads).
provisions.example: A Claimwick check nobody runs goes away with its command.

provisions.heading: Locate Package Versions in the Manifest
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `dependency-version-drift` for a package whose version differs from its manifest pin, and `stack-invalid` for a named stack the manifest does not ship.
provisions.statement: A consumer MUST resolve the standards-selected stack versions from `litespec.manifest.yaml`.
provisions.rationale: The manifest is the version authority for the stacks the standards select, so every consumer resolves the same tested combination. A version pinned in prose or remembered by an agent drifts from that authority with the next manifest change. Consumer dependencies still live in package manifests and lockfiles: only the standards-selected stack versions resolve from `litespec.manifest.yaml`.

provisions.heading: Name Boundaries for Their Business Action
provisions.evidence: Does each changed boundary name state its business action? Check the changed boundary names against the actions they guard.
provisions.statement: A consumer MUST use business operation names, specific command and query mediators, and business-action external ports at boundaries.
provisions.rationale: Components meet at boundaries, and future readers orient themselves there. Business operation names, specific command and query mediators, and business-action external ports state the purpose at that meeting point, so a newcomer places the interaction without opening either side.

provisions.heading: Prefer Direct Owned Dependencies
provisions.evidence: Does each new abstraction name the boundary that justifies it, or the wrapping convention that permits it? Check the new abstractions beside their boundaries and the wrapping convention.
provisions.statement: Use a selected framework type directly inside the architecture layer that owns it until an architectural boundary exists.
provisions.rationale: Using a selected framework type directly keeps one concept instead of two: the abstraction and what it hides. A project-owned abstraction earns its place for provider replacement, a test boundary, a stable domain concept, or an architecture boundary. Wrapping the framework everywhere else doubles the API the team maintains without isolating any real change.

provisions.heading: Prefer Local Code Until Reuse Is Real
provisions.evidence: Does each new shared unit serve two real consumers under one accurate name, or fall under the sharing convention? Check the new shared units beside their consumers and the sharing convention.
provisions.statement: Keep operation-specific code in its operation folder until two real consumers need the same precise behavior.
provisions.rationale: Operation-specific code kept beside its operation stays easy to change with the operation. Shared code needs a name and a responsibility that stay accurate for both consumers, but the first consumer rarely knows what the second needs. Holding out for two real consumers means the shared unit covers behavior both actually need.

provisions.heading: Prove Enforceable Boundaries Mechanically
provisions.evidence: Does each changed enforceable boundary name a reference, test, or lint rule that proves it? Check the changed boundaries beside their references, tests, and lint rules.
provisions.statement: A consumer MUST prove each enforceable boundary mechanically: a reference, visibility, an architecture test, a behavior test, or a lint rule.
provisions.rationale: A boundary stated only in prose holds until the first commit that ignores it. Mechanical proof fails the build or the check the day the boundary breaks. Specifications then explain the decisions that need judgment, while tools guard the constraints that do not. Enforceable boundaries include project and package references, compiler visibility, permission guards, store constraints, and lint rules.
provisions.example: A project-reference test proves Claimwick's Domain has no Infrastructure reference.

provisions.heading: Record Stricter Edge Rules as Conventions
provisions.evidence: Does every stricter edge rule have a cited convention? Check the project conventions beside the changed records.
provisions.statement: A project that keeps a stricter edge rule MUST record it as a cited convention.
provisions.rationale: LiteSpec checks declared edges and leaves stricter taste to each project. A stricter rule recorded as a cited convention stays visible and checkable beside the records it constrains, instead of surviving as habit in a few heads.

provisions.heading: Share No Transaction Across an Edge
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `record-invalid` for an effect entry that names `sharesTransaction` or a use case that `runs` another use case.
provisions.statement: An edge between records MUST NOT share a transaction, so each use case commits only its own writes.
provisions.rationale: An edge that shares its caller's transaction makes two use cases one unit of work: the called use case rides on a commit it does not own, a failure in either rolls back both, and neither use-case record says what it commits anymore. Running every follow-on act from a reaction to the fact the first act raised gives each use case its own commit, its own failure handling, and its own record. The schema holds no field for transaction sharing, so the rule holds by construction. Settled by [decision/0064-raise-facts-and-send-nothing-from-handlers](decision/0064-raise-facts-and-send-nothing-from-handlers).
provisions.example: Claimwick's reimbursement commits the expense and raises its reimbursed fact, and a reaction in the reporting module answers the published fact in its own transaction.

provisions.heading: State the Strength of Every Provision
provisions.evidence: Does every added provision state its strength and scope? Check the provisions the change adds.
provisions.statement: Every provision MUST state whether it is required, a default, or advisory, and where it applies.
provisions.rationale: Strength words work only when each one means exactly one thing. With the strength stated, an agent tells binding from advisory without a check existing, and a check stays an aid where one is cheap and sure, never the condition for a provision to exist.

provisions.heading: Take Every Name from the Intent Above It
provisions.evidence: Does every act carry the name the record above it states in its use case, method, event, permission, route, and screen label? Compare the names of one act across its record, its handler, its endpoint, and its screen.
provisions.statement: Every layer below a record MUST carry the name that record gives an act, a name chosen for what the act does in the business.
provisions.rationale: A name claims what happens, so the right name comes from asking what the act really does, including how it can end. The record that states the act decides the name, and the use case, the aggregate method, the event, the permission, the route, and the screen label repeat it. A check that reports two names for one act reports drift, not the answer: the fix brings every layer to the name the intent states, and the intent changes first when its own word is wrong. A rename made only to quiet a check leaves one act with two names, as does a name kept in one layer while the others move. Settled by [decision/0026-one-name-for-each-concept](decision/0026-one-name-for-each-concept).
provisions.example: In Claimwick, finance staff send an approved expense's payout to the bank, and the bank can refuse it when the company account cannot cover it. The act is a submission, not a payment, so the use case is `submit-payout`, the method `SubmitPayout`, the event `PayoutSubmitted`, the permission `submit-payout`, and the screen button reads "Submit payout". A later command records whether the bank paid or refused.

provisions.heading: Treat Code Beyond Silent Intent as Evidence for an Owner Question
provisions.evidence: Does every piece of working code outside Intent have an owner question carrying it? Check the owner questions beside the uncovered code.
provisions.statement: A consumer MUST treat working code that Intent does not cover as evidence for a question to the owner, not as a defect to delete and not as a source to copy into Intent.
provisions.rationale: When Intent is silent and working code exists, a decision went unrecorded. Deleting the code destroys behavior users rely on, and copying it quietly into Intent turns code into a promise nobody stated. A question carries the behavior to the owner with the code as evidence, and the answer lands in Intent first.
provisions.example: A positivity guard in Claimwick's submit-expense handler that no rule states becomes an owner question citing the guard, while the code stays until the answer lands in Intent.

provisions.heading: Write Every Record About the Software
provisions.evidence: Does every new record state the software rather than company business? Compare each new record with the code, results, tests, or infrastructure it translates into.
provisions.statement: Every record MUST state what the application does, holds, refuses at runtime, or runs on.
provisions.rationale: A goal, problem, feature, research record, or constraint qualifies when it translates into code, results, tests, or infrastructure. Running the company stays out: it enters only as a constraint or as dated research.
provisions.example: A Claimwick goal that translates into payout code and tests qualifies, while a sales target does not.

provisions.heading: Accept Every Retained Personal Data Class in Intent
provisions.evidence: Does every pseudonymized, retained, or exempt personal or sensitive class name its accepting requirement or decision? Check `basedOn` on each data class.
provisions.statement: Each personal or sensitive data class kept with `pseudonymize`, `retain`, or `exempt` MUST name the Intent requirements or decisions accepting it in `basedOn`.
provisions.rationale: Keeping personal data past erasure is a business choice, not a technical default: the statute or the business accepts it, with the reason on record. Pseudonymized data stays personal data, so it needs the same acceptance as retained data. Naming the accepting requirements or decisions in `basedOn` keeps the choice reviewable where the promise lives.

provisions.heading: Classify Every Aggregate Data Field
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `classification-drift` for a field whose `classification` differs from its data class.
provisions.statement: Each aggregate MUST list its data fields with their meaning, classification, and data class in `data`.
provisions.rationale: Without a classification, personal facts sit beside public ones with nothing marking which is which, and every handler guesses. A meaning with a classification of public, internal, personal, or sensitive tells every later reader how each field is handled, and the data class ties the field to its erasure position and its retention. The classification of a field matches its data class, and the fields live in `data` on the aggregate record file.

provisions.heading: Complete the Subject Export Before Erasure
provisions.evidence: Does every export-first class complete its export before an erasure run? Check the run evidence beside each class.
provisions.statement: A data class with `exportFirst` MUST complete the subject export before its erasure runs.
provisions.rationale: Erasure destroys the only copy of data the subject may still want: identity documents, message history, and purchase records. Completing the export first gives the subject that data while it still exists, so erasure never destroys what the subject asked to keep elsewhere.
provisions.example: Claimwick makes finance download the tax-relevant data before a shredder runs, and refuses to shred when anything changed after that download.

provisions.heading: Declare Every Data Class with Its Erasure Position
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `erasure-undeclared` for a personal or sensitive field with no declared position, `retention-enforcement-missing` for a class nothing enforces, and `data-class-fields-drift` for a data class `fields` list differing from the fields naming the class.
provisions.statement: Each data class MUST declare its classification, its fields, its purpose, its erasure position, its basis, its retention period with the date it counts from, and the enforcement that carries it out.
provisions.rationale: Erasure declared per field drifts: one field keeps a new position while its twin keeps the old one. Declaring the position once per class, with per-field exceptions beside it, keeps one decision in one place. The position is `erase`, `pseudonymize`, `anonymize`, `retain`, `exempt`, `tombstone`, `discard`, `cascade-only`, or `transferred`. The `basis` names the constraint, requirement, and decision identifiers behind the retention; the period is an ISO 8601 duration or `{ "mode": "none", "reason": "..." }` with its start in `periodStartsAt`; the enforcement names the `job/` or `use-case/` identifiers carrying out the erasure. A pseudonymized class stays personal with its basis, and an anonymized class can no longer identify anyone. The `erasure-undeclared` check reports a personal or sensitive field with no declared position, and `retention-enforcement-missing` reports a class nothing enforces.
provisions.example: In Claimwick, the submitter-contact class declares `personal`, `pseudonymize`, its purpose, and its accepting requirement, while the expense-ledger class declares `internal`, `retain`, a statutory seven years from the financial year end, and the finance expiry job.

provisions.heading: Discard Rows That Leave No Trace
provisions.evidence: Does any `onErasure` entry keep a marker where no marker duty exists? Check the entries on the aggregate pages.
provisions.statement: A data class with no duty to keep a marker MUST use `onErasure: discard`.
provisions.rationale: A tombstone is still a row: it takes storage, appears in counts, and invites readers to treat a gone subject as present. Where no reference and no audit needs the marker, deleting the row outright keeps the store honest.
provisions.example: Lago discards a customer: the profile is hidden and its relations end, while finalized invoices and credit notes stay as the ledger.

provisions.heading: Keep a Tombstone Where Deletion Stays Visible
provisions.evidence: Does every class referenced after erasure carry a tombstone marker with its kept fields? Check the marker entries on the aggregate pages.
provisions.statement: A data class whose rows outlive erasure as references MUST use `onErasure: tombstone` with the fields its marker keeps.
provisions.rationale: Some rows stay referenced after they are gone: remote servers hold copies, audit trails cite row ids, and support tools link to deleted accounts. Erasing the row breaks those references, while keeping it breaks the erasure duty. A tombstone keeps the row id and the erasure date and drops every other field, so references resolve to a marker that says the subject is gone.
provisions.example: ZITADEL deletes a user by moving it to a terminal state and deleting its read-model rows while the events stay for audit, and Sentry writes a tombstone for a discarded issue so that later events for it are dropped at intake instead of stored again.

provisions.heading: Keep Tombstone Fields Minimal
provisions.evidence: Does every tombstone entry keep only the row id and the erasure date, unless the project lists wider fields with their rules? Check the entries beside the project listing.
provisions.statement: A tombstone keeps the row id and the erasure date, and no other field.
provisions.rationale: Every field on a tombstone is data kept past erasure. The row id and the date satisfy references and audits; anything wider needs its own rule.

provisions.heading: Move Data to Its Next Controller Instead of Erasing
provisions.evidence: Does every handed-over class entry name its receiver and handover record? Check the entries on the aggregate pages.
provisions.statement: A data class handed to another controller MUST use `onErasure: transferred` with the receiver and the handover record.
provisions.rationale: Custody does not always end in erasure: a branch closes and a successor takes its readers, a company is acquired, or a contract moves to a new processor. The data survives under a new controller, so the record names the receiver and the handover both sides signed instead of a deletion that never happened.
provisions.example: A library support tool sends a loan summary and the reader message to a hosted AI model to draft a reply; the position names the model provider, its region and its retention, and the product stores none of it.

provisions.heading: Purge Erased Data from Restored Backups
provisions.evidence: Does every restore runbook name its sweep job? Check the restore runbooks.
provisions.statement: A restore runbook MUST name the sweep job that re-applies erasure after the restore.
provisions.rationale: A backup holds data as it was, including rows erased since. Restoring it resurrects subjects the product promised to forget. The sweep job re-applies every erasure decided before the restore, so the restore brings the system back without bringing the erased data back with it.
provisions.example: The database restore runbook names `job/privacy.sweep-restored-erasure`, which runs before traffic returns and deletes every row erased since the backup.

provisions.heading: Record Which Duty Wins Each Conflict
provisions.evidence: Does every data class `exceptions` entry name its winning duty with its basis? Check the `exceptions` on each data class.
provisions.statement: Each retention conflict MUST name the winning duty and its basis in the data class `exceptions`.
provisions.rationale: Keeping for audit and erasing for the subject collide on the same row: the invoice the statute keeps sits beside the name the subject erases. Without a recorded winner, each implementer picks one. Naming the winning duty with its basis in the data class `exceptions` keeps one decision where every reader finds it.
provisions.example: Claimwick keeps the expense ledger for seven years under tax law while erasing the submitter contact. ZITADEL keeps its audit events while erasing the user they describe, under the same rule.

provisions.heading: Remove Child Rows Through Their Parent Only
provisions.evidence: Does every child class entry carry cascade-only with its parent class, with parent erasure tests that clear the children? Check the entries and tests beside each child class.
provisions.statement: A data class erased only as a cascade from a parent erasure MUST use `onErasure: cascade-only` with the parent it follows.
provisions.rationale: Some rows have no subject of their own: line items belong to an invoice, receipt files belong to an expense, and usage rows belong to a customer. A direct erasure request names the parent, never the child, so the child follows the parent erasure and refuses a request addressed to itself.
provisions.example: Cal.com deletes a user by removing the account and letting the database cascade remove the rows that hang off it, with no retention schedule. A product following this rule declares cascade-only and names the cascade path.

provisions.heading: Require a Fresh Export After Changes
provisions.evidence: Does every erasure run after mid-window edits wait for a fresh export completed first? Check the run evidence beside each erasure.
provisions.statement: Erasure under `unchangedSinceExport` MUST stop and ask for a fresh export when the data changed since the last export.
provisions.rationale: An export taken last month does not cover rows written yesterday. Erasing on that stale copy destroys rows the subject never received. Stopping for a fresh export keeps the export-first promise true at the moment of erasure.
provisions.example: A reader who corrected their address after exporting it gets a fresh export first, and the erasure waits for it.

provisions.heading: Route Every External Erasure Through an Operation or Event
provisions.evidence: Does every external system declare its erasure call, forwarding event, or reason mode with acceptance? Check the external systems beside their erasure routes.
provisions.statement: Each external system MUST declare its erasure as `{ "mode": "call", "operation": "external-system/<name>#<operation>" }`, `{ "mode": "event", "event": "integration-event/<name>" }`, or `{ "mode": "unsupported", "reason": "..." }`, `{ "mode": "manual", "reason": "..." }`, or `{ "mode": "not-applicable", "reason": "..." }`, each with its acceptance.
provisions.rationale: Personal data forwarded to a processor without an erasure route stays there past erasure: the product forgets while the processor remembers. Declaring the call operation, the forwarding integration event, or one of the three reason modes with its reason and its Intent acceptance states the route beside the system.

provisions.heading: Run One Sweep Job per Data Class
provisions.evidence: Does every sweep job page cover one data class, unless the project names the classes each job covers? Check each sweep job page beside the project naming.
provisions.statement: Each sweep job covers one data class.
provisions.rationale: One sweep per class keeps a failure small: a broken sweep delays one class while the others complete. A shared sweep is one failure away from resurrecting every class at once.

provisions.heading: Scope Erasure to What the Subject Requested
provisions.evidence: Does every erasure use case cite the request it answers and touch only the data in it? Check the erasure use cases beside their requests.
provisions.statement: Erasure that answers a subject request MUST use `reach: requested` and touch only the data the request names.
provisions.rationale: A subject who asks to delete one order does not ask to delete the account, and a subject who asks to delete the account names everything. The requested reach ties the erasure to the request it answers, so a narrow request cannot widen into a broad deletion and a broad request cannot stop at one row.
provisions.example: A request naming one hold erases that hold and leaves the reader's other loans untouched.

provisions.heading: State the Erasure Sentence in Intent
provisions.evidence: Does every Intent requirement carry the confirmation sentence before the release that shows it? Check the requirement beside the release.
provisions.statement: The literal sentence the subject reads about an erasure MUST stand in Intent before the erasure ships.
provisions.rationale: The sentence on the confirmation screen is the promise: what goes, what stays, and for how long. Only the product team decides what the product promises, so Behavior cannot word it. Stating it in Intent puts the exact sentence readers see beside the requirement it fulfills.
provisions.example: Mastodon shows on its account deletion form that content other servers have cached may persist, next to the promise that the account and its posts are removed; that sentence is the user-facing copy for a requested reach.

provisions.heading: Apply Release Access Controls
provisions.evidence: Does every restricted release path carry authentication and authorization? Check the guards on each restricted path.
provisions.statement: A release with restricted access MUST provide authentication and authorization.
provisions.rationale: Restricted behavior without authentication accepts callers nobody identified, and without authorization it accepts actions nobody permitted. Both decisions call for a trusted identity and a declared permission before the behavior ships.

provisions.heading: Check Intent and Behavior Changes with the Book
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` exits zero when it reports no G finding, such as `record-invalid`.
provisions.statement: An Intent or Behavior change MUST pass the G checks with the book.
provisions.rationale: G checks read records only: shape, references, links, reachability, coverage, and the Behavior rules the check list names. Without them, a renamed record or a moved file silently breaks the references other pages rely on, and the book renders a graph that no longer holds. `litespec model check --since <ref>` blocks only on findings about records and code changed since `<ref>` and reports the rest, so an adopting project clears new findings first.

provisions.heading: Identify Immutable Release Artifacts
provisions.evidence: Does every release record name its source commit and artifact reference? Check the record header beside each artifact.
provisions.statement: A release record MUST name its source commit and its immutable artifact reference.
provisions.rationale: Without both references, evidence from one build can stand in for another, and nobody can tell which build a record proves. The source commit names the verified input and the artifact reference names the deployed output, which binds the record to one build.

provisions.heading: Keep Generated Contracts Stable
provisions.evidence: Does any contract diff hold timestamps, machine paths, or unstable order? Check the generated diff beside each contract.
provisions.statement: A generated application contract MUST be stable and exclude timestamps, machine paths, and nondeterministic ordering.
provisions.rationale: Timestamps, machine paths, and unstable ordering make every regeneration look like a behavior change. Deterministic output keeps contract diffs reviewable, so a reviewer sees only the changes that matter.

provisions.heading: Keep Release Records Non-Authoritative
provisions.evidence: Does any release record restate a specification or copy a scenario? Check the record against the linked specifications.
provisions.statement: A release record MUST NOT restate a specification or copy a scenario.
provisions.rationale: Specifications own behavior and scenarios. A release record that restates them becomes a second copy, and the copies drift until nobody knows which one holds. Linking outward keeps one home for each fact.

provisions.heading: List Included Release Behavior
provisions.evidence: Does every record list each included flow, use case, and extension? Check the behavior list on each release record.
provisions.statement: A release record MUST list included flows, use cases, and selected applicable extensions.
provisions.rationale: Operators and reviewers need to know what an artifact contains and, by omission, what it does not. Listing the flows, use cases, and extensions states the behavior boundary exactly.

provisions.heading: Qualify Each Stack Reader with Fixtures
provisions.evidence: Does every gating S reader show passing fixture runs? Check the fixture results beside the stack reader.
provisions.statement: A stack reader MUST pass its known good and known bad fixtures before it gates with S checks.
provisions.rationale: An unqualified reader blocks on noise or passes on silence, and each mistake trains the team to ignore its findings. Passing a known good tree and reporting each planted defect in a known bad tree proves the reader sees what it claims before it blocks any change.
provisions.example: The .NET reader passes the clean tree and reports the planted undeclared write before its S findings block.

provisions.heading: Record Accepted Debt as a Waiver
provisions.evidence: Does every accepted debt show a gap waiver with an expiry date, an exit, and `closedBy`? Check the waivers beside each debt.
provisions.statement: Accepted debt MUST live as a gap waiver with an `expiresOn` date, an `exit` and `closedBy`.
provisions.rationale: Accepted debt with no expiry date is forgotten work. A gap waiver with an `expiresOn` date, an `exit`, and `closedBy` turns it into a dated promise whose findings are covered until the date and whose `waiver-expired` reports after it. The [waivers page](waivers.md) states the waiver shape.
provisions.example: Claimwick ships month-end export without its archive proof, so the debt lives as a gap waiver with an `expiresOn` of 2027-03-01, an `exit`, and `closedBy` naming `use-case/spending.export-expenses`; `waiver-expired` reports it after that date.

provisions.heading: Record the Release Artifact
provisions.evidence: Does every release show one record naming its immutable artifact? Check the release records beside each artifact.
provisions.statement: A release MUST create one release record for its immutable artifact.
provisions.rationale: Evidence scattered across builds and reports answers no single question: nobody can say what one artifact proved. One release record per immutable artifact binds every result to the exact output it proves, so each artifact carries its own evidence.

provisions.heading: Regenerate Application Contracts
provisions.evidence: Does any committed contract differ from a fresh generation? Check the contract diff beside the source change.
provisions.statement: A source change MUST regenerate OpenAPI and frontend API types when it changes their source contract.
provisions.rationale: OpenAPI and frontend API types derive from a source contract, and clients build against the committed copies. A source change that leaves those copies stale ships clients built against a contract the server no longer honors.

provisions.heading: Report Verification Exactly
provisions.evidence: Does every completion report name its commands, outcomes, scope, omissions, differences, limits, and covered use cases? Check the report beside the change.
provisions.statement: A completion report MUST name exact commands, outcomes, evidence scope, skipped checks, generated differences, scope limits, and covered use cases.
provisions.rationale: A vague report lets unrun checks hide among completed ones. Naming exact commands, outcomes, scope, omissions, and limits tells a reviewer precisely what the evidence covers and what it does not.

provisions.heading: Resolve Release Blockers
provisions.evidence: Does any release depend on an expired waiver or an external claim without excluding the behavior? Check the waivers and claims beside the owning records.
provisions.statement: A release MUST settle every expired waiver and every external claim it depends on, or exclude the affected behavior from every owning record.
provisions.rationale: An expired waiver is a promise past its date, and an unverified external claim behind released behavior is a promise with unsettled terms: a provider fact, a law text, or a term nobody rechecked. Settling each one, or excluding the affected behavior from every owning record, keeps the Intent and release records agreeing on what shipped. `waiver-expired` reports every expired waiver.

provisions.heading: Run Backend Release Checks
provisions.evidence: Does every backend change show a passing release build and suite results? Check the build and suite reports beside the change.
provisions.statement: A backend change MUST pass the release build and the backend test suites.
provisions.rationale: The release build compiles the solution in release mode, catching the conditional and optimization-gated breaks a debug build hides. The architecture, integration, and acceptance suites the size requires prove layering, wiring, and behavior in turn. Skipping any of them ships backend code the project's own suites don't fully prove.

provisions.heading: Run Boundary-Selected Checks
provisions.evidence: Does every change show a passing result for each check its boundaries select? Check the change report against the boundary table.
provisions.statement: A release change MUST run every check selected by its changed backend, frontend, flow, Intent, Behavior, and extension boundaries.
provisions.rationale: Each boundary carries failures the others can't see: frontend checks say nothing about migrations, and backend suites say nothing about rendered screens. Running every check the changed boundaries select keeps each change evidenced where its failure lives. A narrow category that passes alone certifies only part of the change.

provisions.heading: Run Extension Checks
provisions.evidence: Does every affected extension show its stated verification evidence? Check the extension evidence beside the change.
provisions.statement: A selected project or applicable local extension MUST run its stated verification when affected.
provisions.rationale: An extension adds behavior, tests, and operating surface beyond the baseline, and its stated verification is the only evidence written for that surface. Skipping it releases extended behavior the baseline checks never examine.

provisions.heading: Run Flow Checks
provisions.evidence: Does every flow change show passing flow tests? Check the flow reports against the deployed boundary.
provisions.statement: A flow change MUST run its flow tests.
provisions.rationale: A flow change alters the connected path, so only a flow test through the deployed public boundary can prove it still reaches its outcome. Narrower suites keep passing while the flow itself breaks.

provisions.heading: Run Frontend Release Checks
provisions.evidence: Does every frontend change show passing install, lint, type, test, and build results? Check the frontend reports beside the change.
provisions.statement: A frontend change MUST run frozen installation, lint, type checking, tests, and production build checks.
provisions.rationale: Each step guards a different failure: frozen installation pins dependencies, lint and type checking catch static defects, tests prove behavior, and the production build proves the shipped bundle compiles. A frontend that skips one arrives at release with that whole class of defect unchecked.

provisions.heading: State Each Release as a Complete Record
provisions.evidence: Does any release record depend on an earlier record to be judged? Read the record alone beside its links.
provisions.statement: A release record MUST state its complete behavior and evidence without depending on an earlier release record.
provisions.rationale: A release judged from fragments is judged by archaeology: the reader digs through other records to fill the gaps. A complete record lets one reader judge one release from one page, with no upgrade guide filling in.

provisions.heading: Store Release Records Together
provisions.evidence: Does every release record sit under `.litespec/releases/`, or does a recorded release path convention name where it lives? Check the release paths against the convention.
provisions.statement: Keep release records under `.litespec/releases/`.
provisions.rationale: One folder for release records tells a maintainer where to find the evidence for any artifact. A record filed elsewhere looks missing while readers open the folder and find nothing there.
provisions.example: `.litespec/releases/2026-08-21.md` records one immutable artifact and its evidence.

provisions.heading: Verify Connected Flows
provisions.evidence: Does every completed flow show a passing test through the deployed boundary? Check the flow tests beside each included flow.
provisions.statement: A completed flow MUST connect verified use cases to one observable outcome through a deployed public boundary.
provisions.rationale: Use cases that pass in isolation can still fail together: wiring, permissions, and data cross boundaries the isolated tests never touch. A flow test that runs verified use cases to one observable outcome through the deployed public boundary proves the connected path customers actually take.

provisions.heading: Answer the Constraints Question
provisions.evidence: Does `.litespec/project.yaml` state which outside constraints apply, or record an empty answer? Check the project file.
provisions.statement: A consumer MUST state in `.litespec/project.yaml` whether any outside constraint applies to the project.
provisions.rationale: A product can break a law the team never named. An empty answer proves the team asked the question and found no outside rule binding the project. A later reader can then tell a project with no constraints apart from one that never looked.
provisions.example: A clinic booking system records that medical-device regulation does not apply to appointment scheduling.

provisions.heading: Claim Conformance Only When Every Applicable Provision Holds
provisions.evidence: Does the project meet every provision that applies to each layer it claims? Check `layers` in `.litespec/project.yaml`, the waiver records under `.litespec/governance/waivers/`, and the checks that run for those layers.
provisions.statement: A consumer MUST meet every provision that applies to each layer it claims in `layers` before claiming conformance to LiteSpec for those layers.
provisions.rationale: A conformance claim tells a reader that the whole claimed part of the contract holds, not only the parts the project chose to follow. A claim of `intent` and `behavior` takes in the provisions about the record model, and a claim of `implementation` or `proof` also takes in the provisions that tie each layer to the records. A [waiver](waivers.md) outranks the provision or findings it covers while it stands, so a project that records each waiver still meets this provision. A waiver past its expiry date reports `waiver-expired` and no longer outranks them. An unrecorded gap in a claimed layer breaks the claim for that layer, and leaves any layer the project does meet untouched.
provisions.example: A consumer claims all four layers with `litespec`, selects the dotnet stack and the caching extension, and claims conformance when every page those selections apply holds and their checks pass, with each waiver recorded. A consumer that claims `intent` and `behavior` claims conformance when the provisions about the record model hold, while its own code layout and tooling stay outside the claim.

provisions.heading: Claim the Record Layers the Project Uses
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `project-invalid` for a project file without `layers`, with a value other than those the table allows, or with a layer whose parent is not claimed.
provisions.statement: A consumer MUST name each record layer it claims in `layers` in `.litespec/project.yaml`, with `litespec` or `own` for Implementation and Proof, leaving layers out only from the bottom.
provisions.rationale: Teams adopt LiteSpec in parts: the record model alone, records with marked code, records with acceptance tests, or all of it, with their own architecture or test practice where they have one. Naming each layer lets every tool check exactly the part the team uses, so a missing test project is not a finding for a team that claims no Proof, and a team that keeps its own code layout still gets its marks checked. Leaving layers out from the bottom keeps every remaining link whole, because each layer points up to the one above it. Settled by [decision/0027-projects-claim-record-layers](decision/0027-projects-claim-record-layers).
provisions.example: The running Claimwick example claims all four layers with `litespec`. A product that marks its code in its own layout and proves no scenarios yet claims `intent`, `behavior`, and `implementation: own`, and `model check` reports no `use-case-unverified` finding for it.

provisions.heading: Declare a Consumer That Has No Backend
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `stack-invalid` for a `client-only` project that names a backend stack.
provisions.statement: A consumer with no server of its own MUST declare the `client-only` shape and record a decision naming the surfaces left without coverage.
provisions.rationale: The shape decides which backend pages still apply. A `client-only` product keeps a domain model, so the backend architecture, domain, and application pages that the manifest lists under `shapes` still apply to it. Persistence, the HTTP API, and API testing have no target without a server, and the decision names those uncovered surfaces. Adding a server only to obtain conformance contradicts `litespec/core/principles#add-new-machinery-only-for-a-current-requirement`, which permits new machinery only for a current documented requirement.
provisions.example: `litespec/quality/ci#run-applicable-gates-on-every-pull-request` already permits skipping a gate whose surface does not exist, so a missing backend gate is a recorded consequence rather than an unexplained absence.

provisions.heading: Keep Every LiteSpec File Under One Folder
provisions.evidence: Does any file LiteSpec creates, reads, or governs sit outside `.litespec/` or at the repository root? Look at the repository tree beside the project's `.litespec/` folder.
provisions.statement: A consumer MUST hold every file LiteSpec creates, reads, or governs under one folder, `.litespec/`, at the repository root.
provisions.rationale: Without one folder, readers and tools hunt the tree for LiteSpec material scattered across the repository. One folder with one name in every consumer makes the material identifiable at a glance. A reader, a tool, or an agent finds the whole contract in one place, moves or deletes it without hunting, and keeps it apart from the application's code, tests, and infrastructure. Generated output inside it stays covered by its `.gitignore`, so a checkout never mixes committed records with built files. Every path in `.litespec/project.yaml` stays relative to the repository root, so moving the folder never rewrites the paths inside it. A command finds the consumer by walking up from the working folder to the first folder that holds `.litespec/project.yaml`.
provisions.example: Claimwick holds its project file, glossary, example cast, and its Intent, Behavior, Implementation, Proof, and Governance folders under `examples/claimwick/.litespec/` (in a real consumer, at its repository root), beside its application code and tests, which keep their own places. An agent asked to read the contract opens that one folder, instead of collecting a root project file, a documentation tree, a model folder, and a book folder from four places.

provisions.heading: Keep One Bounded Context
provisions.evidence: Does the project keep one business language and one deployment boundary? Check the module pages and `.litespec/project.yaml`.
provisions.statement: A consumer MUST keep one business language and deployment boundary.
provisions.rationale: One business language and one deployment boundary keep every module, record, and use case in a single consistent model. Modules organize related language, models, use cases, and code without becoming independent services or bounded contexts. A second language or boundary splits the project into systems the records, links, and checks can no longer hold together.
provisions.example: A publishing product keeps Posts, Authors, and Comments as modules in one context, with one shared language.

provisions.heading: Measure Capacity Before Expansion
provisions.evidence: Does each added cache, replica, queue, or partition follow recorded load, latency target, and observed constraint, or a capacity convention? Check the capacity records beside each expansion.
provisions.statement: Record current load, latency target, and observed constraint before adding caches, replicas, queues, or partitioning.
provisions.rationale: Caches, replicas, queues, and partitioning each answer a different limitation, and only measurements show which one the project hit. Expanding first and measuring later adds machinery that can hide the real bottleneck. Recording current load, the latency target, and the observed constraint before expanding proves the added capacity answers the observed limit.

provisions.heading: Point Behavior Docs at the Behavior Root
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `project-invalid` for a project record without `paths.behaviorDocs`.
provisions.statement: A consumer MUST set `paths.behaviorDocs` in `.litespec/project.yaml` to the folder that holds its Behavior records.
provisions.rationale: Tools never see a Behavior tree the project record does not name, so its records skip every check. The builder joins records, queries, diffs, and the book from one declared root. One declared folder keeps authors and tools on the same tree.
provisions.example:
```yaml
paths:
  behaviorDocs: .litespec/behavior
```

provisions.heading: Record Selected Extensions
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `project-invalid` for a selection without a criterion.
provisions.statement: A consumer MUST list every selected extension in `selectedExtensions` in `.litespec/project.yaml`, each with its criterion.
provisions.rationale: Without a written selection, extensions drift in through dependencies and prose while the checks apply a different set. A later reader cannot tell which condition justified each extension, or whether it still holds. Writing each selection with its criterion keeps the project record as the one place that decides which extension boundaries apply.

provisions.heading: Record Unsupported Scope Decisions
provisions.evidence: Does a project decision name each architecture outside the supported boundary the project adopts? Check the project decisions.
provisions.statement: A consumer MUST record a separate project decision for microservices, multiple contexts, native clients on a platform with no mobile stack, other platforms, event sourcing, active-active regions, or large pipelines.
provisions.rationale: Each of these architectures changes the assumptions this page rests on: one language, one deployment, one API, and one database. Without a recorded decision, the project drifts outside the supported scope while claiming its checks still apply.
