provisions.rationale: The code already states what it does, so a comment that restates it adds words a maintainer must keep true without adding knowledge. The reason a boundary exists, the constraint a caller must respect, or the failure a member reports is what the next reader cannot recover from the code alone. History belongs in the commit that made the change, where a reader looking for it finds it; commented-out code is history with no commit to explain it. An API summary states the contract first: what the member does, what it needs, what it returns, and which failures belong to the contract, in the form the stack's pages state.
provisions.example: A Claimwick handler comment states why the approval check runs before the payout call. It names no step the code below it already shows, and holds no earlier version of the call.

provisions.heading: Compare Real Options in Each Decision Record
provisions.evidence: Does every decision record compare real options on the same points and state what would reopen the choice, without recounting the discussion? Check the decision records the change adds.
provisions.statement: Every decision record MUST compare its real options on their merits in Options, then state the chosen outcome in Decision and what would reopen it in Revisit Conditions.
provisions.rationale: A decision record exists for a reader who was not there when the choice was made. That reader needs the forces, the alternatives, and the consequences, not the discussion that produced them. Options compared on the same points let a later reader rejudge the choice when the world moves; a record that names only the winner forces the whole argument to run again. What would reopen the choice belongs in the record beside the choice, so a stable decision stays stable until the named condition holds. Any option singled out from the decision carries its own sentence saying why it stands apart.
provisions.example: A Claimwick decision compares a receipt threshold of EUR 25 with EUR 50 on refusal rate and approver load, chooses EUR 25, and names a refusal rate above the stated bound as what would reopen it.

provisions.heading: Give Each Explanation File Its Fixed Sections
provisions.evidence: Does every explanation file use its record type's fixed sections in order, under its H1 title? Check the explanation files beside the records the change adds against the explanation-section table.
provisions.statement: Every explanation file MUST use the fixed sections of its record type, in the order the explanation-section table gives, with the record title as its one H1.
provisions.rationale: A fixed section list answers the same questions on every record of one type, so a reader who learned one problem page reads the next without relearning where the evidence sits. Each list answers what a cold reader needs: who has the need, what it costs, what the record connects to, and what good looks like. A problem earns its sections because its reader judges a pain: who has it, each way it fails them, what they do instead, what it costs them, the evidence for it, and what shows each failure has ended. Each section is a plain noun, so the heading tells a reader what the section holds before they read it. Free sections may follow the fixed ones; they never replace one. Settled by [decision/0043-use-plain-noun-sections](../intent/decisions/0043-use-plain-noun-sections/0043-use-plain-noun-sections.md), which gives each record type one list of plain noun sections.
provisions.example: The Claimwick problem explanation for waiting expenses runs Affected Users, Failure Cases, Current Workaround, Cost, Evidence, Resolution Criteria. The evidence stands in its own section instead of inside a pointer to another page.

provisions.heading: Give Each Paragraph One Idea
provisions.evidence: Does every paragraph carry one idea on one line, with lists only for parallel items? Check the explanation files and documents the change adds.
provisions.statement: Every paragraph in an explanation file or document MUST carry one idea, on one line in Markdown, with a list only where the items are truly parallel.
provisions.rationale: A reader hunting for one fact should not have to untangle a paragraph that holds a rule, an exception, and a fallback in one block. One idea per paragraph puts each fact where a scanning reader finds it, and one line per paragraph keeps diffs readable, so a changed sentence shows as one changed line. A list drawn from prose that is not parallel hides the reasoning that connects its items: connected reasoning stays in prose, and only parallel items become a list.
provisions.example: The Claimwick decision explanation gives Revisit Conditions its own paragraph. A reader looking for what would reopen the choice finds that paragraph without reading the example above it.

provisions.heading: Interpret Fields in Explanations, Never Restate Them
provisions.evidence: Does any explanation file restate a field value instead of interpreting it? Check each explanation file against its record's fields.
provisions.statement: Every explanation file MUST interpret its record's fields in plain words without restating a field value.
provisions.rationale: An explanation that copies a field value becomes a second copy that drifts with the next edit to the record. Interpretation says what the record means, why it matters, and how it reads beside its neighbors, with context and an example the fields cannot hold. Proposed by decision 0070.
provisions.example: A Claimwick feature explanation says the approval reminders end the wait that costs employees weeks, instead of copying the feature's `offering`.

provisions.heading: Keep Each Record Sentence Within Twenty-Five Words
provisions.evidence: Does any record statement or summary carry a sentence past 25 words that holds no condition a shorter sentence would drop? Check the statements and summaries the change adds.
provisions.statement: Every sentence in a record `statement` or `summary` SHOULD hold at most 25 words.
provisions.rationale: A record sentence carries one fact a builder implements. A sentence past 25 words often carries two facts joined by a comma, so the reader weighs both at once or misses the second. Twenty-five words is a house limit chosen for scanning, not a measured limit of what readers parse, and the count is mechanical so every record is counted the same way. The glossary `meaning` bound is the same bound, checked by `litespec model check` as the advisory `term-meaning-invalid`. A longer explanation belongs in the explanation file, split into sentences that each carry one fact. Proposed by [decision/0057-narrow-the-writing-rules-to-meaning](../intent/decisions/0057-narrow-the-writing-rules-to-meaning/0057-narrow-the-writing-rules-to-meaning.md).
provisions.example: "Employees wait three weeks for reimbursement while approvers batch decisions monthly." The sentence holds 11 words and one fact.

provisions.heading: Keep Release Phases and Plans Out of Records
provisions.evidence: Does any record name a release phase, a later step, or a future plan where the product as it stands, a vision, an owner question, or a backlog item belongs? Check the records the change adds.
provisions.statement: Every record MUST state the product as it stands, with no release phase, later step or future plan in its prose.
provisions.rationale: A phrase such as "in the first release" or "a later step" dates the record the day the release ships, and it promises a behavior no requirement holds. A destination the product heads for is a vision, an open choice is an owner question or a backlog item, and a limit of the current product is stated as a limit, not as a plan to lift it. Proposed by [decision/0054-write-each-shared-record-rule-once](../intent/decisions/0054-write-each-shared-record-rule-once/0054-write-each-shared-record-rule-once.md).
provisions.example: A permission record states "The role cannot be limited to one business", not that staff will narrow the role in a later release.

provisions.heading: Keep the Conditions When Shortening
provisions.evidence: Does every shortened form keep each condition of the claim it shortens? Check the summaries, conclusions, statements, and opening paragraphs the change adds against the claims they shorten.
provisions.statement: Every `summary`, `conclusion`, `statement` and opening paragraph that shortens a claim MUST keep each condition of the claim it shortens, such as where entitled to deduct, for quarterly filers or to the extent allowed.
provisions.rationale: A shortened form that drops a condition states a wider claim than its source, and a reader builds or decides against the wider claim. Shortening stays the aim, so a form keeps the words that carry a condition and drops the rest. This rule outranks the sentence bound in `litespec/core/writing#keep-each-record-sentence-within-twenty-five-words` whenever the two pull apart. Proposed by [decision/0054-write-each-shared-record-rule-once](../intent/decisions/0054-write-each-shared-record-rule-once/0054-write-each-shared-record-rule-once.md).
provisions.example: "Finance reimburses the expense" states more than Claimwick does. "Finance reimburses the approved expense" keeps the condition the policy holds.

provisions.heading: Name Observable Behavior Instead of Intensifiers
provisions.evidence: Does any sentence use an intensifier or claim an experience where the behavior or a measured target belongs? Check the records and explanation files the change adds.
provisions.statement: Every record and explanation file MUST state the observable behavior or the measured target in place of an unsupported intensifier or experience claim, such as seamlessly, easily, instantly, at once, or quickest.
provisions.rationale: The reader of a record has to build or test what it says. An intensifier reads as a promise while hiding the criterion behind it: "the owner sees at once which account differs" names no behavior a tester can check, and "quickest sign" claims a comparison nobody measured. Stating what the product shows, or the number it meets, gives the builder something to build and the tester something to pass or fail.
provisions.example: A Claimwick feature writes "The approver sees each waiting expense with the number of business days it has waited", not "The approver instantly spots late expenses".

provisions.heading: Open Each Explanation File with a Paragraph
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `explanation-opening-missing` for an explanation file with no prose between its H1 and its first H2.
provisions.statement: Every explanation file MUST hold one paragraph of prose between its H1 title and its first H2 section, saying what the record is in plain words, who it concerns and the consequence at stake.
provisions.rationale: A reader who opens an explanation from a link reads the opening paragraph first and decides from it whether the record concerns them. The paragraph stands alone, so the record is understood before any section is read. A heading with no paragraph under it sends the reader straight into a section that assumes context they do not have yet. Proposed by [decision/0049-literal-flow-words-concrete-consequences](../intent/decisions/0049-literal-flow-words-concrete-consequences/0049-literal-flow-words-concrete-consequences.md).
provisions.example: The Claimwick problem explanation for waiting expenses opens with one paragraph: employees wait three weeks for reimbursement, approvers batch decisions monthly, and the wait costs the company more than the money it holds. Only then does its Affected Users section begin.

provisions.heading: Open Each Summary with Who and What Is at Stake
provisions.evidence: Does every summary open with who and what is at stake? Check the first sentence of each summary the change adds.
provisions.statement: Every `summary` MUST restate who it concerns and what is at stake in its first sentence, with any pointer to another page after that content.
provisions.rationale: The summary is the lead a cold reader meets in the book, before any field table or link. A first sentence that restates who and what is at stake lets that reader judge the record without opening its links; a bare pointer such as "described on the launch page" gives them nothing to judge and breaks the moment the pointed page moves. A pointer that follows the content helps the reader who wants more; a pointer that replaces the content helps no one.
provisions.example: A Claimwick problem `summary` opens "Employees wait three weeks for reimbursement while approvers batch decisions monthly." Who waits and what it costs stand in the first sentence, and any link follows after it.

provisions.heading: Put the Actor First
provisions.evidence: Does every sentence that describes an action open with its actor, in the active voice and the present tense? Check the statements and summaries the change adds.
provisions.statement: Every sentence in a record that describes an action MUST name its actor as its subject, in the active voice and the present tense.
provisions.rationale: A sentence that opens with its actor states who does what before the reader reaches the verb, and the present tense states what holds today rather than what a plan intends. Passive forms hide the actor, and future forms promise a behavior no record states. Second person belongs only on tutorial and how-to pages, where the reader is the actor; records stay in the third person, as the text-kind table on the [Record Language](language.md) page states. A sentence that states a fact, a state, or a calculation may take its object or its condition as its subject, as in "The statement closing date determines the comparison date." Passive voice that hides who acts stays a finding. Proposed by [decision/0057-narrow-the-writing-rules-to-meaning](../intent/decisions/0057-narrow-the-writing-rules-to-meaning/0057-narrow-the-writing-rules-to-meaning.md).
provisions.example: Claimwick writes "The approver approves the expense within five business days." The actor opens the sentence, and the present tense states what holds.

provisions.heading: Take Each Example Detail from the Cast or a Cited Record
provisions.evidence: Does every name, date, and number in each Example come from the cast or a cited record, with no rule of its own? Check the Example sections the change adds against the cast.
provisions.statement: Every name, date and number in an `Example` section MUST come from the example cast or from a record the explained record cites, each appears only where it shows something about that record, and the `Example` states no rule of its own.
provisions.rationale: An Example that brings in a figure no record holds shows the reader a number that rests on a rule nobody states, and the reader takes the number for the rule. A fixed cast keeps every Example cumulative, so one name means one person across the documentation. An Example that states a rule would be a second copy of a record's statement, which drifts. Proposed by [decision/0054-write-each-shared-record-rule-once](../intent/decisions/0054-write-each-shared-record-rule-once/0054-write-each-shared-record-rule-once.md).
provisions.example: A Claimwick module example uses the 48.90 EUR fare and the 25 EUR receipt threshold, both as the example cast and the policy record state them, and adds no third amount.

provisions.heading: Use Literal Words
provisions.evidence: Does every title and sentence use the literal word, with each term defined or linked? Check the titles, verbs, and first uses the change adds against the glossary.
provisions.statement: Every title and sentence MUST use the literal word for what it names, with each term defined on first use or linked to the glossary.
provisions.rationale: A metaphor reads smoothly while hiding what the project means: each reader pictures a different act behind the same flourish, and a metaphor title hides its subject in every list that shows it. A literal phrase names the act itself, so no reader has to decode it. A loose verb such as handles, holds, touches, or lands hides the act the same way: "one transfer entry touches both accounts" leaves open what happens to each balance, while "one transfer entry reduces the sending account's balance and increases the receiving account's balance" states it. Plain wording keeps the precise term of the domain, such as opening balance or closing date, where a looser word would lose the meaning. A word is loose when it leaves the act unclear in its sentence; a field or domain term used in its defined sense, such as an actor that holds a role, is not loose. A stock phrase is the same loose form: "It matters because the figures must be correct" names no consequence, while "A wrong box amount means a correction return, and a late return means a fine" names the consequence and who bears it. Each concept keeps its one glossary term, as `litespec/core/authoring#use-one-term-for-one-concept` states; this provision adds only that a term a cold reader may not know is defined where it first appears or linked to its glossary entry. Proposed by [decision/0049-literal-flow-words-concrete-consequences](../intent/decisions/0049-literal-flow-words-concrete-consequences/0049-literal-flow-words-concrete-consequences.md) and [decision/0057-narrow-the-writing-rules-to-meaning](../intent/decisions/0057-narrow-the-writing-rules-to-meaning/0057-narrow-the-writing-rules-to-meaning.md).
provisions.example: A Claimwick problem is titled "Expenses Wait Weeks for Reimbursement". The title names the wait and the delay literally, with no figure of speech to decode.

provisions.heading: Use One Mechanical Form for Each Fact
provisions.evidence: Does every page use American spelling, the serial comma, numerals for measured quantities, long-form prose dates, and straight quotes, with no contraction inside a record? Check the prose the change adds.
provisions.statement: Every page MUST use American spelling, the serial comma, numerals for numbers of 10 and above and for every quantity with a unit, ISO dates in fields and long-form dates in prose, straight quotes, and ASCII characters except in exact quotations and names, which keep their characters.
provisions.rationale: One mechanical form per fact keeps every search, diff, and listing exact: `license` on one page and `licence` on another splits every lookup, and a curly quote or a typographic dash renders differently in terminals, generated context, and plain-text tools. Numerals for measured quantities keep a count scannable beside its unit, while small counts in prose stay words a reader absorbs without stopping. An ISO date in a field sorts and checks as data; the same date in prose reads "2 November 2026", in the order a person says it. Contractions belong on documentation pages, where the voice is a person explaining; records hold none, because a record states a fact in its shortest checkable form. ASCII is LiteSpec's preference for its own pages, as `litespec/core/authoring#keep-authored-prose-ascii-safe` states; exact quotations and names keep their characters.
provisions.example: Claimwick prose writes "The tenant keeps receipts for 7 years, files them by month, quarter, and year, and closes the period on 2 November 2026." The field beside it holds `2026-11-02`.

provisions.heading: Write Each Changelog as a Release Comparison
provisions.evidence: Does every entry state the present behavior, who it affects, and what the reader does, with no former behavior described outside the changelog? Check the entries the change adds.
provisions.statement: Every changelog entry MUST state the present behavior, who it affects and what the reader does, comparing with the previous release only inside the changelog.
provisions.rationale: A changelog serves a reader deciding whether to upgrade and a reader checking what changed after upgrading. Both need the observable change, its condition, and the required action, never an inventory of the work. Stating the present state first lets every other page describe what is true today without carrying a former behavior; the changelog is the one place where the comparison with the previous release belongs. A breaking change, a removal, and a security fix each state what stops working, who is affected, and the replacement or action, in the entry itself rather than behind a link.
provisions.example: A Claimwick changelog entry states "Submitting an expense without a receipt above the threshold is refused. Employees attach the receipt before submitting." The behavior, the reader, and the action stand in the entry.

provisions.heading: Write Each Documentation Page as One Kind
provisions.evidence: Does every documentation page do one job, open as its kind opens, and state its reader and purpose in its first lines? Check the opening lines of each documentation page the change adds against the documentation-kind table.
provisions.statement: Every documentation page MUST do one of the four documentation jobs, open as that kind opens, and state its reader and its purpose in its first lines.
provisions.rationale: A tutorial that stops to explain a trade-off loses the reader mid-path, and a reference page that teaches leaves the reader hunting for the value they came to look up. One job per page puts each fact where its reader looks for it, and the opening tells a reader from a search result within two sentences whether this page answers their question. A README earns its first screen the same way: what the folder holds, who reads it, and where each reader goes next, before any file list. The page styles and their sections live in the [Authoring Standard](authoring.md); this provision states the prose each kind opens with.
provisions.example: A Claimwick how-to page opens "Remind an approver who has held an expense past three business days." The reader and the one problem solved stand before the first step.

provisions.heading: Write Each Statement as a Fact Without Modal Words
provisions.evidence: Does every record statement hold one present-tense sentence with no modal word? Check the statements the change adds.
provisions.statement: Every record `statement` MUST hold one sentence in the present tense with no modal word.
provisions.rationale: A statement states what holds, as a fact a builder implements. A modal word such as must, should, shall, may, can, or will turns the fact into an intention, a permission, or a promise, and each reader grades its strength differently. One sentence keeps one commitment per statement, so a change to one commitment changes one statement. The value style on the [Record Language](language.md) page states the same form; this provision states the prose reason and the check covers every record type.
provisions.example: Claimwick states "An expense above the threshold carries a receipt." The sentence states what holds, with no modal word grading it.

provisions.heading: Write Every Record Title in Title Case
provisions.evidence: Does every record title use Title Case, carry no final period, and hold at most eight words? Check the titles the change adds.
provisions.statement: Every record title MUST use Title Case, carry no final period, and hold at most eight words.
provisions.rationale: A title is the record's name in book lists, outlines, tabs, and search results, so it reads as a name, never as a sentence. Title Case capitalizes every major word and lowercases a, an, the, and, but, or, nor, for, so, yet, as, at, by, in, of, off, on, per, to, up, via, with, from, into, over and than unless the word stands first or last. One casing rule for every title is the only casing rule a check enforces the same way everywhere; mixed casing makes two records of one kind read as two kinds. Eight words keeps the whole title on one scannable line in a list while leaving room for the longest form, a problem clause naming the failure and its consequence. LiteSpec headings follow the same casing under `litespec/core/authoring#use-controlled-capitalization`.
provisions.example: The Claimwick requirement title reads "Expense Above Threshold Carries Receipt", five words in Title Case with no final period, naming the fact the requirement holds rather than a bare noun such as "Receipts".

provisions.heading: Write for the Reader Who Arrives Cold
provisions.evidence: Does every record, explanation file, and page open with who and what is at stake, with no later section repeating the opening? Check the first sentence of each page the change adds.
provisions.statement: The opening paragraph of every record, explanation file and documentation page MUST name who it concerns and what is at stake, before any pointer to another page.
provisions.rationale: Most readers land on one page from a list, a search result, or a link, with nothing read before it. A page that opens with its subject and its stake answers that reader on its own; a page that opens with a pointer sends them elsewhere before giving them anything. Each section after the opening answers its own question instead of repeating the opening. The tone throughout is a product explaining itself plainly: plain words, checkable facts, and honest roles, with no selling and no decoration. Proposed by [decision/0057-narrow-the-writing-rules-to-meaning](../intent/decisions/0057-narrow-the-writing-rules-to-meaning/0057-narrow-the-writing-rules-to-meaning.md).
provisions.example: A Claimwick problem opens "Employees wait three weeks for reimbursement while approvers batch decisions monthly." A reader who has opened no other page knows who waits and what it costs them.

provisions.heading: Assert Output Structure Instead of Wording
provisions.evidence: Does every mediated query scenario assert fields, codes, and cited sources instead of exact words? Read the scenario assertions.
provisions.statement: A scenario for a model-mediated query MUST assert the output structure and never its wording.
provisions.rationale: Model wording shifts between runs: the same facts arrive in different sentences. A scenario asserting exact words fails on a paraphrase, while a scenario asserting structure, fields, codes, and cited sources passes on every true answer.
provisions.example: The scenario asserts the answer carries `orderId` and one cited source, not the sentence around them.

provisions.heading: Bound Tool Calls per Query
provisions.evidence: Does every mediated query state a per-run tool-call bound, and do the run tests honor it? Read the query definitions beside the run tests.
provisions.statement: A model-mediated query MUST bound how many tool calls one run makes.
provisions.rationale: A model in a loop calls tools until the budget or the patience runs out. A bound on calls per run caps the cost and the latency up front, so one looping run cannot spend the month's budget.
provisions.example: The support answer query allows eight tool calls per run and refuses the ninth.

provisions.heading: Name the Closed Tool Set
provisions.evidence: Does every mediated query name its closed tool set, with no calls outside it? Read each query's tool set beside the tool calls its tests record.
provisions.statement: A model-mediated query MUST name the closed set of tools the model calls.
provisions.rationale: A model with an open tool set invents tools, reaches past its grant, and surprises every review. Naming exactly what the model touches gives the grant, the tests, and the audit one list to read.
provisions.example: The support answer query names `orders.lookup` and `docs.search` as its only tools.

provisions.heading: Pin a Deterministic Stub in Proof
provisions.evidence: Does every mediated query test run against the pinned stub version instead of a live model? Read the test configuration beside the stub version.
provisions.statement: Proof for a model-mediated query MUST run against a deterministic stub pinned by version.
provisions.rationale: A live model answers differently each run, so a test against it proves nothing twice. A deterministic stub pinned by version answers the same way every run, so Proof checks the product's handling instead of the model's varying output.
provisions.example: The support answer tests run against `stub-answers v4`, which returns one fixed tool trace per prompt.

provisions.heading: Record Every Model Run
provisions.evidence: Does every run log entry hold a prompt hash, the tools called, and an outcome, or does the AI documentation name other evidence? Read the run log.
provisions.statement: Each model run writes its prompt hash, the tools called, and the outcome to the run log.
provisions.rationale: Production answers need after-the-fact review: what was asked, what the model touched, and what came back. The run log holds the three without storing full prompts.

provisions.heading: Record Provenance in the Output
provisions.evidence: Does every mediated query answer carry the model, the tools called, and the sources read? Read the provenance on each answer.
provisions.statement: A model-mediated query MUST return provenance naming the model, the tools called, and the sources read.
provisions.rationale: An answer without provenance gives nobody a way to check it: nobody knows which model wrote it, which tools fed it, or which sources back it. Provenance names the three, so every answer carries its own audit trail.
provisions.example: The answer returns `model: support-7, tools: [orders.lookup], sources: [order-8841]`.

provisions.heading: Refuse Unknown Tools
provisions.evidence: Does every mediated query test refuse a run that calls a tool outside the closed set? Read the refused-run tests.
provisions.statement: A model-mediated query MUST refuse a run that calls a tool outside its closed set.
provisions.rationale: Models drift: a prompt tweak or a version change can add a call nobody declared. Refusing the run at the first unknown tool keeps the closed set closed in production, not just on paper.
provisions.example: A run that calls `billing.refund` outside its set is refused before the call leaves the product.

provisions.heading: Anchor the Audit Chain Outside Its Own Store
provisions.evidence: Does the store publish a checkpoint where its own operators cannot rewrite it? Check the checkpoint destination and the threat model.
provisions.statement: An audit store SHOULD publish a periodic checkpoint of its chain head to a destination that the store's own operators cannot rewrite.
provisions.rationale: A chain proves that records agree with each other, but anyone holding the store can recompute the whole chain and keep it agreeing. A checkpoint held somewhere the operators cannot rewrite fixes the chain as it stood at that moment. A later recomputation disagrees with the checkpoint, which exposes it.
provisions.example: The checkpoint is the chain head and its record count, published at a stated interval. A separate append-only destination, a timestamping authority, and a transparency log each qualify.

provisions.heading: Audit Async Work at Request Time
provisions.evidence: Does every deferred run write its audit record when requested rather than when it runs? Check the audit rows beside the requesting calls.
provisions.statement: Work that runs after its request MUST write its audit record at request time.
provisions.rationale: The actor, the origin, and the grant exist when the request arrives; the later run carries worker identity under system auth, which says nothing about who asked. Writing the record at request time ties the attempt to the caller who made it. A record written when the background run starts would attribute every scheduled and deferred act to the worker instead of the requester.

provisions.heading: Audit Bulk Reads Inside One Boundary
provisions.evidence: Does every above-threshold query produce a record with the subject count? Check the bulk query paths.
provisions.statement: A query returning personal data for more subjects than its declared threshold MUST produce an audit record, inside one tenant or account boundary as well.
provisions.rationale: The cross-boundary rule catches a disclosure to the wrong party, but it misses an export of every record a party may read one at a time, which is the shape a copied dataset has. A query above the declared threshold therefore writes a record even inside one boundary. [Article 30 of the GDPR](https://gdpr-info.eu/art-30-gdpr/) asks what categories of data were processed and by whom, and an unrecorded bulk read answers neither.
provisions.example: Claimwick records the threshold in its adoption decision. A list endpoint whose page size can exceed it audits the read with the subject count rather than naming each subject.

provisions.heading: Audit Every Bulk Export
provisions.evidence: Does every export produce a record naming the requested scope? Check the export paths.
provisions.statement: An export that returns a set of records to a caller MUST produce an audit record naming the requested scope.
provisions.rationale: Bulk extraction is the highest-consequence read in most products: one call moves a dataset across the boundary. Naming the requested scope states what left the system. Without it, the project learns the shape of a leak from the party that received it.

provisions.heading: Audit Every Required Category
provisions.evidence: Does the declared selection cover all eight required categories? Check it against the eight categories this provision names.
provisions.statement: An audit selection MUST include authentication, authorization denial, grant change, monetary action, tenant configuration, personal-data read, bulk export, and background-process change.
provisions.rationale: Each listed category answers a question a security review, a customer, or a supervisory authority asks after an incident: who signed in, who was refused, who changed a grant, who moved money, and the rest. A trail that omits a category has no answer when that question arrives. The list fixes the floor so no project discovers the gap during its first review.

provisions.heading: Audit Only Selected Commands
provisions.evidence: Does every audited category carry a recorded selection reason? Check the declared selection.
provisions.statement: A project MUST NOT audit every Command without a recorded selection.
provisions.rationale: A trail that records every Command buries the sensitive action inside routine traffic, and the reviewer who has to read it stops reading. Volume then defeats the review the trail exists to support. A recorded selection keeps the trail small enough to read.

provisions.heading: Audit Reads of the Trail
provisions.evidence: Does every completed trail read produce an audit record? Check the trail read path.
provisions.statement: A read of the audit trail MUST itself produce an audit record.
provisions.rationale: Reading the evidence is itself a sensitive action: the trail shows who did what across the whole product. A read that writes no record leaves the reviewer outside the trail. Recording each read puts the reviewer inside the same accountability as everyone else.

provisions.heading: Chain Records to Expose Tampering
provisions.evidence: Does every stored record carry the chained SHA-256 hash over the canonical serialization? Check the stored chain values.
provisions.statement: An audit store MUST chain each record to its predecessor with a SHA-256 hash over a canonical serialization of both.
provisions.rationale: The hash chain detects an edit and a removal, because a changed or missing record breaks every value after it. Detection is the obligation: it lets a reviewer prove the trail is intact. Prevention at a higher cost is not required. The algorithm is named because two implementations that each choose their own cannot verify each other. A verifier written later cannot recompute a chain whose algorithm no one recorded. Canonical serialization is named for the same reason. A hash over a serialization that reorders fields verifies nothing.
provisions.example: The chain value is `SHA-256(previousHash || canonical(record))`, where `canonical` sorts object members and encodes every timestamp and number one fixed way.

provisions.heading: Commit a Success Record with Its Business Change
provisions.evidence: Does every succeeded record commit inside its business transaction? Check the success write path.
provisions.statement: An audit record with a `succeeded` outcome MUST commit in the same database transaction as the change it describes.
provisions.rationale: One transaction makes the action and its evidence inseparable: the change commits with its record or neither commits. Separate writes admit both an unrecorded action and a record of a rolled-back action. Either one leaves the trail disagreeing with the data it describes.

provisions.heading: Correct Mistakes with a New Record
provisions.evidence: Is every correction a new record that points at the earlier one? Check the correction records.
provisions.statement: A correction to the trail MUST be a new record that references the earlier one.
provisions.rationale: An edited history carries no evidential value, because the reviewer cannot tell a correction from a cover-up. A new record that references the earlier one keeps both visible: the mistake and its fix. The trail then shows its own repairs instead of hiding them.

provisions.heading: Declare Audit Details on the Command Type
provisions.evidence: Does every Command carry the declaration attribute with its action, target kind, category, and reason selector, or a recorded local convention? Check the Command types.
provisions.statement: Declare the action, target kind, category, and reason selector as an attribute on the Command type, beside the use-case `audit` field.
provisions.rationale: The declaration sits with the code it describes, so a review reads both at once. The use-case page carries the audit position or exemption, while the attribute carries the action, target kind, and category the producer writes. The reason selector names the message field holding the reason value, so the pipeline reads the declared reason without handler help. A selection kept in a separate file drifts from the Commands it names.

provisions.heading: Declare Which Commands Are Audited
provisions.evidence: Does every command use case state its audit position or an exemption with its justification in its `audit` field? Check each use case page.
provisions.statement: Every command use case MUST declare its audit position in its `audit` field, or declare an exemption with its justification.
provisions.rationale: An audit selection that lives only in code is invisible: a reader cannot tell an unaudited command from an audited one whose call is missing. The `audit` field states a level of `required`, `optional`, or `none` with its target, or an exemption with its justification, so each omission becomes a visible statement. A level of `none` means the command is not audited. `litespec/core/use-cases#state-the-audit-position-of-every-command` states the field, and review reads the selection instead of hunting for missing calls.
provisions.example: A Claimwick command that lists public help pages declares an exemption, because reading public text is not a sensitive action.

provisions.heading: Delete Records When Their Retention Ends
provisions.evidence: Does any stored record outlive its category's declared retention? Check the stored rows against the adoption decision.
provisions.statement: An audit deployment MUST delete a record after the retention period declared for its category.
provisions.rationale: Each category declares its retention in the adoption decision, and the deployment deletes records when that period ends. Deleting on schedule keeps retention defensible: everything kept has a declared reason, and nothing kept lacks one. An indefinite period is the hardest retention to defend, and the easiest to fix while the design is still open.

provisions.heading: Enforce Append-Only Through Storage Privilege
provisions.evidence: Does any writing account hold update or delete on the audit store? Check the granted store privileges.
provisions.statement: An audit store MUST refuse update and delete through the privileges granted to the writing account.
provisions.rationale: An audit store that relies on absent code paths stays append-only until someone writes the missing path. Revoked privileges refuse update and delete no matter what the code tries. A reviewer verifies a privilege in the database instead of auditing every line for a write that should not exist.
provisions.example: The application account holds `INSERT` and `SELECT` on the audit table, and it holds neither `UPDATE` nor `DELETE`.

provisions.heading: Exclude Derived Audit Trails
provisions.evidence: Does any trail write derive from events, triggers, or change capture? Check the producer source.
provisions.statement: An audit trail MUST NOT be derived from domain events, database triggers, or change data capture.
provisions.rationale: Domain events, triggers, and change data capture describe committed state change. They carry no refused attempt, no use-case identity, and no request origin, which are the fields a reviewer reads. A trail derived from them answers what changed and never who attempted it.

provisions.heading: Fail the Build for Commands Without an Audit Declaration
provisions.evidence: Does any Command build or start without an audit position or exemption? Check the build or startup gate.
provisions.statement: An automated check MUST fail when a Command declares neither an audit position nor an exemption, with a composition refusal at startup satisfying this rule.
provisions.rationale: The next Command is written by someone who did not read this page. Only an automated gate catches it: the build or startup fails while the declaration is missing. A selection that depends on every author remembering is a selection with holes.

provisions.heading: Keep Audit Infrastructure in One Location
provisions.evidence: Does every audit part live in the documented location or the recorded local convention? Check under `Infrastructure/Auditing/`.
provisions.statement: Keep the audit record, its store, the producer, and the integrity job under `Infrastructure/Auditing/`.
provisions.rationale: The record, the store, the producer, and the integrity job form one evidence mechanism. One Infrastructure location keeps that mechanism reviewable as a whole instead of scattered across the codebase.

provisions.heading: Keep Secrets and Payment Data from the Trail
provisions.evidence: Does any stored record contain a secret or a payment instrument value? Check the stored audit rows.
provisions.statement: An audit record MUST NOT contain a secret, as `litespec/quality/security#keep-secrets-out-of-tracked-and-observable-data` states, or a payment instrument value.
provisions.rationale: The trail is retained, widely readable, and append-only, which is the worst combination for a secret: retention extends the exposure and append-only removes the repair. A credential or payment value written once stays readable for the whole retention period. Secrets and payment values therefore travel in the systems built to hold them, never in the trail.

provisions.heading: Keep State Copies from Audit Records
provisions.evidence: Does any stored record contain a before or after state copy? Check the stored audit rows.
provisions.statement: An audit record MUST NOT contain a copy of the state before or after the audited change.
provisions.rationale: The domain event stream already holds each change under its own retention. Copying before and after state into the trail duplicates that storage and widens every record with data the reviewer did not ask for. The trail adds the actor and the reason value, which nothing else holds, and leaves the change itself to the stream.

provisions.heading: Limit Personal Data to Actor and Target Identifiers
provisions.evidence: Does any stored record hold personal data beyond the pseudonymous actor and target identifiers? Check the stored audit rows.
provisions.statement: An audit record MUST NOT contain personal data other than the pseudonymous identifier of the actor and the target.
provisions.rationale: A record holding a name, an address, or a message body turns retention into an erasure conflict: the law asks for deletion and the trail asks for keeping. Pseudonymous identifiers keep the record meaningful while the mapping lives, and erasable once the mapping goes. The record then survives erasure instead of fighting it. A pseudonymous identifier is still personal data where the holder can reverse it, as [the EDPB states](https://edpb.europa.eu/our-work-tools/our-documents/guidelines/guidelines-012020-processing-personal-data-context-art-6-1). The identifier is therefore safe inside the tenant that owns the mapping, and it becomes a disclosure when it leaves that tenant.
provisions.example: An audit export crossing a tenant boundary replaces each identifier with one derived for that export, so the receiving party cannot join the records back to a subject.

provisions.heading: Link Each Record to Its Operation Trace
provisions.evidence: Does every stored record carry the trace identifier of its operation? Check the stored audit rows.
provisions.statement: An audit record MUST carry the trace identifier of the operation that produced it.
provisions.rationale: The audit record states what was attempted, and the diagnostic log states what the software did while attempting it. The trace identifier joins the two, so an investigation moves from evidence to detail in one step. Without it, the investigation stops at the audit record and reconstructs the rest by time.

provisions.heading: Mark Actions Taken Under a Support Grant
provisions.evidence: Does every action taken under an administrative or support grant record that the grant was used? Check those records.
provisions.statement: An action that an actor takes under an administrative or support grant MUST record that the grant was used.
provisions.rationale: Support staff act inside customer data under a grant, and without a marker their actions read exactly like customer actions. The marker makes a no-silent-access commitment demonstrable: every supplier-side action says so on its own record. A reviewer who cannot separate the two cannot verify the commitment.

provisions.heading: Name Each Action After Its Use Case
provisions.evidence: Does every action value name the use case the actor invoked? Check the action column against the use case pages.
provisions.statement: An audit `action` MUST use the identity of the use case that the actor invoked.
provisions.rationale: A reviewer who reads an action value opens the specification of that use case to learn the intended behavior. A separate action vocabulary needs a mapping to those specifications, and the mapping drifts as both sides change. Reusing the use-case identity keeps record and specification joined with no mapping to maintain.
provisions.example: `catalog.add-product` is both the use case the actor ran and the value stored in the audit `action` field.

provisions.heading: Provide a Use Case That Reads the Trail
provisions.evidence: Does the trail read carry its access grant and its declared filters? Check the trail read use case.
provisions.statement: An audited system MUST provide a trail read as a use case with its access grant, filtered by tenant, actor, action, target, and outcome.
provisions.rationale: A trail no use case reads is storage, not a control. The read path is a use case with its own access grant: the actor holds a role whose scope reaches the records, the role allows the permission, and the grant permits the read. Filters on tenant, actor, action, target, and outcome keep each reader inside the records they may see.

provisions.heading: Publish a Copy to the Security Platform
provisions.evidence: Does the local store stay authoritative, with each copy leaving through the recorded convention? Check the delivery path.
provisions.statement: Publish a copy of each record to an external security platform through the outbox, and keep the local store authoritative.
provisions.rationale: Delivery is at-least-once, while evidence needs one durable source. The local store stays authoritative for accountability and the published copy serves detection, so a lost copy never corrupts the evidence.

provisions.heading: Publish Unsuccessful Write Failures
provisions.evidence: Does the deployment publish a write failure count for the unsuccessful path? Check the published metrics.
provisions.statement: An audit deployment MUST publish the write failure count of its unsuccessful-outcome path.
provisions.rationale: The separate connection for unsuccessful records accepts a rare lost record when the process dies between the refusal and the write. Steady loss is a defect, not bad luck, and only a published count tells the two apart. The deployment publishes that count so monitoring tells rarity from breakage.

provisions.heading: Record Every Attempt Outcome
provisions.evidence: Does every record carry a `succeeded`, `denied`, or `failed` outcome? Check the outcome column.
provisions.statement: An audit record MUST carry an outcome of `succeeded`, `denied`, or `failed`.
provisions.rationale: A trail of successes is a change history, not evidence. The refused attempt carries the security signal, and the failed attempt carries the operating signal. Three outcomes keep both signals in the same trail as the successes they qualify. A validation refusal records `failed` with its refusal code; `denied` stays for a refused authorization, so recording a validation refusal as denied would accuse the actor of an access refusal they did not meet.
provisions.example: `succeeded` names a committed change, `denied` names a refused authorization, and `failed` names a permitted attempt that did not complete. In Claimwick, an expense refused for a missing receipt records `failed` with the receipt refusal code, while an approval by an actor without the permission records `denied` with the forbidden code.

provisions.heading: Record Failed Audited Attempts
provisions.evidence: Does every permitted attempt that threw produce a failed record? Check the error paths beside the trail.
provisions.statement: An audited action that the actor was permitted to take and that did not complete MUST produce an audit record.
provisions.rationale: A permitted attempt that throws is neither a success nor a refusal, and without a record it vanishes entirely. Writing it separates an operating defect from an access problem: failures cluster around broken behavior, denials cluster around missing permission. Support reads that split before opening the logs.

provisions.heading: Record Personal-Data Reads
provisions.evidence: Does every cross-boundary personal-data query produce a record? Check the query paths beside the trail.
provisions.statement: A query returning personal data across a boundary MUST produce an audit record, defining the account boundary in the adoption decision where tenancy is absent.
provisions.rationale: A read changes no state and therefore leaves no other trace, so a disclosure without a record cannot be investigated. The audit record on a cross-boundary personal-data query states who read whose data and when. Where tenancy is absent, the adoption decision defines the account boundary this rule watches.

provisions.heading: Record Refused Authorization
provisions.evidence: Does every refused authorization produce a denied record? Check the refusal paths beside the trail.
provisions.statement: An authorization decision that refuses an audited action MUST produce an audit record.
provisions.rationale: Repeated refusal is the first indicator of a compromised or probing account, and no other record holds it: nothing changed, so nothing else was written. Each refusal therefore writes its own record. A trail without refusals shows an attacker who never failed.

provisions.heading: Record the Audit Adoption Decision
provisions.evidence: Does the adoption decision behind the audited Commands name its categories, threshold, access model, integrity method, and records entry? Check that decision record.
provisions.statement: An audit adoption decision MUST record its audited categories, threshold, access model, integrity method, and records entry.
provisions.rationale: Which actions to audit, how long to keep them, and how to protect them are policy choices, so the project declares them once in the adoption decision. A reviewer reads the declared policy before reading the implementation instead of reconstructing it from the code, which would give two reviewers two different policies. The records entry declares where audit records live: the store that holds them and, where tenants exist, that authentication events live in the global trail apart from tenant activity.

provisions.heading: Record the Refusal Code on an Unsuccessful Attempt
provisions.evidence: Does every denied or failed record carry its refusal code? Check the unsuccessful audit rows.
provisions.statement: An audit record with a `denied` or `failed` outcome MUST carry the refusal `code` that the attempt produced.
provisions.rationale: A refused permission and an exhausted precondition need different responses, but both look like failure without a code. The refusal `code` tells the reviewer which one the attempt produced. It also lets trend queries count one kind of refusal across the whole trail. The operation, the outcome, and the refusal code stay separate fields, so a reviewer reads a validation refusal as a failed attempt, not as a denied access.

provisions.heading: Record the Request Origin
provisions.evidence: Does every record produced from an inbound request carry origin, client, and request identifier? Check the inbound-request audit rows.
provisions.statement: An audit record produced from an inbound request MUST carry the request origin address, the client description, and the request identifier.
provisions.rationale: Two records naming one account state nothing about location. The same account acting from two countries within one minute states that the account is compromised, but only when each record carries origin, client, and request identifier. The request identifier also joins the record to its exact request in the diagnostic log.

provisions.heading: Record the Required Audit Fields
provisions.evidence: Does every stored record carry actor, action, target, outcome, business time, record time, and tenant? Check the stored audit rows.
provisions.statement: An audit record MUST contain actor, action, target, outcome, business time, record time, and tenant, fixed where the tenancy extension is absent.
provisions.rationale: Actor, action, target, outcome, the two times, and the tenant together answer who attempted what, against whose data, with what result, and when. Business time states when the action happened and record time states when the evidence was written, so a delayed write stays visible as a delay. The actor carries its kind beside its identifier, and the target carries its own identity apart from the actor, keeping who acted and what was acted on in separate fields. A record missing any of them leaves the accountability question half answered.

provisions.heading: Remove the Identity Mapping on Erasure
provisions.evidence: Does every erasure remove the actor mapping while keeping each audit record? Check the erasure handling and the retained rows.
provisions.statement: An erasure request MUST remove the mapping from actor identifier to person and retain every audit record.
provisions.rationale: Erasure asks that the person stop being identifiable, while accountability asks that the record stay. Removing the mapping from identifier to person satisfies both: the record keeps its evidential value and no longer points at anyone. This works only because the record carries no other personal data.

provisions.heading: Restrict Handler Contribution to Determined Values
provisions.evidence: Does any handler contribution repeat the declared target, the reason value, the actor, the action code, or the timestamp? Check the handler audit calls.
provisions.statement: A handler MUST contribute only the audit values that the handler alone determines.
provisions.rationale: The declaration beside the message already fixes the audit target and the reason value the message carries, as `litespec/backend/application#declare-the-audit-target-and-reason-beside-the-message` requires, so the pipeline records both on every outcome, including a denial. Only the handler knows the values it learns while running, such as a generated target identity or a reason value composed from loaded state. Letting the handler write the rest invites a second copy of each field that drifts from the first.
provisions.example: A Claimwick handler that creates an expense contributes the expense identity it generated, and nothing else: no actor, action code, timestamp, or value the message already carries.

provisions.heading: Scope Every Record to Its Tenant
provisions.evidence: Is every record scoped to the right trail, with tenant data carrying its tenant identity and authentication events in the global trail? Check the tenant column and the global trail.
provisions.statement: Every audit record MUST carry the scope it belongs to: an action inside tenant-owned data carries the identity of that tenant, and an authentication event that belongs to no tenant lives in the global trail apart from tenant activity.
provisions.rationale: The tenant is the filter for every read of the trail: each customer reads its own records and no one else's. A record without a tenant identity serves an internal reviewer and no customer. Scoping every record at write time keeps that filter exact. Authentication events belong to no tenant: a sign-in attempt names an account, not a tenant, so those events live in the global trail apart from tenant activity, where a reviewer reads sign-in evidence without opening any tenant's data.

provisions.heading: Stage the Audit Write Before the Business Commit
provisions.evidence: Does any audit stage run after the business commit stage? Check the pipeline stage order.
provisions.statement: An audit producer that stages a success record MUST run before the pipeline stage that commits the business transaction.
provisions.rationale: A success record staged after the commit reaches a transaction that is already closed, so the write has nowhere to land. The producer therefore runs before the pipeline stage that commits. Pipeline priority states that order outright instead of leaving it to registration order.

provisions.heading: Store the Trail Beside the Business Data
provisions.evidence: Does the trail live in the business database or the recorded local convention? Check the audit store and its privileges.
provisions.statement: Store audit records in the business database, under a separate account holding `INSERT` and `SELECT` privileges.
provisions.rationale: One database provides the atomic success write the transaction rules depend on. A separate account holding only `INSERT` and `SELECT` provides the append-only guarantee.

provisions.heading: Use a Closed Actor Set
provisions.evidence: Does every actor value use one of the five kinds, with devices and processes mapped? Check the actor column.
provisions.statement: An audit actor MUST be one of `person`, `company`, `provider`, `system`, or `guest`.
provisions.rationale: An absent actor collapses three answers into one: a scheduled process acted, a device acted, or no one recorded the actor, and only the third is a defect. The five kinds separate them: a device maps to the person whose account authorized it, with the device as the client description, and a named process maps to `system`. A free-text actor would let each writer spell the same actor differently and break every actor filter.
provisions.example: A library self-checkout records the person actor whose account authorized it, while the origin record names the kiosk.

provisions.heading: Use a Fixed Category Vocabulary
provisions.evidence: Does every category value use the eight-value vocabulary or the recorded local convention? Check the declared selection.
provisions.statement: Classify each audited action as `authentication`, `authorization-denial`, `grant-change`, `monetary-action`, `tenant-configuration`, `personal-data-read`, `bulk-export`, or `background-process-change`.
provisions.rationale: The category drives retention and the review query. A free-text value defeats both, because each writer spells the same category differently.

provisions.heading: Verify the Integrity Chain on a Schedule
provisions.evidence: Does the deployment verify its chain on a schedule and alert on a break? Check the integrity job and its alerts.
provisions.statement: An audit deployment MUST verify its integrity chain on a recurring schedule and raise an alert on a break.
provisions.rationale: Tamper evidence that no one checks proves nothing: a break sits in the store until someone looks. Scheduled verification turns the chain into a standing claim the deployment re-proves on each run. Verification recomputes the chain and checks its head against the external checkpoint, so it detects a changed or truncated tail since the last checkpoint. The alert carries the break to an operator instead of waiting for the next review.

provisions.heading: Version the Audit Record Shape
provisions.evidence: Does every stored record carry an explicit schema version? Check the stored audit rows.
provisions.statement: An audit record MUST carry an explicit schema version.
provisions.rationale: A retained record outlives several shapes of the application that wrote it. An explicit version lets a later reader parse each record in the shape it was written in. Without it, every shape change forces a rewrite of retained evidence.

provisions.heading: Write an Unsuccessful Record Outside the Failed Transaction
provisions.evidence: Does any denied or failed record roll back with its transaction? Check the unsuccessful write path.
provisions.statement: An audit record with a `denied` or `failed` outcome MUST be written on a connection that the failing transaction does not roll back.
provisions.rationale: A denied or failed attempt ends with its transaction rolling back. A record written inside that transaction would roll back with it and vanish. The record therefore travels on a connection the rollback does not touch, so the evidence of a refusal outlives the refusal itself.

provisions.heading: Write Audit Records in the Mediation Pipeline
provisions.evidence: Does every audit write run in the mediation pipeline rather than inside a handler? Check the producer stages and the handler code.
provisions.statement: An audit producer MUST run in the mediation pipeline stages that dispatch the Command.
provisions.rationale: Only the pipeline stages that dispatch the Command observe the whole attempt, including attempts the handler never reaches. An audit call inside the handler misses every attempt that throws before it and every refusal the pipeline makes. The pipeline is therefore the one place that records all three outcomes.
provisions.example: A pre-handler opens the audit scope, a post-handler closes it as `succeeded`, and an error handler closes it as `denied` or `failed`.

provisions.heading: Avoid Unbounded Key Locks
provisions.evidence: Does any lock scheme grow one entry per key without bound? Read the lock state under high-cardinality keys.
provisions.statement: A cache implementation MUST NOT create an unbounded per-key lock inventory.
provisions.rationale: Per-key locks trade duplicate refreshes for memory, and that trade needs a ceiling. Untrusted or high-cardinality keys create one lock entry each, which exhausts memory under attacker-chosen or runaway keys. A bounded lock scheme sheds that state instead of growing it.

provisions.heading: Bound Cache Refresh Work
provisions.evidence: Does any cache refresh without bound on concurrent misses? Read the refresh path under concurrent load.
provisions.statement: A cache implementation MUST bound simultaneous refresh work when concurrent misses could overload its source.
provisions.rationale: When a popular entry expires, every concurrent miss can trigger its own refresh and flood the source the cache was protecting. Bounding simultaneous refresh work holds that flood to what the source tolerates. Request coalescing and jittered expiry are two ways to meet the bound.
provisions.example: One request refreshes a key while concurrent callers await the same bounded work.

provisions.heading: Compose Cache Keys from Result Inputs
provisions.evidence: Does every key carry the data-shape version, each result-affecting input, and the tenant or actor partition? Read the key construction.
provisions.statement: A cache key MUST include its data-shape version, every result-affecting input, and applicable tenant or actor partition.
provisions.rationale: A key without the data-shape version serves old shapes to new callers after a deploy. A key without a result-affecting input serves one caller's answer to a different request. Tenant or actor partition keeps one party's results away from another's.
provisions.example: The key `post-summary:v2:tenant-42:post-17` names the data-shape version, the tenant, and the post, so a new shape, another tenant, or another post reads a different entry.

provisions.heading: Define Cache Invalidation
provisions.evidence: Does every cached value define expiry, invalidating events, an owner, and failure behavior? Read the invalidation contract of each cache.
provisions.statement: A cached value MUST define expiry as a setting record, invalidating write events, an invalidation owner, and behavior after invalidation failure.
provisions.rationale: Every cached value goes stale, and the only choice is whether the project decides the behavior up front or discovers it during an incident. Expiry, invalidating write events, an owner, and failure behavior state how long staleness lasts and who fixes it when invalidation fails. A cache without that contract serves stale data on a schedule nobody chose.

provisions.heading: Define Cache Outage Behavior
provisions.evidence: Does every cache document a source fallback or a degraded response? Read the outage behavior of each cache.
provisions.statement: A cache outage MUST use the source when capacity permits or return a documented degraded response.
provisions.rationale: Cache infrastructure fails like any other dependency. The outage behavior states whether callers fall back to the source or receive a documented degraded response, so an outage degrades the product on purpose instead of by accident.

provisions.heading: Distinguish Cache Misses, Errors, and Degraded Responses
provisions.evidence: Does any cache path share one counter across misses, errors, and degraded responses? Read the emitted metrics.
provisions.statement: A cache path MUST emit a metric distinguishing a cache miss, a cache error, and a degraded response.
provisions.rationale: A fallback that works is invisible. An outage runs until someone notices the source load instead. The three cases need different responses: a miss is normal, an error is an infrastructure fault, and a degraded response is a product behavior change. One counter for all three answers none of them.
provisions.example: The metric carries the cache name and the outcome, following [the OpenTelemetry semantic conventions](https://opentelemetry.io/docs/specs/semconv/) for the client it wraps.

provisions.heading: Exclude Unsafe Cache Key Material
provisions.evidence: Does any key carry a secret, unbounded input, or unhashed personal data? Read the key construction.
provisions.statement: A cache key MUST NOT contain a secret, unbounded raw input, or personal data that is not already a hash.
provisions.rationale: Keys appear in diagnostics, metrics, and provider administration tools. That copies the value into a store no one classified. An email address in a key is a personal-data record in the cache provider's key space. It sits outside every retention and erasure path the project defined. [Data minimization](https://gdpr-info.eu/art-5-gdpr/) applies to an identifier as much as to a field.
provisions.example: A per-account cache key carries the account's opaque identifier. Where a key would carry the address, it carries a hash of it instead, and the entry stays bound to the account that owns it.

provisions.heading: Keep Source Data Authoritative
provisions.evidence: Does any required business data live authoritatively in the cache instead of its source of record? Compare the source of record with the cached copy.
provisions.statement: A cache implementation MUST keep required business data authoritative in its source of record.
provisions.rationale: The cache holds a derived copy that the system can drop at any time. Required business data stays authoritative in its source of record, so losing the cache loses speed and nothing else. A cache that owns the only copy turns every cache outage into data loss.

provisions.heading: Place Cache Access at an Outer Boundary
provisions.evidence: Does any cache access live inside Domain, or outside the recorded local convention? Read the cache call sites.
provisions.statement: Place cache access in Infrastructure or a frontend data boundary.
provisions.rationale: Cache access lives in Infrastructure or a frontend data boundary, behind a port the use case owns when Application needs one. Domain code takes no cache dependency, so business rules read the same with or without a cache. A cache concern inside Domain would couple every rule to the cache's presence.

provisions.heading: Prefer Bounded Staleness
provisions.evidence: Does every long expiry rest on a measured staleness and operating-cost decision? Compare the expiry with the invalidation cost.
provisions.statement: A cache owner SHOULD use a short expiry when precise invalidation costs more than recomputation.
provisions.rationale: Precise invalidation costs design and code, while a short expiry costs one recomputation per window. When recomputation is cheaper, a short expiry bounds staleness without the machinery. A longer expiry then needs a measured decision showing the extra staleness is worth what it saves.

provisions.heading: Record Each Manual Cache Invalidation
provisions.evidence: Does every manual clear leave a record naming actor, scope, and reason? Read the invalidation runs.
provisions.statement: A manual invalidation MUST produce a record naming actor, invalidation scope, and reason, as an audit record in its category when the audit extension is selected.
provisions.rationale: A manual clear changes what every later caller sees, and the data itself shows no trace of it. When a stale-read report arrives later, the investigation has to know whether someone already cleared the entry. [Article 30 of the GDPR](https://gdpr-info.eu/art-30-gdpr/) treats an administrative action over personal data as processing that has a record.
provisions.example: An operator clearing one tenant's cached price list during an incident leaves a record naming the tenant, the operator, and the incident.

provisions.heading: Record Measured Cache Need
provisions.evidence: Does every cache proposal record its observed query, load, latency, cost, and target? Read the proposal behind each cache.
provisions.statement: A cache proposal MUST record its observed query, representative load, latency, source cost, and target.
provisions.rationale: A cache costs invalidation, capacity, and recovery work for as long as it lives. The proposal records the observed query, representative load, latency, source cost, and target so a reviewer weighs that cost against measured gain. A cache added without measurements stays until someone pays to remove it.

provisions.heading: Remove Unjustified Caches
provisions.evidence: Has any cache outlived the measurements that justified its operating cost? Read the owner reviews beside the operating cost.
provisions.statement: A cache owner MUST remove a cache when measurements do not justify its operating cost.
provisions.rationale: A cache earns its place only while the measurements justify its operating cost. Traffic shifts, sources get faster, and a cache that paid for itself last year can cost more than it saves today. The owner rechecks the measurements and removes the cache when they do not justify its operating cost. A cache nobody owns stays forever, and its invalidation bugs stay with it.

provisions.heading: State the Staleness Each Cached Query Accepts
provisions.evidence: Does every cached query carry an eventual freshness object with its duration on its output? Check the served query beside each cache.
provisions.statement: A cached query MUST state its accepted staleness as a `freshness` object with `mode` of `eventual` and its duration in `within`.
provisions.rationale: Accepted staleness is the contract each caller relies on: it states how stale a read may be before it counts as a defect. The served query states it on its output as an eventual freshness object such as `{"mode": "eventual", "within": "PT5M"}`, so the cache and the query share one bound that is reviewed with the use case.

provisions.heading: Add Error Outcomes Only When Old Clients Cope
provisions.evidence: Does every added error outcome leave existing consumers safe on unknown codes? Check the consumer error handling.
provisions.statement: An API owner MUST add an error outcome only when existing consumers safely handle an unknown code.
provisions.rationale: A new error outcome reaches consumers written before it existed. Adding it only when existing consumers handle an unknown code safely keeps old clients working against the new contract. An outcome old clients cannot parse turns their error path into a crash.

provisions.heading: Announce Planned Removals in the Changelog
provisions.evidence: Does every operation scheduled for removal appear in the consumer changelog? Check the consumer `CHANGELOG.md`.
provisions.statement: A public operation scheduled for removal MUST appear in the consumer `CHANGELOG.md`.
provisions.rationale: Headers reach callers at the operation, but teams plan from release notes. Naming each operation scheduled for removal in the consumer `CHANGELOG.md` puts it where consumers already look when they plan. A deprecation missing there reaches only the callers that inspect headers.

provisions.heading: Assign Operation IDs
provisions.evidence: Does every operation exposed to an independent consumer carry a deliberate `operationId`, unless an outside specification fixes its shape? Check the OpenAPI document.
provisions.statement: Every operation exposed to an independent consumer MUST have a deliberate `operationId`, except an endpoint whose shape a specification outside the project fixes.
provisions.rationale: Generated clients turn each `operationId` into a method name, and tools use it to reference the operation. A deliberate identifier keeps those names stable and meaningful. An endpoint whose shape an outside specification fixes is exempt, because the project does not own that contract.
provisions.example: An OAuth redirect endpoint, an OIDC discovery document, a provider webhook receiver, and a well-known resource each follow a shape the other party defines.

provisions.heading: Assign Versioned Operation IDs
provisions.evidence: Does every changed operation in a new version carry a new operation ID? Check the versioned OpenAPI documents.
provisions.statement: A new API version MUST assign a new operation ID when its operation contract changes.
provisions.rationale: The new version needs its own contract names so the retained version keeps its own. A new `operationId` for each changed operation separates the two. Sharing one identifier across versions would let the new contract rename the old one.

provisions.heading: Block Breaking Changes Without Authorization
provisions.evidence: Did every breaking diff fail unless a new version or a recorded decision authorized it? Check the CI runs.
provisions.statement: Continuous integration MUST fail a breaking diff unless a new API version or a recorded consumer decision authorizes it.
provisions.rationale: A breaking change needs a compatibility decision while versioning is still possible: a new API version, or a recorded consumer decision that accepts it. Failing the build forces that decision before release. A warning nobody has to answer authorizes nothing.

provisions.heading: Classify Breaking Contract Changes
provisions.evidence: Does every removal, rename, narrowed value, retyped value, or authentication change carry a breaking verdict? Check the change reviews.
provisions.statement: An API change reviewer MUST classify removal, rename, required input, narrowed value, response, status, or authentication changes as breaking.
provisions.rationale: A consumer can depend on any element of the contract: a field it reads, a status it branches on, or an authentication scheme it implements. Removing, renaming, narrowing, or retyping any of them breaks the consumer that depended on it. Calling each such change breaking routes it to versioning instead of silent release.

provisions.heading: Classify Changes That Reach Independent Consumers
provisions.evidence: Does every contract change that reaches an independently deployed consumer carry a classification? Check the change reviews.
provisions.statement: An API change reviewer MUST classify each contract change that affects an independently deployed consumer.
provisions.rationale: A consumer the project does not deploy still receives every change it ships. Classifying each change decides whether consumers need a new version, a review, or nothing at all. Without a verdict, that decision reaches consumers as a surprise.

provisions.heading: Classify Compatible Additions
provisions.evidence: Does every optional addition record why existing behavior stays unchanged? Check the change reviews.
provisions.statement: An API change reviewer MUST classify an optional field, endpoint, or query parameter as compatible when existing clients retain behavior.
provisions.rationale: An optional field, endpoint, or query parameter asks nothing of existing callers: they send and interpret the same values as before. Classifying these as compatible keeps routine growth cheap. Treating them as breaking would version the API for changes nobody has to adopt.

provisions.heading: Classify Integration Event Changes
provisions.evidence: Does every integration-event change carry a breaking, compatible, or needs-review verdict? Check the event reviews.
provisions.statement: An API change reviewer MUST classify each integration-event change as breaking, compatible, or needing consumer review under `litespec/ext/compat#classify-breaking-contract-changes`, `litespec/ext/compat#classify-compatible-additions`, and `litespec/ext/compat#review-new-enum-values-and-subtypes-with-consumers`.
provisions.rationale: Consumers you do not deploy read integration events as contracts, just as they read HTTP responses. They need the same three verdicts: breaking, compatible, or needs review. Using one shared classification keeps those words meaning the same thing on both surfaces. A separate event verdict would let one change read as compatible for events and breaking for HTTP.

provisions.heading: Classify Unclear Changes as Breaking
provisions.evidence: Does every unclear change carry a breaking verdict with consumer review? Check the change reviews.
provisions.statement: An API change reviewer MUST classify an unclear contract change as breaking and require consumer review.
