provisions.rationale: A severity with no destination is only a label: every alert lands in the same place, and the page that should wake somebody sits beside the ticket that can wait. Routing each severity to its destination, with the response time expected of it, separates the page from the ticket, which is the separation [Prometheus alerting practice](https://prometheus.io/docs/practices/alerting/) states. The limits page declares the routing beside the generated inventory.
provisions.example: Claimwick's two-severity inventory routes `page` to the on-call destination with a stated response time, and `ticket` to the queue reviewed each working day.

provisions.heading: Run Images as Non-Root
provisions.evidence: Does every release image run its application with a non-root user? Check the Dockerfiles and image configuration.
provisions.statement: A release image MUST run its application with a non-root runtime user.
provisions.rationale: A compromised application process inherits the rights of its runtime user. A non-root user confines the attacker to what that user can touch. Root would hand over the whole container.

provisions.heading: Run the Application as PID 1
provisions.evidence: Does every container run the application as its entry process? Check the image entrypoints.
provisions.statement: A container MUST run the application as its entry process.
provisions.rationale: The platform stops a container by signaling its entry process. An application running as PID 1 receives that signal and shuts down on purpose. A wrapper that swallows the signal leaves the platform waiting until it kills the container mid-work.

provisions.heading: Run the End-to-End Suite After Traffic Shifts
provisions.evidence: Does every release run its recorded end-to-end suite after traffic shifts? Check the release evidence.
provisions.statement: A release deployment MUST run the release's recorded end-to-end suite after traffic reaches the new version.
provisions.rationale: An image that builds can still fail where it runs, because routing, configuration, and data differ from the build machine. Running the release's recorded end-to-end suite after traffic shifts tests the deployed path itself. The release record names the suite, so the same tests run every release.

provisions.heading: Separate Public Configuration from Runtime Secrets
provisions.evidence: Does every frontend build keep public configuration separate from server-only secrets? Check the frontend image build.
provisions.statement: A frontend image build MUST distinguish public build-time configuration from server-only runtime secrets.
provisions.rationale: A frontend build produces a browser bundle that anyone can download. Public build-time configuration belongs in that bundle, while server-only runtime secrets travel through mounts or runtime injection instead. The build distinguishes the two classes, so each value lands in its own delivery.

provisions.heading: State Availability Objectives as OpenSLO Files
provisions.evidence: Does every OpenSLO file pass Sloth validation with its generated alerts loaded? Check the Sloth validation output.
provisions.statement: A production release MUST state its availability and latency objectives as OpenSLO files compiled by Sloth.
provisions.rationale: OpenSLO files state objectives as code, and Sloth validates them in CI and compiles them into Prometheus recording rules and burn-rate alerts. OpenTelemetry supplies the signals the objectives read, as `litespec/quality/operations#emit-correlated-diagnostics` states. Sloth and OpenTelemetry are free and maintained under Apache-2.0. Availability stays evidenced in production only.

provisions.heading: Supply Runtime Configuration Externally
provisions.evidence: Do the connection strings, OIDC settings, exporter endpoints, and secrets all live outside the image? Check the deployment manifests.
provisions.statement: A deployment platform MUST supply connection strings, OIDC settings, exporter endpoints, and secrets outside the image.
provisions.rationale: Connection strings, OIDC settings, exporter endpoints, and secrets differ by environment. Supplying them outside the image lets one image serve every environment. Baking them in would force a rebuild and retest for each environment the image enters.

provisions.heading: Tie Alert Thresholds to Requirement Measures
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `alert-threshold-drift` (level A) for an alert rule whose own text carries none of the decimal numbers its requirement's `measure` names.
provisions.statement: An alert rule MUST state every number its requirement's `measure` names in its own expression or threshold.
provisions.rationale: The requirement's measure states the agreed target, and the alert is the one place that target is enforced at runtime. When the requirement changes, nobody re-reads the alert, so a measure that says two seconds and an alert that fires at five drift apart silently. Comparing the numbers is coarse because a measure is prose, so the check advises rather than blocks.
provisions.example: Claimwick's `requirement/approval-reminders.month-end-submission` measures "at least 99 percent within two seconds", and its alert's expression compares the 0.99 quantile against 2.

provisions.heading: Treat Check Warnings as Failures
provisions.evidence: Does any build pass with unreviewed warnings outside recorded suppressions? Check the build logs beside the warnings convention.
provisions.statement: Treat build and lint warnings as failures unless the build configuration records a narrow suppression with its reason.
provisions.rationale: Warnings nobody reviews accumulate until a real defect hides among them. Failing on warnings forces each one to be fixed, or narrowly suppressed with its reason, so a changed compiler, linter, or dependency boundary surfaces immediately.

provisions.heading: Use Stable Service Names
provisions.evidence: Do service, resource, meter, and trace-source names stay identical across environments, or does a service-naming convention name another arrangement? Check the environment configurations.
provisions.statement: Keep service, resource, meter, and trace-source names identical across environments.
provisions.rationale: Dashboards and alerts reference services by name. When a name changes with each deployment, every reference breaks, and each one must be rebuilt before the new deployment can be watched. Identical names across environments keep one dashboard and one alert set working everywhere.

provisions.heading: Verify Before Accepting Worker Output
provisions.evidence: Does every accepted output show a watched verification run? Check the verification runs the agent handing off the work reports.
provisions.statement: An agent handing off work MUST re-run the verification its brief names before accepting worker output.
provisions.rationale: The agent handing off the work owns the result. It re-runs the verification the brief named and watches it pass, because a done claim without that run is a claim, not evidence. Accepting on trust moves the worker's defect into the handing-off agent's change.

provisions.heading: Wait for Replica Readiness
provisions.evidence: Does every deployment wait for new replicas to reach readiness before shifting traffic? Check the deployment controller behavior.
provisions.statement: A deployment controller MUST start new replicas and wait for readiness before shifting traffic.
provisions.rationale: New replicas need time to load before they serve, and a replica that receives traffic mid-startup fails its first requests. The controller starts the new replicas, waits for readiness, and only then shifts traffic, so the new version proves it serves before it becomes the version.

provisions.heading: Write a Brief Before Handing Off
provisions.evidence: Does every brief state goal, context, sources, and output? Check the briefs the agent starting the handoff wrote.
provisions.statement: An agent that starts another agent MUST give it a written brief stating goal, context, sources, and output.
provisions.rationale: Two agents sharing one tree collide without a written split of work. The brief states what the worker owns and what it builds on: its goal, context, sources, and output. When workers collide, the defect lies in the brief rather than in either worker.
provisions.example:
A brief carries four sections, each answering one question for the worker.

```text
Goal: the change the worker owns.
Context: the repository facts the change builds on.
Sources: the records and pages to read first.
Output: the files to change and the report to write.
```

provisions.heading: Write Runtime Logs to Streams
provisions.evidence: Does every containerized application write logs to standard output or standard error? Check the application logging configuration.
provisions.statement: A containerized application MUST write logs to standard output or standard error.
provisions.rationale: A container filesystem vanishes with its replica, so a log file inside the container dies with the evidence it holds. Standard output and standard error hand each line to the platform's log collection, which keeps logs past the life of any one replica.

provisions.heading: Apply Forced Uploads over Newer State
provisions.evidence: Does every forced upload in the device tests overwrite newer server values and leave an overwrite record? Read the device tests for forced uploads.
provisions.statement: An offline upload with `force` MUST apply over newer server state and record the overwrite.
provisions.rationale: Sometimes the device is right and the server is stale: a supervisor corrected the count on the floor while the server held the old one. Force lets the operator say so explicitly, and the recorded overwrite keeps the decision visible instead of hiding it in a silent overwrite.
provisions.example: A corrected count uploads with `force`, overwrites the server value, and leaves an overwrite record naming the operator.

provisions.heading: Describe Device Messages as a Channel Fragment
provisions.evidence: Does every device entry point describe each operation with its payload in the channel shape? Read the protocol blocks on each device entry point.
provisions.statement: A device protocol MUST describe its messages as an AsyncAPI channel fragment with named operations and payloads.
provisions.rationale: Devices and servers evolve apart: a scanner runs last year's firmware against this week's server. A channel fragment names each direction, each message, and each payload in one shape both sides read. A mismatch then shows in the record before it shows on the loading dock.
provisions.example:
```yaml
protocol:
  channel: scanner/check-in
  publish:
    message: check-in.recorded
    payload: { code, nonce, scannedAt }
  subscribe:
    message: check-in.denied
    payload: { code, reason }
```

provisions.heading: Identify Retries with a Nonce
provisions.evidence: Does every mutating message in the protocol blocks carry a client-generated nonce scoped to the device? Read each message in the protocol blocks.
provisions.statement: Each mutating device message MUST carry a client-generated nonce as its idempotency key.
provisions.rationale: A device that loses signal mid-send retries a request the server already applied. The nonce gives the retry a stable identity scoped to the device, so the server answers the repeat from the first attempt instead of lending, paying, or shipping twice.
provisions.example: A loan scan carries `nonce: 7f3a`, and the second delivery of the same nonce returns the first attempt's result.

provisions.heading: Replay Uploads in Queue Order
provisions.evidence: Does every upload test apply offline queues in device order, or has the project named another order? Read the upload tests beside the project's documented order.
provisions.statement: The server applies an offline queue in the order the device queued it.
provisions.rationale: Queue order matches what the operator saw on the device: first scanned, first applied. Another order replays the day out of sequence and surprises everyone reading the log.

provisions.heading: Simulate Offline Uploads Before Applying
provisions.evidence: Does any simulated upload in the device tests write behind the outcome it returns? Read the device tests for simulated uploads.
provisions.statement: An offline upload with `simulate` MUST return its outcome without writing.
provisions.rationale: A device back online after a week holds uploads the world outgrew: prices changed, holds lapsed, windows closed. Simulating the queue shows what would happen before anything is written, so the operator reconciles first and applies second.
provisions.example: A scanner uploads three hundred queued scans with `simulate`, reviews the two the server would refuse, and then uploads for real.

provisions.heading: State Client Rules with Scenarios
provisions.evidence: Does every client rule in the protocol blocks carry the scenarios that prove it? Read the protocol blocks beside the scenarios.
provisions.statement: Each client rule in a device protocol MUST carry the scenarios that prove it.
provisions.rationale: Client rules run where the server cannot see them: validation a scanner applies offline, storage limits a kiosk enforces, queueing a phone does in a tunnel. A rule without scenarios leaves that behavior unproven. Scenarios pin each rule to observable device behavior the product tests against.
provisions.example: The rule `a scanner queues scans while offline` carries the scenario `a scan queued offline uploads on reconnect`.

provisions.heading: Version Protocols by Date
provisions.evidence: Does every protocol version use calendar numbering, or does the device documentation name another scheme? Read the protocol version values beside that documentation.
provisions.statement: Protocol versions use calendar numbering of the form `YYYY.N`.
provisions.rationale: A calendar number tells a support engineer how old a device is at a glance. Any scheme works as long as every device and the server share it.

provisions.heading: Version the Device Protocol
provisions.evidence: Does every protocol block state numbering, overlap, and the upgrade path? Read each protocol block.
provisions.statement: A device protocol MUST state its version rule with numbering, overlap, and the upgrade path.
provisions.rationale: Old firmware cannot be recalled from the field, so several protocol versions stay live at once. Numbering tells a device which version it speaks, overlap tells the server how long to answer old versions, and the upgrade path tells the device how to move forward. Without the three, a server upgrade bricks every device still speaking an old version.

provisions.heading: Call Only Declared Operations
provisions.evidence: Does every `calls` effect name an operation its cited external system declares? Check each effect beside its external system record.
provisions.statement: A `calls` effect MUST name an operation the cited external system declares.
provisions.rationale: The effect names the system and its operation, and the operation states the direction, timeout, retry, response, and cache, so each outside call reads as a declared edge. A call to an undeclared operation ships as an unreviewed dependency. `litespec/core/use-cases#declare-every-effect-with-one-verb-and-its-timing` states the effect verbs, and the `effect-undeclared` check reports an edge the records never declared.
provisions.example: The Claimwick payout effect cites `calls` on the payout bank `send-batch` operation with its timeout and retry count.

provisions.heading: Configure External Clients Through Validated Options
provisions.evidence: Does every external client bind its base address, credentials, timeout, and policy through validated options? Check the client registrations.
provisions.statement: An external client MUST bind its base address, credentials, timeout, and policy through validated options.
provisions.rationale: Base address, credentials, timeout, and policy decide where the client calls and how it behaves. Validated options check each value at startup. A missing or invalid value then fails fast instead of misdirecting the first live call.

provisions.heading: Cover Provider Failure Modes
provisions.evidence: Does the suite test every declared failure mode: timeout, connection failure, transient response, permanent response, malformed payload, rate limit, duplicate delivery, and unexpected response shape? Check the integration test suite.
provisions.statement: An integration test MUST cover timeout, connection failure, transient response, permanent response, malformed payload, rate limit, duplicate delivery, and unexpected response shape.
provisions.rationale: Timeout, connection failure, transient and permanent responses, malformed payloads, rate limits, duplicate delivery, and unexpected shapes each exercise a different path through retry, mapping, and idempotency. A mode without a test leaves its path unverified, so the suite covers all eight and each path proves itself. The timeout mode exercises the unknown outcome: the test shows which `onUnknown` handling the retry follows. An unexpected response shape is the mode a provider produces without failing. A well-formed response can carry a field that moved, a type that changed, or a value no one planned for. The response parses, but the behavior is still wrong, while every other listed mode reports that response as an error. A provider that versions its API changes shape on a schedule, and a pinned version still changes on the day the provider raises it.

provisions.heading: Declare Trust for Inbound Integration Events
provisions.evidence: Does every inbound integration event declare trigger-only or payload trust with its correlation? Check each inbound integration event record.
provisions.statement: An inbound integration event MUST declare `trust` as trigger-only or payload with its correlation.
provisions.rationale: An inbound fact carries one of two trusts: trigger-only wakes a read of the source, while payload is fit to act on. The `trust` declaration states which one, and the correlation states how the event matches, so no handler guesses how far to follow a stranger's fields. `litespec/core/edges#describe-every-integration-event-for-its-direction` states the record, and `litespec/core/edges#name-how-every-inbound-integration-event-arrives` states how each inbound fact arrives: the record names in `arrivesThrough` the webhook entry point the provider calls or the external system whose broker or stream the module subscribes to, and every integration event names in `through` the external system it travels through.

provisions.heading: Define Business-Action Ports
provisions.evidence: Is every Application port named for its business action, with no provider in its name or signature? Check each Application port.
provisions.statement: Application MUST own a public external-service interface named for its business action.
provisions.rationale: What the use case needs is a behavior, such as sending a payout, not a provider. Naming a public interface for that business action states the need with no provider in sight, so Application depends on the behavior while providers come and go behind it.
provisions.example: `IPayoutSender` describes the business action without exposing a payout-bank client.

provisions.heading: Group Provider Code
provisions.evidence: Does every provider's code sit under `Infrastructure/Integrations/{Provider}/`, or under another root the project documentation names? Check the Infrastructure tree.
provisions.statement: Place provider code under `Infrastructure/Integrations/{Provider}/`.
provisions.rationale: One folder per provider keeps provider code inside one Infrastructure boundary under `Infrastructure/Integrations/{Provider}/`. A reader finds everything about a provider in one place.

provisions.heading: Isolate Provider Implementations
provisions.evidence: Does any Application layer code reference a provider SDK or transport type? Check the Application layer folders.
provisions.statement: Infrastructure MUST own provider clients, SDKs, authentication, and transport models.
provisions.rationale: Provider clients, SDKs, authentication, and transport models name provider things in provider terms, so they live in Infrastructure, outside the Application business boundary. A provider SDK upgrade then touches Infrastructure instead of the use case.
provisions.example: `IPayoutProviderClient` is provider infrastructure rather than an Application port.

provisions.heading: Keep Ports Near Use Cases
provisions.evidence: Does every business-action port sit with its Application use cases, or in the shared port folder the project keeps? Check the Application folders.
provisions.statement: Keep business-action ports with their Application use cases.
provisions.rationale: A business-action port exists because its use case needs that behavior. Keeping the port with its Application use cases states the need next to the needer, while a ports folder far from the use cases hides which behavior each port serves.

provisions.heading: Keep Provider Components Together
provisions.evidence: Does every provider folder hold its options, client, models, mappings, and registration, or follow another grouping the project documentation names? Check each provider folder.
provisions.statement: Keep one options class, client, transport models, mappings, and registration module in each provider folder.
provisions.rationale: When the provider changes, its options, client, transport models, mappings, and registration module change together. Keeping them in the provider folder keeps each change in one place, while a registration module stored elsewhere is the file every provider change forgets.

provisions.heading: Keep Provider Internals from API Responses
provisions.evidence: Does any API response expose provider bodies, credentials, headers, exception types, or internal account identifiers? Check the API responses.
provisions.statement: An API MUST NOT expose provider bodies, credentials, headers, exception types, or internal account identifiers.
provisions.rationale: Secrets, implementation details, and sometimes another account's data travel in provider bodies, headers, exception types, and account identifiers. An API that returns them leaks all three to its callers. The mapped project-owned outcome carries the meaning without the internals.

provisions.heading: Process Duplicate Messages Safely
provisions.evidence: Does every inbound provider handler leave exactly one accepted effect for a duplicate event? Check the duplicate-delivery paths.
provisions.statement: An inbound provider handler MUST store or process duplicate events idempotently.
provisions.rationale: After a timeout or an acknowledgement failure, the provider repeats delivery and the same event arrives twice. Idempotent storage or processing leaves one accepted effect. A handler without that protection pays, ships, or notifies twice.

provisions.heading: Protect Non-Idempotent Calls
provisions.evidence: Does every retried non-idempotent provider call rest on provider idempotency and documented replay behavior? Check the retry paths.
provisions.statement: An external client MUST NOT retry a non-idempotent provider call without provider idempotency and documented replay behavior.
provisions.rationale: Retrying a payout, a shipment, or any irreversible provider call can perform it twice. The retry is safe only with provider idempotency behind it and documented replay behavior stating what a repeat does. Without both, the project trades one failed call for two completed effects.

provisions.heading: Record Each Provider as an External System
provisions.evidence: Does every provider have an external system page in the Behavior external systems naming its operations and erasure? Check the external system pages.
provisions.statement: An integration MUST record its provider as an external system naming its operations and erasure.
provisions.rationale: The external-system record draws the boundary around the dependency. Its summary names the party behind the provider, `litespec/core/edges#describe-every-external-system-operation` names every operation the product may call, and `litespec/core/access#declare-erasure-for-every-external-system` names how personal data leaves it. A provider with no record gains new messages and fallbacks without review.

provisions.heading: Reject Formula-Leading Import Values
provisions.evidence: Does every CSV or spreadsheet import reject or neutralize each formula-leading value? Check the import boundaries.
provisions.statement: A CSV or spreadsheet import MUST reject or neutralize a value that begins with a formula-leading character.
provisions.rationale: The formula-leading characters are the equals sign, the plus sign, the minus sign, the at sign, the tab, and the carriage return. Escaping on export protects the user of that export, but not the reader of the next one: a different report can re-export an unchanged imported value without escaping it. [CSV injection](https://owasp.org/www-community/attacks/CSV_Injection) travels through the store, so the boundary that admits the value is where it stops.
provisions.example: An import that rejects the value reports the row and the field. An import that neutralizes it records what it changed. A silently altered value is a data defect nobody can trace.

provisions.heading: Reject Per-Request HTTP Clients
provisions.evidence: Does any HTTP integration construct a new HTTP client per request? Check the HTTP call sites.
provisions.statement: An HTTP integration MUST NOT construct a new HTTP client for each request.
provisions.rationale: Each per-request client skips the central handler configuration and opens sockets the process never reuses. Under load, those exhausted sockets fail calls the provider would have served. Managed clients reuse what per-request construction throws away.

provisions.heading: Retry Transient Failures with Bounded Attempts
provisions.evidence: Which external clients retry without a cap on attempts or without jitter? Check each client's retry policy.
provisions.statement: An external client MUST retry transient failures with bounded attempts and jitter.
provisions.rationale: A provider outage tempts every caller to retry at once, and the synchronized wave hits the provider the moment it recovers. Bounded attempts cap that load, and jitter spreads it over time. An unbounded retry turns each caller into a second outage.

provisions.heading: Run Provider Calls from Event Handlers or Jobs
provisions.evidence: Does every provider call run from an event handler or a job, or carry a waiver naming its compensation? Check the provider call sites beside the waiver records.
provisions.statement: A provider call SHOULD run from an event handler or a job, never from a command handler.
provisions.rationale: A command handler changes its aggregate and nothing else, and each consequence runs after the commit, as `litespec/backend/application#call-external-systems-through-their-ports` requires. An event handler or a job calls the provider after the outbox delivers the fact, with one delivery per handler under `litespec/ext/outbox#give-each-handler-its-own-delivery`. A provider failure then retries without rolling back the accepted change. When the command needs the provider result before it can answer, it records the intent first and an event handler calls the provider.
provisions.example: The Claimwick reimburse-expense command records a pending payout on the expense, and the event handler for the recorded fact calls the payout provider through the business-action port.

provisions.heading: Simulate Integration Boundaries
provisions.evidence: Does every integration test run against WireMock.Net or a protocol-specific local endpoint instead of a live provider? Check the integration test suite.
provisions.statement: An integration test MUST use WireMock.Net or a protocol-specific local endpoint.
provisions.rationale: A live provider account makes tests slow, flaky, and expensive, and some failure modes never occur on demand. WireMock.Net or a protocol-specific local endpoint simulates the network contract under test control, so the suite covers provider behavior without calling the provider.

provisions.heading: Translate Provider Failure Outcomes
provisions.evidence: Does every provider error map to a rejected, accepted, or unknown outcome with a project-owned result and stable diagnostics, and does every unknown case name its `onUnknown` handling? Check the integration failure mappings.
provisions.statement: An integration MUST map each provider error to a rejected, accepted, or unknown outcome with its project-owned result and stable diagnostics, and name the handling of the unknown case in `onUnknown`.
provisions.rationale: Each provider reports failure in its own codes and shapes. Mapping them to project-owned results with stable diagnostics keeps the project failure contract steady while providers change theirs. A rejected outcome names the provider refusal, an accepted outcome names what the provider took, and an unknown outcome names a call whose effect stayed uncertain, such as a timeout. The unknown case names its handling in `onUnknown`: `dedupe-key` reuses the provider deduplication key on retry, `reconcile` settles the effect out of band, and `retry-safe` repeats a call the receiver tolerates twice. The stable codes live in the project error catalog, and `litespec/backend/api#return-stable-problem-details` returns a code from that catalog. An integration that invents one code per provider creates one code space per provider, and a client that branches on failure then learns every code space. The provider error taxonomy feeds the mapping; it is not the mapping's output.
provisions.example: A rejected Claimwick payout file and an unsettled batch both map to the project `payout-refused` code, while the provider's own code travels in diagnostics. A payout call that times out maps to unknown with `onUnknown: dedupe-key`, so the retry reuses the provider key instead of paying twice.

provisions.heading: Use Managed HTTP Clients
provisions.evidence: Does every HTTP integration use `HttpClientFactory` and applicable service discovery? Check the HTTP registrations.
provisions.statement: An HTTP integration MUST use `HttpClientFactory` and applicable service discovery.
provisions.rationale: `HttpClientFactory` centralizes handler lifetime in one place, and service discovery resolves provider addresses in one place. Together they keep HTTP construction out of the use case, where a hand-built client in each call site would scatter both concerns.

provisions.heading: Verify Inbound Provider Messages
provisions.evidence: Does every webhook inbound handler run the checks its arrival requires, and does every subscription inbound handler verify event identity, schema, size, and replay protection? Check the inbound handlers.
provisions.statement: An inbound provider handler MUST verify signature, timestamp tolerance, replay protection, content type, size, schema, and event identity before processing on a webhook arrival, and event identity, schema, size, and replay protection on a subscribed broker or stream arrival.
provisions.rationale: An inbound message arrives from the network, where anyone can send bytes. Signature, timestamp tolerance, replay protection, content type, size, schema, and event identity each guard a different part of that trust boundary, and skipping any one leaves its attack open. A subscribed broker or stream arrival authenticates at the subscription, so each message carries no per-message signature, and the handler verifies event identity, schema, size, and replay protection on each message. Order matters on a webhook arrival: verify the signature first, over the raw body, before parsing the body or running any other check. An unauthenticated caller can reach a parser that runs first. A deserialized body is not the bytes the signature covered.
provisions.example: A failed signature returns `401` with no body. A message that names the failed check tells an unauthenticated caller how to pass it.

provisions.heading: Allow Completion Only with a Current Fencing Value
provisions.evidence: Does any completion write succeed on a stale fencing value? Check the store write path and its fencing tests.
provisions.statement: A Worker MUST mark completion only while its fencing value remains current.
provisions.rationale: A stale fencing value means another replica owns the occurrence now. Completing past that point would write one replica's result over another's ownership. The Worker marks completion only while its value stays current.

provisions.heading: Apply Item-Read Authorization
provisions.evidence: Does every report or export carry an authorization test for the item-read rules? Check the authorization tests.
provisions.statement: A report or export MUST enforce actor, role, ownership, tenant, and sensitive-field rules that apply to item reads.
provisions.rationale: A report that reads ten thousand rows at once crosses the same actor, role, ownership, tenant, and sensitive-field boundaries as ten thousand single reads. Enforcing the item-read rules on the bulk path stops the report from exposing rows its user may not open one by one.

provisions.heading: Audit Export Reads
provisions.evidence: Does every export query state its `audit` reason and target? Check the export query beside the report.
provisions.statement: An export query MUST state its `audit` reason and target.
provisions.rationale: An export file concentrates sensitive rows into one downloadable object. The use case states why the bulk read is audited and where the audit lands. Without the stated audit, the concentrated read leaves no trace a reviewer can follow.

provisions.heading: Audit Manual Replay
provisions.evidence: Does every manual replay add an audited attempt under the same occurrence identity? Check the replay command and the audit rows.
provisions.statement: A manual replay MUST create a new attempt for the same occurrence identity: an audit record when audit is selected, a standalone record otherwise.
provisions.rationale: A manual replay creates a new attempt under the same occurrence identity: an audit record where audit is selected, a standalone record otherwise. The replay keeps the original scheduled instant and its history. A replay recorded as a new occurrence would rewrite when the work was due.

provisions.heading: Avoid Speculative Reporting Systems
provisions.evidence: Does every reporting system trace to an accepted current query or export? Check the reporting code and the use case pages.
provisions.statement: A project MUST NOT create reporting infrastructure for possible future analytics.
provisions.rationale: A reporting system built for analytics the product might never need charges its full operating cost from day one while serving no accepted query. Each report or export earns its infrastructure with a current cost boundary, not a guess about future analysis.

provisions.heading: Confirm Bulk Money Actions Out of Band
provisions.evidence: Does every bulk money command ask for the out-of-band code before moving money? Check the command handlers.
provisions.statement: A bulk money command MUST require its `confirmBy` code from outside the session.
provisions.rationale: A preview confirms the set, but the session itself can be hijacked, shared, or left open. An out-of-band code arrives on a channel the session doesn't control, so the confirmation proves the person, not just the browser.
provisions.example: Claimwick's bulk release asks for the six-digit code sent to the finance phone before moving any money.

provisions.heading: Declare Export Paging
provisions.evidence: Does every export query state `paging` with `mode` of `pages` or `none` with its reason? Check the export query beside the report.
provisions.statement: An export query MUST state `paging` with `mode` of `pages` or `none` with its reason.
provisions.rationale: An export reads many rows at once, so it states how the read is bounded. `{"mode": "pages", ...}` bounds each run, and `{"mode": "none", "reason": "..."}` states why the export reads all rows at once. Without the declaration, a bounded export looks the same to a reviewer as one that grows with the table.

provisions.heading: Define Export Encoding and Columns
provisions.evidence: Does every export format state a character encoding and stable columns in its format record? Check each format record.
provisions.statement: An export format MUST use explicit character encoding and a stable column contract.
provisions.rationale: An export without a stated encoding arrives garbled on the first machine that guesses differently. Columns that shift per release break every parser built on them. Explicit encoding with a stable column contract lets consumers parse the file without guessing either.

provisions.heading: Define Report Limits
provisions.evidence: Does every report bound hold a setting record beside the report? Check each report's setting records.
provisions.statement: A report specification MUST state each bound as a setting record: maximum date range, rows, execution time, concurrent jobs, output size, and storage lifetime.
provisions.rationale: Each report cost dimension needs its own cap: date range, rows, execution time, concurrent jobs, output size, and storage lifetime. Setting records hold all six, so a runaway report hits a documented bound instead of an exhausted database, a full disk, or a surprise invoice.

provisions.heading: Derive Stable Occurrence Identity
provisions.evidence: Does every occurrence identity in the store carry the schedule ID and the scheduled instant? Check the occurrence identity column.
provisions.statement: A scheduled-job store MUST derive each occurrence identity from its schedule ID and scheduled instant.
provisions.rationale: Schedule ID plus scheduled instant gives each planned time one stable identity across retries and replicas. Retries of one occurrence then share their idempotency scope, and two replicas recognize the same occurrence.

provisions.heading: Dispatch Jobs Through Application Commands or Ports
provisions.evidence: Does every job handler call only an Application Command or a declared Application port? Check the handler calls.
provisions.statement: A scheduled job MUST dispatch an Application Command or a declared Application port.
provisions.rationale: The job record names the use case it runs, and the use case boundary lives in Application. Each job therefore dispatches an Application Command or a declared Application port. The schedule stays a trigger while the behavior stays owned.

provisions.heading: Escape Formula-Leading Export Values
provisions.evidence: Does every exported value starting with a formula character go out escaped, outside the formula fields the team fills on purpose? Check the CSV and spreadsheet writers.
provisions.statement: A CSV or spreadsheet export MUST escape formula-leading values unless the team intentionally fills a field with a formula.
provisions.rationale: A value starting with `=`, `+`, `-`, or `@` becomes a live formula when the export opens in a spreadsheet. It runs in the opener's application, with the opener's data. Escaping those values keeps data as data, except in a field the team intentionally fills with a formula.

provisions.heading: Exclude Machine-Local Time
provisions.evidence: Is every production job source free of machine-local clock reads? Check the job sources for local time calls.
provisions.statement: Scheduled-job production code MUST NOT depend on machine-local time.
provisions.rationale: Machine-local time follows each host's configuration, so production code that reads it schedules differently on a developer machine, in staging, and in production. Schedules read their time from the injected clock and the declared zone instead.

provisions.heading: Generate Monotonic Fencing Values
provisions.evidence: Does every fencing value in the store rise per occurrence, with no stale value completing? Check the store write path and its fencing tests.
provisions.statement: A scheduled-job store MUST generate each fencing value monotonically per occurrence.
provisions.rationale: Each fencing value rises monotonically per occurrence, so a later claim always presents a higher value than an earlier one. A Worker that lost its lease presents a stale value, and `litespec/ext/jobs#allow-completion-only-with-a-current-fencing-value` refuses completion on a stale value.

provisions.heading: Keep Jobs off Direct Storage and Web Endpoints
provisions.evidence: Is every job source free of direct Marten session or DbContext mutations and WebApi endpoint calls? Check the job sources and their imports.
provisions.statement: A scheduled job MUST NOT mutate a Marten session or DbContext directly, bypass Domain behavior, or call WebApi endpoints.
provisions.rationale: A job that mutates a Marten session or DbContext directly, bypasses Domain behavior, or calls WebApi endpoints skips the command boundary. That boundary carries the authorization, transaction, and validation the job needs. Jobs enter through use case messages like every other caller.

provisions.heading: Keep Raw SQL in Infrastructure
provisions.evidence: Does all raw report SQL and connection handling sit inside Infrastructure code? Check the report query sources.
provisions.statement: Infrastructure MUST own raw reporting SQL and connection handling.
provisions.rationale: Raw SQL names tables, dialects, and connection handling that belong to one provider. Keeping it in Infrastructure lets Application and Domain state what the report means, without depending on how one database phrases it.

provisions.heading: Keep Report Definitions in Application
provisions.evidence: Does every report definition sit inside its module, when the report-definition convention names no other place? Check the report definition sources.
provisions.statement: Keep report definitions in Application under their module.
provisions.rationale: What a report means and who may run it are business choices. Keeping the definition in Application under its module puts those choices beside the module's other rules, instead of buried in query code.

provisions.heading: Keep Report Providers in Infrastructure
provisions.evidence: Does all SQL and storage code sit inside Infrastructure, when the report-provider convention names no other place? Check the report provider sources.
provisions.statement: Keep SQL, row mappings, and storage providers in Infrastructure.
provisions.rationale: SQL text, row mappings, and storage calls change per provider, while the report's meaning stays fixed. Keeping them in Infrastructure swaps the provider without touching the report's business rules.

provisions.heading: Keep Schedule Definitions Separate from Commands
provisions.evidence: Does any schedule definition sit inside Command behavior, when the project keeps them apart from it? Check the handler code and the schedule records.
provisions.statement: Keep schedule definitions separate from Command behavior.
provisions.rationale: Timing policy changes when operations needs a new rhythm; Command behavior changes when the business needs a new outcome. Keeping schedule definitions separate from Command behavior lets each change alone. A schedule buried in the handler makes every timing change a code change.

provisions.heading: Keep Worker Orchestration Separate from Report Rules
provisions.evidence: Does any Worker orchestration code sit inside report rules, when the report-orchestration convention names no other place? Check the report rule sources.
provisions.statement: Keep the scheduling, chunking, and progress tracking of a report in Worker code, apart from the rules that define the report.
provisions.rationale: Scheduling, chunking, and progress tracking run the report; they don't define it. Keeping Worker orchestration apart from the report's rules lets either change without dragging the other along.

provisions.heading: Limit Job Duration
provisions.evidence: Does every job declare a duration bound, with completions recorded inside it? Check the handler code and the occurrence store.
provisions.statement: A scheduled job MUST complete within a bounded duration.
provisions.rationale: Each job bounds its duration, so a Worker stops without stranding work it can no longer watch.

provisions.heading: Limit Job Retries with Backoff and a Poison State
provisions.evidence: Does every schedule declare bounded attempts, cancellation-aware backoff, and a poison state? Check the schedule records and the retry code.
provisions.statement: A scheduled job MUST use bounded attempts, cancellation-aware backoff, and a poison state for permanent failure.
provisions.rationale: Without the bound, one poison occurrence eats the Worker's whole capacity. Bounded attempts with cancellation-aware backoff cap what one failed occurrence consumes, and a poison state parks the permanently failing occurrence instead of retrying it forever.

provisions.heading: Observe Job Cancellation
provisions.evidence: Does every job handler wait with cancellation and end its current step when cancellation fires? Check the handler code and its cancellation tests.
provisions.statement: A scheduled job MUST observe cancellation.
provisions.rationale: Each job observes cancellation, so an occurrence ends its current step instead of running past the moment an operator asked it to stop.

provisions.heading: Order Queue Items by Score
provisions.evidence: Does every queue listing sort by a score that cites its calculation rule? Check the listing queries.
provisions.statement: A work queue MUST order its items by a score that cites a calculation rule.
provisions.rationale: A queue without an order gets cleared by habit: newest first, loudest first, easiest first. A score citing a calculation rule pins the order to declared inputs, so the riskiest or most valuable item surfaces first by rule instead of by accident.
provisions.example: Claimwick's dispute queue orders by `rule/dispute.urgency-score`, which weighs amount, age, and evidence gaps.

provisions.heading: Order Unscored Queues by Age
provisions.evidence: Does every queue without a score list oldest first, or name a fallback order in the queue documentation? Check the queue listings and the queue documentation.
provisions.statement: A queue without a score lists its oldest item first.
provisions.rationale: Age is the honest fallback: the item waiting longest goes first. Any other fallback works, when the queue states it.

provisions.heading: Parameterize Report SQL
provisions.evidence: Does every report query pass actor, tenant, filter, range, sort, and pagination values as parameters instead of SQL text? Check the query code.
provisions.statement: A reporting query MUST parameterize every actor, tenant, filter, range, sort, and pagination value.
provisions.rationale: A report feeds actor, tenant, filters, ranges, sorting, and pagination into SQL that reads across the database. Binding each of those values as a parameter keeps tenant and actor isolation intact, and closes the injection hole string concatenation opens.

provisions.heading: Persist Occurrence Recovery Points
provisions.evidence: Does every occurrence row carry a last scheduled, started, and completed time? Check the occurrence table schema.
provisions.statement: A scheduled-job store MUST persist each occurrence's last scheduled, started, and completed time.
provisions.rationale: After a restart, the Worker must tell missed work from completed work. Last scheduled, started, and completed times persist per occurrence to draw that line. Memory alone can't hold it, because the restart wipes it.

provisions.heading: Persist Occurrence State
provisions.evidence: Does every occurrence row carry a scheduled, processing, completed, or dead-letter state, with only safe execution details? Check the occurrence rows.
provisions.statement: A scheduled-job store MUST persist scheduled, processing, completed, and dead-letter state with safe execution details.
provisions.rationale: Operators and recovery code need to see where each occurrence stands. The four states persist with attempt, lease, start, completion, and safe error data: scheduled, processing, completed, and dead-letter. Without them, work in flight is indistinguishable from work not yet started.

provisions.heading: Place Handlers with Owned Behavior
provisions.evidence: Does every job handler sit in the folder of what it runs, when the project names no other job handler layout? Check the handler folders beside the project documentation.
provisions.statement: Place each job handler in the `Application/` folder of the use case it runs, or with the notification it sends or the system it calls when it runs none.
provisions.rationale: A job handler lives in the `Application/` folder of the use case its `runs` entry names, so the use case folder shows every way the use case starts. One that runs no use case lives in the module `Notifications/` folder of the notification it sends, or the `ExternalSystems/` folder of the system it calls, under `litespec/workspace/naming#place-each-trigger-with-what-it-runs`. The module owns both the business action and what its schedule means. A handlers folder far from the behavior separates each schedule from its reason.

provisions.heading: Prefer UTC Schedules
provisions.evidence: Does every schedule state UTC or a business-local time requirement with its IANA time zone? Check each schedule record.
provisions.statement: A scheduled job MUST use a UTC schedule unless its specification names a business-local time requirement and its IANA time zone.
provisions.rationale: A daylight-saving transition makes a wall clock run one hour twice and skip another. A local schedule therefore runs twice on one date each year and skips an hour on another. That behavior is correct for a job whose meaning is local, such as a nightly statement at 9 AM for a user, and a defect for every other job. Naming the time zone in the specification states the transition behavior for a later reader.

provisions.heading: Prevent Duplicate Completion
provisions.evidence: Does any lease path admit more than one completion per occurrence across overlapping replicas? Check the lease claim code and its concurrency tests.
provisions.statement: A scheduled-job lease MUST prevent two replicas from completing the same occurrence.
provisions.rationale: Overlapping replicas must not complete the same occurrence twice. The lease admits one completion per occurrence. Two completions would bill, notify, or reconcile the same planned work twice.

provisions.heading: Protect Export Output
provisions.evidence: Does every export output sit in approved object storage with a named contact, an expiry, and a short-lived authorized download? Check the export storage configuration.
provisions.statement: An export worker MUST store output in approved object storage with a named contact, an expiry, and a short-lived authorized download.
provisions.rationale: An export file concentrates sensitive rows into one downloadable object that outlives the request that built it. Approved object storage with a named contact, an expiry, and a short-lived authorized download gives that object controlled access and a defined end instead of a permanent public link.

provisions.heading: Record the Schedule on the Job Record
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `schedule-invalid` (level G) for a job schedule that is neither an `every` duration nor a `cron` expression; each scheduled job record states its timezone.
provisions.statement: A scheduled job MUST record its schedule in structured form with its timezone on its job record.
provisions.rationale: Tools can't parse prose for a schedule. The job record states when the work runs as `every` or `cron` with its timezone, which tools read directly. A schedule kept outside the record runs with no recorded moment attached, so misfire behavior has no stated time to measure against. The [automation page](../core/automation.md) states the record fields, and the `schedule-invalid` check reports a schedule no tool can read.

provisions.heading: Record Why Each Report Needs Its Infrastructure
provisions.evidence: Does every report use case page record the report, volume, plan, target, maximum, and operator? Check each use case page.
provisions.statement: A reporting proposal MUST record the report, representative data volume, plan or limitation, latency target, maximum result, and operator.
provisions.rationale: Reporting infrastructure costs a Worker, storage, and operating attention. Before building any of it, the team writes down the report, a representative data volume, the plan or limitation, the latency target, the maximum result, and the operator. The use case page carries that record, with why a normal request projection falls short of the boundary.

provisions.heading: Release Claims Past Their Lease
provisions.evidence: Does every claim test show an untouched item returning to the queue after its lease expires? Check the claim tests.
provisions.statement: A claimed item MUST return to the queue when its claim lease expires.
provisions.rationale: Claims are held by people who go home. A claim with no expiry parks the item forever. The lease returns stale claims to the queue, so an abandoned item waits for the next person instead of for nobody.
provisions.example: A Claimwick payout claimed Friday and untouched returns to the queue when its one-hour lease expires.

provisions.heading: Remove Occurrences Past Retention
provisions.evidence: Is every stored occurrence within its schedule's retention setting record? Check the store rows beside the setting records.
provisions.statement: A scheduled-job store MUST remove occurrences older than the schedule's retention setting record.
provisions.rationale: Occurrences older than the retention setting record leave the store so the key space stays bounded. The key space grows with the schedule's frequency and its retention: a per-second schedule kept for a year holds more than 30 million rows. [Quartz states the same practice](https://quartz-scheduler.net/documentation/best-practices.html) for a persistent job store.
provisions.example: A daily schedule that retains occurrences for 90 days holds 90 rows. A minute schedule with the same retention holds more than 100,000 rows. That is a different storage decision.

provisions.heading: Renew Only Owned Leases
provisions.evidence: Does any replica renew a lease after a failed renewal, or keep running an occurrence it lost? Check the replica logs and the renewal tests.
provisions.statement: A Worker replica MUST renew only its active lease and stop when renewal fails.
provisions.rationale: A failed renewal means another replica owns the occurrence now. A replica that kept going would complete work it no longer owns. The loser stops instead, so each replica renews only the lease it holds, and only while it stays active.

provisions.heading: Resolve Dependencies Inside an Execution Scope
provisions.evidence: Does every occurrence resolve scoped dependencies inside a disposed execution scope, when the project names no other scope boundary? Check the job execution code and the project documentation.
provisions.statement: Resolve scoped dependencies inside an execution scope and dispose the scope after the Command completes.
provisions.rationale: Each occurrence resolves its scoped dependencies inside one execution scope, disposed after the Command completes. The scope isolates one occurrence's dependencies from the next. A shared scope would leak one occurrence's state into another.

provisions.heading: Resume Batch Work from Its Cursor
provisions.evidence: Does every batch job name its resume position in its cursor, with a scenario for the remainder after a halfway failure? Check the job records and the scenario tests.
provisions.statement: A job that works through items in batches MUST name where resume state lives in its `cursor`.
provisions.rationale: A batch that fails halfway resumes instead of restarting. The cursor holds where the run stopped. Without it, the next run replays finished items or skips unfinished ones, and a scenario covering the remainder has no stated position to assert.

provisions.heading: Review Report Plans
provisions.evidence: Does every report have a review record showing query plans and indexes checked against representative data? Check the review records.
provisions.statement: Each report SHOULD have its query plans and indexes reviewed against representative data.
provisions.rationale: A query that flies over a hundred local rows can scan millions in production. Reviewing query plans and indexes against representative data shows the true cost before the report ships, rather than after it slows the database.

provisions.heading: Run One Command per Selected Item
provisions.evidence: Does every job run one command per item in its `selection` within its `batchSize`, each in its own unit of work? Check the job record selection and the handler code.
provisions.statement: A job MUST run one command per item in its `selection` within its `batchSize`, each in its own unit of work.
provisions.rationale: The selection states what each run selects, the batch size bounds how many items one batch takes, and `runs` names the command run per item. Each item runs as one command in its own unit of work, as `litespec/backend/application#issue-per-record-work-from-a-job` requires, so a failed item replays without replaying its batch.

provisions.heading: Run Over-Budget Exports in the Worker
provisions.evidence: Does every export past its request budget run in a Worker, with the budget in a setting record? Check the export use cases and their setting records.
provisions.statement: An export exceeding its request budget MUST run through Worker, with the budget a setting record the export's use case names.
provisions.rationale: An export that outlasts its request budget holds an HTTP connection open: the user waits while the server counts threads. Running it in a Worker returns the request immediately. The budget in its setting record tells the team exactly when an export outgrows the request path.

provisions.heading: Run Scheduled Jobs in Worker
provisions.evidence: Does every scheduled job run in the Worker sources, outside WebApi request handling? Check the Worker project and the WebApi endpoints.
provisions.statement: A scheduled job MUST run in Worker outside WebApi request handling.
provisions.rationale: Scheduled work needs two things request handling doesn't have: a scheduler that owns each schedule's lifetime, and a shutdown order that stops replicas in a controlled way. That is why scheduled work runs in a Worker, outside WebApi request handling.

provisions.heading: Scope Command Idempotency by Occurrence
provisions.evidence: Does every retry of one occurrence use its occurrence identity as the idempotency scope? Check the command idempotency keys.
provisions.statement: A scheduled job MUST use its occurrence identity as the command idempotency scope.
provisions.rationale: Every retry of one occurrence replays the same scheduled business action. The occurrence identity scopes the command idempotency key to make that hold. A key scoped any wider would merge separate occurrences into one.

provisions.heading: Scope Export Output to the Tenant
provisions.evidence: Does every export store output under a tenant-scoped path in object storage? Check the export storage paths.
provisions.statement: An export MUST store its output under a tenant-scoped object-storage path.
provisions.rationale: Export addresses are predictable. In a shared folder, one tenant can guess another tenant's file name. A tenant-scoped storage path puts each tenant's exports under its own prefix, so a guessed address stays inside the guesser's own data.

provisions.heading: Scope Occurrences and Leases by Tenant
provisions.evidence: Does every occurrence and lease row carry tenant scope in a product that isolates tenants? Check the occurrence and lease table schemas.
provisions.statement: A scheduled-job occurrence and its lease MUST carry tenant scope when the product isolates tenants.
provisions.rationale: In a product that isolates tenants, one tenant's schedules must trigger, block, and expose only that tenant's work. Scoping each occurrence and its lease to one tenant keeps that boundary. Unscoped leases would let a replica mix tenants inside one occurrence.

provisions.heading: Show a Preview Before Bulk Money Actions
provisions.evidence: Does every bulk money command render every affected item with its amount before acting? Check the preview step of each command.
provisions.statement: A bulk money command MUST render a preview of every affected item before acting.
provisions.rationale: One wrong filter multiplies one mistake into hundreds when money moves on many items at once. The preview lists every affected item with its amount, so the person confirms the set they meant instead of the set they typed.
provisions.example: Claimwick's bulk release previews forty-two payouts totaling EUR 18,400 before asking for confirmation.

provisions.heading: Show the Score Beside Each Item
provisions.evidence: Does every queue row show its score with the inputs that set it? Check the queue rows in the interface.
provisions.statement: A queue listing MUST show each item score with the inputs that set it.
provisions.rationale: A hidden score is an oracle: people work around an order they can't see or trust. Showing the score with its inputs lets each person check the order and challenge the inputs instead of the queue.
provisions.example: Each Claimwick dispute row shows `urgency 82: EUR 1,900, 6 days old, evidence missing`.

provisions.heading: State Clock Behavior for Business-Local Schedules
provisions.evidence: Does every business-local schedule record its IANA zone and the skipped and repeated local-time behavior? Check each schedule record.
provisions.statement: A business-local schedule MUST record an IANA time-zone identifier and define skipped and repeated local-time behavior.
provisions.rationale: Daylight-saving transitions omit one local hour and repeat another. A business-local schedule records its IANA time-zone identifier and defines what happens to occurrences in the skipped and repeated hours. Without that definition, each transition silently drops or doubles the local work.

provisions.heading: State How Missed Occurrences Recover
provisions.evidence: Does every schedule state skipped, once-replayed, or interval-replayed behavior for missed occurrences? Check each schedule record.
provisions.statement: A scheduled-job specification MUST define skipped, once-replayed, or interval-replayed behavior for missed occurrences.
provisions.rationale: Downtime and delay leave occurrences past their time. The specification states whether each missed occurrence is skipped, replayed once, or replayed per interval. The choice controls the business effect: a skipped reminder stays silent, while a replayed one arrives late.

provisions.heading: State the Claim Mode
provisions.evidence: Does every queue use case state its claim field as disabled, optional, or required? Check the use case pages.
provisions.statement: A work queue MUST state its claim mode as disabled, optional, or required.
provisions.rationale: Two people clearing the same item double-pay, double-approve, or double-refuse. The claim mode keeps two hands off one item: items need no claim, accept an optional hold, or require one before action.
provisions.example: Claimwick's payout queue requires a claim before release, while its review queue leaves claiming optional.

provisions.heading: Stop Jobs During Graceful Shutdown
provisions.evidence: Does every Worker shutdown path drain running occurrences before stopping schedule polling? Check the shutdown code in the Worker.
provisions.statement: A scheduled job MUST stop accepting new work during graceful shutdown.
provisions.rationale: A job that keeps accepting work during shutdown turns every deploy into a wait for work that never ends. Stopping intake lets the running occurrences drain, and the Worker stop.

provisions.heading: Store Execution Leases
provisions.evidence: Does every lease row in PostgreSQL carry an owner, an expiry, and a fencing value? Check the lease table schema.
provisions.statement: A scheduled-job store MUST record lease owner, expiry, and fencing value in PostgreSQL.
provisions.rationale: Each planned occurrence carries a lease with its owner, expiry, and fencing value in PostgreSQL. The lease names the one replica that may complete that occurrence. The `lease` field on the job record names the lock each run claims. The outbox extension cites this definition for its own claims.

provisions.heading: Support Report Cancellation
provisions.evidence: Does every report honor a cancel request and remove expired output? Check the cancellation tests.
provisions.statement: A report implementation MUST support cancellation and remove expired outputs.
provisions.rationale: Closing the tab leaves the report running, and an export nobody downloads still occupies storage. Cancellation stops the abandoned work, and expiry removes the abandoned file, so neither consumes resources indefinitely.

provisions.heading: Test Time Transitions
provisions.evidence: Does every job test use an injected clock and cover representative time-zone transitions? Check the job test sources.
provisions.statement: A scheduled-job test MUST use an injected clock and representative time-zone transitions.
provisions.rationale: Tests on the real clock can only wait for the next transition to arrive. An injected clock moves time to any transition on demand, so representative time-zone transitions run deterministically instead of once a year in production.

provisions.heading: Tolerate Duplicate Execution
provisions.evidence: Does any job Command or side effect record more than one accepted effect after a replayed occurrence? Check the replay tests.
provisions.statement: A scheduled job Command and side effect MUST tolerate duplicate execution after lease or process failure.
provisions.rationale: A lease or process failure can replay a job whose completion stayed uncertain. The job Command and its side effects tolerate that duplicate execution. Work that assumes exactly-once execution breaks on the first uncertain failure.

provisions.heading: Treat Unavailable Schedule Stores as Outages
provisions.evidence: During a store outage, is every Worker log entry backed off and rate-limited, with no occurrence poisoned? Check the Worker logs and the outage tests.
provisions.statement: A Worker MUST treat an unavailable scheduler store as the store outage `litespec/ext/outbox#report-store-outages-separately-from-delivery-failures` defines, with backed-off, rate-limited logging.
provisions.rationale: An unavailable scheduler store is an outage of the dependency, not a failed occurrence. The Worker treats it as the store outage `litespec/ext/outbox#report-store-outages-separately-from-delivery-failures` defines, with backed-off, rate-limited logging. Retry and poison outcomes belong to claimed occurrences, not to a store nobody can reach.

provisions.heading: Write Runbooks for Inspection, Replay, and Disable
provisions.evidence: Does every schedule have a runbook record for inspection, manual replay, and disable? Check the runbook records beside the schedules.
provisions.statement: Each schedule MUST have Runbook records for inspection, manual replay, and disable.
provisions.rationale: Stalled, failed, or unsafe schedules need controlled operator actions: inspection, manual replay, and disable. Runbook records carry those procedures, because an operator without them improvises against the store during the incident. Each procedure names the interface that performs it: a command, an endpoint, or a configuration value. A procedure that says "disable the schedule" without naming the switch stays undiscovered until the incident it was written for. Writing straight to the schedule store instead would bypass the occurrence identity `litespec/ext/jobs#derive-stable-occurrence-identity` depends on.
provisions.example: Claimwick's disable procedure names the configuration value or the administrative endpoint that stops the schedule, and states what happens to an occurrence already claimed.

provisions.heading: Align Backup Deletion Behavior
provisions.evidence: Does every backup and replica operation follow the documented deletion guarantee? Check the backup and replica procedures.
provisions.statement: Backup and replica operations MUST follow the documented deletion guarantee.
provisions.rationale: Every copy the product keeps falls under the deletion promise, including backups and replicas that restore for months after the live row disappears. When backup behavior stays undocumented, the team promises erasure it cannot deliver and learns the gap during an audit or a restore.

provisions.heading: Audit Lifecycle Changes
provisions.evidence: Does every lifecycle operation write an audit record, or a standalone record where audit is not selected? Check each operation's writes.
provisions.statement: A lifecycle operation MUST record its audit as an audit record when audit is selected and a standalone record otherwise.
provisions.rationale: A subject-access or legal-hold dispute asks first who deleted what and when. The audit entry lets a reviewer answer from the record.

provisions.heading: Authorize Lifecycle Access Paths
provisions.evidence: Does every administrative or restore query run on a named path with explicit authorization? Check the query paths and their authorization.
provisions.statement: An administrative or restore query MUST use a named path with explicit authorization.
provisions.rationale: Restore and administration queries reach records normal queries cannot see, so they need a path of their own with checks of their own. Without the named path, a privileged read hides inside normal query code and inherits normal authorization, which grants too much to too many callers.

provisions.heading: Authorize Lifecycle Changes
provisions.evidence: Does every lifecycle operation check its documented authorization before changing the record? Check each operation's authorization check.
provisions.statement: A lifecycle operation MUST apply its documented authorization.
provisions.rationale: Deleting or restoring the wrong record harms a customer or breaks a legal duty. The authorization check runs before the record changes, because a check that runs after can only report harm it already allowed.

provisions.heading: Default to Hard Delete
provisions.evidence: Does every deletion with no retention or restore requirement remove the row in the delete transaction? Check the delete transaction code.
provisions.statement: A lifecycle implementation MUST use hard delete when no accepted retention or restore requirement applies.
provisions.rationale: When no use case needs the data back, removing the row deletes the least and keeps the least: no hidden state, no filtered queries, and no purge job to write and watch. A team that keeps deleted rows just in case pays for retention without a requirement and answers subject-access exports with data it promised to delete.
provisions.example: A Claimwick expense deleted without a retention duty removes the expense row in the delete transaction.

provisions.heading: Define Document Lifecycle Behavior
provisions.evidence: Does every document implementation define document state, filtered queries, indexes, purge transformations, and contract evolution? Check each document implementation.
provisions.statement: A Marten lifecycle implementation MUST define document state, filtered queries, indexes, purge transformations, and contract evolution.
provisions.rationale: A document store keeps whatever the aggregate writes. The team states how each lifecycle state lands in the document: which state the document carries, which queries filter it, which indexes serve those queries, how a purge rewrites the document, and how the contract changes when the shape does. Without those choices, the business transition lands in storage by accident and each query invents its own filter.

provisions.heading: Define Post-Deletion References
provisions.evidence: Does every specification define post-deletion behavior for references, exports, and unique constraints? Check each specification's deletion section.
provisions.statement: A lifecycle specification MUST define post-deletion behavior for cross-aggregate references, exports, and unique constraints.
provisions.rationale: Other records can point at the deleted one, exports can carry its values, and a unique value such as an expense reference number can become available again. When the specification stays silent, each developer guesses: one nulls the reference, another keeps it, and a duplicate value slips through or a report breaks. Writing the behavior down gives every reference, export, and constraint one answer.

provisions.heading: Define Relational Lifecycle Behavior
provisions.evidence: Does every relational implementation define columns, query filters, partial indexes, migrations, and named filter behavior? Check each relational implementation.
provisions.statement: A relational lifecycle implementation MUST define columns, query filters, partial indexes, migrations, and named filter behavior.
provisions.rationale: A relational table keeps retained rows beside active ones. The team states which columns mark the state, which query filters hide retained rows, which partial indexes keep active values unique, which migrations add all of it, and what each named filter means. Without those choices, a unique constraint blocks a legitimate reuse or a query returns rows the lifecycle retired.

provisions.heading: Exclude Inactive Records from Normal Reads
provisions.evidence: Is every normal query free of deleted or archived records? Check the query filters beside the active state.
provisions.statement: A normal query MUST exclude deleted or archived records.
provisions.rationale: An employee browsing expenses expects live data. Deleted and archived records in that list confuse the employee and leak data the lifecycle retired. Normal queries therefore read only the active state, while the named privileged paths serve the records outside it.

provisions.heading: Exclude Persistence-Only Lifecycle Behavior
provisions.evidence: Does every lifecycle transition run through behavior beyond persistence filters or property setters alone? Check the transition code and the persistence filters.
provisions.statement: A lifecycle rule MUST NOT rely only on persistence filters or property setters.
provisions.rationale: A query filter or a property setter runs without the business checks. It filters rows in storage while the aggregate never learns the transition happened. The product then enforces lifecycle in two places that disagree, and a new query that skips the filter exposes data the lifecycle retired.

provisions.heading: Keep Archive Records Module-Owned
provisions.evidence: Does every archive record sit under its owning module, or in the shared archive area the project keeps? Check the module folders.
provisions.statement: Keep archive records under the owning module.
provisions.rationale: Meaning and archive meaning belong together: the module that defines what the record means also defines what its archive means and who may read it. An archive kept elsewhere sits under two modules, and its access checks drift from its home module.

provisions.heading: Keep Purge and Archive Work Bounded and Observable
provisions.evidence: Does every purge and archive run resume after interruption within declared bounds and show progress? Check the purge and archive tests.
provisions.statement: A purge or archive operation MUST be resumable, bounded, cancellation-aware, and observable.
provisions.rationale: A purge or archive job can run for hours across millions of rows, and a deployment, a failure, or an operator stops it midway. Resumable, bounded, cancellation-aware work restarts where it stopped instead of from the beginning, and observable progress tells the operator whether it moves or stalls.

provisions.heading: Model Lifecycle Operations in Domain
provisions.evidence: Does every aggregate expose delete, archive, and restore methods where those operations apply? Check each aggregate's methods.
provisions.statement: A Domain aggregate MUST expose delete, archive, and restore as explicit behavior when those operations apply.
provisions.rationale: Delete, archive, and restore change what the business promises about a record. The aggregate owns them the way it owns any rule: one method per operation, with the checks beside the change. When the operation lives anywhere else, two callers implement it two ways and the checks drift apart.

provisions.heading: Model Retained Lifecycle States
provisions.evidence: Does every retained record carry a business reason and a named state transition? Check each retained record beside its state transitions.
provisions.statement: A soft-deleted or archived record MUST have a business reason and explicit state transition.
provisions.rationale: A record that stays after deletion or moves to an archive still affects the product: it appears in some reads, skips others, and can return. A named state with a named transition shows that behavior in the aggregate itself, so a reader sees which transitions exist and which checks each one runs. Without the transition, the retained data is a row the code treats specially in scattered places.
provisions.example: `Archive` changes aggregate state after the authorization and audit checks succeed.

provisions.heading: Name Soft-Delete Timestamps
provisions.evidence: Does every soft-delete timestamp use `deleted_at_utc`, or another column the documentation names? Check the schema columns.
provisions.statement: Use `deleted_at_utc` when a soft-delete timestamp is required.
provisions.rationale: One name for the deletion timestamp lets every reader and query recognize it on sight. The event and the unit remove the two guesses a reviewer otherwise makes.

provisions.heading: Preserve Legal-Hold Data
provisions.evidence: Does every retention run preserve held data past its retention date? Check the retention run code beside the hold records.
provisions.statement: A retention job MUST preserve data under legal hold.
provisions.rationale: A legal hold suspends the duty to delete. The named data stays until the hold releases, even when its retention date passes. A retention job that ignores the hold destroys evidence the organization had a duty to keep.

provisions.heading: Record Lifecycle Scope
provisions.evidence: Does every lifecycle record name classification, retention, deletion trigger, hold, export, restore, and backup? Check each lifecycle record.
provisions.statement: A lifecycle record MUST name classification, retention, deletion trigger, hold, export, restore, and backup.
provisions.rationale: A record's lifetime raises one set of choices: what kind of data it is, how long it stays, what triggers deletion, and how holds, exports, restores, and backups behave. Naming them all in one lifecycle record keeps them reviewable together.
