Without that record, the choices scatter across tickets and memory, and a deletion runs before anyone checks the retention bound. Retention bounds live in setting records.

provisions.heading: Record Retention Progress
provisions.evidence: Does every retention run persist progress for the next run to resume from? Check the retention run code.
provisions.statement: A retention job MUST record its progress.
provisions.rationale: A retention run can stop midway through millions of rows. Recorded progress tells the next run where to resume, and observable progress tells the operator whether the job moves or stalls.

provisions.heading: Record the Release of a Legal Hold
provisions.evidence: Does every legal-hold release record the actor, data covered, reason, and resumed retention? Check the release records.
provisions.statement: A legal-hold release MUST record actor, data covered, reason, and resumed retention: an audit record when audit is selected, a standalone record otherwise.
provisions.rationale: A hold suspends the duty to erase, and releasing it resumes that duty from a date the team can name. Without a release record, nobody can state when the suspension ended. A subject [erasure request](https://gdpr-info.eu/art-17-gdpr/) then has no answer date, and the next retention run cannot tell which data is deletable again. The record also tells the retention job exactly which data resumed which retention date.
provisions.example: A release record names the hold, the release date, and the retention date the covered data carries.

provisions.heading: Reject Hidden Lifecycle Flags
provisions.evidence: Does every lifecycle transition run through explicit behavior instead of a storage-only flag? Check the transition code.
provisions.statement: A lifecycle implementation MUST NOT use a hidden boolean as its sole lifecycle behavior.
provisions.rationale: A boolean column that only the storage layer reads can flip without running the business checks: no authorization, no audit entry, and no named transition a reviewer can find. The record then looks deleted in one query and active in another, depending on which filter the query remembered. An explicit lifecycle operation keeps the flag, where one exists, as an effect of the transition rather than the transition itself.

provisions.heading: Separate Query-Shaped History
provisions.evidence: Does every query-shaped history live in a read model instead of on its aggregate, unless the project keeps it on the aggregate? Check the aggregate code beside the read models.
provisions.statement: Use a separate read model when archived history is query-shaped instead of an aggregate invariant.
provisions.rationale: History kept for display, such as a list of past expenses, constrains nothing the aggregate protects. It lives cheaper as a read model beside the record. Folding it into the record widens the transaction boundary for data no invariant needs.

provisions.heading: Test Provider Lifecycle Paths
provisions.evidence: Does the suite test the normal and lifecycle query paths on the selected provider? Check the lifecycle tests.
provisions.statement: A selected persistence provider MUST test normal and lifecycle query paths.
provisions.rationale: Filters, indexes, and migrations behave differently per provider: a filter that works on documents can fail on tables. Tests that read through both the normal path and the lifecycle path on the selected provider catch the difference before a customer does.

provisions.heading: Avoid Catalog-Only Locale Claims
provisions.evidence: Does every shipped locale come from the locale decision rather than from catalog files alone? Check the shipped locales beside the locale decision.
provisions.statement: A product MUST NOT infer supported locales from catalog files alone.
provisions.rationale: A catalog file proves only that someone wrote translations. It says nothing about routes, fallback, selection, or detection, so a product that counts locales by counting files announces a language its routes cannot serve and its fallback never reaches.

provisions.heading: Avoid Duplicate Localized URLs
provisions.evidence: Does every localized content item serve from exactly one indexable URL? Check the served URLs of each content item.
provisions.statement: A localized application MUST NOT publish multiple indexable URLs for the same localized content.
provisions.rationale: When two addresses serve the same language, search engines split the page's rank between them, and canonical links point two ways. One indexable address per language keeps search, sharing, and caching pointed at the same page.

provisions.heading: Complete or Fall Back Catalog Values
provisions.evidence: Does every supported locale contain its required keys or resolve them through its declared fallback? Check each locale catalog beside the fallback chain.
provisions.statement: Each supported locale MUST contain required keys or use its declared fallback.
provisions.rationale: A missing translation with no declared fallback becomes a runtime surprise: the interface shows a key, an empty string, or the wrong language, and nobody chose which. The declaration states the fallback locale and what a missing key does at build time. A key missing from the default locale fails the build. No fallback exists for it, and the interface renders its identifier. A key missing from a non-default locale reports a warning and falls back. Shipping one untranslated string costs less than blocking a release on it.
provisions.example: A catalog check runs in the frontend lint gate, so both outcomes are visible before review, not in a browser.

provisions.heading: Define One Locale Route Shape
provisions.evidence: Does every locale reach the application through the documented route shape? Check the route definitions.
provisions.statement: A localized application MUST define one documented locale route shape.
provisions.rationale: Users, links, crawlers, and caches all address a localized page, so one route shape gives each language one predictable address. A path segment is the default shape: it gives every localized page a distinct address that links, crawlers, and cache entries can each name. A cookie or header shape serves every locale from one address instead, so a shared cache and a search index each see only one of them. A product with no public pages, whose locale belongs to the signed-in account, documents one of those shapes instead of inventing a fourth.
provisions.example: `/nl/orders/42` places the locale in the documented path segment, so a crawler and a shared cache each address one language.

provisions.heading: Follow the Validation Message Grammar
provisions.evidence: Does every validation message state the field label, the fault, and the accepted input without technical wording? Check the validation messages in each locale.
provisions.statement: A validation catalog MUST state the field label, what is wrong, and what is accepted, without technical wording.
provisions.rationale: A validation message that names the field, the fault, and the accepted input tells the user how to fix the entry in any language, while a message with only one of the three leaves the user guessing. The three-part shape holds across languages; each language's sentence pattern lives in the labels of the field's glossary term and the language's writing page.
provisions.example: The glossary term for a Claimwick expense field carries the sentence pattern for each supported language.

provisions.heading: Format Values with Active Locale
provisions.evidence: Does every date, number, currency, plural, list, and relative time render through the active-locale formatters? Check the formatting calls.
provisions.statement: A localized interface MUST format dates, times, numbers, currency, plurals, lists, and relative time by active locale.
provisions.rationale: Dates, times, numbers, currency, plurals, lists, and relative time each follow the user's conventions, and a date the user misreads becomes a missed appointment or a wrong payment. The platform supplies all of them. [The `Intl` namespace](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/Intl) has `DateTimeFormat`, `NumberFormat`, `PluralRules`, `ListFormat`, and `RelativeTimeFormat`. Each one carries the locale data the browser already ships. A project-written formatter for any of these is a second locale database that no one updates. Its plural rules are wrong for the first language with more than two forms.
provisions.example: Create one formatter instance per locale and reuse it. Construction is the expensive part.

provisions.heading: Handle Unavailable Locale Segments
provisions.evidence: Does every unsupported or missing locale segment redirect under the documented product policy? Check the redirect tests.
provisions.statement: A localized application MUST redirect unsupported or missing locale segments according to product policy.
provisions.rationale: Readers mistype addresses and follow stale links, so a locale segment can name a language the product never shipped, or go missing entirely. Without a documented policy, each route answers differently: one shows the default language, another shows an error, and a crawler indexes both as content.

provisions.heading: Keep Locale Selection Explicit
provisions.evidence: Does every request carry the locale in the URL or a documented session preference instead of ambient request state? Check the request handling for the locale.
provisions.statement: Keep locale selection in the URL or documented session preference.
provisions.rationale: A locale stored in the URL or a documented session preference travels with the request, so any developer can see which language a page serves and link to it. An implicit global locale hides in process state, where one request can read another's language and no link reproduces the page.

provisions.heading: Keep Stable Error Codes Locale-Neutral
provisions.evidence: Is every stable API error code identical across locales? Check the error code values in each locale's responses.
provisions.statement: A stable API error code MUST NOT change by locale.
provisions.rationale: Integrations and support tools match on the error code. A code that changes per language forces every consumer to list every translation before handling one failure. The code stays fixed while the human-readable message beside it translates.

provisions.heading: Localize Public Presentation Content
provisions.evidence: Do public metadata, form labels, validation messages, and user-safe errors all follow the active locale? Check each rendered page.
provisions.statement: Public metadata, form labels, validation messages, and user-safe errors MUST follow the active locale.
provisions.rationale: A Dutch page with an English title, English form labels, or an English error tells the user the translation stopped halfway and tells a search engine the page serves two languages. Metadata, labels, validation messages, and user-safe errors follow the active locale with the page around them.

provisions.heading: Name Messages by Meaning
provisions.evidence: Does every catalog key use a semantic name citing a glossary term instead of a source-language sentence? Check the catalog keys.
provisions.statement: A locale catalog MUST use semantic keys that cite glossary terms rather than source-language sentences.
provisions.rationale: A key that copies the English sentence breaks its meaning the day English rewords it: every other language still points at the old sentence. A semantic key names the intent instead, citing the glossary term that holds the word's labels per language, so wording changes in any language without disturbing the key.
provisions.example: `orders.cancel.confirmation` identifies intent without copying the English sentence.

provisions.heading: Preserve Locale-Neutral Business Data
provisions.evidence: Is every domain value and API contract locale-neutral outside an explicitly localized exchange? Check the domain values and contracts.
provisions.statement: Domain values and API contracts MUST remain locale-neutral unless a use case explicitly exchanges localized content.
provisions.rationale: An expense state or a price stored in Dutch breaks the moment an English speaker opens it, and an API contract that shifts per language forces every consumer to negotiate wording before reading data. Business values and wire contracts stay in one neutral form, and only the interface translates them for display. A use case that genuinely exchanges localized content, such as a product description the merchant writes per language, names that exchange explicitly.

provisions.heading: Record Supported Locale Behavior
provisions.evidence: Does the locale decision list the supported locales, the default locale, the fallback chain, user selection, and browser detection? Check the locale decision record.
provisions.statement: A localization decision MUST list supported locales, default locale, fallback chain, user selection, and browser detection.
provisions.rationale: Catalogs, routes, and formatters all read the same five choices, and the choices interact. Writing them once in the decision, before building any of the three, gives every part one contract to follow. Without it, each part guesses its own fallback, and the product answers each missing translation differently.

provisions.heading: Resolve Every Shown Identifier
provisions.evidence: Does every screen render glossary labels instead of raw codes, outside user-facing reference numbers? Check the rendered screens.
provisions.statement: A screen MUST resolve every closed-set code it renders to its glossary label and never render the raw code, excluding user-facing reference numbers.
provisions.rationale: A code such as a refusal ground or a billing state is a contract value built for systems, while the glossary label beside it is copy built for users. A screen that renders the raw code shows one untranslated fragment in an otherwise translated page and forces the user to decode it. Resolving every shown code keeps the whole screen in the user's language, except reference numbers the user quotes back.
provisions.example: A Claimwick shipment row shows the glossary label for `shipment-delayed` in the active locale.

provisions.heading: Split Catalogs by Module When Needed
provisions.evidence: Is every catalog whole unless measured size calls for a split, or the project chose a feature split from the start? Check the catalog files beside the size measurements.
provisions.statement: Split catalogs by module only when catalog size requires it.
provisions.rationale: Small catalogs read better whole: one file per locale shows every key at a glance and survives a rename without cross-file edits. Splitting waits until measured size, such as slow loads or conflicting edits, proves one file no longer serves.

provisions.heading: Store User-Facing Copy in Catalogs
provisions.evidence: Does every user-facing sentence live in the locale catalogs instead of source code? Check the source files for literal copy.
provisions.statement: A localized application MUST store user-facing copy in locale catalogs.
provisions.rationale: Copy in source code reaches translators only through developers, and each wording change becomes a code change with a review, a build, and a deployment. Holding every user-facing sentence in one catalog per locale lets translators edit wording while developers edit behavior.

provisions.heading: Use BCP 47 Identifiers
provisions.evidence: Does every locale identifier use BCP 47, or another identifier form the documentation names? Check the locale identifiers in the catalogs and routes.
provisions.statement: Use BCP 47 locale identifiers.
provisions.rationale: BCP 47 is the identifier form routes, catalogs, browsers, and libraries recognize: one tag such as `nl` travels unchanged from the address bar to the catalog lookup. A home-grown form needs translation at every boundary and puzzles every new developer.

provisions.heading: Use One Catalog Root
provisions.evidence: Does every catalog sit under the application-owned root, or under another root the documentation names? Check the catalog folders.
provisions.statement: Keep catalogs under one application-owned locale root.
provisions.rationale: One application-owned root tells every developer and tool where catalogs live, so a new locale lands beside the old ones instead of in a folder nobody checks. Scattered catalogs split the set, and one of them misses the fallback check.

provisions.heading: Keep Secrets and Personal Data Out of Descriptions and Logs
provisions.evidence: Do any tool descriptions or log lines carry a secret or personal value? Read the tool descriptions and the server's log calls.
provisions.statement: Tool descriptions and logs MUST carry no secret, as `litespec/quality/security#keep-secrets-out-of-tracked-and-observable-data` states, and no personal data in any field.
provisions.rationale: Tool descriptions travel to the model on every call, and logs persist for operators long after the call ends. A secret copied into either grants access to whoever reads it next, and personal data in either spreads beyond the consent that collected it. Descriptions and logs name the fields without carrying the values.

provisions.heading: Pass Server Instructions at Initialize
provisions.evidence: Does every initialize response carry an `instructions` value covering transport, audience, write surface, and refusal behavior? Read the server's initialize handler and its test.
provisions.statement: An MCP server MUST pass an `instructions` value at initialize stating its transport, its audience, its write surface, and its refusal behavior.
provisions.rationale: The client loads server instructions once per session from the MCP initialize response, while each tool description loads per call. That split puts scope and policy at the server level, where they hold for every call: transport, audience, write surface, and refusal behavior. Tool mechanics stay in the tool descriptions, which the model reads when it chooses a tool. Without server-level instructions, each tool repeats the policy differently or omits it, and the model plans calls the server then refuses.
provisions.example: "Runs over stdio, one account per process, against the hosted API. Reads cover the account's own data, and three tools create or change records. A policy refusal returns the refusal code, and a write needing a person's confirmation refuses until they give it."

provisions.heading: Record the Server as an Entry Point
provisions.evidence: Does every shipped MCP server have an `mcp` entry point titled for it? Read the entry point list.
provisions.statement: A project shipping an MCP server MUST record it as an entry point of kind `mcp` whose title names the MCP server.
provisions.rationale: Entry point records name how callers arrive, and `litespec/core/edges#give-each-entry-point-a-kind` keeps one closed set of kinds. An MCP server is a channel a local model client calls, so it takes the kind `mcp` with its title naming the protocol it speaks. Without that record, the server's reach stays invisible to anyone reviewing the access records.

provisions.heading: Refuse Each Write Until the Person Confirms
provisions.evidence: Does every writing tool refuse until the person confirms? Read each writing tool's handler and its tests.
provisions.statement: Every tool that writes MUST refuse until the person confirms the write.
provisions.rationale: A model misreads intent the way any agent does: it can pause the wrong subscription or delete the record the user asked about. Refusing each write until the person confirms keeps the person behind every change while leaving reads fast. Without confirmation, one misunderstood sentence becomes a changed record nobody confirmed.

provisions.heading: Scope Each Tool to Named Use Cases
provisions.evidence: Does every tool description name the use cases and permissions it reaches? Read each tool description beside its use case grant.
provisions.statement: Each tool MUST name the use cases and permissions it reaches.
provisions.rationale: Each tool opens product behavior to a model acting for the user. Naming exactly which use cases and permissions each tool reaches lets a reviewer tell whether a tool reads one account or writes across many. Without the named scope, a broad tool ships without the scrutiny its reach needs.

provisions.heading: State the Distribution and Update Path
provisions.evidence: Does the server documentation state how to install and update the server? Read the server's documentation.
provisions.statement: The server documentation MUST state how a user installs and updates the server.
provisions.rationale: The server runs on the user's machine, not on the product's servers, so no deployment pipeline updates it. Without documented install and update steps, users run stale servers with stale tool descriptions, and a security fix waits on users who never learn it exists.

provisions.heading: State the Refusing Side on Each Refusal
provisions.evidence: Does every refusal carry a `Needs:`, `Needs confirmation:`, or `Refused:` prefix, or does the documentation name another vocabulary? Read the tools' refusal messages.
provisions.statement: Prefix an input-shape refusal with `Needs:`, a human-confirmation refusal with `Needs confirmation:`, and a server-side refusal with `Refused:`.
provisions.rationale: A refusal without a source sends the model guessing: it rephrases input the server rejected on policy, or it waits for a person when its own input was malformed. The prefix names the failing side. The model repairs its own input after `Needs:`, asks the person after `Needs confirmation:`, and reports the server after `Refused:`, instead of retrying a refusal no retry satisfies.

provisions.heading: Write One Tool Description for One Decision
provisions.evidence: Does every tool follow the title, behavior, parameter polarity, and side-effect rules? Read each entry in the declared tools directory.
provisions.statement: An MCP tool MUST title its action imperatively, describe its behavior declaratively, use positive parameter polarity, and state its side effects.
provisions.rationale: The model plans its calls from the title and description the [MCP specification](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2025-06-18) carries to it. An imperative title names the action, while a declarative description states what happens instead of commanding the caller, so the server's guidance and the model's own plan do not compete. A positive boolean such as `paused` avoids the inverse polarity a model answers wrongly, and a stated side effect answers the reviewer who asks what the call changed.

provisions.heading: Accept Repeated Delivery
provisions.evidence: Does every event handler keep correct state when the same message arrives twice? Check the handler tests that deliver a message twice.
provisions.statement: An event handler that receives an outbox delivery MUST handle the same message more than once.
provisions.rationale: The target can accept a message while the Worker crashes before recording completion, and the requeued claim then dispatches it again. Delivery promises at-least-once, so every event handler handles the same message more than once without corrupting its state.

provisions.heading: Audit Outbox Replay
provisions.evidence: Does every replay record its actor, reason, time, and failure without editing the payload? Check the replay code and its audit records.
provisions.statement: An outbox replay MUST record actor, reason, time, and failure without editing the payload: an audit record when audit is selected, a standalone record otherwise.
provisions.rationale: A replay dispatches a message the system already handled or dead-lettered. The team records who replayed it, why, when, and which failure it answers. Without that record, a duplicate delivery looks like a dispatcher bug rather than an operator's decision, and no one can reconstruct the choice.

provisions.heading: Avoid Automatic Durable-Bus Adoption
provisions.evidence: Does every dispatcher run on project-owned records, or on a durable bus with a pinned manifest entry and a documented choice? Check the manifest and the dispatch transport.
provisions.statement: Use project-owned Marten records and Worker dispatch unless a manifest-pinned durable package passes a shared-transaction integration test.
provisions.rationale: A durable bus package earns its place only when an integration test proves it commits the message in the same transaction as the business work. Until that evidence exists, project-owned Marten records with Worker dispatch carry delivery without depending on behavior no one verified.

provisions.heading: Classify Message Kinds
provisions.evidence: Does every outbox record name its message kind, with each integration event citing its record? Check the record type and the messages staged.
provisions.statement: An outbox record MUST name its message kind as integration event, flow-step command, or provider side effect, with an integration event citing its integration-event record.
provisions.rationale: An integration event, a flow-step command, and a provider side effect each dispatch through their own owners and transports, so the record names which one it holds. The integration event cites its integration-event record, so the staged message traces to the published fact it carries.

provisions.heading: Cover Undispatched Records in the Rollback Runbook
provisions.evidence: Does every rollback runbook cover the records the new writer staged but no one dispatched? Check each rollback runbook record.
provisions.statement: A rollback Runbook MUST include records created by the new writer but not yet dispatched.
provisions.rationale: Rolling back the deployment does not roll back the store. Records the new writer staged but no one dispatched stay behind. The rollback Runbook names how the previous version handles them. Without that plan, they sit undispatched with no owner and no reader.

provisions.heading: Declare Published Facts as Integration Events
provisions.evidence: Does every delivered integration event have a record carrying direction, payload, trust, and, for an outbound event, `translates`? Check each event type beside its record.
provisions.statement: Each integration event the outbox delivers MUST have an integration-event record carrying direction, payload, trust and, for an outbound event, the domain event it translates.
provisions.rationale: A published fact without a record is a promise nobody versioned: readers depend on fields no page states, and a field change breaks them without a diff. The integration-event record states the direction, the payload with its classifications, and the trust readers place in it. The [edges page](../core/edges.md) states the declaration and the record.

provisions.heading: Define Claim Ownership
provisions.evidence: Does every claim take an owner, expiry, and fencing value inside a short transaction? Check the claim code in the outbox store.
provisions.statement: An outbox claim MUST use a short transaction with the lease owner, lease expiry, and fencing value that `litespec/ext/jobs#store-execution-leases` defines.
provisions.rationale: Several Workers poll the same store, so each dispatch attempt needs one owner. The lease owner, the lease expiry, and the fencing value name that owner. The short transaction takes the claim without holding locks into the delivery itself.

provisions.heading: Deploy Readers Before Writers
provisions.evidence: Does every release plan deploy compatible readers before its additive writers? Check the deployment order in the release runbook.
provisions.statement: A release MUST deploy compatible readers before writers for additive event versions.
provisions.rationale: In a mixed-version rollout, old and new records sit in one store. Deploying compatible readers before the writers that emit new shapes keeps every record dispatchable at each step. The reverse order strands new records until the readers catch up.

provisions.heading: Dispatch Claimed Records in Worker
provisions.evidence: Does every Worker loop dispatch a bounded batch and record each outcome? Check the dispatcher's claim and batch code.
provisions.statement: A Worker MUST claim pending outbox records, dispatch a bounded batch, and record success or retry information.
provisions.rationale: Dispatch needs time, retries, and network calls that no request transaction can hold. The Worker claims pending records, dispatches a bounded batch, and records each outcome. The request then commits fast while delivery proceeds on its own schedule.

provisions.heading: Dispatch Flow-Step Commands in a New Scope
provisions.evidence: Does every flow-step command dispatch through `ICommandMediator` in a fresh Worker scope, or is inline running a documented choice? Check the dispatcher's flow-step code.
provisions.statement: Dispatch a flow-step command through `ICommandMediator` in a fresh Worker scope.
provisions.rationale: A flow-step command is a full command with validation, authorization, and its own transaction, not a subroutine of the dispatcher. Sending it through `ICommandMediator` in a fresh Worker scope runs the whole application pipeline for it.

provisions.heading: Document Delivery Guarantees Before Sending
provisions.evidence: Does every durable-delivery specification document its guarantee, downstream boundary, duplicate behavior, retry horizon, and recovery runbook? Check each specification.
provisions.statement: A durable-delivery specification MUST document delivery guarantee, downstream boundary, duplicate behavior, retry horizon, and recovery runbook.
provisions.rationale: Delivery crosses a system boundary, so the team agrees up front on the guarantee, the boundary, the duplicate behavior, the retry horizon, and the runbook that recovers when delivery fails. Without that agreement, the writer assumes once-only delivery while the target assumes retries, and both discover the mismatch in production. The agreement lands before the first message does.

provisions.heading: Emit Excluded Reactions and Jobs After Commit
provisions.evidence: Does every fact raised under an excluded reaction or job publish after the commit succeeds, with no outbox record staged? Check the pipeline's publish step for the use cases those reactions and jobs run.
provisions.statement: The facts raised by the use case a reaction or job the outbox excludes runs MUST be published after that use case's commit succeeds, without staging an outbox record.
provisions.rationale: Without an outbox record, nothing survives a crash between the commit and the publish, so the pipeline publishes the raised facts right after the commit succeeds and accepts the loss. Publishing before the commit would be worse: it would fire for a change the database then rolls back. The reaction or job itself publishes nothing; the pipeline's staging step does.

provisions.heading: Exclude Request-Transaction Dispatch
provisions.evidence: Does any request path dispatch a durable message inside the request transaction? Check the endpoint and command handler paths.
provisions.statement: WebApi MUST NOT dispatch a durable message inside the request transaction.
provisions.rationale: A network call inside the request transaction holds database locks while the outside world answers, and a slow target slows every request behind it. The request commits only to make the message eligible. The Worker performs the delivery later.

provisions.heading: Give Each Handler Its Own Delivery
provisions.evidence: Does every handler receive its own delivery with its own retries and dead letter? Check the outbox delivery records for each handler.
provisions.statement: The outbox MUST deliver an event to each of its handlers as a separate delivery with its own retries and dead letter.
provisions.rationale: One delivery shared by all handlers retries every handler when one fails. Each handler therefore gets its own delivery with its own retries and dead letter. Each of those deliveries still ends in repeat-safe handling, under `litespec/ext/outbox#accept-repeated-delivery`.
provisions.example: In the library product, a loan-borrowed event feeds a due-notice handler and a statistics handler. The notice delivery retries on its own schedule while the statistics delivery stays complete.

provisions.heading: Group Outbox Infrastructure
provisions.evidence: Does every outbox infrastructure file sit under `Infrastructure/Messaging/Outbox/` or another home named in the documentation? Check the outbox code folders and the project's documentation.
provisions.statement: Keep outbox record, storage, claim, and dispatch infrastructure under `Infrastructure/Messaging/Outbox/`.
provisions.rationale: The outbox record, storage, claim, and dispatch code form one mechanism with one owner. Keeping it under `Infrastructure/Messaging/Outbox/` puts every persistent dispatch question in one folder instead of scattered across the project.

provisions.heading: Identify Repeated Delivery
provisions.evidence: Does every event handler check the message ID or business key at its Command or side-effect boundary? Check each handler's boundary.
provisions.statement: An event handler that receives an outbox delivery MUST use message ID or a business idempotency key at its Command or side-effect boundary.
provisions.rationale: Handling a repeat means recognizing it: the message ID or a business idempotency key gives the event handler a stable identity to check at its command or side-effect boundary. Without that key, the handler processes the repeat as new work and pays, notifies, or ships twice.

provisions.heading: Isolate the Worker Host
provisions.evidence: Does the outbox Worker host live in its own project, or is the shared hosting a documented choice? Check the solution's projects.
provisions.statement: Keep the outbox Worker host in its own project.
provisions.rationale: The Worker runs as its own process with its own lifetime, scaling, and configuration, apart from the request host. Its own project keeps that independence visible and stops request concerns from leaking into dispatch configuration.

provisions.heading: Keep Provider Mapping with Integration
provisions.evidence: Does every provider mapping live in the integration that owns its side effect, or is shared-path hosting a documented choice? Check the dispatch code and the integration projects.
provisions.statement: Keep Integration Event-to-provider mapping in the integration that owns the side effect.
provisions.rationale: Each provider speaks its own transport with its own mapping, retries, and quirks. The integration that owns the side effect owns that mapping, so a provider change touches one integration instead of the shared dispatch path.

provisions.heading: Keep Published Events Available for Read Model Rebuilds
provisions.evidence: Is every integration event a read model names kept apart from delivery for as long as a rebuild may need it, with erased fields removed or the key shredded? Check the event log's retention beside the read models that read it.
provisions.statement: A project MUST keep every integration event a read model names in `from`, `erasedBy` or `removedBy` apart from the outbox's delivery records for as long as a read model may need rebuilding from it, with erased personal fields removed or the event key shredded.
provisions.rationale: A new read model, or a changed one, fills from the events the owner already published. An outbox that deletes delivered records after a few days leaves a new read model nothing to replay, and every new read model then needs a hand-written backfill from the owner's tables, which is the coupling the read model exists to remove. Keeping the published events in a log apart from delivery lets a projection replay history. The log holds personal fields, so the erasing event a read model names in `erasedBy` also erases the field in the log: a retained event keeps its shape with the erased personal fields removed, or with its key shredded, so no rebuild restores them. The read model keeps an erasure tombstone for the erased key and applies it on rebuild, under `litespec/core/automation#erase-a-read-model-personal-field-with-its-owner`. Settled by [decision/0065-read-another-module-through-a-read-model](decision/0065-read-another-module-through-a-read-model).
provisions.example: In Claimwick, the reporting module rebuilds its reimbursed-expense read model by replaying the kept expense-reimbursed events, while the outbox deletes its delivery records after seven days. A retained event for an erased expense replays without the erased personal fields.

provisions.heading: Model Outbox Lifecycle States
provisions.evidence: Does every outbox state have a sealed record under the abstract base with a documented transition? Check the outbox state types and their transitions.
provisions.statement: An outbox record MUST model its lifecycle as an abstract state base with one sealed record for each of pending, processing, dispatched, and dead-letter.
provisions.rationale: `pending` becomes `processing`, and `processing` becomes `dispatched`, `pending`, or `dead-letter`, while audited replay moves `dead-letter` back to `pending`. Three of the four states carry data the others do not: `processing` holds a lease expiry, `dispatched` holds a dispatch time, and `dead-letter` holds a failure reason and an attempt count. A four-value label forces those onto nullable columns that mean something in one state each. That is the shape `litespec/backend/domain#model-every-closed-set-as-a-type-hierarchy` removes everywhere else.
provisions.example: `OutboxState.Processing` carries one unexpired lease before a dispatcher records `OutboxState.Dispatched` or a retry state.

provisions.heading: Preserve Message Identity During Retry
provisions.evidence: Does any retry or replay path mint a new message ID? Check the dispatcher's retry and replay code.
provisions.statement: An outbox dispatcher MUST preserve message ID across retry and replay.
provisions.rationale: The target suppresses a repeat by recognizing its identity. That works only when every retry and replay carries the same message ID. A dispatcher that mints a new ID per attempt turns each retry into a new message the target processes again.

provisions.heading: Protect Active Worker Compatibility
provisions.evidence: Can every active Worker read the type and schema version of each new message the WebApi emits? Check the Worker's readers against those messages.
provisions.statement: New WebApi code MUST emit a message only after every active Worker can read its type and schema version.
provisions.rationale: WebApi writers and Worker dispatchers deploy independently, so a writer can run ahead of the oldest active Worker. When the writer emits a shape that Worker cannot read, those messages dead-letter on arrival through no fault of their own.

provisions.heading: Publish Backlog Indicators
provisions.evidence: Does the deployment publish all six backlog indicators? Check the metrics the Worker exports.
provisions.statement: An outbox deployment MUST publish pending count, failed count, oldest pending age, attempts, dispatch duration, and success rate.
provisions.rationale: Pending count, failed count, oldest pending age, attempts, dispatch duration, and success rate together show whether delivery keeps up. Growth in the backlog or its age reveals a stall, while duration and success rate reveal a struggling target. Without these indicators, the first sign of failure is a customer asking where their message went.

provisions.heading: Read Records from Every Coexisting Version
provisions.evidence: Does the dispatcher hold a reader for every application version that can coexist? Check the dispatcher's version selection and its tests.
provisions.statement: A deployed dispatcher MUST process records from every application version that can coexist during rollout or rollback.
provisions.rationale: During rollout and rollback, several application versions share one store and write different valid shapes into it. The dispatcher reads from every version that can coexist, or the deployment itself causes delivery failures. Each message record therefore carries its own shape version, and the dispatcher picks a reader from that value. Adding an optional member with a defined absent-value behavior needs no new version. Removing a member, renaming one, narrowing a type, or changing a discriminator needs a new version, and the reader for each version stays until no record carries that version.

provisions.heading: Reduce Polling When the Store Is Unavailable
provisions.evidence: Does every Worker loop back off and rate-limit its logging when the store is unavailable? Check the Worker's poll loop and its outage tests.
provisions.statement: A Worker MUST apply bounded backoff and rate-limited logging when its outbox store is unavailable.
provisions.rationale: A Worker that polls a dead store on a tight loop writes an exception per iteration, filling disks and log quotas before anyone reads the first one. Bounded backoff with rate-limited logging keeps the Worker alive and quiet until the store returns.

provisions.heading: Reject Independent Outbox Commits
provisions.evidence: Does any outbox writer use a separate connection or commit? Check each writer source and its path into the business session.
provisions.statement: An outbox writer MUST NOT use another connection or independent commit for required durable delivery.
provisions.rationale: Two commits on two connections can split around a crash: the business change persists while the message rolls back, or the message persists for a change that never happened. Sharing one PostgreSQL database does not make separate transactions atomic, so the message joins the business transaction instead.

provisions.heading: Release Claim Transactions Before Calls
provisions.evidence: Does any claim transaction stay open across a network call? Check the Worker's dispatch path.
provisions.statement: A Worker MUST NOT hold an outbox claim transaction open during a network call.
provisions.rationale: A network call to a slow target can last seconds or minutes. Holding the claim transaction open across that call pins database locks and connection slots, starving the Workers behind it. Releasing the claim first lets the database serve other work while the call runs.

provisions.heading: Report Store Outages Separately from Delivery Failures
provisions.evidence: Does every outbox metric use the right instrument type for store availability and claimed-message outcomes? Check the metrics the outbox publishes.
provisions.statement: A dispatcher MUST distinguish an unavailable outbox store from a failed claimed message.
provisions.rationale: A dead outbox store and a failed delivery ask for different recoveries: the first needs a database restored, the second needs one destination investigated. Each carries its own signal. The store's availability is a gauge the readiness endpoint reads, while a claimed message's outcome is a counter carrying the result, following [the OpenTelemetry metrics specification](https://opentelemetry.io/docs/specs/otel/metrics/). A single error counter cannot tell an operator whether to restore a database or investigate one destination.

provisions.heading: Requeue Expired Claims
provisions.evidence: Does every expired claim return to eligible work? Check the requeue query in the outbox store and its tests.
provisions.statement: An outbox store MUST return expired claims to eligible work.
provisions.rationale: A Worker can die between claiming a record and dispatching it. Returning expired claims to eligible work lets a live Worker pick them up. One crash then delays a message instead of losing it.

provisions.heading: Restrict Completion to Current Lease Owners
provisions.evidence: Does every record update check the current lease and fencing value? Check each update statement in the outbox store.
provisions.statement: A Worker MUST update an outbox record only while it owns the matching lease and fencing value.
provisions.rationale: A Worker that lost its lease through a crash, a pause, or an expiry can wake up after another Worker claimed the same record. Checking the lease and fencing value before each update stops the stale Worker from overwriting the current owner's result.

provisions.heading: Restrict Message Retry to Claimed Records
provisions.evidence: Does any retry or poison-handling path act on a record that holds no claim? Check the dispatcher's retry and poison code.
provisions.statement: A Worker MUST apply message retry and poison handling only to claimed outbox records.
provisions.rationale: Retry and poison handling act on a claimed message. When the store itself is down, no claim exists and no message waits for delivery. Running retry logic against the outage double-counts attempts and can dead-letter messages whose only fault was an unreachable store.

provisions.heading: Retry Delivery with Bounded Backoff and Jitter
provisions.evidence: Does every retry schedule use a bound, backoff, and jitter? Check the dispatcher's retry code.
provisions.statement: An outbox dispatcher MUST use bounded exponential backoff with jitter.
provisions.rationale: A failing target with ten thousand pending messages meets a retry storm when every message retries at once on a fixed interval. Bounded exponential backoff with jitter spreads those retries over time and caps the total, so the target recovers instead of drowning.

provisions.heading: Serialize Durable Messages
provisions.evidence: Does every pending durable message reach a serialized outbox record? Check the outbox writer and its record type.
provisions.statement: An outbox writer MUST serialize each pending durable message into an outbox record.
provisions.rationale: The command scope ends when the request ends. Dispatch happens later, in a Worker that never saw the request. Serializing the message into an outbox record gives that Worker everything it needs once the scope is gone.

provisions.heading: Set Delivery Alerts
provisions.evidence: Does every alert threshold sit in a setting record derived from a use-case delivery target? Check the setting records beside each use case.
provisions.statement: An outbox deployment MUST set alert thresholds as setting records from its use-case delivery target.
provisions.rationale: A shipment notice delayed an hour and a receipt delayed a week carry different business consequences. Each use case therefore sets alert thresholds from its own delivery target. Setting records hold those thresholds, so the alert fires when a delay passes what the business accepted.

provisions.heading: Skip the Outbox for Manually Repeatable Work
provisions.evidence: Does any reaction or job whose loss the operators accept still carry outbox records? Check the outbox records and the reactions and jobs they name.
provisions.statement: A project MUST NOT activate outbox for a reaction or job whose loss the operators accept and which they can repeat manually.
provisions.rationale: Outbox storage, dispatch, retries, and replay exist to prevent loss. A reaction or job whose loss the operators accept, and which they can repeat by hand, needs none of that machinery. Its `onFailure` states how failures are handled, and the use case page records that the loss is accepted.

provisions.heading: Stage After-Commit Effects in the Outbox
provisions.evidence: Does every raised domain event and translated integration event stage in the transaction of its aggregate changes, through the one global step? Check the pipeline's staging step and the outbox writes beside it.
provisions.statement: A use case MUST stage each domain event its act raises, and each integration event translating one of them, in the outbox in the same transaction as its changes.
provisions.rationale: A raised fact promises that what follows it will run: staged in the same transaction, the change and its message share one fate. One global pipeline step stages each raised domain event for the reactions of its module and each integration event whose record translates it, built from the domain event alone, as `litespec/backend/application#emit-declared-integration-events-after-commit` requires. No user code stages or publishes, so this step is the one stager. A message sent from memory instead would vanish on a crash between the commit and the send, and every follow-on act runs from a reaction to a staged fact.

provisions.heading: Stage Messages with Business Work
provisions.evidence: Does every pending durable message stage inside the scoped session of its aggregate changes? Check each command post-handler and its session.
provisions.statement: A command post-handler MUST stage pending durable messages in the same scoped business session as its aggregate changes.
provisions.rationale: The business change and its message share one fate: both persist or neither does. Staging the message in the same scoped business session as the aggregate changes puts both under one commit, so a crash can never leave an accepted change without its message or a message without its change.

provisions.heading: Stop Dispatch When the Host Is Not Ready
provisions.evidence: Does every unready host stop dispatching and polling stores that cannot serve requests? Check the readiness check and the Worker's dispatch loop.
provisions.statement: A Worker host exposing readiness MUST gate dispatch and stop polling stores that cannot serve requests.
provisions.rationale: A host that reports unready still serves traffic it cannot finish when its Workers keep polling dead stores. Gating dispatch on readiness stops that polling, so the host fails fast and recovers instead of churning against storage that cannot answer.

provisions.heading: Stop Retrying Permanent Failures at the Bound
provisions.evidence: Does every permanent failure stop at its retry bound with its investigation and replay data kept? Check the dispatcher's failure classification and its tests.
provisions.statement: An outbox dispatcher MUST classify permanent failures, stop automatic retry at its retry bound, and retain safe investigation and replay data.
provisions.rationale: Some failures never clear on retry: a deleted destination, a rejected payload, or a revoked credential. Retrying those forever burns resources and buries the real backlog. The dispatcher classifies them, stops at its retry bound, and keeps the evidence an operator needs to investigate and replay safely.

provisions.heading: Store Failure and Completion Evidence
provisions.evidence: Does every outbox record keep its last error summary and completion time? Check the record type and its update code.
provisions.statement: An outbox record MUST retain its last error summary and completion time.
provisions.rationale: When delivery stalls, the operator opens the record first. The last error summary says why the previous attempt failed, and the completion time says which records finished. Without that evidence on the record, each investigation starts from scattered logs instead.

provisions.heading: Store Required Message Fields
provisions.evidence: Does every outbox record carry identity, kind, type, schema version, time, payload, tenant, state, attempt, and next-attempt data? Check the outbox record type.
provisions.statement: An outbox record MUST contain message identity, kind, stable type, schema version, time, payload, tenant, state, attempt, and next-attempt data.
provisions.rationale: Three readers share the record: the dispatcher, the retry logic, and the operator. Identity and type route the message, the schema version picks its reader, time and tenant scope it, and state, attempt, and next-attempt data drive the retry. A field stored nowhere forces one of those readers to guess.

provisions.heading: Version Message Types
provisions.evidence: Does every outbox message carry a stable type name and an explicit schema version? Check each outbox message type.
provisions.statement: An outbox message MUST use a stable type name and explicit schema version.
provisions.rationale: An outbox record outlives the deployment that wrote it, so the dispatcher meets records written by several versions at once. A stable type name with an explicit schema version tells the dispatcher which reader parses each record. Without that pair, one shape change breaks every record written before it.

provisions.heading: Wait for Target Acceptance Before Completing
provisions.evidence: Does any outbox record mark completion before the target accepts the message? Check the Worker's completion code and the target's acceptance response.
provisions.statement: A Worker MUST NOT mark an outbox record complete before the target boundary accepts it.
provisions.rationale: Marking a record complete before the target accepts it declares a delivery that never happened. No retry follows, because the record looks done. The Worker therefore waits for the target boundary's acceptance before recording completion.

provisions.heading: Bound Plan Amounts in Settings
provisions.evidence: Does every plan allowance live in a setting the gated use case cites? Read the gated use cases beside their settings.
provisions.statement: Each amount a plan allows MUST live as a setting the gated use case cites.
provisions.rationale: An allowance buried in code changes only with a release, with each plan's number hiding in a different branch. A setting states the range, the setter, and the bound behavior, and the gated use case cites it, so raising a tier edits the setting instead of the code. `litespec/core/access#cite-the-setting-or-plan-behind-every-entitlement` requires the citation, and `litespec/core/use-cases#tie-every-setting-default-to-a-requirement` holds a commercial default to its requirement.
provisions.example: The export-row cap lives as `setting/spending.max-export-rows` with an operator-set value, and the export command cites it.

provisions.heading: Gate Behavior Through Permissions
provisions.evidence: Does every gated use case declare a permission in its grant that only an entitled plan grants? Read each gated use case's grant.
provisions.statement: A gated use case MUST declare a permission that only an entitled plan grants.
provisions.rationale: The permission chain already joins actors to use cases: the actor holds a role, the role allows a permission, and the use case declares it in its grant, as the [access page](../core/access.md) states. A plan grants its permissions through that chain, so entitlement is a grant like any other, not a second access system beside the first.

provisions.heading: Hide Unentitled Actions on Screens
provisions.evidence: Does any screen offer an action the acting plan does not entitle? Read each screen's actions.
provisions.statement: A screen MUST NOT offer an action the acting plan does not entitle.
provisions.rationale: The server refuses what the plan does not entitle, and the screen reflects that refusal before the call. A button for an unentitled action invites a failure the product already decided. Hiding or disabling the action shows each plan only what it may run.

provisions.heading: Record Each Plan Once
provisions.evidence: Does every plan have its own record with its entitlements? Read the requirement pages under `.litespec/intent/`.
provisions.statement: A consumer selecting `plans` MUST record each plan once with its name and entitlements.
provisions.rationale: A plan named in two places disagrees the day one updates without the other: one record promises what the gate refuses. One record per plan holds the name and the entitlements, so a plan change is one edit in one place.
provisions.example: The team plan's record names the export use case it unlocks and the row cap it allows.

provisions.heading: Refuse Runs Beyond Entitlement
provisions.evidence: Does every run past its plan end in the named refusal result? Read the use case tests for plan limits.
provisions.statement: A use case run past its plan MUST end in the refusal result the use case names for that run.
provisions.rationale: A run past its plan is a refusal like any other: it ends in the named refusal result with its stable code, as the [behavior page](../core/behavior.md) states. Callers branch on one code instead of guessing from an error page, and the code stays stable while prices and allowances move.

provisions.heading: Resolve the Acting Plan from Trusted Context
provisions.evidence: Does every acting plan resolve from verified subscription state rather than caller input? Read the plan resolution code.
provisions.statement: The product MUST resolve the acting plan from verified subscription state, never from caller input.
provisions.rationale: The plan decides what runs, so only verified subscription state resolves it: a plan the caller supplies itself is a choice, not a fact. The [multitenancy extension](tenancy.md) treats tenant identity the same way.

provisions.heading: Resolve the Acting Plan in the Authorization Pipeline
provisions.evidence: Does every use case find the acting plan in the authorization pipeline, or does a plan-resolution convention name where? Read the authorization pipeline and that convention.
provisions.statement: Resolve the acting plan where the pipeline authorizes the use case.
provisions.rationale: Authorization already runs in the pipeline with the actor and the target in hand. Resolving the plan there gives every use case the same answer from the same verified state, instead of each handler querying subscriptions its own way.

provisions.heading: Authenticate and Authorize Subscriptions
provisions.evidence: Does any connection test accept an unauthenticated connection, or a scoped subscription without an authorization check? Read the connection and subscription tests.
provisions.statement: A realtime server MUST authenticate each connection and authorize every user-, tenant-, or resource-scoped subscription.
provisions.rationale: A connection proves who the caller is; it says nothing about which user's, tenant's, or resource's updates the caller may hear. Each user-, tenant-, or resource-scoped subscription checks its own authorization, so one valid connection cannot listen in on another tenant's data.

provisions.heading: Bound Realtime Resources
provisions.evidence: Does each of the four deployment bounds have a setting record beside the deployment? Read the setting records and the deployment configuration.
provisions.statement: A realtime deployment MUST set four setting-record bounds: concurrent connections per host, receive message size, parallel invocations per connection, and client timeout.
provisions.rationale: Each open connection holds memory and each message costs CPU, so a flood of either starves the host. The deployment sets four bounds as setting records: concurrent connections per host, receive message size, parallel invocations per connection, and client timeout. Each value comes from the deployment's own connection count and message size and the observation behind it. [The platform's realtime security guidance](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/signalr/security) names the same settings.

provisions.heading: Declare Realtime Freshness
provisions.evidence: Does every realtime-served query declare immediate freshness on its output? Read the served query beside the realtime use case.
provisions.statement: A query served over realtime MUST declare a `freshness` object with `mode` of `immediate` on its output.
provisions.rationale: A realtime channel delivers an update seconds after the change, so the served query promises that speed on its output as `{"mode": "immediate"}`. Without that promise, a client reading the live value has no way to know how stale it may be.

provisions.heading: Measure Polling Before Choosing Realtime
provisions.evidence: Does every realtime use case page record polling behavior, measured cost, update target, expected connections, and recovery behavior? Read each realtime use case page.
provisions.statement: A realtime use case MUST document polling behavior, measured cost, update latency, expected connections, and recovery behavior.
provisions.rationale: Open connections cost memory, CPU, and operating attention on every host, so the team writes down what polling costs, what the update target requires, how many connections to expect, and how recovery works before choosing transport. The use case page carries that record, so a later reviewer sees which measurements justified the choice.

provisions.heading: Place Realtime Code at Outer Boundaries
provisions.evidence: Does any realtime transport code sit outside the documented boundaries without a realtime-placement convention? Check the WebApi, Infrastructure, and `lib/realtime/` folders.
provisions.statement: Keep hubs or endpoints in WebApi, publication adapters in Infrastructure, and browser connections under `lib/realtime/`.
provisions.rationale: Hubs, endpoints, publication adapters, and browser connections speak transport and provider detail, not business rules. Keeping them at the outer boundaries leaves each business feature owning only the narrow functions it calls.

provisions.heading: Reconnect and Refresh Authoritative State
provisions.evidence: Does every client reconnect with bounded backoff and refresh authoritative state after a gap? Read the recovery tests.
provisions.statement: A realtime client MUST reconnect with bounded backoff and refresh authoritative state after a connection gap.
provisions.rationale: Connections drop, and notifications sent during the gap are lost. Bounded backoff reconnects without hammering the server, and refreshing authoritative state after the gap replaces whatever the missed notifications would have changed.

provisions.heading: Record the Transport and Its Platform Support
provisions.evidence: Does every realtime use case page name its transport choice and expected hosted-platform support? Read each use case page.
provisions.statement: A realtime use case MUST record its transport choice and expected hosted-platform support.
provisions.rationale: Hosted platforms cap connection duration, idle timeouts, and transport upgrades, and each host caps them differently. Recording the transport choice with its expected platform support surfaces the mismatch before deployment instead of during the first long-lived connection.

provisions.heading: Reject Cosmetic Realtime Adoption
provisions.evidence: Does every realtime decision cite a measured update requirement? Read the use case page beside each realtime transport.
provisions.statement: A product MUST NOT activate realtime only to make an interface feel immediate.
provisions.rationale: Realtime transport that serves only a feeling of immediacy spends connection capacity and operating attention without moving any target. The extension asks for a measured update requirement first, so polling stays where polling suffices.

provisions.heading: Reject Unbounded Slow-Client Buffering
provisions.evidence: Does any server code path buffer a slow client's stream without a bound or backpressure? Read the connection and send code.
provisions.statement: A realtime server MUST NOT buffer an unbounded stream for a slow client.
provisions.rationale: A client that reads slower than the server writes grows its buffer without end, consuming host memory meant for every subscriber. Bounded buffering with backpressure disconnects or slows the laggard, so one slow reader does not starve the rest.

provisions.heading: Revalidate Long-Lived Access
provisions.evidence: Does any connection keep streaming after its token or session expires? Read the revalidation tests.
provisions.statement: A realtime server MUST revalidate long-lived access according to token and session lifetime.
provisions.rationale: A connection can outlive the grant that opened it: tokens expire, roles change, and sessions end. Revalidating access on token and session lifetime closes the connection whose grant died instead of streaming updates to a caller who no longer qualifies.

provisions.heading: Subscribe Through Narrow Functions
provisions.evidence: Does any feature subscribe to the raw connection instead of a use-case-specific function? Read each feature module's realtime calls.
provisions.statement: Let feature modules subscribe through narrow use-case-specific functions.
provisions.rationale: A feature touching the raw connection spreads subscription strings and payload shapes through business code. Narrow use-case-specific functions show each subscription's inputs and effects beside the feature that owns them.

provisions.heading: Tolerate Notification Ordering Differences
provisions.evidence: Does any duplicate or reordered notification leave client state wrong? Read the client state tests.
provisions.statement: A realtime client MUST safely handle duplicate and out-of-order notifications.
provisions.rationale: The transport can deliver a notification twice or deliver two of them out of order. A client that applies each notification as an absolute update corrupts its state on the first duplicate. A client built for repeats and reordering converges on the truth either way.

provisions.heading: Use Server-Sent Events for Notifications
provisions.evidence: Do all one-way notifications travel over server-sent events? Read the notification endpoints in code.
provisions.statement: A one-way server notification use case MUST use server-sent events.
provisions.rationale: A notification that flows one way, from server to browser, has no use for a bidirectional channel with groups and fallback. Server-sent events carry it over plain HTTP, which passes through proxies and firewalls without extra negotiation.

provisions.heading: Use SignalR for Interactive Messaging
provisions.evidence: Does every bidirectional use case run on SignalR groups, messages, and fallback? Read each use case's hub code.
provisions.statement: A use case requiring bidirectional messages, server groups, or transport fallback MUST use SignalR.
provisions.rationale: Two-way messages, server-managed groups, and transport fallback need a channel built for interaction, which one-way events cannot provide. SignalR supplies all three, so the use case that needs them takes SignalR instead of stretching events past their shape.

provisions.heading: Declare the Release Stage
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `project-invalid` for a `stage` selection with a missing or unknown `releaseStage`.
provisions.statement: A consumer MUST declare `pre-production` or `production` as its release stage in `.litespec/project.yaml`.
provisions.rationale: The release stage is a project fact, not a waiver from any rule, so it lives as data in the `stage` selection. `releaseStage` holds `pre-production` or `production`, while each deferral lives in its own waiver record. Without the declared stage, tools and reviewers have no way to tell which provisions the project owes today.
provisions.example:
A consumer with no customer data in any deployment declares the early stage.

```yaml
selectedExtensions:
  - id: stage
    criterion: no deployment holds customer data
    releaseStage: pre-production
```

provisions.heading: Defer Named Provisions Until Promotion
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` refuses a deferral waiver naming an unknown provision, and any deferral in `production`; `litespec model check` reports `waiver-expired` for a waiver past its `expiresOn`.
provisions.statement: A `pre-production` consumer MUST record each deferred provision as a gap waiver expiring at promotion with `closedBy` naming the promotion decision, with a `production` consumer carrying no deferred provision.
provisions.rationale: An early-stage deferral without a named end becomes permanent by neglect. Each waiver carries `kind: gap`, names the deferred provision in `covers`, sets the date its deferral ends in `expiresOn`, and names the promotion decision in `closedBy`, so promotion closes every deferral at once.
provisions.example:
Each deferral is a waiver covering its provision until promotion.

```yaml
type: waiver
id: waiver/compat-classification-until-promotion
title: Compat Classification Until Promotion
kind: gap
covers:
  - litespec/ext/compat#classify-breaking-contract-changes
paths:
  - apps/api/**
reason: No consumer reads the contract before the first deployment.
exit: Promotion to production ends the deferral and the classification applies.
expiresOn: 2026-12-01
closedBy:
  - decision/0001-promote-to-production
```

provisions.heading: Promote Through a Recorded Decision
provisions.evidence: Does the promotion decision stand in git before the first deployment holds customer data, with every deferred provision ended? Read the decision records under `.litespec/intent/decisions/` beside the deferrals they end.
provisions.statement: A consumer MUST record its promotion to `production` as a decision before its first deployment holds customer data, ending every deferred provision.
provisions.rationale: Promotion is the moment relaxed provisions end, and an unrecorded moment never arrives. The relaxed provisions last until somebody notices they never ended. The decision stands in git before the first deployment holds customer data, so the data sits under full rules from day one. The decision also covers the migration and cutover work that moves customer data into production.

provisions.heading: Apply Cross-Tenant Disclosure Policy
provisions.evidence: Does every cross-tenant response follow the documented not-found or forbidden policy? Check the API tests.
provisions.statement: A cross-tenant resource response MUST use the documented not-found or forbidden policy.
provisions.rationale: A caller that names another tenant's resource forces an answer: pretend it does not exist, or admit it exists and refuse. The product documents one policy and applies it to every cross-tenant response, so callers cannot probe for resources through inconsistent answers.

provisions.heading: Audit Actions Taken Under Delegation
provisions.evidence: Does every action taken under delegation record the delegation grant used? Check the audit records of delegated actions.
provisions.statement: An action that an actor takes under delegation MUST record the delegation grant used.
provisions.rationale: An acted-for action without a marker reads exactly like the delegator's own action, and a reviewer then cannot tell who actually acted. Recording the delegation grant used puts the acting party on the record beside the delegator. `litespec/ext/audit#mark-actions-taken-under-a-support-grant` states the same marker for administrative grants.

provisions.heading: Avoid Unplanned Isolation Models
provisions.evidence: Does every mixed isolation model trace to a decision with a data evolution plan? Check each mixed model beside its decision.
provisions.statement: A multi-tenant system MUST NOT mix isolation models without a decision and data evolution plan.
provisions.rationale: One part of the product on shared tables and another on separate databases answer which rows each tenant sees in two ways. Without a decision and a data evolution plan for the mix, backup, restore, and incident response each guess which guarantee covers which data.

provisions.heading: Declare Delegation Grants on Both Sides
provisions.evidence: Does every delegation declare both a delegator grant and an acting grant? Check each delegation's grants.
provisions.statement: A delegation MUST declare the delegator grant naming who may be acted for and the acting grant naming who may act.
provisions.rationale: Delegation lets one actor act for another. A grant on one side alone leaves the other side unreviewed, so the delegator grant names the role whose scope may be acted for and the permissions open to delegation, and the acting grant names the role permitted to act and the pairing it acts under. `litespec/core/access#grant-across-tenants-only-through-declared-delegation` requires both declarations.
provisions.example: A Claimwick assistant acts for a manager only where the manager delegation grant and the assistant acting grant both name the pairing.

provisions.heading: Define Tenant Isolation
provisions.evidence: Does the adoption decision name its isolation model with its guarantee and operating trade-off? Check the adoption decision.
provisions.statement: A multi-tenant decision MUST define shared-table, schema, or database isolation and state its guarantee and operating trade-off.
provisions.rationale: Shared tables, separate schemas, and separate databases isolate differently and operate differently, and each choice moves work between queries, migrations, backups, and scaling. Naming the model with its guarantee and its operating trade-off tells every later choice which isolation it can rely on.

provisions.heading: Isolate Administrative Cross-Tenant Access
provisions.evidence: Does every administrative cross-tenant use case require a platform-scope permission, with an audit record for every run? Check the use case permissions beside the audit trail.
provisions.statement: An administrative cross-tenant operation MUST require a permission the actor holds through a role whose scope is platform, writing an audit record.
provisions.rationale: Support and operations sometimes reach across tenants, and that exceptional reach needs exceptional control: a permission held through a role whose scope is `platform`, with an audit record for every use. Without both, one support login becomes an unscoped key to every customer's data. Grants that let one tenant act for another follow [Declare Delegation Grants on Both Sides](#declare-delegation-grants-on-both-sides) instead.

provisions.heading: Limit Every Delegation in Time
provisions.evidence: Does every delegation carry an expiry or a revocation path? Check each delegation record.
provisions.statement: A delegation MUST carry an expiry or a revocation path.
provisions.rationale: Without an end, a grant outlives its reason: the assistant keeps acting after the engagement ends, and nobody reopens the pairing because no date asks for it. An expiry ends the pairing on its date, and a revocation path ends it on demand. Either way, the end is stated beside the grant instead of left for an incident to discover.

provisions.heading: Pass Tenant Scope Explicitly
provisions.evidence: Is the Domain free of ambient tenant state reads, or does the tenant-scope convention name how the Domain receives scope? Check the Domain code.
provisions.statement: Pass tenant scope through Application messages or trusted ports rather than ambient Domain request state.
provisions.rationale: Domain logic that reads the tenant from ambient request state depends on the host to run at all, which complicates tests and reuse. Passing the scope through Application messages or trusted ports keeps the tenant visible in the call and the Domain free of host state.

provisions.heading: Protect Tenant Diagnostics
provisions.evidence: Is every error, log, metric, and trace output free of another tenant's identifiers and data? Check the output samples in the tests.
provisions.statement: Errors, logs, metrics, and traces MUST NOT reveal another tenant's business identifiers or data.
provisions.rationale: Errors, logs, metrics, and traces travel to people the API never authorized, on support screens, dashboards, and log stores shared across tenants. Scrubbing other tenants' identifiers and data from diagnostics keeps the disclosure policy whole past the API boundary.

provisions.heading: Prove Delegated Calls with Scenarios
provisions.evidence: Does every delegation prove an allowed call and a refused call with scenarios? Check the delegation scenarios.
provisions.statement: A delegation MUST prove an allowed call and a refused call with scenarios.
provisions.rationale: A pairing described only in prose hides where its grant stops: the allowed assistant and the uninvited one read alike. One scenario walks an allowed call, and another ends a call without delegation in the derived forbidden result, pinning the boundary as checked facts. `litespec/core/access#prove-hierarchies-derived-trust-and-delegation-with-scenarios` requires both scenarios.

provisions.heading: Record an All-Tenant Operation
provisions.evidence: Does every all-tenant run record the actor, operation, reason, tenant count, and reached tenant identifiers up to the adoption bound? Check the run records.
provisions.statement: An all-tenant operation MUST record actor, operation, reason, tenant count, and reached tenant identifiers up to the adoption decision bound.
provisions.rationale: A documented scope states what an operation may touch, not what one run touched, and the run is what a tenant asks about after an incident. An all-tenant run is also the one case where no single tenant's audit trail holds the whole event. [The OWASP logging guidance](https://owasp.org/www-project-cheat-sheets/cheatsheets/Logging_Cheat_Sheet) treats an administrative action over many subjects as one event to record: actor, operation, reason, tenant count, and reached tenant identifiers up to the adoption decision bound. When the `audit` extension is selected, the record is an audit record; otherwise it stays a standalone record.
provisions.example: A support export covering every tenant records the operator, the export, the tenant count, and the incident it was run for.

provisions.heading: Record Delegation Grants with Roles
provisions.evidence: Does every delegation grant sit on its role page, or where the delegation-records convention names? Check the role pages beside that convention.
provisions.statement: Record each delegation grant on the role page that holds it.
provisions.rationale: Each grant qualifies its role: the delegator role names who may be acted for, and the acting role names who may act. Recording the grant on its role page keeps the pairing beside the permission it extends, so a review reads both at once.

provisions.heading: Record the Tenant Adoption Decision
provisions.evidence: Does the tenant adoption decision name the source, storage model, isolation guarantee, administrative access, evolution path, and enumeration bound? Check the decision under `.litespec/intent/decisions/`.
provisions.statement: A consumer selecting `tenancy` MUST record a decision naming tenant source, storage model, isolation guarantee, administrative access, evolution path, and enumeration bound.
provisions.rationale: Tenant source, storage model, isolation guarantee, administrative access, and evolution path interact across every boundary, so one decision records them together before code assumes any of them. The enumeration bound caps how many tenant identifiers an all-tenant record lists.

provisions.heading: Reject Unrestricted Tenant Input
provisions.evidence: Does any tenant resolver path accept a tenant identifier from request data? Check the tenant resolver code.
provisions.statement: A tenant resolver MUST NOT accept an unrestricted tenant ID from request data.
provisions.rationale: Any caller can name any tenant when the tenant ID comes straight from request data. Rejecting unrestricted input keeps the request from choosing a data boundary outside its authenticated context.

provisions.heading: Resolve Tenant Identity from Trusted Context
provisions.evidence: Does every trusted host boundary resolve the tenant from an authenticated source? Check each boundary's tenant resolution.
