provisions.statement: A trusted host boundary MUST resolve tenant identity from verified claims, host mapping, or another authenticated source.
provisions.rationale: The tenant decides which data the request may touch, so only a trusted host boundary resolves it: verified claims, host mapping, or another authenticated source. An identity the caller supplies itself is a choice, not a fact.

provisions.heading: Scope Delegated Grants to Named Permissions
provisions.evidence: Does every delegation name its delegated permissions, with none opened to all permissions? Check each delegation's permission list.
provisions.statement: A delegation MUST name the permissions it delegates, never all permissions.
provisions.rationale: A delegation open to every permission hands the whole tenant to the acting party: one pairing meant for reading reports also moves money. Naming each delegated permission bounds the pairing to what the delegator intended. Each new permission then needs its own review in the pull request before the acting party holds it.

provisions.heading: Scope Every Use Case to Its Tenant Reach
provisions.evidence: Does every use case declare own, cross, public, or none in its access tenant scope? Check each use case's access declaration.
provisions.statement: Every use case in a multi-tenant product MUST declare its tenant scope as own, cross, public, or none in `access`.
provisions.rationale: The tenant scope bounds which tenant data the call may touch: `own` stays inside the caller tenant, `cross` reaches across tenants, `public` works beyond tenant boundaries, and `none` touches no tenant data. Without the scope, a read inside one tenant and a read across all tenants look the same. `litespec/core/access#scope-every-grant-to-its-tenant-reach` states the values.
provisions.example: A Claimwick expense report declares `own`, a finance search across companies declares `cross`, a public catalog declares `public`, and a health check declares `none`.

provisions.heading: Scope Persistence Sessions to the Tenant
provisions.evidence: Does every session-creation path resolve the tenant through its provider's own tenancy support? Check each provider's session creation.
provisions.statement: A multi-tenant persistence implementation MUST resolve its tenant at session creation through the selected provider's own tenancy support.
provisions.rationale: Session creation is the point that matters: a session opened without a tenant serves an unscoped next query. Resolving the tenant then, through the selected provider's own tenancy support, scopes every query the session runs, so no query carries the concern alone. Filtering per query instead leaves every new query one omission away from reading across tenants. The baseline provider resolves the tenant from the registered tenancy at session creation; an Entity Framework Core implementation resolves it when the context is created and applies it through a query filter convention.

provisions.heading: Scope Tenant Operations
provisions.evidence: Does every backup, restore, replay, deletion, export, support, and investigation procedure document one-tenant or all-tenant scope? Check each procedure.
provisions.statement: Backup, restore, replay, deletion, export, support access, and incident investigation MUST document one-tenant or all-tenant scope.
provisions.rationale: Each of backup, restore, replay, deletion, export, support access, and incident investigation touches more data than one normal request. Documenting each as one-tenant or all-tenant tells the operator how much data the run touches before it starts.

provisions.heading: Scope Tenant-Owned Records
provisions.evidence: Does every tenant-owned document, query, constraint, cache key, outbox record, reaction, job, export, and storage path in code carry tenant scope? Check the code for each kind.
provisions.statement: Every tenant-owned document, query, unique constraint, cache key, outbox record, reaction, job, export, and object-storage path MUST include tenant scope.
provisions.rationale: Tenants meet at documents, queries, unique constraints, cache keys, outbox records, reactions, jobs, exports, and object-storage paths. Leaving tenant scope out of any one of them discloses or mixes customer data through exactly that gap.

provisions.heading: Use One Tenant Accessor
provisions.evidence: Does every trusted host boundary read the current tenant through one accessor, or through the place the tenant-access convention names? Check the tenant accessors in code.
provisions.statement: Use one current-tenant accessor at the trusted host boundary.
provisions.rationale: Every boundary reads the current tenant. Two accessors can disagree about which tenant is current, so one accessor at the trusted host boundary gives every reader the same answer from the same trusted source.

provisions.heading: Use Typed Tenant Identities
provisions.evidence: Does every tenant reference carry the `TenantId` type, or another type the tenant-identity convention names? Check the tenant references in code.
provisions.statement: Represent tenant identity with a strongly typed `TenantId`.
provisions.rationale: A bare string tenant ID passes anywhere a string passes: into an actor field, an aggregate key, or a log line. A strongly typed `TenantId` turns each of those mistakes into a compilation failure instead of a production failure.

provisions.heading: Verify Actor and Target Tenancy
provisions.evidence: Does every protected operation refuse when the actor and target tenants mismatch? Check the authorization tests.
provisions.statement: A protected multi-tenant operation MUST confirm actor and target tenancy, with the needed permission held at the resolved scope and the target belonging to it.
provisions.rationale: Checking the caller alone leaves the target unchecked: an authorized caller can still name a resource from another tenant. The operation confirms both sides through one chain: the actor holds a role for the resolved tenant, the role allows the permission, the use case declares that permission in its grant, and the target belongs to the same scope.

provisions.heading: Bind Blazor Routes to Their Address
provisions.evidence: Does every route entry declare exactly one `@page` directive and read query values only through `[SupplyParameterFromQuery]` properties? Check the route files.
provisions.statement: A Blazor route entry MUST declare its address in one `@page` directive and take its query values as `[SupplyParameterFromQuery]` properties.
provisions.rationale: The `@page` directive is the one place the router reads an address, and a query property the framework fills keeps the input typed.
provisions.example: The Claimwick expense list declares `@page "/expenses"` and takes its page number as a `[SupplyParameterFromQuery]` property.

provisions.heading: Build Blazor Forms on the Shared Form Entry Point
provisions.evidence: Does every Blazor form build on the shared form entry point? Check the form components under `Routes/` and `Modules/`.
provisions.statement: A Blazor form MUST build on the form entry point of the shared package, which wraps `EditForm`.
provisions.rationale: One entry point gives every form the same field wiring and the same display for a refusal on its field.
provisions.example: The Claimwick expense claim form in `Modules/expenses/` uses the shared form entry point, with no `EditForm` of its own.

provisions.heading: Declare Blazor Outside the Controlled UI Contract
provisions.evidence: Does every Blazor frontend declare an entry point record naming Blazor and its replacement boundaries? Check the entry point records.
provisions.statement: A Blazor frontend MUST declare an entry point record naming Blazor and the boundaries that replace the controlled UI contract.
provisions.rationale: The controlled contract covers React and Svelte, so a Blazor frontend with no declaration reads as a frontend with nothing to check. Naming Blazor and its replacement boundaries reports it as a frontend with named replacements instead.
provisions.example: The Claimwick Blazor entry point record names Blazor and the shared package boundaries standing in for the controlled contract.

provisions.heading: Keep Blazor Test Mocks to the Owned Boundaries
provisions.evidence: Does any test replace the component model, `NavigationManager`, or the typed store? Check the test doubles.
provisions.statement: A Blazor test MUST NOT replace the Razor component model, the `NavigationManager` service, or the typed store.
provisions.rationale: Those three are the stack's own behavior, and a stand-in for any of them tests the stand-in instead of the screen.
provisions.example: A Claimwick expense list test renders the real component and seeds the typed store with claims.

provisions.heading: Keep Class and Style Bindings Out of Blazor Page Code
provisions.evidence: Do any Blazor components under `Routes/` or `Modules/` set a `class` or `style` attribute? Check the `.razor` files there.
provisions.statement: A Blazor component under `Routes/` or `Modules/` MUST NOT set a `class` or `style` attribute on any element.
provisions.rationale: The shared package's composites own spacing, size, and placement, so a class or style attribute in route code is a second layout that no composite answers to.
provisions.example: The expense total in `Routes/ExpenseList.razor` draws through a shared composite and sets no class attribute.

provisions.heading: Keep Layouts and Error Components Unmarked
provisions.evidence: Do any layout or error components carry a screen mark? Check `Frame/` and the route files.
provisions.statement: A Blazor layout component or error component MUST NOT carry a screen mark.
provisions.rationale: A layout or error component draws no screen of its own, so a mark on it links an address to a screen it does not show.
provisions.example: The Claimwick `Frame/MainLayout.razor.cs` carries no `<implements>` mark.

provisions.heading: Keep the Blazor Frame, Routes, and Modules
provisions.evidence: Does every Blazor file sit in `Frame/`, `Routes/`, or `Modules/`? Check the project tree.
provisions.statement: A Blazor frontend MUST hold the frame in `Frame/`, one `.razor` file per address in `Routes/`, and the use-case code in `Modules/`.
provisions.rationale: Three fixed roots let a reader and a tool find the frame, the addresses, and the use-case code in the same place in every Blazor frontend.
provisions.example: The Claimwick expense console keeps its frame in `Frame/`, its expense list route in `Routes/ExpenseList.razor`, and its expense use-case code in `Modules/expenses/`.

provisions.heading: Load Blazor Route Data Before Its View Renders
provisions.evidence: Does every route view wait for its `OnInitializedAsync` before drawing a read? Check each route file.
provisions.statement: A Blazor route entry MUST read each value it shows from the typed store in `OnInitializedAsync` before its view renders.
provisions.rationale: The typed store is the one shared cache on this stack, so a load there before the first render gives the view one answer for each read.
provisions.example: The Claimwick expense list loads its claims from the typed store, showing its loading state until the load finishes.

provisions.heading: Localize Blazor Copy Through a Pinned Dictionary Library
provisions.evidence: Does every copy call site use the pinned dictionary library with fill, plural, typed keys, and a declared fallback? Check the copy call sites.
provisions.statement: A Blazor frontend MUST resolve its copy through a dictionary library pinned in `packages.nuget` that meets the locale-dictionary contract.
provisions.rationale: A pinned library keeps every sentence in one dictionary per language, with the fill, plural, and fallback behavior the contract states.
provisions.example: The Claimwick console resolves the "Receipt required" sentence through its pinned dictionary library in every language it ships.

provisions.heading: Mark Each Blazor Route Entry with Its Screen
provisions.evidence: Does every route entry carry a screen mark on its partial class? Check each `.razor.cs` file under `Routes/`.
provisions.statement: A Blazor route entry MUST carry the `<implements>` mark of the screen it renders on its partial class in its `.razor.cs` file.
provisions.rationale: The mark links the address to the screen record the way a .NET handler carries its use-case mark, so the builder and the check read one link.
provisions.example: The Claimwick `ExpenseList.razor.cs` carries `/// <implements>screen/claimwick-app.expense-list</implements>` on its partial class.

provisions.heading: Name Blazor Drawings with the Visual Suffix
provisions.evidence: Does every file holding a custom drawing end with `.visual.razor`? Check the project tree.
provisions.statement: A Blazor file holding a drawing no composite makes MUST end with `.visual.razor`.
provisions.rationale: The suffix marks the one place outside the composites, so a reader and a tool find every custom drawing in one search.
provisions.example: The Claimwick receipt-scan preview lives in `ReceiptPreview.visual.razor`.

provisions.heading: Render Raw HTML Only Through MarkupString
provisions.evidence: Does every raw HTML write go through a `MarkupString` value? Check for `MarkupString` and raw markup in the `.razor` files.
provisions.statement: A Blazor component MUST pass raw HTML to the page only as a `MarkupString` value.
provisions.rationale: `MarkupString` is the one type Blazor renders without encoding, so every raw HTML sink is a type a search finds.
provisions.example: The Claimwick expense note renders its sanitized HTML through `(MarkupString)`, matching its recorded sanitization decision.

provisions.heading: Run Blazor Logic Tests on xunit.v3
provisions.evidence: Does every logic test run in a plain .NET test project on the pinned `xunit.v3`? Check the test projects.
provisions.statement: A Blazor frontend MUST run its logic tests as plain .NET test projects on `xunit.v3`, the version `packages.nuget` pins.
provisions.rationale: Logic tests need no browser, so a plain .NET runner keeps them fast, and one pinned runner keeps every test project on the same version.
provisions.example: The Claimwick expense total rule has its test beside its module, in an xunit.v3 test project.

provisions.heading: Show Route Failure in the Frame's Route Error Component
provisions.evidence: Does every route failure render through `Frame/RouteError.razor`? Check the route files and the frame.
provisions.statement: A Blazor route MUST show its failure through `Frame/RouteError.razor`, which draws the shared problem state.
provisions.rationale: One route error component gives every route failure the same recovery and the same problem state.
provisions.example: When the Claimwick expense list fails to load, `Frame/RouteError.razor` shows the problem state with its trace identifier.

provisions.heading: Use a Layout for the Blazor Shell
provisions.evidence: Does every route render inside the shell layout instead of repeating frame markup? Check the route files.
provisions.statement: A Blazor shell MUST be a layout component that inherits `LayoutComponentBase` and holds the frame every child route shares.
provisions.rationale: A layout draws the shared frame once, so each route draws only its own page.
provisions.example: In the Claimwick console, `Frame/MainLayout.razor` holds the navigation bar and cross-route values, and every expense route renders inside it.

provisions.heading: Validate Blazor Route Parameters Before Loading
provisions.evidence: Does every route load validate each address parameter before reading it? Check each route's load.
provisions.statement: A Blazor route entry MUST validate each address parameter before its load reads it.
provisions.rationale: An address comes from outside the component, so a load that reads an unchecked value fails inside the page instead of at its boundary.
provisions.example: The Claimwick expense list rejects a page number below one before reading the typed store.

provisions.heading: Add a Missing Composite to the Shared Package
provisions.evidence: Does every layout, control, or surface drawn by two pages live in the shared package exports? Look in the shared package exports and the drawing pages.
provisions.statement: A layout, a control, or a surface a second page needs MUST be added to the shared UI package, not written inside an application.
provisions.rationale: The second page needing a layout, control, or surface proves the piece is shared, not page-specific. Written inside one application, it is reviewed against one use, styled for one context, and invisible to the floorplans that would carry it, so the third page writes it a third time or copies the first copy. Adding it to the shared package puts it where every page finds it and where its design is judged against every use.

provisions.heading: Compose Composites in Page Code
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `ui-import-invalid` with the file and the refused import, tagged `[litespec/frontend/components#compose-composites-in-page-code]`. Run it at the consumer root.
provisions.statement: A component under a route or module folder MUST import only the shared package's documented entry points.
provisions.rationale: A composite fixes its layout and exposes only the inputs its job needs, so every page using it draws the same shape. If page code could reach past the composite to the primitives, one page would tune spacing or order for itself, and the next page would copy that tuning instead of the composite. The product would then hold as many layouts as pages.
provisions.example:
An expense section in the expenses app draws its facts, its state, and its commands through shared composites, declaring no element, class, or style binding.

```text
EntitySection "title"
  StatusBadge "state"
  DetailActions "commands"
```

The section imports only the shared package entry point, so the layout it draws is the one the shared package owns for every other entity page.

provisions.heading: Expose Card and Section Titles as Headings
provisions.evidence: Does every visible card, panel, and section title render as a heading at its correct level? Look in the route suite output, which resolves each as a heading.
provisions.statement: Render a visible card, panel, or section title as a heading at its correct level.
provisions.rationale: Some primitive sources render a title prop as a plain text element. That removes the title from the page outline, so screen-reader users lose it as a navigation point and the route suite's heading check misses it. Rendering the title as a heading at its correct level keeps the outline and the test in agreement.

provisions.heading: Keep Component Inputs Narrow
provisions.evidence: Does every composite receive values and callbacks instead of a client, a store, or an aggregate? Look in the shared package component signatures.
provisions.statement: A composite MUST receive the values and callbacks it needs, not a client, a store, or an aggregate.
provisions.rationale: The shared package serves applications it was not written against. A composite taking a client, a store, or an aggregate takes one application's data model as its input, so it fits no application with a different model, and a change to that model breaks the shared package. Values and callbacks keep the composite free of any application's shape: the page translates its model into plain inputs, and the composite renders what it is given.

provisions.heading: Keep Domain Values Typed Until Display
provisions.evidence: Does every display string come from the presentation boundary with an explicit locale and zone? Look in the presentation boundary and the components feeding it.
provisions.statement: Keep branded and generated identifier types until the presentation boundary converts them.
provisions.rationale: Dates, money, and status values carry meaning a display string loses: the instant, the amount, the code. Converting early spreads formatting choices across every component touching the value, and each one picks its own locale and zone. Keeping the typed value until the presentation boundary converts it in one place, with explicit locale and zone behavior.

provisions.heading: Keep Error Boundaries Scoped
provisions.evidence: Does every route failure render on the route error surface, and does every component boundary leave its surroundings usable? Look in the route error surfaces and the boundary components.
provisions.statement: Use the route error surface for route failure, and a component boundary only where recovery keeps the page usable.
provisions.rationale: An error boundary catching a failure with no recovery of its own hides the error and leaves the surrounding page broken but silent. The route error surface owns route failure, with a designed recovery. A component boundary earns its place only where the rest of the page stays usable without the failed part. Each stack page names the error surface for its stack.

provisions.heading: Keep Shared UI in One Package
provisions.evidence: Does every shared primitive and composite live in the shared package? Look in the workspace packages and the application sources.
provisions.statement: A workspace MUST hold its shared primitives and its composites in one shared UI package, with no copy in an application.
provisions.rationale: Two applications holding one primitive each drift at the first upstream update: one copy changes, the other still compiles, and nothing reports the split. The two applications grow into two visual languages. One package gives every application the same component, so one update reaches every screen.
provisions.example: The shared UI package holds the primitives in one folder beside the composites, and the composites import them.

provisions.heading: Make Touch Targets Fit a Finger
provisions.evidence: Does every pointer target on a touch layout measure at least 44 by 44 pixels? Look in the route suite output at the phone breakpoint.
provisions.statement: Size every pointer target at least 44 by 44 pixels where the primary pointer is coarse, and keep the 24 by 24 pixel minimum everywhere else.
provisions.rationale: The 24 pixel minimum of WCAG 2.5.8 stops a mouse user from missing a control, but a finger covers more than that: a staff member approving expenses on a phone taps Reject when they meant Approve. A larger target on coarse pointers keeps dense desktop tables while giving touch layouts room. The mobile stacks already size targets for a finger.

provisions.heading: Name Components for Their Role
provisions.evidence: Does every component name state the role it plays? Look in the shared package and module sources.
provisions.statement: Name a component for the role it plays, such as `ExpenseLinesSection` or `ReplayDeliveryDialog`.
provisions.rationale: A name such as `ExpenseComponent` or `GenericModal` describes the file type, so it fits any component and tells a searcher nothing. A name stating the role, such as `ExpenseLinesSection` or `ReplayDeliveryDialog`, tells the next author what the component does before they open it, and keeps two components for two jobs from sharing one vague name.

provisions.heading: Place a Drawing No Composite Makes in an Exception File
provisions.evidence: Does all custom styling sit in the files whose names mark drawings outside the composites, using only semantic theme tokens? Look in the exception files each stack page names.
provisions.statement: An exception file MUST declare custom styling only with semantic theme tokens.
provisions.rationale: Some drawings have no composite: a budget treemap, a receipt-scan preview, or a public marketing frame. Refusing them entirely would push the drawing into arbitrary values no token governs, which is harder to find and restyle than a declared exception. The exception file keeps the drawing visible: its name says the page draws outside the composites, and semantic tokens keep it inside the product palette. Each stack page names the file pattern marking an exception for its stack.

provisions.heading: Prefer a Composite over a Primitive
provisions.evidence: Does any page source import a primitive where the shared package provides a composite? Look in route and module imports.
provisions.statement: Page code MUST import a composite wherever the shared package provides one.
provisions.rationale: The composite holds the product's decision for one job: its layout, its behavior, and its tone. The bare primitive holds none of those, so a page importing it makes each decision again for itself, and two pages answer the same question two ways. Refusing the replaced primitive in page code sends every page to the decision already made.
provisions.example: Where the package provides a composite, page code uses it: `Card` becomes `Section`, `Table` becomes `DataTable`, `Badge` becomes `StatusBadge`, and `Input` and `Field` become the form fields.

provisions.heading: Render Control States
provisions.evidence: Does every control render disabled and pending, blocking a second submission while one is in flight and keeping recovery usable? Look in the shared package components.
provisions.statement: A control MUST render disabled and pending so that a second submission stays impossible while one is in flight and recovery stays usable.
provisions.rationale: A control with no disabled state invites a second submission while the first is still in flight, and a control with no pending state shows no sign anything is happening. Blocking the duplicate submission and keeping recovery usable gives the user one safe path: wait, or recover. State names are glossary terms, as under `litespec/frontend/components#render-data-states`.

provisions.heading: Render Data States
provisions.evidence: Does every data component render loading, empty, error, forbidden, and ready, with state names from the glossary? Look in the shared package components and the glossary.
provisions.statement: A data component MUST render loading, empty, error, forbidden, and ready.
provisions.rationale: A component rendering only its ready state leaves the user with a blank region while data loads, after it fails, or when there is nothing to show. Each missing state is a screen with no design and no test visiting it. Naming every arrival state up front gives each one a designed drawing. A route adds `not-found` under `litespec/frontend/rendering#define-every-route-state`, because a missing target resolves at the route rather than inside a component. Each state name is a term in the project glossary.

provisions.heading: Sanitize Untrusted Rich Content
provisions.evidence: Does every untrusted rich content render carry a recorded decision naming the sanitizer, the allowed elements and attributes, the link policy, and the test cases? Look in the decision records and the rendering components.
provisions.statement: A component MUST NOT render untrusted rich content without its recorded sanitization decision.
provisions.rationale: Rich content written by one user renders in another user's browser, so unsanitized markup is a script injection path: whoever writes the content runs code as every user. The recorded decision names the sanitizer, the allowed elements and attributes, the link policy, and the test cases, so the boundary stays explicit and reviewable instead of a different ad-hoc escape on every page.

provisions.heading: Show a Focus Indicator That Stands Out
provisions.evidence: Does every control show a focus indicator at 3:1 against its surroundings on keyboard focus? Look in the route suite output and the shared package's focus styles.
provisions.statement: A control MUST show, on keyboard focus, an indicator that reaches 3:1 contrast against the colors next to it, drawn in place of any platform indicator it removes.
provisions.rationale: WCAG 2.4.7 Focus Visible and 1.4.11 Non-text Contrast: a keyboard user finds their place on the page by the indicator alone, and a faint ring on a gray row is no place at all. The indicator shows on keyboard focus rather than on every click, so pointer users see no ring they did not ask for, and keyboard users always see one. The Approve button on an expense row, for example, shows a ring staying visible on the selected row's tinted background.

provisions.heading: Support Keyboard, Focus, Labels, and Announcements
provisions.evidence: Does every interactive UI support keyboard operation, visible focus, semantic elements, programmatic labels, and status announcements? Look in the route suite output.
provisions.statement: Interactive UI MUST support keyboard operation, visible focus, semantic elements, programmatic labels, and asynchronous status announcements.
provisions.rationale: Keyboard operation, visible focus, semantic elements, programmatic labels, and status announcements come free with platform controls, and all five break at once in a custom control. A mouse-only control locks out keyboard users, a missing label leaves screen-reader users guessing, and a silent update leaves anyone missing the screen change unaware of it. Starting from a platform control keeps all five properties, and the composite keeps them for every page using it. The five properties above are the ones a component can satisfy on its own. [WCAG 2.2](https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/) adds criteria that only a flow or a page can satisfy, so each route answers them where the criterion applies: | Criterion | Level | What it means for the UI | |:---|:---|:---| | 1.3.5 Identify Input Purpose | AA | A field collecting information about the user names its purpose, so the browser can fill it. | | 1.4.11 Non-text Contrast | AA | A control's boundary, state, and focus indicator reach 3:1 against what surrounds them. | | 2.2.2 Pause, Stop, Hide | A | Content that moves or updates on its own for more than five seconds can be paused. | | 2.4.11 Focus Not Obscured (Minimum) | AA | A focused control stays at least partly visible under a sticky header, bar, or panel. | | 2.4.12 Focus Not Obscured (Enhanced) | AAA | A focused control stays fully visible. | | 2.4.13 Focus Appearance | AAA | The focus indicator meets the stated minimum area and contrast. | | 2.5.1 Pointer Gestures | A | Every swipe, pinch, or multi-point action has a visible single-pointer alternative. | | 2.5.7 Dragging Movements | AA | Every drag action has a single-pointer alternative. | | 2.5.8 Target Size (Minimum) | AA | A pointer target measures at least 24 by 24 pixels, or meets the stated spacing. | | 3.2.6 Consistent Help | A | A help mechanism sits in the same relative order on every page that has one. | | 3.3.4 Error Prevention (Legal, Financial, Data) | AA | A command that moves money or changes recorded data can be reviewed, confirmed, or reversed. | | 3.3.7 Redundant Entry | A | Information already given in the same process is not asked for again. | | 3.3.8 Accessible Authentication (Minimum) | AA | Sign-in offers a path with no cognitive function test. | | 3.3.9 Accessible Authentication (Enhanced) | AAA | That path asks for no object recognition or personal content test either. | | 4.1.3 Status Messages | AA | A status that appears without a focus move reaches assistive technology through a live region. | The level column marks which target each criterion belongs to: AA for every project, AAA for a project that targets AAA.

provisions.heading: Use a Composite for a Content Image
provisions.evidence: Does every content image render through the shared image component with the text policy for its kind? Look in page sources for unwrapped images.
provisions.statement: An informative or decorative image MUST render through the shared image component, which owns its shape, its sizing, and its fallback.
provisions.rationale: An informative image needs meaningful alternative text, and a decorative image needs empty alternative text so assistive tools skip it. A source and label written directly in a page bypass both rules: the author tracks which kind each image is and writes the matching text, on every page. The shared image component owns the shape, the sizing, the fallback, and the text policy, so each image gets the handling its kind needs. The raw-element rule refuses unwrapped images in page code under `litespec/frontend/components#use-composites-for-layout-and-interaction-in-page-code`.

provisions.heading: Use Composites for Layout and Interaction in Page Code
provisions.evidence: Does any layout or interactive element appear in route and module sources? Look in route and module sources; each stack page names the refused elements and the composite each refusal names.
provisions.statement: A component under a route or module folder MUST NOT declare a layout or interactive element.
provisions.rationale: A raw element is only markup: no focus handling, no state behavior, and no accessibility wiring. Each page declaring one rebuilds behavior the composite already carries, usually worse. The lint refusal names the composite to use instead, so the author gets the replacement in the same message as the refusal, with no search through the shared package.

provisions.heading: Use Declared Visual Variants
provisions.evidence: Does every repeated variant use the shared variant helper with theme tokens? Look in the shared package components.
provisions.statement: A repeated component variant MUST use theme tokens through the shared package's variant helper rather than repeated literal values.
provisions.rationale: When each composite writes its own pixel values, colors, or conditional branches for one variant, the copies start equal and drift with every later edit, because nothing points the author at the other copies. The variant helper holds each variant once, in theme tokens, so a change to the variant reaches every composite using it, and every value stays inside the theme.

provisions.heading: Write No Class Name in Page Code
provisions.evidence: Does any class or style binding appear in route and module sources? Look in route and module sources; each stack page names the bindings its lint refuses.
provisions.statement: A component under a route or module folder MUST NOT declare a class or style binding.
provisions.rationale: The floorplan and the display composites own every spacing, size, and placement choice on a page. A class or style binding in route code is a second layout answering to no composite, and the next route copies it because it looks like the local way to draw. Two sources of layout disagree on the first redesign. Keeping classes out of page code leaves the floorplan as the one place a visual change lands. Each stack page names the class and style bindings this rule covers for its stack.

provisions.heading: Announce the Outcome of an Optimistic Update
provisions.evidence: Does every reconciled outcome differing from the shown value announce through a live region? Look in the route tests asserting the announcement.
provisions.statement: An optimistic update MUST announce its reconciled outcome through a live region when the server result differs from the value shown.
provisions.rationale: A rollback is a silent visual change: the shown value changes back with no event a screen reader announces. The user heard the optimistic value confirmed and hears nothing when it is withdrawn, so they act on a value the server refused. Announcing the reconciled outcome through a live region tells them what actually holds. [The ARIA live-region technique](https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG21/Techniques/aria/ARIA19) is the mechanism, and a test of the route asserts the announcement.

provisions.heading: Assign State to the Narrowest Owner
provisions.evidence: Does every value live with its narrowest owner: the query cache, the address, form state, or component state? Look in the state declarations.
provisions.statement: A value MUST live with the narrowest owner that can hold it: server data, then the address, then form state, then the component's own state.
provisions.rationale: A value with the smallest audience that can use it re-renders only the components needing it, and its changes stay visible where they happen. The [Where State Lives](#where-state-lives) concept names the order and what keeping a value above its owner costs.

provisions.heading: Brand Every Identifier from the Contract
provisions.evidence: Does every generated identifier carry its branded type, and does every route loader parse identifier parameters with the generated schema? Look at the generated client's identifier types and the route loaders.
provisions.statement: Give each identifier of the published contract its own branded type in the generated client, from the identifier's named schema component, and parse each route parameter that holds an identifier with the generated schema in the route loader.
provisions.rationale: The backend gives every identifier its own type, but a client typing every identifier as `string` lets a caller pass an expense identifier where a receipt identifier belongs. The call compiles and fails at runtime. A branded type per identifier turns that swap into a compile error. Deriving the brands from the contract's named identifier components needs no hand-kept list, so a new identifier is branded the moment the contract names it. Parsing route parameters with the generated schema gives a route the branded value at its edge. The brands stay until the presentation boundary converts them, as `litespec/frontend/components#keep-domain-values-typed-until-display` states.
provisions.example: `listExpenseReceipts(expenseId: ExpenseId, receiptId: ReceiptId)` refuses `listExpenseReceipts(receiptId, expenseId)` at compile time, and the receipt route reads `ExpenseIdSchema.parse(params.expenseId)`.

provisions.heading: Build a Form on the Shared Form Library
provisions.evidence: Does every form build on the shared package form entry point and its registered field components? Look in the form sources and the shared package form entry point.
provisions.statement: Build a form on the shared package's form entry point and its registered field components.
provisions.rationale: A form library used directly in every use-case folder gives each folder its own fields, its own validation wiring, and its own error display, and none of them knows how to show a refusal on its field. The shared package's form entry point and registered field components hold those decisions once, so every form validates, renders, and refuses the same way.

provisions.heading: Classify State
provisions.evidence: Does every aggregate introducing state name its durable, device-local, or derived classification? Look on the aggregate pages.
provisions.statement: An aggregate introducing state MUST classify it as durable, device-local, or derived.
provisions.rationale: The classification decides what happens to the state: durable state is persisted, versioned, and exported, device-local state is persisted but excluded from export, and derived state is never persisted. Without a declared classification each reader guesses, and a value the user made can end up unpersisted while a computed value ends up stored and stale.
provisions.example: The expense draft for the Rotterdam client visit is durable state, the device copy of the receipt photo is device-local state, and the expense total for EXP-1042 is derived state computed from its lines.

provisions.heading: Compose a Screen from Each Owner's Query
provisions.evidence: Does every screen showing several modules' data call each owner's query and join the answers itself? Look at each screen's `offers` beside the queries it calls.
provisions.statement: A screen that shows data from several modules MUST call each owning module's own query and join the answers itself, rather than call one query that reads another module's data.
provisions.rationale: A query existing only to show another module's data couples two modules for one page: the owner grows a reader method named for that page, and the reading module calls it in its query handler. The screen already knows both answers it needs, so it calls each owner's query side by side and joins the answers itself. Every query stays inside its own module, and the screen record's `offers` lists both use cases, so the composition stays visible in the model. Settled by [decision/0065-read-another-module-through-a-read-model](decision/0065-read-another-module-through-a-read-model).
provisions.example: A finance page showing each reimbursed expense beside its payout status calls the spending module's list-expenses query and the payout module's list-payouts query, and joins the two lists by expense identifier in the page.

provisions.heading: Generate the Client from the Published Contract
provisions.evidence: Is every client, type, schema, and operation option generated from the published OpenAPI document? Look in the generated client directory and the contract it names.
provisions.statement: A frontend MUST generate its client, types, schemas, and operation options from the API's published OpenAPI document.
provisions.rationale: A handwritten copy of a request, a response, or a schema drifts from the contract silently: the API changes, the copy still compiles, and the page sends a request the API no longer accepts. The failure surfaces at runtime, in front of the user. A generated client turns the same contract change into a compile error in every application at once, at every call site the change affects.

provisions.heading: Keep a Calendar Date Free of a Time Zone
provisions.evidence: Does every date with no time of day travel and display as a calendar date? Look in the date sends and renders beside the trip, payout, and billing reads.
provisions.statement: A date with no time of day, such as a trip day, a payout day or a billing month, MUST travel and display as a calendar date, never as an instant converted through a time zone.
provisions.rationale: A trip starting 8 October shows as 7 October to a reader west of the server once the date passes through a zone. The calendar date means the same day to every reader, wherever they sit. The frontend sends and renders the date itself, with no zone attached.

provisions.heading: Keep Schemas Use-Case Specific
provisions.evidence: Does every form schema and view model live in its owning use-case folder? Look in the use-case folders and the shared schema locations.
provisions.statement: Keep a form schema or a view model in its owning use-case folder, and let a second use case that needs the same shape declare its own.
provisions.rationale: A schema shared before its second use case exists is a contract written for one reader. The second use case then either contorts itself to fit or breaks the first reader by changing the shared shape. Keeping each form schema or view model in its owning use-case folder, with a copy where a second use case needs the same shape, keeps each use case free to change for its own reasons, as `litespec/backend/architecture#give-each-use-case-its-own-models` states for the server.

provisions.heading: Keep Secrets Out of Browser Storage
provisions.evidence: Is any refresh token, provider secret, or privileged credential stored in browser storage or a browser-visible variable? Look in the storage writes and the public variables.
provisions.statement: A frontend MUST NOT store a refresh token, a provider secret, or a privileged credential in browser storage or a browser-visible variable.
provisions.rationale: Local storage, session storage, IndexedDB, and a build-time public variable are all readable by any script on the page. A secret kept there is available to the same injected script the secret is meant to resist. Refresh tokens, provider secrets, and privileged credentials therefore stay out of the browser entirely. A preference the user chooses, such as a theme or a locale, is no secret and can be stored under a named key in the frame.

provisions.heading: Keep the Client Boundary in the Frame
provisions.evidence: Do all client configuration, problem mapping, and download helpers sit in the frame root instead of a use-case folder? Look in the frame root and the use-case folders.
provisions.statement: Place the client configuration, problem mapping, and download helpers in the frame root, keeping them out of every use-case folder.
provisions.rationale: The client configuration, the problem mapping, and the download helpers serve every use case. A copy in each use-case folder turns one change to the base address or the headers into an edit per folder, with the missed folder failing at runtime. The frame root holds them once, where every use case reaches them and none duplicates them.

provisions.heading: Keep the Session in an API Owned Cookie
provisions.evidence: Does any token sit in frontend sources instead of the API-owned HTTP-only cookie? Look in the API session handling and the frontend sources.
provisions.statement: The API MUST hold the browser session in an HTTP-only cookie, with frontend code holding no token.
provisions.rationale: Anything a script can read, any script on the page can read, including one an attacker injected. Tokens kept in frontend code or browser storage are therefore readable by the same attack the session is meant to resist. The API runs the authorization code flow instead and keeps the tokens encrypted in an HTTP-only cookie the browser sends on its own, so frontend code holds no token. A refused sign-in lands on a signed-out page rather than on an error, because the user is not signed in.

provisions.heading: Localize Copy Through Locale Dictionaries
provisions.evidence: Does every copy resolve through the locale dictionaries with fill, plural, chunking, typed keys, and a declared fallback? Look in the locale dictionaries and the copy call sites.
provisions.statement: Copy MUST resolve through locale dictionaries with fill and plural support, one chunk per language, and typed keys with a declared fallback.
provisions.rationale: One sentence written in two components drifts at the first rewording: the author finds one copy and misses the other. A dictionary per language keeps each sentence in one place, keyed by a typed key the compiler checks, with fill and plural support so variable content and counts render correctly in every language. One chunk per language keeps a user's download to the language they read, and a key the catalog lacks fails where the declared fallback says it fails instead of rendering a raw key.
provisions.example: A workspace carrying its own dictionary machinery still meets the same contract: typed keys, fill and plural support, one chunk per language, and a declared fallback.

provisions.heading: Make Optimistic Behavior Recoverable
provisions.evidence: Does every optimistic update declare its client identity, conflict behavior, rollback, and reconciliation path, and does every money, irreversible, or uncertainly authorized action wait for the server? Look in the optimistic update definitions.
provisions.statement: An optimistic update MUST declare its stable client identity, its conflict behavior, its failure rollback, and its reconciliation path.
provisions.rationale: An optimistic update shows a value the server has not confirmed. Without a stable client identity, the retry after a failure creates a duplicate. Without declared conflict behavior, two writers overwrite each other silently. Without a rollback path, a failed update leaves the shown value wrong. Declaring identity, conflict behavior, rollback, and reconciliation up front makes each case designed instead of improvised. Money, irreversible actions, and uncertain authorization skip optimism entirely and wait for the server result.

provisions.heading: Map Every Failure to One Problem Type
provisions.evidence: Does every failure render through the one problem type? Look in the frame problem mapping and the error surfaces.
provisions.statement: A frontend MUST convert every failure into one problem type, deciding from its code.
provisions.rationale: A raw response body carries whatever the API included: field names, internals, sometimes data kept from the user. Rendering it leaks that content, and each failure looks different, so the user gets no consistent recovery path. One problem type gives every failure the same shape: the page branches on the published code, so its decision survives a reworded message, and the problem carries the trace identifier support needs to find the request.

provisions.heading: Name the Zone for Every Timestamp
provisions.evidence: Does every timestamp formatter receive an explicit IANA zone resolved from the shown record? Look in the formatter call sites.
provisions.statement: A formatter rendering a timestamp MUST receive an explicit IANA time zone, resolved by the caller from the record the screen shows.
provisions.rationale: An instant from the API carries no zone, so a formatter left to pick one shows the user's own zone: a payout cut-off reads as midnight in the user's city instead of the office's. The caller resolves the zone from the record the screen shows: a record with its own zone states it, otherwise the account's zone applies, and an account choosing none falls back to UTC. Passing the zone explicitly names whose day each timestamp belongs to.

provisions.heading: Place a Field Refusal on Its Field
provisions.evidence: Does every field problem reach its field through the frame helper, with the form open until resolved or abandoned? Look in the forms and the frame helper.
provisions.statement: A field problem MUST reach the field it names through the frame's one helper, with the form staying open until resolved or abandoned.
provisions.rationale: A problem on its field shows the user what to fix where they fix it, through the frame's one helper. Above a long form, a summary links to each field in error, so a problem below the fold stays one tap away. The summary is a navigation aid added to the messages on each field, and it replaces none of them. The form stays open until each problem is resolved or the user abandons the form, so no input is lost to a closed dialog.

provisions.heading: Place a Refusal Beside What Was Refused
provisions.evidence: Does every refusal render beside the refused record or control, with the application's sentence and the code in the markup? Look in the screen's page files beside the refusing controls.
provisions.statement: A refusal MUST render beside the record or control that was refused, in the sentence the application holds for that code.
provisions.rationale: A refusal at the top of a page says that something failed but not what, so the user scans the page for the control that caused it. Beside the refused record or control, the refusal answers both questions at once. The sentence comes from the application's own dictionary for that code rather than from the response body, so the words stay consistent and translatable. The code in the markup lets a test provoke the refusal by name.
provisions.example: Submitting an expense above the receipt threshold with no receipt refuses with `spending.receipt-missing` under `result/submit-expense.receipt-missing`. The page renders the application's sentence for that code beside the Submit control, carries the code in the markup so a test provokes it by name, and keeps the trace identifier in the detail in copyable form.

provisions.heading: Read a Permission from the Session
provisions.evidence: Does every offered command stay within the permissions the session actor holds at the record scope? Look in the page command guards and the session shape.
provisions.statement: A page MUST offer a command only when the session actor holds its permissions at the record's scope, with the API deciding every command.
provisions.rationale: Permissions are the project's permission records: an actor holds a role, a role allows permissions, and a use case needs permissions. The page reads the permissions the signed-in actor holds from the session the API returns, and offers only the commands those permissions allow at the record's scope. The user meets no offer ending in a refusal. The API still decides every command, so an action offered in error is refused rather than executed.

provisions.heading: Regenerate the Client Rather Than Editing It
provisions.evidence: Does the committed client match fresh generation output, with no hand edits below the generated directory? Look in the generated directory and the generator command.
provisions.statement: Regenerate the client from the document, and edit nothing under the generated directory.
provisions.rationale: A hand edit under the generated directory works until the next generation overwrites it: the change appears sound and then silently disappears. Regenerating from the document keeps the committed output provably equal to the contract. A reviewer regenerates and compares, and any difference is either a contract change or an edit belonging outside the generated directory.

provisions.heading: Route a Personal Value in a Header
provisions.evidence: Does every person-naming value travel in a contract-declared header instead of the query string? Look in the contract headers and the call sites.
provisions.statement: A value naming a person MUST travel in a request header rather than the query string, with the contract declaring the header each operation reads.
provisions.rationale: A query string leaks three ways: proxies log it, the browser keeps it in history, and the next page the user opens receives it as the referrer. A value naming a person therefore travels in a request header the contract declares per operation, reaching the API without landing in any of those places. The address keeps its own copy for filters and paging, so a filtered list stays a link somebody can share.

provisions.heading: Route Use Cases Through Application
provisions.evidence: Does every screen and component invoke an Application handler carrying a `Command` or `Query` role suffix, instead of composing Domain calls or writing storage? Look in the screen and component sources.
provisions.statement: A frontend MUST invoke an Application handler carrying a `Command` or `Query` role suffix for each use case rather than compose Domain calls or write storage.
provisions.rationale: The handler is the one place a use case exists: its validation, its rules, and its result. A screen or component composing its own sequence of Domain calls and storage writes creates a second definition that no record names and no test pins down. Routing every use case through a handler keeps the screen or component a caller and the handler the definition.
provisions.example: The expense screen invokes the submit-expense Application handler for EXP-1042 rather than composing the Domain expense calls and writing the expense store itself.

provisions.heading: Set the Write Marker on Every Request
provisions.evidence: Does every write carry the configured marker header of the form `X-<Project>-Request`? Look in the client configuration and the API write acceptance.
provisions.statement: A client MUST send its marker header on every write, with the API accepting a cookie-authenticated write only when it carries that header.
provisions.rationale: A browser attaches its cookies to a cross-site request on its own, so the cookie alone cannot tell the page's own write from a forged post submitted from another site. The marker header tells them apart: the page's client adds it to every write, and a page on another site adds no custom header without a preflight, which the API grants to no foreign origin. The API therefore accepts a cookie-authenticated write only when the header is present. The header name varies by project, so configuration owns it rather than code; it has the form `X-<Project>-Request` with the value `1`.

provisions.heading: Update the Cache a Command Changed
provisions.evidence: Does every successful command invalidate exactly the queries whose answers it changed? Look in the command call sites and the cache keys.
provisions.statement: A successful command MUST invalidate every query whose answer it changed, and no other query.
provisions.rationale: A page renders the cached answer, not a new request, so the query cache owns freshness. A command leaving a changed query cached shows the old record until something else happens to refetch, and the user's own write appears to have no effect. Invalidating exactly the queries the command changed refreshes what changed; invalidating more costs a needless request per affected page.
provisions.example: The generated client holds both sides of one write: the expenses route calls the submit operation with the expense values, and the list reads through the list operation. After the submit succeeds, the page invalidates the list query and no other query, so the list shows the new expense without refetching unrelated pages.

provisions.heading: Use One Configured Client per Application
provisions.evidence: Does every read and write pass through the one configured client? Look in the frame client configuration and the call sites.
provisions.statement: A frontend MUST configure the generated client once, and route every read and write through it.
provisions.rationale: The configured client owns four decisions: the base address, the credentials, the headers, and the mapping from a failure to a problem. A call building its own request opts out of all four at once: it can point at the wrong host, miss the session cookie, skip the write marker, and surface a raw failure outside the page's problem shape. Routing every read and write through the one client keeps those decisions in one place.

provisions.heading: Validate a Form with the Generated Schema
provisions.evidence: Does every form validate against the generated request schema extended with application rules? Look in the form sources and the generated schemas.
provisions.statement: A form MUST validate against the generated schema for its request body, extended with the application's own rules rather than replaced by them.
provisions.rationale: The generated schema states what the API accepts, so it holds even where the browser accepts more. Validating the form against it refuses bad input before the request leaves the page. The application extends the schema with the message shown for each rule and any rule beyond the contract's reach, rather than replacing it, so the form refuses everything the API refuses.

provisions.heading: Accept App Links in the Host Activity
provisions.evidence: Does the host Activity receive app links on both a cold start and while running? Check the intent filter and both overrides.
provisions.statement: The host Activity MUST receive app links in `OnCreate` and `OnNewIntent`, through an `IntentFilter` with `AutoVerify` set.
provisions.rationale: Handling both entry points lets a cold start and a link that arrives while the app runs open the same screen, and `AutoVerify` lets the platform open the app instead of a browser.
provisions.example: A link to `https://claimwick.example/claims/` opens the claim screen its path names, whether the app was closed or open.

provisions.heading: Apply System Insets to Each Screen
provisions.evidence: Does every screen keep its controls and text clear of the system bars and cutouts? Check the screen layouts and the inset handling.
provisions.statement: A screen MUST apply the system bar and display cutout insets it reads from `WindowInsets` to its controls and text.
provisions.rationale: The window supplies these insets, so reading them from `WindowInsets` keeps controls and text clear of the bars and cutouts on every device.
provisions.example: The Claimwick expense claim screen pads its submit button by the system bar inset while its background draws full bleed.

provisions.heading: Declare Android Outside the Controlled UI Contract
provisions.evidence: Does every Android frontend declare an entry point record naming Android and its replacement boundaries? Check the entry point records.
provisions.statement: An Android frontend MUST declare an entry point record naming Android and the boundaries that replace the controlled UI contract.
provisions.rationale: The controlled contract covers React and Svelte, so an Android frontend with no declaration reads as a frontend with nothing to check. Naming Android and its replacement boundaries reports it as a frontend with named replacements instead.
provisions.example: The Claimwick Android entry point record names Android and the native view review standing in for the controlled contract.

provisions.heading: Hold One Navigation Controller in the Platform Project
provisions.evidence: Does navigation run through the one controller owned by the host Activity, with no screen navigating on its own? Check the screen classes and the host Activity.
provisions.statement: The Android app MUST hold its navigation controller in one class in the platform project, owned by the host Activity.
provisions.rationale: One controller holds the current screen, the open overlay, and the history, so no screen navigates on its own.
provisions.example: The Claimwick host Activity creates the one controller class, and every expense screen raises events to it.

provisions.heading: Keep Android Core Test Mocks to the Owned Boundaries
provisions.evidence: Does any core test replace a Domain type or an Application handler? Check the test doubles.
provisions.statement: A core test MUST NOT replace the Domain types or the Application handlers it proves.
provisions.rationale: A stand-in for the code under test proves the stand-in, so the test reaches the rule only through the real types and handlers.
provisions.example: The Claimwick expense claim test builds a real Domain claim and calls the real submit handler, replacing only the platform storage adapter.

provisions.heading: Keep Hosts and Failure Views Unmarked
provisions.evidence: Do any host Activities or failure views carry a screen mark? Check the platform project.
provisions.statement: A host Activity or a failure view MUST NOT carry a screen mark.
provisions.rationale: A host or failure view draws no screen of its own, so a mark on it links an address to a screen it does not show.
provisions.example: The Claimwick host Activity class carries no `<implements>` mark.

provisions.heading: Keep Screen Styles in Resources
provisions.evidence: Does every screen take its colors and text styles from `Resources/values/styles.xml`, with none set in code? Check the screen classes.
provisions.statement: A screen MUST take its colors and text styles from `Resources/values/styles.xml` and set no style value in code.
provisions.rationale: Resources hold every color and text style in one place, and a screen that sets a value in code is a second style that no resource answers to.
provisions.example: The Claimwick expense total uses the `TotalText` style from `Resources/values/styles.xml`, setting no color in its screen class.

provisions.heading: Keep the Android Frame, Routes, and Modules
provisions.evidence: Does every screen class sit under `Screens/` and call Application handlers instead of holding use-case logic? Check the platform project and the core projects.
provisions.statement: An Android frontend MUST hold its frame in the host code of the platform project, its routes as screen classes under `Screens/`, and its use-case code as Application handlers.
provisions.rationale: Three fixed homes let a reader and a tool find the frame, the screens, and the use-case code in the same place in every Android app.
provisions.example: The Claimwick Android app keeps its navigation host in `Claimwick.Android`, its expense list screen in `Screens/Expenses/`, and its expense handlers in the Application project.

provisions.heading: Mark Each Android Screen with Its Screen Record
provisions.evidence: Does every screen class under `Screens/` carry its screen mark? Check each screen file.
provisions.statement: A screen class under `Screens/` MUST carry the `<implements>` mark of the screen it renders, in the form the .NET stack states.
provisions.rationale: The mark links the screen to its record the way a .NET handler carries its use-case mark, so the builder and the check read one link.
provisions.example: The Claimwick `ExpenseListScreen` carries `/// <implements>screen/claimwick-app.expense-list</implements>`.

provisions.heading: Read Android Copy Through the Generated Resource Class
provisions.evidence: Does every screen read its copy through the generated `Resource` class? Check the screen classes and the layouts.
provisions.statement: A screen MUST read every copy string through the generated `Resource` class, with its fallback in `Resources/values/strings.xml`.
provisions.rationale: The generated class gives every copy key a typed name, and the default values folder gives every key a fallback when a language lacks it.
provisions.example: The Claimwick expense list reads its empty-state sentence as `Resource.String.ExpenseListEmpty`, with the Spanish file supplying the translation.

provisions.heading: Request Audio Focus Before Playing Sound
provisions.evidence: Does every screen that plays sound request audio focus first and pause on focus loss? Check the playback call sites.
provisions.statement: A screen that plays sound MUST request audio focus with an `AudioFocusRequest` before it plays, and pause when focus is lost.
provisions.rationale: One speaker serves every app, so the platform arbitrates only the apps that ask for focus, and pausing on loss yields to navigation prompts and calls.
provisions.example: The Claimwick confirmation chime plays only after the app holds audio focus, and a phone call pauses it.

provisions.heading: Request Permissions at the Point of Use
provisions.evidence: Is every runtime permission requested through `RequestPermissions` when its action starts, none in `OnCreate`? Check the host Activity and the action handlers.
provisions.statement: The Android app MUST request each runtime permission through `RequestPermissions` when the action that needs it starts, never in `OnCreate`.
provisions.rationale: A request at the point of use arrives when the visitor knows what it is for, and the same permission answers a question the visitor just asked.
provisions.example: The Claimwick app requests the camera permission when the visitor taps Scan receipt, not at launch.

provisions.heading: Route the Back Gesture Through the Activity Dispatcher
provisions.evidence: Does every back gesture reach the controller through the Activity's dispatcher, leaving the app only from the first screen? Check the host Activity and the controller.
provisions.statement: The host Activity MUST deliver the system back gesture to the navigation controller through its `OnBackInvokedDispatcher`.
provisions.rationale: The dispatcher is the platform's own path for the back signal, so predictive back reaches the controller as the same overlay-then-screen-then-leave order on every screen.
provisions.example: On the Claimwick expense detail screen, a back gesture closes an open overlay first, then steps back to the expense list.

provisions.heading: Run Android Core Tests on xunit.v3
provisions.evidence: Does every core test run in a plain .NET test project on the pinned `xunit.v3`, with no emulator? Check the core test projects.
provisions.statement: The Android app MUST run its core tests as plain .NET test projects on `xunit.v3`, the version `packages.nuget` pins.
provisions.rationale: Core tests need no emulator, so a plain .NET runner keeps them fast, and one pinned runner keeps every core project on the same version.
provisions.example: The Claimwick expense claim rule has its test in an xunit.v3 project beside the Domain project it proves.

provisions.heading: Store Navigation State in the Activity Bundle
provisions.evidence: Does the host Activity save and restore the controller's navigation state through its `Bundle`? Check the host Activity and the controller.
provisions.statement: The host Activity MUST save the navigation controller's state in its `Bundle` from `OnSaveInstanceState` and restore it in `OnCreate`.
provisions.rationale: The platform ends the process in the background when memory runs short, and the saved bundle returns the visitor to the same screen with the same overlay and history.
provisions.example: When the platform ends the Claimwick process, the app reopens on the expense detail screen with its overlay still open.

provisions.heading: Store Persisted State in App-Private Storage
provisions.evidence: Does all persisted state and user media live under `Context.FilesDir`, written atomically? Check the storage adapters.
provisions.statement: Persisted state and user media MUST live under `Context.FilesDir`, written atomically.
provisions.rationale: The app's own sandbox keeps the data away from other apps and the shared media library, and an atomic write keeps the previous complete file if a write stops midway.
provisions.example: The Claimwick receipts the visitor adds are copied into the app's files directory, replacing their previous copy only after the new one is whole.

provisions.heading: Use the System Pickers for Media
provisions.evidence: Does every screen pick photos and files through the system pickers, with no storage permission requested for it? Check the picking call sites and the manifest.
provisions.statement: A screen MUST pick photos through the Photo Picker action `android.provider.action.PICK_IMAGES` and files through `android.intent.action.OPEN_DOCUMENT`.
provisions.rationale: Both pickers grant access to the chosen items only, so the app needs no storage permission to read one receipt.
provisions.example: In the Claimwick app, adding a receipt photo opens the Photo Picker, and the visitor's choice is the only image the app receives.

provisions.heading: Call the Server Only Through the Generated Client
provisions.evidence: Does every backend call in a `server` app go through the generated client in `{ProjectName}.Client`? Check the backend call sites.
provisions.statement: A `server` consumer's app MUST call the backend only through the generated client in `{ProjectName}.Client`.
provisions.rationale: The generated client owns the base address, the credentials, the headers, and the mapping from a failure to a result. A call that builds its own request opts out of all four at once: it can point at the wrong host, miss the session, and surface a raw failure outside the handler's result shape. Routing every backend call through the one client keeps those decisions in one place. This realizes litespec/frontend/data#use-one-configured-client-per-application.

provisions.heading: Copy Picked Media into the App
provisions.evidence: Does every media import copy the media into app-private storage instead of storing the picker's URI? Check the media imports.
provisions.statement: Media picked from the device MUST be copied into app-private storage on import rather than kept as a reference to the picker's URI.
provisions.rationale: The platform can revoke a picker's URI when the picker closes, and the source file can move or vanish. A screen holding only the URI shows a broken image after either. Copying the media into app-private storage on import keeps the app's copy under the app's own control.

provisions.heading: Keep Persisted State in App-Private Storage
provisions.evidence: Does all persisted state and user-added media live in app-private storage, written through a temporary file? Check the storage writes.
provisions.statement: Persisted state and media the user adds MUST live in the app's private storage, written atomically.
provisions.rationale: App-private storage keeps the user's data inside the app's own sandbox, away from other apps and from the shared media library. A crash mid-write leaves a half-written file, so each write lands in a temporary file that then replaces the target, keeping the previous complete file until the new one is whole. Media the user adds travels with the state that references it, so an export or a reinstall keeps both together.
provisions.example: A filed Claimwick expense report persists as versioned durable state in app-private storage, with its photographed receipts beside it in the same private files.

provisions.heading: Load Persisted State Once
provisions.evidence: Does all persisted state load once at startup into the typed store, with screens showing a loading state until it is ready? Check the startup sequence and the screen loading states.
provisions.statement: Persisted state MUST load once at startup into a typed store that screens read from, with screens showing a loading state until it is ready.
provisions.rationale: Storage reads are slow and can fail, so the product reads once at startup into a typed store that screens read from. A screen that reads storage on render pays an input-output call per frame and can render half-loaded state. A screen renders its loading state until the store finishes loading, so it never shows an unloaded store as ready.

provisions.heading: Refuse Commands While Offline
provisions.evidence: While offline, does every screen show its failure state and queue only what a recorded local convention names with its replay order? Check the command call sites and the offline screens.
provisions.statement: While the network is unavailable, a screen shows its failure state and queues no command; the user retries the command in the foreground when the network returns.
provisions.rationale: A command queued offline runs later against state the user cannot see, so an expense submitted on a train can land after its trip closed or its approval policy changed. Showing the failure state keeps the refusal on the screen that caused it, and queuing nothing keeps every command tied to the screen that sent it. A project that needs offline capture writes its own convention with its replay rules, instead of letting each screen improvise a queue.
provisions.example: With no network, filing expense EXP-1042 for the Rotterdam client visit shows the failure state on the expense screen and sends nothing; the user submits the expense again when the network returns.

provisions.heading: Return Every Refusal in a Typed Result
provisions.evidence: Does every handler return a typed union of success and each named refusal, with every screen mapping each refusal to a message? Check the handler result types and the screens.
provisions.statement: A handler MUST return a typed result union covering success and each named refusal, with each screen mapping every refusal to a message.
provisions.rationale: Signaling a refusal through `null`, an empty collection, or a bare boolean tells the caller that something was refused but not what. Every caller then guesses, and two callers guess differently. A typed result union names success and each refusal, so each screen maps every refusal to the message the application holds for it. This realizes litespec/frontend/data#map-every-failure-to-one-problem-type.

provisions.heading: Declare Only Used Permissions
provisions.evidence: Does every permission in the app manifest serve a current feature? Check the app manifest beside the features.
provisions.statement: The app manifest MUST declare only the permissions the app's current features use.
provisions.rationale: Each declared permission is a promise the app's features must keep: a declaration without a feature asks for the trust nothing uses. Stale declarations accumulate as features leave, and each one asks the user a question no feature needs. Declaring only what current features use keeps the manifest an honest list of the app's needs.

provisions.heading: Hold Audio Focus While Playing Sound
provisions.evidence: Does every audible playback request audio focus first and pause on focus loss? Check the playback code.
provisions.statement: An app playing audible sound MUST request audio focus and pause when it loses focus.
provisions.rationale: One speaker serves every app, so playback without focus talks over navigation prompts, calls, and other players. Requesting focus before playing lets the platform arbitrate between them. Pausing on focus loss yields to whatever took it, and resuming waits for focus to return rather than grabbing it back.

provisions.heading: Keep Device Work in the Foreground
provisions.evidence: Does every background service, scheduled job, and push handler have a project decision naming it? Check the background work beside the decision records.
provisions.statement: Run no background service, scheduled job, or push handler without a project decision naming it.
provisions.rationale: Background work runs where the user cannot see it, spending battery and data on a schedule the app chose. A project decision naming the service, job, or handler records why the work cannot wait for the foreground and what it costs. Without that decision, every device feature runs while the app is visible and stops with it.

provisions.heading: Pause Media in the Background
provisions.evidence: Does all sound and video pause when the app leaves the foreground and resume only on return? Check the lifecycle handling.
provisions.statement: Sound and video MUST pause when the app leaves the foreground and resume only when it returns.
provisions.rationale: An app the user cannot see goes quiet: background sound from a hidden app reads as a bug, and background video decodes frames nobody watches. Pausing when the app leaves the foreground frees the speaker and the decoder for the app now in front, and resuming only on return keeps playback tied to the visible screen.

provisions.heading: Pick Media Through Permissionless System Pickers
provisions.evidence: Does every photo and file pick go through the permissionless system picker where the platform offers one? Check the picking call sites.
provisions.statement: An app MUST pick photos and files through the system picker that needs no storage permission when the platform offers one.
provisions.rationale: A permissionless system picker shows the user exactly what the app receives: the chosen items and nothing else. Requesting broad storage access instead asks for the whole library to read one photo, which the user has good reason to refuse. Using the permissionless picker where the platform offers one keeps the app's access to what the user chose.

provisions.heading: Request a Permission at the Point of Use
provisions.evidence: Is every runtime permission requested from the action that needs it, none at launch? Check the permission requests.
provisions.statement: A runtime permission MUST be requested when the user starts the action that needs it, never at launch.
provisions.rationale: Asked at launch, a permission arrives before the user knows what it is for, so the safe answer is no. Asked when the user starts the action that needs it, the same permission answers a question the user just asked. Each request names the feature waiting on it, so refusing it disables that feature rather than the app.

provisions.heading: Draw Edge to Edge with Insets
provisions.evidence: Does every screen draw edge to edge with its controls and text inside the system bar and cutout insets? Check the screen layouts.
provisions.statement: Screens MUST draw under the system bars and apply the system bar and cutout insets to their controls and text.
provisions.rationale: Drawing under the system bars uses the whole display, but controls and text under a bar or a cutout are unreadable and untappable. Applying the system bar and cutout insets moves controls and text into the visible area while backgrounds keep the full-bleed look. Each stack page names the inset source for its platform.

provisions.heading: Follow the System Back Gesture
