provisions.evidence: Does the back gesture close the overlay first, step back one screen, and leave only from the first screen? Check the back handling.
provisions.statement: The system back gesture MUST close the open overlay first, then step back one screen, and leave the app only from the first screen.
provisions.rationale: Users learn one back behavior per platform: the gesture dismisses what is on top before it leaves where they are. An app that leaves from a deeper screen, or that traps the gesture on the first screen, breaks a habit the whole platform teaches. Overlay first, then one screen back, then out from the first screen matches that habit on every screen. Each stack page names how the platform's back signal reaches the controller.

provisions.heading: Honor Reduced Motion
provisions.evidence: With animations off, does every screen replace looping motion and video with a still state? Check the screens with animations off.
provisions.statement: When the system turns animations off, a screen MUST replace looping motion and video with a still state.
provisions.rationale: Some users turn animations off because motion causes discomfort, so a screen that keeps looping motion ignores an explicit request. A still state shows the same content without the movement: the final frame, the resting layout. Applying the system's setting on every screen keeps the whole app honoring one choice.

provisions.heading: Meet Touch and Text Accessibility
provisions.evidence: Does every interactive view carry a content description and the platform-minimum touch target, with text scaling with the system font scale? Check the views, the text styles, and the accessibility device tests the Mobile Testing page names.
provisions.statement: Every interactive view MUST carry a content description, meet a minimum touch target of 48 dp on Android or 44 pt on iOS, and scale its text with the system font scale.
provisions.rationale: A view without a content description is silent to a screen reader, and a target below the platform minimum is missed by the finger it was drawn for. Text fixed at one size ignores the user who enlarged the system font to read at all. Meeting the platform target size and scaling with its font scale keeps every screen usable with the platform's own accessibility settings. The device tests on the [Mobile Testing](testing.md) page prove each screen against this rule.

provisions.heading: Own Navigation in One Controller
provisions.evidence: Does all navigation state live in the one controller, with screens raising events instead of navigating? Check the controller and the screens.
provisions.statement: The current screen, the open overlay, and the history MUST live in one controller per app, with screens raising events instead of navigating.
provisions.rationale: A screen that navigates itself keeps a second history nobody else reads, so back behavior and deep links disagree with what the screen shows. Holding the current screen, the open overlay, and the history in one controller gives navigation one answer for every question. Events keep screens decoupled from the controller, so the controller alone decides what each event opens.

provisions.heading: Release Media with Its Screen
provisions.evidence: Is every player, animator, and decoded image released or cancelled when its view leaves the window? Check the view teardown.
provisions.statement: A player, animator, or decoded image MUST be released or cancelled when its view leaves the window.
provisions.rationale: Media holds memory and hardware that the app stops showing once its view leaves the window. A player that keeps playing, an animator that keeps running, or a decoded image that stays resident drains the battery and starves the screen the user now sees. Releasing or cancelling with the view ties each resource's life to the screen that uses it.

provisions.heading: Render with the Platform's Own Views
provisions.evidence: Does every product screen render with the platform's native UI toolkit, none in a WebView or cross-platform layer? Check the screen implementations.
provisions.statement: A mobile app MUST render every screen with the platform's native UI toolkit, with no product screen in a WebView or a cross-platform UI layer.
provisions.rationale: The platform's native toolkit gives each screen the platform's behavior for focus, text input, and accessibility without extra work. A WebView or a cross-platform layer reimplements that behavior and lags behind it, so the screen feels foreign on its own platform. One toolkit also keeps every screen testable through the platform's own device tests.

provisions.heading: Restore the User's Place
provisions.evidence: Does every process recreation return to the screen the saved navigation state names? Check the saved-state handling.
provisions.statement: Save the controller's navigation state in the platform's saved-state mechanism so a process recreation returns to the same screen.
provisions.rationale: The platform destroys background processes when memory runs short. Without saved state, recreation drops the user on the first screen; with the controller's navigation state in the platform's saved-state mechanism, the user returns to the same screen with the same overlay and history. Each stack page names the saved-state mechanism for its platform.

provisions.heading: Route App Links to Flow Entry Screens
provisions.evidence: Does every app link open the flow entry screen and record it names, resolved through the one controller? Check the app link handling and the controller.
provisions.statement: A screen a flow can be entered from MUST open directly from its app link, with the controller resolving the link to that screen and its record.
provisions.rationale: A flow that starts outside the app, in a message or a browser page, lands on the screen the link names rather than on the first screen with the work still to find. The controller resolves the link, so a cold start and a link that arrives while the app runs open the same screen with the same history behind it. Each stack page names how its platform delivers the link to the controller.
provisions.example: A Claimwick approval message for expense EXP-1042 carries an app link that opens the approval screen for EXP-1042, with the expenses list behind it for back.

provisions.heading: Keep Core Projects Platform-Free
provisions.evidence: Does every core project target plain .NET with no platform SDK reference? Check the core project files and sources.
provisions.statement: Domain, Application, Infrastructure, and Client core projects MUST target plain .NET and reference no platform SDK type.
provisions.rationale: A core project that names a platform SDK type compiles only for that platform, so a second platform app copies the core instead of reusing it. Targeting plain .NET with no platform reference keeps the core compiling for every platform unchanged, with platform differences behind the interfaces Application owns and the adapters in the platform projects.

provisions.heading: Match Core Projects to the Product Shape
provisions.evidence: Does every `client-only` solution hold Domain, Application, and Infrastructure projects, and every `server` solution the Client project with no Domain copy? Check the solution tree.
provisions.statement: A mobile consumer MUST hold Domain, Application, and Infrastructure core projects in the `client-only` shape, and a `{ProjectName}.Client` core project with the generated API client instead of them in the `server` shape.
provisions.rationale: Where the rules live decides what the app holds. A product with no server carries its own domain model in Domain, Application, and Infrastructure projects. A product with a server keeps its rules there, and the app holds a Client project with the generated API client instead, reaching every rule through that client. A copy of the rules in the app drifts from the server's rules on the first change, and the app then enforces a rule the server does not hold.

provisions.heading: Organize Screens by Module
provisions.evidence: Does every screen sit under `Screens/`, in its module folder in a multi-module product? Check the platform project tree.
provisions.statement: A screen MUST live under `Screens/` in the platform project, in a folder for its module when the product has more than one module.
provisions.rationale: A reader holding a module record finds its screens by path when screens group by module, the way the frontend module mirror maps use cases to folders. One folder for a single-module product would add a level that distinguishes nothing, so its screens sit directly under `Screens/`. Use-case code reached from a screen lives in Application, so the screen folder holds the screen and the handler holds the behavior. This realizes litespec/frontend/structure#mirror-the-backend-use-case-path-in-kebab-case only as far as the screen path follows the module name.

provisions.heading: Place Platform Adapters in the Platform Project
provisions.evidence: Does every platform API surface have one adapter type in the platform project behind an interface Application owns? Check the platform project adapters.
provisions.statement: Place adapters for players, pickers, sensors, and storage locations in the platform project behind an interface Application owns, one type per platform API surface.
provisions.rationale: Each platform API surface gets one adapter type in the platform project, implementing an interface declared in Application. That puts every platform call behind a testable boundary the core tests can substitute. The platform project is the only layer naming the platform SDK, so each adapter resolves to its platform API by name. This realizes litespec/frontend/structure#place-cross-route-values-in-the-frame.

provisions.heading: Use the Mobile Solution Tree
provisions.evidence: Does every mobile app live in the one solution at `apps/mobile/`, with core projects under `src/` and one `{ProjectName}.{Platform}` app project per platform? Check the `apps/mobile/` tree.
provisions.statement: A consumer selecting a mobile stack MUST hold its mobile apps in one solution at `apps/mobile/` with core projects under `src/` and one app project per platform named `{ProjectName}.{Platform}`.
provisions.rationale: One solution gives every platform app one core to share, so a second platform reuses the domain model unchanged. Core projects under `src/` separate shared code from the platform apps that consume it, and one app project per platform named `{ProjectName}.{Platform}` makes each platform's screens findable by name. A reader moves from the solution to a screen by rule rather than by search. This replaces the API solution path in `litespec/workspace/structure#use-the-canonical-root-tree`, because a client-only consumer has no API directory.
provisions.example:
```text
apps/mobile/
  {ProjectName}.Mobile.slnx
  src/
    {ProjectName}.Domain/
    {ProjectName}.Application/
    {ProjectName}.Infrastructure/
    {ProjectName}.Android/
  tests/
    {ProjectName}.Domain.Tests/
    {ProjectName}.Application.Tests/
    {ProjectName}.Android.Tests/
```

The framework-generated `bin`, `obj`, and `publish` folders stay untracked.

provisions.heading: Prove Screens on a Device or Emulator
provisions.evidence: Does every screen a use case reaches have a device test driving it on an emulator or a device? Check the device tests beside the screens.
provisions.statement: Each screen a use case reaches MUST have a device test that drives it on an emulator or device.
provisions.rationale: Screens render through the platform toolkit, so only a device test meets them where users do: layout, insets, back behavior, and accessibility. A screen no device test drives is proved by nothing, whatever the core tests cover. Driving each screen a use case reaches on an emulator or device keeps every reachable screen proved. This realizes litespec/frontend/testing#match-test-level-to-risk.

provisions.heading: Prove Touch and Text Accessibility on a Device
provisions.evidence: Does every screen have a device test checking content descriptions, platform-minimum touch targets, and text scaling with the system font scale? Check the device tests beside the screens.
provisions.statement: A device test for each screen MUST check that every interactive view carries a content description and the platform-minimum touch target, and that text scales with the system font scale.
provisions.rationale: A screen that looks right at the default font size can still hide its commands from a screen reader, miss the finger a target was drawn for, or clip text a reader enlarged. Checking descriptions, targets, and scaling on a device meets the screen with the platform accessibility settings its visitors use, not the settings the developer happened to keep. This proves `litespec/frontend/mobile/screens#meet-touch-and-text-accessibility` on each screen.

provisions.heading: Test the Core as Plain .NET
provisions.evidence: Does every core test project run on the plain .NET runner with no emulator? Check the core test projects.
provisions.statement: Domain, Application, Infrastructure, and Client tests MUST run as plain .NET test projects with no emulator.
provisions.rationale: Its tests need no emulator, device, or platform host, because the core holds no platform type. Plain .NET test projects in xunit.v3, the framework the manifest pins, keep them fast. A core test that needs a device proves the layering already broke, and the fix belongs in the layering rather than in the test setup. This realizes litespec/frontend/testing#match-test-level-to-risk.

provisions.heading: Try the Release Build on Hardware Before Publishing
provisions.evidence: Does every release record one physical device per platform with the result of the hand check? Check the release records.
provisions.statement: Install the release build and try it by hand on one physical device per platform before publishing, and record the device and result.
provisions.rationale: Emulators approximate performance, sensors, and vendor behavior, and hardware differs on all three. Trying the release build by hand on one physical device per platform meets the app as users will. The recorded device and result make the check reviewable; a release without that record ships on emulator evidence alone.

provisions.heading: Declare the Compact Behavior
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `ui-catalog-invalid` tagged `[litespec/frontend/patterns#declare-the-compact-behavior]` for a breakpoint outside the breakpoints map or a compact option naming no recorded option. Run it at the consumer root.
provisions.statement: Each pattern MUST name one breakpoint and state whether the chosen option reflows below it or a named option replaces it.
provisions.rationale: A pattern with no compact statement breaks on a narrow screen, or each route redraws it for the phone in its own way and the product ships as many compact layouts as routes. Naming one breakpoint and stating whether the chosen option reflows below it or a named option replaces it settles the phone layout once. The breakpoint is a key in the catalog's breakpoints map, so every pattern measures against one width scale.
provisions.example: The entry names breakpoint `compact`; below it expense rows render as cards.

provisions.heading: Draw Each Screen as a Wireframe Before It Is Built
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `wireframe-invalid` for a wireframe block the wireframe language rejects, `wireframe-reference-unknown` for a wireframe action, state or refusal that names nothing the screen reaches, and `wording-alias` for a wireframe, result sentence or label that uses a glossary alias where the term exists. Run it at the consumer root.
provisions.statement: Each screen MUST carry one wireframe block in its explanation file, drawn in the wireframe language this page states.
provisions.rationale: The wireframe is the blueprint the screen is built from: the product owner settles the structure, the actions, and the words before any route exists, and the builder draws that drawing with the project's own components inside the page frame the screen names. Each action names a use case the screen offers, each state names a glossary term of the record shown, and each refusal names a result of an offered use case, so the drawing stays bound to the records. Proposed by decision 0089.
provisions.example:
The Claimwick expense record carries this wireframe before its route exists.

```wireframe
page
  breadcrumb "Expenses" "EXP-1042"
  header
    heading "EXP-1042"
    status "Paid" positive
    action primary "Message spender"
```

provisions.heading: Implement a Chosen Pattern Once
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `ui-catalog-invalid` tagged `[litespec/frontend/patterns#implement-a-chosen-pattern-once]` for a named component path that does not exist or an adopted status with no components. Run it at the consumer root.
provisions.statement: The shared UI package MUST implement each chosen pattern once at the source paths the catalog names per platform.
provisions.rationale: A route redrawing the pattern instead of composing the shared implementation makes a second decision the catalog does not track: it looks like the pattern, drifts from it, and no entry records the difference. Implementing each chosen pattern once in the shared UI package, at the source paths the catalog names per platform, gives every route the same behavior to compose.
provisions.example: The catalog names one shared source path per platform, so every expense route composes its platform path.

provisions.heading: Keep a Visual Registry
provisions.evidence: Does every product-added option appear in the registry at compact and full widths? Look in the product registry.
provisions.statement: Review LiteSpec options on the pattern's page on the LiteSpec site, and draw only product-specific options in a product registry at compact and full widths.
provisions.rationale: An option seen beside its rivals is judged on appearance rather than on its description, which is how owners actually choose. The pattern's page on the LiteSpec site already draws every LiteSpec option at desktop and phone widths, so a product registry only needs to draw the patterns and options the product added, at compact and full widths.

provisions.heading: Keep One Pattern Catalog
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `ui-catalog-invalid` tagged `[litespec/frontend/patterns#keep-one-pattern-catalog]` for a missing catalog, a duplicate id, an unknown group, an unknown library pattern, or a renamed option. Run it at the consumer root.
provisions.statement: A workspace with a controlled frontend MUST keep one pattern catalog at `paths.uiPatterns` in `.litespec/project.yaml`, valid against the schema.
provisions.rationale: An interface decision kept in one catalog is found before it is remade: the next author reads the entry and builds the chosen option. A decision kept in chat, in a review thread, or in one author's memory is decided again on the next page, and the two answers differ. One catalog at the configured path, valid against the schema, keeps every decision searchable and every choice comparable.
provisions.example:
The project file points at the catalog.

```yaml
paths: {}
```

provisions.heading: Keep the Catalog Platform Neutral
provisions.evidence: Does any pattern name a component library outside its implementations? Look in the catalog entries outside implementations.
provisions.statement: A pattern MUST name behavior and structure, never a component library.
provisions.rationale: A pattern names behavior and structure: which parts sit where, in what order, with which actions. Each platform binds that behavior to its own components through `implementations`, so one catalog serves every selected stack. A component library named in the pattern itself would force a second catalog per platform, and the two would diverge.
provisions.example: An option describes a menu listing sort fields rather than naming the component rendering it.

provisions.heading: Promote Pattern Improvements
provisions.evidence: Has every accepted product-neutral proposal reached the LiteSpec pattern page as a new or refined option? Look in the LiteSpec pattern pages and the accepted proposals.
provisions.statement: Send an accepted proposal that is not specific to one product to the LiteSpec pattern page, as a new option or a refined one.
provisions.rationale: An improvement learned in one product usually applies to every product, so keeping it local starves the shared patterns. Sending an accepted, product-neutral proposal to the LiteSpec pattern page, as a new option or a refined one, lets every later product start from it, while each product keeps its own choices. The proposal travels through `litespec/frontend/patterns#report-pattern-feedback-after-the-work` and reaches the pattern page after the owner accepts it.

provisions.heading: Record Every Option Considered
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `ui-catalog-invalid` tagged `[litespec/frontend/patterns#record-every-option-considered]` for a choice or extension naming no recorded option, and the catalog schema requires at least two options with rationale and cost. Run it at the consumer root.
provisions.statement: Each pattern MUST record at least two options with rationale and cost, and name the chosen option.
provisions.rationale: Recording at least two options with their rationale and cost turns a preference into a decision the next team can revisit. When the chosen option stops fitting, the team reads the recorded cost of the alternative instead of repeating the research from nothing. An option recorded without its cost gives them no basis to compare. Settled by [decision/0028-one-default-and-two-pattern-options](decision/0028-one-default-and-two-pattern-options), which caps each pattern at its Default and two options.
provisions.example: An expense list considers two sort options: clickable headers and a menu listing sort fields. The entry records the rationale and cost of each, then names the chosen one.

provisions.heading: Record Who Chose
provisions.evidence: Does every decision record `owner` or `recommended`, with no agent proposal posed as an owner choice? Look in the catalog decisions.
provisions.statement: Each pattern decision MUST record its source as `owner` or `recommended`.
provisions.rationale: The source tells the reader whether the choice is settled. A recommended choice stands until an owner confirms or changes it. An agent leaves its own choice marked as recommended, so no automated choice poses as a human decision. The catalog then shows at a glance which choices are settled and which still await review.
provisions.example:
The Claimwick catalog starts its expense header entry from `litespec/frontend/patterns/record-detail#record-header`, keeps the pattern option IDs, and records the owner choice.

```yaml
id: expense-header
group: record-detail
library: litespec/frontend/patterns/record-detail#record-header
decision:
  option: title-state-breadcrumb-one-primary-action
  source: owner
compact:
  breakpoint: compact
  behavior: The header stacks under the title.
implementations:
  svelte:
    status: adopted
```

The entry names the pattern's default option with `owner` as the source, so the choice stands as settled and the platform team builds it in its own components.

provisions.heading: Report Pattern Feedback After the Work
provisions.evidence: Does every pattern proposal in a completion report carry its pattern id, change, reason, and affected option? Look in the completion reports.
provisions.statement: Finish the task on the chosen pattern, then report a proposal in the completion report with pattern id, change, reason, and affected option.
provisions.rationale: An agent spotting a better option finishes the task on the chosen pattern first: it changes no decision on its own and stops for no mid-task question. The proposal goes in the completion report with pattern id, change, reason, and affected option, where the owner accepts, refuses, or defers it. An accepted proposal updates the catalog with its implementation under `litespec/frontend/patterns#update-the-catalog-with-the-code`.

provisions.heading: Start from a LiteSpec Pattern
provisions.evidence: Does every entry start from its LiteSpec pattern through `library`, or record why no pattern fits, keeping the pattern option IDs and names? Look in the catalog entries.
provisions.statement: Start each catalog entry from its LiteSpec pattern, through `library`, and keep the pattern's option IDs, option names, and default.
provisions.rationale: Starting from the LiteSpec pattern keeps choices comparable across products and keeps the default visible beside the product's own options. Keeping the pattern's option IDs and names lets one product read another's catalog without translation. A product choosing a different option records its reason in the entry, so the choice stays reviewable.

provisions.heading: State the Implementation Status
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `ui-catalog-invalid` tagged `[litespec/frontend/patterns#state-the-implementation-status]` for a partial or pending entry with no gap. Run it at the consumer root.
provisions.statement: Each platform entry MUST state one status and the gap when that status is `partial` or `pending`.
provisions.rationale: The status tells a team adopting the catalog what exists in code on each platform and what is still a drawing. A partial or pending entry states its gap, so the missing work is named rather than discovered. The Concepts section defines the four values.
provisions.example: A `pending` entry for one platform states in `gap` what is missing there.

provisions.heading: Update the Catalog with the Code
provisions.evidence: Does every option switch, added option, and extension update the catalog entry in the same change, and does every single-route departure name a decision record? Look in the change diffs and the catalog entries.
provisions.statement: A change that switches option, adds an option, or extends a pattern MUST update the catalog entry in the same change as its implementation.
provisions.rationale: When the catalog waits for a later change, the code ships, the follow-up slips, and the entry describes behavior no route renders. Updating the entry in the same change as its implementation keeps the two in agreement by construction. A route deliberately departing from the chosen option names a decision record instead, so the departure stays reviewable.
provisions.example: A route departing from the chosen option names a decision record, such as `.litespec/intent/decisions/0014-expense-sort-menu/0014-expense-sort-menu.yaml`.

provisions.heading: API Keys and Webhooks
provisions.evidence: Does the built key list, secret dialog, or delivery list differ from the wireframe the catalog entry chose? Open the built keys or webhooks screen beside the catalog entry recording the chosen option and its reason.
provisions.statement: `keys-table-with-the-grants-in-line`
provisions.rationale: The keys table with the grants in line states what each key may do, and last use tells finance whether it still runs. That is why it is the default. The secret dialog pairs with it at creation, where the new secret shows once and cannot be read again. The endpoint with its delivery log is the runner-up; prefer it on the webhooks tab, where deliveries are the work. Never show the secret outside the creation dialog: a secret that can be read again is not a secret. Keep the key list and the endpoint list on separate tabs: a key grants access, and an endpoint receives updates.

provisions.heading: Budget Limits and Advances
provisions.evidence: Does the built code table, condition editor, or advance balance differ from the wireframe the catalog entry chose? Open the built budget screens beside the catalog entry recording the chosen option and its reason.
provisions.statement: `code-table-with-use-and-state`
provisions.rationale: The code table with use and state shows value, use, and dates in one scan. A leaked code opens from its row and is retired in its editor. That is why it is the default. The condition editor is the runner-up; prefer it for creating or revising a code with several conditions. The advances list is the alternative when the balance of the money held is the question. Never ship the claims-only list: claims explain the past, and finance manages the codes. A code with a handful of fields is issued from the list; a code with conditions opens the editor.

provisions.heading: Connecting the Payment Account
provisions.evidence: Does the built account card, capability checklist, or method cost differ from the wireframe the catalog entry chose? Open the built payment setup beside the catalog entry recording the chosen option and its reason.
provisions.statement: `connected-account-with-the-methods-below`
provisions.rationale: The connected account card with the methods list gives connection state and methods each a place, with costs in line. That is why it is the default. The capability checklist is the runner-up; prefer it while the connection is new and methods still need approval. The costs table is the alternative when finance compares methods on last month's payouts. Never show the methods without the account card: a method means nothing while the account is disconnected. Before the company connects an account, the page names that state and offers one connect command, with no methods list.

provisions.heading: Importing Data from a File
provisions.evidence: Does the built import flow, column match, or dry-run count differ from the wireframe the catalog entry chose? Open the built import flow beside the catalog entry recording the chosen option and its reason.
provisions.statement: `imports-with-the-refused-rows-below`
provisions.rationale: The imports table with the refused rows below keeps history and repairs on one page. That is why it is the default. The column mapping is the runner-up; prefer it at import time, where the file's columns meet the product's fields. The dry run is the alternative before a large file lands, where the count of refusals decides whether to continue. Never ship the upload alone: an import without its refused rows hides the work it creates. Never show one list for refusals from several imports; each import groups its own refused rows.

provisions.heading: Show a New Secret Once
provisions.evidence: Does any newly created credential stay readable after its creation dialog closes? Open the creation flow for keys and secrets on a built settings screen.
provisions.statement: A screen MUST show a newly created API key or secret in full only once, at creation.
provisions.rationale: Anyone who later opens the page can copy a secret that stays readable: on a shared screen or in a screenshot. Showing the secret once, at creation, forces the person creating it to store it in a vault or an environment file right away, so no later visit can leak it.
provisions.example: Dana creates the Accounting export key; the secret shows once in the creation dialog, and afterward the keys table names the key's grants and last use.

provisions.heading: Show What a Role Allows Before Granting It
provisions.evidence: Does any invitation or role change go out without listing what the role allows? Open the invite and role-change flows on a built team screen.
provisions.statement: An invitation or role change MUST show what the chosen role allows before it is sent.
provisions.rationale: Role names such as Spender or Approver hide what they actually grant. A sender who sees only the name can hand out reimbursement rights by mistake. Showing the granted capabilities beside the name lets the sender confirm the access itself before the invitation goes out.
provisions.example: When Dana invites Nina as Spender, the dialog lists that Spenders submit expenses and attach receipts but cannot reimburse, before Dana sends the invitation.

provisions.heading: Subscription Invoices
provisions.evidence: Does the built invoice sheet, invoice list, or plan and mandate differ from the wireframe the catalog entry chose? Open the built billing screens beside the catalog entry recording the chosen option and its reason.
provisions.statement: `invoice-sheet-with-its-lines`
provisions.rationale: The invoice sheet with its lines reads as the document the books need, with the mandate and the download beside it. That is why it is the default. The plan page with the mandate is the runner-up; prefer it for changing the plan rather than reading a month. The invoice list is the alternative for the history of months, where state and total are the facts. Never show usage lines without their rates: a metered figure without its rate cannot be checked. Never bury a failed payment in the list; the invoice states the failure and the next retry.

provisions.heading: Team Members and Their Roles
provisions.evidence: Does the built member list, permission matrix, or staff card differ from the wireframe the catalog entry chose? Open the built team or roles screen beside the catalog entry recording the chosen option and its reason.
provisions.statement: `members-with-the-invitations-below`
provisions.rationale: The members table with invitations below answers three questions in one scan: who is in, who is invited, and what each person may do. That is why it is the default. The permission matrix is the runner-up; prefer it on the roles page, where capabilities are compared across roles. The cost-centre cards are the alternative for a staff group that claims for one cost centre with access that ends on a date. Never ship the matrix as the team page: the team page manages people, and a capability grid hides who holds what. The invite command opens a dialog in place, with the role and its capabilities beside the address. A reader who cannot manage the team sees the same list without the row commands.

provisions.heading: Changing a Record That Already Exists
provisions.evidence: Does every built edit flow match the wireframe its catalog entry chose? Open the built save, impact-first, and autosave edits beside the catalog entry recording the chosen option and its reason.
provisions.statement: `one-save-per-page`
provisions.rationale: The default is one Save for the whole page: a reader who changed three things saves once, and an unsaved note says what is still pending. The impact statement is the runner-up, for changes that break something. Autosave is the other alternative, and it earns its place only for free text, beside the version history in the Changing Something That Has Already Happened pattern. Never ship the inline list-row edit on this wide table: it hides validation.

provisions.heading: Changing Something That Has Already Happened
provisions.evidence: Does every built correction flow match the wireframe its catalog entry chose? Open the built past-change edits, dated corrections, and refusals beside the catalog entry recording the chosen option and its reason.
provisions.statement: `the-old-value-stays-on-the-record-beside-the-new`
provisions.rationale: The default keeps the old value beside the new: an expense filed last month still resolves to the trip it was filed for. The dated correction is the runner-up where a fact was entered wrong. The refusal naming the newer way is the other alternative where no safe edit exists. Never ship a silent overwrite of anything priced or paid: the record must show what it was before.

provisions.heading: Confirm or Undo Every Removal
provisions.evidence: Does every built removal ask first or offer a way back? Open the archive, delete, void, and suspend flows on built screens.
provisions.statement: Every removal MUST either offer undo or ask for confirmation before it runs.
provisions.rationale: Staff remove the wrong record by misreading a row or misclicking, and without a way back the record is gone. An undo toast restores a reversible removal in one click, while a confirmation dialog makes an irreversible removal a deliberate choice. Either way, the reader gets a moment to catch the mistake before it becomes permanent.

provisions.heading: Creating a Record and Then Filling It In
provisions.evidence: Does every built draft-first flow match the wireframe its catalog entry chose? Open the built name-first creates, setup guides, and required-field creates beside the catalog entry recording the chosen option and its reason.
provisions.statement: `create-with-a-name-fill-the-rest-later`
provisions.rationale: The default is to create with a name and fill the rest later. The record exists as a draft, and every later addition is its own audited command. The home-page setup guide is the runner-up and the required companion, because a draft nobody finishes is a dead record. Everything required before the record exists is the other alternative, for a record that has to be whole before anyone sees it. Leave out a create that writes nothing until the final publish step: if the browser loses the page, the whole form goes with it.

provisions.heading: Creating One Record
provisions.evidence: Does every built creation form match the wireframe its catalog entry chose? Open the built dialog, page, and file-import starts beside the catalog entry recording the chosen option and its reason.
provisions.statement: `a-dialog-for-two-or-three-inputs`
provisions.rationale: One to four inputs belong in the dialog: the list stays visible behind it, and a single verb commits the create. Past four inputs, or when the form needs sections, the full page is the runner-up and the right choice. The file import is the other alternative, for the days when many records arrive at once and a dialog per record would take all day. Never ship a form inside a table row: it breaks the table structure and hides validation.

provisions.heading: Duplicating a Record
provisions.evidence: Does every built copy flow match the wireframe its catalog entry chose? Open the built duplicate dialogs, carry checklists, and row-menu copies beside the catalog entry recording the chosen option and its reason.
provisions.statement: `a-dialog-that-says-what-the-copy-carries`
provisions.rationale: The default is the dialog that says what the copy carries. A duplicate that silently drops the ceilings is worse than no duplicate. The carry checklist is the runner-up where the parts vary per company. One click from the row menu is the other alternative, and it earns its place for budget codes and plan entries, which carry no spenders. Never ship one-click duplication for a trip: a silent copy drops the ceilings a trip needs. An expense is never duplicated, because it is one spender's claim.

provisions.heading: Inviting a Team Member
provisions.evidence: Does every built join flow match the wireframe its catalog entry chose? Open the built email invites, links, and pending lists beside the catalog entry recording the chosen option and its reason.
provisions.statement: `invite-by-email-with-the-role-chosen-first`
provisions.rationale: The default is to invite by email with the role chosen first: person, role, and scope are all named on one dialog. The pending list with resend and revoke is the runner-up and the required companion, because an invitation waits far longer than sending takes. The invite link is the other alternative for trip crew on one trip, where forty people are not typed by hand. Never ship an open invite link for staff roles: anyone holding it joins. A request to join is refused: the company invites, and nobody applies.

provisions.heading: Publishing and Unpublishing a Draft
provisions.evidence: Does every built publish flow match the wireframe its catalog entry chose? Open the built publish, unpublish, and per-channel controls beside the catalog entry recording the chosen option and its reason.
provisions.statement: `publish-with-the-readiness-check-beside-it`
provisions.rationale: The default is to publish with the readiness check beside it: the reader reads what spenders will find before they find it. Per-channel publish is the runner-up for companies that publish in more than one place. Unpublish with the spender consequences stated is the other alternative, because filed expenses outlive the command. Never ship a silent unpublish: the page must say that filed expenses stay valid.

provisions.heading: Putting a List in Order by Hand
provisions.evidence: Does every built manual ordering match the wireframe its catalog entry chose? Open the built drag handles, move commands, and typed numbers beside the catalog entry recording the chosen option and its reason.
provisions.statement: `drag-handles-in-the-list`
provisions.rationale: Drag handles in the list are the default: direct, visible, and the order saves as it changes. Move up and Move down in the row menu are the runner-up and the required companion, because drag alone leaves keyboard and screen-reader users behind. Typed position numbers are the other alternative for a jump across a long list. Never ship typed position numbers alone: two rows both numbered 3 are a question the page cannot answer.

provisions.heading: Refuse a Second Send While One Is in Flight
provisions.evidence: Which built command controls show no pending state, or send twice when pressed twice in a row? Open the built submits and pays, press each twice quickly, and read what the API received.
provisions.statement: While a command is in flight, the control that sent it MUST show a pending state and refuse a second send until the first settles.
provisions.rationale: A double click on Submit creates two expenses or pays a payout twice. A pending state tells the reader the first send is still running, so there is no reason to press again, and refusing the second send keeps one press to one command.

provisions.heading: Removing Several at Once
provisions.evidence: Does every built bulk removal match the wireframe its catalog entry chose? Open the built count-and-money dialogs, background jobs, and dry-run plans beside the catalog entry recording the chosen option and its reason.
provisions.statement: `a-dialog-naming-the-count-and-the-money`
provisions.rationale: Up to about twenty-five rows, the default is the dialog that names the count and the money, because those two figures are what the reader checks. Past that size the background job is the runner-up, and a report lands afterwards. The dry-run plan is the other alternative where rows can refuse, because a page shows every refusal before anything runs. Never ship a typed count for an ordinary bulk remove: typing 200 trains copy and paste, which is the reflex the pattern exists to break.

provisions.heading: Removing Something
provisions.evidence: Does every built single removal match the wireframe its catalog entry chose? Open the built archive, delete, and trash flows beside the catalog entry recording the chosen option and its reason.
provisions.statement: `archive-with-what-archiving-means`
provisions.rationale: Archive is the default: it is reversible, keeps the audit trail, and the Archived view is the way back. The thirty-day trash is the runner-up where readers reach for the word delete. The delete dialog is the other alternative for records that have to go, and it says what is kept. Never ship a bare delete for anything with history: the dialog must name what survives.

provisions.heading: Restoring an Archived Record
provisions.evidence: Does every built restore flow match the wireframe its catalog entry chose? Open the built archived views, record-page banners, and undo toasts beside the catalog entry recording the chosen option and its reason.
provisions.statement: `restore-from-the-archived-view`
provisions.rationale: Restore from the archived view is the default: the view is the way back, and each row says where its record returns to. The record-page banner is the runner-up for anyone arriving by link. The Undo toast is the other alternative in the seconds after archiving, not as the way back days later. Never ship a restore that silently un-archives parents or overwrites a newer name: both need their own dialog.

provisions.heading: Scheduling a Change for Later
provisions.evidence: Does every built dated change match the wireframe its catalog entry chose? Open the built scheduled changes, code timelines, and spender previews beside the catalog entry recording the chosen option and its reason.
provisions.statement: `a-change-with-a-date-listed-with-the-record`
provisions.rationale: The default is a change with a date, listed with the record: current and coming values sit side by side with a cancel. The code timeline is the runner-up where ceilings change on fixed dates. The spender preview is the other alternative where spenders read the value, because a fee change is judged by the line they see. Never ship overlapping schedules on one record: one record cannot become two fees on the same date.

provisions.heading: Show the Created Record
provisions.evidence: Does every built create flow end at its new record? Open the create dialogs, pages, and bulk flows on built screens.
provisions.statement: A successful create MUST take the reader to the created record or show it in place.
provisions.rationale: After creating, the reader needs proof that the record exists with the values entered, and the created record itself is that proof. A create that ends on an empty form or a bare toast leaves the reader unsure whether it worked, so they create it again and produce a duplicate.

provisions.heading: Bar That Stays While the Reader Works
provisions.evidence: Does every built persistent band match the wireframe its catalog entry chose? Open the built deployment and deadline bands beside the catalog entry recording the chosen option and its reason.
provisions.statement: `a-neutral-band-for-what-this-page-is`
provisions.rationale: Ship the neutral band stating a fact about the deployment, the same band on every page. The bar on the record page is the runner-up for facts true of one record only, drawn as a notice on that record. Never ship the bar naming a deadline: a full-width caution band paints the whole page, and its tone covers work the page is not about.

provisions.heading: Confirming a Command That Cannot Be Taken Back
provisions.evidence: Does every built irreversible step match the wireframe its catalog entry chose? Open the built confirmation dialogs beside the catalog entry recording the chosen option and its reason.
provisions.statement: `name-the-object-state-the-consequence-offer-the-alternative`
provisions.rationale: The default dialog names the object, states the consequence in numbers, and offers the alternative in the same surface. The runner-up shows the consequence as numbers, and it is the better choice wherever money moves, because the reader sees the number before confirming. Never ship the undo toast for an irreversible cancellation: an undo there is a second command rather than a reversal.

provisions.heading: Context Menu Where the Pointer Is
provisions.evidence: Does every built right-click menu match the wireframe its catalog entry chose? Open the built row and bulk menus beside the catalog entry recording the chosen option and its reason.
provisions.statement: `a-right-click-menu-on-a-row`
provisions.rationale: Ship the right-click menu on the row: the row's own commands at the pointer, nothing added, nothing missing, and closed by clicking elsewhere. The bulk-selection menu is the runner-up for bulk work, where the menu rewrites itself for the selection count. Never ship silence: silence hands the gesture to the browser, whose commands act on the page rather than the record.

provisions.heading: Dialog with a Long Body and a Sticky Footer
provisions.evidence: Does every built scrolling dialog match the wireframe its catalog entry chose? Open the built pinned footers beside the catalog entry recording the chosen option and its reason.
provisions.statement: `a-scrolling-body-with-a-pinned-footer`
provisions.rationale: Ship the scrolling body with a pinned footer: one scrolling body, one pinned footer, nothing else. The summary pinned above the footer is the runner-up wherever money moves, because the reader sees the totals above the footer before confirming. Never ship the dialog with no pinned footer: buttons that scroll away ask the reader to agree first and find the way to confirm after.

provisions.heading: Drawer Beside the List
provisions.evidence: Does every built side preview match the wireframe its catalog entry chose? Open the built drawer variants over and next to the list, with the catalog entry recording the chosen option and its reason.
provisions.statement: `read-only-record-beside-the-list`
provisions.rationale: Keep the read-only record beside the list. The list keeps its scroll position and its filters while the record reads beside it, and nothing in the drawer is editable, so the drawer cannot turn into a task. Prefer the tabbed drawer when support compares reversals across facts, history, and messages. Never ship the filter drawer: filters belong in the toolbar, and a drawer over the results hides the list those filters describe.

provisions.heading: Hold a Toast While a Modal Is Open
provisions.evidence: Does every built toast wait until an open modal dialog closes? Raise each toast while a modal dialog is open and watch where it lands.
provisions.statement: A toast raised while a modal dialog is open SHOULD wait until the dialog closes.
provisions.rationale: The page behind a modal is inert, so a toast raised over it can be neither read nor used. Waiting until the dialog closes delivers the news when the reader can act on it: the toast still arrives, only late enough to be heard.

provisions.heading: Keep Tab Free to Leave a Menu or Popover
provisions.evidence: Does Tab leave every built menu and popover? Open each menu and popover with a keyboard and press Tab until focus leaves.
provisions.statement: Tab MUST move focus out of an open menu or a non-modal popover and close it.
provisions.rationale: A menu that keeps Tab cycling inside it strands a keyboard user on one row of the payout list. Only a modal dialog or drawer holds focus inside itself, because the page behind it waits until it closes. Anything less than a modal that traps Tab fails WCAG 2.1.2 No Keyboard Trap.

provisions.heading: Keep the Page Behind a Modal Still
provisions.evidence: Does the page behind every built modal keep its scroll position and layout width? Open and close each modal over a scrolled list and watch the page.
provisions.statement: The page behind a modal overlay SHOULD keep its scroll position and its layout width while the overlay opens and closes.
provisions.rationale: When the page jumps or shifts sideways as the overlay opens, the reader loses their row in the list behind. Keeping the scroll position and the layout width holds their place through the interruption, so closing the overlay returns to the same view, not a nearby one.

provisions.heading: Keep Unsaved Input Through a Dismissal
provisions.evidence: Does every built dialog or drawer keep unsent input through a dismissal? Open each dialog and drawer holding unsent input and try a press outside it, the close control, and the Escape key.
provisions.statement: A dialog or drawer holding unsaved input MUST ignore a press outside it and ask before its close control or the Escape key discards that input.
provisions.rationale: A stray click beside a half-typed payout note wipes out the work, and retyping it from memory invites errors. Ignoring the stray press, and asking before the close control or the Escape key discards anything, gives the reader one chance to keep what was typed. For money movements this is WCAG 3.3.4 Error Prevention (Legal, Financial, and Data), which asks that the reader verify, check, or reverse the submission.

provisions.heading: Keyboard Shortcut Help Overlay
provisions.evidence: Does every built shortcut list match the wireframe its catalog entry chose? Open the built grouped grids beside the catalog entry recording the chosen option and its reason.
provisions.statement: `a-grouped-grid-of-shortcuts`
provisions.rationale: Ship the grouped grid of shortcuts: three groups, one grid, every key the application honors, all closed by the same key. The this-page-only list is the runner-up on dense pages, where it answers the only keys that work there. Never ship tooltips alone: they hide the catalog from exactly the reader who would learn it fastest.

provisions.heading: Menu of a Row's Commands
provisions.evidence: Does every built row menu match the wireframe its catalog entry chose? Open the built grouped menus beside the catalog entry recording the chosen option and its reason.
provisions.statement: `a-menu-with-groups-and-a-destructive-item-last`
provisions.rationale: Keep the menu with groups and the destructive item last after a separator, with nothing disabled without a reason. The runner-up is the menu that states the reason beside a disabled item. It is the better choice where a command is often disabled, because the reason in place beats a hover. Arrow keys move between items, Tab leaves the menu, and Escape closes one level and returns focus to the opener. Never ship a confirmation inside a menu. A confirmation there is a dialog over a menu, which is the same nesting the project forbids for dialogs.

provisions.heading: Name the Command on a Confirm Action
provisions.evidence: Does every built confirmation label its commit button with the command it runs? Open the confirm dialogs on built screens.
provisions.statement: A confirmation dialog MUST label its confirm action with the command it runs.
provisions.rationale: Staff often scan only the buttons before clicking, so the button text is the last chance to say what happens. A button labeled `OK` or `Yes` forces the reader to reread the dialog title to learn what they are confirming, and under time pressure they click without rereading and run the wrong command.

provisions.heading: Pause a Timed Toast While It Is in Use
provisions.evidence: Does every built timed toast pause while the pointer is over it or focus is inside it? Trigger each timed toast, hover it, tab into it, and watch the timer.
provisions.statement: A toast that closes on a timer MUST pause that timer while the pointer is over it or focus is inside it.
provisions.rationale: An Undo that disappears while the reader moves toward it is lost, and the command it would have reversed stands. Pausing the timer while the toast is in use gives the reader the time the movement takes. This is WCAG 2.2.1 Timing Adjustable, which asks that a time limit be adjustable, extendable, or removable.

provisions.heading: Place Initial Focus on the Safe Action
provisions.evidence: Does every built irreversible confirmation open with focus on its safe action? Open each confirmation with a keyboard and note where focus lands.
provisions.statement: A confirmation for a command that cannot be taken back MUST place initial focus on its safe action.
provisions.rationale: When focus lands on the destructive button, a held Enter key runs the command before the reader has read the question. Starting on the safe action, such as `Keep the run`, makes the command take a deliberate move, so a hurried reader confirms nothing by accident.

provisions.heading: Return Focus When an Overlay Closes
provisions.evidence: Does every built overlay return focus to its opener when it closes? Open and dismiss each dialog, drawer, popover, menu, and toast on built screens with a keyboard.
provisions.statement: An overlay MUST return focus to the control that opened it when it closes.
provisions.rationale: Keyboard and screen-reader users navigate by focus position, so closing an overlay must put them back where they started. Focus that falls back to the top of the page strands them far from their row in a long list, and they must tab through the whole page to continue.

provisions.heading: Short Panel That Opens Beside a Control
provisions.evidence: Does every built hover card or hint match the wireframe its catalog entry chose? Open the built popovers and previews beside the catalog entry recording the chosen option and its reason.
provisions.statement: `a-popover-that-explains-what-a-term-means`
provisions.rationale: Keep the popover that explains what a term means. A defined term carries its glossary entry where it is read, and only for terms the application has defined. The runner-up is the row preview popover. It suits dense lists where a hover card saves a navigation, and it has to open on focus as well as hover. Never ship a menu and a popover for the same thing. The pair teaches that floating layers stack, and stacked layers leave readers unsure which one to dismiss.

provisions.heading: Short Task in a Dialog
provisions.evidence: Does every built two-input task match the wireframe its catalog entry chose? Open the built small dialogs beside the catalog entry recording the chosen option and its reason.
provisions.statement: `two-or-three-inputs-one-dialog`
provisions.rationale: The default is one dialog shape for commands with one to four inputs: title, fields, one verb, no navigation. The runner-up is the task on the page, and it is the better choice for commands that repeat all day, where leaving the page costs more than the dialog saves. Never ship a dialog over a dialog. A helper that supports the nesting does not make the nesting readable.

provisions.heading: Toast at the Edge of the Screen
provisions.evidence: Does every built edge notice match the wireframe its catalog entry chose? Open the built confirmations and linked results beside the catalog entry recording the chosen option and its reason.
provisions.statement: `a-confirmation-that-closes-by-itself`
provisions.rationale: Keep the self-closing confirmation for success, where the message leaves on its own and nothing goes with it. The runner-up is the toast that links to the result, which suits commands whose result lives elsewhere, because the link going away costs nothing. Never ship two actions on one toast: two buttons turn a transient message into a small panel with a timer. Never ship a toast as the only route to a result either.

provisions.heading: Announce Each Status by Its Urgency
provisions.evidence: Does every built page announce routine news politely and add its live regions at load? Trigger each status with a screen reader and note which region speaks.
provisions.statement: A page MUST announce each status through one of two live regions present when the page loads: a polite region for routine news and one assertive region for a session about to end, a lost connection holding unsent input, or a failed money command.
provisions.rationale: A live region added at the moment of the message is often not read, so both regions exist from the page load. Assertive messages interrupt whatever the reader hears, so only blocking news earns them: a session about to end, a lost connection holding unsent input, or a failed money command. This is WCAG 4.1.3 Status Messages, which asks that status changes be announced without moving focus.

provisions.heading: Back Office Is Down for a Short While
provisions.evidence: Does every built maintenance screen match the wireframe its catalog entry chose? Open the built advance notices, maintenance pages, and read-only windows beside the catalog entry recording the chosen option and its reason.
provisions.statement: `told-ahead-of-time-on-every-page`
provisions.rationale: The default is the advance notice on every page. A window nobody meets by surprise is a window finance can plan around, and the printed payout lists are the plan. The runner-up is the maintenance page itself, which is what every page becomes while the window runs. Read-only access suits a short window where the records still answer a call. A lone message stays out as the only signal: a Thursday message tells once, and only the back office itself reminds on Sunday at 02:00.

provisions.heading: Command That Worked
provisions.evidence: Does every built success notice match the wireframe its catalog entry chose? Open the built confirmations, toasts with undo, and quiet saves beside the catalog entry recording the chosen option and its reason.
provisions.statement: `evidence-on-the-page-not-only-a-toast`
provisions.rationale: The default is evidence on the page. State, money, and timeline all say what changed after a reversal. The runner-up is the toast with `Undo`; prefer it for a reversible change such as hiding a policy from the portal. The quiet saved line is the other alternative for a settings form where the values are already the evidence. No message at all stays out: a screen reader user gets no signal, which fails WCAG 4.1.3.

provisions.heading: Command the API Refused
provisions.evidence: Does every built refusal notice match the wireframe its catalog entry chose? Open the built refused commands, with codes and fixes, beside the catalog entry recording the chosen option and its reason.
provisions.statement: `the-refusal-sentence-its-code-and-a-way-to-fix-it`
provisions.rationale: The default is the refusal sentence with its code and its fix. It meets WCAG 3.3.1 and 3.3.3 in one place. The runner-up is the refusal inside the dialog that sent it; prefer it where closing would lose what the reader typed, such as a reversal amount. The disabled button with its reason is the other alternative for a refusal the page can predict. A refusal only on the record timeline stays out: a reader who sent the command from elsewhere never returns to find it.

provisions.heading: Connection Is Gone
provisions.evidence: Does every built offline screen match the wireframe its catalog entry chose? Open the built stale banners, failed reads, and refused pages beside the catalog entry recording the chosen option and its reason.
provisions.statement: `a-banner-saying-what-is-stale-and-what-still-works`
provisions.rationale: The default is one band saying what is stale, when it was read, and what still works. A stale page the reader can read beats a page that shows nothing. The runner-up is the failed read state, which suits a page with nothing to show because the read itself failed. Showing nothing is the other alternative for a page where acting on stale money would move the wrong money. Whatever the reader typed stays on the page while the connection is gone, and every failed read offers its retry. Queuing a command that moves money stays out: a reversal nobody confirmed is a liability, and the page says plainly that the money has not moved.

provisions.heading: Fact Somebody Has to Read Before Acting
provisions.evidence: Does every built must-read notice match the wireframe its catalog entry chose? Open the built page notices, section notices, and side columns beside the catalog entry recording the chosen option and its reason.
provisions.statement: `a-neutral-notice-above-the-page`
provisions.rationale: The default is one neutral sentence above the page, with no tone and no band. It says why the page holds its state and stays out of the work. The runner-up is the notice inside the section it is about; prefer it where the fact changes what the reader does in that section only. The side column is the other alternative for a record where the fact changes the next step. A full-width toned band for one record stays out: it paints other work with the same alarm.

provisions.heading: Keep the Reader's Input Through a Failure
provisions.evidence: Does every built form keep its typed values after a refused save? Open the failed submits on built forms and check every field.
provisions.statement: A failed save MUST keep the reader's unsaved input on the screen.
provisions.rationale: Retyping a whole form to fix one refused field wastes the reader's time and introduces new typos. Worse, readers who lose work to a failure stop trusting the form: they copy long answers elsewhere before saving.

provisions.heading: Keep Unsent Input When the Connection Drops
provisions.evidence: Does every built route keep typed input when the connection drops and offer a retry? Drop the connection on each route holding unsent input and try the retry.
provisions.statement: A route that loses its connection MUST keep the user's unsent input and show the error state with a retry action.
provisions.rationale: A long expense form lost to a train tunnel is typed again or abandoned. Keeping the unsent input on screen with a retry action turns the dead connection into a wait: the reader retries the read instead of retyping the form.

provisions.heading: Loading
provisions.evidence: Does every built waiting state match the wireframe its catalog entry chose? Open the built skeletons, thin bars, and scrims beside the catalog entry recording the chosen option and its reason.
provisions.statement: `skeletons-at-the-real-row-height`
provisions.rationale: The default is skeletons at the real row height. Nothing moves when the data lands, even on a slow phone read. The runner-up is the thin bar over the old rows; prefer it for a re-read where the reader keeps their place, such as a changed filter. A scrim is the other alternative for a wait the reader must not work through. Showing nothing at all stays out: any read slower than a blink reads as a failed page.

provisions.heading: Mark a Loading Region Busy
provisions.evidence: Does every built loading region stay silent in live regions and expose its busy mark or progress role? Trigger each load with a screen reader and inspect the loading markup.
provisions.statement: A loading region MUST expose its state through markup, as busy on the region or as role and value on a progress bar, and not through a live region announcement.
provisions.rationale: A `Loading` announcement on every read buries the messages that matter. A region marked busy with `aria-busy="true"` stays silent while assistive technology reports its state on request, and a progress bar with its role and value says how far the read has come. Announcements stay for the news that matters.

provisions.heading: Move Focus to a Refusal
provisions.evidence: Does every built refusal move focus to itself or to the first field it names? Refuse each command with a keyboard and note where focus lands.
provisions.statement: After the API refuses a command, focus MUST move to the refusal or to the first field it names.
provisions.rationale: A sighted reader sees the refusal where it appears. A keyboard or screen-reader user otherwise never meets it. Moving focus to the refusal, or to the first field it names, puts every reader at the same place. This is WCAG 3.3.1 Error Identification, which asks that each error be described in text.

provisions.heading: Nothing Has Ever Existed
provisions.evidence: Does every built first-run screen match the wireframe its catalog entry chose? Open the built empty lists and setup guides beside the catalog entry recording the chosen option and its reason.
provisions.statement: `positive-title-one-action`
provisions.rationale: The default is the positive title with one action. It is the smallest shape, and the only option that asks nothing of a reader who has nothing yet. The runner-up is the setup guide on Home; prefer it when the first expense needs steps across several pages. Sample rows are the other alternative for a page whose shape is learned by using it. A table with a dashed sample row stays out: it shows a record that does not exist and leads nowhere when opened.

provisions.heading: Nothing Matches What Was Asked For
provisions.evidence: Does every built no-results screen match the wireframe its catalog entry chose? Open the built filtered empties and filter panels beside the catalog entry recording the chosen option and its reason.
provisions.statement: `different-copy-and-it-names-the-term`
provisions.rationale: The default is the copy that names the term. It says what failed and what to change, with the count proving the data exists. The runner-up is the table that keeps its headers; prefer it where readers filter all day and want the columns to stay put. The filters panel is the other alternative for a page whose filters are the whole question. An empty state with no action at all stays out: a search that names its term can always offer to clear it.

provisions.heading: Reader May Not Do This
provisions.evidence: Does every built forbidden view match the wireframe its catalog entry chose? Open the built refused commands, absent tabs, and read-only sections beside the catalog entry recording the chosen option and its reason.
provisions.statement: `the-commands-are-refused-each-with-its-grant-named`
provisions.rationale: The default is the explained action. Each refused command names the role that grants it, and the record stays readable; on a call, reading the record is the point. The runner-up is the read-only section with values as text; prefer it where a form that fails on `Save` hurts more. The absent tab is the other alternative for a capability the reader should never see offered. Refusing the whole page stays out: a support agent needs the spender name on a call, and the refusal hides more than it protects.

provisions.heading: Sign-In Ran Out
provisions.evidence: Does every built expired session match the wireframe its catalog entry chose? Open the built sign-out pages, warnings, and re-authentication dialogs beside the catalog entry recording the chosen option and its reason.
provisions.statement: `a-dialog-over-the-work-which-stays-where-it-is`
provisions.rationale: The default is the dialog over the work, which stays where it is. It keeps unsent work on screen and names the one thing to do. The runner-up is the warning before the end, which suits a reader still at the desk who never meets the expired state. The signed-out page is the other alternative for a reader with no page to keep. A toast alone stays out: the message leaves in seconds and the typed work leaves with it.

provisions.heading: Somebody Else Saved First
provisions.evidence: Does every built conflict screen match the wireframe its catalog entry chose? Open the built field-level refusals, field-by-field merges, and conflict dialogs beside the catalog entry recording the chosen option and its reason.
provisions.statement: `the-refusal-above-save-with-her-value-under-the-field`
provisions.rationale: The default is the refusal above `Save`, with her value under the field. It refuses in the dictionary's words and fixes only what collided, with no dialog and no lost keystroke. The runner-up is the field-by-field choice, which suits a record where both people changed several fields. The whole-record dialog is the other alternative for two people who rewrote the same long notes. A lock that reloads her whole version stays out: it deletes Ben's notes to resolve an arrival time.

provisions.heading: Something Went Wrong on Our Side
provisions.evidence: Does every built server-failure screen match the wireframe its catalog entry chose? Open the built failure states, outcome pages, and failed sections beside the catalog entry recording the chosen option and its reason.
provisions.statement: `the-shipped-failure-with-its-reference`
provisions.rationale: The default is the failure with its reference. It words the failure once, says what did not move, and gives support something to read back. The runner-up is the outcome page; prefer it where the money sentence deserves a page of its own. The failed section suits a page whose other sections still read. Old data with a quiet line stays out: figures the server could not confirm are misinformation, and a quiet line does not make them honest.

provisions.heading: State What Failed and the Next Step
provisions.evidence: Does every built failure message name the cause and the way forward? Open the refused commands and failed reads on built screens.
provisions.statement: A refusal or error message MUST state what failed and the next step the reader can take.
provisions.rationale: A message that only says something went wrong leaves the reader guessing whether to retry, fix input, or ask for help. Most readers retry blindly or give up. Naming what failed plus the one next step turns the dead end into a task the reader can complete.

provisions.heading: This Record Does Not Exist
provisions.evidence: Does every built missing-record screen match the wireframe its catalog entry chose? Open the built not-found pages, section notices, and removal notices beside the catalog entry recording the chosen option and its reason.
provisions.statement: `not-found-with-the-way-back`
provisions.rationale: The default is `Not found`, with the way back. It names the record, covers the three ways a record goes missing, and offers the list and the search. The runner-up is the section that says so while the page stays; prefer it for a child missing from a parent that exists. Naming who removed a record and when suits a record the reader saw yesterday. The bare code stays out: a code means nothing to a reader, and a dead end with a number on it is still a dead end.

provisions.heading: Too Many Tries
provisions.evidence: Does every built rate-limit screen match the wireframe its catalog entry chose? Open the built waits, usage figures, and stop pages beside the catalog entry recording the chosen option and its reason.
provisions.statement: `the-button-waits-and-says-how-long`
provisions.rationale: The default is the button that waits and says how long. It turns the limit into a 40-second wait with its reason attached, which is all a reader who ran 12 exports needs. The runner-up states the limit before it hits; prefer it for a reader planning a month of exports rather than one too many. The stop page suits a limit measured in minutes. The spinner that never says why stays out: a wait the reader cannot name reads as a page that broke, and reloading restarts it.

provisions.heading: Work That Runs Without You
provisions.evidence: Does every built background job match the wireframe its catalog entry chose? Open the built trays, job pages, and finished notices beside the catalog entry recording the chosen option and its reason.
provisions.statement: `an-activity-tray-like-an-upload-panel`
provisions.rationale: The default is the activity tray. It stays visible on every page, it never holds the reader, and it answers progress without being asked. The runner-up is the job page with the failures listed; prefer it for a bulk reversal where two of 31 need a person and the rest do not. The finished notice suits a job nobody needs to watch. The dialog that holds the reader stays out: minutes of a blocked page are the cost this pattern exists to remove.

provisions.heading: Address Field
provisions.evidence: Does every built location input match the wireframe its catalog entry chose? Open the built lookups, country shapes, and map pins beside the catalog entry recording the chosen option and its reason.
provisions.statement: `postcode-lookup-that-fills-the-street`
provisions.rationale: The default is the postcode lookup. Two short values the reader knows produce the street they would mistype. The runner-up asks country first; prefer it for companies outside the lookup coverage. One search that fills the address is the other alternative for a reader who knows the street but not its spelling. The postcode stays optional for a country that has none, and every lookup offers manual entry beside it. A single free-text address box stays out: one line never splits back into street, postcode, and city.

provisions.heading: Capacity Field
provisions.evidence: Does every built ceiling input match the wireframe its catalog entry chose? Open the built splits, steppers, and overage messages beside the catalog entry recording the chosen option and its reason.
provisions.statement: `a-number-with-the-warehouse-ceiling-restated`
provisions.rationale: The default is the number with the budget ceiling restated. One field, the budget it draws from, and what is left sit on the same screen. The runner-up is the split across codes; prefer it on the budget page, where the question is the whole budget rather than one code. Claimed as a read-only fact beside an editable ceiling is the other alternative where claimed must never be typed. A capacity with no ceiling stated stays out: a number without its budget is a number that overspends.

provisions.heading: Choosing a Record
provisions.evidence: Does every built record picker match the wireframe its catalog entry chose? Open the built searchable pickers and recent lists beside the catalog entry recording the chosen option and its reason.
provisions.statement: `searchable-picker-showing-names`
provisions.rationale: The default is the searchable picker over names: nobody types an identifier, and search beats scrolling for every list longer than a screen. The runner-up shows one distinguishing fact per row; prefer it where records share a name. The plain select is the other alternative for a short, fixed list. A bare identifier field stays out: a code such as CC-0C893968A2 is not a value a reader can type or check.

provisions.heading: Choosing One of a Few Options
provisions.evidence: Does every built single-choice control match the wireframe its catalog entry chose? Open the built radios, segments, and plan cards beside the catalog entry recording the chosen option and its reason.
provisions.statement: `a-radio-list-with-a-description-per-option`
provisions.rationale: The default is the radio list with a description per option, since each choice carries the sentence that lets a reader tell names apart that sound alike. The runner-up is the segmented control; prefer it for two or three short values with no descriptions. The select is the other alternative for a long list on a settings page. The native multi-select stays out: it needs a modifier key for a second value and hides which values are chosen, so a checkbox list replaces it.

provisions.heading: Color Field
provisions.evidence: Does every built accent picker match the wireframe its catalog entry chose? Open the built swatches, wells, and contrast readouts beside the catalog entry recording the chosen option and its reason.
provisions.statement: `hex-field-with-a-swatch-and-a-contrast-readout`
provisions.rationale: The default is the hex field with a swatch and a contrast readout. It takes any color, shows it, and states the ratio the validation enforces. The runner-up is the approver-button preview, which shows the ratio rather than stating it. Preset swatches are the other alternative for a reader who does not know a hex value. A free color with no contrast check stays out: a pale accent ships white text nobody can read.

provisions.heading: Date and Time Field
provisions.evidence: Does every built calendar input match the wireframe its catalog entry chose? Open the built date, duration, and range fields beside the catalog entry recording the chosen option and its reason.
provisions.statement: `one-text-field-with-a-calendar-that-opens-beside-it`
provisions.rationale: The default is one typed field with a calendar beside it: there is always a way to type, and the calendar serves a reader who would rather click. The runner-up is three text inputs; prefer it where accessibility review demands it, at the cost of the slowest entry in the form. A date and a time on one row are the other alternative where a form always takes both. The native date input stays out: it draws the browser chrome instead of the application control.

provisions.heading: Email Body Editor
