provisions.evidence: Does every built message composer match the wireframe its catalog entry chose? Open the built subject-plus-body forms and variable chips beside the catalog entry recording the chosen option and its reason.
provisions.statement: `subject-plus-body-with-variable-chips`
provisions.rationale: The default is subject plus body with variable chips. The sentence is written once and the facts are placed where they belong. The runner-up is the side-by-side spender preview; prefer it because a template is proven once it is seen filled. Plain text with a variable list is the other alternative where a mail client must read text. A template with no preview stays out: variables are spelled in one place and filled in another, and only a filled copy shows that they meet.

provisions.heading: Expose a Field Error to Assistive Technology
provisions.evidence: Does every built field expose its invalid state and point at its error while the error shows, and carry neither before it is touched? Open the built forms and read each field's attributes with its error shown and hidden.
provisions.statement: A field MUST set `aria-invalid="true"` and point `aria-describedby` at its error only while the error shows.
provisions.rationale: A visible error message alone reaches only sighted readers. Marking the field invalid and pointing at the error message tells assistive technology which field failed and what the message says, which is what WCAG 3.3.1 Error Identification and WCAG 4.1.2 Name, Role, Value ask for: an error described in text, and a field exposing its state. An untouched empty required field carries neither mark, so it is never announced as invalid before the reader reaches it.

provisions.heading: Keep Submit Enabled to Reveal Errors
provisions.evidence: Does any built submit control disable itself while the form holds errors? Open the built forms with errors in them and press each submit.
provisions.statement: A submit control MUST stay enabled while the form holds errors, so pressing it moves focus to the summary or the first field in error.
provisions.rationale: A greyed-out submit button gives no reason and no way forward. A submit that stays enabled can be pressed, and pressing it carries the reader to the summary or to the first field in error, which names what to fix. The form still refuses the submit, and keeps every entered value.

provisions.heading: Mark Every Required Field
provisions.evidence: Does every built required field show a visible marker and carry the `required` attribute, and does each form explain the marker above its first field? Open the built forms and read each required field plus the line above the first one.
provisions.statement: Every required field MUST carry the `required` attribute and a visible marker that the form explains once, above its first field.
provisions.rationale: WCAG 3.3.2 Labels or Instructions asks that a required field say so before it is submitted. A visible marker tells sighted readers which fields they must fill, and the `required` attribute tells the same to screen readers. Explaining the marker once, above the first field, teaches it for the whole form, so every field needs only the mark itself.

provisions.heading: Match the Keyboard to the Value
provisions.evidence: Does any built numeric, code, or identifier field keep the default text keyboard with no recorded reason? Open the built fields and read the project's recorded convention beside them.
provisions.statement: Set `inputmode` on a numeric or code field for its value, and turn off autocorrect and autocapitalize on an identifier field such as an IBAN or a reference.
provisions.rationale: A reader entering an amount or a booking reference meets keys for the value instead of the full alphabet. On an identifier field, autocorrect stays off, so it never rewrites an IBAN or a booking reference.

provisions.heading: Money Field
provisions.evidence: Does every built amount input match the wireframe its catalog entry chose? Open the built amount, currency, and total fields beside the catalog entry recording the chosen option and its reason.
provisions.statement: `text-input-currency-in-the-label-symbol-inside`
provisions.rationale: The default is the text input with the currency in its label: the label names the currency for a screen reader, and the field accepts any typed amount with a comma or a point as the decimal separator. The restated payout total is the runner-up: it belongs on every amount an approver sees, because it stops the fee from surprising either side at payout. Preset chips are the other alternative where one round amount repeats. The stepper stays out: a continuous amount cannot be reached by stepping.

provisions.heading: Name Every Field with a Visible Label
provisions.evidence: Does every built field show a visible label naming its value? Open each form on the built screens and read every field's label.
provisions.statement: Every field MUST carry a visible label that names its value.
provisions.rationale: A placeholder vanishes on the first keystroke, so a filled field with no label beside it no longer says what it holds. Screen readers announce the label aloud, and sighted staff read it when they return to a filled form to check each value before saving. Without a visible label, both groups have to guess what each value means.

provisions.heading: Picking a Period
provisions.evidence: Does every built range picker match the wireframe its catalog entry chose? Open the built presets, month pickers, and painted calendars beside the catalog entry recording the chosen option and its reason.
provisions.statement: `two-date-inputs-with-presets`
provisions.rationale: The default is two typed dates with presets: one tap covers the common windows, typing covers the rare ones, and both edges stay visible. The runner-up is the painted calendar; prefer it on reporting screens where the window itself is the question. The month picker is the other alternative for a report running by calendar month. Presets alone with no typed fallback stay out: no preset reaches the filing-to-payout window the payout check wants.

provisions.heading: Refuse Enter While Text Is Being Composed
provisions.evidence: Does any built field acting on Enter submit half-composed text from an input method? Open the built tag inputs and other fields acting on Enter, and confirm a candidate with Enter.
provisions.statement: A field that acts on the Enter key MUST ignore it while an input method is composing text.
provisions.rationale: Someone typing a vendor name in Japanese or Chinese presses Enter to confirm a candidate in the input method, not to submit anything. If a tag input or inline rename acts on that keystroke, it files half-composed text. Ignoring Enter until composition ends keeps the submitted value whole.

provisions.heading: Repeatable Group
provisions.evidence: Does every built code group match the wireframe its catalog entry chose? Open the built stacked cards and inline tables beside the catalog entry recording the chosen option and its reason.
provisions.statement: `stacked-cards-one-per-type`
provisions.rationale: The default is stacked cards: one card per code with its ceiling and allocation readable at once, and one command to add another. The runner-up is the table with inline editing; prefer it for reviewing many codes, where changing three ceilings costs three fields and no navigation. One section per repetition is the other alternative for creation, where each code is new. A group whose repetitions cannot be removed stays out: a code added by mistake leaves without taking its claimed amounts with it.

provisions.heading: Reporting a Refused Submit
provisions.evidence: Does every built submit-error report match the wireframe its catalog entry chose? Open the built summaries and per-field messages beside the catalog entry recording the chosen option and its reason.
provisions.statement: `a-summary-above-the-form-plus-a-message-on-each-field`
provisions.rationale: The default is the summary with focus, plus per-field messages. It meets WCAG 3.3.1 and 3.3.3, and the links carry the reader to each field. The runner-up validates on leaving each field; prefer it as a complement, never a replacement, since it confirms good values early but leaves a reader facing three errors with no overview. Messages on the fields only are the other alternative for a short form. The dialog summary stays out: it hides the form the reader must fix. Whatever the form reports, it keeps every entered value, as [Keep the Reader's Input Through a Failure](feedback-and-states.md#keep-the-readers-input-through-a-failure) states.

provisions.heading: Show a Field Error After the Field Is Left
provisions.evidence: Does any built field show an error while it is still being typed in, or keep one after the value turns valid? Open the built forms, type in each field, leave it, fix it, and watch when each message appears and clears.
provisions.statement: A field error MUST appear only once the user leaves the field with a changed value or submits the form, and disappear as soon as the value becomes valid.
provisions.rationale: An error shown mid-typing scolds a value the reader has not finished, and one that lingers after the fix makes the reader doubt the repair. The message appears once the field is left or the form is submitted, and it clears as soon as the value turns valid.

provisions.heading: Slug or URL Field with a Preview
provisions.evidence: Does every built address input match the wireframe its catalog entry chose? Open the built slugs, transliterations, and availability checks beside the catalog entry recording the chosen option and its reason.
provisions.statement: `slug-with-the-live-address-under-it`
provisions.rationale: The default is the slug with its live address under it: the reader types the short part and reads the full address before saving. The runner-up transliterates from the name; prefer it at creation, where typing the same words twice is pure overhead. The address as a fact is the other alternative once it is shared. An address that stays unreadable until after it is saved stays out.

provisions.heading: State Each Field's Purpose
provisions.evidence: Does every built field collecting information about the user carry the `autocomplete` token for its purpose? Open the built forms and read the token on each such field.
provisions.statement: A field collecting information about the user MUST carry the `autocomplete` token for its purpose.
provisions.rationale: Without the token, the browser cannot offer the stored bank account holder or email, so the reader retypes both on every claim. With the right token, the browser fills each value once, and the reader checks it instead of typing it. That is what WCAG 1.3.5 Identify Input Purpose asks for: the purpose of each such field must be programmatically determinable.

provisions.heading: Switch or a Checkbox
provisions.evidence: Does every built toggle match the wireframe its catalog entry chose? Open the built switches, checkboxes, and instant applies beside the catalog entry recording the chosen option and its reason.
provisions.statement: `a-switch-with-the-label-and-its-consequence`
provisions.rationale: The default is the switch with its consequence stated: the label says what is on, and the line under it says what turning it off does. The runner-up applies instantly with an undo toast; prefer it for low-risk settings a reader flips often. A checkbox is the other alternative where the off state is the default. A switch whose label names the control instead of the outcome stays out.

provisions.heading: Tag Input
provisions.evidence: Does every built tag chip match the wireframe its catalog entry chose? Open the built chips, popover lists, and inherited tags beside the catalog entry recording the chosen option and its reason.
provisions.statement: `chips-with-type-to-add-and-suggestions`
provisions.rationale: The default is chips with type-to-add and suggestions. New words are allowed and old ones are offered, so `travel` is spelled once. The runner-up is a checkbox list in a popover; prefer it where the tag set is closed and counted. Free text split on commas is the other alternative where a list is pasted in. Free text with no suggestions stays out: it grows `travel`, `Travel`, and `travel-meals` side by side.

provisions.heading: Take a Name in One Field of Any Script
provisions.evidence: Does any built name entry split the name, or refuse letters outside Latin? Open the built staff and spender forms and enter a name in a non-Latin script.
provisions.statement: A person's name MUST be one field that accepts letters of any script.
provisions.rationale: Given and family names are not universal, so splitting them forces staff into parts their name lacks, and a Latin-only rule refuses real staff. One field accepting letters of any script holds every name the back office meets.

provisions.heading: Text Field and Its States
provisions.evidence: Does every built text input match the wireframe its catalog entry chose? Open the built labels, counts, and growing areas beside the catalog entry recording the chosen option and its reason.
provisions.statement: `label-above-help-under-six-states-on-one-page`
provisions.rationale: The default is the six-state reference page, the only option pinning every state one field draws. The runner-up confirms a good value inline; prefer it on create forms, where it saves a refused submit. Floating labels are the other alternative for a compact form. The placeholder-as-label stays out: it vanishes on the first keystroke, and its color misses contrast.

provisions.heading: Upload Field
provisions.evidence: Does every built file input match the wireframe its catalog entry chose? Open the built drop zones, CSV reads, and progress rows beside the catalog entry recording the chosen option and its reason.
provisions.statement: `a-drop-zone-that-states-what-it-accepts`
provisions.rationale: The default is the drop zone stating its types and size limit: nobody learns the limit by being refused. The runner-up is one progress row per file; prefer it for imports of several files, where one bar per file beats one bar for all. A CSV upload stating its columns first is the other alternative where the file must match a fixed shape. A CSV upload with no stated columns stays out: a file refused for a format nobody stated is a refusal the application caused.

provisions.heading: Work That Is Not Saved
provisions.evidence: Does every built unsaved marker match the wireframe its catalog entry chose? Open the built dirty flags, drafts, and save bars beside the catalog entry recording the chosen option and its reason.
provisions.statement: `a-visible-unsaved-marker-beside-the-save`
provisions.rationale: The default is the visible unsaved marker beside Save: a reader never has to remember whether anything was typed. The runner-up pins a save bar to the top; prefer it for long settings pages where the form actions scroll out of view. Autosave with a saved marker is the other alternative for a note written over several sittings. Silent autosave on money or access stays out: each save would be an audited command, and an audit entry per keystroke batch is not a trail a reader can follow.

provisions.heading: Align Money to the Right with Its Currency
provisions.evidence: Does every built money column right-align its figures and show a currency on each? Open the money columns on built tables.
provisions.statement: A table MUST right-align a money column and show the currency of every amount in it.
provisions.rationale: Right alignment lines up place value down the column, so a reader compares hundreds against thousands at a glance instead of reading each figure digit by digit. Showing the currency on every amount keeps EUR 125.00 distinct from a bare 125.00, so an export or a screenshot never leaves finance guessing which money it shows.

provisions.heading: Announce a List's Result Count
provisions.evidence: Does every built list announce its result count after a filter or search, and its selection total after a selection change, once per change? Change the view and the selection on built lists and listen for the announcement.
provisions.statement: A list MUST announce its result count after a filter or search and its selection total after a selection changes, once per change through the page's polite status region.
provisions.rationale: A filter narrows 268 expenses to 58, and a screen-reader user sitting on that list hears nothing: the rows changed under them. A bulk selection of "3 selected, EUR 412.00" stays silent too, so the reader acts without knowing the scope. Announcing the result count after each filter or search, and the selection total after each selection change, through the page's polite status region, keeps both in the open. Announce once per change, through the region in `litespec/frontend/patterns/feedback-and-states#announce-each-status-by-its-urgency`. This is WCAG 4.1.3 Status Messages.

provisions.heading: Bulk Action Bar
provisions.evidence: Does the built selection bar match the wireframe the catalog entry chose? Open the built count bars, pills, and dialogs beside the catalog entry recording the chosen option and its reason.
provisions.statement: `a-bar-above-the-table-naming-the-count`
provisions.rationale: A bar above the table names the count and the money, and on a reversals page that total is the thing a reader checks before acting. The runner-up is a floating pill for reversible bulk work, such as resending receipts or tagging, where the pill leaves the table in place. Never ship the bar at the foot: on a long table the action sits off screen while the checkboxes that enabled it do not.

provisions.heading: Choosing the Columns
provisions.evidence: Does the built column set match the wireframe its catalog entry chose? Open the built choosers and saved views beside the catalog entry recording the chosen option and its reason.
provisions.statement: `five-columns-nothing-removable`
provisions.rationale: Five fixed columns cover the five questions a reader asks of a row: which expense, who spent, when, what state it is in, and how much. That is what fits at 1440 pixels without scrolling, so it stays the default. The runner-up is the Columns popover: add it once more than one team asks for a sixth fact, such as method or cost centre. Saved views come later, when finance and the auditors want different tables of their own. Never ship the question-shaped headers: they cost width and read as a form.

provisions.heading: Exporting the List
provisions.evidence: Does the built download flow match the wireframe the catalog entry chose? Open the built CSV buttons, dialogs, and background exports beside the catalog entry recording the chosen option and its reason.
provisions.statement: `one-export-button-that-downloads-csv`
provisions.rationale: One Export button downloads the filtered rows as CSV, so the accountant's job costs one click and no decisions. Prefer a background export past a few thousand rows, where a direct download would time out. Never ship copy as the only export: copying the visible page silently drops every row past the pager.

provisions.heading: Filters
provisions.evidence: Do the built filter controls match the wireframe the catalog entry chose? Open the built controls, panels, and facet buttons beside the catalog entry recording the chosen option and its reason.
provisions.statement: `one-filter-per-category-visible`
provisions.rationale: One visible control per category shows what can narrow the table without opening anything, and each category keeps its own control. The runner-up is faceted buttons with counts: prefer it once a category holds more than a few values and the reader needs the split before choosing. Never ship every category inside one dropdown: it hides the applied state and breaks the stated rule.

provisions.heading: Grouped Rows
provisions.evidence: Do the built group headers match the wireframe the catalog entry chose? Open the built day, trip, and flat groupings beside the catalog entry recording the chosen option and its reason.
provisions.statement: `grouped-by-day-with-subtotals`
provisions.rationale: Grouping by day with subtotals answers what today paid without a chart and without leaving the list. The runner-up is grouping by trip with collapse toggles: prefer it once trips grow long enough that one day of rows stops fitting. Collapsed rows stay findable, because the browser's find opens the group that holds a match. Never ship two group levels: month-then-day nesting turns the list into a tree that paging cannot cross.

provisions.heading: Inline Row Expansion
provisions.evidence: Do the built expandable rows match the wireframe the catalog entry chose? Open the built expense lines and decision states beside the catalog entry recording the chosen option and its reason.
provisions.statement: `expand-to-the-order-lines`
provisions.rationale: Expansion shows the expense lines: what the spender claimed, which is the question asked from the list. The runner-up adds decision state to the lines; prefer it on the decision list, where handover is the work. Never ship expand-all: twenty expanded rows make a page nobody can scan, and one click fires a read per row.

provisions.heading: Keep a List's View in Its Address
provisions.evidence: Does every built list keep its filters, sort, page, and expanded groups after a reload? Change the view on each built list and reload the address.
provisions.statement: A list MUST keep its filters, sort order, and page in the URL, and its expanded groups where it groups rows.
provisions.rationale: Readers pass list views around: they open one expense and come back, they refresh, they paste a link to a colleague. When the filters, sort order, page, and expanded groups live in the URL, all three return to the same rows. Without that, opening one record wipes out the filters the reader set, and a pasted link opens the unfiltered first page instead of the rows under discussion.

provisions.heading: Keep the Header Row in View
provisions.evidence: Does every built tall table keep its header in view while scrolling, with no focused row hidden under it? Scroll built long lists with the keyboard.
provisions.statement: Keep the header row of a table taller than the viewport visible while it scrolls, with no focused row hidden under it.
provisions.rationale: On a long expense list the header scrolls out of sight, and the reader scrolls back up to relearn which column is which. A header fixed in place keeps the names visible, but a focused row sliding under it looks lost even though focus sits on it. Keeping the header visible while scrolling, with no focused row hidden under it, answers both. This is WCAG 2.4.11 Focus Not Obscured.

provisions.heading: Make a Scrolling Table a Named Region
provisions.evidence: Does every built sideways-scrolling table take keyboard focus, carry a name, and show a cue at each edge it can still scroll? Open built wide tables at 390 px and tab to each table edge.
provisions.statement: A table that scrolls sideways MUST sit in a named region that takes keyboard focus and shows a cue at each edge it can still scroll.
provisions.rationale: A sideways scroll without a focus stop is pointer-only, so a keyboard user on a 390 px screen has no other way to reach the columns past the edge, and without a cue at the edge a sighted user has no sign that more columns exist. A named region gives the table a stop in the tab order and a name for assistive technology, and the edge cue shows there is more to scroll to. This is WCAG 2.1.1 Keyboard.

provisions.heading: Mark the Sorted Column
provisions.evidence: Is every built sortable header a button, and does only the sorted column carry the direction mark? Open built tables and read each sortable header and the sorted column.
provisions.statement: A sortable column header MUST be a button inside its header cell, with `aria-sort` and its direction on the sorted column only.
provisions.rationale: A screen-reader user needs to hear which column orders the list and to change it like any other button. A header drawn as plain text hides the sorting, and a sorted column with no mark keeps the order silent even though the rows follow it. The button shape plus `aria-sort` with its direction on the sorted column gives both. This is WCAG 1.3.1 Info and Relationships.

provisions.heading: Money Column
provisions.evidence: Does the built amount column match the wireframe the catalog entry chose? Open the built aligned figures and reversal columns beside the catalog entry recording the chosen option and its reason.
provisions.statement: `number-only-right-aligned`
provisions.rationale: Keep the number only. Each cell shows the currency with the figure, so an export or a screenshot never leaves finance guessing which money it shows. Prefer the reversed part under the charged amount where reversals are the work rather than the exception. Never ship money as a share of the total: a derived percentage column answers a question no expenses list is asked.

provisions.heading: Pagination
provisions.evidence: Does the built page control match the wireframe the catalog entry chose? Open the built chevrons, load-more buttons, and compact pagers beside the catalog entry recording the chosen option and its reason.
provisions.statement: `count-left-numbered-pages-right`
provisions.rationale: The count with numbered pages lets the reader jump while the range still says where they are. The runner-up is the compact pager, for tight widths where nobody jumps further than one page at a time. Never ship the jump field: typing a page number and pressing Enter is slower than clicking for almost every reader.

provisions.heading: Pinned and Resizing Columns
provisions.evidence: Do the built fixed columns match the wireframe the catalog entry chose? Open the built frozen first columns beside the catalog entry recording the chosen option and its reason.
provisions.statement: `the-order-column-pinned-while-the-rest-scroll`
provisions.rationale: The expense column stays pinned while the rest scroll: the row stays named at any scroll position, and it costs no control. The runner-up pins the actions too; prefer it once rows carry inline commands that must stay reachable. Never ship draggable widths in a first release: per-user widths are stored state that support cannot see and screenshots cannot hold.

provisions.heading: Row Actions
provisions.evidence: Do the built row commands match the wireframe the catalog entry chose? Open the built inline actions, row menus, and side previews beside the catalog entry recording the chosen option and its reason.
provisions.statement: `one-inline-action-the-rest-in-a-row-menu`
provisions.rationale: One inline command keeps the common job one click away while the row stays narrow, and the rest live in the row menu. Prefer the side preview where acting needs the record context, such as the lines before a resend. Never ship hover-revealed actions: hover fails on touch, and a second focusable render doubles the table for no gain.

provisions.heading: Row Density
provisions.evidence: Does the built row height match the wireframe the catalog entry chose? Open the built 24, 32, and 40 pixel rows beside the catalog entry recording the chosen option and its reason.
provisions.statement: `40-pixels-the-default`
provisions.rationale: Stay at 40 pixels: two lines fit, the row scans, and it matches the default size. The runner-up is 32 pixels, for a working queue where every row is read once and acted on. Never ship a density control the reader sets: most readers set it once, and a screenshot suite then holds three versions of every page. The phone answer is a record list.

provisions.heading: Searching with Highlighted Matches
provisions.evidence: Does the built list search match the wireframe the catalog entry chose? Open the built highlighted cells and scoped searches beside the catalog entry recording the chosen option and its reason.
provisions.statement: `matches-highlighted-in-the-cells`
provisions.rationale: Highlight the matches in the cells, so the reader sees why each row matched without opening it. Prefer a scope control once readers search across trips and must say which one. Never ship a match column on its own: it spends a column stating what the highlight already shows.

provisions.heading: Shape a List by Its Container
provisions.evidence: Does every built list switch between table and cards by the width of its holding region? Open built lists in narrow panels on a wide screen.
provisions.statement: Switch a list between its table and its cards by the width of the region that holds it, not the width of the screen.
provisions.rationale: A list does not always get the full screen. The expense table inside a record's side panel has a phone's width on a desktop screen, and a screen-wide breakpoint would keep it a table where cards read better. Measuring the region that holds the list switches each list at the width it actually has, so one list on a page stays a table while its neighbor turns to cards.

provisions.heading: Sorting
provisions.evidence: Do the built sort controls match the wireframe the catalog entry chose? Open the built arrows and phone sort controls beside the catalog entry recording the chosen option and its reason.
provisions.statement: `every-sortable-header-carries-an-arrow`
provisions.rationale: Every sortable header carries its own arrow, which states that headers sort on touch screens too. The runner-up is headers on a desktop with a Sort control on the phone list: it becomes necessary the moment the table becomes rows below 640 pixels. Never ship multi-column sort: no finance question needs two keys.

provisions.heading: Status in a Column
provisions.evidence: Do the built state badges match the wireframe the catalog entry chose? Open the built tones, badges, and reason lines beside the catalog entry recording the chosen option and its reason.
provisions.statement: `tone-only-on-the-states-that-block`
provisions.rationale: Only the states that block get a tone: Disputed and Awaiting payment take a badge because somebody must act, while Paid and Completed stay plain words. Prefer the reason on a second line for a disputes queue, where the word alone never answers why. Never ship progress marks: four blocks per row on a 268-row list cannot serve a lifecycle that branches.

provisions.heading: Table's Own States
provisions.evidence: Do the built table states match the wireframe the catalog entry chose? Open the built no-data, failed-read, and slow-read states beside the catalog entry recording the chosen option and its reason.
provisions.statement: `no-data-yet-table-replaced`
provisions.rationale: Each state gets its own sentence for its own fact: no data yet replaces the table, a failed refresh keeps the chrome and names how old the rows are, and a slow read names what is loading. Never ship a bare spinner over the table body: rows that shift when the data lands move the row the reader already chose.

provisions.heading: The Layout of a Short List
provisions.evidence: Does the built short-list layout match the wireframe the catalog entry chose? Open the built cards, table rows, and date-led lists beside the catalog entry recording the chosen option and its reason.
provisions.statement: `trip-cards-with-a-budget-bar`
provisions.rationale: Cards with a progress bar: a handful of trips reads better as cards than as rows, and the bar answers the only question the list exists for. The runner-up is a date-led list; prefer it once the year holds dozens of trips and cards stop fitting. Never ship a month calendar for this question: it answers when, which the list is never asked.

provisions.heading: Align Figures in a Column
provisions.evidence: Does every built figure column line up by place? Open built amount, count, and quantity columns and read down each one.
provisions.statement: An amount, count, or quantity shown in a column MUST use tabular figures, so digits of equal place sit under each other.
provisions.rationale: Proportional figures give each digit its own width, so equal places in a column stop lining up and the column wanders. A reversal column that wanders is misread at a glance, and the wrong row pays for it. Tabular figures give every digit one width, so hundreds sit under hundreds down the whole column.

provisions.heading: Choosing a Period
provisions.evidence: Does the built period control match the wireframe its catalog entry chose? Open the built chevrons, preset ranges, and filter chips beside the catalog entry recording the chosen option and its reason.
provisions.statement: `chevrons-either-side-of-the-period-as-the-heading`
provisions.rationale: Ship chevrons beside the heading with a month dropdown: walking a month is one click, and jumping avoids twelve clicks. The runner-up uses presets with typeable bounds, which fits charts and exports where the period is not a month. Never ship the period as a filter chip: the period is the subject, not a refinement.

provisions.heading: Counting Things
provisions.evidence: Does the built tally match the wireframe its catalog entry chose? Open the built sidebar counts, tiles, and report-backed counts beside the catalog entry recording the chosen option and its reason.
provisions.statement: `counts-in-the-sidebar-on-the-rows-that-hold-work`
provisions.rationale: Keep counts where the reader would otherwise fetch them: the sidebar rows that hold work carry them, and the tabs above a list carry them. The runner-up is the stat tiles with their measure stated. Tiles are the better choice for the home page, where the question is how large the month is. Never ship counts with the report that produces them: the report name is system language on a number page.

provisions.heading: Figure Against an Earlier Period
provisions.evidence: Does every built comparison tile match the wireframe its catalog entry chose? Open the built deltas, sparklines, and KPI tables beside the catalog entry recording the chosen option and its reason.
provisions.statement: `tiles-with-a-delta-pill-and-the-previous-figure`
provisions.rationale: Ship the tiles with a delta pill and the previous figure in words: the comparison is visible and the basis is stated. The runner-up is the tiles with sparklines, and it fits the home page where the shape of the month matters more than one earlier figure. Never ship a bare percentage with no basis: up 12 percent without the basis is a claim, not a comparison.

provisions.heading: How Much Fits Before It Breaks
provisions.evidence: Does the built dense table match the wireframe its catalog entry chose? Open the built 390-pixel lists and two-column tables beside the catalog entry recording the chosen option and its reason.
provisions.statement: `the-full-width-with-nothing-truncated`
provisions.rationale: Keep the table at desktop width with two-line cells and no truncation, and switch to the record list under 640 pixels. That pair answers honestly at both widths. The runner-up wraps rather than truncates, which fits where one column holds names of any length. Never ship shortened figures near a statement: a rounded money figure is not a money figure.

provisions.heading: Mark a Moment with Its Machine Value
provisions.evidence: Does every built date or moment carry its machine value? Open built dates and read each time element for its ISO value.
provisions.statement: Render a date or moment in a time element that carries its ISO 8601 value.
provisions.rationale: People write one moment many ways: 8 Oct, October 8, next Tuesday. Assistive technology and the browser read the exact value from the machine form, not the reader's wording of it. The ISO 8601 value in the time element keeps the cited moment exact even where the words stay short.

provisions.heading: Numbers at Phone Width
provisions.evidence: Does every built narrow figure match the wireframe its catalog entry chose? Open the built pairs, per-row figures, and halved charts at 390 pixels beside the catalog entry recording the chosen option and its reason.
provisions.statement: `kpis-in-pairs-with-the-orders-under-them`
provisions.rationale: Ship the two-column KPI pair with the record list under it: the figures of the day stay visible and every expense keeps its amount right-aligned. The runner-up is the aligned statement, and it fits finance pages where the adding up is the point. Never ship the desktop table unchanged at 390 pixels: a table that scrolls sideways for its money column hides the answer.

provisions.heading: Show the Currency of Every Amount
provisions.evidence: Does every built figure show its currency? Open the amounts on built tables, statements, and charts.
provisions.statement: Every amount MUST show its currency.
provisions.rationale: A bare 125.00 reads fine until a second currency arrives; then each bare figure becomes a guess, and a pasted number carries no way to settle it. A currency on every amount keeps EUR 125.00 distinct from GBP 125.00 on every screen and export.

provisions.heading: Showing an Identifier
provisions.evidence: Does every built code display match the wireframe its catalog entry chose? Open the built monospaced, labeled, and copyable codes beside the catalog entry recording the chosen option and its reason.
provisions.statement: `a-code-monospaced-labeled-and-copyable`
provisions.rationale: Ship the labeled, monospaced, copyable code on the record: it is the shape of the rule and the one thing a support case needs quoted. The runner-up is the identifier as the record name, and it fits records with no human name, such as a payout reference. Never ship the page with no identifier: a record nobody can quote is a record support cannot help with.

provisions.heading: Spend Against the Budget
provisions.evidence: Does every built fill-rate view match the wireframe its catalog entry chose? Open the built bars, countdowns, and capacity tables beside the catalog entry recording the chosen option and its reason.
provisions.statement: `a-bar-with-sold-held-and-left-in-words`
provisions.rationale: Ship the progress bar with claimed, held, and left in words: one glance says how far the budget has burned and what is still movable. The runner-up is the per-kind spend table, and it fits when one kind is gone and the others are not. Never ship the countdown alone: EUR 468 left without the budget size hides whether the budget is nearly gone or barely touched.

provisions.heading: Spending by Expense Kind
provisions.evidence: Does every built mix chart match the wireframe its catalog entry chose? Open the built bars, tiles, and donuts beside the catalog entry recording the chosen option and its reason.
provisions.statement: `horizontal-bars-with-the-figure-on-each-row`
provisions.rationale: Ship the horizontal bars with the figure on each row: every kind reads with its count and its money in one glance. The runner-up is the table with a bar in each row, and it fits once kinds gain states such as disputed or reversed. Never ship the donut alone: an angle nobody can read exactly is decoration, not a figure.

provisions.heading: Spending over Time
provisions.evidence: Does every built trend chart match the wireframe its catalog entry chose? Open the built columns, areas, and sparklines beside the catalog entry recording the chosen option and its reason.
provisions.statement: `daily-columns-with-the-total-above`
provisions.rationale: Ship the daily columns with the total above and the peak labeled: they answer how much and when in one glance. The runner-up is the cumulative line against the previous quarter, and it fits once the budget has a quarter to beat. Never ship the chart without its table: a figure nobody can read exactly is a figure nobody can cite.

provisions.heading: State the Time Zone of a Shared Moment
provisions.evidence: Does every built shared moment state its zone? Open the dates and times on built screens read across zones.
provisions.statement: A moment shown to readers in different time zones MUST state its time zone.
provisions.rationale: Without a stated zone, 09:32 in Amsterdam reads as 09:32 in London, and two readers plan the same payout window an hour apart while finance meets only one of them. A stated zone keeps the moment the same for every reader.

provisions.heading: Statement That Adds Up
provisions.evidence: Does the built totals page match the wireframe its catalog entry chose? Open the built groups, subtotals, and payout endings beside the catalog entry recording the chosen option and its reason.
provisions.statement: `groups-subtotals-and-a-grand-total`
provisions.rationale: Keep groups, subtotals, and a grand total, with a count under each line. The count is the only completeness check. The runner-up ends in the payouts the statement became, which fits finance work against bank lines. Add links on every line later, as a behavior of the pick. Never ship the one-figure option as the statement: it hides how the figure was reached.

provisions.heading: Two VAT Rates on One Page
provisions.evidence: Does every built mixed-rate view match the wireframe its catalog entry chose? Open the built splits, badges, and per-rate summaries beside the catalog entry recording the chosen option and its reason.
provisions.statement: `the-vat-split-under-the-order-total`
provisions.rationale: Ship the VAT split under the expense total: the spender total stays one figure and the books get both rates. The runner-up is the per-rate report with taxable bases, and it fits quarter end when finance files the return. Never ship amounts with no VAT note at all: a lawful amount states what the tax is.

provisions.heading: Vendor's Invoice to the Company
provisions.evidence: Does every built supplier bill match the wireframe its catalog entry chose? Open the built documents, states, and usage lines beside the catalog entry recording the chosen option and its reason.
provisions.statement: `the-invoice-as-a-document-with-the-usage-behind-each-line`
provisions.rationale: Ship the document-style invoice with the usage behind each line: finance sees what the fee paid for without opening another page. The runner-up is the paid invoice with its mandate reference, which is the better state of the same document once the money has moved. Never ship the invoice without its VAT lines: a business invoice without VAT is not an invoice.

provisions.heading: When the Money Arrives
provisions.evidence: Does every built payout view match the wireframe its catalog entry chose? Open the built upcoming, weekly, and past views beside the catalog entry recording the chosen option and its reason.
provisions.statement: `upcoming-payouts-with-the-sales-each-one-holds`
provisions.rationale: Ship the list of upcoming payouts with the expenses each one holds: the company sees what goes out and when in one place. The runner-up is the past payouts table with bank references, and it fits finance reconciling against the bank. Never ship the single next-payout tile as the page: one arrival without the ones after it cannot plan a month.

provisions.heading: Writing a Moment
provisions.evidence: Does the built date text match the wireframe its catalog entry chose? Open the built absolute, relative, and weekday forms beside the catalog entry recording the chosen option and its reason.
provisions.statement: `one-form-per-table-with-the-zone-stated-once`
provisions.rationale: Keep one form per table and state the zone once in the header, so a column reads as a column. The entry point names the option its screens render in `formats.moment`. The runner-up puts absolute over relative, which fits dispute and payout surfaces where recency leads. Never ship relative-only dates on a reconciled page: nothing there can be cited.

provisions.heading: Writing an Amount
provisions.evidence: Does the built money text match the wireframe its catalog entry chose? Open the built codes, symbols, and red negatives beside the catalog entry recording the chosen option and its reason.
provisions.statement: `code-and-two-decimals-in-the-reader-s-language-with-a-true-m`
provisions.rationale: Ship the code format in the reader's language with a true minus. It keeps one convention and settles decimals, negatives, and separators at once: each currency shows the decimals it defines. The runner-up is the plain code table, which shows the same choice without reversal rows. The entry point names the option its screens render in `formats.money`. Choose the symbol with the code in the header only when the finance screens and the spender screens show the same form. Never ship the no-currency option: it loses the currency in exports. Never ship mixed decimals: they break the alignment tables exist for.

provisions.heading: Account Menu
provisions.evidence: Does the built sign-in menu match the wireframe its catalog entry chose? Open the built account controls, in the sidebar foot or header, beside the catalog entry recording the chosen option and its reason.
provisions.statement: `an-avatar-menu-in-the-header`
provisions.rationale: The avatar menu in the header is the default because it holds the account page, the access statement, and sign-out in one control. The sidebar foot is the runner-up, but it sits far from the top of a long page. The account as a page reached from the menu fits a console where account, email, sign-in, and close are separate pages. Never ship a bare sign-out link: an account with no page turns the language, sessions, and closing the account into support messages.

provisions.heading: Breadcrumb
provisions.evidence: Does the built parent chain match the wireframe its catalog entry chose? Open a built four-level trail, with its truncation and parent links, beside the catalog entry recording the chosen option and its reason.
provisions.statement: `the-trail-as-the-parent-chain`
provisions.rationale: The parent chain is the default because it states where a record sits in the tree, with the last item marked current. The trail that truncates from the left is the runner-up for four-level chains: its overflow menu keeps the current page visible. The current title as a sibling menu fits records whose siblings get opened together. Never ship with no trail at all: on a phone the sidebar is closed, so the trail is the only statement of where a record sits.

provisions.heading: Command Palette
provisions.evidence: Does the built jump-to dialog match the wireframe its catalog entry chose? Open the built palette, with its grouped results and recent items, beside the catalog entry recording the chosen option and its reason.
provisions.statement: `cmd-k-dialog-with-grouped-results`
provisions.rationale: The grouped Cmd+K dialog is the default because it puts pages above records, so one typed query answers both where to go and what to open. Recent items first are the runner-up for cost centre and support work that moves between a few records. Search scoped to the current area fits a reader who is already in the right list. Never ship command verbs with a preview as the default palette: every verb becomes a second path to a use case.

provisions.heading: Draw Sibling Pages as Links, Not Tabs
provisions.evidence: Is every built row of sibling pages a navigation landmark of links instead of a tab list? Open each built row, and check the address changes and the Back button returns.
provisions.statement: A row of sibling pages MUST be a navigation landmark of links with `aria-current="page"` on the current page, leaving the tab list for switching panels within one page.
provisions.rationale: A screen reader announces a tab list as panels on one page, so a reader who opens Receipts from a tab expects the address to stay and the Back button to skip it. A navigation landmark of links tells the truth: each page has its own address, and the Back button returns to the page before it. WCAG 2.2 criterion 1.3.1 Info and Relationships and criterion 4.1.2 Name, Role, Value require the announced role to match the behavior.
provisions.example: On the Standard expense page, the Amounts, Receipts, Reversals, and Details row looks like tabs but is built as links: opening Receipts changes the address, and the Back button returns to the previous page.

provisions.heading: Give Every Page Its Own Address
provisions.evidence: Can every built screen be opened directly from its copied address? Paste three copied addresses into a fresh tab.
provisions.statement: Every page MUST have its own URL that opens it directly.
provisions.rationale: A direct address lets a reader share, bookmark, and reopen a page, and lets a notification or a record link to it. Without it, support cannot send the page under discussion, and a refresh drops the reader back to the start.
provisions.example: A dispute notification links to expense EXP-1042; pasting that address into a fresh tab opens the same record, not the console home.

provisions.heading: Header Bar
provisions.evidence: Does the built top band match the wireframe its catalog entry chose? Open the built trip header, with its company name and deployment identity, beside the catalog entry recording the chosen option and its reason.
provisions.statement: `the-bar-with-the-company-name`
provisions.rationale: The bar with the company name and the acting person is the default because it states the two facts a support conversation needs first: which company, and who is acting. The bar as the breadcrumb is the runner-up when the trail would otherwise repeat the page title. The deployment identity band fits a sandbox deployment, where naming the deployment keeps it from being confused with production. Never ship with no bar at all: burying the theme and language in the sidebar foot turns a visible control into three taps.

provisions.heading: Help and Support
provisions.evidence: Does the built guidance entry match the wireframe its catalog entry chose? Open the built help surfaces, from sidebar entry to contextual hints, beside the catalog entry recording the chosen option and its reason.
provisions.statement: `contextual-help-beside-the-page-it-explains`
provisions.rationale: The guide for the current page in a side panel is the default because it answers the question without leaving the record. A help page from the sidebar is the runner-up: an index for a reader who knows what to ask. Help search inside the command palette fits a console where navigation queries already go to one input. Never ship with no help entry: a finance lead stuck at the office with a queue has nowhere else to turn.

provisions.heading: Icons in the Frame
provisions.evidence: Which built label or action carries an icon outside the set the catalog entry chose? Open the built frame, with its labeled actions and marked current item, beside the catalog entry recording the chosen option and its reason.
provisions.statement: `an-icon-beside-every-label`
provisions.rationale: An icon beside every label is the default because the icon reinforces the label instead of replacing it, which makes seven areas easy to scan. Icons only for the actions, with words for the areas, are the runner-up where the icon budget is short. Words alone fit a small set of areas with no icon set to keep. Never ship icons that carry state in the frame: the theme and language as bare glyphs force the reader to hover over each to tell them apart.

provisions.heading: Language and Theme
provisions.evidence: Do the built locale and appearance controls match the wireframe the catalog entry chose? Open the built controls, in the header and account menu, beside the catalog entry recording the chosen option and its reason.
provisions.statement: `the-theme-following-the-system-with-an-override`
provisions.rationale: The default splits the two switches. The theme follows the device, because few readers change it during a day and the device already states the preference; System, Light, and Dark stay in the account menu for the reader who overrides it. The language stays in the header showing its value, because a wrong language makes every other word unreadable. Both switches in the header, each showing its value, are the runner-up for a product whose staff switch theme during a shift. Never ship with no language switch: one language is a commercial decision about which companies Claimwick serves, and Claimwick already serves companies in two languages.

provisions.heading: Mark the Current Section
provisions.evidence: Does every built screen highlight the area holding its open page? Open three screens reached by link, notification, and search.
provisions.statement: The navigation MUST mark the section that holds the current page.
provisions.rationale: A marked section tells a reader who arrived from a link, a notification, or a search which area holds the open page. Without it, every page looks like the start, and the reader reopens the sidebar to learn where they already are.
provisions.example: Ava opens expense EXP-1042 from a notification; the Expenses area stays highlighted in the sidebar, so she knows which area holds the record.

provisions.heading: Notification Inbox
provisions.evidence: Does the built attention list match the wireframe its catalog entry chose? Open the built inbox and bell, with triage and unread states, beside the catalog entry recording the chosen option and its reason.
provisions.statement: `a-bell-in-the-header-with-a-dropdown-panel`
provisions.rationale: A bell with a dropdown panel is the default because it keeps the count visible on every page and answers what changed without leaving the list being worked. The inbox page is the runner-up for support days with dozens of items, where triage needs filters. Needs attention on the home page fits a console where the first page is the only queue. Never ship with no notifications: polling seven areas by hand is how a dispute deadline gets missed.

provisions.heading: Sidebar
provisions.evidence: Does the built area list match the wireframe its catalog entry chose? Open the built console frame, with its grouped areas and marked item, beside the catalog entry recording the chosen option and its reason.
provisions.statement: `grouped-areas-with-expandable-sub-items`
provisions.rationale: Grouped areas with expandable sub-items are the default because two levels hold all seven areas, with each sub-item indented under its area and the current item marked. Groups with live counts are the runner-up for areas that hold a queue, such as reversals, where the count saves a visit. Recent pages above the areas fit a reader who resumes the same few records. Never ship a flat list of every page: past a hundred entries the list is an index, not a map, and that lookup job belongs to the command palette.

provisions.heading: Tabs Within a Page
provisions.evidence: Does the built tab row match the wireframe its catalog entry chose? Open the built in-page tabs, with the active tab in the URL, beside the catalog entry recording the chosen option and its reason.
provisions.statement: `the-shipped-tab-row-with-the-tab-in-the-url`
provisions.rationale: The tab row with the active tab in the URL is the default because a pasted link carries the facet. The row looks like tabs but is built as navigation links, one address per page, following Draw Sibling Pages as Links, Not Tabs. The current page is marked by more than color, with weight or an underline. Tabs drawn as real links are the runner-up and the most defensible alternative: middle click and the Back button behave as a reader expects. Headed sections on one page fit a record with a handful of facets that all fit. Never ship a segmented control for facets: three segments are its ceiling, and it can't carry counts or overflow.

provisions.heading: Workspace Switcher
provisions.evidence: Does the built cost centre picker match the wireframe its catalog entry chose? Open the built switcher, with recent workspaces first, beside the catalog entry recording the chosen option and its reason.
provisions.statement: `a-workspace-switcher-at-the-top-of-the-sidebar`
provisions.rationale: A workspace switcher at the top of the sidebar is the default because it moves the whole console without visiting the list. The trail sibling menu is the runner-up on record pages four levels deep, where the sidebar context is far away. Recent workspaces first in the palette fit a reader who switches by keyboard. Never ship back-to-list as the only path: it costs the most to exactly the companies with the most cost centres.

provisions.heading: Calendar or Schedule Page
provisions.evidence: Does the built date view match the wireframe its catalog entry chose? Open the built month grids, agendas, and week lanes beside the catalog entry recording the chosen option and its reason.
provisions.statement: `month-grid-with-trips-marked`
provisions.rationale: The default builds the month grid. Ninety-three trips ahead need density, and the grid shows the month the list cannot. The agenda list is the runner-up: choose it on a phone, where seven columns become unreadable whichever way they are drawn. The week lanes are the other runner-up for a company with few cost centres and a clash to spot. Never ship the week lanes as the default: two cost centres fit, and the third cost centre breaks the shape.

provisions.heading: Editor Page
provisions.evidence: Does the built preview screen match the wireframe its catalog entry chose? Open the built form-plus-preview splits, drawers, and floating panels beside the catalog entry recording the chosen option and its reason.
provisions.statement: `form-left-live-preview-right-one-save`
provisions.rationale: The default builds the form left with a live preview right. Every control writes straight into the preview, and nobody saves to find out what a change looks like. The floating panel is the runner-up: choose it when the visual dominates, such as a cover image judged at real size. The preview drawer is the other runner-up when the form needs the full page. Keep the preview beside the form or over it: a preview above the form scrolls away with every edit, which defeats a live preview.

provisions.heading: Error or Not-Found Page
provisions.evidence: Does the built dead end match the wireframe its catalog entry chose? Open the built not-found, outage, and refused views beside the catalog entry recording the chosen option and its reason.
provisions.statement: `centered-not-found-with-links-back`
provisions.rationale: The default builds the centered not-found with links back. It says what happened, says where to go, and does both in one glance. The permission refusal is the runner-up: choose it whenever the page knows who can resolve it, because Back is not a fix. The full-page outage is the other runner-up when a provider failure blocks the page. A retry button on a page that will never exist is a promise that cannot be kept, so name the state and the next step instead.

provisions.heading: Form Page
provisions.evidence: Does the built input screen match the wireframe its catalog entry chose? Open the built sections, labeled blocks, and one-question flows beside the catalog entry recording the chosen option and its reason.
provisions.statement: `one-section-one-column-of-fields-cancel-beside-save`
provisions.rationale: The default builds one section, one column, Cancel beside the submit action. A single command reads as a list of questions with one place to submit and one place to leave. The stacked blocks are the runner-up when the form carries several labeled groups, such as the expense, the amounts, and the budget. The one-question-per-screen flow is the other runner-up when each answer changes the next question and nothing may be skipped. Three steps for work that fits one page is one step too many.

provisions.heading: Home Page
provisions.evidence: Does the built start screen match the wireframe its catalog entry chose? Open the built queues, tiles, and next actions beside the catalog entry recording the chosen option and its reason.
provisions.statement: `work-first-tiles-second`
provisions.rationale: The default builds work first, tiles second. The manager reads the queue and stops, and the figures wait below for the curious reader. The my-work split is the runner-up: choose it once assignment is a real command and two people share one queue. The tiles-first layout is the other runner-up, for a reader who opens the page to check a number. Never ship the tiles-first layout as the default: three stat tiles push the queue below the fold, and the page reads as a report instead of a task list.

provisions.heading: List Page
provisions.evidence: Does the built collection screen match the wireframe its catalog entry chose? Open the built searches, views, and filter bars beside the catalog entry recording the chosen option and its reason.
provisions.statement: `search-and-a-state-filter-only`
provisions.rationale: The default builds search plus one state filter. Two controls answer the two questions readers ask, who is this and what state is it in, and a bare list needs only the filter added. The row of views is the runner-up for the states a reader returns to. The dense filter bar is the other runner-up past a few hundred rows across many spenders, where the query is restated in words. A list page holds one table: a second table is a second route wearing a disguise. Views can replace the state filter, but they never replace the search box.

provisions.heading: Live Operations Page
provisions.evidence: Does the built live view match the wireframe its catalog entry chose? Open the built counts, cost centres, and exception views beside the catalog entry recording the chosen option and its reason.
provisions.statement: `the-count-the-cost-centres-the-exceptions`
provisions.rationale: The default builds the count with cost centres and exceptions. The finance lead reads one number first, then the per-cost-centre split, then only what needs a person. The exceptions-only view is the runner-up: choose it on the wall display once the day is steady and the count is already known. The full-screen count is the other runner-up for a display read from across the room. A page that lists every payout is a log, not a live view, so keep the count in the header and the exceptions above the fold.

provisions.heading: Name the Page in One Heading
provisions.evidence: Does every built screen carry exactly one top-level heading that names it? Open every built page and read its top-level heading.
provisions.statement: Each page MUST show one top-level heading that names the record, list, or task it holds.
provisions.rationale: One heading names the open record, list, or task, so a reader who arrives from a link or a search knows where they landed. With two headings, both compete for that job: the reader guesses which line to trust, while assistive tech announces the wrong one.

provisions.heading: Onboarding or Setup Page
provisions.evidence: Does the built first-run guide match the wireframe its catalog entry chose? Open the built checklists, wizards, and templates beside the catalog entry recording the chosen option and its reason.
provisions.statement: `checklist-with-a-progress-bar`
provisions.rationale: The default builds the checklist with a progress bar. It states the three steps, shows which is done, and waits without leading. The stepper wizard is the runner-up: choose it when a step cannot be skipped and the next depends on the last. Starting from a template is the other runner-up when the first trip is a known shape. Three saves for a first run are three chances to leave the company half set up.

provisions.heading: Outcome Page
provisions.evidence: Does the built result screen match the wireframe its catalog entry chose? Open the built statements, references, and refusal outcomes beside the catalog entry recording the chosen option and its reason.
provisions.statement: `one-statement-one-next-step`
provisions.rationale: The default builds one statement with one next step. A reader who came to learn whether it worked leaves in one glance. The refusal outcome is the runner-up, for the same frame with the fix in the primary place. The confirmation band is the other runner-up when the flow leaves a reference the reader must keep. A moment is not a place: an outcome the reader may need to return to belongs on a page, not in a toast.

provisions.heading: Queue
provisions.evidence: Does the built batch-selection screen match the wireframe its catalog entry chose? Open the built select-all banners, play modes, and per-row checkboxes beside the catalog entry recording the chosen option and its reason.
provisions.statement: `select-all-on-the-page-banner-for-the-rest`
provisions.rationale: The default builds select-all on the page, then the rest from a banner. It is the clearest answer to the select-all problem: the header checkbox selects the 25 rows on screen, and the banner offers all 31 as an explicit second act. Money deserves the second click. The play mode is the runner-up: choose it when each decision needs different information and batch work is rare. A checkbox on every row is the other runner-up for a queue whose bulk job is small and capped. Keep the search box and the filter in place while rows are selected: a bulk bar that replaces the toolbar makes the layout jump mid-decision and hides the controls the reader wants to refine it.

provisions.heading: Record Page
provisions.evidence: Does the built single-record screen match the wireframe its catalog entry chose? Open the built summaries, tabs, and asides beside the catalog entry recording the chosen option and its reason.
provisions.statement: `summary-sections-aside-for-history`
provisions.rationale: The default builds the summary with sections and history in the aside. What defines the record runs down the main column, while history supports it from the side. The properties rail is the runner-up: choose it when the aside must carry editable values rather than history. The tabs layout is the other runner-up for a record with more facets than three sections allow. Never put the record's facts in the header: a dense header pushes every command below the fold on a phone and fights the breadcrumb trail for space.

provisions.heading: Report Page
provisions.evidence: Does the built figures screen match the wireframe its catalog entry chose? Open the built period pickers, range controls, and trend cards beside the catalog entry recording the chosen option and its reason.
provisions.statement: `chevron-pair-with-the-period-as-the-heading`
provisions.rationale: The default builds the chevron pair with the period as the heading. A reader cannot mistake a chevron for a tab, and the month select still allows a jump across months. The cards with sparklines are the runner-up: choose them mid-month when the question is trend rather than settlement. The typed range is the other runner-up for a report over an arbitrary span. Label each month control with its direction: a pair of unlabeled buttons leaves the reader guessing which one goes back.

provisions.heading: Settings Home
provisions.evidence: Does the built setup index match the wireframe its catalog entry chose? Open the built grouped links, settings trees, and search indexes beside the catalog entry recording the chosen option and its reason.
provisions.statement: `grouped-links-one-line-each`
provisions.rationale: The default builds grouped links. Each area names what it holds, the page never grows a form, and thirty routes fit in a handful of sections. The left navigation is the runner-up: choose it once areas gain enough depth to deserve their own tree. The searchable list is the other runner-up for a reader who knows the name of the setting. Group by the thing, never by how often it changes: readers look for a thing, not for how often they change it.

provisions.heading: Keep Destructive Commands Out of the Primary Place
provisions.evidence: Does any built record header give a destructive command the primary style? Open the headers on built record screens and read each command's tone.
provisions.statement: A destructive command MUST NOT take the primary action's place or style in a record header.
provisions.rationale: The primary place draws the hurried click, so it holds only the safe next step. A destructive command styled or placed as primary, such as Void the expense, turns a routine visit into a retired policy or a voided expense, with no step between intent and loss.

provisions.heading: Previous and Next Record
provisions.evidence: Does the built neighbor step match the wireframe its catalog entry chose? Open the built jump searches and list drawers beside the catalog entry recording the chosen option and its reason.
provisions.statement: `chevrons-beside-the-breadcrumb`
provisions.rationale: The default keeps the chevrons beside the breadcrumb. They keep the list order and cost almost no space. The jump-by-search option is the runner-up, and fits readers who know the next record number rather than its neighbor. Prefer the list drawer on triage queues where the reader skims many records. Never ship movement without a position: chevrons that never say 4 of 268 leave the reader lost in the queue.

provisions.heading: Property List with Copy
provisions.evidence: Does the built copyable fact match the wireframe its catalog entry chose? Open the built confirmations and identifier cards beside the catalog entry recording the chosen option and its reason.
provisions.statement: `every-identifier-copies`
provisions.rationale: The default keeps the always-visible copy button on each identifier, so support reaches for it without hunting. The in-place confirmation is the runner-up, and fits records where a miscopied reference causes real mistakes. Prefer the grouped card only where identifiers are quoted together, such as a reference pasted into a dispute. Where the same copy control repeats in every row of a table, it shows on hover and on keyboard focus, stays visible on a touch screen, and a repeated click restarts its confirmation instead of being ignored. Hover-only copy fits nowhere: touch screens have no hover, and the button would never appear. Never ship a property list whose long values clip without a way to expand them.

provisions.heading: Record Aside
provisions.evidence: Does the built side column match the wireframe its catalog entry chose? Open the built decision panels and ownership rails beside the catalog entry recording the chosen option and its reason.
provisions.statement: `history-in-the-aside-sections-in-the-main-column`
provisions.rationale: The default gives the aside to history. History supports the expense without describing it, which is exactly what the aside slot is for. The decision panel is the runner-up, and the better choice on records that wait for someone, such as a dispute with a deadline. Prefer the people and labels aside on records a team hands between shifts. Never ship an empty aside by accident: an expense with nothing pending and no history reads as a rendering fault.

provisions.heading: Record Attachments
provisions.evidence: Does the built file section match the wireframe its catalog entry chose? Open the built evidence groups and thumbnail grids beside the catalog entry recording the chosen option and its reason.
provisions.statement: `a-file-list-with-a-drop-zone`
provisions.rationale: The default keeps the file list with a drop zone. Each row names the file and its kind, who added it, and its size, and the drop zone invites the next file. The evidence-grouped option is the runner-up, and fits a dispute, where Ben asks for kinds rather than files. Prefer the thumbnail option only where images dominate, such as receipt photos. Never ship a section that is only a drop zone: a record whose files hide behind an upload control reads as empty.

provisions.heading: Record Change History
provisions.evidence: Does the built audit trail match the wireframe its catalog entry chose? Open the built per-field histories and full-page logs beside the catalog entry recording the chosen option and its reason.
provisions.statement: `history-as-a-tab-on-the-record`
provisions.rationale: The default keeps the history tab on the record. It keeps one route, and the tab state stays in the URL. A reader checking a claim opens History without losing the expense. The per-field history is the runner-up, and fits disputes about one value such as the email that carried the receipt. Prefer the full-page log only for long-lived records whose trail outgrows a tab. Never ship the money-only trail as the audit: the edits that explain the money are missing there.

provisions.heading: Record Header
provisions.evidence: Does the built title row match the wireframe its catalog entry chose? Open the built facts option and overflow menu beside the catalog entry recording the chosen option and its reason.
provisions.statement: `title-state-breadcrumb-one-primary-action`
provisions.rationale: The default keeps the title, the state, the breadcrumb, and one primary action. The state beside the title answers the first question on every record. The overflow menu is the runner-up, and the better choice once a record carries four or more commands. Prefer the facts option only where the record's own facts are the reason to open it, since a tall header pushes the sections below the fold. Never ship a header with no title: every page carries exactly one `h1`, which automated checks enforce.

provisions.heading: Record Notes
provisions.evidence: Does the built annotation feed match the wireframe its catalog entry chose? Open the built scope toggles and mixed feeds beside the catalog entry recording the chosen option and its reason.
provisions.statement: `a-notes-section-with-the-composer-on-top`
provisions.rationale: The default keeps the notes section with the composer on top. The newest note reads first, and internal scope is the default, so nothing leaks to the spender. The internal-or-spender composer is the runner-up, and fits records where staff write to the spender from the same box. Prefer notes mixed into the timeline only where what the team wrote explains what the system did next. Never ship notes without a scope marker: a reader who cannot tell internal from spender-visible will write the wrong one.

provisions.heading: Record Summary
provisions.evidence: Does the built fact block match the wireframe its catalog entry chose? Open the built copy buttons and figure tiles beside the catalog entry recording the chosen option and its reason.
provisions.statement: `facts-about-the-record-itself`
provisions.rationale: The default keeps the facts about the record itself. A trip summary states when, where, and what it may spend: the identity of the record rather than its support. The copyable identifiers option is the runner-up, and the better choice on records a reader quotes elsewhere, such as an expense read out on the phone. Prefer the tiles option only where the reader checks four figures at a glance rather than reading facts line by line. Never ship values with no section: a row of values standing on the canvas breaks the rule that a section is the only box.

provisions.heading: Record Tabs
provisions.evidence: Does the built facet row match the wireframe its catalog entry chose? Open the built side rails and three-tab rows beside the catalog entry recording the chosen option and its reason.
provisions.statement: `four-tabs-with-the-active-one-in-the-url`
provisions.rationale: The default keeps four tabs with the active one in the URL. Four stays inside every cited ceiling, and each panel repeats its tab label as a heading. The side rail is the runner-up, and the better choice past five facets or where one facet is a long form. Prefer three tabs with the fourth as its own page only where the fourth facet is long enough to stand alone. Never ship tabs with icons in their labels: icons are forbidden in tab labels, since they add a second channel for one meaning.

provisions.heading: Record the Reader May Not Change
provisions.evidence: Does the built locked record match the wireframe its catalog entry chose? Open the built access requests and whole-page refusals beside the catalog entry recording the chosen option and its reason.
provisions.statement: `the-commands-are-refused-the-record-is-not`
provisions.rationale: The default keeps the refused commands on a readable record. Auditors can read an expense and cannot reverse it, and each refusal names the grant that would allow it. The ask for access option is the runner-up, and the better choice where access is routinely granted, such as an intern joining finance. Prefer the whole-page refusal only where the record itself is out of the reader's reach: it names the grant, and it costs the reader every fact on the page. Never ship a role switcher on production: acting as somebody is a development capability, and the button would be a security hole with a label on it.

provisions.heading: Record Timeline
provisions.evidence: Does the built event feed match the wireframe its catalog entry chose? Open the built filters and history tables beside the catalog entry recording the chosen option and its reason.
provisions.statement: `newest-first-with-actor-and-timestamp`
provisions.rationale: The default keeps the newest-first timeline with actor and timestamp, since it answers who and when on every line. The filtered timeline is the runner-up, and the better choice once a record carries dozens of entries across kinds. Prefer the table option only where the history is the record rather than context. Never group the main history by actor: it destroys the chronological order a timeline exists to give.

provisions.heading: Related Records
provisions.evidence: Does the built relation link match the wireframe its catalog entry chose? Open the built previews and editable tables beside the catalog entry recording the chosen option and its reason.
provisions.statement: `each-relation-is-a-link-with-its-state`
provisions.rationale: The default ships the link with state list. Each relation is a link carrying its own state, so a reader can jump and knows what they will find. The preview card is the runner-up, and the better choice where the parent facts decide the next step, such as a receipt read against its trip. Prefer the editable table only where the relation itself is the work, such as the exceptions to a policy. Never ship a cross-reference line in the description: it cannot carry the parent state, and it hides where a reader does not look.

provisions.heading: Show One Primary Action in a Record Header
provisions.evidence: `litespec-maintain validate` emits `PATTERN_INVALID` for a wireframe header holding two primary actions.
provisions.statement: A record header wireframe MUST show at most one primary action.
provisions.rationale: One primary action names the step readers take most often next on the record, such as Message spender on expense EXP-1042. With two equal buttons, the reader compares labels on every visit, and a hurried click lands on the wrong command.

provisions.heading: Whole Record Screen
provisions.evidence: Does the built record page order its parts as the wireframe its catalog entry chose? Open the built summary, money-first, and tabbed screens beside the catalog entry recording the chosen option and its reason.
provisions.statement: `summary-three-sections-history-in-the-aside`
provisions.rationale: The default keeps the record-page shape with a summary, three sections, and history in the aside. Spender, lines, and money each keep their own section.
