The money-first layout is the runner-up, and fits finance readers who reconcile payments against reversals. Prefer the tabbed layout only once a record outgrows three sections. Never ship the phone layout as the desktop page: stacked sections waste most of the width there.

provisions.heading: Build the Server Data Cache per Request
provisions.evidence: Does every server-rendered frontend construct its data cache inside each request, reusing none across requests? Check the server request setup.
provisions.statement: A server-rendered frontend MUST construct its data cache inside each request.
provisions.rationale: A server renders for many users at once. A data cache shared across requests serves the next user the previous user's answer, leaking one actor's data to another with no error to report it. Constructing the cache inside each request gives every user a fresh cache that dies with the response.

provisions.heading: Define Every Route State
provisions.evidence: Does every data-driven route define its loading, empty, error, forbidden, not-found, and ready behavior, with an absent address on the shared outcome page? Check the route state definitions.
provisions.statement: A data-driven route MUST define its loading, empty, error, forbidden, not-found, and ready behavior.
provisions.rationale: A blank region while a request is pending or failed gives the user no signal: the page reads no different when loading than when broken. Defining each state up front gives it a designed drawing, and the root not-found handling draws the shared outcome page for an absent address. These six are the states a route has. A control adds `disabled` and `pending` under `litespec/frontend/components#render-control-states`, because both describe a control rather than a route. A route adds `not-found`, which a control does not, because a missing target resolves at the route.

provisions.heading: Keep Authenticated Caching Explicit
provisions.evidence: Does every cached actor-specific read declare its cache key, partition, invalidation owner, and security review beside the read definition? Check the read definitions setting cache keys.
provisions.statement: Actor-specific data MUST declare its cache key, partition, invalidation owner, and security review before caching, beside the read definition setting the key.
provisions.rationale: A cache entry that ignores whose data it holds serves one actor's answer to another user: the classic leak behind a shared cache. Declaring the cache key, the partition, the invalidation owner, and the security review beside the read definition forces each cached actor-specific read to name its boundary before it caches. An uncached read is the safe default, and a cache partitioned per request is the safe server shape.

provisions.heading: Keep Layouts Stable
provisions.evidence: Does every layout hold only the frame and the providers every child route needs? Check the layout definitions.
provisions.statement: Keep a layout to the frame and the providers every child route needs.
provisions.rationale: A layout wraps every route beneath it. A feature-specific provider placed in a shared layout forces unrelated routes to carry its download, its state, and its failure modes. Keeping each route's cost to what it uses means the layout holds only what every child needs.

provisions.heading: Keep Proxy Behavior at the Edge
provisions.evidence: Does every development and edge proxy rule route only, deciding neither identity nor authorization? Check the proxy rules.
provisions.statement: A development or edge proxy rule MUST route only, and never decide who the actor is or what the actor may read.
provisions.rationale: A development or edge proxy runs before the request reaches the API, with no view of the record or the permissions an authorization decision depends on. A proxy rule that decided who the actor is or what the actor may read would enforce a different boundary than the API, and the two would disagree on the first edge case. Leaving identity and authorization to the API keeps one boundary instead of two.
provisions.example: A development proxy forwards `/api` and `/auth` to the API and changes nothing else: no header decides the actor, and no rule filters what the actor may read.

provisions.heading: Keep Server-Only Code Identifiable
provisions.evidence: Does every module reading a request header, cookie, or server secret sit in a file named and placed for the server? Check the server file names and places.
provisions.statement: Keep a module reading a request header, a cookie, or a server secret in a file whose name and place show the server ownership.
provisions.rationale: A module that reads a request header, a cookie, or a server secret breaks when it runs in the browser, and worse, it can drag the secret into the client download. A file whose name and place show server ownership turns an accidental browser import into a build error, and carries the same fact to a reader browsing the tree.

provisions.heading: Load Each Route and Each Language Separately
provisions.evidence: Does every route and every language ship as its own download, with no icon set or language loaded whole? Check the route bundles and the dictionary loader.
provisions.statement: A frontend MUST load each route and each language as its own download, with no icon set or language loaded whole.
provisions.rationale: A user opens one address and reads one language, so downloading every route and every language up front wastes time on code and copy outside that path. Each route and each language ships as its own download: a user in Dutch who stays on the dashboard downloads neither English nor the routes outside that path. No icon set or language loads whole for the same reason.
provisions.example: A dictionary loader returns one language, not the whole dictionary. Each route file or folder ships as its own download.

provisions.heading: Load Route Data Before Rendering
provisions.evidence: Does every route load each read it needs through the one shared cache before its view renders? Check the route loaders and the cache definitions.
provisions.statement: A route MUST load each read it needs through one shared cache before its view renders.
provisions.rationale: A view that renders before its reads complete shows a spinner after it appears, then swaps the spinner for content. That is two drawings for one navigation, with layout shifting between them. Loading through one shared cache puts the data in place for the first drawing, and the router keeps no second copy that could disagree.
provisions.example: An expense record route loads the expense and every read its sections need, before the view renders.

provisions.heading: Move Focus on a Route Change
provisions.evidence: Does every route move focus to the new route's top-level heading after a navigation inside the application? Check the route suite output.
provisions.statement: A route change inside the application MUST move keyboard focus to the new route's top-level heading.
provisions.rationale: A full page load starts focus and the screen reader at the top of the new page. A client-side navigation instead replaces the content under a focus that stays on the link just used, or falls back to the page body. A keyboard user then tabs through the old position, and a screen-reader user hears nothing change. Moving focus to the heading reads the new page's title and starts the next Tab from there, as WCAG 2.4.3 Focus Order expects.
provisions.example: Opening EXP-1042 from the expense list lands focus on the heading "EXP-1042, Ava, EUR 125.00".

provisions.heading: Prefetch a Route on Intent
provisions.evidence: Does every route prefetch land in the shared cache, with no second router cache? Check the router prefetch wiring.
provisions.statement: A frontend MUST prefetch the route the user signals intent toward, without treating that prefetch as a cache beyond the shared cache.
provisions.rationale: When the user signals intent toward a route, by hovering a link or focusing a menu item, prefetching loads that route's data into the shared cache before the navigation starts, so most navigations render from data already in place. The prefetch fills the shared cache only, because a router keeping its own second cache would serve a stale answer beside the fresh one.

provisions.heading: Read Route Data from the Route Cache
provisions.evidence: Does every view read through the cache entry its route filled, and does every failed read reach the route error boundary? Check the view data reads and the route loaders.
provisions.statement: A view MUST read route data through the same cache entry its route filled.
provisions.rationale: A view that reads under another key issues a second request for data the route already loaded, and the two answers can disagree when the data changes between them. Reading through the same entry renders the data the route approved. A failed read reaches the route's error boundary, which draws the shared problem state instead of a half-rendered view.

provisions.heading: Split Long Client Work
provisions.evidence: Does every client task longer than 50 milliseconds yield between chunks? Check the browser performance traces of the heaviest routes.
provisions.statement: Split client work that runs longer than 50 milliseconds, such as an import preview or a report total, into chunks that give the browser a turn between them.
provisions.rationale: While script runs, the page answers no click and no key. A staff member previewing 1,204 imported payouts sees a frozen screen and clicks again. Giving the browser a turn between chunks keeps every input answered within one frame, and the total blocking time the measured checks record stays low.

provisions.heading: Use a Shared Layout for a Shell
provisions.evidence: Does every shell sit in a shared layout, adding no address segment? Check the layout definitions.
provisions.statement: Give a shell a layout holding the frame every child route shares.
provisions.rationale: A shell is the frame every child route shares: navigation, header, and providers. A shared layout holds it without adding an address segment, so the shell stays out of links and every child route renders inside the same frame.

provisions.heading: Validate Address Parameters with a Schema
provisions.evidence: Does every route declare its address parameters, filters, and page in a validated schema? Check the route parameter schemas.
provisions.statement: A route MUST declare its address parameters in a validated schema, including its filters and its page.
provisions.rationale: Without a schema, a malformed address renders a page from nonsense values, and a filter kept outside the address is lost on the first share or navigation away. A validated schema makes the address the whole input: a shareable address restores the same filters and page, and validation refuses a malformed address at the boundary.
provisions.example: The expense list schema declares its own text field and spreads the shared paging fields.

provisions.heading: Keep a Route Entry Thin
provisions.evidence: Does every route entry hold only its input, load, and component, with no reusable logic and no reference to another route entry? Check the route entries.
provisions.statement: A route entry MUST hold its input, its load, and its component, with no reusable logic and no reference to another route entry.
provisions.rationale: A route entry serves one address: its input, its load, and its component. A column definition or validation rule written in a route entry stays unreachable from the second route that needs it, so the second route writes its own copy. A reference from one route entry to another ties one address to another, so changing the first breaks the second. Reusable logic lives in modules instead, where both routes import it.
provisions.example: An expense list route validates its search input, prefetches its read, and composes one screen from module components.

provisions.heading: Keep a Use Case Folder Flat
provisions.evidence: Does every use-case folder hold files with no subfolder? Check the module tree.
provisions.statement: A folder named for one use case MUST hold files and no subfolder.
provisions.rationale: A subfolder inside a use case folder names a grouping the backend does not have, so the one-to-one mirror between the two trees stops at that point. Past the subfolder, the reader can no longer translate names by rule, and nothing reports where the translation broke. Files directly in the use case folder keep the mirror checkable to the bottom.

provisions.heading: Keep Applications Independent
provisions.evidence: Does any frontend import source from another frontend? Check the import statements.
provisions.statement: A frontend MUST NOT import source from another frontend.
provisions.rationale: An import from another application's source ties the two together: a change to one breaks or redeploys the other. Each application owns its routes, its environment, its session handling, its words, its tests, and its deployment, so it can change, test, and ship on its own. Code two applications genuinely share moves down into a shared package, which names neither application.

provisions.heading: Keep Shared Packages Free of Application Code
provisions.evidence: Does any shared package hold page composition, feature state, authentication policy, or application components? Check the shared package sources.
provisions.statement: A shared package MUST NOT contain page composition, feature state, authentication policy, or application components.
provisions.rationale: Page composition, feature state, authentication policy, or application components kept in a shared package would bind every application to one application's choices. Shared packages hold only what serves every frontend and names none of them: the generated client, the shared UI package, the locale dictionaries, and the frontend tooling. Application-specific code stays in the application, where it can change without touching the rest.

provisions.heading: Mark Each Route with Its Screen
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `mark-missing` (level S) for a route entry with no mark, `mark-count-invalid` (level S) for one with more than one, and `mark-unknown` (level S) for a mark naming no screen of the route's entry point.
provisions.statement: A route entry MUST carry one mark naming the screen it renders, in the form its stack page states.
provisions.rationale: The route is where a screen record becomes code, and its folder or file name only resembles the screen. One mark makes the link written and checkable. A web route exports the same typed `litespec` constant a use-case module exports, so a wrong identifier fails the consumer's type check against the generated union, and `litespec model check` reports it as `mark-unknown` where no type check ran. A Blazor component or an Android destination carries the .NET mark the .NET reader already reads. Each stack page states its route entry, the file or class that carries the mark, and that layouts, error pages, and route groups are not route entries: the [Svelte Stack](web/svelte/stack.md), [React Stack](web/react/stack.md), [Blazor Stack](blazor/stack.md), and [Android Stack](mobile/android/stack.md) pages state theirs. The use cases a screen offers are not marked on the route; the builder computes them from its calls.
provisions.example: The `<script module>` of the Claimwick expense list page exports `export const litespec = { implements: "screen/claimwick-app.expense-list" } as const satisfies LiteSpecMark;`, naming the screen it renders.

provisions.heading: Mirror the Backend Use Case Path in Kebab Case
provisions.evidence: Does every use-case folder sit at `{module}/{aggregate}/{use-case}/`, or at `{module}/use-cases/{use-case}/` for a module-level use case, in kebab case and resolve to the backend folder of the same names? Check the module tree and the structure test proving the mirror.
provisions.statement: A use-case folder MUST sit under the modules root at `{module}/{aggregate}/{use-case}/` in kebab case, or at `{module}/use-cases/{use-case}/` for a query describing no one aggregate, resolving to the one backend use case folder of the same names inside its `UseCases/` folder.
provisions.rationale: A reader holding a specification page finds the frontend code by translating three names to lowercase folders. No second map, index, or naming register stands between the specification and the code, so an agent given a use case identifier resolves its frontend folder by rule. The backend holds one folder per use case, so the mirror names one folder. The frontend structure test holds the mirror on every build, under `litespec/frontend/testing#prove-the-module-mirror-in-a-structure-test`.
provisions.example:
One backend folder and its frontend counterpart are the same path in two spellings:

```text
<backend>/Orders/Orders/UseCases/SearchMerchantOrders/
<frontend>/modules/orders/orders/search-merchant-orders/
```

In Claimwick, `use-case/spending.list-expenses` lists expenses. The backend implements it under `Spending/Expenses/UseCases/ListExpenses`, and the web frontend serves it from the same path in kebab case, `lib/modules/spending/expenses/list-expenses`, beside the screen record `screen/claimwick-app.expense-list`.

```text
<backend>/Spending/Expenses/UseCases/ListExpenses/
<frontend>/modules/spending/expenses/list-expenses/
```

The three backend names become three lowercase folder names, while the `UseCases/` segment carries no frontend spelling.

A query that describes no one aggregate keeps its record home under `use-cases/` beside its module, so its folder mirrors that home with two names instead of three. A query named `use-case/spending.read-spending-summary` would live at `<frontend>/modules/spending/use-cases/read-spending-summary/` and `<backend>/Spending/UseCases/ReadSpendingSummary/`. The running Claimwick example holds no such module-level query.

The diagram shows the backend path beside its frontend mirror, with one arrow per translated segment.

![The backend folder Spending, Expenses, ListExpenses beside the frontend folders spending, expenses, list-expenses, with one arrow mapping each backend segment to its kebab-case spelling.](../assets/diagrams/frontend-use-case-path.svg)

provisions.heading: Order Imports from Routes to Shared Packages
provisions.evidence: Does every import point from a route to a module to the frame to a shared package, with none in the reverse direction? Check the import statements.
provisions.statement: An import MUST point from a route to a module to the frame to a shared package, and never in the reverse direction.
provisions.rationale: A module importing a route ties use-case code to one address, and a shared package importing an application ties every application to one application's choices. Each reverse import collapses two layers into one. One direction, from routes to modules to the frame to shared packages, keeps addresses, use-case code, cross-route values, and shared code in separate layers, with each layer usable without the layers above it.
provisions.example:
The allowed dependency path runs one way:

```text
Routes -> modules -> frame -> shared packages
```

That direction refuses three imports: a module reaching a route, a shared package reaching an application, and a frame module reaching into one module's use-case folder for a second module's data.

provisions.heading: Organize a Frontend into Frame, Routes, and Modules
provisions.evidence: Does every frontend file sit in the frame, routes, or use-case modules? Check the frontend folder roots.
provisions.statement: A frontend MUST organize its code into a frame, routes, and use-case modules.
provisions.rationale: Every new file raises one question: is it cross-cutting, is it an address, or does it serve one use case. Without the split, shared values hide inside routes, use-case code hides inside shared folders, and no author can tell where a new file belongs. The three parts answer the question, so each file has one home.
provisions.example:
Each stack page maps the same three parts onto its own toolchain:

```text
{frontend}/
  frame/     client configuration, session, language, permissions, formatting, shell data
  routes/    one entry per address
  modules/   one folder per backend module, aggregate, and use case
```

provisions.heading: Place a Shared File in the Folder That Owns It
provisions.evidence: Does every file read by several use cases sit in the narrowest folder holding every consumer? Check the aggregate and module folders.
provisions.statement: A file read by several use cases of one aggregate MUST sit flat in that aggregate's folder.
provisions.rationale: A file read by several use cases of one aggregate belongs flat in that aggregate's folder: the lowest folder holding every consumer. There it sits beside its consumers, found by browsing rather than through an index, and moving it changes nothing outside the aggregate. A file read by several aggregates rises one more level, to the module folder, by the same rule.
provisions.example: Three expense queries share one tab strip, so the tab strip sits flat in the aggregate folder. A file read by several aggregates sits flat in the module folder.

provisions.heading: Place Cross-Route Values in the Frame
provisions.evidence: Which cross-route values or browser uses sit outside the frame? Check the frame.
provisions.statement: A frontend MUST place cross-route values in its frame: client configuration, session read, language choice, permissions, formatting, and shell data.
provisions.rationale: A route holding a cross-route value keeps a copy beside every other route's copy, with nothing keeping the copies equal. Client configuration, session read, language choice, permissions, formatting, and shell data cross every route, so the frame holds each once, where every route reaches it. A browser API a use-case module needs belongs in the frame for the same reason: a module renders and reads data rather than touching the device.

provisions.heading: Place Tests at Their Ownership Boundary
provisions.evidence: Does every logic test sit beside its module, and does every browser suite sit under the one tests root per frontend? Check the module folders and the tests roots.
provisions.statement: Place a logic test beside its module, and keep browser suites under one tests root per frontend.
provisions.rationale: Scattering browser suites beside modules would split the fixtures and the runs, because browser suites share one fixture set and one deployment per frontend. One tests root per frontend keeps them together. A logic test instead sits beside its module, where it is found from the code it covers and runs with it.

provisions.heading: Reject a Folder Name That Owns Nothing
provisions.evidence: Does any folder under an application's `src` carry a refused name? Check the application folder tree.
provisions.statement: A folder under an application's `src` MUST NOT be named `shared`, `common`, `utils`, `util`, `helpers`, `misc`, `components`, `hooks`, `types`, or `services`.
provisions.rationale: A folder named `shared`, `utils`, or `components` refuses nothing. Every author with a file of unclear ownership drops it there, so the folder collects unrelated code that escapes review against the use cases it serves. Finding a file then means searching a pile instead of translating a use case path. Refusing these names forces each file into the folder that owns it. The rule covers an application's `src`, not a shared package's internals, which the package owns.
provisions.example: A shared query three use cases read sits flat in the aggregate folder, not in a `shared/` folder beside them.

provisions.heading: Use Explicit Public Entry Points for Shared Packages
provisions.evidence: Does every application import stop at the documented public entry points of shared packages? Check the application imports and the package manifests.
provisions.statement: Expose a shared package only through its documented public entry points.
provisions.rationale: An application importing an internal path couples itself to that layout, so the next rearrangement breaks the application. A shared package rearranges its internals between releases, while its documented public entry points are the stable surface it keeps.

provisions.heading: Assert Each Declared Refusal by Its Code
provisions.evidence: Does every declared refusal get reached and asserted by result code in some evidence specification? Check the evidence specifications.
provisions.statement: An evidence specification for a use case declaring a refusal MUST reach that refusal and assert it by its result's code.
provisions.rationale: A refusal the test leaves unreached renders where no reader looks: in a log, or nowhere at all. Reaching it and asserting it by its result's code proves two things at once: the page renders the refusal, and the code the page shows is the code the result declares. The scenario records the situation that reaches it, so the test also documents how the refusal is provoked.
provisions.example: The refusal alert carries the code, so the assertion names it.

provisions.heading: Assert the Result a Scenario Ends In
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `proves-unreached` (level S) for a browser test reaching the screen whose assertions in the same test hold neither the refusal code nor the success result's declared text or code.
provisions.statement: A browser test that proves a scenario MUST assert the result the scenario ends in by its refusal code or by the success result's declared text or code.
provisions.rationale: Reaching the screen shows only that the page opened; the assertion shows the ending the result promises. Holding the refusal code or the success text in the same test ties the proof to the named result. A money-moving use case that a test only reads leaves completion unshown, so the test submits it.
provisions.example: The browser specification for `scenario/list-expenses.listing-own-expenses-succeeds` opens the expense list on `screen/claimwick-app.expense-list` and asserts the expenses table: the listed ending the success result `result/list-expenses.listed` promises.

provisions.heading: Isolate Browser Tests
provisions.evidence: Does every browser test create or identify its own data, authentication context, and expected state? Check the browser specifications.
provisions.statement: A browser test MUST create or identify its own data, its own authentication context, and its own expected state.
provisions.rationale: A test that depends on execution order or on leftover data fails for reasons unrelated to the change under review, and passes only when the suite runs in one order. Creating its own data, its own authentication context, and its own expected state makes each test runnable alone and in any order. A test spends no seeded record; it creates the record it needs.

provisions.heading: Keep Test Support Narrow
provisions.evidence: Does every test support file hold only render helpers, one shared API helper, and locator helpers? Check the test support files.
provisions.statement: Limit test support to render helpers for required providers, to one API helper that every specification shares, and to the locator helpers.
provisions.rationale: Test support grows easily into render frameworks, data builders, and custom runners: a second application with its own untested surface. Limiting it to render helpers for required providers, one shared API helper, and locator helpers keeps it small. A change to the actor header or the idempotency key then reaches the fixtures rather than every specification.

provisions.heading: Mark Each Browser Test with the Scenario It Proves
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `mark-unknown` (level S) for a `proves` annotation naming no record a test may prove, or naming a flow.
provisions.statement: A browser test that proves a scenario MUST carry a `proves` annotation naming that scenario.
provisions.rationale: A title tag claims proof without anything reading it, so the builder cannot count it. The written annotation is the link the builder counts: it names the lowest record the test verifies, exactly as a backend test mark does, and it is built by the `proves` helper the generated records file exports. A wrong identifier fails the consumer's type check against the generated union, and `litespec model check` reports it as `mark-unknown` where no type check ran.
provisions.example: The browser specification at `apps/web/tests/expenses/list-expenses.spec.ts` in the Claimwick example carries `proves("scenario/list-expenses.listing-own-expenses-succeeds")`. That mark makes the specification the evidence for the listing scenario.

provisions.heading: Match Test Level to Risk
provisions.evidence: Does all pure logic take a logic test, all navigation and integration a browser specification, and every address the route contract? Check the test files beside the modules and under the tests roots.
provisions.statement: A frontend MUST use a logic test for pure logic, a browser specification for navigation and integration, and the route contract for every address.
provisions.rationale: A browser run costs seconds and a deployment; a unit test costs milliseconds and nothing else. Proving pure logic through the browser slows the suite without strengthening it, while proving navigation with unit tests proves nothing about the running page. Matching the level to the risk proves each risk at the cheapest boundary that represents it.

provisions.heading: Name the Flow a Flow Test Covers
provisions.evidence: Does every browser test that drives several screens carry a `flow` annotation naming the flow and a `proves` mark for each scenario it drives and asserts? Check the browser tests and their annotations.
provisions.statement: A browser test that drives several screens MUST carry a `flow` annotation naming the flow and a `proves` mark for each scenario it drives and asserts.
provisions.rationale: A flow is not a proof target: it is achieved through use cases, so a flow test proves the scenarios it drives, and flow coverage is computed from them. The `flow` annotation tells a reader which flow the test rehearses without claiming that the flow itself is proven. Reworded by [decision/0049-literal-flow-words-concrete-consequences](decision/0049-literal-flow-words-concrete-consequences).
provisions.example: The submit-and-reimburse flow test carries `flow: flow/submit-and-reimburse` and a `proves` mark for each scenario it drives and asserts on each screen it reaches.

provisions.heading: Prove Each Scenario at One Boundary
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `proves-duplicate` (level A) for a scenario with `proves` marks on more than one test.
provisions.statement: A scenario MUST carry one `proves` mark, on the test at the cheapest boundary that represents its risk.
provisions.rationale: Marking both boundaries on one scenario makes the slower test a second witness nobody needs, and doubles the work when the scenario changes. An API test proves a business outcome faster and more steadily than a browser test, and a browser test is the only proof that a page offers the use case and renders its result. A scenario whose risk is the outcome is proved at the API, and a scenario whose risk is what a person sees is proved in the browser.
provisions.example: `scenario/list-expenses.listing-own-expenses-succeeds` is proved by the browser specification at `apps/web/tests/expenses/list-expenses.spec.ts`, the cheapest boundary that shows what a person sees on the expense list. A scenario whose risk is a business outcome alone is proved at the API boundary instead.

provisions.heading: Prove the Module Mirror in a Structure Test
provisions.evidence: Does the structure test resolve every module folder to a backend use-case folder, and does it name no refused folder? Check the structure test.
provisions.statement: A frontend calling the API MUST hold a test asserting that its module tree resolves to the backend use-case folders and names no refused folder.
provisions.rationale: Without a check, the backend adds or renames a use case and the frontend tree silently stops matching, so the translation lands nowhere. The module mirror is the claim that makes a specification findable from a folder path: translate three names, land on the code. A test asserting the mirror on every build, and naming no refused folder, keeps the translation true. The same test can also assert no import between use case folders or between modules, which no lint rule checks.
provisions.example: The structure check resolves each folder name against the backend's module tree, as the Vitest structure test on [Web Testing](web/testing.md) shows.

provisions.heading: Reach a Screen That Offers the Scenario's Use Case
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `proves-unreached` (level S) for a browser test whose `page.goto` targets match no screen offering the claimed scenario's use case.
provisions.statement: A browser test that proves a scenario MUST reach a screen that offers the scenario's use case by a `page.goto` literal or template matching that screen's `address`.
provisions.rationale: A test that only clicks through navigation names no screen it proved on, so proof becomes a claim instead of exercised behavior. Driving the use case through the page a person uses keeps proof on the exercised path. Matching the `page.goto` target against the screen `address` templates gives the deterministic reach the reader computes.
provisions.example: The evidence specification opens `/expenses`, the address of `screen/claimwick-app.expense-list`, which offers `use-case/spending.list-expenses`. That navigation is the reach the check reads.

provisions.heading: Read the Deployment for Its Identifiers
provisions.evidence: Does every browser test read the record identifiers it needs from the running deployment instead of hard-coding them? Check the browser specifications.
provisions.statement: Read a record identifier a browser test needs from the running deployment, and fall back to an absent identifier when the deployment holds none.
provisions.rationale: A hard-coded record identifier passes against the deployment it was copied from and fails against the next deployment, where that record does not exist. Reading the identifier from the running deployment keeps the test true wherever it runs. Falling back to an absent identifier still visits the route as a not-found page, which is a state a reader can reach anyway.

provisions.heading: Run Browser Checks Through the Command Line
provisions.evidence: Does every browser suite run through the command line, addressable per route and per file? Check the suite runner and the CI invocation.
provisions.statement: A browser suite MUST run through the command line, addressable per route and per file.
provisions.rationale: A check that runs only inside an editor plugin or a proxy runner leaves the next investigator with no way to repeat it. The command line is the interface every runner shares: the developer, the drill, and the integration job all invoke the same command. Addressable per route and per file, the suite also runs just the check under review instead of the whole suite.

provisions.heading: Test Observable States
provisions.evidence: Does every test assert observable behavior, in each state its situation reaches, instead of internal state? Check the test assertions.
provisions.statement: A frontend test SHOULD assert observable behavior in each state applicable to what the test covers: loading, empty, error, forbidden, not-found, pending, validation, and success.
provisions.rationale: An assertion on internal state passes while the rendered page stays broken, because nothing ties the variable to what the reader sees. Asserting observable behavior in each state the test's situation reaches ties the test to the reader's view instead. The scenario states which states its situation reaches, from loading and empty through error, forbidden, not-found, pending, validation, and success. The project records each state as a term with labels per language.

provisions.heading: Use Network Mocks for Component Tests
provisions.evidence: Does every component and logic test that needs HTTP answer through contract-generated network mocks, with the generated client in the path? Check the component tests and the mock generation.
provisions.statement: A component or logic test that needs HTTP MUST serve its answers through network mocks generated from the published contract.
provisions.rationale: A mocked client replaces the generated code with a guess of what it returns, so the test proves the mock rather than the component. A network mock generated from the published contract answers the same HTTP request the browser would send instead. The generated client stays in the path it takes in production, and the component is tested through the client the page actually uses.
provisions.example: The workspace keeps one mock-generation command that regenerates them from the published OpenAPI document.

provisions.heading: Compose Each Route from One Floorplan
provisions.evidence: Does every route render exactly one floorplan, or record a freestyle decision? Look in the route sources and in the suite output that reads the floorplan name from each frame.
provisions.statement: A route MUST render exactly one floorplan from the declared set, unless it is a recorded freestyle route.
provisions.rationale: The floorplan fixes the layout, the heading position, and the slots, so a reviewer reads which floorplan a route composes and knows what the page looks like before opening it. The slots take domain values only: the aggregate state, the use cases that state permits, and the refusal results of the called use case. Exactly one floorplan per route keeps each page to one known shape, unless it is a recorded freestyle route.
provisions.example: The Claimwick expense record composes `EntityPage` and fills its slots from the expense: its facts, its state, the actions that state permits, and its related records.

provisions.heading: Declare Each Frontend Outside the Contract
provisions.evidence: Does every frontend outside the controlled platforms declare an entry point record with its platform and replacement boundaries? Look in the entry point records.
provisions.statement: A frontend outside the controlled platforms MUST declare an entry point record naming that platform and the boundaries replacing this contract.
provisions.rationale: A device client with no shared component and no router sits outside the floorplan set and the component rules: the contract's checks do not apply to it. Declaring an entry point record that names its platform and the boundaries replacing this contract keeps the decision visible, instead of letting the frontend report as one with nothing to check.

provisions.heading: Give Every Input a Visible Boundary
provisions.evidence: Does every input boundary reach 3:1 against its surface in each declared scheme? Look in the token definitions and the rendered form fields.
provisions.statement: The boundary of a text field, select, checkbox, radio, or switch MUST reach 3:1 contrast against the surface it sits on.
provisions.rationale: WCAG 1.4.11 covers non-text contrast. A reader with low vision finds a field by its edge, and a field drawn at the faint separator step disappears into the page. Its own boundary token keeps separators quiet and controls findable.
provisions.example: The amount field on the Claimwick expense form keeps a visible edge on the card behind it in both color schemes, so it stays findable where a separator would fade.

provisions.heading: Justify Each Freestyle Route with a Decision Record
provisions.evidence: Does every freestyle route name the decision record that justifies its layout? Look in the freestyle routes and the decision records.
provisions.statement: A route that composes no declared floorplan MUST name the decision record that justifies its layout.
provisions.rationale: A route that composes no declared floorplan is either the first consumer of a floorplan that does not exist yet or a genuine one-off. Naming the decision record that justifies its layout makes either case reviewable and keeps the declared set closed. A second route of the same shape is the signal to add the floorplan instead of recording another freestyle route.

provisions.heading: Keep a Blocked Command Visible with Its Reason
provisions.evidence: Does every command blocked only by state or role stay visible and disabled with its reason beside it? Look in the command surfaces.
provisions.statement: Leave a command blocked only by the current state or role visible and disabled, with the reason beside it.
provisions.rationale: A user looking for an action needs to learn it exists and why it is unavailable, such as a missing permission or an unmet precondition. A control that vanishes instead reads as a product that does not offer the action at all. Staying visible and disabled with the reason beside it teaches both the existence and the block.

provisions.heading: Keep Each Behavior Package Justified and on Baseline
provisions.evidence: Does every behavior package name its decision record and render through baseline components and tokens? Look in the package declarations and the decision records.
provisions.statement: A behavior package MUST name the decision record justifying it for the capability it supplies, and render through baseline components and tokens.
provisions.rationale: A behavior package adds a capability the design baseline lacks, such as a chart or a rich editor, and naming the decision record that justifies it for that capability keeps the decision tied to the need. The decision follows the capability rather than the visual catalog, so no package duplicates a component the design baseline already provides. Rendering through baseline components and tokens keeps the new capability inside the product's look.

provisions.heading: Keep Layout Inside Floorplans
provisions.evidence: Does any route file declare layout outside its floorplan and display composites? Look in the route sources.
provisions.statement: Route code MUST NOT declare layout outside its floorplan and display composites.
provisions.rationale: A layout declaration in a route file is a second layout beside the floorplan: the route draws its own spacing while claiming the floorplan's shape. The next route copies the declaration because it looks like the local way to draw, and the floorplan stops describing what routes render. Floorplan and display composites own layout, so one change there reaches every route composing them.

provisions.heading: Keep Token Values in One Token File
provisions.evidence: Does every token value live in the named token file and follow the W3C Design Tokens format? Look in the token file and the stylesheets.
provisions.statement: A project MUST keep every token value in the one token file the design contract's Tokens section names, written in the W3C Design Tokens format, version 2025.10.
provisions.rationale: When values scatter across stylesheets, each limit depends on a hand-run script that runs once and is forgotten. Design tools and token converters have no file they read, and the check has no file to judge. One token file gives every value a home that tools read: components read the stylesheet generated from it, and the check reads it to judge every limit. Proposed by decision 0089.

provisions.heading: Keep Tokens in One Definition
provisions.evidence: Does any application declare its own token value, or does any shipped definition carry a literal color? Look in the application and shared token definitions.
provisions.statement: An application MUST use the shared token definition and declare no value, with no literal color in any shipped definition.
provisions.rationale: One token definition is what makes two applications look like one product. An application uses the shared definition and declares no value of its own, so no second definition introduces a value the first has no opinion about. A definition the shared package ships declares no literal color, so every value traces to the one token file the design contract names.

provisions.heading: Link Each Screen to Its Next Screens
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `screen-unreachable` for a screen no other screen leads to that is not its entry point's start, and `screen-dead-end` for a screen that leads nowhere and offers no use case. Run it at the consumer root.
provisions.statement: Each screen MUST name every screen a person reaches from it in one step in `leadsTo`.
provisions.rationale: The screens and their links are the navigation, and they exist in records before any route is built. The book draws each entry point as a map of places and connections, and each flow as a strip of its step screens. A screen that no other screen leads to strands its readers unless it starts its entry point. A screen that leads nowhere and offers no use case ends their task with nothing done. Proposed by decision 0089.
provisions.example: The Claimwick expense list names the expense record and the new expense form in `leadsTo`. A reader on the list reaches the record to act on one expense, or the form to start a new one, each in one step.

provisions.heading: Map Each Page Frame to Its Floorplan
provisions.evidence: Does every page frame the product uses name its component and its when-to-use rule in the Page Frames section? Look in the design contract.
provisions.statement: The `Page Frames` section of the design contract MUST map each page-frame pattern the product uses to the floorplan component that implements it, each with a when-to-use rule.
provisions.rationale: Without a when-to-use rule, authors choose floorplans by resemblance. Two authors pick different floorplans for one kind of page, and users meet the same kind in two layouts. A map from each page-frame pattern to its component, with the rule that selects it, makes the choice mechanical. A floorplan outside the map is a decision for the shared package, not a choice a route makes on its own. Proposed by decision 0089.
provisions.example:
Claimwick's Page Frames section states each page frame, its component, and the question that selects it:

```markdown
## Page Frames

| Page frame | Component | Use it when the user |
|:---|:---|:---|
| `list-page` | `ListPage` | Finds one record among many. The page shows the result count. |
| `record-page` | `EntityPage` | Acts on one record: its facts, its state, and the actions that state permits. |
| `form-page` | `FormPage` | Supplies the input of one command, with one primary action. |
```

provisions.heading: Meet the Limits of Every Token Role
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `design-token-limit-failed` for a token role that misses its limit in a declared scheme. Run it at the consumer root.
provisions.statement: Every token value in each declared color scheme MUST meet the limit the Concepts table states for its role.
provisions.rationale: Readable text and findable controls are measured limits, not pinned values: a palette passes when every role meets its limit, whatever values it holds. Judging values instead of limits refuses a readable palette for differing from the baseline while waving through a baseline value on a new surface. The manifest baseline stays as defaults chosen because they pass, and a project sets its own values with no waiver while they meet the limits. Proposed by decision 0089.
provisions.example: Claimwick's card edge differs from the page by 1.2:1 in both schemes, so cards read as separate surfaces while separators stay quieter.

provisions.heading: Name Money and Moment Formats on Each Entry Point
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `sentence-language-missing` for a written refusal result with no sentence for a language its use case's entry points declare. Run it at the consumer root.
provisions.statement: Each entry point MUST name the money and moment forms its screens render in `formats`, rendered with the locale data (CLDR) of the reader's language and the currency and country the record carries, with no format string, separator, or symbol written in code.
provisions.rationale: One record serves readers in several languages, and each language writes its separators its own way. The entry point names one money option and one moment option from the money and moment patterns, and each screen renders them with the locale data (CLDR) of the reader's language and the currency and country the record carries. A form fixed in code shows one reader the wrong separators and hides the choice from every check. Proposed by decision 0089.
provisions.example: The same Claimwick expense of EUR 1,212.35 reads `EUR 1.212,35` for a Dutch reader and `EUR 1,212.35` for an English reader.

provisions.heading: Name the Evidence for Each UI Change
provisions.evidence: Does every change name the evidence the matrix assigns to its class? Look in the change descriptions and the named evidence.
provisions.statement: A primitive, composite, token, source, floorplan, or route change MUST name the evidence in the matrix in this section.
provisions.rationale: Each change class carries different risk: a token change reaches every route in every density profile, while a primitive change reaches one component. The matrix maps each class to the narrowest evidence that represents its risk, so each change runs the proof its reach requires and no more. | Change class | Narrowest evidence | |:---|:---| | Primitive or variant | The component test for that primitive | | Floorplan or display composite | The route suite on one route that composes it | | Token or global style | The route suite on one route in each profile | | Route | The route suite on that route, and every test proving a result it calls | | Pattern decision | The catalog entry changes with its implementation | | Fork | The fork record and the component test | | Behavior package | The accessibility check for the capability it supplies |

provisions.heading: Name the Reference Behind Each Page Type
provisions.evidence: Does every route name its page type reference, or its decision record for a freestyle route? Look in the route sources.
provisions.statement: Every route MUST name its page type's reference, with a freestyle route naming its decision record instead.
provisions.rationale: An author with no named reference invents a page from primitives, and the next author invents another page for the same type. Naming the page type's reference keeps every page of one type on the one drawing it derives from, so the type stays one design. A freestyle route names its decision record instead, since it derives from no reference.

provisions.heading: Pass Every Route Suite Check
provisions.evidence: Does every discovered route pass each route suite check? Look in the suite output and the CI job logs.
provisions.statement: Every route MUST pass each route suite check.
provisions.rationale: The route suite visits every route and asserts each check the Concepts section names: the floorplan, the reference, accessibility, the heading, the landmark, reflow, text spacing, target size, keyboard use, the focus move on a route change, each color scheme, reduced motion, status announcements, and the formats. The suite discovers its routes from the application route definition, so a new route is checked with no new specification. Every route passing every check keeps each address inside the contract by default.

provisions.heading: Pin the Baseline in the Shared Package
provisions.evidence: Does the pinned baseline install once, and only in the shared UI package? Look in the shared package manifest, the shared lock file, and each application manifest.
provisions.statement: A workspace MUST install the pinned baseline from `litespec.manifest.yaml` into its shared UI package once.
provisions.rationale: The design baseline installed once in the shared UI package gives every application the same primitives at the same pinned version. Installing per application makes a copy per application, and each copy drifts on its own update schedule with nothing reporting the split. An additional design-baseline source is permitted only under a waiver recorded against this provision.

provisions.heading: Publish a Design Contract
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `ui-design-contract-invalid` tagged `[litespec/frontend/ui#publish-a-design-contract]` for a missing contract, a missing metadata block, a package mismatch, or a missing required section. Run it at the consumer root.
provisions.statement: A workspace MUST publish one design contract with its shared UI package, carrying the required sections: Baseline, Tokens, Page Frames, Vocabulary, Motion, Browser Support.
provisions.rationale: An author that has read no contract picks their own tokens, motion, browser features, and components for each page. The picks differ on the next page, and the user sees the difference as clutter: same product, different looks. One design contract published with the shared UI package keeps every answer in one file. Baseline names the pinned design baseline and its version, Tokens names the path of the token values file, Page Frames maps each page-frame pattern the product uses to the component that implements it, Vocabulary names the composites a page reaches for, Motion states the durations and what each becomes under the reduced-motion setting, and Browser Support states the target every platform feature is judged against. The contract names no screen: each screen names its own page frame on its record. Proposed by decision 0089.
provisions.example:
Claimwick publishes its contract with `@claimwick/ui`. The metadata block names the package, the token file, and the component behind each page frame it draws:

```yaml
schemaVersion: 2
package: "@claimwick/ui"
profile: application-balanced
tokens: tokens/claimwick.tokens.json
pageFrames:
  list-page: ListPage
  record-page: EntityPage
  form-page: FormPage
```

provisions.heading: Record One Shared UI Package
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `ui-package-invalid` for controlled frontends with no `ui.package` in `.litespec/project.yaml`, and `ui-dependency-invalid` tagged `[litespec/frontend/ui#record-one-shared-ui-package]` for a second general-purpose visual dependency. Run it at the consumer root.
provisions.statement: A workspace MUST record one shared UI package in `.litespec/project.yaml`.
provisions.rationale: Two general-purpose visual systems in one workspace make every component choice ambiguous: each screen picks its source, and the product ships two looks. Recording one shared UI package in `.litespec/project.yaml` settles the source for every controlled frontend. A frontend outside the contract declares another platform and says what replaces the contract.

provisions.heading: Restrict Styling to Semantic Tokens
provisions.evidence: Does any style use a raw value instead of a semantic token? Look in the stylesheets and the shared package definition.
provisions.statement: A style MUST use a semantic token rather than a raw value.
provisions.rationale: A raw value in a style answers to no token. The theme leaves it unchanged through every restyle, and the next author copies the value instead of the token. The shared package definition is the authoritative style surface, holding the tokens, the fonts, and the documented resets. A style built from semantic tokens stays inside the product's visual language by construction.

provisions.heading: Select a Command Surface by Size
provisions.evidence: Does every command use the surface the Concepts table assigns to its input? Look in the command surfaces.
provisions.statement: A command MUST use the surface the Concepts table assigns to its input.
provisions.rationale: The surface fits the input: a button for a reversible action, a confirmation dialog for an irreversible one, a form dialog for one to four inputs, and a form page beyond that. A form dialog with more inputs than the table allows scrolls, loses its title, and hides the refusal beside the field that caused it. An oversized surface for a small command costs the user attention the command has no use for.

provisions.heading: Select a Density Profile for Each Frontend
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `ui-frontend-invalid` for a controlled frontend with no `ui` block declaring its density profile or a profile outside `public-light`, `application-balanced`, `admin-dense`. Run it at the consumer root.
provisions.statement: Select one density profile from `public-light`, `application-balanced`, or `admin-dense` for each controlled frontend.
provisions.rationale: Density is a property of the audience: `public-light` suits a surface a user meets once, `application-balanced` suits a surface a signed-in staff member works in, and `admin-dense` suits a surface an operator reads all day. All three profiles share one design baseline, so choosing per frontend changes density without changing the visual language.

provisions.heading: Select a Tone from the Closed Set
provisions.evidence: Does every application map each state to a tone in one exhaustive table of glossary terms? Look in the application state mapping.
provisions.statement: A state indicator MUST take one tone from the closed set, each application declaring its state-to-tone mapping once as an exhaustive table of glossary terms.
provisions.rationale: A page that picks its own color picks a meaning nobody agreed to: the same red celebrates on one screen and warns on another. One state-to-tone mapping per application, declared once as an exhaustive table of glossary terms, makes the same state read the same way on every screen. A new state fails to compile until its tone and its word exist, so no state ships uncolored or mislabeled.

provisions.heading: Show the Trace ID in Error Detail
provisions.evidence: Does every visible error show its trace identifier in copyable form in the detail? Look in the error surfaces.
provisions.statement: Every visible error MUST show its trace identifier in copyable form in the error detail, from the problem body or the `X-Trace-Id` header.
provisions.rationale: Support reads the trace identifier to find the failed request, and the user copies it from the detail without retyping. Shown in copyable form from the problem body or the `X-Trace-Id` header, it connects the user's report to the server's logs. The headline carries what happened in words; the identifier belongs in the detail.

provisions.heading: Enforce Trusted Types on Raw Markup
provisions.evidence: Does every raw markup sink run inside the named policy, with the frontend sending the Trusted Types directive? Check the Content Security Policy header and the violation reports.
provisions.statement: A web frontend SHOULD send `require-trusted-types-for 'script'` in its Content Security Policy and pass every raw markup string through one named policy that calls the sanitizer `litespec/frontend/components#sanitize-untrusted-rich-content` records.
provisions.rationale: A recorded sanitizer protects only the calls that remember to use it. Trusted Types makes the browser refuse any raw string written into `innerHTML` or a similar sink, so a component that forgets the sanitizer fails in testing instead of in a staff member's browser. Framework runtimes and libraries also write markup through those sinks. A team first sends the policy as `Content-Security-Policy-Report-Only`, reads the reports, and enforces it once every reported sink passes through the named policy.

provisions.heading: Keep Component Boundaries Typed
provisions.evidence: `svelte-check` fails on an untyped Svelte prop, event, or snippet, and the consumer-supplied type-check command fails on an untyped React prop or event. The consumer's configuration provides the type-check command.
provisions.statement: A component MUST type its props, its events, and its snippets under strict mode.
provisions.rationale: An untyped prop fails at the call site the next author writes, which is the most expensive place to learn a shape: after writing the code that uses it. Strict mode turns that failure into a build error at the author's own call. Typed events and snippets do the same for what the component reports and what it lets callers fill in. React components carry props and events; Svelte components add snippets.

provisions.heading: Refuse Page Code Violations with ESLint
provisions.evidence: Does any refused element, binding, or layout utility show in the consumer's lint output outside visual files in route and module code? Check the lint output the consumer's configuration produces in CI.
provisions.statement: Route and module code MUST pass the ESLint rules that refuse raw layout and interactive elements, class and style bindings, and layout utilities outside visual files, with each refusal naming the composite to use.
provisions.rationale: A lint gate that only refuses leaves the author searching the shared package for the replacement. A refusal that names the composite answers with the error. The refusal-to-composite map is approved once per stack, and each stack page names the mechanism that enforces it. Visual files stay allowlisted, because a drawing no composite makes has no composite to name. This gates litespec/frontend/components#use-composites-for-layout-and-interaction-in-page-code, litespec/frontend/components#write-no-class-name-in-page-code, and litespec/frontend/ui#keep-layout-inside-floorplans.

provisions.heading: Add the TanStack Query Plugin to the Client Generator
provisions.evidence: Does every client generator configuration add the `@tanstack/react-query` plugin? Check the generator configuration of each React frontend.
provisions.statement: The client generator MUST add the `@tanstack/react-query` plugin.
provisions.rationale: The plugin gives every generated read a query key, so the cache entries of every route share one shape.
provisions.example: The library product's client generator adds `@tanstack/react-query`, giving each generated loan read a query key.

provisions.heading: Apply the Page-Code Lint to Route and Module Code
provisions.evidence: Does any route or module file use a refused import or JSX element without a lint finding? Run the page-code lint, then compare its findings with the files under `src/routes` and `src/modules`.
provisions.statement: The page-code lint MUST apply import restrictions and JSX element restrictions in route and module folders, with visual files allowlisted.
provisions.rationale: A lint refusal that names the composite to use lets the author replace a raw element when writing it, not in review. Visual files stay allowlisted because a drawing no composite makes has no composite to name.
provisions.example: In `src/routes/loans.tsx`, the lint refuses a raw `div` and names the `Stack` composite to use instead.

provisions.heading: Declare Route Search Parameters in validateSearch
provisions.evidence: Does every route declare its search parameters in `validateSearch` before reading them? Check each route file under `src/routes`.
provisions.statement: A route MUST declare its search parameters in `validateSearch`.
provisions.rationale: A declared check runs before the route reads a parameter, so the route receives a typed value or a refusal.
provisions.example: The library loan list declares its page number in `validateSearch`, so the loader reads a checked number.

provisions.heading: Hold a Route's Parts in Its Route File
provisions.evidence: Does every route file hold its search parameters, its loader, and its component? Check each file under `src/routes`.
provisions.statement: A route file MUST hold its search parameters, its loader, and its component.
provisions.rationale: One file for the three parts lets a reader see an address, its inputs, its data, and its screen together.
provisions.example: The library loan list keeps its page number, its loader, and its component in its route file.

provisions.heading: Keep Layouts, Error Components, and Route Groups Unmarked
provisions.evidence: Do any layout routes, error components, or route groups carry a screen mark? Check the non-entry files under `src/routes`.
provisions.statement: A pathless layout route, an error component, or a route group MUST NOT carry a screen mark.
provisions.rationale: A layout, an error component, or a group draws no screen of its own, so a mark on it ties an address to a screen it does not show.
provisions.example: The library product's underscore layout route carries no screen mark.

provisions.heading: Keep React Test Mocks to the Owned Libraries
provisions.evidence: Does any test replace the rendering library, the router, or the query library? Check the mocks in each test file.
provisions.statement: A test MUST NOT replace the rendering library, the router, or the query library.
provisions.rationale: Those three are the stack's own behavior, and a stand-in for any of them tests the stand-in instead of the screen.
provisions.example: The library loan list route test runs against the real router and query library, replacing only the network call.

provisions.heading: Keep the React Frame, Routes, and Modules
provisions.evidence: Does every file under `src` sit in `src/app`, `src/routes`, or `src/modules`, with one file per address? Check the `src` tree of each React frontend.
provisions.statement: A React frontend MUST hold the frame in `src/app`, one file per address in `src/routes`, and the use-case code in `src/modules`.
provisions.rationale: Three fixed homes let a reader and a tool find the frame, the routes, and the use-case code in the same place in every React frontend.
provisions.example: The library product keeps its frame in `src/app`, its loan list route in `src/routes/loans.tsx`, and its loan use-case code in `src/modules/loans`.

provisions.heading: Keep the Tone Table in One States File
provisions.evidence: Does every state-to-tone mapping live in `src/app/states.tsx`? Search the `src` tree for tone maps.
provisions.statement: The state-to-tone table MUST live in `src/app/states.tsx`.
provisions.rationale: One file holds every state's tone, so a state reads the same tone on every route.
provisions.example: The library product maps its overdue state to its warning tone in `src/app/states.tsx`.

provisions.heading: Load Intent Targets Before Navigation
provisions.evidence: Does every preloaded link fill the query cache before navigation? Check the router link setup in the `src` tree.
provisions.statement: Intent preloading MUST fill the query cache before navigation.
provisions.rationale: A preload on hover or focus fills the cache before the click, so the target route draws from data it already holds.
provisions.example: In the library product, hovering the loan link fills the loan page key, and the click draws the list from the cache.

provisions.heading: Mark Each React Route Entry with Its Screen
provisions.evidence: Does every route entry export its screen mark from its route file? Check each route file under `src/routes`.
provisions.statement: A route entry MUST export its screen mark from its route file as the same typed constant a use-case module exports.
provisions.rationale: A mark in the route file ties the address to its use case where the address is declared, so the builder and the check read one link. A wrong identifier fails the consumer's type check against the generated union.
provisions.example: The library loan list exports its typed screen mark from its route file for the loan list screen.

provisions.heading: Name Drawings with the Visual Suffix
provisions.evidence: Does every file holding a custom drawing end with `.visual.tsx`? Check the component folders.
provisions.statement: A file that holds a drawing no composite makes MUST end with `.visual.tsx`.
provisions.rationale: The suffix marks the one place outside the composites, so a search finds every custom drawing in one pass.
provisions.example: The library loan due-date sparkline lives in `LoanSparkline.visual.tsx`.

provisions.heading: Prefetch Route Reads in the Loader
provisions.evidence: Does every route prefetch its reads in its loader? Check each loader under `src/routes`.
provisions.statement: A route MUST prefetch its reads in its loader.
provisions.rationale: A loader fills the query cache before the component draws, so the first render has its data.
provisions.example: The library loan list loader fetches the loan page for the checked page number before the component draws.

provisions.heading: Read Route Data with useSuspenseQuery
provisions.evidence: Does every route data read use `useSuspenseQuery` over the key its loader filled? Check each route file under `src/routes`.
provisions.statement: A route file MUST read its route data with `useSuspenseQuery` over the key its loader filled.
provisions.rationale: Reading the filled key keeps the component on the data the loader fetched.
provisions.example: The library loan list component reads its loan page through `useSuspenseQuery` over the key its loader filled.

provisions.heading: Render Raw HTML Only Through dangerouslySetInnerHTML
provisions.evidence: Does every raw HTML write go through `dangerouslySetInnerHTML`? Check for `innerHTML` and raw markup in the component files.
provisions.statement: A React component MUST pass raw HTML to the page only through `dangerouslySetInnerHTML`.
provisions.rationale: One named prop makes every raw HTML sink a name a search finds, and a review can check each use.
provisions.example: The library loan note passes its sanitized HTML through `dangerouslySetInnerHTML`, matching its recorded sanitization decision.

provisions.heading: Resolve Copy Through the Dictionary Library
provisions.evidence: Does every copy call site use the dictionary library with fill, plural, typed keys, and a declared fallback? Check the copy call sites under `src`.
provisions.statement: The dictionary library MUST meet the locale-dictionary contract that the web data page states.
provisions.rationale: One contract keeps every sentence in one dictionary per language, with the same fill, plural, and fallback behavior.
provisions.example: The library product resolves its overdue-loan sentence through its dictionary library in every language it ships.

provisions.heading: Run the Registry Build Command
provisions.evidence: Does every registry build script run `shadcn build`? Check the scripts in each frontend's `package.json`.
provisions.statement: The registry build command MUST be `shadcn build`.
provisions.rationale: One registry command builds UI artifacts the same way in every React frontend.
provisions.example: The library product builds its UI registry with `shadcn build`.

provisions.heading: Show Route Failure in the Route Error Component
provisions.evidence: Does every route failure render in the route error component? Check the error handling of each route under `src/routes`.
provisions.statement: A route failure MUST render in the route error component, which draws the shared problem state.
provisions.rationale: One error component gives every route failure the same problem state and the same recovery.
provisions.example: When the library loan list fails to load, the route error component shows the shared problem state with its trace identifier.

provisions.heading: Use Named Props for Class and Style Bindings
provisions.evidence: Does every class or style binding use `className` or `style`? Check the JSX in the component files.
provisions.statement: A class or style binding in a React component MUST use `className` or `style`.
provisions.rationale: Two fixed prop names keep styling in one vocabulary that the lint and a reviewer can read.
provisions.example: The loan row in `src/app/components/LoanRow.tsx` sets its tone through `className` and uses no `style` prop.

provisions.heading: Use the Shared Package Form Hook
provisions.evidence: Does every React form build on the shared package form hook? Check the form files under `src`.
provisions.statement: A React form MUST build on the form hook of the shared package.
provisions.rationale: One entry point gives every form the same field wiring and the same display for a refusal on its field.
provisions.example: The library loan request form builds on the shared form hook, with no form library of its own.

provisions.heading: Use the TSX File Extension on Shared Files
provisions.evidence: Does every shared React file use the `.tsx` extension? Check the `src` tree of each React frontend.
provisions.statement: A shared React file MUST use the `.tsx` extension.
provisions.rationale: One extension lets the compiler, the lint, and a search treat every shared React file the same way.
provisions.example: The library product holds its shared loan status helper as `src/app/loan-status.tsx`.

provisions.heading: Declare Titles and Indexing Policy on Every Route
provisions.evidence: Does every public route define its title, description, canonical address, and indexing policy, with every private route carrying a `noindex` marker? Check the route metadata.
provisions.statement: A public route MUST define its title, its description, its canonical address, and its indexing policy, while a private route refuses indexing.
provisions.rationale: A public route's title, description, canonical address, and indexing policy are what a search result and a shared link show. Without them the page arrives as a bare address. A private route refuses indexing, because an indexed console address exposes to search what a signed-in user believes is private.
provisions.example: A channel route states `og:*` tags and one alternate per language. A console route ships a `noindex` meta tag in its document.

provisions.heading: Generate the Records File into the Frame
provisions.evidence: `litespec model render` writes each frontend's file into its frame from its own entry points, and `litespec model check` reports `mark-unknown` (level S) for a mark naming a use case or screen outside its frontend's entry points.
provisions.statement: A frontend's generated `litespec-records.ts` MUST sit in its frame folder and hold only the use cases and screens of that frontend's own entry points.
provisions.rationale: The records file is a cross-route value every module and route imports, which is what the frame holds. On both stacks it sits in the frame folder: `src/app/` on React and `src/lib/app/` on Svelte, so no stack-specific folder is needed. A union holding every browser use case of the project would let one frontend mark a use case only another frontend reaches, and the type check would pass; a union per frontend makes that mistake a type error. The file exports the `UseCaseId` and `ScreenId` unions, the `LiteSpecMark` type, and the `proves` helper browser tests annotate with.
provisions.example: `litespec model render` writes `apps/web/src/lib/app/litespec-records.ts` for the Claimwick web frontend, whose `UseCaseId` holds the use cases its entry point reaches and nothing else.

provisions.heading: Locate the Frame in the App Folder
provisions.evidence: Do all cross-route values and browser uses sit in the frame folder their stack page names? Check the frame folder and the route and module sources.
provisions.statement: A frontend MUST place cross-route values in the frame folder its stack page states: client configuration, session read, language choice, permissions, formatting, and shell data.
provisions.rationale: Client configuration, session read, language choice, permissions, formatting, and shell data cross every route. Filed in the frame folder, each has one home; filed in a route, each exists once per route with copies to keep equal. A browser API reached from a use-case module belongs here too, because a module renders and reads data rather than touching the device. This realizes litespec/frontend/structure#place-cross-route-values-in-the-frame.

provisions.heading: Mark Each Use-Case Module with Its Use Case
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `mark-missing` (level S) for a use-case folder exporting no `litespec` constant, and `mark-unknown` (level S) for one naming a use case its path does not mirror; for a folder at `{module}/use-cases/{use-case}/` the mirrored use case is the one its module and use-case segments name, with no aggregate segment.
provisions.statement: A frontend use-case folder MUST export one `litespec` constant whose `implements` names its use case, typed against the generated union of use-case identifiers.
provisions.rationale: The folder path mirrors the backend use case, which tells a reader where to look but tells a tool only a resemblance. A typed constant is the frontend mark in both mark styles: a mistyped identifier fails the consumer's type check against the generated union, and `litespec model check` reports it as `mark-unknown` where no type check ran. The route files import the module instead of restating the identifier. The calls a screen makes through the generated client remain the computed `calls` link; the mark adds the written link from the screen to the use case it serves. A query folder at `{module}/use-cases/{use-case}/` mirrors a use case with no one aggregate, so its expected mark still names `use-case/<module>.<use-case>`, from the module and use-case segments alone.

provisions.heading: Refuse Stack-Specific Folder Names
provisions.evidence: Does any React folder take the name `lib`, or any Svelte folder under `src/lib` the name `stores`? Check the frontend tree.
provisions.statement: A React folder MUST NOT be named `lib`, nor a Svelte folder under `src/lib` be named `stores`.
provisions.rationale: A `lib` folder on React would sit beside `src/app` as a second frame, and `src/app` already holds the frame. A `stores` folder on Svelte would gather shared state in one place, while the rules put shared state in the frame or beside its readers. Refusing both names stops the second home before anything moves into it.

provisions.heading: Use the Frontend Application Tree
provisions.evidence: Does every frontend tree follow the frame, routes, and modules layout its stack page states? Check the frontend tree.
provisions.statement: A frontend MUST use the frame, routes, and modules layout its stack page states.
provisions.rationale: The frame, routes, and modules layout gives every file one predictable home: cross-route values in the frame, one address per route file or folder, and use-case code under the module that owns it. A reader moves from a use case to its code by path alone, on either stack. This realizes litespec/frontend/structure#organize-a-frontend-into-frame-routes-and-modules.
provisions.example:
React:

```text
apps/{frontend}/
  src/
    app/       the frame: client configuration, session, language, permissions, formatting, shell data
    routes/    one file per address, compiled into a typed route tree
    modules/   one folder per backend module, aggregate, and use case
  tests/
    unit/      logic tests
    routes/    the route contract suite
    e2e/       evidence specifications
  package.json
  vite.config.ts
```

Svelte:

```text
apps/{frontend}/
  src/
    routes/    one folder per address, with a page per folder
    lib/
      app/       the frame: client configuration, session, language, permissions, formatting, shell data
      modules/   one folder per backend module, aggregate, and use case
  tests/
    unit/      logic tests
    routes/    the route contract suite
```
