A new package joins the narrowest layer that needs it. A central version entry does not authorize every layer to reference that package; the table decides who takes what. A consumer references conditional packages only after their extension activates.

provisions.heading: Follow the Declared Dependency Graph
provisions.evidence: Does each layer and module dependency follow the declared graph? Read the references between layer folders under `apps/api/src` and the imports in `apps/`.
provisions.statement: A dependency between layers or modules MUST follow the declared graph and add no other edge.
provisions.rationale: The declared graph lists the crossings review checks. An undeclared edge lets a layer reach past its boundary while review finds no graph that forbids it. Each new edge then needs an explicit decision instead of arriving silently with an import.

provisions.heading: Keep Application Free of Provider Packages
provisions.evidence: Does the Application layer reference only messaging abstractions, read abstractions, and the declared read boundary? Read those folders and the manifests that serve them.
provisions.statement: Application MUST depend only on messaging abstractions, required read abstractions, and the one declared read boundary.
provisions.rationale: Application coordinates use cases through abstractions, while Infrastructure hides the technology behind them. A provider package in Application makes the coordination layer depend on the technology Infrastructure was meant to hide, so a provider change reaches two layers. Only messaging abstractions, required read abstractions, and the one declared read boundary stay.

provisions.heading: Keep Domain Dependency-Free
provisions.evidence: Does any Domain layer folder need an external package or framework? Read the Domain layer folders and the manifests that serve them.
provisions.statement: The Domain layer MUST depend on no external package or framework.
provisions.rationale: Business rules outlive frameworks, and Domain holds the business rules. Depending on no external package or framework keeps the rules testable and portable on their own. Persistence, messaging, web, injection, serialization, and logging libraries all stay outside.

provisions.heading: Keep Frontend Applications Isolated
provisions.evidence: Does any import in one frontend name another application's source or another module's internal feature files? Search the frontend imports.
provisions.statement: A frontend MUST NOT import another application's source or another module's internal feature files.
provisions.rationale: When one frontend imports the source of another, neither can change its internals without checking the other, so the two release as one. The same holds for the internal feature files of another module. Sharing goes through a shared package with a documented public entry point that depends on no application.

provisions.heading: Keep Generated Packages Dependency-Light
provisions.evidence: Does the generated API types package carry no dependencies, with the shared client limited to the generator runtime, its query plugin, and those types, or does the client package manifest name the project's own client dependency set? Read the generated package manifests.
provisions.statement: Keep generated API types free of dependencies and limit the shared client to the pinned generator's runtime, its query plugin, and those types.
provisions.rationale: Generated types mirror the API contract, and the shared client only carries them to queries. Keeping the types free of dependencies and the client limited to the generator runtime, its query plugin, and those types keeps regeneration a pure function of the contract. A generated package that owns state, UI behavior, or authentication policy is no longer regenerable.

provisions.heading: Keep Providers in Infrastructure
provisions.evidence: Do database providers, external SDKs, and resilience, discovery, and serialization adapters appear only in the Infrastructure layer folders? Read those folders and the manifests that serve them.
provisions.statement: A database provider, external SDK, resilience, discovery, or serialization adapter MUST live in Infrastructure.
provisions.rationale: Database providers, external SDKs, and resilience, discovery, and serialization adapters all change with their technology. Keeping them in Infrastructure keeps each provider change inside one layer, apart from the read boundary the ownership table assigns to Application.

provisions.heading: Keep Test Dependencies in Test Projects
provisions.evidence: Does any production project manifest reference an assertion, substitution, host, container, or architecture-test package, or does the project documentation name the shipped helper and its reason? Read the production project manifests.
provisions.statement: Keep assertion, substitution, host, container, and architecture-test packages inside test projects.
provisions.rationale: Assertion, substitution, host, container, and architecture-test packages exist to verify code, not to run it. Once a production project references one, it ships to production with its own dependencies and advisories. Keeping them inside test projects keeps the shipped graph free of verification weight.

provisions.heading: Pin Every Dependency Version Centrally
provisions.evidence: Does every version resolve through central management or the committed lockfile within the manifest major where one exists, with no version inline in a module file? Read the central version files and the module files.
provisions.statement: Every dependency version MUST resolve through central management or the committed lockfile, within the major `litespec.manifest.yaml` pins where it pins one.
provisions.rationale: An inline version in one module file is invisible to the file that should own it, so two modules drift to two versions of the same package. Central management or the committed lockfile resolves every version in one owned place. The manifest pins the major of each baseline package, so a consumer takes a patch without waiting for a LiteSpec release, and it pins an exact version only where a check depends on exact output. The manifest belongs to the LiteSpec release rather than to the consumer, so the exact versions of a consumer live beside its code, admitted by `litespec/workspace/dependencies#approve-new-packages-explicitly`. Settled by [decision/0036-pin-third-party-packages-to-their-major](decision/0036-pin-third-party-packages-to-their-major).
provisions.example: The Claimwick central version file holds Marten at 9.50.2 while the manifest pins `9.x`, so a patch lands without a LiteSpec release. Its receipt PDF library sits exact in the same file with a decision record, because the manifest names only the baseline stack.

provisions.heading: Take Web UI Packages from the Approved Baseline
provisions.evidence: Does each React frontend take UI packages only from `uiBaseline`, and each Svelte one only from `uiBaselineSvelte`? Read each frontend manifest beside `litespec.manifest.yaml`.
provisions.statement: A React web frontend MUST take its UI packages from the `uiBaseline` in `litespec.manifest.yaml`, and a Svelte web frontend from `uiBaselineSvelte`.
provisions.rationale: A fixed UI baseline keeps every screen drawing from the same design system, styling, base components, icons, and utilities. Taking UI packages only from `uiBaseline` for React and `uiBaselineSvelte` for Svelte keeps that set reviewed and versioned in one place. Each baseline pins the design system, styling, base components, icons, and the utility packages the installed source imports directly.

provisions.heading: Align Business Names Across Layers
provisions.evidence: Does one business name for each module span Domain, Application, endpoints, features, and documentation, or does the project documentation name the project's own per-layer names? Read the module names in each layer.
provisions.statement: Use one business name for a module across Domain, Application, endpoints, features, and documentation.
provisions.rationale: One business name per module keeps every layer pointing at the same word: the Posts module maps to `Shop/Posts`, `features/posts`, and `.litespec/behavior/modules/posts` without translation. A second name in any layer reads as a second concept that does not exist.

provisions.heading: Anchor Aggregate-Owned Types on the Aggregate Root
provisions.evidence: Does each aggregate-owned type name in `apps/api/src` begin with its aggregate root name, through nesting or prefix? Read the type names beside their aggregates.
provisions.statement: An aggregate-owned type's qualified name MUST start with its aggregate root's full name.
provisions.rationale: Leading with the root name reveals the owner without folder context. The rule covers events, states, child entities, values, and discriminated unions. A type nested inside a declaring type inherits the prefix of that type through its qualified name, so `PostState.Published` satisfies the rule, while a flat `PostStatePublishedState` repeats the anchor twice.
provisions.example: `PostPublishedEvent` and `PostState.Published` both lead with `Post`. `PublishedState` declared at namespace level does not.

provisions.heading: Avoid Generic Type Names
provisions.evidence: Does each type name in `apps/api/src` avoid the listed generic names where a narrower name exists, or does the project documentation name the kept name and its reason? Read the type names.
provisions.artifact: aggregate, state-record, value-object, domain-event, use-case, command-handler, query-handler, validator, reaction, port, repository, endpoint, migration, job
provisions.statement: Avoid `Manager`, `Helper`, `Processor`, `Common`, `Utility`, `BaseService`, `DataService`, `MessageBus`, `Engine`, `Facade`, `Wrapper`, and `Factory` when a narrower name exists.
provisions.rationale: A generic name invites unrelated responsibility, because nothing in it excludes the next addition. A narrower name states what the type does and, by exclusion, what it does not. `Factory` is generic on a class but exact on a named static aggregate factory method, so the default covers the class and not the method.

provisions.heading: Derive Boundary Names from the Ubiquitous Term
provisions.evidence: Does each route segment and JSON field name derive from its current aggregate or ubiquitous term, or does the project documentation name the project's own boundary naming? Read the routes and contracts beside the glossary.
provisions.statement: Derive route segments and JSON field names from the current aggregate or ubiquitous term.
provisions.rationale: Route segments and JSON field names are the contract clients read. Deriving them from the current aggregate or ubiquitous term, the shared Domain word for the concept, keeps the contract speaking the Domain language. Renaming a Domain concept then renames its boundary names with it, so the contract and the language stay aligned.

provisions.heading: Keep Namespaces Aligned with Folders
provisions.evidence: Does each namespace start with its product name and follow the folders beneath the project root, or does the project documentation name the project's own namespace root? Read the namespaces beside the folders.
provisions.artifact: aggregate, state-record, value-object, domain-event, use-case, command-handler, query-handler, validator, reaction, port, repository, endpoint, migration, job
provisions.statement: Start a namespace with the product name and follow the folders beneath the project root.
provisions.rationale: A namespace that starts with the product name and follows the folders beneath it puts each type exactly where its namespace says. Including `src` or `apps` couples the type name to a workspace layout decision. The project root is the directory holding the project file, so every folder above it stays outside the namespace.

provisions.heading: Name Exceptions by Failed Rule
provisions.evidence: Does each exception name state its failed rule, with Domain rejections in `{DomainType}{Reason}Exception` form leading with the aggregate root? Read the exception names.
provisions.statement: An exception name MUST state the rule that failed, using `{DomainType}{Reason}Exception` for a Domain rejection.
provisions.rationale: An exception name is the first diagnosis: it states which rule failed on which type. The form `{DomainType}{Reason}Exception` puts both in the name, and the `DomainType` is the aggregate root or an anchored owned type, so the name always starts with the aggregate root.

provisions.heading: Name Repository Variables After Their Interface
provisions.evidence: Does each repository parameter, field, or local carry the name of its interface without the `I` prefix? Read the repository use sites.
provisions.artifact: command-handler, query-handler, validator, reaction, repository, job
provisions.statement: Each repository parameter, field or local MUST be named after its interface without the `I` prefix, ending in `Repository`.
provisions.rationale: A short plural name hides which aggregate the variable guards. `orders` can be a list, a query, or the repository, and each reader guesses. Naming the variable after its interface keeps one name per repository at every use site, so a reviewer reads the dependency from the name alone.
provisions.example: A parameter of type `IExpenseRepository` is named `expenseRepository`, and a field of type `ILoanRepository` is named `loanRepository`.

provisions.heading: Name Result Parts After Their Result
provisions.evidence: Does each type nested in a use-case result carry the full result name as its prefix? Read the result types.
provisions.statement: Each type nested in a use-case result MUST be named after the result it belongs to, as `{UseCase}QueryResult{Part}` or `{UseCase}CommandResult{Part}`.
provisions.rationale: A result part named for its own shape instead of its result collides with every other use case shaping the same thing: two summaries named `PostSummary` answer different queries with different fields. Leading with the full result name keeps each part beside the result it belongs to in every listing, and keeps command coordination apart from query projection without opening the file.
provisions.example: `ListPostsQueryResultItem` belongs to `ListPostsQueryResult`, and `ReadLoanQueryResultHold` belongs to `ReadLoanQueryResult`.

provisions.heading: Place Each Trigger with What It Runs
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `code-placement-drift` (level S) for an event handler or job class outside the folder its record's effects name.
provisions.statement: Each event handler and job class MUST live in the `Application/` folder of the use case its record runs, or, when it runs none, in the module `Notifications/` folder named for the notification it sends or the module `ExternalSystems/` folder named for the system it calls, with an event handler named `{Action}On{Fact}Handler`.
provisions.rationale: A reaction and a job are triggers, like an endpoint, and a trigger belongs to what it triggers. Placed with its use case, the handler names the command of that use case from inside the folder of the use case, so no command leaves its folder for a caller to reach it, and the folder shows every way the use case starts. A folder named for a fact instead gathered the commands of several use cases under one name, and it never showed every reaction to the fact, because those reactions span modules. The question of what happens when a fact is recorded is answered by the model query on the event and by the handler names, which carry the fact. Settled by [decision/0063-place-each-trigger-with-what-it-runs](decision/0063-place-each-trigger-with-what-it-runs).
provisions.example: `Lending/Holds/UseCases/ExpireHold/Application/ExpireHoldOnLoanReturnedHandler` runs the expire-hold use case when a loan is returned, and `Lending/Notifications/LoanDue/SendDueNoticeOnLoanBorrowedHandler` only sends the due notice.

provisions.heading: Reveal Asynchrony and Cancellation in Operation Names
provisions.evidence: Does each asynchronous operation name reveal asynchrony, with each cancelable operation signature taking cancellation explicitly? Read the public signatures in `apps/api/src`.
provisions.artifact: command-handler, query-handler, validator, reaction, port, repository, endpoint, migration, job
provisions.statement: An asynchronous operation MUST reveal its asynchrony in its name and accept cancellation explicitly when the operation is cancelable.
provisions.rationale: A caller decides from the signature whether to await and what to cancel, so both answers belong in the signature: the name reveals the asynchrony and a cancelable operation accepts cancellation explicitly. An operation is cancelable when it performs I/O or awaits, and anything else has nothing to cancel.

provisions.heading: Use Architectural Suffixes
provisions.evidence: Does each type name and each frontend file name carry the suffix its role assigns in the Role Suffixes table? Read the names beside the table.
provisions.artifact: state-record, domain-event, use-case, command-handler, query-handler, validator, reaction, repository, endpoint, job
provisions.statement: An architectural type MUST carry the suffix its role assigns in the Role Suffixes table.
provisions.rationale: A short name hides the role: `{UseCase}Handler` never says whether it coordinates a command or projects a query, and `{UseCase}Request` never says it is passive boundary data. Full suffixes put the role in the name, so a reader sorts types without opening files.
provisions.example:
An event handler names its act and the business fact without the `Event` suffix. `NotifySubscribersOnPostPublishedHandler` answers `PostPublishedEvent` and sits with what it runs (`litespec/workspace/naming#place-each-trigger-with-what-it-runs`). The name carries no technical suffix for the fact, so `NotifySubscribersOnPostPublishedEventHandler` is wrong, while the event type keeps its `Event` suffix (`litespec/workspace/naming#anchor-aggregate-owned-types-on-the-aggregate-root`).

Application types keep their full suffix. The short forms `{UseCase}Result`, `{UseCase}Handler`, and `{UseCase}Validator` drop the command-or-query distinction the full name carries. A result part carries the full name of its result, as `litespec/workspace/naming#name-result-parts-after-their-result` states, not a bare summary name like `PostSummary`. The full role suffix distinguishes command coordination from query projection without opening the file.

HTTP transport types keep their full suffix too. The short forms `{UseCase}Request` and `{UseCase}Response` drop the boundary marking. The `Model` suffix marks the type as passive boundary data rather than an operation or rich business object. Other project-owned, passive HTTP DTOs also name their concrete role and end in `Model`, such as `ListPostsResponseItemModel` or `PaginationModel`.

A polymorphic transport model mirrors a Domain discriminated union (`litespec/backend/api#mirror-each-closed-set-on-the-wire`). Its abstract base names the concept and each sealed case names its case, with both ending in `Model`: `FulfillmentOutcomeModel` and `ShippedFulfillmentOutcomeModel`.

The transport name drops the aggregate prefix of the Domain union, such as `OrderFulfillmentOutcome`, while its discriminator string keeps the stable case code of the Domain union unchanged.

provisions.heading: Use Current Language Features
provisions.evidence: Does production code target the pinned language version and use its current constructs? Read the toolchain pins and the language idioms in `apps/api/src`.
provisions.artifact: aggregate, state-record, value-object, domain-event, use-case, command-handler, query-handler, validator, reaction, port, repository, endpoint, migration, job
provisions.statement: Production code SHOULD target the pinned language version and use its current construct over an older equivalent.
provisions.rationale: A pinned language version gives every writer the same constructs. Using the current construct over its older equivalent keeps one idiom across the codebase instead of one per author. In the dotnet stack that means collection expressions, pattern matching, and primary constructors, which express the same intent with less incidental code.

provisions.heading: Use Intent-Revealing Boolean Names
provisions.evidence: Does each boolean property and method name in `apps/api/src` start with `Is`, `Has`, `Can`, or a precise verb? Read the boolean names.
provisions.artifact: aggregate, state-record, value-object, domain-event, use-case, command-handler, query-handler, validator, reaction, port, repository, endpoint, migration, job
provisions.statement: A boolean property or method SHOULD use `Is`, `Has`, `Can`, or a precise verb.
provisions.rationale: A boolean answers a yes-or-no question, so its name asks one. The prefixes `Is`, `Has`, `Can`, or a precise verb make the question explicit: `HasLines` and `CanPublish` state a condition. `LinesPresent` and `CheckPublish` state neither a question nor an answer, so the caller reads the body to learn the polarity.

provisions.heading: Use Predictable Frontend Names
provisions.evidence: Does each frontend folder use kebab-case, each component file and export PascalCase, and each React hook file `use-{name}`? Read the frontend tree.
provisions.statement: A frontend folder MUST use kebab-case, a component file and its export PascalCase, and a React hook file `use-{name}`.
provisions.rationale: Every file gets one predictable name: kebab-case folders, PascalCase components with matching exports, and `use-{name}` hooks. One mapping lets a reader move between the documentation tree and the source tree without translation, and lets an agent derive the file from the feature name.

provisions.heading: Declare Size and Application Stacks in Project Config
provisions.evidence: Does `.litespec/project.yaml` at the workspace root declare `size` and one stack for the backend and for each frontend? Read the file.
provisions.statement: `.litespec/project.yaml` MUST declare `size` as `small` or `large` and one stack for the backend and for each frontend.
provisions.rationale: Size decides which record types and test projects apply: `small` or `large` selects the required-record set of the project. Each stack decides which technology pages and checks apply to its application. Declaring both in `.litespec/project.yaml` lets tools and reviewers read the selection from one file. The [scope page](../core/scope.md) states the full selection.

provisions.heading: Keep Generated API Contracts in Packages
provisions.evidence: Do generated OpenAPI types sit in `packages/api-types/` with the thin client in `packages/api-client/` once two frontends consume the API, or does the single frontend keep both outputs? Count the API consumers and read their imports.
provisions.statement: Place generated OpenAPI types in `packages/api-types/` and a thin client in `packages/api-client/` when more than one frontend consumes the API.
provisions.rationale: Generated OpenAPI types and their thin client belong to every frontend that reads the API. With more than one consumer, `packages/api-types/` and `packages/api-client/` hold one copy each. A single frontend may keep both locally until a second consumer appears.

provisions.heading: Keep Orientation Documents Separate from Canonical Records
provisions.evidence: Does each `README.md` under `.litespec/` link to its record and restate no record content? Read each README beside its record.
provisions.statement: A README under `.litespec/` MUST link to the record rather than restate its content.
provisions.rationale: A README orients while a record decides. A README that restates a decision becomes a second authored source that drifts from the record it summarizes, until the two disagree and neither is trusted. Linking to the record keeps one source with many pointers.

provisions.heading: Keep Production and Test Code Separate
provisions.evidence: Do production files sit under `apps/api/src/` and test files under `apps/api/tests/`, with no test helper shipped beside production code? Walk both folders.
provisions.statement: Production code MUST live under `apps/api/src/` and test code under `apps/api/tests/`.
provisions.rationale: Production code lives under `apps/api/src/` and test code under `apps/api/tests/`, so the two graphs stay apart by path. The split makes a test dependency reaching production code visible in the path itself, and keeps test helpers from shipping with the product.
provisions.example:
The backend tree looks like this:

```text
apps/api/
  <backend project manifest>
  src/
  tests/
```

provisions.heading: Keep Project Records Under the Root LiteSpec Directory
provisions.evidence: Does every record path sit under the root `.litespec/` directory? Walk the tree from the workspace root.
provisions.statement: Project records MUST live under the root `.litespec/` directory.
provisions.rationale: Project records describe the product, not the standard and not the code. Placed inside the application tree, they disappear when the application is rewritten. The root `.litespec/` directory keeps records where they survive replacing the standard or rewriting the application.

provisions.heading: Keep Runnable Applications Under Apps
provisions.evidence: Does each directory under `apps/` run on its own, with each directory under `packages/` imported by an application? Read the workspace root and the imports in `apps/`.
provisions.statement: An independently runnable frontend, API, or deployed host MUST live under `apps/{name}/`.
provisions.rationale: Each root folder makes one promise: `apps/` runs, and `packages/` is reused. A reusable package under `apps/` or deployable code under `packages/` inverts that promise, so neither location tells the reader what it holds. One home per kind keeps the promise readable.

provisions.heading: Keep the Generated Model Out of Source Control
provisions.evidence: Is any path under `.litespec/model/` tracked in git? `git ls-files .litespec/model` prints nothing when the folder stays untracked.
provisions.statement: The generated `.litespec/model/` folder MUST stay out of source control.
provisions.rationale: The model builder writes generated working files there, such as frontend facts, while it builds the model from records, code, routes, tests, and test runs. Tracking them commits derived files beside their sources, so every commit carries stale working files until somebody rebuilds. The folder is rebuilt rather than reviewed.

provisions.heading: Limit Shared TypeScript Packages
provisions.evidence: Is each package under `packages/` imported by at least two consumers, or does it carry generated output shared by design? Read the imports in `apps/`.
provisions.statement: A shared TypeScript package MUST have at least two consumers or carry generated output shared by design.
provisions.rationale: A shared package with one consumer pays versioning, publishing, and cross-package edits for an audience of one. Requiring two consumers, or generated output shared by design, keeps sharing deliberate. The baseline permits shared configuration, generated API types, a thin client, and CSS theme tokens.

provisions.heading: Name Frontends by Audience
provisions.evidence: Does each directory under `apps/` carry an audience name, or does `frontends` in `.litespec/project.yaml` name the project's own frontend names? Read the `apps/` folders and the project file.
provisions.statement: Name a frontend for its audience, such as `web`, `admin`, `portal`, or `docs`.
provisions.rationale: The name `apps/web` says who the frontend serves, while `apps/frontend` says only what it is built with. Naming each frontend for its audience keeps the folder meaningful when the technology changes. The names `frontend`, `client`, and `app` name the technology rather than the audience it serves.

provisions.heading: Use the Canonical Root Tree
provisions.evidence: Does the workspace tree match the canonical tree in this section, with each record at its type's home under `.litespec/`? Walk the tree from the workspace root.
provisions.statement: A consumer workspace MUST use the canonical root tree declared in this section.
provisions.example:
A consumer workspace uses this shape:

```text
{repo}/
  .config/
    dotnet-tools.json
  .litespec/
    project.yaml
    glossary.yaml
    product.yaml
    intent/
      goals/ visions/ problems/ constraints/ decisions/ research/ actors/ roles/ flows/
      features/
        {feature}/
          {feature}.yaml
          requirements/
            {requirement}/
              {requirement}.yaml    one requirement, in its own folder
      requirements/                 product requirements
        {requirement}/
          {requirement}.yaml
    behavior/
      rules/                            cross-module invariants only
      external-systems/                 create with the first product-level external system
      entry-points/
        {entry-point}/
          entry-point.yaml
          screens/
            {screen}/{screen}.yaml
      modules/
        {module}/
          permissions.yaml
          use-cases/ rules/ reactions/ jobs/ read-models/ notifications/ settings/ integration-events/ external-systems/
          aggregates/
            {aggregate}/
              aggregate.yaml
              use-cases/
                {use-case}/
                  {use-case}.yaml   results and scenarios as entries
              domain-events/ rules/
    implementation/
      decisions/ api/ guides/ operations/ patterns/ writing/ runbooks/
      operations/
        limits.yaml                     create with the first limit record
        secrets.json                    create with the first secret
        log/                            create with the first operations entry
      entry-points/
        {entry-point}/                  UI catalog, captures and patterns
      modules/
        {module}/
          decisions/ runbooks/
    governance/
      waivers/                       create with the first waiver record
      modules/
        {module}/
          waivers/
    proof/                              generated registers, gate files and run outputs; no authored records
    model/                              generated; ignored
  apps/
    api/
      <backend project manifest>
      src/
      tests/
    {frontend}/
    apphost/                            when one host runs more than one application
  packages/
  AGENTS.md
  <toolchain pin file>
  package.json                          when a frontend or TypeScript package exists
  pnpm-lock.yaml                        when a frontend or TypeScript package exists
  pnpm-workspace.yaml                   when a frontend or TypeScript package exists
```

A backend stack binding names the files that realize the entries in angle brackets.

Neither the backend application nor a frontend application sits at the workspace root. Under `behavior/modules/`, each module folder holds its typed folders, and `aggregates/` holds one folder per aggregate in plural kebab-case form.

A named record lives in its own folder as `<name>/<name>.yaml`, with its explanation `<name>.md` beside it. Each record file lives at the home the [model page](../core/model.md) names for its type. A requirement is a named record in its own folder inside the folder of its feature.

An entry lives in its home file: permissions in the permissions file of their module, results and scenarios in their use case file, and rules and domain events in their aggregate file or type folder. Each entry point is one record in its own folder, with its screens beside it.
